Italy has extended temporary border controls with Spain for another 15 days amid continued concerns over the situation in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, local media reported Wednesday.
Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi decided to extend checks at air and maritime borders after consulting the Committee for the Analysis of Immigration and Border Security, which met earlier Wednesday, Italian news agency ANSA reported.
The Interior Ministry said the decision was prompted by the situation in Ceuta, particularly the persistence of concerns that had previously led authorities to introduce the controls.
Checks at Italy's air and maritime borders with Spain will therefore remain in force for another 15 days, the ministry said.

Around 72,000 people irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30-31, according to official Spanish government estimates.
More than 3,000 migrants, including several hundred minors, are still living on the streets of the Spanish enclave in North Africa, according to the latest estimates.
While temporary accommodation facilities have been established, authorities said up to 200 people voluntarily return to Morocco each day.

Robots won’t replace armored vehicles, says Ukrainian company that builds both. It reveals one job they can’t do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:48:46 UTC
06:48:46 KST

Robots will not replace armored vehicles on the battlefield, says a company that builds both. Ground robots are a new tool that lets Ukraine distribute risk more smartly, but they cannot do everything a crewed armored vehicle can, above all pulling wounded soldiers out under fire, says Ukr Armo Tech's chief executive Hennadii Khirhii, in an interview with RBC-Ukraine.
Ukraine has a serious shortage of armored vehicles, from evacuation carriers to tracked fighting vehicles, with the focus shifting to hulls that offer heavy mine protection and built-in electronic warfare. For medical-evacuation armor alone, Khirhii says, the deficit is often put at 80 percent.
Robots can ease some of that, hauling ammunition and supplies to the front without risking a crew, but they are a complement, not a substitute, a view frontline commanders also confirm.
Robots share the load, not replace it
Where a robot can do the job, Khirhii says, there is no sense sending in heavy armor and the people inside it to face danger. For carrying ammunition or food, unmanned ground vehicles are useful. But evacuating the wounded is different: that usually needs, at least for the second leg, a protected medical vehicle in which care can begin on the move, with room for transfusions and resuscitation that a robot's capsule cannot provide.
"A UGV doesn't cancel the armored vehicle, just as the drone didn't cancel artillery," he says.
The limits show at evacuation
Ukraine has leaned hard into robotic logistics and casualty evacuation, running more than 100,000 such missions this year to keep medics and crews off exposed roads, but the robots themselves now draw Russian drone and artillery fire, and they cannot replace medical personnel.
One commander has called ground robots too slow for evacuation and easy targets, arguing brigades still need staffed evacuation teams and light-armored vehicles.
Commanders want both
The lesson from the front is not robots instead of armor, but robots alongside it. What matters, Khirhii says, is a smart combination of machines for each mission, with people's safety and the task's practicality first. The front today needs both armored vehicles and ground robots, he continues, and it needs a great amount of both.

Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge

Breadcrumb
Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a 20 percent cut to the number of generals and admirals in the US military, intensifying concerns that the Trump administration is reshaping the armed forces around its political and ideological agenda.
Hegseth portrayed the cuts as an exercise in "accountability", suggesting that officers who failed to embrace his drive to purge what he calls "woke" policies from the military had been removed.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base on Wednesday.
"We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent."
"So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board," he added. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
The announcement comes amid mounting concerns among Democratic lawmakers and some current and former military officials that the Trump administration is eroding the traditionally non-partisan character of the US armed forces and making adherence to its political agenda increasingly important for senior officers.
Since returning to office last year, President Donald Trump and Hegseth have removed a succession of senior military leaders, often without publicly explaining the reasons for their dismissal.
They include former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Charles "CQ" Brown, who Trump fired without explanation in February 2025, as well as the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, a Navy admiral assigned to NATO and three senior military lawyers.
Hegseth has also fired or blocked the promotions of scores of generals and admirals during his tenure, according to US media reports.
The upheaval has prompted warnings from some former senior officers about the potential creation of a loyalty culture within the military.
H.R. McMaster, a retired Army general who served as Trump's national security adviser during his first term, recently warned against creating "a climate in which everything's a loyalty test".
Hegseth rejects accusations that the changes amount to a political purge, insisting that Trump is entitled to select the military leadership he wants and that his reforms are intended to restore an apolitical force focused on combat effectiveness.
In Wednesday's address, however, he explicitly linked the fate of senior officers to their response to his previous efforts to reshape military culture.
Hegseth said officers who "responded positively" to a speech he delivered to senior commanders last year were now "leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations", while those who did not "no longer work here".
"We are no longer the woke department, or the weak department," Hegseth said.
"Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors -- just tough, ready, committed troops."
Hegseth ordered major cuts to the military leadership in May 2025, including a 10-percent reduction in the overall number of generals and admirals and a 20-percent cut to the highest four-star ranks.
During his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon bureaucracy was top-heavy and that resources should instead be directed towards combat capabilities.
"It's going to be my job, working with those that we hire and those inside the administration, to identify those places where fat can be cut, so it can go toward lethality," he told lawmakers.
His campaign has extended beyond the military's senior ranks. The Pentagon has dismantled diversity programmes and Hegseth this week moved to end tenure for future civilian faculty at US military academies, saying the institutions should refocus on their "warfighting" mission.
Critics argue that the combination of ideological changes and unexplained dismissals risks encouraging officers to tailor their conduct to the political preferences of the administration.
Hegseth, meanwhile, has cast the changes as necessary to reverse what he regards as years of misplaced priorities at the Pentagon.
"The media calls that a purge," he said on Wednesday. "I call it accountability."

Ohio woman sues hospital for allegedly amputating wrong leg during surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:47:06 UTC
06:47:06 KST

An Ohio woman is suing a hospital after doctors allegedly amputated the wrong leg during a scheduled operation last year.
Sharon Jacks, 74, of Meigs county, alleged that she went to Selby general hospital in September 2025 to undergo a planned below-the-knee amputation of her right leg. Instead doctors removed her left leg during the procedure, according to the lawsuit, which was filed earlier this month in Washington county court in Marietta, where the hospital is based.
Her attorney, Brad Layne, said the error ultimately left Jacks, an army veteran, a double amputee after doctors at another hospital in Ohio had to remove the correct leg four months later.
According to the 32-page complaint, Jacks “suffered physical injury, permanent disability, pain and suffering, emotional distress, humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, medical expenses and other damages”.
Jacks and her husband named nine defendants in the lawsuit, including the hospital and Jacks’ medical and surgical teams, accusing them of gross negligence, battery and reckless conduct.
“Defendants acted willfully, wantonly, recklessly, maliciously, and with conscious disregard for the substantial certainty of catastrophic injury,” the complaint alleged.
The amputation of Jacks’ lower right leg was recommended as part of a treatment plan for a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, according to the lawsuit, and she “consented only to surgery involving her right lower extremity” and “never consented to amputation of her left lower extremity”.
According to the complaint, medical records show that the surgical team conducted two “time-outs” before the procedure. In surgery, these pauses are supposed to be used to confirm the patient’s identity, the planned procedure and the correct surgical site. But “despite multiple opportunities … to identify and correct the error”, the team proceeded to amputate the wrong leg, it alleged.
“The performance of surgery upon the wrong extremity constituted a complete failure of basic safety procedures,” the lawsuit said.
In a statement to WBNS-TV, the hospital acknowledged that “this was an avoidable event, and that our expected operating room procedures were not followed.”
The statement added: “Those involved were held accountable for their actions and are no longer in their positions.
“We are saddened by what occurred, and our team continues to keep this patient and their family in our prayers.”
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages on behalf of Jacks.

The US Blacklists Alleged Venezuelan Cyber Crime Mastermind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:38:00 UTC
06:38:00 KST

Reported by
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Wednesday announced it had placed on a special blacklist Aníbal Alexander Canelón Aguirre— a Venezuelan who appears on the FBI’s "Ten Most Wanted" list—identifying him as a key link in a financial network for the notorious crime group Tren de Aragua.
Canelón Aguirre is wanted by the Justice Department for allegedly leading a multi-million dollar ATM fraud scheme. Authorities accuse him of masterminding a jackpotting operation involving malware that when installed allows thieves to direct the bank machine to spew out money.
The alleged Venezuelan hacker topped a list of six Venezuelans and three Mexicans whose names were announced Wednesday as having been added to a group of specially designated nationals. It effectively locks them out of the global financial system. Six of the named are co-defendants of Canelón Aguirre in a U.S. prosecution.
The accused hacker has been on the run, lending his tech skills to the likes of a Romanian mafia operating along Mexico's white-sand beaches and became the cyber "engineer" of the infamous Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang.
Appearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee two weeks ago, the FBI Director Kash Patel announced that federal authorities had apprehended a long-sought fugitive, claiming the arrest effectively cleared the agency’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list.
"Just this past weekend, we captured a thug down in Venezuela who is on our most wanted list and on the run for years. He has been captured, apprehended, and is on his way back to the United States of America. That's ten of ten," Patel told lawmakers.
Patel did not formally identify the suspect or provide operational details, offering no information on how the operation was carried out and whether Venezuelan authorities assisted. He only said that the arrested person was en route to the United States to face prosecution.
OCCRP reached out the Venezuelan government for comment but did not get a response.
An FBI spokesman declined to elaborate on the director’s remarks and as of Wednesday afternoon Canelón Aguirre, 49, remains on the agency’s website for the current 10 Most Wanted Fugitives.
He was added to the list on March 12, 2026, becoming the first alleged cybercriminal ever to appear on it. The agency was offering up to a million dollars for information leading directly to his arrest and described him as armed and dangerous.
Known as "El Ingeniero," "Prometeo" or "Prometheus," Canelón Aguirre is accused by the FBI of being the alleged creator of a malware tied to Tren de Aragua (TdA), a Venezuelan gang that has spread to half a dozen South American countries after emerging from a Venezuelan prison around 2012.
The scheme allowed a network to loot millions of dollars from ATMs across several U.S. states starting at least in January 2024. The technique is known as jackpotting: malicious software takes control of the ATM and forces it to dispense all the cash it holds.
“Within TdA, the jackpotting proceeds would then be transferred among members and associates of the organization in an effort to conceal the fact that they are illegally obtained proceeds,” according to the indictment of Canelon and colleagues.
Prosecutors claim that the proceeds were then moved through a money-laundering network tied to Tren de Aragua, an organization Washington has designated a foreign terrorist group. U.S. authorities describe the structure as combining high-level cybercrime with financing for a transnational criminal organization. OCCRP was among the first to warn of the nascent criminal organization spreading into the U.S. in its November 2023 series Narcofiles: The New Criminal Order.
The arrest warrant against Canelón Aguirre was issued in Omaha on December 9, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Nebraska, as part of a case that already includes dozens of defendants. He was charged with conspiracy to commit bank fraud, conspiracy to commit bank burglary and intentionally damage a protected computer system as well as to commit money laundering and provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization.
Also charged in the same indictment is Jimena Romina Araya Navarro, known in Venezuela as "Rosita" from a Venezuelan comedy show, who is accused of playing a role in the 2012 prison break of the leader of the Tren de Aragua, Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flore. His alias is "Niño Guerrero," and he escaped from the notorious Tocorón prison. The broader jackpotting case now totals 87 defendants nationwide across the United States. Araya Navarro was not among those placed under the Treasury blacklisting.
Before becoming Tren de Aragua's "engineer," Canelón Aguirre had already been flagged in connection with a different kind of criminal structure. According to an intelligence brief from Mexico's Security Cabinet (Gabinete de Seguridad), dated October 30, 2020, and a report from Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) on Romanian criminal groups, Canelón was identified as the developer of the malware known as Ploutus.D.
This software, the intelligence brief suggested, was used by the organization known as the Riviera Maya Gang, led by Romanian national Florian Tudor, alias "El Tiburón" ("The Shark"), to empty ATMs in the tourist zone of Quintana Roo, which includes Cancún, and in the United States.

The West tried to rein in Russian oil. What went wrong?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:33:18 UTC
06:33:18 KST

The West tried to rein in Russian oil. What went wrong?
Nearly four years after Western governments set out to squeeze Russia’s oil revenues, Moscow is shipping crude worth more per week than at any point since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
The gross value of Russia’s seaborne crude exports surged to $2.75 billion in the week through September 27, the highest weekly figure in four years, according to tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Shipments averaged 3.71 million barrels per day over the latest four weeks, their highest since early August.
The rebound exposes a central problem with the Western strategy. Sanctions were designed to keep Russian oil on the global market to avoid a supply shock while forcing Moscow to sell it more cheaply.
Instead, Russia rerouted crude from Europe to China, India, and other markets, built alternative shipping networks, and reduced its reliance on Western services. Now, soaring global prices fueled by the US-Israeli war on Iran are making those barrels more valuable.
The plan: Keep Russian oil flowing but slash Moscow’s earnings
When the West moved against Russian oil in 2022, it faced an obvious problem: Russia was too large an exporter to remove from the market without risking a surge in global prices.
The EU was also Moscow’s biggest oil market. Europe took more than half of Russia’s oil exports in 2021, while Russia was the EU’s largest crude supplier, accounting for roughly a quarter of its imports. China, by comparison, was Russia’s largest single-country buyer.
The EU banned most seaborne Russian crude imports in December 2022, while the G7-led bloc imposed a $60-per-barrel price cap. Western shipping, insurance, and other maritime services could still handle Russian crude, but only if it was sold below the ceiling. Sanctions on petroleum products followed in February 2023.
The logic was simple: cut Russia’s revenues without removing its oil from the global market. The strategy therefore depended on keeping Russian crude flowing while using Western dominance of shipping and insurance services to constrain its price.
The plan backfired.
What went wrong?
The $60 cap initially coincided with steep discounts on Russia’s flagship Urals crude. But Moscow gradually reduced its dependence on Western shipping and insurance services by which the ceiling was supposed to be enforced.
Even the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) – a Helsinki-based research organization that has repeatedly advocated tougher sanctions on Moscow – now says the policy has “failed to impose a durable constraint on Russian crude export earnings.” It says the measure worked only for limited periods on Urals, while other grades and export channels were largely unaffected.
The EU repeatedly tightened the mechanism, lowering the ceiling first to $47.60 and then to $44.10 per barrel from February 2026. The latter was intended to remain 15% below the average market price for Urals.
Yet Urals averaged $60.22 a barrel in July – roughly $16 above the EU and UK ceiling. Russia’s ESPO crude, heavily oriented toward Asian buyers, has also consistently traded above both the old and new caps, according to CREA.
Brussels has responded by sanctioning hundreds of tankers, targeting traders, and tightening restrictions on third-country entities accused of helping Moscow circumvent the measures. Russian crude, however, continues to flow.
Four years later: Where is Russian oil going?
Russia did not stop selling oil when its biggest European customers turned away. It found other customers.
China and India emerged as the dominant destinations for Russian crude, while Türkiye also increased its role. In July alone, India imported $6.25 billion worth of Russian crude – a record high for a second consecutive month – while seaborne deliveries to China were 16% higher than a year earlier, according to CREA.
Russia also built up shipping capacity outside the traditional Western system. By June, sanctioned “shadow” tankers were carrying 66% of its seaborne crude exports, compared with just 31% aboard G7-linked vessels, CREA estimates.
Sanctions changed the routes, ships, and customers. They did not stop millions of barrels of Russian crude from reaching the global market.
Why is Russian oil worth more now?
The biggest twist has come not from Brussels or Washington, but from the Middle East. The US-Israeli war on Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed global crude prices sharply higher, while attacks on regional energy infrastructure have further strained supplies.
The result is precisely the type of supply shock Western governments sought to avoid when designing the price cap – and Russia is among the producers benefiting from higher prices.
On a four-week basis, the gross value of Russia’s crude shipments has risen to $2.39 billion per week, up $290 million from the previous four-week period, according to Bloomberg.
The price shock has also complicated efforts to tighten the squeeze. Earlier this year, the EU considered a maritime-services ban that would have gone beyond the price cap by directly targeting Russia’s ability to ship oil. But soaring prices following the Hormuz disruption prompted a rethink over fears that squeezing Russian exports could worsen the global shortage, according to CREA.
The EU subsequently suspended automatic adjustments to its Russian crude price cap until July 2027, while retaining the option of an earlier review.
The dilemma is the same one Western governments faced in 2022: squeeze Russian supply too hard and global prices could rise further – making the barrels that still reach the market more valuable.
Not all barrels are created equal: The refinery factor
The surge in the value of Russia’s crude exports does not tell the whole story.
Ukrainian drone attacks have disrupted Russian refineries, reducing domestic processing and leaving more crude available for export. Moscow has also restricted diesel shipments to protect domestic supplies.
Russian oil-product loadings fell to 4.7 million tons in July, their lowest level on record and less than half the 9.6 million tons shipped a year earlier, according to CREA. Seaborne crude revenues, by contrast, rose 7%. Russia has also raised its 2026 crude-export forecast while cutting its outlook for refined-product shipments.
The crude boom is therefore being partly offset by weaker fuel exports. At the same time, reduced refinery activity is freeing up more unprocessed oil for shipment abroad – where higher global prices have increased its value.
Europe doubles down
Despite the limits exposed by the price-cap system, Western governments are continuing to tighten restrictions and pressing European states that still rely heavily on Russian energy to cut their remaining ties.
Slovakia and Hungary have resisted demands for a rapid cutoff, arguing that refineries, pipelines, and other infrastructure built around Russian supplies cannot simply be switched to alternatives overnight.
The dispute returned to the fore this week when German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul traveled to Slovakia and urged it to move away from Russian oil and gas and increase pressure on Moscow.
Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar pushed back, saying the country’s infrastructure was built around Russian supplies and that an immediate cutoff would create “enormous problems.”
The West’s Catch-22
The West can sanction more tankers and traders, tighten enforcement, pressure remaining buyers and target third-country networks. The EU’s latest sanctions package added another 41 vessels to a list that already includes 632 ships and targeted entities in China, India, Türkiye, Kazakhstan, and the UAE.
But directly targeting Russian export volumes brings the original dilemma back into focus: the West kept Russian barrels on the market because it feared soaring oil prices – only for soaring oil prices to make those barrels more valuable.

While Spain blocks evictions, Portugal forges on with bill to hasten them
LISBON, Sept 30 - Portugal's parliament approved on Wednesday, in the first reading, a contentious rental market overhaul aimed at speeding up evictions and ending rent controls on new leases in what the centre-right government hopes will encourage landlords to put more homes on the market.
The reform, criticised by tenants' associations as "savagery", sharply contrasts with developments in neighbouring Spain where the leftist government on Tuesday decreed a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, along with other measures, amid protests against evictions and rising rents.
The general outline of the reform was approved after the far-right party Chega unexpectedly abstained after having expressed its objections during the debate, while all left-wing parties voted against.

<p xmlns=""> "This reform proposal is sheer savagery," Antonio Machado, head of the Lisbon Tenants' Association, told Reuters, saying that it would "further skew the rental market in favour of landlords" and only lead to higher rents rather than alleviate the housing affordability crisis.

"This is not just a personal achievement, but a badge of honor for an entire camp in Israel – a proud and determined camp fighting for the democratic character of our country and for solidarity and social justice," she wrote. Lazimi said the recognition gave her renewed momentum ahead of what she called "the most important elections the State of Israel has ever known."
Democrats chairman Yair Golan also congratulated Lazimi on X, citing TIME's description of her as a "charismatic leader" and "superstar of the Israeli left."
"This year in TIME100 Next. Next year in the government," Golan wrote.
Lazimi has become one of the most prominent figures in Israel's Zionist left. She first drew national attention in 2022, when she unexpectedly finished first in the Labor Party primary, and her standing has grown since Labor merged with Meretz to form the Democrats.
In the party's primary in July, she received more than 90 percent of the vote and secured the top spot on its slate behind chairman Yair Golan.
The primary drew more than 97,000 voters, with Lazimi finishing ahead of fellow incumbent lawmakers Gilad Kariv and Efrat Rayten. The Democrats have sought to consolidate Israel's Zionist left while also incorporating prominent figures from the anti-government protest movement.
Lazimi's political profile has been built around social-democratic issues including public housing, food security and economic inequality, alongside a highly visible role in protests against Netanyahu's government and the judicial overhaul. She has also become known for combative speeches in the Knesset and for confronting coalition members directly.
Lazimi has increasingly become a target of attacks from coalition lawmakers. Likud MK Nissim Vaturi recently called her "worse than Hamas" and an "enemy from within," while United Torah Judaism MK Yitzhak Pindrus said protesters blocking roads should be shot in the legs, adding: "But start with Naama Lazimi." Lazimi filed complaints over both remarks and accused members of the government of inciting violence against her.
TIME's annual TIME100 Next list aims to spotlight emerging figures across politics, culture, business and other fields whose influence the magazine expects to grow.

Ukraine’s training facilities get boost: EU is funding centers where its army prepares soldiers, with Denmark putting in €33 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:31:50 UTC
06:31:50 KST

The EU is putting money into the places inside Ukraine where the army trains its soldiers. The bloc will fund the modernization of several military training centers in Ukraine, upgrading facilities, housing, and equipment, with Denmark administering the funds and the Come Back Alive charity carrying out the work, the Defense Ministry said.
The Ministries of Defense of Ukraine and Denmark previously signed a Letter of Intent to implement a project to modernize one of the Armed Forces of Ukraine's training centers. Under this agreement, Denmark allocated about €33 million to training infrastructure, living and sanitary conditions, equipment, and drones for training defenders.
The money goes into the centers
The support will pay to modernize several training sites: better living quarters for the troops who cycle through them, upgraded facilities, and improved infrastructure, the ministry says.
The project runs under the EU's diplomatic and military-planning bodies, the European External Action Service, the Military Planning and Conduct Capability, and the bloc's military-assistance mission for Ukraine, with the Come Back Alive foundation carrying it out alongside the Defense Ministry.
Halan calls training a foundation
The aim is a modern environment for preparing soldiers.
"Modernized centers let us train the military on real combat experience," Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan says, thanking the EU and every partner country.
Training inside Ukraine, she says, is as fundamental to defense as ammunition and equipment, because weapons do not work without people trained to use them. The modernized sites, the ministry says, are meant to let Ukraine prepare its own forces to a higher standard, faster, and closer to the front.
Denmark administers the funds
The project is an EU initiative, open to any partner willing to contribute, with Denmark as the fund administrator. The ministry thanked the EU, Denmark, and Come Back Alive for support it says raises the quality of Ukraine's training.

How Hong Kong’s foreign carer scheme aims to get ahead of ageing city
The pilot scheme to bring in specially qualified carers will upset the market equilibrium, but the shake-up will be to Hong Kong’s benefit
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Mike Rowse is an independent commentator. 
When I first heard about the Hong Kong government’s plans to allow the importation of specially qualified carers to look after the elderly, my mind turned to some colloquial English expressions. The first was “set the cat among the pigeons”, which basically means to say or do something that causes a good deal of trouble, alarm, anger or controversy in a peaceful situation.
The immediate trigger for this thinking was a brief reference in Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address to the government introducing a pilot scheme in which domestic helpers with more advanced training and experience could be brought in to take care of the elderly living at home.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han expanded on the idea in a subsequent press briefing. In short, carers possessing a suitable certificate of expertise and three years’ relevant experience could expect to be paid 10 to 20 per cent more than the normal helper salary. The minimum wage for domestic workers is currently HK$5,100 (US$650) per month.
The government will also strengthen its support for carers by regularising the pilot schemes on training for domestic helpers in elderly care and care for people with disabilities.

Trump administration files complaint against judges over media comments
Seven Minnesota judges face ethics complaint after speaking publicly about the US president’s immigration crackdown.
The United States Justice Department has filed a misconduct complaint against seven federal judges in Minnesota who spoke publicly about the pressure their courts came under during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
The judges spoke to The New York Times this month about dealing with a flood of cases during Operation Metro Surge, an immigration crackdown that led to thousands of arrests in the Minneapolis-St Paul area from December to February.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release
- list 2 of 4White House bars CNN from Air Force One for Trump’s upcoming trip
- list 3 of 4US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue third-country deportations
- list 4 of 4US judge rules Wisconsin mosque leader Salah Sarsour can be deported
The Justice Department says it crossed an ethical line by talking publicly about the cases.
Attorney General Todd Blanche accused the judges of showing “obvious bias” against the Trump administration and called on them to step aside from any cases involving the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
“When we have a situation like we have now, where you have a judge, a couple of judges, just not only violating the canons in our view but also showing bias in what they’re saying, we have no choice but to act,” Blanche told reporters.
The judges say they did nothing wrong. A spokesperson for Minnesota’s federal court system said legal experts had found that the judges were “well within the ethical rules” when they spoke to the newspaper.
The complaint is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and the judiciary, which has blocked some of the president’s policies and, in several cases, accused government lawyers of failing to follow court orders.
One of the judges named in the complaint, Patrick Schiltz, alleged that the government did not comply with nearly 100 court orders related to immigration enforcement in January alone.
In one ruling, he wrote that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “is not a law unto itself”.
Schiltz was nominated by Republican President George W Bush and previously clerked for conservative Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia.
He later told The New York Times that what happened in Minnesota’s federal courts during the crackdown “created a grave threat to the rule of law”.
Schiltz also pointed to guidance issued by a federal judicial ethics panel in February, saying that judges can speak publicly about issues such as the rule of law and judicial independence.
“That is exactly what I did,” he said.

Unknown Publisher

War at the expense of orphans and pensioners: Russia’s regions cut social spending — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
In Tula Oblast, more than 54 million rubles in social assistance were allocated to military personnel. In St. Petersburg, they plan to cut the budget by 70.2 billion rubles.
Russian regions are being forced to sacrifice key social expenditures to satisfy the Kremlin’s growing wartime demands. This is reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that, for example, the authorities of Tula Oblast took more than 54 million rubles ($637,000) allocated for social support for residents and redirected them to payments for military personnel. In particular, payments to foster parents for the upkeep of orphaned children, as well as funds for low-income families, pensioners, and labor veterans, were cut.
An even larger budget sequestration is being carried out in St. Petersburg: officials are proposing cutting budget expenditures by 70.2 billion rubles ($828 million). The city is reducing funding for education, healthcare, and housing and utilities. At the same time, expenditures on payments to war participants and their families are being additionally increased by 6.4 billion rubles ($75.5 million)
They point out that the regions are taking such steps against the backdrop of a significant deficit in local budgets.
"To maintain the flow of "cannon fodder" for the Kremlin, regional authorities are effectively taking money away from orphans, medical workers, and pensioners," the CCD concludes.

The share of Russians collecting aid for Russian servicemen fell from 42% to 28% over the year. 81% are ready to end the war as early as tomorrow.

Ukraine urges US to sanction entities supporting Russia’s Starlink rival

Ukraine urges US to sanction entities supporting Russia’s Starlink rival
- Ukraine urges the US to sanction Russian entities aiding the development of the Rassvet satellite network, a domestic rival to SpaceX’s Starlink, to prevent real-time targeting of Ukrainian territory.
- Russia aims to operate Rassvet by 2027, posing a significant threat, while Starlink remains banned in Russia and Ukraine seeks expanded satellite coverage to counter missile attacks.
- Ukraine highlights Russia's attacks on US businesses in Ukraine and calls for stronger sanctions and better air defence to protect both civilians and American investments amid ongoing conflict.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Ukraine is urging the United States to impose sanctions on several Russian entities that it says are helping develop Moscow’s Rassvet satellite network as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink, its acting ambassador said on Sept 30.
Denys Sienik, deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, told reporters that Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network, saying its goal to start operations in 2027 would pose grave risks to Ukraine.
“If they launch Rassvet by the end of 2026, they will be able to target to hit Ukrainian targets real time on our territory,” Sienik said, adding that he would share details with the US government and Congress about the firms and individuals that Kyiv accuses of aiding Rassvet.
Ukraine plans to issue its own national sanctions against the entities linked to the network, Sienik said, adding: “If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this programme possible for Russia and that will be a game-changer.”
Russia plans to start operating Rassvet, a smaller version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system, in 2027, Alexei Shelobkov, chief executive of Iks Holding, the company developing the service, said in June. The company launched its first 16 low-orbit satellites in March and plans to reach 900 over several years.
SpaceX currently has over 10,000 satellites in orbit. Starlink is banned in Russia, and the use of its equipment is subject to fines.
Western nations have targeted the infrastructure behind Russia’s space-based communications efforts, but gaps remain. Kyiv has been pressing Washington to expand sanctions against a broader group of Russian companies and individuals.
Ukraine has been clamouring for access to expanded Starlink satellite internet coverage so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory, a message backed by Finnish President Alexander Stubb last week.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defences to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
Sienik also expressed frustration about the lack of US response when American firms were hit in Ukraine, noting that US officials had complained loudly when Ukraine had targeted US assets in the Caspian Sea, resulting in closer cooperation and more precise targeting.
But Washington remained silent in terms of messaging to Moscow when US firms in Ukraine were struck, and officials were even reluctant to name the companies affected, he said.
Sienik last week posted details of US firms being hit by Russia missiles in Ukraine, including offices of Boeing, Flex and Bunge.
A Coca-Cola facility in the Kyiv region was also hit in September, along with a logistics facility serving McDonald’s, he said in his message on X.
“It is not a coincidence, Russia knows what it is doing by attacking regular businesses operating in Ukraine, supported by American investment and serving civilian needs,” he wrote.
“While Russia must be deprived of the possibility to cause more deaths and destruction by strong sanctions, Ukraine must have enough air defence capabilities to protect itself but also to ensure the security of the American businesses operating and investing in Ukraine.” REUTERS

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has praised the profound solidarity between Türkiye and Palestine following an emotive friendly football match hosted in the central Turkish province of Konya.
"Tonight in Konya, the friendly match between Konyaspor and the Palestine national football team was an exceptional example of the brotherhood, solidarity and unity of hearts between our countries," Erdogan stated in a message shared on the X platform.

Tributes to Palestinian children

The fixture took place on Wednesday evening as the centrepiece of dedicated "Palestine Day" commemorations in Konya, featuring emotional tributes and ceremonies designed to draw global attention to the thousands of children who have lost their lives in Palestine.
On the pitch, the match delivered competitive drama.
Konyaspor opened the scoring inside two minutes courtesy of Melih Ibrahimoglu, before the Palestine national team responded with two clinical goals from Mohammed Sandouqa in the 12th and 25th minutes to seize a 2–1 advantage.
Konyaspor striker Mostafa Mohamed found an equaliser in the 28th minute to level the scoreline before the break.
Despite persistent attacking opportunities created by both sides throughout an energetic second half, neither team could break the deadlock, concluding the historic friendly in a 2–2 draw.

2026 Global South Modernization Forum calls for effective use of AI
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:23:18 CST
06:23:18 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Global South Modernization Forum was held in Cairo on Wednesday under the theme "The Rise of Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Modernization in the Global South."
More than 100 experts and scholars from nearly 30 countries and regions attended the forum.
Participants said innovation in artificial intelligence (AI) technology presents enormous opportunities while also posing governance challenges.
At the 18th BRICS Summit earlier this month, Chinese President Xi Jinping put forward important initiatives to empower new industrialization with AI and promote open-source and inclusive AI development, outlining a direction for AI development that serves the common good, they said.
Modernization in the Global South is at a crucial stage of overcoming development constraints, addressing capacity gaps and transforming growth drivers, they said, calling for effective use of AI to continually strengthen the internal drivers of development.
Participants said AI is a shared asset of all humanity and urged Global South countries to seize this historic opportunity to use AI to empower a wide range of industries and improve people's well-being.
They called for improving global AI governance, practicing genuine multilateralism, bridging the AI divide and ensuring that development and security reinforce each other.
They also urged greater exchanges and mutual learning in AI, a commitment to open-source development, openness, cooperation and sharing, and deeper theoretical and practical research to ensure that AI better benefits humanity.
The forum was jointly hosted by the State Council Information Office of China, the Party School of the Communist Party of China Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Peking University, Renmin University of China and Cairo University.
The event featured four parallel forums. "The Rise of the Global South: An Atlas of Academic Research on Modernization in the Global South" and "Top 10 Buzzwords in Global South Modernization Research of 2026" were released at the forum.
Academic exhibitions, youth exchanges and think tank seminars were also held before and after the forum. ■

Exclusives
Intelligence and technology
Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest. Chains of Russian drones keep crossing near the Belarus border, Ukraine's Air Force says.
Ukrainian combat simulator, used to train more than 500,000 troops, can now be ordered from NATO’s supply catalogs by single code. Each trainer assigned a 13-digit NATO Stock Number.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges. Russia opens a massed assault on the grid.
Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach. A Ukrainian robot drives to the front, then swims.
Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module. The Mangal launcher carries two cameras, picks out drones on its own, and mounts on a vehicle or a fixed post.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters. Ukraine can jam Russian drones into drifting off course—a satellite relay overhead would let them fly straight through the jamming and strike.
International
EU wants reforms before more money. Kyiv wants Europe to touch Russia’s frozen billions. The push comes as Ukraine seeks access to €210 billion in immobilized Russian central-bank assets to help cover its needs.
Humanitarian and social impact
Ukraine brings 14 more children home from Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast. One of them was being forced onto Russia’s military rolls. This year's returns from the occupied south now reach 204.
Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram bomb while children in grades 1–4 were studying there. The bomb hit as about 40 children sheltered inside, one of many Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities and villages over the past 24 hours.
Kyiv’s supermarkets are the new front line as Russia hunts civilian life before winter. Officials say the Kremlin is blending drone strikes, sabotage, and bot-farm propaganda to break the capital before the cold arrives.
Russian troops seize drone-dropped food in occupied Oleshky, accusing recipients of cooperating with Ukraine. Some people go missing, a local official says. One family in Oleshky was taken "to the basement" and has since disappeared without a trace, an Oleshky official says.

7 killed, 4 wounded in attack on vehicle in C. Syria: state media
China

2026-10-01

Security and investigation teams work at the site of an attack on a vehicle in the countryside of Homs province, Syria, Sept. 30, 2026. Seven people were killed and four others wounded on Wednesday when unidentified assailants attacked a vehicle in Syria's central Homs province, state news agency SANA reported. (Str/Xinhua)
DAMASCUS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Seven people were killed and four others wounded on Wednesday when unidentified assailants attacked a vehicle in Syria's central Homs province, state news agency SANA reported.
The attack targeted the vehicle while it was crossing the Masyaf Bridge in the Homs countryside, SANA said, without immediately providing details about the attackers' identities or motives.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a Britain-based war monitor, said the vehicle belonged to the Al-Matin company and was carrying engineers and workers when it came under attack on the bridge near the Houla area.
The Observatory initially reported several deaths and injuries, saying the wounded were transferred to medical facilities for treatment. Security forces were deployed to the area following the attack and began procedures at the scene, it added.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, and the type of weapon used remained unclear as of Wednesday evening.
Al-Matin is a Homs-based industrial group whose operations include manufacturing and engineering-related activities. The company lists its facilities in the Hassia Industrial City and says it employs around 700 employees across engineering, technical, and production departments.

BERLIN, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- German inflation accelerated to 3.3 percent in September, its highest level since late 2023, as a sharp rise in energy prices continued to push up consumer costs, preliminary data showed Wednesday.
The rate rose from 2.9 percent in August after hovering at elevated levels in recent months, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
Energy prices jumped 14.9 percent year-on-year in September, accelerating sharply from a 10.5-percent increase in August, the data showed.
Inflationary pressures in Europe's largest economy have intensified in recent months as the conflict in the Middle East has driven up energy prices.
To ease the impact of high fuel prices and rising inflation, the German government has announced a temporary fuel tax cut from Oct. 1 through the end of the year, at an estimated total cost of 2.5 billion euros (2.8 billion U.S. dollars).
"The fuel tax cut is likely to dampen inflation again by around 0.3 percentage points in October," said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Hamburg-based Berenberg.
The measure, however, is expected to provide only temporary relief as broader energy-related price pressures remain elevated.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, noted that gas storage levels were below 60 percent at the end of September, historically low for this time of year.
"Low gas storage levels are likely to lead to higher gas prices over the coming weeks, translating into higher retail prices at the start of next year," he said, adding headline inflation could remain above 2 percent until the end of 2027.
Persistent inflation pressures are also reflected in a joint forecast released last week by Germany's five leading economic institutes, which projected inflation to rise from 2.2 percent in 2025 to 2.8 percent this year and further to 3.2 percent in 2027, before easing to 2 percent in 2028. ■

Roundup: Dutch food industry looks to innovation ecosystem for transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:58 CST
06:22:58 KST

THE HAGUE, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Dutch food industry is seeking to transform by building an innovation ecosystem that links research institutions, companies, private investors and government to turn emerging technologies into commercially viable solutions for a more sustainable food system.
For Cosun, a Dutch agricultural cooperative with more than 8,000 sugar beet growers, innovation is closely tied to making greater use of plant-based raw materials and reducing waste.
"We really try to make sure that we valorize our co-products to the maximum," said Fanny Weinbreck, chief R&D officer at the Cosun Innovation Center in Dinteloord, in the Dutch province of North Brabant, on Tuesday.
Rather than using co-products simply for energy or animal feed, Cosun seeks higher-value applications, including food ingredients, plant-based proteins and fibers.
The cooperative works with universities, research institutes, startups, incubators and corporate partners through an open-innovation network.
According to Weinbreck, the model helps established food companies provide a pathway for emerging technologies to move beyond the laboratory and toward commercial applications.
For startups, the challenge is likewise to move technologies from the laboratory into commercial production.
GOA Ventures, a Dutch startup focused on seaweed processing based in Yerseke in the Dutch province of Zeeland, is working with research institutions to scale up its technology toward commercial production.
"The Netherlands has provided an ecosystem in which startups like ours can develop these technologies, work with research institutes such as NIOZ (Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research) and move from an initial idea toward commercial-scale production," said Theo M. Verleun, CEO and co-founder of the company, on Tuesday.
The company's current demonstration facility processes about 15 kilograms of seaweed a day and is being used to test the technology and work with research and investment partners.
"The next challenge is to demonstrate that the technology can work economically and at industrial scale," Verleun said.
But financing remains a challenge in the transition of the food industry in the Netherlands.
The Protein Brewery, a Dutch company developing protein and fiber ingredients through fermentation, has progressed from laboratory research to pilot production and commercial manufacturing.
"The first investment was based on the fact that the technology was very robust," said Thijs Bosch, CEO of The Protein Brewery in Breda, in the Dutch province of North Brabant, on Monday.
The company raised its first investment around 2020, when interest rates were low and investors were actively backing sustainable food technologies. Fundraising has since become more difficult as interest rates have risen and investors have become more cautious, Bosch said.
"Now it's extremely difficult because interest rates are high. Many funds themselves are having trouble raising money," he said.
Peter Wennink, former CEO of Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML, also highlighted the funding challenge for startups and early-stage technologies in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, on Monday.
"We have to acknowledge that lack of funding for startups and early-stage development is a critical issue," Wennink told hundreds of founders and entrepreneurs looking to scale up, connect and innovate at LEVEL UP 2026 event.
The Dutch government's 2026-2030 coalition agreement explicitly identifies biotechnology, genetics, cultured meat and innovative fermentation as technologies that will play a role in future food production. It says the government will support private investment through grants and credit schemes and work with agribusinesses and knowledge clusters to scale up proven innovations. ■

Feature: Across borders, Chinese pianists find a voice in Chopin
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:50 CST
06:22:50 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Piano melodies flowed through a concert hall in Warsaw, gathering strength before softening into delicate phrases. As the final notes faded, the audience rose to its feet in applause.
For Chinese pianist Wang Zitong, returning to Poland for this performance in September meant renewing a connection forged through Chopin's music a year earlier.
It was here, at the 19th International Chopin Piano Competition in October 2025, that she won third prize and the prestigious best sonata performance award. Invitations from around the world soon followed, opening doors to a wider international stage.
Born into a musical family in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Wang grew up surrounded by piano music.
At 13, she left for the United States to pursue her musical ambitions, studying at the Curtis Institute of Music and later the New England Conservatory.
Over more than a decade of study, the piano became woven into her daily life. "Music is both a way for me to express my feelings and my profession. I feel very fortunate that the two can be one and the same," she said.
Long before the Chopin competition, music had become an indispensable part of Wang's life. As her professional career has developed, so too has her understanding of Chopin.
Through reading Chopin's biographies and letters, studying his musical manuscripts and visiting places associated with his life across Europe, Wang has come to see a connection between the emotional expression in his music and the subtlety and restraint she finds in Chinese culture.
For the young pianist, this cultural experience has offered a personal perspective on Chopin, allowing performers and listeners from different backgrounds to find common ground through music.
Wang's feelings about Chopin's music are shared by fellow Chinese pianist Lyu Tianyao, whose life far from home has deepened her understanding of his works.
Lyu began learning the piano at five. On the day she jointly won fourth prize and the award for best concerto performance at the 2025 competition, she had just turned 17.
Her decision to move to Chopin's homeland was inspired by Polish pianist Katarzyna Popowa-Zydron. Deeply moved by Popowa-Zydron's playing at a masterclass in China, Lyu resolved to study with her, a decision that took her to Poznan in November 2024.
After spending two years away from her family during the Spring Festival because of concert commitments, Lyu knows what it means to miss home. That homesickness, she said, has helped her connect with what she describes as the apparent simplicity of Chopin's music.
She brought that personal understanding to the stage for Warsaw audiences in September, playing Chopin with an orchestra. Later that month, she also performed at a Chinese National Day reception in the city at the invitation of the Chinese Embassy.
As invitations to perform multiply, Lyu is discovering an increasingly personal connection with her audience. When listeners approach her in tears, she recognizes something of her younger self in them.
She hopes her performances can give them strength, she said, while their support, in turn, enriches her music.
"I am grateful to every one of them," she said. "It brings me such joy that we can connect through music, and that what I play can reach their hearts." ■

Tunisia amends cybercrime law to replace prison terms with fines for first offenses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:48 CST
06:22:48 KST

TUNIS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Tunisia has amended Article 24 of Decree-Law No. 54 of 2022 on combating offenses related to information and communication systems and networks, replacing prison sentences for certain offenses involving false information with financial penalties for first-time offenses, according to the Tunisian official gazette, Journal of the Republic of Tunisia, published Wednesday.
Under the amendment, the previous penalty of five years in prison and a fine of 50,000 Tunisian dinars (about 16,786 U.S. dollars) has been replaced by a fine of 10,000 to 20,000 dinars.
The provision applies to anyone who deliberately uses information and communication systems or networks to produce, promote, publish, transmit, or prepare false news, data or rumors, or fabricated, forged or falsely attributed documents, with the aim of violating the rights of others, harming public security or national defense, or spreading terror among the population.
The same fine applies to the deliberate use of information systems to disseminate false information or fabricated or forged documents, or data containing personal information or falsely attributing acts to others, with the intent to defame, damage reputation, cause material or moral harm, incite attacks, or promote hate speech.
For repeat offenses, the amended provision stipulates six months in prison and a fine of 50,000 dinars. Penalties are doubled when the target is a public official.
The amendment was reviewed Tuesday at a Council of Ministers meeting chaired by Tunisian President Kais Saied at the Carthage Palace. ■

06:22:44 KST

OSLO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Denmark's government released its annual climate program on Wednesday, warning that the projected margin for meeting its 2030 emissions reduction target had narrowed sharply.
The country is still expected to meet its target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 70 percent from 1990 levels by 2030. The projected margin has fallen to 0.4 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, down from 1.5 million metric tons in last year's assessment, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Utilities said.
Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa warned that even a few delays could wipe out the remaining margin, making closer monitoring of implementation essential.
"We have come a long way, but we are not there yet," she said in the ministry's statement.
The program introduces an assessment of uncertainties surrounding the main expected contributions to emissions reductions through 2030 and 2035. It examines risks sector by sector to identify where closer monitoring and timely policy decisions are needed.
Agriculture remains a particular concern. The program projects that emissions covered by the target for agriculture, forestry and land use will fall by about 52 percent by 2030 compared with 1990, below the binding reduction target of 55 to 65 percent.
The government plans to review progress toward the agricultural target in 2027 and is prepared to take further action if the sector remains off track, according to the program.
Denmark's Climate Act, adopted in 2020, requires the government to publish an annual climate program assessing progress toward national targets and whether they can be achieved. ■

Under the proposal put forward by Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry, artists and cultural figures would be required to sign a publicly available declaration condemning Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and supporting its territorial integrity.
Those who refuse would be barred from working in Lithuania completely.
However, signing such a declaration poses significant risks for Russian citizens. Since the full-scale invasion, Russia has prosecuted numerous civilians for anti-war statements and has also moved against Yabloko – its only registered liberal party – whose ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in August along with an 11-year prison sentence for its deputy chairman.
In July, Turkey deported a 24-year-old anti-war activist Ariadna Litvinova to Russia, where she faces up to seven years in prison for writing slogans such as “Peace to Ukraine” on banners at a pro-war exhibition in St. Petersburg.
Rights advocates said the case was part of a wider pattern of transnational repression targeting Russian anti-war exiles.
Moscow courts have also ordered the arrest in absentia of anti-war pop singer Monetochka, who now lives and performs in Europe, and sentenced novelist Boris Akunin to 14 years in prison in absentia after he voiced support for Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported.
Such sentences would take effect if the exiled artist returned to Russia or were extradited.
Rising tensions with Moscow
The measures come amid heightened tensions between NATO members, particularly the Baltic states, and Moscow.
On Sept. 11, Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Lithuania would “disappear from the map of the world” if it lifted its long-standing ban on nuclear weapons.
Russia’s embassy in Belgium warned on Sept. 28 that Moscow was ready to use its entire arsenal if NATO countries tried to isolate Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave bordering Lithuania.
NATO dismissed the warning, condemning Russia’s irresponsible nuclear rhetoric while reiterating that it is a defensive alliance. Vilnius rejected the threat by framing the warnings as a form of psychological pressure.
The warning came days after Putin claimed on Sept. 25 that the rights of Russian speakers were being violated in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, while insisting that Russia had no plans for military action against Europe.
The Kremlin used similar unfounded claims to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Trump demands Powell resign from Fed board over headquarters renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:17:01 UTC
06:17:01 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday demanded that Jerome Powell immediately resign from the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors over cost overruns in the central bank's headquarters renovation.
Trump said he had asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to review an inspector general's report on the project.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump cited findings of deficiencies in the management of the Washington, DC, renovation project and accused Powell of failing to control its costs.
"This is Jerome Powell's fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!" Trump wrote.
He said he had instructed Blanche to study the report and determine what action to take over a project that, according to his post, would cost at least $2.5 billion.
Trump threatened legal action if Powell refused to step down, saying the US government should sue him "for either corruption or incompetence."
The inspector general's review, however, found no grounds for a criminal referral and no administrative misconduct, while identifying significant shortcomings in the Fed's oversight of the renovation.
Powell remains a Fed governor after his term as chair ended in May.
Trump highlighted passages stating that the Fed board did not obtain a project cost estimate from its construction manager until January 2026, three-and-a-half years after construction began and after more than $2 billion in construction costs had been awarded.
According to the passages quoted in his post, the board had also failed to establish a guaranteed maximum price by July 2026, leaving it without cost certainty and without transferring material risk to the construction manager.
Trump predicted that the final bill could reach $3.5 billion or $4 billion and claimed he could have completed the renovation for $25 million while preserving the buildings’ historic appearance. 
Dispute over interest rates
The renovation has become a focal point of Trump's broader dispute with Powell over interest rates and the central bank's independence.
In January, Powell disclosed that the Justice Department had served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas threatening a criminal indictment related to his June 2025 Senate testimony about the renovation.
Powell said the threat stemmed from the Fed setting interest rates according to its assessment of economic conditions rather than the president's preferences.
He described the renovation and his congressional testimony as pretexts for the pressure.
In April, Powell said the Justice Department had provided assurances that it would not reopen the investigation without a criminal referral from the Fed's inspector general. 
Renovation of 2 historic buildings
The project covers the Marriner S. Eccles Building, the Fed board's headquarters, and the neighboring 1951 Constitution Avenue Building.
The Fed has listed the board-approved renovation budget at $2.46 billion.
It said the work aims to modernize building systems, remove asbestos and lead contamination, improve safety and accommodate modern workplace technology.
Construction costs alone rose from an estimated $921 million in February 2020 to $2.018 billion by December 2024, according to the watchdog's findings.
The Fed has attributed overruns to inflation, unexpected remediation expenses and additional requirements from agencies reviewing the project.

Google announces Gemini 4 flagship AI model after months of delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Google restricts access to new AI model over safety concerns
- Google is limiting access to its new AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to cybersecurity experts due to safety concerns and potential misuse by hackers.
- The model excels in software engineering, legal, financial tasks, and cyber defence, detecting flaws missed by other AI systems.
- Google and other AI firms are implementing safeguards and working with the US government to ensure safe, phased AI deployment amid rising cybersecurity risks.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO - Google on Sept 30 said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.
“Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach,” wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google’s chief AI architect, in a blog post announcing the model.
Google said it is voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and will gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.
The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organisations.
Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.
The announcement came a day after President Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including Google chief Sundar Pichai and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.
Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.
Google said Argon excels at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber defence, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.
Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information – something other advanced models had missed, Google said.
Google said Argon is designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyberattacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.
Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI have built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.
Google said it is monitoring the model’s reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.
The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of AI company Hugging Face. AFP

Why the closure of Russian publisher Individuum is such a loss for Russian-language literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:02:59 UTC
06:02:59 KST

Why the closure of Russian publisher Individuum is such a loss for Russian-language literature
Individuum is closing. In its 11 years, the publisher’s team showed that there was another way to publish literature in Russian: with energy, flair (just look at their covers), and speed. Founded by people with media backgrounds, the publisher always understood what interested readers at any given moment. Literary critic Alex Mesropov explains why its closure cannot be ignored.
Many people have a favorite Individuum book.
In 2020, I picked up Brian Raftery’s “Best. Movie. Year. Ever.” and realized I was no longer surprised to see nonfiction published in Russia in paperback, with original cover designs — just like in the West. It’s the kind of book you want to display prominently on your shelf.
And that’s before you get to what’s inside: Raftery’s book explores the landmark films of 1999 that many millennials remember from childhood. The publisher had thought of everything: owning such a beautiful book made you feel special, while its subject connected you with other readers — fans of “The Blair Witch Project” or “The Sixth Sense,” for instance.
Perhaps that was Individuum’s greatest achievement: choosing its books made you feel both unique and part of something shared and important.
The people at Individuum were true publishing nonconformists: they wanted to publish radically different books in Russian — and that led to a genre they called “adventure nonfiction.”
They also made sure their books were professionally produced. I think many, if not all, of those who worked with them would confirm how different their approach was from that of other Russian publishers. Original design, thorough editing, their own research and fact-checking, decent pay, attention to authors’ views — everything reflected their professionalism.
Individuum reminded us that independent publishing involves more than selfless devotion to culture. Everyone involved deserves respect, and that should be normal.
Perhaps they managed all this because they had worked outside the book industry. Alexey Dokuchaev and Mikhail Vrubel, who founded Individuum in 2015, came from media and film. Felix Sandalov, who became editor-in-chief in 2018, had worked in the media for more than a decade, including at Afisha in its heyday. Maxim Balabin, who later became the publisher’s art director, had also worked there. Their books were available as ebooks through the easy-to-use Bookmate service. In other words, they all understood modern media, how it changes reading habits, and what interests young readers.
So what was new about their “adventure nonfiction”? Individuum knew that many people in Russia had unique professional experiences that could interest others — all that remained was to turn those experiences into gripping books. Publishers had previously overlooked these experiences: Russian nonfiction was very conservative.
But in the Russian media of the late 2000s and the first half of the 2010s, people with unusual experiences had already begun sharing them. You could find excellent long-form writing that connected personal stories with issues of public importance. Individuum approached the writers with a proposal: let’s turn your long-form pieces into great books. Whether you were an anthropologist or a reporter, a young mother or a stage actor made no difference. Everyone had a right to tell their story, especially if their experience was unlike anyone else’s.
This approach produced books that became hits in 2019–2021 and cemented Individuum’s reputation as one of Russia’s leading publishers: Olga Allenova’s “Forpost” (“Outpost”), Daniil Turovsky’s “Vtorzheniye” (“Invasion”), Robert Garayev’s “Slovo patsana” (“A Boy’s Word”), Maxim Semelyak’s “Znachit, uragan” (“That Means a Hurricane”), and others. These books explored different — often ugly — sides of contemporary Russia. They brought readers stories that had been pushed out of public view: uncomfortable testimony about the terrorist attack in Beslan, the story of Russian hackers working for the Kremlin, a chronology of the rise of criminal culture in Tatarstan in the 1990s, and the rightward turn of Russia’s cultural elite in the 2000s.
The writers’ personal perspectives made these stories emotionally engaging and, surprisingly, even universal (good editing probably had a lot to do with that). Writers and readers found a sense of solidarity: it turned out that professional anthropologists, doctors, and reporters with international experience worried about the same things as ordinary young city dwellers. You could even talk about those problems with the authors in terms you both understood: the editors had made sure the books were clearly written. Readers would then go to book launches and fairs, where they met these authors, sometimes also running into them at vodka bars or rallies. And all of this was thanks to one independent publisher.
Individuum did more than publish the latest Russian-language nonfiction — it also released a wide range of translations. These included internationally acclaimed classics of journalism that had long been unavailable in Russian, such as John Hersey’s “Hiroshima,” as well as unusual books about women’s place in society, from Stoya’s “Philosophy, Pussycats, & Porn” to Christine de Pizan’s “The Book of the City of Ladies,” written in the 15th century.
Its fiction was distinctive, too: think of the novels and short stories of Roman Mikhailov, who quickly attracted a community of fans, or Charlie Kaufman’s “Antkind” — a brilliant, challenging novel by a director whose work is equally brilliant and challenging.
The publisher had an excellent instinct for what to release. Producing a timely book quickly, without sacrificing quality, became routine. Have all your friends taken up birdwatching? Here’s a classic on the subject. Or become technology skeptics? Here’s a book for you. Is everyone arguing about gender? Here’s the big new book from the United States.
That remained true throughout, including the last two years, when Alexey Kiselyov was editor-in-chief. Bold new bestsellers kept coming out during that period, too — under very different, very difficult conditions.
Since 2022, the publisher has done more than stay relevant — it has become even more relevant. As everyone watched the state destroy documentary theater in Russia, Individuum published a book by the founder of Teatr.doc. As years of debate continued over mass killings and who bore responsibility for them, it published a book about genocide and retribution.
When books in Russia began appearing with passages removed because of censorship, it released an edition of “Yevgeny Onegin” with cuts. And when the state began persecuting publishers, it released a scholarly study of literary policy in the Third Reich.
The publisher’s team had faced pressure from law enforcement even before the war, but the first truly devastating blow hit its imprint, Popcorn Books, in 2025. It was Popcorn Books that had published the young adult hit “Leto v pionerskom galstuke” (“Pioneer Summer”).
A call by one “well-wisher” to set fire to the publisher’s office was followed by a sequence of events familiar from the news of recent years. The Justice Ministry added employees and authors of Popcorn Books and Individuum to its register of “foreign agents.” Online booksellers — including Labirint — began withdrawing their books from sale. Novels and nonfiction with queer themes disappeared from stores after the “international LGBT public movement” was declared extremist.
The forced sale of Individuum to businessman Denis Kotov in 2022 and the transfer of control to the publisher Eksmo in 2023–2024 did not change the situation. The criminal prosecution known as the “publishers’ case” began in May 2025, when three Individuum employees were charged under a law concerning an “extremist organization.” In 2026, they received suspended sentences.
In this appalling situation, public support from the frightened book industry was barely visible. Only the publisher’s readers offered real help. But there were obstacles even here: Moscow’s Non/fiction and several other book fairs repeatedly refused to let Individuum participate — often at the last moment, when staff were already setting out books at their booths. In 2026, the publisher said it was closing.
Still, Individuum will not disappear without a trace. And its legacy goes beyond books. A community formed around the publisher in which young writers, editors, translators, and other professionals learned a great deal from one another. Some have left the country and others have stayed, but there is no doubt that these young publishing professionals will, in one way or another, carry on the work Individuum began. The gripping, bold books about contemporary life that readers have grown accustomed to over the past 11 years will continue to appear in Russian.
