Catholic clergy sexually abused nearly 1,000 Massachusetts children over decades, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:53:09 UTC
04:53:09 KST

More than 270 Catholic clerics sexually abused nearly 1,000 children across three Massachusetts dioceses over several decades, according to a report released by the state’s attorney general’s office on Wednesday.
The eight-year-long investigation did not result in new indictments, the office said, claiming that some conduct identified was not a crime under Massachusetts law at the time it occurred, and that in other cases the applicable statute of limitations had expired.
However, three cases were referred to different district attorney’s offices and one of those resulted in criminal charges. The majority of the abuse occurred before 2002.
“The evidence gathered during this investigation also shows that, for decades, and especially before 2002, church officials in all three dioceses knew about the sexual abuse of children yet did not take effective action to prevent it or to examine the institutional failures of leadership that led to scores of children being victimized at the hands of abusive priests,” the report stated.
The attorney general’s office said the report was “the first comparable public accounting of the institutional failures within the Fall River, Springfield and Worcester dioceses”.
The abuses in the archdiocese of Boston drew international attention after the Boston Globe published its Pulitzer-winning coverage in 2002, and prompted other investigations around the world that found similar cases of sexual abuse.
“I strongly urge the dioceses and the broader church to take these recommendations seriously and implement greater, meaningful changes to strengthen child protection and improve responses to allegations of abuse,” the Massachusetts attorney general, Andrea Joy Campbell, said at a press conference.
“Behind every one of those numbers is a child whose safety was violated, a family that was changed forever and a survivor who carried that abuse for years, and in many cases decades. They continue to carry this trauma even today,” Campbell said.
“I know many survivors have been waiting a long time to see these findings made public. I understand the frustration that comes with that wait. It is my hope that today is a meaningful step forward toward truth, accountability and healing that survivors deserve,” she added.
Only one of the three dioceses responded to the report in a statement. “We will study the attorney general’s report to identify any additional improvements that can be made to respond to victims of past abuse and to continue to strengthen efforts to keep children safe,” said the diocese of Worcester in a statement.
The diocese of Worcester did not apologise on Wednesday for its clerics’ behavior, but pointed to an apology by Bishop Robert J McManus, who wrote in 2022 that he was “profoundly sorry for the abuse of minors by priests” within his diocese.
“I continue in my commitment with the help of many collaborators to do everything we can to ensure such abuse does not happen again,” he said at the time. The diocese of Worcester also highlighted that no charges were filed.
Many of the individuals identified in the report are also deceased, the report said. “Any legal limitations do not diminish the seriousness of what this investigation found. The office believes that while criminal law cannot provide justice for all survivors today, the office still has a responsibility to tell the truth of what happened.”

For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. From secret orders to fighter jets: How Israel responds to an in-flight terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:52:09 UTC
04:52:09 KST

The tense hours endured Wednesday morning by passengers aboard a Flydubai flight were also nerve-racking for Israelis and especially for the country’s security forces, as the circumstances were initially unclear and the IDF prepared for the possibility of a hijacking.
Shortly after the alert was received, two Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled to escort the aircraft while officials assessed how to respond.
The deployment was carried out under procedures the IDF regularly drills for scenarios in which a civilian aircraft heading to Israel deviates from its route, fails to respond to radio calls, transmits a distress or emergency signal or is suspected of being hijacked.
If necessary, fighter jets are scrambled to identify and escort the aircraft, while authorities also consider closing the airspace.
The fighter jets are intended to provide a response to hijackers or terrorists and prevent the incident from escalating or causing additional casualties, including damage to strategic sites as well as harm to passengers and crew.
Scrambling fighter jets also provides the option, if necessary, of shooting down the aircraft or alternatively escorting it securely to a safe airport for landing.
At the same time, a decision to shoot down a civilian aircraft is an exceptionally rare one and would be made only after consultations with senior security officials acting under the direction of the political leadership.
Such a scenario is intended to prevent far greater and more severe harm, such as mass casualties on the ground in addition to those aboard the aircraft, or an attack on strategic assets that could cause major damage to national security.
Amid the spread of unverified information on social media, the Air Force stressed that activation of the relevant order — whose name is barred from publication — does not necessarily indicate a security incident.
The Air Force maintains continuous readiness to deal with a range of airborne threats and prevent unauthorized entry into Israeli airspace. Its systems operate around the clock to monitor the skies, identify irregularities and detect threats, while maintaining the ability to scramble and deploy aircraft within a short period of time.
The readiness is based on a continuous aerial picture, forces kept on alert and regular drills for a range of scenarios. The goal is to allow early identification of an unusual event, rapid decision-making and a response tailored to the way the incident develops.
One of the scenarios routinely practiced by the Air Force involves civilian aircraft heading to Israel.
Under a dedicated order, the military can respond to situations in which there is concern that an unusual event is developing, including the possibility of airborne terrorism, a hijacking or an attempt to deliberately crash an aircraft with its passengers on board.
The order may be activated in a range of circumstances, including when an aircraft deviates from its planned route, fails to answer radio calls, transmits a distress signal, suffers a technical malfunction or experiences a medical emergency requiring an emergency landing.
Once the order is activated, measures are taken to protect the airspace, at times including closure of the entire airspace, with the aim of preventing more serious harm.
At the same time, as occurred Wednesday morning, fighter jets can be scrambled to identify and escort the civilian aircraft.
A continuous assessment is then carried out until the circumstances are understood and the concern is resolved.
The Air Force regularly drills its response, with an emphasis on shortening response times and moving quickly from identifying an irregularity to understanding the situation and activating the appropriate response.
The IDF stresses that activation of the order does not necessarily mean there is suspicion of a security incident.
In some cases, it may be triggered by a technical malfunction, a communications problem, a deviation from the flight path or human error by the flight crew.
Every unusual incident is examined and handled until the concern is removed and the situation is fully clarified.
The Air Force continues to keep forces on alert to defend Israel’s skies and borders in both routine and emergency situations, with the ability to shift rapidly from normal operations to an operational response as events develop.

19:47:32 UTC
04:47:32 KST

Israel suspended Flydubai flights to Ben Gurion Airport for six days on Wednesday following the suspected terror attack aboard one of the airline’s Dubai-Tel Aviv flights earlier in the day.
The suspension could be extended depending on the findings of the investigation into the incident. Flydubai currently operates as many as 10 flights a day to Israel.
The decision followed a tense discussion in which Transportation Minister Miri Regev urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to immediately halt the airline’s operations until the circumstances of the incident were clarified.
According to Israeli officials, the Omani co-pilot is suspected of attempting to carry out a terror attack and crash the aircraft. The report said the attempt was thwarted by another pilot with the help of Israeli passengers aboard the flight.
Regev argued that Flydubai had violated the aviation agreement between Israel and the UAE, which she said allows only pilots from countries that maintain diplomatic relations with Israel to land in the country.
An Israeli official said the Omani pilot had never previously landed in Israel.
“This is a mega-event,” a Transportation Ministry official said in explaining Regev’s position. “We came very close to a major disaster that was prevented.”
Regev also demanded that Israeli airlines immediately be allowed to resume flights to Dubai with Israeli security screening. Israeli carriers are currently unable to operate the route because of a dispute over security requirements.
Emergency codes trigger Israeli response
The Flydubai aircraft took off from Dubai at 7:05 a.m. and was scheduled to land at Ben Gurion Airport at about 9:30 a.m.
Roughly 90 minutes into the flight, as the plane entered Jordanian airspace, it transmitted squawk code 7700, the international general emergency signal. It later transmitted code 7500, indicating unlawful interference or a possible hijacking.
The aircraft then turned back toward Saudi Arabia and began flying at a lower altitude over the kingdom before heading south and then west.
There were 174 passengers aboard, including 27 children.
The hijacking alert prompted urgent consultations among Israel’s political and security leadership. Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz and IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir held emergency consultations, while Israeli fighter jets were scrambled.
A major Israel-UAE air link
Flydubai is a relatively young airline, founded by the Dubai government in 2008 and beginning operations a year later. Despite its close association with Emirates, it is not an Emirates subsidiary.
For Israeli travelers, Flydubai’s importance grew rapidly after the Abraham Accords.
On Nov. 26, 2020, the airline operated its first regular commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The aircraft received a traditional water-cannon salute at Ben Gurion Airport, with a delegation led by the airline’s CEO aboard.
Flydubai began with two daily flights, or 14 per week, between Tel Aviv and Dubai, also giving Israeli passengers access to onward connections across Asia, Africa and the Far East.
Its operation expanded sharply in the years that followed, reaching as many as 10 flights a day in each direction during parts of 2026.
Within a few years, a route born out of Israel-UAE normalization had become one of the busiest air links between Israel and an Arab country.

There will never be a player who changes my ideas. Never."

How does Trump’s White House AI accord work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:44:42 UTC
04:44:42 KST

How does Trump’s White House AI accord work?
Trump announces voluntary pact on AI, urging companies to self-police amid growing calls for strict safety regulations.
Amid calls for regulation, United States President Donald Trump met with artificial intelligence executives at the White House to put in place a voluntary pact, called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.
The agreement, which was signed by executives at Meta, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic on Tuesday, calls on companies to put in place guardrails internally to help monitor security risks, with four layers of control.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump backs AI self-regulation at tech summit but is it enough?
- list 2 of 4OpenAI launches ‘dots,’ personal AI assistant ‘built to handle everything’
- list 3 of 4Trump unveils new site to simplify access to government services
- list 4 of 4Trump, tech bosses sign voluntary pact pledging ‘robust’ AI safeguards
What does the White House Accord do and what doesn’t it do?
The agreement calls for companies to maintain internal controls, establish an internal team to oversee these controls, work with independent outside auditors and create an independent board committee to review the results.
The pact, however, is voluntary and not legally binding. It does not establish penalties for companies that fail to comply. The pact does not require companies to publicly disclose audit results or give the government an enforcement role. Companies also retain control over how the safeguards are implemented.
The agreement does, however, leave open the possibility that its measures could eventually become mandatory. It says that, over time, it might “make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations”.
“There’s going to be a tremendous self-policing aspect,” Trump told reporters, adding that it is “morally binding”.
On the White House lawn, alongside the executives, Trump claimed that AI companies had done a great job at self-policing.
Google CEO Sundar Pichai also touted the agreement on social media.
“We are committed to working with other industry leaders to establish norms and build public confidence. The White House Accord and the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities signed today is a solid basis for moving forward – it contains real tangible steps to promote safe development, while delivering the economic and scientific benefits of this technology,” Pichai said in a post on X.
Why are AI companies calling for more regulation?
The agreement comes despite calls by some of the same companies for government-mandated safety standards.
In September, Chris Lehane, chief global affairs officer at OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, called for Congress to establish mandatory national AI safety standards.
“Industry-led standards would complement – not replace – mandatory federal safeguards and democratic oversight,” Lehane said in a post.
In June, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for “more serious and binding regulation of AI”. In July, Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, called for an AI watchdog led by the US.
The calls for guardrails come amid reports that some employees at those companies have raised concerns about whether increasingly sophisticated AI systems are being adequately watched.
Two employees at OpenAI warned executives that testing of the company’s new models was not being properly monitored. The warnings were reportedly not acted upon ahead of incidents in which the models behaved in unintended ways, according to The New York Times.
What are lawmakers proposing?
Pushes for legally binding regulations are coming from Congress rather than the White House.
Earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, warned that AI technology could pose an existential threat to humanity within the next decade, prompting renewed attention from lawmakers.
Among the most comprehensive proposals comes from Independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar, a Democrat from Texas.
The two lawmakers introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which, if passed, would permanently ban the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator establishes safety rules.
The bill would also create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence to monitor frontier AI systems – a term used to describe the most advanced AI systems – as well as oversee dangerous capabilities and supervise the destruction of artificial superintelligence if needed.
The legislation would impose harsh penalties for violations, such as up to 20 years in prison for individuals.
It comes amid a bipartisan bill introduced last week by Senators Chris Coons, a Democrat from Delaware; Brian Schatz, a Democrat from Hawaii; Katie Britt, a Republican from Alabama; and James Lankford, a Republican from Oklahoma.
The AI Systems Transparency Act would require AI companies to disclose what data they collect and what measures they have in place to prevent their systems from going rogue or being misused by bad actors.
What does ‘superintelligence’ actually mean?
The White House named the accord the White House Accord on Super Intelligence amid Trump’s push to rename “artificial intelligence” on government documents.
In the technology industry, “superintelligence” refers to a form of AI that exceeds human intellectual capabilities.
Trump, however, has directed executive branch agencies to use “Super Intelligence” or “SI” in place of “artificial intelligence” or “AI” in official communications.
On Tuesday, Trump outlined a new executive order that says that “Super Intelligence” refers to technologies and systems covered by the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence and directs the creation of a new federal definition within 60 days.

Displaced by war, young Sudanese turn to entrepeneurship to survive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:43:47 UTC
04:43:47 KST

Displaced by war, young Sudanese turn to entrepeneurship to survive
Displaced by war and shut out of formal jobs, young Sudanese are turning to art, small businesses, and entrepeneurship to rebuild their livelihoods.
Yousra Hussein’s career was on the rise. She had graduated with a degree in medical laboratory sciences from Nahda College in 2022, and then began developing a women’s empowerment initiative – Golden Women – in the western Sudanese city of Nyala, in the same year.
The initiative organised psychosocial support sessions and training workshops in marketing and entrepreneurship that helped more than 70 women. Yousra wanted to help young women like her seeking work, but often lacking the experience and practical skills needed to pursue available opportunities.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Nigeria and Ghana suffer huge AFCON 2027 qualifying shocks
- list 2 of 3US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue third-country deportations
- list 3 of 3Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises
Things were going well until Sudan’s civil war began in April 2023, upending her life. By June, Yousra and her family fled Nyala to Sennar, a city in central Sudan that she had never visited.
“Before the war, I was ambitious and had many dreams,” Yousra told Al Jazeera. “I started from zero in Sennar, without work experience or connections.”
Unable to find work in a city that she was unfamiliar with, she began offering nail services from home, charging the equivalent of about $10 to $15, and saving what she could to help her family.
Then, fighting between the two belligerents in Sudan’s war – the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces – spread to Sennar in mid-2024, forcing Yousra and her family to flee once again, this time to Kassala in eastern Sudan.
Once again, Yousra was starting from scratch, and Sudan’s economy was collapsing as a result of the war. With few jobs available, and the growing need Yousra saw for women to earn money to support their families, she has resurrected her Golden Women initiative.
But while she has been able to raise some income through the initiative, funding remains a major obstacle. Yousra said young Sudanese entrepreneurs have limited access to skills training and institutional support, as well as struggling with bank requirements for guarantees that many cannot provide. She also pointed to complex registration procedures and taxes as barriers to establishing and sustaining a business.
War-driven jobs crisis
Yousra’s experiences reflect a wider collapse in jobs and livelihoods.
In a 2024 joint report by the United Nations Development Fund and the International Food Policy Research Institute, 31 percent of the 3,000 urban households surveyed had been displaced, while the share reporting no employment or income rose from 1.6 percent before the war to about 18 percent by the time of the survey. Full-time employment also fell by half.
The World Bank, meanwhile, estimates that even as the economy grew modestly last year, with the government attempting to stabilise the areas of Sudan under its control, the percentage of the population living in extreme poverty rose from 33 percent in 2022 to 59 percent in 2025.
For young people whose education and livelihoods have been disrupted, the shrinking labour market has pushed some towards entrepreneurship and informal work as they search for ways to support themselves and their families, but they may not have the skills or experience to go into business for themselves.
International and government-backed programmes have been initiated to help some Sudanese develop the skills that they’ll need to run businesses.
The International Labour Organization said in May that its i-UPSHIFT programme had reached 500 young people in Kassala, providing entrepreneurship training, mentorship, and business incubation. Thirty-eight youth-led teams – involving 160 participants, including 66 internally displaced people – went on to pitch business and social-enterprise ideas.
Sudan’s Ministry of Youth and Sports says it has also promoted vocational training and youth-led projects. Minister Ahmed Adam Ahmed told Al Jazeera that two youth conferences had been held in Atbara and Kassala in an attempt to understand the views and aspirations of young people, as part of an effort to equip young people with practical skills that could help them earn an income.
Ahmed explained that one of the first conference’s outcomes was a proposed industrial city in River Nile State intended to support youth-led enterprises.
“Projects were also directed towards implementation in states considered safe, with some already under way,” Ahmed said. “The second conference in Kassala focused on practical applications and innovation, particularly artificial intelligence and the use of agricultural waste.”
Turning art into a livelihood
The struggle to earn a living after displacement affects many Sudanese. Mahira, a 30-year-old visual artist who did not wish to give her full name, moved to Port Sudan after her home in Khartoum was damaged during the war.
She now paints decorative pieces and murals, earning about 1 million Sudanese pounds ($130 at parallel market exchange rates) to help support her husband and son, but has worked a variety of jobs since being displaced.
Before the war, she graduated with a degree in French and completed a diploma in fine arts, both from Sudan University of Science and Technology.
“Since the war began, my main concern has been finding any income, no matter how much, to meet my family’s daily needs, despite how difficult it has been to find opportunities and funding,” she told Al Jazeera.
Mahira initially took on several jobs in Port Sudan, including making soap, applying henna and makeup, and styling clothes. She then began working in home decoration after she volunteered to paint the walls of a woman’s house in the Salbouna neighbourhood.
“Everyone was surprised by my skills in decorating and beautifying homes,” she said. “After that, requests started coming from other residents in the neighbourhood asking me to paint and decorate their homes.”
She later turned to more of her artistic work, conducting workshops on concrete art – an art form that uses cement-based materials to create decorative and artistic pieces – and teaching traditional dance at shelters. She worked with nongovernmental organisations running psychosocial support and skills-training programmes for displaced people.
Mahira now hopes to stage an exhibition featuring paintings that challenge hate speech and promote peaceful coexistence, while also giving her a way to market her work and build a more sustainable income.
At the same time, the exhibition would cost at least 8 million Sudanese pounds ($1,000), but Mahira says she has no savings and earns only about 1 million pounds per month. And yet, Mahira is still optimistic that she can raise the funds, and believes in the benefits the exhibition will bring – not just to herself.
“We need to promote peace and peaceful coexistence in Sudan, because the war has affected society and fuelled hate speech based on ethnic and tribal identity,” she told Al Jazeera.

French court sentences 13 men over deadliest small-boat crossing to UK
Six people smugglers are found guilty of involuntary homicide after 31 migrants died in the English Channel in 2021.
A French court has sentenced 13 men to up to 10 years in prison for their roles in the deadliest small-boat crossing by migrants trying to reach the United Kingdom from France.
The court in Paris found six of the men guilty of involuntary homicide on Wednesday, handing down prison terms of between six and 10 years. Prosecutors said they organised the crossing of a small boat that was unfit for navigation on the open sea, was overloaded with 31 passengers and lacked appropriate life jackets.

The remaining seven men were found guilty of lesser criminal charges and were sentenced to up to four years in jail. There were 14 defendants on trial, one of whom was acquitted.
The court said the smugglers were driven by greed and were “profiting from the vulnerability of exile candidates”.
“When it costs the lives of 31 people and the sea becomes a cemetery, there is a price, and the court said that the price they had to pay was justice and prison time,” said Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for victims’ families.
The migrants, mostly Iraqi Kurds, drowned after the UK-bound small boat carrying them from northern France capsized in the English Channel in November 2021. Four of the bodies were never found, while two men survived.
Seven military personnel are still being investigated for allegedly failing to help the survivors. They all deny any wrongdoing.
The sentencing of the 13 men comes as France and the UK end their pilot scheme that allowed Britain to return migrants from France deemed not to have the legal right to remain in the country.
In return, the UK accepted an equivalent number of migrants whose asylum claims were likely to be granted.
The scheme was due to expire on Thursday. However, unverified reports say the UK government wanted the programme to continue.
The UK Interior Ministry confirmed earlier on Wednesday that new applications were no longer being accepted.

06:45 GMT: According to local media, the plane FZ1073 lands safely at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk.
Flightradar24 receives the aircraft’s final tracking signal at 06:58GMT at Tabuk airport.

Millions of Aussie websites could be caught up in a quiet shake-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:32:48 UTC
04:32:48 KST

in brief
- New rules that could make it more difficult to register .com.au websites have been proposed.
- However, other experts suggest the changes will not be as dramatic as they are being made out to be.
A quiet policy shift within Australia's web address regulatory body has industry experts concerned that millions of local websites could be pushed offline, even as the government urges a wait-and-see approach.
Last month, the board of the .au Domain Administrator (auDA) approved "in-principle" recommendations from an independent panel that would overhaul eligibility rules for domestic website registrations.
The decision, recently announced by auDA, will see the long-standing "close and substantial connection" rule scrapped. Companies and organisations will soon no longer be able to register web addresses based on products, services, or events, but will instead have to link their websites to their name alone.
Domain industry experts estimate that "potentially millions" of Australian websites could be impacted and that "confidence" in the .com.au domain address could be shaken if the proposed changes go ahead.
auDA said in a statement to SBS News that rule changes have yet to be finalised and that "most" domain name holders are expected to meet the new requirements.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Under the current rules, businesses are allowed to register website names that are related to their services — such as applepies.com.au for a bakery — but under the new rules, they could need a much more closely aligned Australian company name to match the site.
"The independent review recommendation is intended to strengthen the connection between a com.au or net.au domain name and the domain name holder's official business identity, helping maintain the trust Australians place in .au domain names," the auDa statement said.
"The Panel found the current criteria can create inconsistency in how the allocation rules are applied, can be seen as unfair to small businesses, and in some instances may result in consumer harm."
'More red tape'
Former auDa chair and domain lawyer Erhan Karabardak voted against the change on the divided advisory panel. He said the policy "throws the baby out with the bathwater" and will fail to address the problem it was designed to.
"We still don't understand what the justification was," Karabardak said.
He said the policy change stems from a desire to curb domain investors and "monetised" web portfolios from claiming generic domain names to sell them to legitimate businesses.
However, he argued commercial domain investors will simply work around the change by registering multi-word business names with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and that everyday users will end up paying more.
"Whenever a business wants to register a generic name, product, or service, they're going to have to firstly pay for a business name — $47 a year — and then pay for a domain name," he said. "It's effectively doubling the cost of registering a .com.au or .net.au domain name."
Schools, charities, and small businesses that want a temporary domain name to promote an event could struggle to do so under the new rules.
Registrants will see the process as "more red tape" and opt to use a different domain address like .com where there are fewer rules, Karabardak said.
Improving trust in the age of AI
While the announcement of the change has sparked concern among industry insiders, some have urged caution until the full details are known.
Patrick Myles, an independent domain industry consultant, told SBS News that he expects the number of registrants who might be impacted will be "pretty small" and that updates to business organisational practices are a routine part of day-to-day operations.
"I'm in this category myself," Myles said. "I have multiple domains, and some of them are less associated with my business than others so [the changes] might impact me a bit, but it doesn't worry me at all."
In an era of declining trust in global institutions and declining relevance of domain names as artificial intelligence changes how users access the internet, Myles said protection of national domain names is increasingly important.
"If you don't support the policies around your country code ... it basically becomes existential," Myles said.
Myles, who has worked for auDA previously, said the changes proposed are "one of the best ways to ensure that the brand of .au is retained and it is kept as strong as it can be in a very, very cloudy world".
While the requirements for registering a .com.au domain could become stricter, Myles advises anyone who fails to meet the new standards to register an .au address, which has fewer requirements.

What is and isn't changing today as Thriving Kids begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:31:48 UTC
04:31:48 KST

What is and isn't changing today as NDIS alternative Thriving Kids begins
The first phase of the $4 billion National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) alternative for kids under nine with developmental delay or autism who have "low to moderate" support needs begins today.
Thriving Kids is intended to offer children and families a baseline level of support in places they already live, learn and play, without needing a diagnosis or specialist referral.
While running under a national model, each state and territory will run their own iteration of Thriving Kids.
Here's what you need to know about the system, what's changing today, and what your state or territory is saying about it.
What's changing today?
Not much.
Today simply marks the first stage of the program, with the launch of what are being called "general supports".
That includes the Thriving Kids Autism Helpline (1300 654 789) delivered by autism organisation Amaze, which will provide autism-specific information, guidance and connections to relevant services.
An online resource hub, delivered by the Raising Children Network, contain information, practical resources and guidance to help families support their child's development.
A Medicare-funded three-year-old developmental health check is set to start on November 1, aiming to give families cheaper access to a doctor to help catch developmental concerns early.
States and territories will then gradually phase in "targeted supports", which involve more intensive supports such as playgroups and allied health therapies, with full rollout expected to be reached by January 2028.
"We are absolutely committed to making sure that for children under the age of nine, those Thriving Kids services are fully up and running [by then]. We're not going to let parents and children fall between two stalls," federal minister Mark Butler said.
How is 'low to moderate' defined?
This is the $4 billion question, but one we don't have an exact answer for yet.
"Thriving Kids is going to be available for children that have mild to moderate support needs. But at the moment, it's really unclear exactly what that means," Children and Young People with Disability Australia chief executive Skye Kakoschke-Moore said.
"It's also unclear how families who might have more than one child with mild to moderate support needs are going to be supported."
Does this mean my child will be kicked off the NDIS?
Not today.
The government says there will be no changes to how people access the NDIS until January 2028 — the date Thriving Kids is expected to be completely rolled out and when new eligibility criteria, currently being designed, will be in place.
"We'll have two systems operate in parallel. Children are still able to be enrolled in the NDIS from now until the end of next year in the same way they have been … but at the same time we will be rolling out new Commonwealth supports and new state supports," Mr Butler said.
Children with "permanent" and "significant" disability, including developmental delay and autism, will remain eligible for the NDIS beyond 2028.
Anecdotal evidence from disability advocates and allied health professionals suggests some children have been removed from the NDIS before Thriving Kids begins, something the government strenuously denies.
What are the other big questions?
Advocates are worried about what will happen to the children who are no longer eligible for the NDIS, but too old for Thriving Kids.
Mr Butler said he is talking to the states about the development of supports outside the NDIS for other groups, including kids over nine. But considering Thriving Kids isn't ready yet, many are sceptical about how timely or effective such a program for over-nines may be.
Concerns have also been flagged about whether children with "moderate" support needs will be adequately catered for and how Thriving Kids will be properly delivered in already stretched education settings.
Additionally, while families will not need a diagnosis to access Thriving Kids supports, it's still unclear what they will need.
The new assessment process that will determine whether a child goes into Thriving Kids or the NDIS is also yet to be designed.
While that change and others don't kick in until the start of 2028, giving governments more time to prepare, that also means another year of uncertainty for families.
It's also unclear how well Thriving Kids will cater for the specific needs of Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse children, who have historically faced barriers engaging with disability supports.
SNAICC, an advocacy group for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, said Aboriginal community-controlled organisations (ACCOs) are trusted places already providing wraparound, culturally strong support for families, and so they must be sufficiently resourced and involved in delivery.
How did we get here?
Thriving Kids was announced last August with the federal government under growing pressure to reduce the growth of the NDIS, which cost more than $50 billion last financial year.
Statistics from June 2025 showed 11 per cent of all kids between five and seven years of age were on the scheme.
The states and territories shut their disability services when the NDIS began, leaving families with nowhere else to go if they wanted support.
The Albanese government earlier this year agreed to boost states and territory hospital funding in exchange for them taking on more of a role in disability support.
What your state says
With Thriving Kids set to look a little different in each jurisdiction, the ABC contacted all states and territories to ask what families can expect over the next 15 months.
Queensland is yet to formally sign up to the program and is therefore not included in these responses.
NSW
Read more
A spokesperson for the Department of Communities and Justice said families in NSW could continue to access the services they currently do.
When up and running, they said Thriving Kids would include a range of supports, including:
- supported playgroups
- parenting programs and peer support for families, carers and kin
- information and advice about child development
- help finding and connecting with services
Some children requiring extra help may also receive short term allied health support, with those services to become available in 2027, the spokesperson said.
The government will provide more information about accessing Thriving Kids supports when ready and new service providers will start becoming available from now and throughout 2027, they said.
The spokesperson said Thriving Kids had been designed to reflect the needs of different communities across NSW — including Aboriginal families, multicultural families and families living in regional and remote areas — and parents could ask for help even if they were unsure what support they needed.
Western Australia
Read more
A spokesperson for the West Australian government said its most recent budget included $361 million in funding over five years for Thriving Kids services, which would include:
- information and advice support so families and caregivers have assistance to navigate different service systems
- family support programs, such as playgroups, peer supports and community groups to build capacity, skills, and connect with others
- targeted, time-limited therapeutic supports for children with more moderate needs
They said the Department of Communities has spoken with more than 300 service providers across the state this year, and heard from families and experts about ensuring Thriving Kids works for the state's "unique geographical, service and population characteristics".
Some services will be established through a grants program, they said, while the Aboriginal Health Council of Western Australia (AHCWA) and Council of Aboriginal Services Western Australia (CASWA) would help develop a partnership that includes mobilisation of Aboriginal community-controlled expertise.
"We will continue to work closely with families, people with lived experience and service organisations to ensure that Thriving Kids support works appropriately for WA," the spokesperson said, with more information available online here.
Victoria
Read more
The Victorian government said initiatives starting from today included:
- information and guidance to help families understand available supports
- access to the Advocating for Children with Disability Support Line
- more publicly funded autism assessments and places in the Strengthening Parent Support program
- more training for early years educators to help identify developmental concerns earlier
From January 2027, allied health and support services to help children build everyday skills will begin at six initial sites in Bendigo, Hobsons Bay, Hume, Loddon, Maribyrnong and Melton, before expanding to the rest of the state throughout the year.
Starting in the initial delivery sites, families will also have access to two new developmental checks – one as each child starts kindergarten, and one as they start school.
The government said the Department of Education would lead delivery of the targeted supports and development checks, as well as managing triaging and intake. The checks will be undertaken by allied health professionals and clinicians.
"These initial supports will lay the foundation for the full complement of services to be delivered across the state from 2028." Minister for Children Lizzie Blandthorn said.
South Australia
Read more
The South Australian government said it was expanding its Preschool Boost program and Child Health and Development Checks, while also funding qualified facilitators and allied health professionals to work with families at the state's 140 facilitated playgroups.
Further initiatives, including autism-specific supports, will be announced in coming weeks, it government said.
The government said the commissioning of the state's targeted supports would start in the first half of 2027, with delivery expected by the end of the year.
A Thriving Kids Ministerial Forum is set to be established to give families, early childhood and disability providers, peak bodies and others a voice in the design and rollout of supports.
"Thriving Kids is about helping and empowering children and families to access the right support at the right time," Human Services Minister Katrine Hildyard said.
"We want South Australian children and families navigating some difficulties and differences to know that they are not alone, that there is support close to home."
Tasmania
Read more
A spokesperson from the Tasmanian Department of Health said Thriving Kids supports would be "introduced over time", with the "full range" of services in place from January 1, 2028.
"Initial supports will include supported playgroups and Early Childhood Connectors in every region to connect families with services and supports. Further information will be provided over the coming weeks," they said.
The department will continue building workforce capability, strengthening local services and engaging families, carers, providers, advocates and Aboriginal communities, they added.
ACT
Read more
From today, families with questions about their child's development can call the Thriving Kids ACT Information and Navigation phone line on (02) 6205 5500 for advice and connections to support services.
The government said it would work with stakeholders and progressively roll out a range of targeted supports over the next 15 months, including:
- time-limited therapy and functional assessments through the Child Development Service, with new allied health staff
- new intake and referral services to help families understand their child's needs and undertake developmental screenings in local Child and Family Centres
- targeted services for priority cohorts, including for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders and CALD families
- community awareness initiatives to improve understanding of developmental delay and neurodivergence
"We acknowledge these changes will impact many families, carers and kin of children who need developmental support. Thriving Kids is a new approach to early intervention, and represents an important step towards to making support easier to access and navigate," Disability, Autism and Neurodiversity Minister Suzanne Orr said.
Northern Territory
Read more
Disability Minister Jinson Charles said existing services and support arrangements would continue while Thriving Kids was progressively introduced.
He said targeted supports would be provided through a phased uplift and expansion of existing NT Health allied health teams such as the Children's Development Team.
"We understand families want clear information and certainty. Our focus is on making it easier for children to receive support early, based on their developmental needs, without families having to wait for a formal diagnosis or navigate complex systems before asking for help," he said.
The government says consultation with families and stakeholders is underway, and more feedback can be provided via Have Your Say.

U.S. court halted Christa Pike&apos;s execution just hours before it was due to take place
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:30:33 EEST
04:30:33 KST

U.S. court halted Christa Pike's execution just hours before it was due to take place
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. appeals court suspended Christa Pike's execution in Tennessee following her petition for a case review. The state attorney general filed an appeal.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit stayed the execution of Christa Pike just hours before it was due to take place. She was set to become the first woman executed in the state of Tennessee in 206 years. UNN reports this, citing the court’s ruling.
Details
According to the court’s ruling, Christa Pike filed a motion to remand the case to the district court, arguing that the state had recently changed its position in the litigation, under which she had been portrayed as a liar who fabricated sexual abuse.
Pike argues that the state’s acknowledgment of her account of childhood sexual abuse and rape "undermines the foundation" of the trial of her case in state court.
Pike also cites authoritative scholarly sources in support of her argument that the state’s statements regarding her history of sexual abuse tainted the proceedings in state court and the subsequent federal proceedings by introducing harmful stereotypes about survivors of sexual abuse.
"To properly consider and resolve the issues currently before this court, and after carefully weighing all the circumstances, we conclude that a stay of Pike’s execution is necessary. A stay of execution is an equitable remedy. Accordingly, it is hereby ordered: the execution of the applicant is stayed pending further order of this court," the court’s ruling states.
However, one of the circuit judges expressed the view that this case was yet another baseless last-minute attempt to delay a lawful execution.
According to media reports, after the stay was granted, Tennessee’s attorney general immediately appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Witnesses and media representatives remained at the prison in case the Supreme Court allowed the execution to proceed.
Update
In the U.S. state of Tennessee, preparations are underway to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years—50-year-old Christa Pike, who was sentenced to death for murdering a classmate in 1995.
Pike’s execution was scheduled for Wednesday. She was 18 at the time of the crime and became one of the youngest women in the United States to be sentenced to death.
Pike and her boyfriend were found guilty of murdering 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, with whom they attended school in Knoxville. According to prosecutors, Pike viewed the girl as a romantic rival, lured her to a secluded location, where the victim was tortured, and then killed.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee stated on September 28 that he would not pardon Pike. Her attorneys appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking it to halt the execution, while the mother of the murdered Colleen Slemmer supports carrying out the death sentence.
"The application for a stay of execution, submitted to Justice Kavanaugh and referred by him to the Court, is denied. The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied," the Supreme Court’s ruling of September 29 states.

The Battle to Be Your Personal AI Agent Is Here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

Yesterday, I spent the morning at OpenAI’s annual DevDay, where over 2,500 nerds discussed building software and marveled at the latest artificial intelligence models. The biggest reveal of the day was Dots, the company’s new, always-on agents that proactively help complete tasks and make autonomous decisions as they scour the web.
After watching the sometimes messy demos on stage and hearing CEO Sam Altman talk about his experiences using the agents, I was curious what it felt like to boss my own Dot around. I’ve spent most of September testing another cute, cuddly agent, Meta’s Muse, and I wanted to know how OpenAI’s user experience would compare.
I named mine “Toolie” and tweaked it to look like a pink frog. As midnight approached and my partner slept soundly nearby, I started whispering sweet nothings to Toolie. I called my personalized bot through ChatGPT, asking what tasks it was best at. “My strongest work is taking a messy, time-consuming task and turning it into something you can use,” it responded. OK, sure. Let’s get to work.
I asked Toolie to look through my ChatGPT history and flag three tasks that it could immediately get started on. The bot flagged an in-process data request that I needed to send a follow-up email for, and offered to draft a reply. Toolie also noted that my upcoming gay-cation was a bit underplanned, and suggested it could pick some better dinner spots. (More time for me to pack the Speedos!) Then, it offered to go through my reporting notes and refine pitch drafts before I took them to editors. This is my favorite part of the process, so I declined.
Early adopters in Silicon Valley are still obsessed with agents, from Instinct to OpenClaw to Google’s CC. But recent releases like Dots and Muse are pushing them even further mainstream. The chatbot is dead, at least as a hot form factor for developers. Now, everyone wants to build the next big agent—and they want it to dominate. The companies promise that their agents will simplify your life, automating all the boring, exhausting tasks you have no desire to do: booking doctor’s appointments, arranging carpools, sorting through bills.
For now, users will be able to access one Dot, but they’ll soon be able to use multiple Dots. At launch, the agents are only available for subscribers of OpenAI’s Pro plan, which starts at $100 per month. In comparison, Muse is free to use for anyone who wants to download the app or visit the website.
OpenAI leaders see the quality of Dots, powered by the GPT-6 Astra model, as a differentiating factor. “We're starting out as a premium product. It uses a lot of compute,” Altman said during DevDay. While Dots are currently gated for paying subscribers, it may not always be that way. “You should, of course, expect us to do a mass-market thing for billions of people," he said.
These CEOs seem to be taking careful notes on the larger cultural backlash against generative AI, and they may have found their secret weapon: cuteness. From the Labubu stylings of Muse to Dot's two-eyed puffball, developers of always-on agents are leaning aggressively into adorable aesthetics as central to their branding. Previously, I've chatted with experts who said this approach could be disarming for users who may feel affectionate toward the anthropomorphized software.
Developers involved with this wave of personal agents are also leaning into texting-style experiences that feel familiar to a group chat. When I send a task request to Toolie or Muse, it often emoji-reacts—a thumbs up, a heart, really anything—to my messages to tell me that it’s getting to work.
A chatbot, like a blushing prom date, was never going to make the first move. In contrast, proactive agents are made to message you unprompted, especially if you give them a recurring task.
“My Dot just deals with the stuff, tells me if there's anything really urgent, and will respond to what it can,” Altman said. The CEO lets the agent handle his mornings and claims the experience leaves his brain feeling less “polluted” from an inundation of information right after waking up.
The “always-on” design of these agents is a key selling point, though it will be interesting to see which company strikes the best balance between helpful and incessant. For example, Muse reminded me to pay a utility bill that I’ve never had a problem with before and don’t really need pings from an AI tool about.
Still, it’s clear after using them for a bit that the tools actually work—another reason that agents are expanding beyond insider-y Silicon Valley circles and onto your mom’s phone.
I’m not saying that agents are perfect. But when I was testing agents a year ago, they often sucked at interacting with computers. It was error message after error message. Now, I have more trust that the tools might actually be able to complete whatever tasks I throw at them, without getting lost in the digital wilderness.
That said, trust has its limitations. During the setup process for Dots, OpenAI suggested that I connect my Gmail and Google Drive accounts. Some users may feel comfortable with that connection and consider potential risks as a trade-off for automated help, but it’s worth seriously reflecting on what you’re comfortable allowing these agents to access and do on your behalf.
While the agents recently going on rogue hacking sprees were powered by different models with different guardrails, my own guard remains up while using Toolie. The little AI guy needs to earn more of my trust before I let it really automate aspects of my life.
Altman declined to answer questions about whether these Dots are a precursor to the software users will eventually see in OpenAI's long-rumored hardware. Even so, the foundation laid here by Dots for future devices feels pretty evident. It's easy to imagine Toolie becoming my generative AI alarm clock that wakes me up with a daily briefing or an Alexa-style assist that can answer cooking questions while my hands are covered in raw chicken goo.
Competition in the AI agent wars is heating up, but my energy is starting to fade. I call Toolie, one more time through ChatGPT before dozing off, requesting that it generate a morning report going over all the major announcements from this OpenAI developer day as well as important pieces of analysis. While I sleep, Toolie’s out there, always doing something.
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Why Gadi Eisenkot should support Palestinian elections without promising statehood - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:27:12 UTC
04:27:12 KST

I hope that Gadi Eisenkot will be Israel’s next prime minister, even if I am not voting for him. It disturbs me that he refuses to say that he will deal differently with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict than how Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dealt with it since 2009.
I recognize that the trauma of October 7 has changed Israeli society profoundly. But we should also understand that Hamas’s massacre shattered assumptions about security, deterrence, and the possibility of simply containing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Rather than confronting the reality that this conflict cannot be managed and must be resolved, Israeli politics has moved sharply toward the Right and focuses solely on increased military strength as a solution and distrust of Palestinian intentions.
It is therefore understandable that politicians competing for the Israeli mainstream are cautious when talking about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Words such as “Palestinian state” and even “two-state solution” have become politically explosive for many Israelis. And political leaders all too often follow public opinion rather than shaping it.
But avoiding the need to resolve the conflict does not eliminate it.
Netanyahu’s political strategy for many years was based on determined opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel. But preventing Palestinian statehood did not erase the Palestinian aspiration for freedom and self-determination. Three years of devastating war have not made that aspiration disappear. If anything, the issue of Palestinian self-determination has become even more central to the conflict.
Nor has the idea of two states disappeared internationally. Despite profound disagreements over how such an outcome could be achieved, broad international support remains for a negotiated future in which Israel and a Palestinian state exist alongside one another. In September 2026, the vast majority of countries, including Britain, France, Canada, and more than 100 other countries, again publicly reaffirmed support for a two-state solution.
Eisenkot has built much of his public identity around responsibility, sober judgment, and learning lessons from failure. That makes the question of what comes next especially important.
The lesson that Israel must learn should therefore be larger than the failure to “manage” the conflict. The Palestinian national question cannot simply be wished away. Israel cannot suppress Palestinian aspirations, resist them, or postpone dealing with them.
And there is something happening on the Palestinian side that Israelis are barely discussing. Israelis will vote for a new Knesset on October 27. Palestinian legislative elections are scheduled for November 28 – almost exactly one month later.
New Palestinian political lists are entering the process, including representatives of a generation that has never before had the opportunity to vote in a national Palestinian election. What Israel says – or does not say – during this period will inevitably form part of the environment in which Palestinians make that decision.
Why it's important for Israel to support Palestinian elections
There is a remarkably simple message that an Israeli leader could convey without promising a Palestinian state, accepting a particular negotiating formula, or prejudging the outcome of future negotiations.
It is this: If the Palestinian people elect leaders who are sincerely committed to achieving genuine peace between the Palestinian people and the people of Israel, they will find a partner for peace in Israel.
That sentence should not be controversial. It does not ask Israelis to forget October 7. It does not ask them to trust Hamas. It does not prescribe borders, Jerusalem, settlements, refugees, or security arrangements. It does not even require Eisenkot, during an Israeli election campaign, to use the words “two states.”
It simply tells Palestinians that political choices matter. That message could have significance far beyond Israeli domestic politics.
Imagine being a young Palestinian who has never voted in a national election. You have grown up watching negotiations fail, settlements expand, violence recur, and Israeli governments increasingly argue that there is no Palestinian partner. You are now being asked to choose among political movements offering very different visions of the Palestinian future.
One of the central questions confronting such a voter is obvious: Does choosing a peaceful political path actually lead anywhere?
If the answer coming from Israel is silence – if Palestinians conclude that Israel will reject them regardless of whom they elect or what policies those leaders adopt – then advocates of diplomacy have a much harder argument to make. But if a major Israeli leader says clearly that Palestinians who choose leaders committed to genuine peace will encounter an Israeli partner, the political equation changes.
It does not guarantee peace. Nothing could. But it restores the essential principle upon which diplomacy depends: Political choices can produce political consequences.
Such a statement could also resonate internationally. Israel today faces an extraordinarily difficult diplomatic environment. Criticism of Israeli policy has intensified across many countries, international institutions, and younger generations abroad. Whatever Israelis believe about the fairness or motivations of that criticism, the deterioration of Israel’s international standing is a strategic issue that cannot be dismissed.
An Israeli leader saying that Israel remains prepared to pursue genuine peace with genuinely peaceful Palestinian leadership would communicate something important to the world as well: Israel has not abandoned the search for a political future beyond permanent war.
Most importantly, however, this should not be about public relations. It should be about strategy. Israel cannot determine whom Palestinians elect. Nor should it try. But Israeli leaders should understand that what they say influences the Palestinian political debate just as Palestinian rhetoric influences Israelis.
For decades, Israelis have asked a legitimate question: Where is the Palestinian partner? Palestinians have increasingly begun asking the mirror-image question: If we choose a different path, will there be an Israeli partner?
The elections of October and November 2026 provide an unusual moment when both societies will be making political choices almost simultaneously. There is no certainty about what either electorate will decide. But there is an opportunity to establish one principle before those choices are made.
If Palestinians choose leaders genuinely committed to peace with Israel, Israel should be prepared to meet them. That is not a peace agreement. It is not a concession. It is an invitation to choose a different future. And sometimes history begins with something as simple as one sentence.

Joy mixed with fear as US forces leave Iraq amid potential security vacuum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:26:42 UTC
04:26:42 KST

Iraqis celebrated the departure of US forces after more than two decades of war on Wednesday, though many feared that any security vacuum could increase the power of Iran-backed militias or provide an opening for the return of Islamic State (ISIS).
The withdrawal of the final troops, mainly from an airbase in Erbil in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, ended the biggest US war of the century, which brought widespread devastation and chaos from which Iraq has yet to fully emerge.
Iran, which has entrenched its influence in Iraq through allied armed groups and is determined to drive all US forces out of the Middle East, views the US pullout as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
Iraqi troops paraded in vehicles through the streets of Baghdad and the Shi'ite holy city of Najaf to mark the pullout.
The withdrawal "fills our hearts with joy," said Baghdad resident Ahmed Salah, who said he felt reborn at the age of 70. But he also said it was now time for powerful militia groups to surrender their weapons, "and let the government be the one responsible to protect me and you on the ground, sky and water."
Pullout plans drafted under Biden, performed under Trump
The pullout was agreed in 2024 under former president Joe Biden and carried out by the Trump administration even as it waged war against Iran next door.
US forces invaded to topple Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003, triggering years of upheaval and chaos. The Americans initially left at the end of 2011 but came back less than three years later to assist Iraqi forces after Islamic State fighters seized a third of Iraq and imposed violent rule.
US President Donald Trump said that the United States leaves Iraq with "wonderful" Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, saying in a Truth Social post that he would "hopefully be able to handle things very well."
More than 4,500 US troops died in Iraq, around twice as many as in the parallel war in Afghanistan. The Iraq Body Count project says more than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed.
The Pentagon said the United States and its coalition partners formally concluded "Operation Inherent Resolve" and Washington would continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
The Iraqis are expected to lead the effort to secure the country, an ally of both Washington and Tehran, and keep the remnants of Islamic State suppressed.
“The end of the international coalition’s mission does not mean the end of our battle against terrorism, but rather Iraq’s transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability," said Zaidi in a statement.
'Security vacuums can be extremely dangerous'
While the departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, some worry that security forces trained and funded by the United States still can't protect the country.
"The lesson from the past two decades is that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous," said Jassim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi analyst who advises the security forces.
Adil Salman, 45, a high school English teacher, said Iraqis "should not rush to celebrate" the withdrawal.
"Militias still operate outside the state's control and (Islamic State) still has not disappeared," he said. "I'm concerned that the US departure could lead to a new period of instability. In the end, people will judge this decision by one thing: whether security remains stable in the coming years."
Hundreds of supporters of pro-Iranian Iraqi militia groups gathered in Baghdad to celebrate the pullout, chanting "Death to America."
They carried portraits of Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his son and current Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, and top Iranian general Qassem Soleimani, who was killed in a US airstrike on his convoy in Baghdad in 2020.
With US forces present alongside armed groups allied to Iran, Iraq has been caught up in this year's war.
Of the 18 US service members listed as killed since Trump launched Operation Epic Fury alongside Israel's Operation Roaring Lion in February, seven died in Iraq. The last was an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
The withdrawal raises "the possibility that Iran's proxies will feel increasingly empowered in the absence of a Western military presence. These groups may attempt to expand their role in shaping state policies and consolidating their presence within key institutions," said Baghdad-based political analyst Ahmed Younis.
Some Iraqi security officials say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
The last time the US withdrew, the Iraqi army proved no match for Islamic State: soldiers took off their uniforms and fled when the group captured Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city, in 2014.
"The most important question now is whether Iraq's security institutions have prepared a viable Plan B for the post-coalition phase," said Iraqi Army Gen. (ret.) Mohammed al-Jubouri, who led a brigade in the war against Islamic State.

A last-minute push
The funding comes from the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI), a Pentagon program through which the US procures weapons and equipment for Kyiv.
Congress approved the $400 million late last year, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced its allocation in June, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
As of late July, the funds had still not been obligated, according to Reuters.

Ukraine Completes 17 of 42 Resolutions Needed to Unlock $29.5B in Aid
The funds did not have to be spent by the end of the fiscal year on Wednesday, Sept. 30, but they would have expired if not placed under contract by then.

Months of pressure from Congress
At a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on April 30, Pentagon Comptroller Jules Hurst said the funding had recently been released and would be “put to work very shortly.”

Republican Sens. Kevin Cramer and Thom Tillis, along with Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet and Catherine Cortez Masto, also signed it.

The Pentagon’s plan allocated $200 million for weapons, ammunition and explosives, $99.9 million for vehicles, spare parts and equipment.
Another $100 million is intended for services such as transporting military equipment, Reuters reported in July.
The more recent contracts include offensive weapons and spare parts for armored vehicles.
However, the package does not include Patriot interceptors, one of Reuters’ sources said, despite Ukraine’s repeated appeals for more ahead of winter, when Russia is expected to step up attacks on the country’s critical infrastructure.
Currently, the Patriot systems are the only weapons in Ukraine’s arsenal that can reliably down Russian ballistic missiles.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly held last week, US President Donald Trump told President Volodymyr Zelensky that he had made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine licenses to domestically produce Patriots.
He had previously made a similar pledge during the NATO summit in Ankara on July 7-8, but retreated from the commitment weeks later, citing concerns over sharing sensitive weapons technology with other countries.
In the meantime, Ukraine announced that it was signing contracts with partners for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles ahead of winter.
Around the same time, Germany announced it would urgently transfer the PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks.

AI Isn’t the Cause of Education’s Demise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:22:00 UTC
04:22:00 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Students shouldn’t “cheat themselves of the cognitive friction and productive struggle necessary for actual learning.”
This was one of many insights in MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee’s paper titled, “AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training”. In this paper, the committee explores the impact AI is having at MIT on teaching, instructional design, student health, and, most importantly, learning.
The paper argues that AI is deeply impacting learning (at MIT but arguably in general) in the way students approach learning itself, in how teachers design curricula and educational assessments, and in how students and teachers approach the learning enterprise itself.
Ironically, the paper highlights that AI is bringing to the surface what has arguably been a slow degradation in education that’s been happening for decades. AI is accelerating that degradation but is not really the cause of it.
A key thread in the paper is that education is not merely “content delivery.” Rather, it’s a robust experiential enterprise that is based on a contract between the student and the teacher. Learning is both a process and a product:
… the process of education is necessarily a productive struggle, and that the most important product of [a student’s] education is not a GPA or a diploma but themselves: their personal growth and intellectual maturity and the development of their own imagination, insight, and judgment.
This also highlights the root of the decay. Education has become a highly competitive means to getting a good job or prestige or status rather than and end in and of itself. If students don’t value learning primarily for it’s own sake, then using AI tools will only amplify behaviors that help them “get ahead” in the competitive learning landscape.
When it comes to the educational experience itself, the committee argues that learning happens when students are, “disentangling the steps of a mathematical proof with [their] study group, adjusting an experiment over and over until it works, or having a spirited argument with a peer.”
So, not unexpectedly, they see a tremendous value in on-site learning. While that has a strong self-serving odor, their bases for making these claims are not unfounded. When it comes to digital learning and the use of AI, they see both tremendous opportunities and serious risks.
For example, learning that is created using AI tools ,
. . .helps [teachers] develop customized, interactive learning tools that allow students to explore subject content with more depth and for instructors to create learning experiences for their students that are new or newly tailored to each student.
They see a lot of possibilities in what AI tools can do to augment education. Education, they argue, degrades when AI is used to automate it.
For us in the digital education space, the paper summarizes a lot of core educational philosophy that we can and should bring into the materials we’re creating. AI can and should be used. But the Ad Hoc Committee urges us to do so thoughtfully and intentionally.
While the paper is focused on AI’s impact on education at MIT, much of it is transferrable to any learning institution and it is rich with ideas for any instructional designer, teacher, and student. Definitely worth reading in full.

Slower au pair visa approvals hit Australian families
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:20:38 UTC
04:20:38 KST

Families waiting for au pairs face uncertainty as visa delays continue
Johanna Paulina Gorek postponed university for a year and turned down a job at home in Germany to become an au pair in Australia.
But a slowdown of working holiday visa processing times is threatening her plans.
"I had already found a host family in Melbourne who had basically offered me a position, but eventually they decided to cancel because they did not want to wait longer for my visa," she told the ABC.
Ms Gorek said she applied for her visa on September 3 and had spent more than $1,500 on visa application and au pair agency fees.
She wanted to become an au pair to improve her English and learn Australian culture, she said.
"It's so disappointing to still be waiting and not knowing exactly when I will be able to go," she said.
"I'm also worried that the longer I have to wait, the fewer opportunities I will have to find a suitable host family."
The Department of Home Affairs began prioritising processing of onshore visa applications in July.
A spokesperson said it slowed down processing first-year working holiday visas and prioritised second and third-year visas "to better manage demand and ensure the sustainability of the program over the long term".
"The government will now manage first-year WHMs (working holiday makers) processing to deliver an average processing time of approximately three months," the spokesperson said.
"This balanced approach will provide greater control over the impact of WHMs on NOM [net overseas migration], while supporting regional labour market needs."
The department's website recommends that visa applicants not "book flights or make travel, work or study commitments until their visa has been granted".
Au pairs are typically young overseas visitors who live with an Australian host family and help with child care and light household tasks, in exchange for accommodation, meals, weekly pocket money and a cultural exchange experience.
Cultural Au Pair Association of Australia (CAPAA) president Anna Prasad said that before July applications for the working holiday visa (subclass 417) were granted "in a matter of hours".
Ms Prasad, who is also the inbound manager for the American Institute for Foreign Study (AIFS) which facilitates au pair placements, said visas for "hundreds" of AIFS' au pairs had been delayed since July.
She said "high season" for au pairs usually started in July, with 30 to 40 arranged through AIFS arriving on working holiday visas each week, but only 10 to 12 had arrived between then and the second week of September.
"Families are waiting for their au pairs to arrive and they have no other option in some cases," she said.
The number of au pairs who come to Australia is unknown due to the informal nature of the sector, but Ms Prasad said at least 500 were connected with Australian families by the AIFS each year.
Ms Prasad said the processing delays did not put Australia in a good light.
"It's a nightmare,"
"We are starting to see au pairs pull out of placements, choosing to travel to other countries instead for their gap year experience."
Filling gaps in child care
Backpackers' contribution to child care was "overlooked", said Western Sydney University heritage and tourism studies lecturer Donna James.
"A lot of working holiday-makers are filling gaps in child care, particularly for families in remote, regional areas where child care is already very inaccessible,"
"But also for people who are working unusual hours."
Dr James added that au pairs cost less and offered more flexibility than nannies.
However, Migrant Justice Institute co-executive director Laurie Berg said a paper she co-authored in 2018 found that most au pairs worked long hours, were doing work beyond child care and did not have a genuine cultural experience in Australia.
"We need much more detailed official guidance on the rights of au pairs," she said.
"It's really important there are stronger regulations and processes in place to ensure that all parties are safe, secure, and are meeting their legal obligations."
Backpacker visa delays affect families
Some families find au pairs indispensable.
In Perth, university lecturer Renae Barker has had to take annual leave to look after her children while she waits for her family's new au pair to arrive.
"We line up our au pairs, three, four months in advance," she said.
"But at the moment because of the slowdown in processing, we've ended up with a gap between au pairs."
Dr Barker, whose husband works fly-in, fly-out in the mining industry, said au pairs helped with school pick-up and drop-off, along with after-school activities.
She said they offered flexibility, as her job could "be very demanding and often time-sensitive", while her husband was away working for eight days at a time, followed by six days at home.
"We're going to have to pull the kids out of some of their therapies or some of their after-school activities because I can't actually get there,"
She added that an au pair offered more than just help, but also the opportunity for her children to learn about European culture, language and food.
'I feel sorry for making them wait'
Shodai Kitahama, from Japan, said he was still waiting for the working holiday visa that he lodged at the end of July.
"The hardest part for me is that my host family has been waiting for me for a long time,"
"I didn't think the visa process would take this long, so I feel sorry for making them wait."
Mr Kitahama said he wanted to come to Australia to improve his English and experience its culture.
He said the lack of updates on his application had caused him anxiety and made it difficult to make plans.
"I took a break from university and quit my job because I was preparing to go to Australia," he said.
"Right now I'm not working or studying, I'm just waiting to find out when I can leave."
