'US-style medicine model' as big pharma dispensing of GLP-1s condemned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:54:38 UTC
03:54:38 KST

Doctors condemn Eli Lilly move to dispense GLP-1 medication Mounjaro direct to door
In short:
Eli Lilly's new online platform LillyDirect will dispense certain medicines, starting with Mounjaro, directly to a patient's door.
Doctors and pharmacists have criticised the move, arguing it poses a risk to patient safety.
Eli Lilly has defended the online platform, saying it does not circumvent pharmacists or GPs, and will improve affordability and convenience for patients.
A move by a multi-billion-dollar global pharmaceutical company to bypass bricks and mortar pharmacies and deliver its GLP-1 medication Mounjaro directly to consumers' doors has been broadly condemned by doctors and pharmacists, who argue it poses a risk to patient safety.
Eli Lilly has announced its new online platform LillyDirect will dispense certain medicines, starting with tirzepatide, an injectable GLP-1 agonist sold as Mounjaro, which is used to treat conditions like type 2 diabetes and obesity.
Under the model, patients submit an e-script to LillyDirect from their doctor.
The script is then directed to an online third-party pharmacist to dispense, before it is delivered to the patient's home.
The pharmaceutical giant said the new platform allows patients to find competitive pricing without shopping around and does not replace the need for an independent doctor to prescribe the medication.
But Royal Australian College of GPs (RACGP) President Michael Wright said GLP-1 agonists were powerful medications with serious side effects, and needed proper oversight and continuity of care.
He said using online pharmacists to dispense the medication could remove a layer of protection for patients, noting many might already be using telehealth providers to access the e-script in the first place.
"What concerns me about this model is that potentially they can be prescribed in some situations and delivered by someone who doesn't actually have full access to your whole record and I think that really creates risks for patients," Dr Wright said.
The Pharmacy Guild of Australia and the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia said the model of care was "clinically inferior" and reduced opportunities for "face-to-face clinical interaction" where problems could be identified and addressed.
"This proposal is a concern to every Australian who values an independent and patient-focused healthcare system," Pharmacy Guild President Trent Twomey said.
"We should not allow the Americanisation of Australian healthcare."
Eli Lilly advertising online doctors for prescriptions
After protracted negotiations with the federal government, Eli Lilly announced in April it would not proceed with the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) listing process, airing a cluster of grievances including that the price Australia was willing to pay for the drug was too low.
As a result, Mounjaro can cost patients as much as $700 a month privately.
Eli Lilly is bound by competition law and is unable to say how much cheaper the medication is when sold through its platform.
However, social media users who have already begun using the service, which launched last week, have posted the medication costs as much as $50 less.
LillyDirect launched in the US in 2024 where consumers are connected directly with telehealth providers to get their prescription.
The Australian Eli Lilly website advertises two major telehealth providers including Juniper, which has previously been criticised by eating disorder experts for aggressive social media marketing of GLP-1 drugs.
Dr Wright said GLP-1 drugs were not suitable for everyone such as those with a history of eating disorders, and came with serious side effects such as the potential risks of suicidal thoughts and behaviours.
He also noted there had been serious consequences when telehealth providers were not able to access a patient's full history, such as the fatal overdose of a young woman in Melbourne, who convinced multiple telehealth providers she needed large qualities of her medication and stockpiled it.
The case prompted the federal government to introduce sweeping changes to force prescribers to record all medicines-related information under a new national record.
The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency also recently vowed to crack down on reckless prescribing of drugs such as GLP-1s, arguing some telehealth practitioners had "departed from established professional standards."
'An interest in keeping people on the medicine'
Barbara Mintzes from Sydney University's school of pharmacology said online distribution platforms run by pharmaceutical companies were problematic.
"It's putting patients who are using a company's medicine directly in contact with the company that's marketing that medicine and they are a producer of pharmaceuticals, they're not a health care provider — that's quite a different role," Professor Mintzes said.
"Lilly has an interest in keeping people on the medicine that is being prescribed."
The company's experiment with a new distribution model comes as its revenue last quarter blew past estimates, increasing by 48 per cent.
The growth was primarily driven by its injectable weight loss drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound.
In a statement, a Lilly Australia spokesperson said the move would improve affordability and convenience for Australians, arguing Lilly Direct operated within existing regulatory frameworks.
"Australian doctors prescribe the medicine, Australian pharmacists review and dispense prescriptions, and Australian healthcare, pharmacy, privacy and regulatory requirements apply at every stage," they said.
"The LillyDirect platform does not circumvent the role of pharmacists. A registered Australian pharmacist reviews the prescription, dispenses the prescribed medicine and is available to provide advice and counselling to the patient."

Russia warns NATO of possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off
Moscow claims that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade in the Baltic Sea.
Russia has warned NATO it is prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempts to cut off the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, according to a diplomatic document sent to member states.
The diplomatic memo sent on Wednesday claimed Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad”.
NATO’s response came through its Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said that NATO is a defensive alliance and that Russia should “stop the nuclear threats”, calling the document unhelpful.
Rutte also downplayed the seriousness of the threat, saying that “Putin knows that he can never win” in a direct escalation with NATO.
Bordered by Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members, the Russian territory of Kaliningrad sits on the Baltic Sea. The region serves as a major military outpost, housing Russia’s Baltic fleet and nuclear-ready Iskander missile systems.
The exchange comes more than four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine, as tensions increasingly spill into neighbouring states.
Poland has heightened its air defence posture following alleged incursions into its airspace in recent weeks, while Danish authorities said a Russian warship fired two flares near a Danish military helicopter over the Baltic Sea two weeks ago.

ECB President Lagarde signals possible departure months before term ends in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

03:52:39 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde on Wednesday said she could leave office a few months before her eight-year term ends in October 2027 but stressed that she has announced no specific plans.
In an interview with French newspaper La Croix, published on the bank's website, Lagarde addressed speculation about her future and the possibility of running in France's presidential election next year.
She said she did not rule out leaving before the end of her term, but any early departure would be limited to a few months.
"I will still be here in 2027," she said, adding that such a departure would not represent a major upheaval.
Asked whether she would seek the French presidency, Lagarde replied: "That would not be a good idea at all."
The 70-year-old cited the vitality, energy and strength required for the role, alongside the personal sacrifices such a commitment would entail.
She emphasized that her current responsibility was to serve the European public interest.
France faces serious debt challenge
Turning to France's finances, Lagarde warned that public debt approaching 120% of gross domestic product without a clear trajectory to bring it under control constituted a serious problem.
Restoring confidence would require a credible path, shared commitment and reforms, she said.
Lagarde called for simplifying administrative and regulatory frameworks, pursuing labor market reforms and addressing pressures on the pension system stemming from rising life expectancy.
She said the pension model established in the past could not continue indefinitely as people live longer, underscoring the need to adapt it to demographic changes.
European financial system more resilient
Despite those concerns, Lagarde offered a more positive assessment of Europe's financial resilience, saying the financial system was considerably stronger than during the crises of 2008 and 2011.
She pointed to Greece, Portugal and Ireland as examples of countries that endured painful crises, repaired their public finances and subsequently returned to growth that often exceeded the average.
Their experience demonstrated the importance of restoring confidence through credible fiscal plans and sustained reforms, she said.

Indian designers making themselves ‘louder’ – Kanika Goyal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:51:18 UTC
03:51:18 KST

Indian designers making themselves ‘louder’ – Kanika Goyal
Indian designers are moving beyond manufacturing and craft work for global brands and are increasingly presenting their own collections on the international stage, fashion designer Kanika Goyal told RT at the BRICS+ Fashion Summit in Moscow. 
India has long been an important source of craftsmanship and production for the global fashion industry, with much of that work taking place behind the scenes. But a new generation of homegrown labels is increasingly creating the finished product and taking its own design identity overseas. 
“We’ve always been on the back end of things and walking behind the scenes,” Goyal told RT, but said Indian designers are now emerging “in a much louder way,” drawing greater attention to where the craft and techniques behind their work originate. Emerging talent is increasingly “creating the final product” and “putting it on global stage,” she added, saying that “recognition really matters.”
The shift comes as India’s textile exports rose 16.1% year-on-year in August, with ready-made garment exports up 6.1%, according to the Ministry of Textiles. 
The change goes beyond India. Designers from BRICS and other emerging markets are already building strong domestic businesses while reaching audiences outside their home countries. For Goyal, this is less a future Global South-led fashion revolution than a shift that is already underway. 
Russia is among the markets Indian labels could explore more directly. Goyal’s brand previously supplied Russian stores through a Paris-based sales agency before 2022. Shipping, customs, and finding the right partners now influence how designers approach the market, but she sees greater business between the two countries as a possibility.
Goyal’s Arc Echo collection was showcased at Moscow Fashion Week on Sunday. The current edition, which runs through October 1, features more than 350 designers from over ten countries. In 2025, the Fashion Design Council of India presented CoEK-Khadi India and Samant Chauhan at the event, while Russian label Hatsibana later appeared at Lakme Fashion Week in New Delhi under an FDCI–Moscow Fashion Week exchange.
Stronger links between emerging markets could eventually allow designers and buyers to work with each other without routing business through established fashion centers such as Paris, Goyal told RT India. That will, however, require these countries to establish effective commercial structures that make shipping, buying and cross-border partnerships easier.
Social media is also weakening the traditional barriers to global visibility. Designers from smaller cities and countries can now put collections directly in front of international audiences and editors, giving them routes into the industry that previously depended much more heavily on established fashion capitals.

Iranian woman on death row pleads for international help

Breadcrumb
'Do something,' begs Iranian woman after death sentence over protests
An Iranian woman sentenced to death over protests earlier this year has begged the international community to save her life and others facing the death penalty, according to an audio message from prison shared by rights groups on Wednesday.
The plea by Mahboubeh Shahbani, 33, from her jail in the eastern city of Mashhad comes as the authorities executed two more men on charges linked to the mass January protests.
Rights groups accuse Iran of ramping up executions of high-profile prisoners in a bid to intimidate the population and ensure there is no repeat of the protests, which preceded the US-Israeli war against the Islamic republic that erupted on February 28.
"The sentence handed down to me shows that many others are in danger of execution," Shahbani said in a telephone call from the phone for prisoners in Mashhad's Vakilabad prison after her lawyer informed her of the death sentence on September 26.
"I am not worried about myself. I am worried for the others whose sentences have been upheld," she said in the call, an audio recording of which was shared by Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) and US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
It was not immediately possible to verify the authenticity of the message. It was punctuated by an automatic voice saying the caller was a prisoner, which is usual practice for calls from Iranian prisons.
"I call on everyone -- the public, the UN, human rights organisations. Not just for me but for all the others whose sentences have been upheld and who have spent months sleeping in fear and stress at night.
"I call on them to do something," she said.
'I beg everyone'
According to the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), Shahbani was convicted of carrying out actions "to strengthen Israel, the US, and individuals affiliated with opposition groups" in the protests.
But IHR said she had merely used her motorcycle to transport injured protesters. It added she had been moved to solitary confinement after making the call from prison.
"Conditions are extremely bad for the prisoners given the pressures they exert on us," Shahbani said in the message. "I beg everyone to do whatever is in their power."
Iran's judiciary earlier announced the hanging in Mashhad of Ali Hemmati and Majid Nik-Andish on charges linked to the deaths of four members of the security forces in the protests.
According to IHR, since wartime executions resumed in March, 31 people, all men, have been hanged in connection with the January protests and two in connection with the 2022 protests. Dozens more are at risk of execution.
The CHRI said it believed a total of nine women across Iran are at risk of execution on political and security charges.

Air Force Names 7 to Vie for New MMA Drone Program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:49:15 UTC
03:49:15 KST

The Air Force and the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit have narrowed the field to seven companies which will be invited to compete to develop low-cost, semi-autonomous drones to succeed the MQ-9A Reaper, multiple sources confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero all made the cut to continue to develop their candidates for the Massed Modular Aircraft. The companies got the word Sept. 30.
The Air Force and DIU did not immediately respond to queries. Spokespeople from each of the companies either declined to comment or did not respond to queries. It is unclear how many companies submitted proposals, and therefore how many firms were cut from the competition.
An industry source said each company will now submit a proposal to build a prototype MMA.
The Air Force wants to field 500 MMAs by 2032, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
DIU—an acquisition office created to tap into commercial and non-traditional suppliers—sought on July 7 proposals for cheap, attritable drones that could take on the MQ-9’s trademark missions of persistent intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and strike. The Air Force soon confirmed it was working with DIU on the concept.
The solicitation followed the loss of dozens of MQ-9s in operations against Iran earlier this year. DIU said at the time that the military’s reliance on “exquisite” aircraft that cost $30 million or more per tail has become “unsustainable against adversaries utilizing layered defenses enabled by increasingly low-cost antiaircraft capabilities.”
The MQ-9As that were lost did not cost that much, but General Atomics no longer makes that model and instead is offering a larger MQ-9B that can approach or exceed the $30 million level, depending on how it is equipped.
MMA is aiming for a lower price point. DIU’s solicitation sought drones that could fly together in groups large enough to overwhelm an enemy, even if several were shot down, while also forcing the enemy to expend precious anti-aircraft munitions. The Air Force must be able to affordably replace aircraft lost without busting the budget.
Air Force leaders said in a Sept. 3 briefing that they expect to pay about $10 million per MMA airframe, plus whatever sensors or other capabilities are added to it. During that briefing, Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said Secretary Meink pushed to accelerate the MMA fielding schedule in the wake of the Iran losses. Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel, DIU’s military deputy, told reporters that the Pentagon wants to see a prototype within a year of issuing a contract, and field it at scale as soon as 2029.
Responding to the summer solicitation, industry rapidly moved to pitch their concepts. General Atomics pitched a new drone called Wildfire that could carry at least two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, four Joint Strike Missiles, or a similar combination of heavy stand-off weapons.
Swarm Aero, a California startup, proposed a new Group 5 drone dubbed Gamera, and displayed a full-scale model at the Air, Space & Cyber conference.

====================================================================================================

A political dynasty? Why the Bolsonaro family dominates Brazil’s right wing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:48:32 UTC
03:48:32 KST

Sao Paulo, Brazil – Much has changed since the far-right army captain Jair Bolsonaro won Brazil's presidency in 2018.
Last year, the former president was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. In 2023, he was barred from holding public office for eight years after a court determined he abused his political office.
He is currently banned from using social media. His last post was published in July 2025.
And yet, Bolsonaro has forged a powerful political dynasty that is on the verge of returning to power in Brazil's October presidential election.
His eldest son, 45-year-old Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, is in a statistical tie with the race's incumbent, left-leaning President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
A September 24 poll released by the public opinion firm Datafolha showed Lula with a slim lead in a simulated run-off, earning 47 percent support to Flavio's 45 percent, well within the margin of error.
Other pollsters predict an even narrower gap between the two frontrunners.
Like his father, Flavio has faced investigation and scandal. But experts say the Bolsonaro family has endured as a political force in part by harnessing decades of frustration with Lula's Workers' Party (PT).
That resentment, in turn, has transformed into a potent election-season brand.
“There is a hyperfocus on Lula and the PT, who for over two decades have been branded by many conservatives as the ones solely responsible for rampant corruption,” said political scientist Paulo Roberto Souza of the Democracy in Check Institute, an independent research nonprofit.
Embracing 'antipetismo'
Analysts told Al Jazeera that the Bolsonaro family's electoral strength does not come from a base of hardcore supporters.
Bolsonaristas, after all, are only estimated to comprise between 15 and 25 percent of Brazil's electorate. Instead, experts credit "antipetismo" — a trend of hostility against Lula's PT movement — with fuelling the Bolsonaro family's rise to political power.
The PT has won all but one of the last six presidential elections in Brazil. The only exception has been Jair Bolsonaro himself, with his 2018 win.
Jair Bolsonaro did not invent "antipetismo", according to Mario Sergio Lima, a Brazil analyst at Medley Advisors, a political advisory firm.
But his arrival as a presidential frontrunner in 2018 gave the movement a political identity, Lima said. The elder Bolsonaro was able to “condense anti-PT sentiment into his own persona”.
Lima predicted Flavio would likewise benefit from the wave of "antipetismo" when he competes against Lula in the October 4 general election.
“It is easy for anyone who is already against the PT to vote for Flavio or anyone who carries the Bolsonaro name, because Jair managed to personify a feeling that already existed in Brazilian society,” Lima explained.
A family affair
Formerly a long-serving member of Brazil's Chamber of Deputies, Jair Bolsonaro has become the fulcrum for a political movement based around his own nuclear family.
Each of his four sons has embarked on a political career. In October's general election, his second oldest son Carlos is running for a Senate seat. His youngest son Jair Renan is competing for the Chamber of Deputies.
Meanwhile, his third son, Eduardo, moved to the United States in 2025 to lobby President Donald Trump for help with his father’s trial.
He lost his congressional seat that December because of repeated absences, and in June, a Brazilian court ruled that Eduardo's efforts amounted to illegal foreign interference.
Even former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro commands her own political clout, enjoying immense popularity among Brazil's conservative evangelical Christians.
In the lead-up to the 2026 election season, Michelle was floated as a possible right-wing candidate for the presidency. But in December, Jair offered a jailhouse endorsement to his son Flavio.
Though imprisoned, the ex-president remains a powerful figure in the Liberal Party, a right-wing juggernaut.
Columnist Fabio Zanini, a political analyst for Brazil's biggest newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo, described the Bolsonaro family as a nest of competing interests.
“It’s a dysfunctional family. They often fight among themselves,” he said.
But their disparate political activities have created what Zanini calls a “franchise", with influence across different spheres of Brazilian politics.
Flavio himself has sought to channel his father on the campaign trail. In early September, with less than a month remaining until the first round of voting, Flavio rallied on the streets of Juiz de Fora, an industrial city in the country's southeast.
The location was symbolic: His father survived a near-fatal stabbing in downtown Juiz de Fora during his successful 2018 presidential bid.
Flavio used his visit to retrace his father's route, saying he had returned to “complete the journey” Jair was unable to finish.
Overshadowing the conservative field
The right-wing senator was not always his father's heir apparent.
After Jair Bolsonaro’s 27-year prison sentence, Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas was widely rumoured to be a new standard-bearer for the Brazilian right.
Freitas, after all, had served in Jair's cabinet and had comfortably won a 2022 election to lead Brazil’s richest and most populous state. He had also expressed an interest in making a run for the presidency himself.
But Zanini believes that challenging the Bolsonaro family for Brazil's presidency would have come at a steep cost for Freitas, who ultimately sought re-election as governor instead.
“Cutting ties with the Bolsonaros would have been political suicide for Tarcisio. He would have been labelled a traitor or worse,” said Zanini. “So someone like him had no alternative but to back Flavio.”
Other conservative presidential candidates remain far behind Flavio in the pre-election polls.
Combined, figures such as Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema are polling with less than 10 percent support ahead of the first round of voting on Sunday.
Still, the race is expected to proceed to a run-off between Lula and Flavio, with neither candidate projected to win an outright majority in the first round.
While Flavio and Lula are clear leaders in the race, a large number of Brazilian voters have expressed strong disapproval of their campaigns.
A September poll from the research firm AtlasIntel and the publication Bloomberg found that 51.6 percent of respondents said they would refuse to vote for Lula, while 50.6 percent said the same for Flavio.
“Neither of the two main candidates are particularly convincing,” Zanini said of the withering rejection rates.
Instead, he noted that, for many of Brazil’s conservative voters, Flavio's main credential is that “he is seen as the guy who can defeat Lula".
A September surprise
Flavio's presidential ambitions, however, have faced a new obstacle in the final weeks of the election.
Earlier this month, the Supreme Court unsealed documents revealing that Flavio is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and the illegal transfer of funds abroad.
The case revolves around Flavio's interactions with Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced former banker accused of perpetrating one of the largest fraud schemes in Brazilian history.
Brazilian media has reported that Flavio negotiated with Vorcaro to obtain millions in funding for a film about his father.
Flavio, however, has denied wrongdoing and denounced the investigation as politically motivated.
Should Flavio overcome the allegations and win the presidency, Lima — the political analyst at Medley Advisors — says his victory would “definitively cement Bolsonarismo as the undisputed leader of the Brazilian right”.
But even a loss might not break the Bolsonaro family's hold on Brazil’s right wing.
“Even if he loses, it will be by a slim margin, and he’d come out of this election strengthened, potentially setting himself up for another run in 2030," said Zanini, the columnist.
“It would be a defeat for Bolsonarismo, sure, but it wouldn’t be a death blow.”

Unknown

2026-09-30
18:48:09 UTC
03:48:09 KST

analysis
Chalmers promised action on inflation and productivity. The scorecard on both is grim
On the morning after last year's landslide Labor election win, Jim Chalmers declared a shift in priorities for the government's second term.
"The first term was primarily inflation without forgetting productivity," the treasurer told Insiders. "The second term will be primarily productivity without forgetting inflation."
At the midway point of this term, the scorecard on both is grim.
As Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock put it this week: "Inflation is too high and has been driven by domestic capacity pressures."
As for productivity, Bullock was even more blunt: "Productivity is doing nothing."
In response, both the treasurer and prime minister have spent the week on the defensive, highlighting their various efforts to both tackle inflation and kickstart productivity, pinning blame on the war in the Middle East, denying any contradiction with the Reserve Bank, and pointing out where the government is trying to rein in spending, only to be frustrated by the Coalition.
None of it is likely to satisfy anxious households.
What Labor desperately needs is some better news on inflation to restore confidence.
A glimmer of hope?
Chalmers saw a glimmer of hope in yesterday's data.
While annual headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent, largely thanks to higher fuel prices, and the annual underlying rate remained stubbornly stuck at 3.6 per cent, the monthly numbers for August told a slightly better story. Both headline and underlying inflation for the month came down.
Whether the treasurer is right to be optimistic about the monthly numbers or not, the point is he felt vindicated. He argued the data backed his claim about the Iran war being the chief driver of the recent inflation spike.
He showed no signs of changing course on the government's spending plans.
Indeed, Anthony Albanese was yesterday flagging more cost-of-living support measures would be announced in the mid-year budget update in December.
That would be on top of the list of spending measures to deliver free TAFE, free visits to the GP, cheaper medicines, student debt relief and so on.
All politically popular with the various beneficiaries, but all contributing to demand in the economy.
The government insists it has "found room" for the extra spending through cuts elsewhere, but the budget remains stuck in a structural deficit.
The temptation for Labor to offer even more household relief at the end of the year and no doubt more tax cuts before the next election will be strong.
Loading
A new layer of difficulty for Labor
One Nation is already feeding on the grievances of frustrated voters on the right. Now a new Greens leader has emerged on the left with an energetic and overwhelming focus on the cost of living.
After defeating Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young in a contested ballot, unprecedented for the party, David Shoebridge laid out his priorities.
It was all about the hip pocket. Climate change and the Middle East barely rated a mention.
"Things have got harder, much, much harder, for ordinary Australians," Shoebridge said. "We are not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them."
The new Greens leader will be out to prove himself and unite his team. His focus on the plight of stressed younger Australians and his determination to blame Labor for their woes presents a new layer of difficulty for the government.
When Jim Chalmers promised a shift from inflation to productivity, the hope was that the first problem was largely under control.
Halfway through the term, it's clear neither objective is where the government wants it to be, even if it can point with some justification to factors beyond its control.
But it's equally clear the government is not for shifting course.
As political pressure mounts from both the left and right, the risk is that pursuing more short-term relief will only make the long-term challenge harder.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

RT examines human cost of US intervention in Iraq (VIDEO)
Unknown

2026-09-30
18:45:27 UTC

RT examines human cost of US intervention in Iraq (VIDEO)
The Pentagon announced on Wednesday that the last American troops had left Iraq, more than two decades after the US invaded the country.
A handover ceremony at Erbil Air Base in the northern Kurdish region marked the end of the US military presence.
The administration of then-President George W. Bush justified the 2003 invasion by claiming that longtime Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. Washington never substantiated the allegations, while Iraq descended into a quagmire of violence involving Sunni and Shia Muslims as well as Kurds.
US forces pulled out in 2011 amid a slew of war crimes allegations, including the killing of unarmed civilians.
According to some estimates, more than a million Iraqis lost their lives as a result of the conflict, with millions more displaced.
Left in disarray with a weak central government and security forces, Iraq became fertile ground for Islamist militant groups. The crisis came to a head with the emergence of Islamic State, which seized around a third of Iraqi territory and spread into several neighboring countries, proclaiming a ‘caliphate’. Its militants massacred those they deemed insufficiently Muslim, as well as Christians and members of other religious minorities.
Washington intervened again in 2014 with a deployment code-named Operation Inherent Resolve.
RT correspondent Steve Sweeny took a look back at an intervention that upended the delicate balance between Iraq’s sectarian and ethnic groups, plunging the country into years of chaos and violence.

2026-09-30
18:42:31 UTC
03:42:31 KST

Talks to end the Drumcree parade dispute are on a knife-edge after Jamie Bryson, the legal adviser of the Orange Order, said it would “not surrender” to a deal proposed by the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant.
With echoes of the former Democratic Unionist leader Ian Paisley’s “no surrender” mantra of the 1980s, Bryson told supporters in Portadown that Bryant could keep his deal.
He said he had the authority of the Orange Order’s district master to say: “The Portadown District will not surrender the fundamental principle, not now, not last week, not next week, not ever – ever.”
Bryson said the Portadown Orangemen would not “sell out” even if they were offered £20m.
Government sources said they expected talks to continue on Thursday and possibly into Friday.
Earlier today, Bryant said an end to the dispute was “tantalisingly close”, as the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition signalled it would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order also did so.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the nationalist group, said on Wednesday afternoon that he had been through the document drawn up by Bryant and his team.
“Obviously, I can’t divulge what is in it,” he said after a meeting with Bryant. “But if it’s accepted by the Orange Order, it will be accepted by us.”
But after a second meeting with Bryant on Wednesday evening, Bryson rubbished the residents’ leader’s words.
“Do not be panicked by Breandán Mac Cionnaith coming out and saying there is a document on the table. The document can stay on the table because it won’t be accepted by the Portadown District.”
Earlier in the day, Bryant urged parties to “search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise” to break the deadlock, after meeting with both sides at Hillsborough Castle, just outside Belfast.
On Tuesday, Mac Cionnaith had described mediation over the dispute as “dead in the water”.
Bryant said on Wednesday: “I would just appeal to everybody – including the wider community, not just the people I have been meeting in the room – that people are going to have to search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise if we’re going to get to a successful long-term resolution of the situation.”
He added that he and his team were “working flat-out to try and get to a successful resolution, and I think that is tantalisingly close if everybody can just go that extra mile”.
Politicians and others had warned that any parade down Garvaghy Road risked returning Northern Ireland to the bleak days of the Troubles.
But on Sunday a court of appeal overturned a high court injunction banning the Orange Order from processing through the mainly nationalist area, leading to a four-day standoff that has heightened sectarian tensions.
Attempts to march down Garvaghy Road were blocked by protesters, and a small group of Orange Order members has remained at Drumcree church, the starting point of the parade, vowing not to leave until the parade goes ahead.
Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of Northern Ireland’s police force, said the protest stopping the parade was unlawful, and that a major criminal investigation into the blockade was under way. He warned that mob rule must not be allowed to win, and that he would continue to seek a way to facilitate the Orange Order march.
The first minister of Northern Ireland, Michelle O’Neill, visited Garvaghy Road on Wednesday, despite accusations by unionist leaders that she had broken the law by supporting protesters when she went there on Sunday.
Asked if she had broken the law, O’Neill said: “I accept that I made a choice, a choice to stand with the residents of the Garvaghy Road. It is a choice I will continue to make.
“This is very clearly a community which feels under siege, a community that has been put in reverse and retraumatised in terms of what happened 28 years ago.”
The parade was given the go-ahead by the Northern Ireland Parades Commission on Friday, ending a 28-year ban on the Orange Order marching in Garvaghy Road. At a special sitting of the high court the next day, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, but that was overturned on appeal in the small hours of Sunday morning.
Critics of the Parades Commission’s decision included the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, who called it “incomprehensible and wrong”, given that the march prompted some of the most serious violence seen in Northern Ireland in the late 1990s – including the murders of three children – and nearly derailed the 1998 peace process.
On Tuesday, the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition lodged a fresh legal challenge against the march, this time arguing the Parades Commission had “materially misdirected itself” by using historical police assessments over the risk of violence as opposed to a future-looking risk assessment.

Burc Eruygur
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Russia summoned Denmark’s ambassador to Moscow on Wednesday because of an incident earlier this month in which a Russian frigate allegedly fired flares at a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea.
The Foreign Ministry said that it lodged a protest with the ambassador regarding the “unprofessional and provocative” actions of the Danish helicopter directed at the Soobrazitelny corvette of Russia’s Baltic Fleet, which it said took place earlier in neutral waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea.
The corresponding statement said the helicopter made a “dangerous” approach toward the corvette, "threatening navigational safety" among others, and that all warnings transmitted regarding the helicopter's altitude were ignored.
“To draw attention, two signal flares were fired from the corvette in a direction away from the helicopter. The aircraft subsequently ceased its provocative actions and departed the area. These facts are confirmed by objective monitoring data and are indisputable,” said the statement.
It also said the ambassador was informed that Moscow viewed the maneuvers by the helicopter as a “gross violation” of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
“Emphasis was placed on the unacceptability and absurdity of the accusations leveled against Russia by the Danish authorities regarding the incident – accusations that are entirely baseless,” it said.
The statement added that amid heightened tensions in the Baltic region “directly linked to increased anti-Russian military activity by NATO,” it was stressed that a recurrence of the “reckless” actions could lead to escalation and create the risk of a serious incident.
On Sept. 15, the Danish Defense Ministry said that a Fennec helicopter belonging to the Air Force was fired at with flares "in connection with routine photo coverage of a Russian frigate, which was in international waters off Gedser," a coastal town on the island of Falster.
The ministry said the Russian frigate fired two flares at the helicopter during the incident on Sept. 14, with one passing "within a short distance" of the aircraft.
Meanwhile, Denmark also summoned Russia's ambassador in the country over the incident, who later told Russian media that Moscow would thoroughly investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.
In a later statement on Sept. 16, the Russian Defense Ministry said the incident occurred as the corvette operated in international waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea, and that its crew detected the helicopter as it approached the vessel and “failed to respond to calls" made via an international communication channel.
"The corvette's commander made the decision to fire two red signal flares to prevent a provocation by the Danish helicopter, after which the helicopter left the area," it added.
The incident off Denmark came amid escalating tensions across Europe over a series of alleged sabotage attacks and airspace violations that European countries have blamed on Russia.

Greens leader David Shoebridge wants to woo the same angry voters as One Nation — but from the left
The elevation of NSW senator David Shoebridge to the Greens' top job is the clearest indication the party is prepared to swing further to the populist left and fight harder to demolish Labor, especially in its inner-city heartland.
He wasn't the only contender to lead the party — Sarah Hanson-Young and Mehreen Faruqi also put their hands up for the top job.
Faruqi is reportedly divisive inside the party and Hanson-Young, despite being the longest-serving Greens senator, is seen as too moderate, according to sources.
Greens leadership talks are usually done under a cloak of secrecy, driven by consensus. But today's contest broke convention.
Greens whip Nick McKim read out the results of the leader and deputy leadership ballots, a sign the Greens have heard the concerns that they are too secretive.
Transparency can't be something you bang on about if you don't reveal your cards. And the cards they have revealed tell you everything about how they believe politics needs to be played.
Shoebridge moves to the left
The Greens have been frustrated at an inability to capitalise on public anger at the big end of town, and that One Nation have been the only big winners, despite a collapse in support for the two big parties.
The Greens want to replicate the success of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's progressive campaign.
Shoebridge may not have the charisma of Mamdani (let's be honest, few do), but he came straight out of the blocks with over-the-top rhetoric indicating he would focus the party's direction on the cost of living and a strident left-wing economic agenda.
After more than a decade in NSW politics, he entered federal parliament when the Albanese government was elected in 2022 and is known for his relationship with hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon. He holds the Greens' defence and foreign affairs portfolios.
The Greens have long had a tension between the so-called watermelons — those who are more economically focused, old-school lefties — and those who are a product of the environmental movement.
The Greens are desperate to seize the moment rather than follow the Australian Democrats' path, a past Senate balance-of-power party that collapsed because of a deeply unpopular policy compromise on the Goods and Services Tax and ugly infighting.
This moment will test the party. Can they stay together and unite around a more radical leadership?
Loading
Path is harder for Labor
Yesterday Shoebridge vowed to take the fight to both Labor and One Nation and positioned the left-wing party as needing to become the alternative for a growing base of disaffected and raging voters.
His framing is all about Labor and One Nation.
Shoebridge said voters wanted drastic political change, not gradual reform.
"That is the dead politics of Labor, it's the dead politics of the Coalition, and when you really test it, it's the dead politics of One Nation," he said.
"People are desperate for material change. They don't want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know isn't going to change their lives. They want to take on the vested interests."
In a social media statement, Faruqi said she was disappointed by the result.
"Globally, people are struggling against genocide, wars, surging fascism and the twin crises of capitalism making working life too expensive and climate breakdown threatening our future," she said.
"This struggle calls for bold politics and radical action. I did not stand again for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team."
Under Larissa Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and Labor's changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. She vowed to be the leader who would get "shit done".
Shoebridge wants to hold Labor's feet to the fire. He will be a thorn in Labor's side rather than a deal maker.
The government's pathway through the Senate just got a whole lot harder.

The US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers.
The investigation by the Federal Trade Commission is the first official US enforcement action that delves into rogue AI agents, following a surge in incidents first reported in July that have stoked fears among the public that uncontrolled AI could one day harm humans.
The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research group Metr, according to multiple reports.
Anthropic and OpenAI have used Metr to conduct independent investigations into security incidents involving their agentic AI technology.

Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, had concerns about the companies before AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. The incident, in which OpenAI agents probed the AI coding hub for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack, sparked global discussion of the issue.
Ferguson suggested last week in an interview that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any harm they cause. The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI, Ferguson said at an event in Austin.
The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to take reasonable measures to secure consumers’ data.
Donald Trump met with top AI executives on Tuesday, where the companies agreed to establish voluntary standards.
Trump has repeatedly called fears about AI a hoax as he seeks to prioritize US dominance in the technology over regulation. At the same time, he has also said the government can use existing laws against AI companies for any harm they may cause.

Burnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.
Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”
The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.
Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.
Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.
On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.
Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.
Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.
The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.
In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.
No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it.
Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.
But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday welcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.
He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”
An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”
Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goods out of certain supply chains on the continent.
No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London receives signals that there could be an accommodation.
Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding the summit on 20 November.
One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.
A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.

====================================================================================================

Flydubai terror attempt brings to mind the hijackings of 1970s in Israeli consciousness - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:32:43 UTC
03:32:43 KST

For a tense stretch on Wednesday morning, the news carried Israelis back to an older chapter of terror.
Not October 7. Not the bus and café bombings of the Second Intifada. Further back: to the aircraft hijackings of the 1970s, when a flight carrying Israelis could become a hostage crisis and an entire country would wait anxiously to learn where the plane had landed and what would happen to those aboard.
Dawson’s Field in Jordan. Sabena. Entebbe. Names that older Israelis need little explanation for, and that younger Israelis know from the history books.
Then came Wednesday’s alerts, in rapid succession: a flydubai plane en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv transmitted an emergency signal associated with hijacking. The plane changed course in midair. Israeli fighter jets were scrambled.
Suddenly, a routine flight home became the focus of national attention.
Israelis followed updates with bated breath, they were 'our passengers'
Where was the plane? Who was controlling it? Had someone seized it? Were the passengers safe?
Israelis followed the updates with bated breath. Those with relatives or friends aboard faced their own immediate terror. Others needed no personal connection. A plane carrying Israelis, in distress somewhere over the region, was enough.
Each update mattered. A report that contact had been lost deepened the anxiety; the first indications that the plane was not hijacked offered hope.
Then came the news everyone had been waiting for some 90 long minutes: the aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were safe.
Relief.
The first reports suggested an altercation between the pilots rather than a hijacking. That offered further reassurance: perhaps this frightening episode would turn out to have an explanation other than another attempt at the wholesale murder of Israelis.
But subsequent accounts suggested something much darker, and Israeli officials increasingly described the incident as an attempted terrorist attack, with the Omani co-pilot suspected of stabbing the Indian captain and trying to crash the aircraft with all aboard, 9/11 style.
Alongside those reports, however, came accounts of remarkable resourcefulness. Israeli passengers and other crew members had intervened and subdued the suspected attacker. They averted disaster even as the aircraft plunged.
They had refused to remain passive while their lives, and the lives of everyone around them, were in danger.
That brought pride alongside relief. “How Israeli,” many undoubtedly thought.
The older hijacking stories are remembered largely through the commandos who ultimately rescued the hostages. Wednesday’s emerging story centered on passengers and crew helping save themselves, while the emergency was still unfolding in the air.
Ordinary people rose to meet extraordinary danger
Ordinary people on an ordinary journey home had found themselves facing an extraordinary danger. They rose to meet it.
Clips circulated of passengers clapping and singing “Am Yisrael Chai” (the People of Israel live) after the plane landed in Saudi Arabia. The song expressed what many watching at home felt as well: joy that they were alive, pride that passengers had acted, and gratitude that the morning ended in celebration rather than mourning.
The relief extended well beyond the cabin.
Israel is a small country, and in moments like these it feels smaller still. People who have never met became “our passengers.” Their danger was followed on phones across the country. Their survival was a national relief.
That does not erase the country’s divisions. Indeed, by early afternoon, the incident was already being drawn into arguments about the election and the prime minister’s security warnings.
But before that came a simpler, shared response: let them be safe. And then, thank God, they are.
Crucial questions remained on Wednesday about vetting processes for pilots flying to Israel and the sequence of events in the cockpit. False reports and rumors spread quickly. The entire incident will require a thorough investigation.
But the passengers who overcame the co-pilot did not have the luxury of waiting for certainty before acting. Nor could they wait, as in the 1970s, for commandos to come to the rescue. They acted with extraordinary courage and resourcefulness.
Another striking difference from the hijacking era was the geography.
The aircraft was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, a route made possible by the Abraham Accords and normalization between Israel and the United Arab Emirates. It landed in Saudi Arabia, with which Israel still has no formal diplomatic relations.
An Israeli journey home through Dubai is now part of the region’s regular daily life. That would have been difficult to imagine during the era whose memories resurfaced on Wednesday.
Yet the limits of that regional transformation were also apparent. The Saudi authorities refused to permit an Israeli civilian aircraft to collect the passengers. Instead, another flydubai aircraft was sent, a prospect that - understandably, given the ordeal they had just endured - spooked some passengers.
The safe landing in Saudi Arabia was welcome. But the difficulty of arranging their return reminded everyone of the distance that remains between emergency cooperation and normal - even basic human - relations.
Still, the contrast was striking. Israelis experienced a hijacking fear associated with an older Middle East while traveling through a region that has changed profoundly.
That combination - new possibilities alongside enduring threats and dangers - is painfully familiar. And Wednesday abruptly exposed how fragile certain things are that we take for granted: like getting on a plane and expecting to get home safe and sound.
It also revealed how quickly anxiety, relief, and pride can once again become a shared national experience.
“Am Yisrael Chai,” the passengers sang after the plane landed in Saudi Arabia. Indeed. The passengers were alive. They had survived. They could sing.
And a country that for a terrifying hour and a half in the morning could hardly breathe was able to exhale again.

US-led delay in confronting Houthis a ‘grave mistake,’ says former Houthi spokesman - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:32:00 UTC
03:32:00 KST

The US delay in confronting the Houthis in coordination with Saudi Arabia “is a grave mistake that will cost dearly later,” Yemeni politician, writer, and former Houthi spokesperson Ali Al-Bukhaiti told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
According to Axios, US President Donald Trump has rejected multiple requests from Riyadh to strike the Houthis, despite repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi assets. Bukhaiti said the delay was a strategic error that the West could spend years paying for if it is not corrected soon.
“Defeating them after a few more years will be extremely costly for the region and the world, and may become impossible, forcing the world to recognize them as it recognized the Taliban government,” Bukhaiti said. “Worse, the Houthis control an international shipping lane, so the pain will be chronic for the West and the world, unlike the Taliban, who primarily harm their own people.”
Bukhaiti highlighted that, unlike the Taliban, the Houthis lack a large support base and remain a minority movement able to continue operating by exploiting “chaos and divisions of other political actors” and a unifying ideology.
“Washington and the West must therefore understand that the Yemen file is not like Afghanistan, and that defeating the Houthis is far easier than defeating the Taliban - especially with a capable, strong state that has powerful allies inside Yemen, namely Saudi Arabia,” he continued.
“Houthi rule is closer to Alawite rule and Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, and it will unravel in the same way Assad’s system did…They resemble the Taliban only in that they are a cohesive religious movement; they resemble Assad in that they are a minority and most of the population is against them.”
Bukhaiti: Continued Houthi presence means 'end of American imperial era'
Bukhaiti also argued that the West needs to understand that failing to confront the Houthis and allowing their position to grow stronger at a strategic location next to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait would mean “the end of the American imperial era,” with consequences reaching far beyond the Gulf.
“If the United States cannot secure the Middle East, its presence there, and the sea lanes through it, the Chinese will not respect it over Taiwan, nor the Russians over Ukraine - or even Europe - and the world will face a grave danger,” he cautioned. “What is needed is an American strategic mind in the mold of Henry Kissinger, to grasp the extremely dangerous implications of a Houthi takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.”
The Houthis claimed control of Perim Island earlier this month, which sits directly in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its narrowest point.
Now “sitting at zero distance from the shipping lane, the Houthis can now close the strait at any moment without Iranian support,” he explained.
“They can also fight Saudi Arabia and the [internationally recognized] Yemeni forces arrayed against them so long as the war stays as it is: one front active while the others sleep. But if Saudi Arabia chose a full-scale war, committed all allied forces, and forced them to fight together rather than in pieces, the recognized Yemeni government, its allied forces, and Saudi Arabia could successfully topple Houthi rule.”
Despite assessing a strong possibility of a Houthi defeat, Bukhaiti doubted Riyadh retained the “boldness it had in 2015,” suggesting Saudi decision-makers would err on the side of caution, particularly over concerns that Tehran could become more directly involved if a genuine Houthi defeat appeared likely.
He also argued that Riyadh’s confidence in its Arab and American alliances was waning, creating uncertainty that helped pave the way for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed with Pakistan and Turkey in August.
“Once Saudi Arabia reaches a clear agreement with Pakistan and Turkey that they would confront Iran if it intervenes - and once advance warnings are sent to Tehran not to do so - I believe Saudi decision-makers would then launch a full-scale war against the Houthis aimed at bringing them down,” he predicted.
That lack of trust has also prevented the Yemeni majority opposed to the Houthis from taking action. Bukhaiti said economic collapse, unpaid salaries and growing corruption had pushed public anger in Houthi-controlled areas to a high point. However, fear of Houthi repression and a lack of confidence in the internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia had kept people from rebelling.
If Yemenis were given a credible force they could trust to support them, he argued, the public could turn against the Houthis and their rule could collapse rapidly.
Explaining the Houthis’ motives, Bukhaiti identified two apparent aims. First, on the domestic front, he said the Houthis are seeking to ease their economic crisis by pressuring Riyadh to pick up the tab for employee salaries. Second, they aim to “squeeze Saudi Arabia by stopping its ships from passing through Bab el-Mandeb, completing a siege after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz.”
Houthis likely to be a part of eventual Saudi-Iranian peace agreement
The second aim, he argued, is tied to the Houthis’ alliance with the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Any conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government of Yemen, he reasoned, would be addressed in an Iranian ceasefire agreement, protecting the Houthis from potentially having to fight alone in a full-scale war.
He said Tehran and the Houthis remain in close contact, but “the Houthis do not take orders from Iran.” Rather, the group’s leadership is almost free to decide when and to what extent it is willing to risk its own interests and survival for Iran’s benefit.
Though the Houthis are able to make some decisions on their own, Bukhaiti alleged that some members of the group’s leadership are closer to Iran than others and, as a result, the Islamic Republic of Iran “has hidden, dormant tools of influence.”
Those closer to the regime “press” Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi and persuade him that moves aligned with Iran would better serve the movement and are worth certain strategic risks.
“Abdul-Malik al-Houthi lacks a deep grasp of international and regional politics - though he is shrewd at managing the local internal struggle - so he cannot always choose the right decisions,” he claimed.
“He does not submit to Iranian diktats, but his weak regional and international political awareness leads him to accept advice from some of his own commanders who themselves have been shaped by Iranian counsel.”
With the Islamic Republic of Iran already viewed as a “good and honorable ally” by the Houthis’ religious base, accusations that the Houthis are serving Iranian interests over other Yemeni ones would not threaten domestic support, he added.
“Most civilians in areas they govern, however, believe the Houthis are gambling with their lives and interests for Iran’s sake - but those civilians have no influence and are powerless.”
Though the group is likely banking on a ceasefire agreement between Washington and Tehran including them, Bukhaiti stressed that they could not be trusted to honor those commitments.
“The assurances they sent the United States and Israel are deceptive and tactical, meant to keep Washington, Israel, and their regional allies from joining Saudi Arabia against them. They fear an international coalition like the one that brought down ISIS and al-Qaeda, and they know that once Saudi Arabia is sure the United States is with it - or at least will deter Iran from intervening - Saudi and Yemeni forces can topple their rule,” he said.
“Whenever the Houthis decide it serves them to target American ships or bar them from Bab el-Mandeb - if the war in Gaza reignites, another global crisis erupts, or even China or Russia asks, and they cooperate on other files - they will do it. They are an adventurist group and will cut shipping at any moment against America and the rest of the world.”
Bukhaiti insisted that cooperation between Riyadh and Jerusalem would be “dangerous for the Houthis,” but he doubted that such cooperation would ever be confirmed publicly or handled directly, especially as Saudi officials doubt Jerusalem would remain quiet on such dealings.
Despite the danger such a partnership could pose to the Houthis, he argued that opposition to Israel in the region could mean such a coalition risks further legitimizing the Houthis.
“The better course is for Israel to press the United States and the West to form an international coalition…,” he reasoned, adding that it wasn’t necessary to have boots on the ground to win this war.
“Some airpower, political and military support, and a clear green light for Saudi Arabia to wage the campaign against the Houthis until their authority falls in Sanaa and even in Saada would suffice. The US-led coalition must also pledge to cover Saudi Arabia’s back against any Iranian intervention. Then, once those conditions are in place, Saudi Arabia and Yemeni forces would have the ability to topple the Houthis within a few months.”

30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji said Wednesday that direct negotiations with Israel under US auspices are the only way to regain Lebanese territory and allow residents to return to their villages.
Rajji made the remarks during a discussion organized by the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, according to a Lebanese Foreign Ministry statement.
The discussion, chaired by former US diplomat Elliott Abrams, was attended by council members, journalists and representatives of research centers, the ministry said.
It addressed the situation in Lebanon, reasons for delays in implementing the framework agreement, Hezbollah's weapons, the future of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon and relations with Syria's new government, the statement said.
Rajji said Lebanon's priority is to ensure stability, adding that the Lebanese want their country to once again become a cultural, tourism and economic hub in the region.
However, he said this could not be achieved while weapons exist outside state authority.
He described the Lebanese government's decision to restrict weapons to state control as "courageous," saying Lebanon's stability and prosperity require "ending the occupation and Hezbollah handing over its weapons."
"We want peace with all our neighbors," Rajji said.
He also stressed that Iran must "stop interfering in Lebanese affairs" and said the Lebanese army is the country's "only hope."
Rajji welcomed US assistance to the Lebanese military and expressed hope that the support would continue.
He reiterated the government's commitment to direct negotiations with Israel under US auspices, describing them as "the only way to regain the territories and allow residents to return to their villages."
On Sunday, Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem called on Lebanese authorities to “freeze direct negotiations with Israel and move toward indirect negotiations” in order to halt what he described as concessions and correct the course of the talks.
Direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel began on April 14, 2026, with a meeting in Washington under US auspices.
Subsequent rounds addressed a ceasefire, Israeli withdrawal, borders, prisoners and missing persons.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored "framework formula" in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have continued, while Israel still occupies areas in the south, some held for decades and others seized during recent wars and military operations.
Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people and injured 12,413 others, while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.

NASA directive might increase the odds of contaminating Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:25:22 UTC
03:25:22 KST

A new NASA directive seeks to loosen “planetary protection” rules meant to avoid the contamination other worlds with microbial life from Earth.
The policy shift arrived via a message to NASA personnel that was obtained and shared yesterday by the independent watchdog sites NASA Watch and Astrobiology.com. In it, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman writes that procedures for avoiding contamination “must reflect our current scientific knowledge” and argues that this knowledge has shifted since the current rules were established decades ago.
The directive “ensures we can use our incredible data to lower costs on our missions,” says Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate. “This process will also help increase commercial capabilities — getting more missions into space by streamlining space exploration.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In 1964 members of the International Council for Science’s Committee on Space Research (COSPAR), led by the United Nations–affiliated International Council of Scientific Unions (now the International Science Council), feared that the breakneck pace of the space race could lead to spacecraft accidentally contaminating alien worlds with microbial life from Earth. If those interplanetary hitchhikers were sufficiently resilient and numerous to form self-sustaining populations on Mars or other planets, they could forever alter those otherwise-pristine environments and sabotage all future efforts to discover true alien life there. So COSPAR issued a resolution that any mission to another potentially habitable or inhabited world must demonstrate a less than one-in-10,000 chance of exposing such places to terrestrial life capable of interplanetary colonization.
The new directive notes that COSPAR subsequently tightened those rules to account for the flurry of Mars-bound missions, some carrying human crews, that were widely expected to launch in the intervening decades. Codified in 1969, those more stringent and costly restrictions have guided—and greatly limited, some critics say—Mars exploration ever since. But “human exploration did not progress as quickly as all believed,” Isaacman’s message reads, while technology for sterilizing spacecraft has improved markedly. “Our long-standing policies were designed in a different era,” he writes.
Now, the message states, NASA’s rules will immediately be restored to the looser 1964 restriction of less than a one-in-10,000 chance of biocontamination for each Mars-bound mission. And in the meantime, NASA officials will perform a rapid-fire “modernization assessment” of the current science and technology concerning contamination risk, with a December 2026 deadline for delivering recommendations to lower that threshold even further.
A statement from NASA clarified that the new directive isn’t “weakening” existing planetary protection protocols so much as updating them. “This directive moves NASA toward a quantitative, performance-based approach that measures actual contamination risk and applies protections accordingly,” the statement said. Additionally, missions looking for past or present life on Mars—such as NASA’s Perseverance rover—will “continue to carry requirements appropriate to protecting those investigations.”
Such cautions are crucial, experts say, especially since Perseverance has uncovered tantalizing hints of possible ancient biosignatures in some of the rocks it has studied; samples from those rocks are now in limbo, awaiting an as-yet-unclear ride back to Earth for further analysis.
“We are actively seeking to learn if the organics we have found on Mars are biological in origin,” says Linday Hays, NASA’s senior scientist for Mars exploration. This policy change will not threaten that goal, she says, but “will allow us to bring decades of science from our Mars exploration to help make our processes more straightforward for robotic and, in the future, human exploration of the Red Planet.”

DOJ accuses Minnesota federal judges of misconduct for NY Times immigration interviews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:24:35 UTC
03:24:35 KST

The Department of Justice on Wednesday filed a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one Minnesota federal judges on active status for interviews they gave to The New York Times that criticized the Trump administration's handling of immigration enforcement cases in the state.
The DOJ asked the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals to force the recusal of all seven judges who spoke with The Times from any case involving the Department of Homeland Security.
The complaint also asks the 8th Circuit, which handles cases arising from the District of Minnesota, to investigate what the DOJ called "the judges' improper and unethical conduct" in speaking to the newspaper.
The complaint singles out Senior Judge Patrick Schiltz and Senior Judge John Tunheim, who were quoted by name in the article, which ran under the headline "Trump's Minnesota Surge Threatened Democracy, Judge Warns."
Schiltz until July 1 had served as chief judge in the District of Minnesota, having succeeded Tunheim in that role in 2022.
Schiltz had issued a Jan. 28 order demanding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement stop violating orders issued by Minnesota federal judges in cases related to a surge in immigration enforcement actions in the state. Schiltz told The Times that ICE's violations of the orders "created a grave threat to the rule of law."
Tunheim was quoted by The Times after a paragraph that said the judges considered that most of the detainees whose cases they handled "seemed to be ordinary people with homes and jobs," and not immigrants who DHS officials claimed were "the worst of the worst."
"They weren't arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street," Tunheim said, according to The Times.
The other judges spoke to the newspaper on the condition of anonymity.
"Judge Schiltz and Judge Tunheim, at least, have flagrantly violated the Code of Judicial Conduct with their improper and unethical comments to the New York Times," says the complaint by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, Jr.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement, said, "Seven federal judges in the District of Minnesota talked to the New York Times about cases, some of which are on-going, in a manner that the Department of Justice views as a clear violation of their ethical duties."
"Their conduct has undermined public confidence in an impartial judiciary in Minnesota," Blanche said.
A spokeswoman for U.S. District Court in Minnesota defended the judges' contact after CNBC requested comment from Schiltz and Tunheim about the complaint.
"As legal-ethics experts have confirmed, our judges were acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to the New York Times," said Rebeccah Parks, the spokeswoman.
"Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may "speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence,'" Parks said. "Our judges acted within this capacity."
