Ukraine Completes 17 of 42 Resolutions Needed to Unlock $29.5B in Aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:20:36 UTC
03:20:36 KST

Ukraine’s government has now adopted 17 out of 42 resolutions it needs to unlock international financing, with less than three weeks left before its self-imposed deadline.
The Cabinet of Ministers approved four more decisions at its meeting on Wednesday, Sept. 30, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement. The government has entered what he described as a regime of maximum austerity and postponed non-priority spending.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The remaining 25 resolutions must be completed by Oct. 15.
“Over the next two weeks, we need to accelerate the work as much as possible and ensure that every decision is fully implemented,” Koretskyi said, adding that “any delay comes at a very high cost.”
The decisions are required to secure €27 billion ($29.5 billion) in planned international financing by the end of the year, which depends exclusively on Ukraine meeting its reform commitments to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the EU.
The government originally planned to finish the work by Nov. 1 but moved the deadline forward as pressure on public finances grew.
Parliament’s share of the work
The commitments fall into two groups: government measures and legislative changes that require votes in Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada.
Koretskyi thanked lawmakers who supported several of the necessary bills in their first reading last week, calling the process “a joint effort and our shared responsibility.”
Ukraine Plans Fourth Phase of Operation Vivaldi, Zelensky Says
The cabinet has asked parliament to hold an additional plenary session on Oct. 12, a day before lawmakers are scheduled to return from recess. According to UA.News, among the funds at stake is an EU tranche of about €3.7 billion ($4 billion).
President Volodymyr Zelensky has also pressed lawmakers to act on Monday, Sept. 28, saying that if the government meets its commitments by Oct. 15, parliament must follow an equally clear schedule.
A $27 billion defense gap
The push comes as Ukraine’s defense budget faces a $27 billion shortfall.
On Monday, Ukraine’s government announced that it adopted a decision setting the priority order for state expenditures.
Koretskyi said that the government will fund mainly defense, pensions, social payments and public-sector salaries, while postponing nonessential spending.
“Under these conditions, we continue to adopt strict anti-crisis measures to ensure the most important priorities – defense needs and the welfare of our people,” he said.
The government’s budget plans to cover about $7 billion through austerity, including cutting and reallocating spending, while the remaining $20 billion is expected to come exclusively from its Western partners.
“It is time, finally, to stop spending money on non-priority items,” he said, urging local self-government bodies to set similar priorities in their own budgets and to cut spending that is not currently essential.
Throughout 2026, Kyiv has struggled to receive foreign aid on time and in full because of delayed reforms and corruption scandals.
Much of the support comes from the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027, which is to be repaid from reparations owed by Russia, according to the European Council.
The EU has allocated up to €45 billion ($51 billion) of it for 2026, including €17 billion ($19 billion) in budget support and €28.3 billion ($32 billion) for Ukraine’s defense industrial capacities.
Ukraine’s total war costs will reach $155 billion this year, Reuters reported, citing Koretskyi on Wednesday.
It marks the first time Kyiv has published an estimate of its annual war costs, so there is no comparable figure for previous years, though officials say the cost of the war has grown as both sides rely more heavily on missiles and drones.
Funding from Western partners
On Sept. 27, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced almost €710 million ($809 million) in EU support for displaced people and crisis relief worldwide, €52 million ($59 million) of which will be allocated to Ukraine ahead of winter.
European Pravda separately reported that an EU-proposed €100 billion ($115 billion) funding package for Ukraine remains largely undisputed in negotiations on the bloc’s upcoming seven-year budget, spanning from 2027-34.
The EU disbursed €3.3 billion (roughly $3.7 billion) to Ukraine for the procurement of missiles and drones.
Separately, the EU approved a €6.1 billion ($7 billion) defense package for Ukraine on Sept. 11, allowing Kyiv to purchase the PAC-3 Patriot interceptors.
According to von der Leyen, the EU has already mobilised nearly €15 billion (approximately $17 billion) to Ukraine in 2026 alone.

Girls in Gaza forced into child marriage as Israel’s genocide fuels hunger and displacement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:20:30 UTC
03:20:30 KST

Safaa’s face bears marks of fatigue and exhaustion far beyond her 19 years. Squeezed into a torn nylon tent on the sandy coast of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, months into a supposed ceasefire that has done little to ease the hardships of her people, she sits at the entrance with hollow eyes and brittle nails — the visible signs of malnutrition and vitamin deficiency. She is also pregnant, waiting to give birth while gripped by unrelenting fear.
In 2024, her parents married her off with the promise that she would live in better conditions. “There was no house, no walls, no celebration,” she tells Mondoweiss quietly, asking to be referred to by her first name only.
Instead of finding reprieve in her marriage, she found herself responsible for gathering firewood, cooking over an open fire, and washing clothes by hand amid a water shortage — burdens her frail body was not built to bear.
Her pre-war life in Shuja’iyya was the picture of an ordinary childhood. Then their home was struck and leveled in 2023, leaving her family of eight with no roof and no income. Her pregnant mother grew weaker by the day. Safaa herself suffered constant dizziness from malnutrition. When a young man proposed, promising food and stability, she agreed at 15 and was married at 17.
But the illusion collapsed on the first day.
Before October 2023, child marriage in Gaza had been declining. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, the rate of girls married under 18 had fallen from 22.2 percent in 2015 to 17.9 percent in 2022. The war reversed that progress entirely. A 2024 UNFPA survey found that 71 percent of respondents reported growing pressure to marry girls under 18, driven by displacement, poverty, and the collapse of protective systems.
“Girls in Gaza are not choosing marriage. They are being driven into it by hunger, fear, and displacement,” UNFPA Country Representative Nestor Owomuhangi said in April 2025. As such, childhood marriage can put young girls in precarious conditions where they are unable to make educated decisions about their future.
“Under continuous bombardment and repeated displacement, I see parents pushed toward excruciating, zero-option scenarios,” Walaa al-Othmani, a field specialist with the al-Shafi Association for Family Development, told Mondoweiss. “Through my direct work with these families, I witness how extreme deprivation drives them to make the most painful decision: marrying off their young daughters.”
Losing everything
In a narrow, dark corner of a school run by UNRWA in Nuseirat refugee camp sits Manal, 17, wedged between piles of discarded school furniture. Before the war, she was a top student planning to study at an arts college. Today she lives in a chaotic, overcrowded environment where hundreds of displaced families share classrooms and hallways with no privacy, and diseases spread from overflowing sewage and a chronic water shortage.
In 2024, her father convinced her that marriage would protect her and ease the family’s burden. Two of her older sisters had already been married off. She had no say. Within days, she was transformed from a student carrying a school bag into a wife responsible for running a household inside a displacement corridor.
“I never once imagined that I would become a wife living in a classroom crowded with displaced people,” she said, asking to be identified by her first name only. “No protection, no stability, not even a private space to cry. I lost my school and my childhood at the same time.”
The collapse of education was a direct driver. According to UNICEF, more than 97 percent of Gaza’s schools have been damaged or destroyed since October 2023, leaving around 658,000 school-age children without access to formal education. The UN has described this destruction as deliberate and systematic. What was once a protective space for young girls has ceased to exist.
“Child and early marriage is witnessing a marked rise; amidst wartime conditions, some families have come to view it as a safe way to secure their daughters’ futures,” Maryam Zaqout, Director of the Aisha Association for the Protection of Women and Children in Gaza, told Mondoweiss. “Yet, at a time when these girls ought to be in school, we see them carrying their own children and sometimes coming to the association seeking protection from the harsh reality in which they live.”
Al-Othmani describes how the concept of protection has been distorted beyond recognition: girls are being promised security and safety in marriages in exchange for their childhood. “Fathers escape this fear by passing responsibility for the girl to a husband, believing a male presence will shield her,” Zaqout says. “But what we witness on the ground is that this protection is an illusion. The young girl moves to a new tent only to find herself completely unprotected and far more vulnerable to abuse, without her own family there to back her up.”
This is what happened with Amal, the 15-year-old wife whose frail body was subjected to sexual abuse and violence from the first day of her marriage. She lives in the southern edge of Khan Younis, in a sand-battered tent with her family, surviving on a single free meal each day from a communal charity kitchen. At 15, she was married off in a hasty agreement between her father and her aunt, despite her own mother’s objections. Amal found no room to maneuvere. “It felt as though my father simply wanted to get rid of a heavy burden in the tent and cut expenses,” she said.
Since October 2023, Israel has tightened its siege over Gaza, imposing a famine that starved its population and killed dozens. Months into a ceasefire, Gaza’s families remain trapped between hunger and soaring living costs: food prices are still about 235 percent above pre-October 2023 levels, while shortages of cash, jobs, cooking fuel, and clean water make even basic meals difficult to afford. In July, the World Food Program found that 45 percent of households surveyed reported going to bed hungry at least once in the 30 days preceding the survey, with 6 percent experiencing this more than ten times.
On her wedding night, and as a result of sexual violence, Amal’s weak body endured severe bleeding and serious health complications which were exacerbated by a complete lack of medical care or nearby hospitals capable of handling her case. “I thought moving to my husband’s tent might mean better food,” she recalled. “Instead I found myself sinking into something even harsher.”
Soon after, she got pregnant with a baby she quickly lost as a result of malnutrition and overall physicall unwellness. Grappling to navigate the emotional, mental, and physical tool the marriage has had on her, Amal feels numb. “I just wanted to go to school, finish my education, graduate, and not have to constantly worry about having enough food or calculating every bite just to make it last. I didn’t want much from this world — just to breathe freely and see the sea, not something that would choke the life out of me,” she said.
The legislative vacuum
Israel’s assault on Gaza has wiped out the judicial system’s infrastructure entirely — demolishing court buildings, destroying decades of records preserving marriage contracts, paternity records, and custody rulings, and killing or displacing judges and licensed marriage officiants. The result is the total paralysis of the official legislative system.
“Under normal circumstances, Palestinian law and sharia courts enforced strict procedures prohibiting the documentation of any marriage for those under 18, except through stringent judicial exceptions requiring a judge’s approval, medical examination, and social assessment,” al-Othmani explained. “Today, amid the absence of the court, the judge, and the registrar, marriage decisions are made individually inside camp tents — without legal oversight or statutory deterrents.”
Data from the Supreme Sharia Court, cited by the Associated Press, shows that 20.6 percent of the 35,474 marriages recorded in 2024 and 2025 involved a girl under 18, including 627 marriages of girls under 15. Rights advocates warn that even these figures undercount the reality: most child marriages now take place verbally, entirely outside any statistical record.
The collapsed healthcare system also adds to the physical toll these young wives face.
In Zeitoun, east of Gaza City, 16-year-old Fatima suffered three consecutive miscarriages within six months of her forced marriage, a direct result of grueling physical labor, including hauling water and gathering firewood while walking for long distances over rubble, severe malnutrition, and the complete collapse of healthcare in northern Gaza. Before the war, she had opened her own small food stand and had great ambitions. Air strikes destroyed it along with her family’s home in Beit Hanoun. “The war took my home, my work, my dream, my health, and my unborn children,” she told Mondoweiss, explaining that destitution and her family’s struggle to find food drove her into this marriage. “I was completely deprived of medicine or care throughout my miscarriages,” she added, lamenting the circumstances that crushed her dreams and independence.
Only 50 percent of Gaza’s hospitals are functioning even partially, according to the World Health Organization. Pregnant minors face a complete absence of prenatal care, ultrasound checkups, and essential supplements, producing a sharp rise in premature births, uterine rupture, severe hemorrhaging, and recurrent miscarriage. According to UNFPA, approximately 10 percent of all newly registered pregnancies in Gaza now involve adolescent girls.
A last line of defense
Faced with this crisis and the absence of official protection, grassroots initiatives have emerged as the only available response.
The al-Shafi Association for Family Development, working in partnership with UNFPA, operates through three strategies inside the displacement camps: expanding safe spaces and dedicated tents exclusively for adolescent girls; running direct awareness campaigns for parents using medical evidence on the dangers of early pregnancy; and offering legal guidance to families who proceed with a marriage, encouraging them to draft temporary contracts signed by the camp’s mukhtar (a respected elder tasked with mediating disputes) and recognised community figures, preserving dowry rights and proof of paternity until sharia courts reopen.
Al-Othmani describes how eagerly the girls turn up. “They are fully aware of the rights they have lost,” she says, “and are in urgent need of self-care and an outlet for their emotions.”
But the scale of what has been lost cannot be offset by tents and awareness sessions. As the genocide continues and all traces of normalcy are erased, girls continue to be forced into marriage in hopes of better living conditions, purpose, or an escape.
Field estimates place the rate of marriage among girls under 18 at above 35 percent.
Manal still carries her school notebook. Its pages are worn from being leafed through in the displacement corridor where she now lives as a wife. “Every time I remember what my life was supposed to be,” she says, “I feel like I can’t breathe.”

Ukraine war latest: Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for 1st time, Zelensky adviser says

Russia has for the first time used a jet-powered drone equipped with a warhead designed to destroy high-voltage power pylons and steel bridge structures, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Sept. 30.
The development comes as Moscow renews its large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter, launching its heaviest combined attack on energy infrastructure in months overnight on Sept. 30.
"Bad news. Today, the enemy for the first time used a special shaped-charge cutting warhead on a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)," Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technologies, wrote on Telegram.
According to Beskrestnov, the warhead was developed specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and steel bridge structures. It consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four additional destructive modules.
"I think the enemy plans to attack important high-voltage power transmission lines," he said.
Russia's overnight assault involved nearly 190 attack drones as well as ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast was the primary target, while critical infrastructure was also struck in several other regions.
By the evening, emergency power outages had been introduced in the capital and surrounding region as well as in Chernihiv and Zhytomyr oblasts following repeated Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, according to the Energy Ministry.
The Sept. 30 attack marked a sharp escalation in Russia's renewed campaign against Ukraine's power system.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said following the attack.

A drone flew into Moldovan airspace, crashed outside a village, and exploded in the early hours of Sept. 30 amid a Russian mass attack on Ukraine, Moldova's Defense Ministry said.
The drone entered Moldovan airspace around 5:43 a.m. local time and fell down near the village of Hirbovat in the central Anenii Noi district, where it exploded, according to the ministry.
According to preliminary information, no injuries were reported from the explosion. Moldovan police and army teams were headed to inspect the site.

Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
Missile alerts cost Ukraine an estimated $45 million for every hour they force businesses to stop operating, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian in an interview published on Sept. 30.
"If people are in a bunker, business stops," Kravchenko told the Guardian.
Kravchenko said prolonged missile alerts can bring large parts of the economy to a standstill as workers move into shelters, with some alerts lasting for hours.
Ukraine introduced a two-tier air raid warning system on Sept. 2 to reduce the economic disruption caused by prolonged alerts. Red alerts are issued when there is a missile threat and require businesses to halt operations and people to seek shelter. Yellow alerts warn primarily of drone threats and allow many businesses to continue operating.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, but those warnings do not mean there is no danger.
On Sept. 28, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv during a yellow alert while employees were still inside. The attack killed an aide to former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin and injured others.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $10 billion in damage to fixed assets in Ukraine this year alone, according to Kravchenko. Steel plants, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers have all been hit as Moscow increasingly targets infrastructure supporting the country's economy.
Russia has also stepped up attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports and maritime export infrastructure, adding pressure on one of the country's main trade routes.
The government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukrainian air-defense systems to better protect their facilities, Kravchenko said, while acknowledging that businesses cannot fully shield themselves from Russian missiles and drones.

Rwanda open to hosting migrants transferred from Europe, EU lawmakers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

03:17:50 KST

Rwanda open to hosting migrants transferred from Europe, EU lawmakers say
BRUSSELS, Sept 30 - Rwanda had held preliminary discussions with some EU member states about potentially hosting facilities for migrants transferred from those countries, two European Parliament lawmakers said on Wednesday, citing discussions with Rwandan officials.
During their visit to Kigali last week, the lawmakers, Tineke Strik and Anna Strolenberg of the Greens/EFA and Volt groups, said Rwandan officials told them they are open to the idea but that discussions remained at an early stage and no agreements had been reached.
Rwandan officials were not immediately available for comment.
Earlier this month, five European countries said they aimed to strike agreements this year to send migrants without a legal right to remain in the European Union to countries outside the bloc.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands, known as the Group of Five, said they had agreed on concrete steps towards establishing return hubs in a non-EU country as part of a wider European push to increase deportations and curb irregular migration.
The countries have not publicly identified potential host states.
An EU official told Reuters, on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak publicly, that Rwanda was among the countries being considered by the Group of Five.
During their visit, the lawmakers were shown two facilities prepared under Britain's abandoned Rwanda deportation scheme that could potentially be used to house migrants transferred from Europe. One of the sites was a hotel.
The five countries are expected to meet again on Thursday on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council.
Rwanda has in recent years positioned itself as a destination for migrants that Western nations would like to remove, despite concerns by rights groups about human rights in the country.
Last year, Rwanda received migrants deported from the United States after the two countries reached an agreement for the transfer of up to 250 people.
In 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled that a government plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda was unlawful. Rwanda later asked Britain for a £50 million ($63.62 million) payment after the asylum deal was cancelled.
Rights groups have criticised return hub proposals, saying they risk undermining safeguards for migrants and asylum seekers, while supporters argue they could boost returns and deter irregular migration.
"The deportation plans by these five member states are unrealistic, inhumane and costly," Strik said.
Uganda and Rwanda, which host large refugee populations, have also been hit hard by cuts in US foreign aid, forcing humanitarian agencies to scale back food assistance, healthcare and other services for displaced people.
“Uganda and Rwanda are one of the few stable countries in the region. Pressuring these countries by sending even more people is tempting fate,” said Strolenberg. REUTERS

Britain’s MI5 spy agency issued an unprecedented alert on Wednesday to warn that a Chinese organisation was involved in funding academic research into topics such as AI on behalf of Beijing’s state security service.
In its “Espionage Alert”, MI5 said more than 100 UK-based academics had contributed to projects funded by the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), which had “very strong ties” to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), Beijing’s civilian intelligence service.
“MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage,” the alert said.
“UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, covert communications systems and steganography. This activity supports MSS espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security.”

Türkiye joins action framework to tackle global steel overcapacity

30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Türkiye and fellow members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity (GFSEC) adopted an action framework to combat global overcapacity, Trade Minister Omer Bolat said Wednesday.
Bolat said in a statement on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal that members adopted the Comprehensive Framework for Joint Action and a ministerial statement during a meeting on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers’ gathering in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
The forum assessed ways to prevent excess steel capacity from increasingly harming international steel trade, alongside coordination of members’ investment, production and foreign trade policies, he said.
Participating countries agreed to continue efforts to address the problem, Bolat added.
The minister is representing Türkiye at the two-day meeting, held under the US presidency as geopolitical tensions, mounting uncertainty and the risk of economic fragmentation weigh on global trade.
The gathering runs from Sept. 30 to Oct. 1 and is hosted by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
Bolat said Türkiye is sharing its approaches and proposed solutions on preventing food from being used as an instrument of political and economic pressure, addressing structural overcapacity, the most-favored-nation principle and eliminating forced labor from global supply chains.
He said Türkiye would continue efforts under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s leadership to strengthen its influence and competitiveness in global trade, diversify trade relations and defend its interests on international platforms in line with its Century of Türkiye goals.

Intl Register of Damage for Ukraine opens all 43 claim categories for compensation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:15:10 EEST
03:15:10 KST

The International Register of Damages for Ukraine has opened the last three categories out of the 43 categories of claims submitted by the State of Ukraine: "Other property losses," "Environmental Damage," and "Theft and/or Misappropriation of Natural Resources," the President's Office said.
"The International Register of Damages for Ukraine has opened all 43 categories of claims for compensation for damages, losses, or harm caused by Russia's full-scale aggression against Ukraine. The three categories of claims recently opened for the State of Ukraine are: "Other Property Losses," "Environmental Damage," and "Theft and/or Misappropriation of Natural Resources,"" according to a statement posted on the presidential website on Wednesday.
It is reported that claims in the last three categories may be submitted by the state, central, regional, and local authorities, as well as state and municipal institutions and organizations. This makes it possible to document damage to the natural environment, the value of illegally seized or appropriated natural resources, and the damage, destruction, or loss of state and municipal property that are not covered by other categories of claims.
It is noted that there are a total of 21 categories of claims for individuals, 11 categories for legal entities, and 11 categories for the State of Ukraine. These categories cover various consequences of Russia's aggression against Ukraine: the death and disappearance of loved ones, bodily injury, torture, sexual violence, forced displacement, loss of housing, jobs and private businesses, damage to property and infrastructure, economic losses to businesses, damage to cultural heritage and the environment, humanitarian expenditures by the state, and other types of losses.
The International Register of Damages was launched on April 2, 2024. Since then, it has received 195,000 claims, of which more than 65,000 have already been entered into the system, and the rest are currently being processed.
The registry is the first component of the international compensation mechanism for Ukraine. The second component is the International Compensation Commission for Ukraine, which will review the claims on their merits, determine the amount of compensation in each case, and issue decisions. The convention establishing it has been signed by 40 states and the EU, and 10 of them have already ratified it. Twenty-five ratifications are required to establish the commission. The final component of the mechanism will be the International Compensation Fund, from which payments will be made in accordance with the commission's decisions.

Global air passenger demand falls 0.8% in August as Middle East slump deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:14:28 UTC
03:14:28 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Global air passenger demand fell 0.8% year-on-year in August as a deepening downturn at Middle Eastern airlines interrupted the region’s recovery, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said Wednesday.
Total demand, measured in revenue passenger kilometers, declined despite a 0.3% increase in capacity, IATA said.
The passenger load factor, which measures how much available capacity was filled, fell 0.9 percentage points to 85.1%.
Excluding Middle Eastern carriers, global demand increased 0.6%, half the growth rate recorded in July.
“Global demand for air transport contracted by 0.8% compared to August 2025 as the recovery trajectory for carriers in the Middle East was interrupted,” said Marie Owens Thomsen, IATA’s senior vice president for sustainability and chief economist.
Middle Eastern airlines recorded a 14.6% decline in overall passenger demand, while capacity fell 9.3%.
Owens Thomsen said forthcoming data would show whether higher energy prices, which have reduced travelers’ purchasing power, and geopolitical instability were prompting consumers to adjust their travel budgets.
 
Forward schedules for October indicate cautious optimism, with available seats projected to increase 2%, she added.
International demand weakens
International passenger demand fell 0.9% year-on-year, while capacity was unchanged, IATA said. Excluding Middle Eastern carriers, international demand rose 1.3%.
Middle Eastern airlines’ international traffic dropped 14.2%, reversing the gradual stabilization seen since the Iran war began in February, according to IATA.
The contraction on Middle East-Asia routes deepened to 11.7%, compared with an 8.6% decline in July.
European carriers recorded a 2.1% increase in international demand, while traffic on Europe-Asia routes rose 12.2%.
Transatlantic traffic fell 2.4%, with declines across several markets, including the UK and France.
International demand at North American airlines fell 1.7%, while Asia-Pacific carriers registered a 0.1% decline.
African and Latin American airlines both reported international demand growth of 6.7%.
China bucks domestic downturn
Domestic passenger demand fell 0.5% in August despite a 0.7% increase in capacity, IATA said.
The domestic load factor declined 1.1 percentage points to 85.3%.
India recorded the sharpest contraction among the domestic markets covered, with demand falling 7.5%.
US domestic traffic declined 2.9%, while Japan’s fell 2%.
China’s domestic demand rose 5.8%, supported by summer travel, while Brazil and Australia recorded increases of 4.3% and 2.3%, respectively.

Istanbul Arbitration Days spotlights forces reshaping international arbitration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:12:52 UTC
03:12:52 KST

Geopolitical developments, sanctions and artificial intelligence took center stage Wednesday as international arbitration practitioners gathered for Istanbul Arbitration Days 2026.
Participants at Ciragan Palace discussed challenges in cross-border dispute resolution, including geopolitical developments affecting enforcement and arbitral seats, the growing use of AI and efforts to make proceedings more efficient.
Opening the conference, Istanbul Arbitration Centre President Ziya Akinci highlighted the institution's growing caseload and international reach, saying construction disputes represented its largest category of cases.
The center handled 263 cases last year, Akinci said, adding that both the number of cases and amounts in dispute were continuing to increase.
He said the center was also handling cases involving entirely non-Turkish parties and disputes with no connection to Türkiye.
Akinci said 86% of cases handled under its fast-track mechanism last year were completed within the prescribed three-month period.
Geopolitics enters arbitration strategy
Discussions throughout the day highlighted the growing impact of geopolitical developments and sanctions on international arbitration.
Evgeniya Neverova, a counsel at Asari Legal, speaking during a panel on geopolitical realignment and disputes, said lawyers representing Russian and Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) clients have had to develop increasingly case-specific approaches since 2022.
She said sanctions can affect the choice of arbitral institution and seat, payments, selection of counsel, experts and arbitrators, and enforcement of an eventual award.
Neverova said parties increasingly need to consider from the outset where assets are located and whether an award can ultimately be enforced and its proceeds recovered.
In some circumstances, she said, a successful party may obtain an award only for the proceeds to remain in a frozen account because of sanctions restrictions.
Ceyda Akbal Schwimann, a partner at IAS Partners law firm, highlighted differing approaches to sanctions and enforcement across jurisdictions.
She cited recent decisions in the UK and Switzerland involving similar sanctions-related issues that reached different outcomes, describing the divergence as an emerging “enforcement fracture.”
Wolfgang Peter, a founding partner of Peter & Kim, a specialist arbitration and disputes firm, said support for arbitration remains strong, but sanctions, controls on information and technology, and other regulatory restrictions have made its operating environment significantly more complicated.
Heiko Heppner, a partner at Bird & Bird law firm, said growing fragmentation of the global legal order requires lawyers to become better at helping clients navigate conflicting regimes.
Counsel must look beyond prevailing in arbitration itself and consider the entire path toward enforcement and eventual recovery, he said.
Institutions seek faster, more flexible arbitration
Ercument Erdem, founder and senior partner at Erdem & Erdem, said institutional arbitration was moving away from excessive formality toward more active case management, with reforms increasingly focused on speed and efficiency.
“The current direction is clear: less formality, more responsibility,” he said.
Erdem said procedures were increasingly being designed around the needs of individual disputes rather than tradition.
He pointed to changes aimed at faster proceedings, early determination of claims and stronger case management as institutions respond to concerns over arbitration becoming too slow, costly and procedurally complex.
Thomas Francis, a partner at Curtis, Mallet-Prevost, Colt & Mosle LLP, said the growing use of third-party funding was also raising questions beyond who finances a claim to who ultimately owns it, particularly in investment disputes and at the enforcement stage.
He said tribunals were likely to pay increasing attention to the ownership history of claims, including issues involving jurisdiction, quantum and beneficial ownership.
AI puts human judgment under spotlight
Dominic Spenser Underhill, an international arbitrator and solicitor at Spenser Underhill Newmark LLP, highlighted recent cases in which AI-generated legal material contained fabricated or inaccurate authorities.
He argued that professional policies and guidelines alone may not be sufficient to address the risks because AI is developing too rapidly for a rules-based approach alone to provide adequate safeguards.
Underhill stressed the importance of human qualities including intellectual honesty, diligence, prudence and judgment.
He warned that problems involving AI in dispute resolution were likely to “get worse before they get better,” saying lawyers must retain intellectual independence rather than delegate professional judgment to technology.
Erdem said AI could help reduce costs and delays but should not undermine confidentiality, due process or an arbitrator's personal responsibility for decisions.
Greener arbitration
The conference also highlighted efforts to reduce arbitration's environmental footprint through greater use of digital processes, reduced paper consumption and tools to assess the carbon impact of proceedings.
Speakers pointed to sustainability measures adopted for Istanbul Arbitration Days, describing the event's approach as an example for other arbitration organizations and institutions.
Akinci also highlighted the Istanbul Arbitration Centre's environmental initiatives, including efforts to use greener materials and work toward creating an arbitration forest through tree planting.

Overwhelming Cheating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:12:37 UTC
03:12:37 KST

In a comment on an earlier post, a professor suggested as a topic for discussion, “Academic integrity violations becoming commonplace (analog, not just AI!) and what to do about it.”
I’ve certainly heard from many professors about rampant AI-enabled cheating in their courses. Here’s one horror story from an instructor of an online course:
24 students started the course.
7 dropped on the first day immediately after being informed there would be in-person [live] Zoom oral exams. (You can draw your own conclusions about why….)
Of the 17 left, 4 handed in either nothing at all during the course, or at most one assignment (out of five). So, they failed.
That leaves 13 ‘active’ students.
Of these 13, I had to turn in 10 for cheating using AI – and of those 10, 3 continued to use AI to cheat after I had already turned them in for this (and informed them that I had done so). So, they got turned in again. And again. And again. And, in one case, again.
So, of the original 24 students, only 3 did the work required in the course, and did so honestly.
That may be an extreme example, but even some professors teaching in-person courses, including those who have taken steps to reduce the incentives students have to use AI for their coursework, have reported a crushing amount of AI-enabled cheating.
I’ve heard less about an increase in “analog” violations of academic integrity—reports on that welcome— but perhaps an environment in which AI cheating is common diminishes people’s inhibitions against other kinds of cheating.
We’ve discussed in the past ways of preventing AI cheating or trying to make cheating “not worth it.”
That’s all well and good, but one question I’d like to ask about is: What should one do about all the cheating that remains?
Part of the answer to this may come from official university policies. But most of us have the discretion to decide whether to go the “official” route. Do you?
Should we?
How much of a burden will it be to officially report the cheating, given how much there is? Any one case can be time consuming: forms must be completed, extra meetings must be held, hearings may sometimes be required. What if one has 10 or 20 or 50 instances of cheating at the same time?
What is the university’s likely response to the kind of cheating you’re reporting? Are you likely to be supported by the administration? Are the disciplinary measures for those found to have violated the honor code trivial?
What effects will officially reporting the cheating have? Will the student caught be less likely to cheat? Will case confidentiality cut too much against the deterrent effect that reporting one student might have on others?
Is this a collective action problem? One might hope for university-wide measures to curb cheating if enough of it is reported. But such measures may be unlikely to arise if only a few professors here and there report cheating. Any one of us may be skeptical that our own reporting of cheating is going to make enough of a difference, and so be discouraged from reporting, and so no university-wide measures arise. Would it make a difference if faculty members at a university formed a pact to each more carefully attend to cheating and officially report it when they find it?
Discussion of these and related questions welcome.

crystal animal sculptures freeze the open-mouthed gesture of a roar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:10:38 UTC
03:10:38 KST

crystal animal sculptures freeze the open-mouthed gesture of a roar
ferdi b dick’s animal sculptures feature an open mouth and extended tongue in different crystal colors.
the Roar recurs across Ferdi B Dick’s animal sculptures
South African-born sculptor Ferdi B Dick builds many of his animal sculptures around a recurring gesture: an open mouth with an extended tongue, capturing the form of a roar. Rather than representing aggression, Dick connects the gesture to release and exhalation, drawing a parallel with Simhasana, the lion’s breath in yoga practice.
The motif appears throughout his practice at different scales, from mirror-polished stainless-steel public sculptures to gallery works and cast crystal. In Embrace the Amazing Whale, the gesture takes the form of an 8-meter-tall public sculpture on the waterfront of Zhanjiang, China, installed in December 2023. Lion Roar brought the same language to gallery-scale works at Everard Read in Johannesburg in 2023.
Crystal Roar translates the gesture into a smaller and more fragile material form. The series includes Dragon Roar, Lion Roar, Bunnie Roar, and Ellie Roar. Each sculpture begins as a digital model developed using the same tools employed for Dick’s large-scale public works before being cast in crystal through the lost-wax process.
Crystal, color, and light define each sculptural form
Metal oxides are introduced during casting to produce different colors, with each requiring a specific firing temperature. Once cast, the sculptures are cut, ground, sandblasted, and polished by hand. The crystal alters the way each form interacts with light: violet carries and catches light differently from amber, while darker crystal absorbs it. The material gives the sculptures a combination of weight and fragility.
The Crystal Roar works form part of a broader sculptural language that moves between monumental public works, gallery pieces, and smaller collector sculptures. While the scale changes, the recurring gesture remains.
Artist Ferdi B Dick studied 3D animation and ran an animation studio in Cape Town for 20 years before turning to sculpture full-time. He is now based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, with public sculptures installed in Taiyuan, Zhanjiang, and Guangzhou, China.
project info:
name: Crystal Roar
 artist: Ferdi B Dick | @ferdibdick

Sale of Kyiv’s Gulliver for $207 million falls through — reason given

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

03:09:32 KST

Sale of Kyiv’s Gulliver for $207 million falls through — reason given
Kyiv • UNN
No buyer submitted an application for the Gulliver auction on Prozorro.Sale. The next steps will be determined by the supervisory boards of Oschadbank and Ukreximbank.
The auction for the sale of the capital’s Gulliver complex on the Prozorro.Sale system did not take place — no potential buyer submitted an application to participate. Oschadbank reported this on September 30, UNN reports.
The further fate of the asset will now be decided by the supervisory boards of Oschadbank and Ukreximbank.
Details
The deadline for submitting applications to participate in the auction expired on September 30 at 8:00 p.m. By that time, no offers from potential buyers had been received, so the scheduled three-round English auction did not take place.
Oschadbank explained that the next steps regarding the sale of Gulliver would be determined by the supervisory boards of Oschadbank and Ukreximbank. They will take into account the market situation, investors’ readiness to purchase the asset, as well as wartime and security risks. The financial institution’s Chairman of the Management Board, Yurii Katsion, noted that the very fact that the shopping and entertainment center had been put up for sale was already an important stage. According to him, there is interest in the property, but potential buyers are still taking a cautious approach to major investments because of the war.
"We see interest in the asset and understand that investors remain cautious because of wartime risks. We will next assess the readiness of the market and potential investors to purchase the asset and determine possible models and timelines for its sale," Katsion said.
He added that it was important for the state-owned bank to conduct the sale as transparently as possible and achieve the best possible financial result. Among other things, the amounts of taxes and dividends that the banks pay to the state will depend on this.
Context
The Gulliver complex is owned by a consortium of two state-owned banks. Oschadbank owns 80% of the asset, while the remaining 20% belongs to Ukreximbank. The banks’ supervisory boards decided to put the complex up for sale at the end of July 2026. Gulliver’s starting price was set at $207 million. Under the terms of the sale, the buyer was required to pay the full amount on the day the sale and purchase agreement was concluded.

Japan wants to stand up to Russia. Can it stand on its own?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:09:26 UTC
03:09:26 KST

Japan wants to stand up to Russia. Can it stand on its own?
A 15-meter-high bronze memorial towers over the Amur River embankment: a Soviet soldier swings his rifle butt, smashing a Japanese border marker bearing the Imperial Chrysanthemum emblem – a symbol held sacred in Japan.
On September 4 – the day following Victory Day over Militaristic Japan and the End of WWII (as observed in Russia) – the Victory in the East memorial was unveiled at the highest point of the Amur River embankment in Khabarovsk. The monument was created at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin, with the participation of the Russian Military Historical Society and the government of Khabarovsk Krai. The stone border post is an exact replica of a border stone erected by Japan on Sakhalin after the Russo-Japanese War.
The following day, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi demanded the removal of the monument. The depiction of the smashed chrysanthemum, she wrote on X, was absolutely unacceptable and was an affront to the national sentiments of the Japanese people. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi called the monument “unacceptable” and deeply regrettable, and said that Tokyo would continue to press for its removal.
Moscow responded that it would not dismantle or alter the monument. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova even stated that one might as well demand that the wind stop blowing or the sun stop shining.
Beijing seized the opportunity to remind its neighbor of past crimes: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning advised Japan to learn from history, make a definitive break with militarism, and earn the trust of its neighbors through concrete actions.
At first glance, the situation appears unprecedented. In the span of a single month, the Russian president made a historic visit to Iturup; both sides summoned ambassadors; Japan, the US, and Australia held military exercises just 20 kilometers from the Russian border; and now, there’s the issue with the monument and the demand to tear it down. Media outlets speak of a “sharp chill” in relations, a new wave of confrontation in the Russian Far East, and even a potential “second front” of the Cold War.
However, Russian experts who spoke to RT view the situation differently.
A series of coincidences
The situation was triggered not by Russia’s actions, but by the Japanese Ministry of Defense.
On August 4, the Cabinet of Japan approved its annual Defense of Japan White Paper – a record-breaking 598 pages featuring an anime-style cover showing a group of smiling young people against the backdrop of a futuristic city. This year’s theme was “Security for the Future.” The content of the whitepaper was quite pragmatic, however. China was identified as Japan’s greatest strategic challenge; on this list, China was followed by Russia and North Korea; for the first time, the buildup of military power was directly linked to economic prosperity (hence the peaceful cover design).
There is a section on Russian military activity in the Far East: the document notes Tu-95 flights, 214 interceptions of Russian aircraft over the course of the year, the expansion of joint naval patrols with China (in August 2025, a submarine participated in these patrols for the first time), as well as a flight by Russian and Chinese bombers to the area near Shikoku Island in December. There is also a chapter on new methods of warfare, such as the use of mass-produced, low-cost drones and AI in decision-making. For the second consecutive year, the document characterizes Russian military actions in the Southern Kuril Islands as “illegal occupation.”
Nine days later, on August 13, Vladimir Putin visited Iturup. Throughout his years in office, the Russian president had never visited the southern islands of the Kuril chain, which are also claimed by Japan.
Japan’s reaction was immediate. Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable,” Motegi repeated Tokyo’s position about the islands being an “inherent part of Japanese territory,” and the Japanese Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolay Nozdrev. Moscow responded firmly, dismissing the statements of Japanese officials as politically irrelevant, offensive, and legally null and void; it reiterated that Iturup, like the rest of the Kurils, is an integral part of Russia, and that Japanese officials have no right to tell Moscow which regions of the country the Russian president may visit.
On August 15, the anniversary of Japan’s surrender in WWII, Takaichi sent a ‘tamagushi’ (ritual offering) to the Yasukuni Shrine. However, she refrained from going there personally, and the ruling party clarified that the donation was made from personal funds and in Takaichi’s capacity as LDP leader, rather than as head of government. The gesture was calculated to satisfy the domestic audience, without triggering a diplomatic row with Beijing and Seoul.
On August 18, Japanese Ambassador to Russia Akira Muto was summoned to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin lodged a strong protest regarding statements made by the Japanese prime minister and foreign minister, asserting that Russia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction over the Southern Kuril Islands are inviolable, and that any attempts to call this reality into question are unacceptable and illegitimate.
On August 31, another incident occurred, this time involving military exercises. From September 8-24, Japan, the US, and Australia conducted Exercises Orient Shield with some operations taking place on Hokkaido Island, near the Russian border. The Japanese side was informed that provocative military activity near Russia’s Far Eastern borders is absolutely unacceptable; Zakharova specifically noted plans to deploy US land-based Typhon missile systems – capable of firing medium-and shorter-range missiles – during the exercises and warned of compensatory countermeasures.
On September 4, the monument was unveiled in Khabarovsk. That same day, the UN General Assembly voted to adopt the Equal Earth Projection. Japan voted in favor. But a few days later, it demanded a correction: on the online version of the new map, the four Southern Kuril Islands were shaded the same color as the rest of Russia, which Japan found unacceptable.
So there we have it – six incidents in 30 days. Each incident compounds the previous one, and together they form a picture of rapidly deteriorating relations.
Below, Russian experts analyze the situation.
‘Relations have not cooled suddenly’
Vasily Shchepkin – a Japanologist with a PhD in History, senior researcher of the Far East Department at the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and an associate professor at the Higher School of Economics in St. Petersburg – suggests reframing the question.
“In my view, relations between Russia and Japan have not cooled suddenly; they have been in this state for over four years, since the start of Russia’s military operation in Ukraine. Japan joined Western sanctions, and everything that has happened over the past four years is largely a consequence of that,” he said.
Therefore, the rift happened not in September 2026, but in March 2022 – when Tokyo backed the collective West’s sanctions regime, and Moscow responded by withdrawing from peace treaty negotiations, cancelling visa-free travel for Japanese citizens to the Kuril Islands, and halting dialogue on joint economic activity there. Everything that followed was the consequence of that single decision.
So, what happened in August? According to Shchepkin, the current chain of events was a direct result of Putin’s visit to Iturup. Tokyo’s reaction was inevitable. However, he draws attention to a neglected detail. “Aside from statements, no concrete measures have followed so far.”
No actions were undertaken by Japan in September. No new sanctions packages were adopted; diplomats were not expelled, and the remaining projects were not cancelled. As for démarches, the summoning of diplomats, and declarations of unacceptable behavior, all this is standard diplomatic procedure.
“Neither Tokyo nor Moscow seeks to aggravate relations further,” Shchepkin says. “In my view, [relations] are unlikely to deteriorate further, because, speaking of bilateral interaction, neither side wants to halt it or escalate tensions.”
Therefore, we may conclude that Russia-Japan relations, in their current form, are a dependent variable.
“The current state of relations is rather a consequence of other events, which are not directly tied to the Russian-Japanese agenda,” the expert says.
An independent bilateral agenda no longer exists; therefore, we may only speak of the global situation and how it relates to Russia’s Far East.
“We are currently in a sort of deadlock which we return to whenever the global situation gets worse – and particularly when relations between Russia and the US deteriorate,” the expert says. “The US has long been the ‘third force’ on which Russia-Japan relations largely depended.”
Who started it?
While it’s true that relations are frozen, there is no consensus among the parties on who is to blame for this. Russian experts, however, have a clear opinion.
Olga Bonch-Osmolovskaya, a Japanologist with a PhD in History, describes the reasons behind Tokyo’s decision. According to her, after 2022, Japan’s policy ceased to be truly independent. But that is only part of the story.
“It is one thing to politically condemn a distant war and state one’s position for the sake of appearances, given the existence of a sort of ‘suzerain’; it is quite another to actively integrate oneself into the corresponding policy,” she says. Japan chose the latter option. And it did so with particular zeal.
“Driven by what one might call the ‘straight-A student complex’ of the Japanese and their tendency to be highly conscientious, sometimes even fanatical in executing tasks, Japan closely aligned itself with this course, joining the full package of sanctions against Moscow and withdrawing from various forms of cooperation,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says.
The former policy – one that allowed Tokyo to balance between allied obligations and its own interests in the north – was curtailed. Along with it, all the achievements of the previous decade came to naught.
“Russia did not initiate the deterioration of relations with Japan,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says. “It responded and continues to respond to Japanese sanctions and to the increased US military presence.”
There is a fine line between words and capabilities, however. Take Exercises Orient Shield, for example. “During the exercises, all sorts of maneuvers are practiced – the landing of troops, the transfer of ammunition, the deployment of HIMARS systems, air defense systems, etc.”
This explains Russia’s strong reaction. “Of course, no one is saying that this is literally preparation for an attack on the Kuril Islands. But Russia is obliged to evaluate not only statements, but military capabilities,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says.
Intentions change along with governments, but military infrastructure remains. And military officials all over the world take this into account.
The result is a vicious circle: Japan builds up its military potential jointly with the US; in response, Russia strengthens its position in the Far East; then, Tokyo presents this strengthening as an additional justification for further militarization. And the circle repeats itself.
This is confirmed by Japan’s military spending. Japan crossed the 2% defense spending threshold ahead of schedule, a year earlier than the mark outlined in the 2022 strategy. For the current fiscal year, defense spending amounted to a record 8.8 trillion yen, and the request for the next year is already a record 8.9 trillion yen (about $56 billion). In June, the parliament renamed the Air Self-Defense Force into the Air and Space Self-Defense Force; this was the first renaming of one of the three branches of the Self-Defense Forces since their creation in 1954. In August, Takaichi announced further changes: the creation of a Space Operations Group, a Space Domain Awareness (SDA) satellite, and the expansion of the Okinawa Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade into a division.
These actions are mainly directed against Beijing. But considering the geography, they are also directed against Moscow.
Energy instead of diplomacy
Despite all this, there is something that balances the dramatic picture. While diplomats are exchanging demarches, gas carriers are departing from Sakhalin and transporting LNG to Japan.
The Sakhalin-2 project survived sanctions, frozen political dialogue, and demands to dismantle the monument. In June, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control once again extended the special license until December 18, 2026. Such an exception has been issued annually since 2022, and each time it was preceded by negotiations between Tokyo and Washington. Russian LNG, according to the Japanese Ministry of Economy, provided about 9% of Japanese liquefied gas imports in 2025; According to Bonch-Osmolovskaya, the inverse relationship is even stronger – Japan accounted for about 58% of the project’s exports.
Vladimir Nelidov – PhD in History, associate professor of the Department of Oriental Studies at MGIMO, Senior Researcher at the Center for Japanese Studies at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and RIAC expert – considers this to be the main reason why the threats didn’t go beyond words.
“Severing diplomatic relations would be disproportionate,” he says. “The possibilities for introducing additional economic sanctions are also limited: Japan does not have much leverage. For example, it remains involved in Sakhalin oil and gas projects and, I believe, is not ready to sacrifice them.”
Notably, the US administration insisted on Japan’s withdrawal from the Sakhalin projects. However, Tokyo remained. “As far as we can judge, Takaichi either convinced the US or insisted [on doing things her way] and so, despite the position of its senior ally, Japan remained in the projects.”
The second possible lever is humanitarian. Tokyo tries to preserve it, too. “The Japanese side has invested a lot of effort in humanitarian cooperation with Russia. Before the current escalation, the Japanese even proudly said that, despite the lack of political dialogue, cultural festivals and other events continue between the countries.” And Nelidov adds, “in the long term, Japan has perhaps more need for such contacts than Russia.”
Shchepkin supports this idea, adding that even in the past four years, and thanks to the efforts of the pro-Russia lobby within the Japanese Foreign Ministry, cooperation has been preserved in areas like culture, education, and tourism. The current flow of Russian tourists to Japan, the expert adds, is largely a legacy of the Shinzo Abe administration, when the parties agreed to put the territorial issue aside and focus on the economy, culture, and visas.
The general picture is quite clear. Bonch-Osmolovskaya calls it “cold peace” and warns that a complete rupture of relations would not benefit either country: while Japan could technically replace Sakhalin gas, doing so would require time, money, and even greater dependence on US suppliers, whereas Russia would lose revenue from the project. “A definitive break, should it occur, would come at too high a price for both sides,” she says.
Therefore, the limit to how far relations can deteriorate is not determined by diplomacy. It is dictated by the energy balance, and this applies to both parties.
Why Takaichi could not remain silent
A pressing question remains: why did the Japanese Prime Minister issue all these loud statements if no concrete measures were to follow?
Nelidov suggests viewing the situation through the eyes of the Japanese leadership to better understand their logic. Sanae Takaichi rose to power as a nationalist politician and, among other things, a defender of national honor. Her policy is grounded in this.
“Had she failed to react to the Russian president’s visit to the territory claimed by Japan, to the installation of the monument – which [Russia] views as fine, necessary, and valuable, but which the Japanese see as a desecration of a state symbol – or to the military exercises, she would have been torn apart, figuratively speaking, by her own party,” the expert says.
For example, when the US administration imposed sanctions against the International Criminal Court – including its presiding judge, Japanese national Tomoko Akane – Takaichi faced criticism for not standing up for her compatriot firmly enough. “If public opinion and fellow party members demand decisive action from her even in dealings with the US, then what would they say about Russia?”
A scenario in which Tokyo would have remained silent to avoid damaging relations with Moscow is virtually impossible.
Valery Kistanov, head of the Center for Japanese Studies at the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences, drew attention to the details of the protest against the monument in Khabarovsk. Takaichi posted her comment on social media but did not issue an official statement, and major Japanese media outlets (except for right-wing conservative publications) barely covered the story. It didn’t cause a nationwide outcry.
In other words, the statement was addressed not to Moscow, but to fellow party members and the segment of the Japanese electorate for whom the events of 1945 remain an enduring historical wound. The offering made at Yasukuni on August 15 followed the same logic: made from personal funds and without Takaichi herself present, it was intended as a signal to the domestic audience, but was carefully calibrated to avoid provoking a new crisis in relations with Beijing.
The fact that the series of incidents was not followed by any practical actions holds the key to understanding the events of September. This means that a large part of what happened did not concern bilateral relations but was intended for domestic audiences.
However, this does not render the situation entirely harmless. Symbolic commitments tend to become entrenched: a prime minister who has demanded the dismantling of a monument cannot refute their own statement, and a successor would have to start from the same position.
Who benefits?
Experts agree on who benefits from the conflict, though they differ on the implications. “It is clear that the US is the primary beneficiary,” says Bonch-Osmolovskaya. “The worse relations between Moscow and Tokyo become, the stronger Japan’s existing dependence on the US grows in all aspects: weaponry, intelligence, supplies, and security guarantees.” Washington gains a disciplined ally, additional bases for the deployment of forces, and another tool for exerting pressure on the Russian Far East.
However, she adds, “It is important not to reduce the situation to a scenario where the US is some sort of ‘dark empire’ and Japan is merely its puppet.”
In Japan, there are certain beneficiaries of this confrontation as well. Among the proponents of revising post-war restrictions is the defense establishment, which Bonch-Osmolovskaya characterizes as revanchist and nationalistic, and arms manufacturers, for whom expanded exports open up markets that had been closed for nearly 80 years. The image of an external threat serves as a mechanism for legitimization: the longer the list of threats, the easier it is for the parliament to increase military spending and lift export restrictions.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya gives a rather harsh assessment and makes a historical analogy. She believes that the current propaganda is reminiscent of the decades preceding WWII, when Japan designated China as its primary adversary and demonized it; today, a similar process is unfolding regarding Russia. At the root of this, she sees the unresolved trauma of 1945: while the cult of the emperor was formally dismantled and the atrocities of the military machine were acknowledged, the defeat was never truly accepted, and strategic sovereignty was lost.
Nelidov takes a more measured approach, offering a different view that does not suggest malicious intent. The problem, he believes, is the so-called ‘security dilemma’ – a long-standing concept in international relations theory. A state strengthens its defenses; its neighbors, unaware of its true intentions, interpret this as preparation for aggression and arm themselves in response; the first state observes these preparations and continues its military buildup. “The paradox of the security dilemma is that in seeking to protect itself, the state ultimately finds itself in an even more dangerous situation,” he explains.
Another factor also comes into play. “Most Japanese diplomats, politicians, and even military officials have no desire to develop an independent view of the global situation,” Nelidov says, describing Japanese political circles as highly compliant pupils of the West; the few who acknowledge that the situation in Ukraine might be more complex than the prevailing narrative risk becoming outcasts. These sentiments did not emerge in 2022; they were shaped throughout the post-war period by the media and the education system, initially as anti-Soviet views. In Japanese opinion polls, Russia consistently ranks low in terms of public favorability, alongside China and North Korea.
Freezing point
If the current situation resembles ‘freezing point’, it is logical to ask what might drive the relations between Japan and Russia below freezing.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya mentions a specific threshold. “The next stage of deterioration could be the deployment of US long-range systems in Japan,” she says. Russia’s reaction would be predictable: a further military buildup on the Kuril Islands and in Sakhalin. A further contraction of economic ties is also likely; she believes that the fishing industry would suffer first, followed by what remains of trade.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya does not predict a direct military conflict. According to her, if it were to occur at all, it would happen only as part of a larger clash between Russia and the US or a major crisis surrounding Taiwan that dragged in all the neighboring states. In other words, a Russo-Japanese war is impossible as a standalone event – it could only be an episode within someone else’s war.
Nelidov views the situation somewhat differently. He points out that Japan’s defense policy identifies China and North Korea as the primary threats, with Russia ranking third on the list. But even when it comes to China and North Korea, it’s not about direct confrontation but rather an arms race. While this is certainly a negative phenomenon, it is fundamentally different from a direct conflict.
The comparison the expert draws with Europe is interesting. He considers the rhetoric of Berlin, London, Helsinki, and Stockholm far more threatening than that of Tokyo, which demonstrates “virtually no real readiness for aggressive action against Russia.” He is convinced there are certain limits the Japanese side will not cross.
He attributes East Asia’s greater reluctance to engage in direct conflict to accumulated experience: territorial disputes and mutual historical grievances are common in the region, and the elites have learned to manage such crises. For example, following Takaichi’s November statement regarding potential intervention in Taiwan, Tokyo’s relations with Beijing plummeted to their lowest point in a decade, and China imposed economic restrictions; yet within a few months, the situation had stabilized.
“In East Asia, I don’t see the kind of crazy Russophobia and readiness to direct all resources into the conflict that we’re witnessing in Europe,” says Nelidov. “Japan doesn’t intend to go to war with Russia; and neither does Russia want war with Japan. Both sides realize it is not in their interests. There are no strategically vital or fundamental contradictions between them.”
Is there a way to achieve a thaw in relations? All three experts agree that there is no simple solution. Normalizing bilateral ties is impossible until relations between Russia and the West are normalized; the Japanese leadership lacks both the will and the capacity to adopt an independent stance. However, Shchepkin believes that once the conflict in Ukraine ends, Tokyo will be among the first to act: as soon as the sanctions regime is lifted or minimized, Japan will be ready to soften its position and resume dialogue.
However, the opinions of experts diverge when it comes to assessing the current pause in relations. For Nelidov, it is merely another fluctuation in a long history of regional squabbles. For Bonch-Osmolovskaya, it represents a deeper rift: Russia is asserting itself as an independent civilization, while Japan, in response, is becoming increasingly integrated into the US system of control over Eurasia. She advocates neither for reconciliation at any cost nor for territorial concessions, but rather for maintaining energy, economic, and cultural ties as a bridge – “not so much with the Japan of today, but with the Japan that might one day become more independent.”
As Bonch-Osmolovskaya concludes, “Japan cannot simultaneously be an independent civilization and America’s forward military outpost. It will have to make a choice.”

TAP: final bids from Air France-KLM and Lufthansa have been submitted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:08:59 UTC
03:08:59 KST

Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submitted their final bids on Wednesday to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP, closing the bidding phase and leaving the decision to the government.
Air France-KLM and Lufthansa have already submitted their final bids for the privatisation of 44.9% of TAP’s share capital, which are expected to include improvements on the offers submitted on 29 July.
The announcement was made on Wednesday by Parpública. In a statement, the state shareholding manager said it will now draw up a descriptive report on the improvements put forward by the two candidates, "assessing their final overall merit and forwarding it to the members of the Government responsible for the finance and air transport portfolios".
Wednesday was the deadline set by the Government for the airlines competing for TAP. On Monday, the Minister for Infrastructure and Housing, Miguel Pinto Luz, had said that the final bids from the two contenders would be submitted by Wednesday and that the Government would then have 15 days to take a position on the process.
The final bids set out the financial and strategic terms for taking a stake in the Portuguese airline. They will be assessed on the planned investment, fleet development, commitments in areas such as maintenance and sustainable fuels, and respect for labour obligations.
In its statement, Air France-KLM says it "reiterated today its strong and continued interest in TAP Air Portugal by submitting its final proposal for a shareholding of up to 49.9% in the airline".
Quoted in the document, Benjamin Smith, the group’s CEO, states that "interest in TAP is stronger than ever". "Over the past four weeks, our team and our advisers have worked diligently to strengthen our bid, and I am convinced that this revised proposal is the best way forward for TAP, for its management, its employees and its customers, as well as for Portugal," he argues.
According to the Air France-KLM chief executive, the proposal presented "is an ambitious long-term strategic plan" which, in his view, will "better position TAP for the future and safeguard Portugal’s connectivity and sovereignty".
"My personal conviction and our guiding principle remain unchanged: if Air France-KLM is chosen, TAP and Portugal will be the winners in the global aviation market," he maintains, adding that the group’s offer "has been built around a stronger Portuguese flag carrier, with Lisbon as the Air France-KLM Group’s exclusive hub in Southern Europe, offering greater connectivity and a clear intention to create jobs and value across the country".
Lufthansa, in a written statement, stressed that its proposal reflects "the conviction" that, based on its "proven track record of successfully developing network airlines, the Lufthansa Group is the best partner to support TAP’s future growth, strengthen its competitiveness and continue to develop its role as Portugal’s flag carrier".
The process has from the outset envisaged an optional negotiating phase to improve the bids before the investor is chosen. The final decision will also involve a series of formal steps, including approval by the Council of Ministers and securing the green light from the European competition authorities.
The sale of TAP also includes 5% of the shares reserved for employees, with any unsubscribed stake also available to be acquired by the selected investor.

NATO chief confirms receipt of Russian warning over potential Kaliningrad blockade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:08:18 UTC
03:08:18 KST

BRUSSELS, September 30. /TASS/. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte confirmed that the alliance had received a warning from Russia that it would use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if NATO attempted to impose an air or naval blockade on the Kaliningrad Region.
"I’m not at liberty to disclose what they sent us, but this is what they reported, more or less," Rutte said at the Euronews Defense and Space Summit 2026 in Brussels.
At the same time, he urged the Baltic states to stop worrying and NATO members to continue supporting Ukraine and investing in weapons. The NATO chief reiterated that "NATO is a defensive alliance."
Rutte also noted that he doesn’t believe in a threat from Russia.
Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that Russia’s policy documents provide for a nuclear response to any attempts to blockade the Kaliningrad Region and that this is what Russian diplomats are reminding hotheads in Europe about.
Earlier, the Russian Embassy in Brussels said it had sent a diplomatic warning to the Belgian government and NATO headquarters that Brussels’ "reckless and irresponsible" course "sharply increases the risks of a direct armed conflict" with Russia. The embassy also warned that Russia "is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad Region."

China slaps 55% tariff on Brazilian beef, rebuffs bid to borrow Uruguay’s quota
Surtax on its largest market alarms the industry, which is already locked out of the EU and facing higher US duties
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Igor Patrickin Rio de Janeiro
China will charge an extra 55 per cent tariff on Brazilian beef from Thursday after Brazil filled its import quota for the year and has not agreed to let Brazilian exporters use the unfilled quota of neighbouring Uruguay, industry sources said.
The Chinese Ministry of Commerce announced the surtax on Wednesday, a day after China’s customs administration confirmed that Brazil had used all of its 1.106 million-tonne allowance for 2026, and under the rules the extra tariff applies from the third day after a country reaches its limit.
Beef above the quota will now pay 67 per cent, including the regular 12 per cent import duty, a level exporters consider too high to keep selling.
With the quota exhausted, Brazil is effectively shut out of its biggest beef market for the rest of the year.
