Germany debates alleged antisemitism in the Left Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:54:00 UTC
01:54:00 KST

Do Jewish representatives see the Left Party as antisemitic?
September 30, 2026
The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election on September 20. This means there's a good chance that the party's top candidate, Elif Eralp, could become Berlin's next mayor — making her the first member of the Left Party to hold that office.
Preliminary talks with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the environmentalist Green Party are scheduled to take place on October 1. If the talks are successful, it would represent a major step toward forming a coalition government.
Securing a clear commitment from the Left Party against antisemitism within its own ranks is seen as a prerequisite for successful cooperation. Yet doubts still persist about whether the party and its representatives can adequately protect Jewish life in the city.
During the election campaign, a performance at a Left Party event by the rapper Dahabflex made headlines and sparked outrage when he used slogans seen as antisemitic during his performance. And later, at an event held by the Left Party to celebrate its election victory, an appearance was made by Ibrahim Ibrahim — a supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is on the EU's list of terrorist organizations. The leaders of the Left Party have repeatedly distanced themselves from both incidents, both at the federal and state levels.
The Central Council of Jews in Germany is warning
However, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, thinks these statements are mere lip service.
"In the fight against antisemitism, which is tolerated and allowed to run rampant within the party's ranks, the Left Party no longer has any credibility," reads a press statement released two days after the election. Schuster explicitly appealed to the SPD and the Greens not to form a coalition with the election winner.
High-ranking members of the federal government have also spoken out. Wolfram Weimer, government commissioner for culture and media who has no party affiliation, accused the Left Party of "openly flaunting antisemitism" and called into question the €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in funding for the capital's cultural sector for the coming decade — a deal that had already been agreed upon with the Berlin state government. Weimer claimed that many figures in the cultural sector are alarmed by the prospect of a government led by the Left Party.
'Antisemitism and expropriations threaten the economy'
Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also voiced concern. A video titled "Antisemitism and Expropriations Threaten the Economy" is available on her ministry's Instagram account, in reference also to the Left Party's plans to nationalize large private housing companies.
Reiche describes the Left as a party "that openly embraces antisemitism, that instills fear in the Jews of this city, that opposes Jewish life and that cheerfully welcomes organized crime at election parties."
The Left Party is now seeking an injunction to compel the Minister of Economic Affairs to delete the video.
"Reiche is using taxpayer money to spread propaganda against the Left Party on the Economy Ministry's official channel," said Left Party Federal Co-Chair Ines Schwerdtner.
150 prominent Jews come to the defense of the Left Party
In an open letter, a group of 150 prominent Jews from various social backgrounds has voiced support for the Left Party. Among those who signed it are the author Eva Menasse and the former director of the Einstein Forum in Potsdam, Susan Neiman. They advocate for a "social and safe city" and emphasize the importance of voting for different parties.
They explain their motivation as follows: "We are writing this letter because, over the past few weeks, we have heard the same claim time and again: that the Left is dangerous for Jews, and that a coalition involving the party poses a danger to our safety. We reject this claim not because we downplay concerns about our safety, but because we actually take them seriously."
Without naming the party directly, the signatories of the letter wrote that they believe that the greatest enemy of Jewish life is the Alternative for Germany (AfD): "At a time when an in-parts openly fascistic political party is marching towards power across Germany, it is an abdication of responsibility on the part of mainstream media and elements of our own community to continue to pretend that the Left presents the largest threat to Jewish safety."
In light of this, the letter states: "The constant accusations of antisemitism against the Left are not only cynical political weaponization, but they also conflate nearly any criticism of Israel with antisemitism."
The Left Party is the only party in the German parliament that opposes arms deliveries to Israel due to the military operation in the Gaza Strip following the terrorist attack by the radical Islamist group Hamas on October 7, 2023. Based on a resolution passed at its party convention, the Left Party classifies the ensuing war as a genocide.
Elif Eralp wants to build bridges
Human rights organizations and a United Nations (UN) commission have also classified Israel's actions in Gaza against the Palestinian people as a genocide. The Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has invoked Israel's right to self-defense.
The intensifying debate over antisemitism within the Left Party is complicating the formation of a government in Berlin. At a party congress convened on short notice, Elif Eralp, the potential future mayor of Berlin, emphasized that her party has a duty to bring people together and build bridges.
"And in doing so," Eralp said, "it must be absolutely clear that there must never be any calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people must never be made from our platforms."
With these remarks, Eralp once again criticized the antisemitic rapper's performance during the Berlin election campaign. Jewish people must be able to feel safe in Berlin, said Eralp.
"I will strengthen Berlin's diverse Jewish community and combat antisemitism. And Palestinian and Muslim people must also feel seen and safe," Eralp said.
Outside the building where the special party convention was held, about 20 Jewish people expressed their solidarity with the party. A poster in Hebrew and German lay at their feet, reading, "Mazel Tov to the Left," congratulating the party on its September 20 election victory in Berlin.
One of the demonstrators was Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York.
"Antisemitism is real — we know that," Grabell told DW. "But three years of genocide are also real, as are illegal occupation, forced destruction and displacement in the West Bank — that, too, is real."
Grabell emphasized that they were there to support the Left Party in its efforts to advance progressive policies. "We also want to show the diversity of Jewish life in German society. Everyone talks about the different sides — we are also part of Jewish life."
This article was originally written in German.

Iran seeks peace while defending its rights, security and interests: MoD spox

Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik made the remarks on Wednesday at a ceremony in Tehran marking the beginning of the new academic year, where he also highlighted the role of national unity, faith and reliance on domestic capabilities in strengthening Iran’s resilience in the face of external pressure.
“Today, more than a thousand types of domestically produced products and services are being manufactured in the country, some of which have export potential,” he said, attributing these achievements to investment in human capital, knowledge, experience and national determination.

Peace and national security

“If the opposing side accepts Iran’s legitimate rights and conditions, the path to ending the conflict is open,” he said, adding that the Iranian nation would not allow its rights and interests to be disregarded.
His comments came as Iran continues to emphasize diplomacy and engagement alongside the protection of its national interests, with Tehran repeatedly stressing that sustainable regional stability requires respect for national sovereignty, security and legitimate rights.
Talaei-Nik said the strength Iran has developed today is rooted in faith, national unity, popular participation, and reliance on indigenous knowledge and capabilities.
He pointed to the role of the Iranian people, religious faith, and national leadership during the Sacred Defense (Iran-Iraq War) and other critical periods in the country’s modern history, describing popular participation and reliance on domestic capabilities as among the factors that enabled Iran to withstand major challenges.
The spokesman said the development of indigenous capacities has become an important component of Iran’s national resilience, particularly amid continued external pressure and sanctions.
He stressed that the ultimate objective remains the advancement of the country and the creation of a strong, independent, and developed Iran.

Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:53:27 UTC
01:53:27 KST

In the aftermath of Andy Burnham’s speech to the Labour conference, media discussions are focusing on how to define social care and estimate its cost (How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?, 29 September).
Most arguments assume that any new system will look like the existing one, with services outsourced to large companies, using contracts without scope for innovation, with rigidly defined targets, often delivered using poorly rewarded, precariously employed migrant workers.
The reality is that many of the services needed by elderly and incapacitated people – such as cleaning, meal preparation, transport to medical appointments, household repairs and personal services such as podiatry, hair care, physiotherapy, counselling or therapeutic massage – are also required by others and are already freely available in local markets.
The trouble is that they are most often supplied by online platforms such as Uber, Deliveroo or Housekeep with no commercial incentive to address social need.
One solution would be to set up local platforms that supply these services to anyone, regardless of age or disability. If these platforms made sure that all staff were suitably trained, qualified and security-checked, and their vehicles suitably adapted, they could be attractive to all local residents, whose commercial use of them would help subsidise their costs. Social care recipients could be provided with access to them using a voucher system that would be much cheaper than setting up such services from scratch or bundling them in with huge outsourcing contracts.
With suitable public oversight, using platform technology for public good would also bring other benefits to the local economy. Services would be better for all. Workers could upgrade their skills and gain job security. And, instead of being siphoned off to tax havens, any profits could remain, as Burnham might put it, “in every postcode”.
Ursula Huws
London
Andy Burnham’s commitment to a national care service brings welcome clarity to a debate that has too often avoided difficult choices. But before deciding how to pay for care, we must answer a prior question: what should people be able to count on?
Reports that the proposed service may follow Scotland’s model of free personal care raise an important distinction. Removing charges for help with washing, dressing and eating could make a substantial difference. But social care is about much more than these tasks. When we in the coalition government developed the Care Act, we placed wellbeing at its heart. Its purpose extends to dignity, independence, relationships, participation and people’s control over their own lives.
There is a risk that defining a national care service primarily through free personal care narrows our understanding of what social care is for. The two need not be in conflict. Free personal care could form part of a wider national guarantee, grounded in the Care Act’s wellbeing principle and applying to people across adulthood.
The Casey commission has an important opportunity to help establish that wider promise. The question is whether the new service will simply change what people pay, or also strengthen the care and support that they can rely on to live their lives.
Paul Burstow
Former minister of state for care services, 2010-12
Andy Burnham’s decision that proposals for social care reform will not happen until after the next election is the latest instalment in almost two-decade saga of delays.
Since a Labour government first committed to social care reform in 2007, we have seen a succession of unfulfilled promises: the discarded Personal Care at Home Act 2010, David Cameron’s part-implemented Care Act 2014, Theresa May’s failed 2017 proposals, and Boris Johnson’s 2019 pledge on the steps of Downing Street to fix social care – delayed under Rishi Sunak, then scrapped by Rachel Reeves in 2024.
In the years since this saga of broken promises began, both of my parents were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. One of them survives, and our family continues to wait for any meaningful help.
Families living through the reality of the social care crisis do not have the luxury of waiting for another election cycle. Mr Burnham needs to get a move on.
Dr Ruth Charles
Swavesey, Cambridgeshire
 As a 69-year-old in receipt of 20 years’ teacher’s pension and a full state pension, I say by all means take money from pensioners. Scrap national insurance (a retrogressive tax) and increase income tax. Scrap all age-related tax benefits/exemptions. But please don’t hit the triple lock until the state pension reaches parity with most European states (Will pensioners be poorer as a result of Burnham scrapping the triple lock?, 29 September). It is mainly women who rely solely on this inadequate pension, and many of them live alone in rented accommodation. They are the last people who should be asked to make sacrifices.
Sarah James
Monmouth
 As an 86-year-old, I’m sure I am not alone in having anxiety about paying for a care home if the need arises, and am delighted that Andy Burnham is determined to sort out the system at last. While the triple-lock pension increases are very welcome, I’d happily accept their change into simply keeping up with prices as a trade-off for never having to worry about paying for social care.
Michael Miller
Sheffield

From nuclear to hybrid: The key moments from the Euronews Defence Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:53:21 UTC
01:53:21 KST

Euronews hosted on Wednesday its first Defence and Space Summit. Here are the key moments from the day-long gathering, bringing together the NATO Secretary General, ministers, senior officials and industry leaders.
Is Europe ready to defend itself?
That was the central question at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit, which brought together policymakers, lawmakers and industry leaders as Europe grapples with the need to rearm and deter potential threats.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has transformed Europe's security landscape, exposing longstanding weaknesses and forcing governments to rethink defence spending, military capabilities and industrial capacity.
As Russia continues its war in Ukraine and hybrid attacks against European allies increase, the pressure to act is growing.
Here are five key moments from Wednesday's summit.
Radev raises the alarm
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev was among the day's most anticipated speakers. On Wednesday, he challenged the EU's strategy of supporting Ukraine, describing it as a failed attempt at "peace by force".
"The war in Ukraine challenged our critical thinking and realistic approach," he said.
"It challenged our ability to assess the strategic centre of gravity of the opponent. It challenged most of all our ability to design feasible political objectives and to translate them into a sound military strategy and to define a desired end state."
Radev called for greater diplomatic engagement with the Kremlin to end the war and avert what he described as the "worst-case scenario" of a nuclear attack against Europe.
Russia controls the world's largest nuclear arsenal, with an estimated 4,400 stockpiled warheads, including 1,796 strategically deployed.
"There is a nuclear card," Radev said.
"We need to have this into account. We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation."
His remarks came hours after Reuters reported that Russia had sent a document threatening to "use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" to defend its territory.
Rutte reassures allies
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte followed Radev with a very different message for Moscow: "Stop the nuclear threats."
Rutte declined to comment on the reported document but offered a glimpse of NATO's response to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Putin knows he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this seriously," he said. "Of course, we had to reply and make clear to him that NATO is a defensive alliance."
"I think the best way to deal with this is to have a bit of calm," he added.
Rutte also addressed the rise in hybrid attacks targeting Ukraine's allies, including an arson attack at a robotics defence company in Estonia and an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in Germany.
He described the incidents as attempts by Putin to divert attention from the stalled battlefield, fracture Western unity and weaken military support for Kyiv.
Seeking to reassure allies, Rutte said: "There is no immediate threat to NATO territory."
"We will defend every inch of NATO territory, every square kilometre, square mile," he said. "There's no doubt Putin knows this. So that threat is not there. And if anything happens, we are ready to counter it."
Rutte praised Ukraine's gains on the battlefield and its deep strikes inside Russia, but highlighted a critical weakness: air defence.
Russia has used sustained aerial attacks to pummel Ukrainian cities, putting pressure on Kyiv's stocks of air defence interceptors.
"It is crucial now to keep Ukraine strong," Rutte said, urging allies to provide Patriot interceptors. "But Ukraine is not doing worse (now) than some time ago."
Francken warns of 'dark winter'
Despite the reassurances, concern over Europe's security is growing.
Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken warned that Europe was facing a "dark winter" of increasing interference.
"Russia, air attack, air attack, air attack. This is the biggest threat. So we need air defence, air defence, air defence," Francken told the summit.
"We need to have more stocks, more production, scale up production, and a large industrial base. Everything has to go faster."
Francken said Russia had decades of experience in hybrid warfare and argued that Europe should draw on Ukraine's battlefield expertise to keep pace with rapidly changing technology.
"I don't want to have 200,000 drones somewhere in a stock, and in two months you cannot even use them because they're outdated. So we have to adapt," he said.
Francken also acknowledged Belgium's long-standing underinvestment in defence.
"We were like the worst pupil of the NATO class. We had 1% of GDP in defence spending," he said, adding that spending had since doubled.
"But I cannot do in 18 months what has been neglected for 40 years."
Puzder aims at 'Made in Europe'
European security remains closely tied to the United States, NATO's largest military power.
Relations between Washington and European capitals have faced repeated tensions since Donald Trump returned to the White House and pursued an "America First" agenda.
Matthew Whitaker, the US ambassador to NATO, sought to reassure European allies that Washington remained committed to their security.
"We're not stepping back. We're just asking our allies to step forward and join us," he said. "We have continued to say that we're going to stay engaged in Europe."
Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, struck a more confrontational tone, criticising the bloc's push to prioritise "Made in Europe" products in public procurement, including defence.
The policy, which originated in France, has gained support in other EU capitals, although its precise scope remains contested.
"When lives are on the line, capability and availability should determine the solution, not geography," Puzder said.
"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we'll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics."
Puzder instead promoted a "Made in NATO" approach, which would give US defence companies greater access to EU procurement.
"We're stronger when we work together," he said, calling for an alliance that confronts its adversaries with "unity and strength rather than division and self-interest".

A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:53:18 UTC
01:53:18 KST

Reading that Andy Burnham wants to push electoral reform forward and move the UK towards proportional representation (Report, 29 September), I found myself shouting at the screen.
I come from Italy, where I have seen proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents. They reward tribalism (yes, even more than here). They leave large parts of the electorate hostage to the whims of tiny parties, and force parties into ragtag coalitions that produce unstable, ineffective governments. And for all that, people do not seem to feel any better represented.
Having lived in the UK since 2014 and watched its parties with an outsider’s eyes, I still see first past the post as the lesser of two evils.
Brexit exposed a complete lack of leadership in David Cameron’s Conservative party, and it was an act of unprecedented self-harm that we are all still paying for, quite literally. But it also showed that parties outside the big two can exert enough pressure to force the party in power to adapt and, alas, to listen to voters.
Labour, meanwhile, has reinvented itself remarkably: from Ed Miliband’s soft left to Jeremy Corbyn’s more radical programme, and back again when that proved ineffective. Would a major party put itself through so much self-scrutiny without the incentives of first past the post? Or would it have split into several streams, perhaps more representative but far less effective, squandering its history as so many parties of the Italian left have done?
As a settled-status resident who expects to become a citizen this year, and is hoping to vote for Labour at the next general election, I can only say: please don’t do this.
Gian Lorenzo Spisso
Bristol

Unfair method of splitting pensions can add to the pain of divorce | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:53:09 UTC
01:53:09 KST

Your article on the impact of the escalating cost of living on divorce settlements (Unhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyers, 23 September) provides a timely reminder of the financial inequities facing many separating couples.
As a pensions expert, I have regularly encountered a particular imbalance in the splitting of pension assets on divorce. Although the last Labour government enabled pension savings to be taken into account in divorce settlements, there remains, 25 years on, an inherent unfairness in the way many such arrangements are implemented.
Where one partner (usually the husband) has built up valuable pension entitlements through a defined benefit pension, the allocation of those assets on divorce is often based on an equivalent cash value at the point of divorce, known as “external sharing”.
In thousands of such cases, especially those involving private sector pensions, this leads to the undervaluing of pension assets transferred – usually to the wife and, in some cases, by many thousands of pounds.
Divorce is a traumatic enough experience. This fundamental flaw in the legal process compounds unfairness and is both unnecessary and easily rectified. The government should address this urgently to avoid sleepwalking into another pensions scandal. 
Richard Nobbs
Excalibur Actuaries

Russia agrees to share data on ‘extremists’ and ‘terrorists’ with five former Soviet states. Its own terrorism and extremism registry now tops 23,000 names.
The prosecutors general of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan have signed an agreement to cooperate in combating terrorism and extremism, RBC reported.
Under the agreement, the countries will promptly exchange information about terrorist and extremist organizations and individuals whom authorities consider security threats. They will also share information about attempts to infringe on countries’ sovereignty or possible terrorist attacks. The agreement separately mentions foreign fighters returning “to their countries of origin” and their family members.
In Russia, authorities also use extremism and terrorism laws in politically motivated cases. The terrorism and extremism register maintained by Russia’s financial monitoring agency, Rosfinmonitoring, already lists more than 23,000 people. Journalist Yuri Dud was one of the latest additions. Others on the list include Pavel Durov, Vera Polozkova, Leonid Gozman, Tatyana Lazareva, Boris Akunin, and Alexander Nevzorov.
According to the Pervy Otdel project and the think tank Parubets Analytics, 1,145 people were convicted of terrorism in the first half of 2026, compared with 725 such convictions a year earlier.

The Israeli settler movement preparing to return to Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:50:50 UTC
01:50:50 KST

Breadcrumb
The Israeli settler movement preparing to return to Gaza
Northern Gaza border - Tamar Ben Simon, an Israeli from Haifa, brought her three young children to Israel’s border with Gaza on Sunday.
Looking across the fence at the annihilated landscape of Gaza City, near the former Israeli settlement of Nissanit, she sees a future home.
Ben Simon was among thousands attending a demonstration organised by Nachala, a hardline settler movement campaigning to re-establish Israeli settlements in Gaza.
Sunday’s rally called specifically for Israelis to return to Nissanit, which was evacuated during Israel’s 2005 disengagement from the territory.
“I want to live there with my children,” Ben Simon told The New Arab, arguing that doing so would help “protect the security of Israel”.
Ben Simon said she had no problem living alongside Palestinian citizens of Israel. “I live with Arabs. I live in Haifa,” she said, pointing to her friends and former colleagues at a hospital in the city.
But when asked about the Palestinians living in Gaza, she spelt out a different vision: “First of all, in Gaza, there is no future for Arabs. It’s a pity, but they did this to themselves,” she said.
Since 7 October 2023, Nachala has been at the forefront of efforts to re-establish Israeli settlements in Gaza. The movement has close ties to Israel’s far-right, with ministers and coalition lawmakers repeatedly attending and supporting its events.
Among those attending on Sunday was Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. “I hope that even before the elections we will reach Nissanit,” he said, addressing the crowd.
If not, Ben-Gvir, leader of the far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party, said he hoped to serve as defence minister in the next government and “return us to Nissanit, and to the entire northern perimeter, and to all of Gaza”.
The upcoming Israeli election on 27 October was a central theme in speeches, campaign material, and interviews with attendees conducted by The New Arab.
A new front in Israel's far-right politics
The rally also highlighted a political battle on Israel’s right, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud is competing with smaller far-right parties, including Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, for settler votes.
“As we get closer to the election, the far-right religious parties are trying to position themselves as [distinct] from the others, and to draw votes from Likud,” Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, an Israeli organisation that monitors settlement policy in the occupied West Bank, told The New Arab.
Etkes said the push to resettle Gaza allows these parties to present themselves as a force capable of pressuring Netanyahu to resist Washington’s opposition to Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territory.
The US administration’s stated policy for Gaza, as outlined in Trump’s plan, says that Israel will not occupy or annex the territory and calls for the eventual withdrawal of Israeli forces as an international security force takes control
On 5 February 2025, Trump was asked about the prospect of Israeli resettlement in Gaza during an Oval Office meeting with Netanyahu and said, “I don’t see it happening.”
But according to Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, a political commentator and former Israeli diplomat, the resettlement of Gaza is not a question of “if, but when,” and that getting in the way of the settler movement’s ambitions would be politically costly for Netanyahu and others.
“Members of Knesset like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Limor Son Har-Melech were at the demonstration as well as influential rabbis. They will relentlessly campaign for this until they get what they want,” he told The New Arab.
For some of those campaigning to return to Nissanit, the site has a personal significance. Hundreds of Israelis lived in the settlement before it was evacuated in 2005, and some former residents now hope to return.
One attendee, Nissim Avinoam, said he helped establish Nissanit. “I was expelled in 2005, and I came today from Kibbutz Neve Yam. I wanted to see where I was expelled from. It’s my home. I still miss it there, 21 years later,” he said.
But for others, Nissanit is just another conquest on the path to creating greater Israel. “My name is Tehiya Chaim, mother of 11 children, may they multiply, from the settlement of Evyatar in Judea and Samaria,” another woman said.
“Our goal is to raise the flag of Jewish settlement, and to stand and strengthen our Prime Minister, without giving up, until we see Jewish settlement in the Gaza region,” she told The New Arab.
Attendees expressed indifference to the devastated nature of Gaza. They plan on moving there anyway.
“It really doesn’t scare us. We are prepared to build settlements and build cities very quickly. We have logistics teams, we have capability, we have the desire and joy, and the government behind us,” Chaim said.
Waiting for the green light
That preparation has also taken on a grassroots form. According to Ben-Ephraim, prospective settlers have organised into garinim, or settlement nuclei, designed to move into Gaza as soon as they receive a green light from the government.
By April 2025, he said, around 800 families had signed up, with some 30 already living together at temporary sites near Gaza.
A teenage girl who introduced herself as Tamar, from Elad, east of Tel Aviv, said that Israelis needed to “conquer this land. We don’t want Arabs to take it for themselves”.
One of her friends then interjected: “It’s already ours, we are returning it to ourselves,” prompting laughter from the group of girls.
As the sun began to set over the Gaza border, electronic dance music continued to play as a group of young Israeli children lined up at an ice cream truck. Not long afterwards, the distant rumble of successive explosions cut through the music.
On this side of the fence, however, the war formed the backdrop to something resembling a festival.
Fin de Pencier is a Canadian journalist and filmmaker based between Lebanon and Palestine

‘I came to fight him’: Israeli doctor fought Flydubai attacker, then saved wounded captain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:49:54 UTC
01:49:54 KST

Israeli dentist Musaev Shota was one of three passengers who rushed toward the cockpit aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 as the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to crash the aircraft. After helping overpower and restrain the suspected attacker, Shota turned to the badly wounded captain and provided emergency medical treatment that he says helped save his life.
“I didn’t wait. I saw something was wrong and ran,” Shota told ynet after returning to Israel.
He said the captain was in extremely serious condition when he reached him.
“The pilot was in very bad shape, with heavy bleeding from his head and hands,” Shota said. “I was the only doctor on the plane. I managed to stop the bleeding, and the pilot was fairly stable until shortly before landing, when his condition deteriorated somewhat.”
Shota said several passengers joined the struggle to overpower the suspected attacker.
“There were a few brave people there,” he said. “We took control of the attacker and tied him up. Of course it was difficult, but we managed.”
The injured captain remained conscious and communicated with them while lying on the floor, Shota said.
“The pilot was talking to us while he was lying there and told us he was 39 and had two children,” he said. “The attacker stabbed him and cursed him.”
Shota said instinct took over as soon as he heard shouting.
“At that moment you don’t think, you just act,” he said. “There were four of us who took control of the whole situation, and if we hadn’t, we wouldn’t be talking to you now.”
He said another passenger, named Yaniv, was the first to jump into action.
“I saw something wasn’t right and ran forward. I didn’t wait for anyone to call me,” Shota said. “I came to fight the attacker when I heard the screams. I didn’t come to provide medical treatment, but after we tied him up, I treated the stabbed pilot.”
Shota said the suspect continued struggling after being restrained.
“He was thrashing around, so we tied him several times, both his legs and his hands,” he said. “He kept struggling, so we tied him tighter. Then he calmed down and understood that he was in our hands.”
Shota said Saudi medical teams later treated the wounded captain after the aircraft landed in Tabuk.
“I understood from them that he survived and was out of danger,” he said.
The dentist also described the terror inside the cabin as the aircraft rapidly lost altitude.
“We thought we were going to die, 100%,” he said. “The plane lost an insane amount of altitude in half a minute.”
Passengers then began shouting for other pilots aboard the aircraft to get to the cockpit.
“We saw the pilots and started screaming, ‘Bring the pilots,’” Shota said. “Then when one of them went into the cockpit and took control, we understood that we had survived.”

Iran seeks deeper ties with neighbors, puts Caucasus and Central Asia in focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:48:35 UTC
01:48:35 KST

Iran seeks deeper ties with neighbors, puts Caucasus and Central Asia in focus
TEHRAN — Iran is stepping up efforts to expand political, economic and people-to-people engagement with neighboring and friendly countries, with recent high-level contacts with Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan highlighting Tehran’s emphasis on closer ties with its northern neighbors and partners across the Caucasus and Central Asia.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has repeatedly identified relations with neighboring, friendly and like-minded countries as a priority of Tehran’s foreign policy. The latest diplomatic activity with Baku and Tashkent has given fresh impetus to that approach, focusing particularly on trade, investment, transportation, energy, cultural exchanges and the implementation of existing agreements.
Azerbaijan: Turning a shared border into a bridge
In Tehran on Tuesday, Pezeshkian told Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev that the Republic of Azerbaijan occupies a special position in Iran’s neighborhood policy, stressing the need to make full use of the opportunities provided by the two countries’ shared geography and common ties.
Pezeshkian said the common border should be regarded as an opportunity for greater interaction rather than an obstacle to closer relations. He described the two countries as relatives and brothers and called for broader cooperation across scientific, cultural, economic, political and security fields.
The Iranian president also stressed the importance of transportation and communications networks in bringing the two countries and their peoples closer together, calling for the expansion and integration of land, air and rail connections.
The emphasis on connectivity is significant given Iran’s geographical position as a link between the Persian Gulf, the Caucasus, Central Asia and wider Eurasian markets. Strengthening cross-border infrastructure and transit routes can provide a practical foundation for expanding trade and economic exchanges while reinforcing Iran’s role in regional connectivity.
Mustafayev, meanwhile, briefed Pezeshkian on his talks with several Iranian ministers and reaffirmed Baku’s determination to develop relations with Tehran. He stressed the need to follow up on existing agreements and understandings, particularly in transportation and communications, and to make greater use of available capacities.
The Azerbaijani delegation’s visit comes amid continued high-level engagement between the two countries. On September 29, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev also spoke by phone with Pezeshkian, with the two leaders recalling their recent meeting in Bishkek and noting that an Azerbaijani government delegation was in Iran for talks on bilateral issues.
Uzbekistan: Expanding the northern and central Asian dimension
At the same time, Pezeshkian and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev discussed ways to broaden bilateral relations during a telephone conversation on Tuesday.
Pezeshkian said Iran was determined to strengthen ties with Uzbekistan through joint efforts and called for greater use of the two countries’ existing capacities. He also emphasized the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation and strengthening people-to-people contacts.
Mirziyoyev said relations between Tehran and Tashkent were steadily expanding, particularly in economic, investment, cultural and humanitarian fields, and stressed the importance of continued diplomatic exchanges and consultations. The two presidents also exchanged views on regional issues and upcoming events.
The conversation underscores the broader geographical scope of Iran’s neighborhood diplomacy. While Azerbaijan represents a key dimension of Iran’s engagement with the South Caucasus, Uzbekistan provides an important avenue for strengthening ties with Central Asia, a region where Iran seeks to expand trade, transit and economic cooperation.
Connectivity as a Tool of Regional Engagement
For Tehran, the drive to strengthen relations with northern neighbors is not limited to political dialogue. Transportation corridors, border infrastructure and economic connectivity are increasingly viewed as practical instruments for turning geographical proximity into sustained cooperation.
Iran has also emphasized the implementation of bilateral agreements with Armenia, particularly those related to transit routes. During a meeting with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this month, Pezeshkian said developing cooperation with the region and neighboring countries remained a firm policy of Tehran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has similarly said that greater priority has been given to neighboring countries under the Pezeshkian administration, with the stated objective of ensuring peace and security in Iran’s immediate surroundings and creating opportunities for economic, political and cultural cooperation.
The approach reflects Tehran’s longstanding geographic reality: Iran shares borders with the South Caucasus, Central Asia through regional transit networks, the Persian Gulf and South Asia, giving it access to several major trade corridors linking Asia, Europe and the Middle East.
 
 Against this backdrop, closer engagement with Azerbaijan, Armenia, Uzbekistan and other neighboring and regional states forms part of Iran’s broader effort to expand regional cooperation, diversify economic and diplomatic partnerships, and capitalize on its geographic position.
For Tehran, the emphasis is increasingly on converting proximity into connectivity and connectivity into sustained economic and political interaction — particularly across the Caucasus and Central Asia, where transport corridors and regional trade can serve as tangible foundations for closer relations.

Tunisian president eases cybercrime penalties after rights groups' criticism

Tunisian president eases cybercrime penalties after rights groups' criticism
TUNIS, Sept 30 - Tunisian President Kais Saied on Wednesday eased penalties under a cybercrime decree that human rights groups had said was designed to muzzle dissent.
The move marks a rare retreat by Saied since he consolidated control over much of Tunisia's political system in 2021 and came hours after civil society groups, led by the UGTT union, announced plans for a large national march in protest against what they see as curbs on rights and freedoms.
Under the decree amendment, prison terms of up to 10 years in some cases will be replaced by financial penalties ranging from 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,370 to $6,740) for first-time offences. Repeat offenders will face six months in prison and a fine of 50,000 dinars.
Under the previous decree, offenders could face up to 10 years in jail when their target was a public official or equivalent, and could be fined up to 100,000 dinars.
The decree, which came into force in 2022, drew widespread criticism from Tunisian and international rights and press freedom organizations, which described it as repressive and used against journalists, activists and political opponents of Saied.
Several journalists and activists have been jailed in cases involving the decree.
The authorities have defended the legislation as necessary for combatting cybercrime, false information and attacks on individuals and public order.
Saied has repeatedly said that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia and that he will not become a dictator.
Saied seized additional powers after suspending parliament in July 2021 and dissolved it in 2022, moves that his opponents have described as a coup. REUTERS

Context

Details

- Article 115 (intentional murder);
- Article 263 (illegal handling of weapons, ammunition, or explosives).
The issue of choosing a measure of restraint for the suspect by the court is currently being decided.
The investigation is ongoing. All circumstances of the crime are being established.
The investigation is examining several versions and motives for the killing.

US lifts long-standing ban on arms exports to Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:45:28 UTC
01:45:28 KST

The US has said that it lifted its long-standing blanket ban on arms exports to Syria, clearing the way for case-by-case reviews of defence sales and security services to Damascus.
"The Department of State is amending the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) to remove Syria from the list of countries subject to a policy of denial for licenses and other approvals," the agency said in a public notice published in the Federal Register on Wednesday.
The administrative rule formally takes effect on Thursday.
The regulatory adjustment implements a decision authorised August 19 by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who approved a revised defence trade framework permitting authorities to evaluate individual applications for military equipment and security service transactions bound for or originating in Syria.
The regulatory shift arrives as the Trump administration moves to normalise diplomatic and trade relations with Syria following the fall of Bashar al Assad's government in late 2024.
Washington previously terminated comprehensive economic sanctions and removed Damascus from its State Sponsors of Terrorism list as part of a conditional engagement strategy with the new leadership headed by President Ahmed al Sharaa.
The Federal Register document is unpublished as of reporting at 1600GMT and is expected to be released on Thursday.

Passengers recount terrifying attempted hijack of Dubai-to-Israel flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:44:58 UTC
01:44:58 KST

FlyDubai passengers recount terrifying ordeal as pilot allegedly attempted to hijack and crash flight to Israel
Passenger accounts paint a chaotic and terrifying picture of the alleged attempted hijacking of FlyDubai flight 1073 on Wednesday. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed his counterpart and tried to crash the Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft.
"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers he said had helped to "neutralize the pilot."
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack."
"It was the most frightening experience we've ever had in our lives," passenger Ron Levi told CBS News on Wednesday.
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship were aboard the flight.
Here's what we know about how the suspected terror attack unfolded, based on accounts from Levi and other passengers.
"Worse than a free-fall"
"The flight was going well, we were two hours in," Levi told CBS News' Dov Lieber, speaking from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where the plane made its safe emergency landing, piloted by an off-duty flight crew member who happened to be on board.
"All of a sudden, what we thought was turbulence started," said Levi. It kept getting stronger, and "we realized it's not something regular."
"I would say much worse than a free-fall," he said, describing how the plane "started turning all sideways and going up and down in all different kinds of directions, for a pretty long time."
"It's very hard to even to estimate if this was 30 seconds or a minute or more than that … it was just the scariest thing possible."
Levi was sitting in a row of seats with his family, "just holding each other's hands and saying that we love them and just hoping for the best."
"And then shouting started from the front of the plane," he recalled. He saw some people near the front get up.
"Very stressful situation"
Passenger Adam Polo was in row 13, hugging his 6-year-old son while his wife was hugging their 3-year-old daughter. Polo told CBS News he "tried to be cool" for his children and told them, "We will be OK."
"The first couple of minutes was very terrifying; you just feel like you're going to crash, but even after the plane was stabilizing, there was more than an hour where we were in the air without the primary crew members," Polo said.
Polo said he couldn't see much from his seat, but after 15 minutes, he saw a passenger running out of the cockpit covered in blood.
"No one from the crew members told us what was happening," Polo said. "The only ones to give us information was the passengers who stood up with an act of bravery."
Polo, who lives in Israel and was vacationing in Thailand with his family, said everything happened so fast and it was a "very stressful situation."
"I'm a pretty cynical guy, I'm not getting excited easily, but I think it was one of the most exciting moments of my life when the plane touched the ground," Polo said.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot"
Levi said he wasn't close enough to see what happened next, but several other passengers who spoke with Israeli media said one pilot had stabbed the other, details that were also repeated by Netanyahu.
"According to the initial information in our possession, the terrorist's intention was one thing: to crash the plane with all its passengers," said Katz, Israel's defense chief.
Netanyahu said he had spoken with an Israeli passenger who told him that, "somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit together with one of the crew members, and that together they neutralized the pilot who carried out the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems."
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place, she believed somewhere over Jordan.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone, held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."
Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
Netanyahu said the person who "managed to stabilize the aircraft" was "another aircrew member who was on the plane."
"All we heard in the back was shouting," said Levi. "We saw that some people were dealing with stuff, and it kept on going like that for, I think, about 10, 20 minutes until … the shakiness [of the plane] relaxed."
"Rumors started coming, and we realized that it wasn't just turbulence," he said. "It was something … a lot worse than that."
"They're heroes," he said of the people who intervened to stop the attacking pilot. "We owe them our lives."
Levi said he saw people covered in blood.
"They're here with us as well now," he told CBS News from the airport in Saudi Arabia. "These were the people I'm talking about who … jumped into the cockpit even and saved the situation."
According to Ohayon, a doctor and others on board helped treat the pilot for unspecified wounds.
"Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," she said.
"I just want to go home"
An Israeli security official told CBS News on Wednesday that Israel is investigating whether it was intended to be a Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
The pilot was arrested and taken for questioning by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said, adding that Israel was working to bring the passengers back to Israel safely.
"There's another FlyDubai plane here now," said Levi. "People are a bit reluctant to get on it, naturally. … We want to go home, but we want to do it in a safe way."
Asked how he was processing the incident, Levi replied: "Honestly, I'm not even starting. We're all shaking here … I have no idea. I just want to go home."
The flight landed safely in Tel Aviv around 8 p.m. local time Wednesday. Cheers and chants could be heard as the passengers disembarked.

US appeals court halts Tennessee execution of Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:44:16 UTC
01:44:16 KST

US appeals court halts Tennessee execution of Christa Pike
Christa Pike was set to become the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years.
A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped Tennessee from executing death row inmate Christa Pike, intervening less than two hours before she was due to receive a lethal injection.
The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted what it called a “short stay of execution” on Wednesday while judges consider Pike’s argument that evidence of sexual abuse she experienced as a child was not properly weighed when she was sentenced.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
- list 2 of 3Walmart settles US government’s opioid lawsuit
- list 3 of 3Charlie Kirk statue vandalised outside Turning Point USA headquarters
Tennessee officials quickly turned to the US Supreme Court, asking the justices to lift the stay and allow the execution to proceed.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled to die at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Had the execution gone ahead, she would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.
She was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at a Knoxville vocational centre.
Pike was 18 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and another teenager tortured and killed Slemmer. Pike and Shipp were later convicted of first-degree murder. Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her childhood was marked by violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was 11 and 17 years old. They also cited her later diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in seeking to have her sentence reduced to life without parole.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee rejected that clemency request. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has publicly supported the execution.
The case has also attracted international scrutiny, with a group of United Nations human rights experts calling for Pike’s death sentence to be commuted.
Women have accounted for just 18 of the 1,683 executions carried out in the US since capital punishment resumed in 1976. Pike’s case is more unusual still: If the execution ultimately proceeds, she would be the only person in Tennessee’s modern death penalty era put to death for a crime committed as a teenager.

Russia on Wednesday accused European countries of using an alleged Russian threat to justify higher defense spending and rejected claims that Moscow plans to invade Europe.
In a statement, the Russian Embassy in Dublin rejected claims that Russia plans to launch a military invasion of Europe or escalate an alleged hybrid campaign against European countries.
“The slogan of ‘Russian threat’ is being recycled in the Western media on a daily basis,” the embassy said in a statement shared on US social media platform X.
It claimed European countries were seeking to justify higher defense spending and the “overall militarization of Europe,” as well as further financial, military and political assistance to Ukraine.
The embassy said there was nothing to support claims of an “imminent Russian invasion.”
“Moscow’s position on the security situation in Europe has always been consistent and confirmed yet again by President (Vladimir) Putin on September 25 – we have no plans, no reasons and, most importantly, no real motives for aggravating situation with Europe,” it said.
Referring to Gallant Boar 2026, a joint military exercise by Lithuania, Poland and France, the embassy claimed the exercise was “specifically aimed” at Russia’s Kaliningrad region on the Baltic Sea.
“There has been information that NATO is preparing air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and Kaliningrad region,” it said.
The Kaliningrad region is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea between Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory.
Calling the issue a “matter of grave concern” to Russia, the embassy said: “The irresponsible and shortsighted European political elite is playing a dangerous game.”
‘Moscow would be ready to use all its arsenal’
The embassy cited Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov as saying recently: “If the West attacks us, we will respond and it would be completely different war and a very brief one.”
Speaking at the International Youth Festival in Yekaterinburg on Sept. 16, Lavrov said that if Europe attacks Russia, the resulting war would be “completely different” and “very brief.”
The embassy said Moscow would be ready to use its entire arsenal, “including nuclear weapons,” to defend its territory if NATO countries tried to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of Russia.
“Under such scenario, the risk of armed confrontation is high with the likelihood of Russia using preemptive strikes against centers of decision-making in the Alliance countries already at the early stage of the conflict,” it warned.
“It is a matter of utmost seriousness and should be treated by Europe as such,” the embassy added.
On Tuesday, the Russian Embassy in the UK also warned that any attempt by the UK or NATO to blockade the Kaliningrad region would be met with a response using all means, including nuclear weapons.

Ukrainian forces use single ground robot to evacuate four wounded soldiers in constant danger from drones and mines – video
Ukrainian soldiers have evacuated four wounded infantrymen from the contact line in Zaporizhzhia Oblast using a single unmanned ground vehicle (UGV). A video of the operation has been posted by the 7th Rapid Response Corps of the Ukrainian Air Assault Forces.
Details: The evacuation was carried out by soldiers from the 5th Separate Kyiv Assault Brigade, who are performing combat missions on the Huliaipole front. The wounded soldiers were evacuated in two stages: the ground robot delivered two of the soldiers first, and after recharging it went back for the other two.
The video shows the final stage of the evacuation, when the soldiers were being transferred from the UGV to an evacuation vehicle. The mission was fraught with danger due to the constant threat of Russian drone strikes and mines.
Quote from the 7th Corps: "Due to the threat of the enemy using UAVs against the evacuation mission, the ground drone carrying the wounded soldiers had to be escorted by Mavic drones and required air cover from interceptor drones."
Evacuation of four soldiers with a single UGV. Video: 7th Corps
Details: The unit said one of the soldiers evacuated with the help of the UGV was in an "extremely critical condition". All the wounded were first taken to a stabilisation point and then to a hospital.
Quote from the 7th Corps: "Currently, evacuation from the front line remains challenging and requires a combination of various methods and assets. At the same time, where conditions allow, UGVs enable us to perform some tasks remotely and reduce the risk to personnel."
Background:
- The number of missions that employ ground robots has increased by 3.3 times since the beginning of 2026. According to the Ministry of Defence, UGVs carried out 25,143 logistical and evacuation missions on the contact line in August. For comparison, there were 7,511 such operations in January.
- In June 2026, a video released by the 110th Separate Mechanised Brigade showed UGVs being used to conduct a 15-hour evacuation of two wounded soldiers who had been unable to leave their positions for several days following a Russian attack. The drones travelled 56 km to extract the soldiers.

Macron says ‘welcome back’ to Burnham suggestion UK could rejoin EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:40:27 UTC
01:40:27 KST

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU.
“Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday. Macron continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU.
The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference in which Burnham said Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”.
In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” for full EU membership.
Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added.
Earlier, Macron, who has frequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public, said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities.
Sandro Gozi, an Italian Social Democrat, told the Guardian: “Burnham has finally swept away the so-called red lines that have constrained the debate on Britain’s relationship with Europe. That is a welcome and important step.”
The MEP, who co-chairs the EU-UK parliamentary partnership assembly, added: “Europe should respond with the same openness. We should be ready to turn the page and build a new EU-UK partnership, removing unnecessary barriers and restoring much closer economic and political cooperation.”
EU officials welcomed the change in tone but said it was up to the UK to define what it wanted from the future relationship. They have told their British counterparts that the UK is welcome to join the customs union or single market via membership of the European Economic Area.
In recent weeks Brussels has again mooted British membership of the customs union as an answer to the bloc’s Made in Europe policy, which could exclude British clean technology and electric vehicles from valuable European subsidy programmes and public contracts.
But EU officials also stress that joining the customs union would require full alignment with EU trade policy and tariffs. Single market membership means accepting free movement of people, alongside free movement of goods, services and capital.
More than 10 years after the Brexit vote, the EU remains attached to its red lines. A recent proposal from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, that Canada should become the EU’s first-ever associate member, is not seen as a serious option for the UK (or even Canada). The idea is widely regarded by EU insiders as an ill-defined symbolic gesture with no legal basis.
The EU and UK are due to hold a summit in Brussels, with a date in the second half of November expected to be announced in the coming days. The annual gathering was postponed after the resignation of Keir Starmer.
The Burnham government has made resolving Britain’s exclusion from Made in Europe a top priority, but several EU sources say the issue will not be settled at the summit as the EU is yet to agree its internal position on key legislative texts.
France is the staunchest opponent of opening Made in Europe to countries outside the EU, including the UK.
Macron pointed to the limits of the UK seeking close ties with the EU while remaining outside. “You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union, nor can you decide to take what suits you and leave the rest,” he said. “So, come back.”
A European Commission spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

Russian Regions Turn to Residents and Businesses to Fund Bomb Shelters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:40:18 UTC
01:40:18 KST

Authorities in several Russian regions are turning to residents and businesses to pay for bomb shelters and protection against drone attacks, local media reported, as the country restores its civil defense infrastructure amid the war in Ukraine.
Building owners in St. Petersburg have received orders to equip shelters, while apartment residents in Yekaterinburg have been asked to approve charges for converting underground parking facilities. In Omsk, parents of kindergarten children have been asked to contribute toward supplies for a basement shelter.
The measures would shift some preparation costs to households and businesses as Russia works to restore more than 20,000 protective facilities across 82 regions, a program the Emergency Situations Ministry estimates will require about 155 billion rubles ($1.88 billion).
In St. Petersburg, owners of buildings containing civil defense facilities have received notices requiring them to prepare the shelters, BFM news website reported. The St. Petersburg Pharmaceutical Factory was ordered to put an underground facility near the Nevskaya Ratusha complex in order. Similar instructions have been sent to municipal authorities.
The requirements apply both to apartment buildings with existing shelter facilities and to those without them, Nikolai Pitirimov, co-chairman of the board of the St. Petersburg Clean Technologies Cluster for the Urban Environment, told BFM.
Buildings must provide at least temporary shelter, with the responsibility falling on homeowners’ associations, he said.
In Yekaterinburg, residents of one district received notices asking them to vote on equipping shelters in underground parking facilities, local news outlet E1 reported.
The Akademichesky property management company said a one-time charge of 841 rubles ($10.18) per person registered as living in an apartment would appear as a separate item on utility bills. The company said the amount was set by a governor’s decree.
In Omsk, about 2,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, parents at one kindergarten were asked to contribute 200 rubles ($2.42) per child for benches and emergency water supplies in a basement being converted into a shelter, the local outlet Gorod55 reported, citing residents.
City authorities said parents had only been advised to help provide supplies and prepare the basement as their means allowed.
Emergency Situations Minister Alexander Kurenkov said in February that his ministry was restoring more than 20,000 civil defense facilities nationwide.
Russian authorities began a large-scale reconstruction and modernization program for Soviet-era shelters in late May 2025. At the time, Kurenkov said restoring the civil defense system had become increasingly urgent because of the war in Ukraine.

The braised pork political economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:35 UTC
01:39:35 KST

On Sept. 19, restaurant chain Formosa Chang’s third-generation heir Chang Yao-sheng (張耀升) attended a campaign event for Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) in Datong District (大同); he came bearing pineapples and wished Chiang success in his bid for re-election. Chang’s appearance prompted calls from some consumers to boycott the restaurant chain, which was quick to issue a statement saying that Chang had attended the event in a private capacity, and that his participation did not represent the brand’s position.
Someone who has been publicly positioned as the company’s successor cannot really be regarded as an ordinary employee. Chang is free to support any candidate he chooses — just as consumers are free to choose where to spend their money. The sticking point is the different identities he holds: all at once, Chang is an ordinary citizen, the son of the company’s chairman Chang Yung-chang (張永昌), an assistant to the general manager and the company’s future successor. When he walks into a campaign event, it is inevitable that all the public sees is the third-generation face of Formosa Chang.
This private-turned-public appearance is particularly sensitive because Datong District, where Formosa Chang’s roots were established, is one of the more staunchly pan-green areas on Taipei’s political map. In 2020, Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) won nearly 64 percent of the district’s vote; and in the 2022 Taipei mayoral election, it was the only district in which the Democratic Progressive Party’s candidate, Chen Shih-chung (陳時中), led against the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Chiang. Chang Yao-sheng’s decision to publicly support the KMT mayor in the brand’s home territory was more than a personal political statement; it directly touched the local community where Formosa Chang first built its reputation. In a highly polarized political environment, a single move can tear at the emotional ties of longtime customers and turn what was originally an apolitical form of trust into a sense of betrayal.
Starting out as a roadside stall in Datong District, Formosa Chang transformed the humble Taiwanese dish of braised pork over rice into a Chinese-style restaurant chain with a clearly defined market position. Consumers choose it not for political reasons, but for convenience and dependability. This controversy might generate short-term publicity, and some supporters of the pan-blue camp or those opposed to online pile-ons might opt to patronize the chain in solidarity. However, those who wish to boycott the chain have plenty of options for pork rice and boxed meals elsewhere, while its most vocal supporters might not necessarily offer long-term patronage themselves.
The situation represents a conflict between rights and responsibilities in corporate governance. While Chang Yao-sheng enjoys political visibility because of his status as successor, brand risks are borne collectively by the company, its employees and other members of the founding family. Franchisees and frontline staff are the most vulnerable parties when a boycott of a restaurant chain occurs, and the headquarters’ insistence that Chang Yao-sheng was acting in a personal capacity offers a thin fig leaf at best.
Succession in a family business is not simply about inheriting shares and job titles; it also means managing one’s symbolic power. Chang Yao-sheng is free to choose his political preference, but he cannot pretend that the decision is a personal matter and nothing more.
Ko Chia-chih is an insurance broker.

Doctor encourages people to stay active as they age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:35 UTC
01:39:35 KST

An 83-year-old took the pitcher’s mound as a 103-year-old stepped up to bat ahead of a baseball match between the Uni-President Lions and WeiChuan Dragons in Tainan, with one doctor saying it gave the audience a lesson in how to stay active while aging.
Shih Wu-chi (石武吉), 83, is a volunteer at National Cheng Kung University’s Center for Sports Science and Healthy Aging. He pitched for He Kuo-chao (何國昭), who is 103 years old.
Center director Lin Li-chuan (林麗娟) had invited orthopedic surgeon Chen Chien-hung (陳建宏) to take part in the event.
Photo courtesy of Dr. Orthealth Clinic in Tainan
The scene was more powerful than any health education presentation, said Chen, who is a specialist on osteoporosis, sarcopenia and preventive medicine for middle-aged and older adults.
The two older adults took to the field and showed that growing older does not mean stepping away from an active life, he said.
Instead, old age marks the beginning of another chapter of learning, pursuing dreams, sharing and contributing, Lin said.
At his clinic, some people in their 50s or 60s think that they should reduce their movement as they worry about wearing out their knees or getting hurt in a fall, Chen said.
Meanwhile, others still go to the market, eat with friends and do the things they want to do well into their 70s, 80s and 90s, like the two older people who stepped onto the baseball field, he said.
“The healthier your body, the farther you can go from home,” Chen often tells older patients.
As long as they maintain proper bone and muscle strength, and balance, they can continue to go out for activities daily, rather than gradually seeing their world shrink, he said.
Chen reminds sedentary older people not to go too far at once, as someone who has not exercised for a long time should gradually increase their activity level, he said.
What matters is not how much you can accomplish on any one day, but finding an approach that suits you, and is safe, gradual and sustainable, he added.

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) plans to propose amendments to the Criminal Code to allow caning as a punishment for certain crimes, after a proposed caning referendum was vetoed by the Central Election Commission (CEC) last month, KMT Legislator Hung Meng-kai (洪孟楷) said yesterday.
The party is proposing between three and 12 strokes as punishment for serious crimes, including drug driving that results in death or serious injury, child abuse resulting in death or serious injury, aggravated sexual assault and large-scale fraud, Hung said.
The CEC reviewed the referendum proposal on caning on Aug. 28 and ruled that it did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act (公民投票法).
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) and Hung held a news conference at the KMT caucus on their bill.
As the referendum was rejected, the party plans to submit the draft amendments to the legislature for discussion and review, Hung said.
Caning would only be used for the most serious crimes and be handed out by the courts on a case-by-case basis and under strict guidelines, he said.
Courts would consider the infringement of legally protected interests, the number of victims, the method of the offense, criminal proceeds, the perpetrator’s attitude after the crime and the risk of reoffending, he added.
The draft amendments would propose that caning be used as a punishment for large-scale fraud convictions with sentences of at least three years in prison and involving proceeds of at least NT$5 million (US$156,976) or at least three victims, he said.
The maximum would remain at 12 strokes even when multiple offenses are combined for sentencing, he said.
Caning would not be used on anyone younger than 18 at the time of the offense, or 65 or older, and doctors would first conduct assessments and issue a written opinion.
If a doctor determines that caning poses a serious health risk, it would be stopped immediately, he added.
If caning cannot be carried out, it would be replaced by a prison sentence.
Democratic Progressive Party caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said that KMT lawmakers “love caning,” but would not use it for crimes such as offenses committed by legislators, large-scale economic crimes or treason.
In cases of sexual assault, the priority should be providing assistance to victims and prevention of such crimes, rather than corporal punishment, Chuang said.
For aggravated fraud, focus should be placed on recovering victims’ losses and dismantling criminal organizations rather than assuming that caning would make criminal organizations disband or ensure that the money would be recovered, he added.

Photo: AP

“Playoff-style hockey,” Forsling said. “That felt like a playoff game to me. It was awesome, really fun.”
The NHL said it marked the third time in its modern era (since 1943-44) that the two previous Cup winners met in a season-opening game, the others coming in 1962-63 and 2019-20.
The Panthers had reached the Stanley Cup Final for three straight years and won it all in 2024 and last year, twice eliminating the Hurricanes in the Eastern Conference Final in that run. They also brought in Jacob Markstrom to take over the crease anchored by Sergei Bobrovsky during those title runs.
That is why Florida coach Paul Maurice pointed out it is a new team, even with so many championship holdovers, and why the Panthers sat on the bench to watch the Hurricanes’ pregame ceremony.
“You get a chance to see what you want so bad,” Maurice said. “We think it’s really important that the teams respect each other for those achievements, whether it’s an individual player hitting a milestone or certainly a Stanley Cup. 16:39:31 UTC
01:39:31 KST

Japan has started its first nationwide survey of animal cafes amid concerns over animal welfare, hygiene and public health, a government official said, bringing greater scrutiny to the popular but lightly regulated sector.
The desktop survey, which began this month, will examine the number of facilities, the types of animals they house and the conditions they are held in, and how visitors interact with the animals.
Exotic animal cafes, where visitors can interact with species ranging from otters to owls and marmots, have become popular attractions for Japanese and foreign tourists. However, researchers say some facilities keep threatened species, raising concerns about animal welfare and the trade in wildlife.
Photo: Reuters
Japan lacks standards governing such cafes and handling of many exotic species, Japanese Ministry of the Environment official Takuya Ishikawa said.
“There has been strong public interest, including from animal welfare groups, which have regularly shared findings from their own research with the ministry,” Ishikawa said. “Experts on a government advisory panel have also frequently raised concerns about potential problems at such cafes.”
Cafes with domesticated animals including cats and dogs will also be included in the survey.
The Japanese government also plans a public awareness campaign, acknowledging that it had not done enough to inform public about the risks of interacting with exotic animals.
The prospect of tighter oversight has been welcomed by some in the industry.
“Japan is clearly lagging behind when it comes to [animal welfare] regulation,” said Syaina Nozaki, manager of Owl Otter Cafe in Kamakura, near Tokyo, which houses rescued animals.
Nozaki said that she hoped that regulations would help distinguish facilities like hers from less responsible operators focused solely on profit.
Japan, which has a large domestic pet market, ranked as the world’s second-biggest importer of live reptiles and mammals by value in 2024, a report by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) last month said, highlighting risks including invasive species introduced through pet releases and the spread of zoonotic diseases.
Of about 80 registered wildlife animal cafes in Tokyo and Osaka, three-quarters were also registered to sell animals, a separate report by WWF and Hokkaido University said.
Researchers visiting 25 cafes found more than 1,700 animals on display, 27 percent of them threatened species. More than 90 percent of the cafes displayed animals considered at high risk of causing injury through contact, while samples from four cafes tested positive for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, which can cause bloody diarrhea.
