Ansarallah’s gains could reverberate beyond Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:36:01 UTC
00:36:01 KST

Ansarallah’s gains could reverberate beyond Saudi Arabia
TEHRAN - In a commentary published on its website, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace said that victories by Yemen’s Ansarallah forces against Saudi-backed forces have brought them within 80 miles of Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, which houses the United States’ only permanent and largest military base on the African continent.
The article, written by Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in Carnegie’s Middle East Program, and Lesley Anne Warner, a visiting scholar with the Endowment’s Africa Program, argues that the fallout from Ansarallah’s advance could extend beyond Saudi Arabia.
Testifying before Congress last year, General Michael Langley, then the commander of U.S. Africa Command, warned that Ansarallah already possessed the capacity to strike the base facilities, should they decide to escalate attacks against the United States or its interests.
The article adds that military interventions by both the Biden and Trump administrations against Ansarallah forces ended in “strategic defeats”.
The following is a slightly edited version of the article:
Earlier this month, Ansarallah, an armed political movement that has controlled much of Yemen’s territory for more than a decade, took control over Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. Their rapid capture of the Port of Mokha marked the group’s first major military advance in nearly five years. It also further threatened global oil trade at a time when the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz (by Iran in response to the U.S.-Israeli war of aggression) has spiked energy prices worldwide.
Ansarallah initially stayed out of direct involvement in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Still, their advance into Mokha reflects a steady escalation between Saudi Arabia and Ansarallah since mid-July, after the collapse of an initial U.S.-Iranian memorandum of understanding. On September 19, Ansarallah bombed a fuel depot at the main airport in Riyadh, sending a plume of black smoke over the Saudi capital.
This development reflects both the dynamics of a no-longer-frozen domestic Yemeni conflict and continued fallout from the U.S.-Iranian military and diplomatic stalemate in the Persian Gulf. It has also raised the possibility of additional U.S. intervention in the region against Ansarallah, though President Donald Trump has thus far declined to use force against the group.
Ansarallah’s advance gives them control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a crucial chokepoint at the southern end of the Red Sea. It also raises the possibility of opening a second front in the current Persian Gulf conflict—one that could target Saudi oil facilities and threaten an additional Red Sea chokepoint for global energy trade and other goods shipments. Past attacks on Red Sea traffic have already curtailed shipping through the strait while raising insurance and security costs on the remaining vessels.
Previous air campaigns by Saudi Arabia (with the support of other countries) sought to dislodge Ansarallah. However, these efforts contributed to a humanitarian catastrophe in Yemen and entrenched the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces in a fraught stalemate with Ansarallah. Later military interventions by both the Biden and Trump administrations against Ansarallah forces likewise ended in strategic defeats.
The latest advance also calls Saudi Arabia’s bluff that it could contain Ansarallah on its own, through a combination of quiet diplomacy and the unification of fragmented forces.
In the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, Ansarallah now controls the island of Perim (also known as Mayyun), which allows them to harass and disrupt maritime traffic. The advance also brings Ansarallah within 80 miles of Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, which houses Combined Joint Task Force–Horn of Africa and is the United States’ only permanent military facility on the continent. 
 
 Since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas conflict and the resulting impact on maritime insecurity in the Red Sea, Djibouti has reportedly not allowed the United States to use its base for offensive operations against Ansarallah. The country has continued to play a balancing act between its criticism of Israel’s approach in Gaza and its utility as a relatively secure, geostrategic country that houses several foreign military bases.
When testifying before Congress last year, General Michael Langley, then the commander of U.S. Africa Command, warned that Ansarallah already possessed the capacity to strike the base facilities, should they decide to escalate attacks against the United States or U.S. interests.
How does this affect Saudi Arabia’s energy shipping?
Ansarallah’s control of Red Sea shipping corridors (at least the southern end) compounds a disastrous period for Saudi energy shipments. Around the same time as the Bab al-Mandeb takeover, the kingdom’s crucial East-West Pipeline was severely damaged. That energy corridor, combined with Red Sea ports in Jeddah and Yanbu, had allowed Saudi Arabia to offset a significant portion of the U.S.-Iran war’s direct economic costs.
The one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures, however, risks forcing Saudi Arabia into relying more on fraught “dark crossings” of the Strait of Hormuz—or face a dramatic drop in oil revenues. Tellingly, the kingdom has already begun canceling key oil shipments to Europe.
Ansarallah’s gains further complicate efforts by the Arab Persian Gulf states to establish a common position for negotiating with Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
There’s also a Somaliland dimension to this that doesn’t get much attention outside specialist circles.
Following Operation Al-Aqsa Flood on Oct. 7, 2023, and continuing during the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran this year, Ansarallah has targeted Saudi commercial vessels in the Red Sea—including more recently near the 18-mile-wide Bab al-Mandeb that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The Bab al-Mandeb is a maritime chokepoint through which roughly 12 percent of seaborne-traded oil travels, and the uptick in threats has forced many vessels to reroute around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope. This has increased the strategic value of Somaliland, that declared independence from Somalia in 1991, and has added to the view in some Washington-based foreign policy circles that the United States should recognize Somaliland’s independence.
The Mogadishu-based federal government has never recognized Somaliland, treating it as an autonomous region. Tensions between Somaliland’s capital, Hargeisa, and Mogadishu escalated in 2024, when Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, granting landlocked Ethiopia a fifty-year lease on approximately 20 kilometers of Somaliland’s coastline for a naval base and commercial port access, with the prospect that the former would extend formal diplomatic recognition to the latter in return. The memorandum provoked fierce opposition from Mogadishu, which accused Addis Ababa of violating its territorial integrity. In December 2024, Turkey brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia, which committed both parties to respect each other’s territorial integrity and work toward “mutually advantageous” commercial arrangements for Ethiopian port access.
In defense policy circles, increased U.S. military engagement in Somaliland could be perceived as a hedge for the U.S. military presence in Djibouti, where President Ismail Omar Guelleh has been in power for almost three decades and is approaching his eighties. In addition, with the establishment of China’s first overseas military installation in Djibouti in 2017, Djibouti is the only place on the planet that has a permanent military presence from both the United States and China.
Until Israel’s unilateral recognition of the region as an independent state in December 2025, no country had ever recognized Somaliland. There has been speculation as to whether the United States would follow suit, due to Trump’s close relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his frequent disparagement of people of Somali descent as well as Somalia as a whole. In addition, Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi (also known as Irro) was in Washington recently, making the case for Somaliland recognition. As yet, there are no public indications that the executive branch has changed U.S. policy on recognition of Somaliland as an independent country.
It remains to be seen if Ansarallah forces can consolidate their hold on port cities such as Mokha and Dhubab, as well as the Red Sea island of Perim.
It also remains to be seen to see whether domestic pressure mounts on Saudi de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman to “do something” about the security dilemma facing the kingdom, as happened in the run-up to Saudi Arabia’s intervention in Yemen last winter. Currently, Saudi commentators are more focused on exhorting the international community to take action.
So far, Trump has demurred, with U.S. diplomats reaching out to Ansarallah counterparts mainly to ensure that the conflict does not directly implicate the United States. Saudi Arabia has reportedly reached out to China instead to try to restrain Ansarallah forces via Iran.
From the U.S.-Africa policy perspective, it remains to be seen whether the worsening of the security environment in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa provides additional justification for increased U.S. engagement. In fact, non-recognition of Somaliland has not inhibited high-level U.S. engagement with the region. A recent State Department report to Congress noted that the U.S. military “has regular engagements with Somaliland authorities and is exploring areas for potential cooperation.”
The United States has also been exploring a closer relationship with Eritrea, which sits north of Somaliland and Djibouti along the Red Sea. Last week, Washington allowed sanctions to expire on members of the ruling party and security forces tied to Eritrea’s conduct during the 2020–2022 conflict in northern Ethiopia, when it was on the side of the Ethiopian government. Given anticipation of renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia (and that Ethiopia and Eritrea have again fallen out and would be on opposite sides of the conflict), overlaid on rising insecurity in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb, I would not be surprised if these developments provide additional justification for U.S. engagement with Eritrea—notwithstanding the country’s human rights record.
The impact on maritime security, given the slight uptick in Somali piracy, which peaked over a decade ago also needed to be watched. Back then, a combination of industry-led measures and multinational naval patrols addressed the threat, but there are a few new variables this time around. One is that international order is more contested, meaning less coherence around military and nonmilitary means of addressing the evolving threats in the Bab al-Mandeb. The second is that the cross-strait relationships are now more evolved and strategic. The third is that the battlespace has evolved: Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia already use drones for reconnaissance, and the latter group conducted its first confirmed drone strikes in January 2025. Given trends in commercial off-the-shelf drone technologies in the Sahel and West Africa, an expansion in use cases for these technologies seems likely.
Higher insurance costs for the shipping industry as a result of insecurity and higher freight costs associated with any need to reroute from the Bab al-Mandeb around the Cape of Good Hope is anticipated. These costs will inevitably be passed on to consumers. In particular, African economies have already weathered a succession of geopolitical shocks in recent years, with little time in between to increase their resilience, and they will have to brace for higher commodity costs.

‘We don’t need handouts’: Key takeaways from Putin’s first address to Russia’s new parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:33:14 UTC
00:33:14 KST

‘We don’t need handouts’: Key takeaways from Putin’s first address to Russia’s new parliament
Russian President Vladimir Putin has addressed the newly elected State Duma for the first time, outlining priorities from economic self-reliance and social spending to defense and long-term national security.
Speaking at the opening session of the ninth convocation of the lower house of parliament on Wednesday, Putin urged lawmakers to avoid economic missteps and “destructive populism,” stressing that Russia has the resources it needs to achieve its goals without outside assistance.
Here are the key takeaways from the president’s address.
‘We don’t need handouts’
Russia will not go around the world “begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” Putin said while discussing the country’s finances and the new federal budget.
“Firstly, because it is humiliating. Secondly, nobody will give us anything, we know that very well. And thirdly – and most importantly – we don’t need it,” he said.
Putin described Russia’s financial system and economy as confident, but warned that mistakes are “absolutely unacceptable.”
He called for a balanced and realistic budget, while demanding that the government fully fund national projects and federal programs and meet all of its social commitments.
Putin also called for measures to boost investment and urged lawmakers to reduce administrative barriers for businesses.
Security and the Ukraine conflict
Defense and support for Russian troops and their families should remain among parliament’s top priorities, Putin said.
Lawmakers must focus on issues of “state importance,” strengthen the country’s defense capabilities and “do everything for our victory,” according to the president.
Putin also welcomed veterans of the Ukraine conflict elected to the new parliament, saying they had already demonstrated their commitment to the country “on the battlefield.”
He said national unity would allow Russia to “achieve its goals” and provide “reliable guarantees of security and sovereignty” for generations to come.
Developing the new regions
The first sitting coincided with Russia’s Day of Reunification, marking four years since Moscow incorporated the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics and the Kherson and Zaporozhye regions following referendums in September 2022.
Putin described the vote to join Russia as “clear” and “lawful,” and said the entire country is now involved in rebuilding and developing the territories.
The four regions are represented in the State Duma for the first time following this month’s election.
Putin said residents who went to the polls despite shelling and threats had demonstrated that the Russian people “cannot be broken or intimidated.”
Election shows ‘national unity’
The September 18-20 vote was accompanied by a massive Ukrainian drone raid targeting Moscow and other Russian regions.
Russian officials said more than 1,600 UAVs were repelled, including 450 on approaches to the capital, describing the unprecedented attack as an attempt to disrupt the elections. At least two civilians were reported killed in Moscow Region.
Putin said the turnout and election results had reaffirmed the strength of Russia’s multiparty political system and national unity in the face of what he called “historic challenges.”
The ruling United Russia party secured 349 of the State Duma’s 450 seats. Putin told the newly elected deputies that they bore a “particular responsibility” to voters and urged them to remain closely engaged with the people they represent.

Gulf media delays reporting on flydubai hijacking, consider Israeli sources unreliable - analysis

An initial review of Gulf media reactions to the crisis aboard a flydubai flight that rapidly lost altitude and then landed in Saudi Arabia shows most media are taking a cautious approach to reporting the details.
While Israeli officials increasingly view the incident as an attempted hijacking and a disaster that was narrowly avoided by heroes on the plane, many reports in the Gulf appeared wary of reporting details at this point.
Hours after the incident unfolded, and after video showed bloodied passengers and crew, Al-Arabiya noted in the late afternoon that “a flydubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an altercation occurred in the cockpit, the airline says.”
The report noted that “Flight FZ1073, which was traveling from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion International Airport, was secured by off-duty flydubai crew members who were traveling on board, according to the airline.”
Relying on the airline, the report said the crew diverted the aircraft and landed it in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. “All passengers and crew members were safe and accounted for, flydubai said…The airline said the reasons and motives behind the incident remained unknown at this early stage and would be subject to a formal investigation.”
Gulf media sources did not report the incident hours after it occurred
A further look at Gulf media revealed that some media outlets did not even report the incident, despite many hours having passed.
Other media provided only basic details. The National in the UAE, for instance, noted that “flydubai pilots taken to hospital after stabbing on Tel Aviv flight.
Saudi authorities say all passengers safe and accounted for after emergency landing in the kingdom. Video: Hijacking ruled out as flydubai flight lands safely in Saudi Arabia.” Gulf News in the UAE had not reported on the incident by 17:35 UAE time. Al-Ain media had also not covered it by the same time.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia had more coverage. Arab News noted, “Flydubai passenger jet pilots in bloody mid-air fight, Israeli media reports. Plane landed safely at Tabuk airport, all passengers are accounted for, the airline says. An Israeli official says pilots sent emergency signals after a physical altercation. Mystery surrounded the forced landing in Saudi Arabia of a flydubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, as conflicting accounts of the incident raised fears of a possible hijacking.”
Gulf media cautious, considers news from Israel unreliable
As noted above, Al-Arabiya had covered it. It also included an interview with a passenger where the passenger had said the co-pilot had stabbed the pilot. “The co-pilot stabbed the pilot and tried to bring the plane down.”
In Bahrain, the Daily Tribune had no articles on the story by 16:38 Bahrain time, which is 17:38 in the UAE. In Oman, the Muscat Daily also had no coverage at that time. Similarly, the media site Al-Jarida had no coverage by that time.
The difference in coverage between Israel and the Gulf was clear. Gulf media was more cautious. This is not entirely surprising. The Gulf prefers caution. Many media also prefer official statements. There was a statement from flydubai by the late afternoon. However, in the absence of other statements, many were reluctant to report further.
Well-known professor and author Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, who has a large following on X/Twitter, noted that “Israeli sources regarding the flydubai flight are not credible and are seeking to achieve a media scoop at the expense of reliability. Awaiting clarification from the Dubai Media Office.”

What the data really shows about ‘settler violence’ in the West Bank - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:33:04 UTC
00:33:04 KST

Fresh sanctions were recently imposed against Israel by the UK, France, and other governments, which cited – as did British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband – “ethnic cleansing perpetrated by settler terrorists.”
This argument was also front and center in the recent UN General Assembly, in a series of heated anti-Israeli speeches by world leaders. Yet newly obtained exclusive data from the Israeli Police through a freedom of information request cast serious doubt over the widely repeated “settler violence” narrative.
The “settler violence” campaign has been extremely effective in convincing European governments, and even some supporters of Israel, that hordes of Jewish terrorists attacking Palestinians are one of the top security challenges of the Middle East and pose a strategic threat to the prospects for peace.
Yet very rarely do politicians present verifiable evidence that illustrates what exactly they mean by “settler violence.” Statements often include a smoke screen of ominous warnings but provide few measurable metrics.
The data we obtained reveal a striking gap between the dire rhetoric and the unvarnished numbers.
First, nationalist violence among Israeli settlers has seen a sharp, 57% decline between 2023 and 2025. October 7 and the ensuing war have actually led to a sharp decrease in cases, amid a heightened military presence throughout the territories and the attention diverted to Gaza: 969 complaints in 2022, 1,066 in 2023, then 679 in 2024, and merely 614 incidents in 2025.
Unlike the acceptable method in the US, the data provided by the Israeli Police covers all complaints and hotline reports, without filtering out verified incidents.
But even taken at face value, this represents a crime rate of 3.07 per 10,000 people, an extremely low rate compared to Palestinian terrorism, crime in Israel’s other regions, antisemitic incidents in Europe, or crime rates in many large US cities.
Among Palestinians, abundant terrorist attacks, including murder and foiled suicide bombings, amount to 37.1 cases per 10,000 Palestinians – more than 12 times more than Israeli settlers.
Second, qualitatively – not just quantitatively – these figures represent not cases of murder, but delinquency, such as property theft, agricultural vandalism, or vehicle arson.
About 5-7% of the counted reports covered settlers confronting Israeli security forces rather than attacks on Palestinian civilians.
Vandalism and assault are doubtlessly crimes, but considering them as a state-sponsored effort of ethnic cleansing or as terrorism is absurd.
Third, openings of investigation files by the Police Interrogation Unit soared by 27% year over year, from 802 in 2024 to 1,024 in 2025, alongside dozens of criminal indictments – 40 in 2024 alone.
Most cases are prosecuted by the State Attorney’s Office, rather than the Police, and logically many more indictments are filed beyond these. This directly contradicts the widely quoted claim that Israel does little to prosecute perpetrators – even actively abetting them.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Issac Herzog, and even US Ambassador Mike Huckabee all personally condemned these crimes as “criminal acts of violence” that are committed by “a handful of hooligans who are violating the law, disturbing the IDF in fulfilling its missions, and harming Israel’s global reputation.”
The data follows the narrative
A larger prism tells us that vocal critics of “settler violence,” including heads of state, rely on extremely problematic figures, provided by impartial actors. The UN as well as the EU have both come under criticism for abandoning basic professional standards in their reporting on Israel.
The same goes for virtually any topic concerning Israel: Miliband cited the widely repeated and inflated figure of 70,000 fatalities in Gaza, a figure provided by the UN but has already been debunked as exclusively relying on data provided by Hamas’ “Health Ministry” – by the UN’s own admission.
The same applies to “settler violence,” where the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) cited as its sources “municipal authorities, Palestinian District Coordination Offices, UN agencies, human rights organizations, and media reports,” without naming any specific sources.
As previously revealed, a look at the OCHA database reveals that of the 6,285 alleged “settler violence” incidents it cites, 27.1% took place in Jerusalem, another 21% covered mere visits by Jews to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem (alongside Muslim worshippers and tourists), while others involve tensions between Israeli police and rioters in Jerusalem.
Testifying before the Knesset, the then-commander of the Central Intelligence Unit of the Israeli Police’s Judea and Samaria District, Avishai Mualem, confirmed the above-mentioned steep decline, as well as the false complaints phenomenon by Palestinians and far-left anarchists: “When 191 cases were opened, 90 of them were confirmed as false complaints around the South Hebron Mountain district. … In the Jordan Valley district, there were 70 incidents, of which 50% also ended up as false complaints.”
The EU, on its part, cites the far-left Israeli NGO B’tselem as the exclusive source for its figures. Unsurprisingly, its roughly $3.7 million budget originates primarily from the EU, the UN, and European governments, the same entities that later use the data to compile damning reports on Israel.
B’tselem falsely claims that “settler attacks” against Palestinians have seen a “sharp increase,” and its database includes multiple incidents such as “road blocking,” “verbal confrontations and threats,” and incidents in which “settlers stole a flock of grazing sheep.”
All of these may constitute wrongdoing but are far from fitting neatly within the customary understanding of ethnic cleansing or terrorism – nor are they uncommon in any large city in Europe or in the US.
Much lower crime rate than Baltimore
Indeed, compared with crime statistics elsewhere, 614 complaints of violent crimes attributed to a Jewish population of 462,000, or 3.07 per 10,000 people, is far below the rates in Baltimore (143.4) or New York City (70), representing over 46 and 22 times higher crime rates than Judea and Samaria, respectively.
Judea and Samaria also boast Israel’s lowest overall crime rate, by a wide margin: in 2024, the civil crime rate in Judea and Samaria reached 64 violent cases per 10,000 people, 1.4 times lower than Tel Aviv (91.7), and 2.1 times lower than the South (135.4).
Sharp increase in Palestinian terrorism
These incidents pale especially in comparison to the rate at which Israeli settlers themselves are targeted by Palestinians on a daily basis, including two different attacks last week alone, one of which resulted in the murder of Netanel Shukrun.
Rescuers Without Borders counted 6,389 attacks by Palestinians against Israelis in 2024 and 5,013 attacks in 2025. These figures include murder and shooting attacks, rather than mere vandalism or theft.
The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) reports a 291% surge in the foiling of “substantial attacks” in Judea and Samaria between 2022 and 2025, in a coordinated effort with the IDF to arrest thousands of terrorists: 472 attacks were foiled in 2022, compared with 1,374 in 2025.
Once again, far from graffiti incidents, these were planned suicide bombings, hostage taking, and explosive cars.
Factoring in both actual and foiled Palestinian attacks, this amounts to 37.1 cases per 10,000 Palestinians – more than 12 times more than Israeli settlers.
Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria are routinely targeted by Palestinian terrorism: 71 Israelis were murdered in 2024 and 2025, while 744 were injured. Those victims include three Israelis murdered in January 2025 when a Palestinian gunman opened fire at bus line 55 en route to their settlement and two Israelis, including a 16-year-old, murdered at a gas station near their settlement. The two phenomena are simply incomparable in scale or lethality.
Palestinian state-sponsored terrorism
While the Israel Police has increased the opening of investigation files by 27%, and the Chief Prosecutor’s Office is indicting dozens of suspected offenders, the Palestinian Authority has been leading actual state-sponsored terrorism.
Not only does it fail to investigate Palestinian terrorism, but it actively rewards it by allocating over $10 billion in financial benefits to terrorists over the past decade alone.
While the top brass of Israel’s leadership condemned these delinquent attacks, Palestinian Authority chairman Mahmoud Abbas hailed the “martyrs,” a term widely used for terrorists, as the “stars in the sky of the Palestinian nation’s struggle.”
Abbas further stressed before the UN General Assembly that “even if we were left with just one penny, we would pay it to the families of the martyrs and prisoners.”
Based on evidence or a political objective?
The purpose of this analysis is not to excuse violence nor present a whataboutism argument. Anyone who commits a crime should be held accountable to the full extent of the law, as many of them eventually are.
Rather, the point is narrower: to put a widely circulated claim in proportion, and facts ahead of narratives, particularly in a region plagued by genuine terrorism and strategic security threats.
The data showed that while documented incidents of wrongdoing or criminal offenses among the Israeli settler population do occur, the “settler violence” narrative rests on shaky foundations, nor does it fit the established legal definition of ethnic cleansing.
There is no public record of Miliband referring to the genuine ethnic cleansing against Christians in Nigeria, where at least 50,000 people have been murdered, nor in Syria, where Israel ultimately intervened militarily to prevent further bloodshed.
Instead, Miliband dedicated a passionate 21-minute address to 614 cases of vehicle arson and graffiti.
The true objective of the “settler violence” campaign may be much simpler than debate over numbers: serving as a tool in the arsenal of smearing Israel’s very presence in the territories and putting political pressure to make concessions.
Israel, on its part, may do well in making these figures public and accessible, alongside the traditional defense of the overall law-abiding residents in Judea and Samaria.
We are all exposed to disinformation online, and in an online environment inundated with widely repeated claims, verifying them is becoming increasingly harder. Yet heads of state should distinguish facts from politics and take a sober, more balanced approach to an otherwise complicated conflict.
The author is an independent national security analyst and the host of the podcast Underscore. He was the founder and executive director of the David Institute for Security Policy under IDSF – the Israel Defense and Security Forum.

Russia draws up measures to control bear population after spate of deadly attacks

Russia draws up measures to control bear population after spate of deadly attacks
Sept 30 - The Russian government said on Wednesday it was drawing up urgent measures to control the population of brown bears that has spiralled out of control in some regions, with at least 22 people killed in attacks.
In the latest attack, reported by state media, a 23-year-old man out gathering berries was killed by a bear this week in Kamchatka, in Russia's far east.
Last week, a Russian woman in Siberia was fatally mauled by a bear in her garden, amid a nationwide spate of killings that experts blame on climate change and human incompetence.
"It is clear that as the population grows, so too does the number of problems. Systemic measures are needed to ensure that humans and animals can coexist safely and to maintain the necessary balance," said Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev.
"In this regard, the Russian government is currently preparing a series of priority measures," he said.
The government said it would look at lifting hunting quotas on brown bears, would establish regional population limits, give local authorities extra powers to control their numbers, and identify regions that need more financing to tackle the problem.
The population of brown bears has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000, in part due to shorter and milder winters. At least 22 people have been killed by bears across Russia, the world's largest country, since this spring, the RIA state news agency said.
Experts cited in Russian media have said bears have been forced to look further afield for food this year because an early and dry spring meant there was a lack of berries for them to feed on in September.
People are also guilty of leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears and of ignoring safety rules, experts say.
Investigators in Krasnoyarsk in Siberia — home to nearly 27,000 bears according to environment ministry data — said last week that they had opened a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing it of negligence that led to the deaths of seven people in September alone.
The federal environment ministry has sought to play down the spate of attacks, saying that around 20 to 30 cases of bear attacks have been recorded annually in recent years, but that social media and smartphones are making such attacks seem more widespread. REUTERS

A man appeared on a live Channel 12 News broadcast on Wednesday, posing as a passenger who had been aboard the plane involved in a reported attempted hijacking. During an interview with reporter Tamir Steinman, he claimed that "the plane started going up and down," and that a passenger on board shouted "Allahu Akbar."
The hoaxer continued describing the alleged dramatic moments on the flight, saying passengers feared something had happened to the pilot and that the aircraft could crash. "We had no understanding of what was happening up front. There was insane pressure," he said.
As the conversation continued, however, his story began to raise doubts. The prank became clearer when he was asked who he was with. "I’m here with my brother Nevo," he said, before adding: "It’s short for Nebuchadnezzar."
At that point, it became obvious that the caller was not an actual passenger on the plane. The incident occurred amid heightened reports surrounding the flight and highlighted how, even during a live broadcast of a security incident, false information can make it onto the air.
Hoaxer's friend warned Channel 14 about the antics, so he went to Channel 12 instead
According to a post published afterward by one of the hoaxer’s friends, the incident was a preplanned attempt to "troll media systems in Israel." The friend claimed that he had warned Channel 14 staff about the impersonation attempt, but that the hoaxer simultaneously contacted Channel 12 News researchers, passed the screening process, and went on air within minutes.
The post claimed that during the interview, the hoaxer provided false details, invented names for himself and his brother, and claimed that both were on the flight. It also claimed that no one on the production team stopped the interview in time and that the hoaxer ultimately ended the conversation after feeling the prank had "already become too embarrassing."
The post’s author sharply criticized Channel 12 News’ handling of the incident, calling it "journalistic clownery." He claimed that the fact that the hoaxer managed to pass screening and remain on air for several minutes demonstrated a failure to verify the identities and credibility of interviewees during a developing event.
The incident quickly became a subject of jokes on social media, but it also raised broader questions about the process of verifying real-time testimonies, particularly during sensitive security incidents in which false information can spread within minutes. Channel 12 News declined to comment.

The figure surpassed expectations of 68,000 and accelerated from August's downwardly revised increase of 36,000.
Service providers added 59,000 jobs, while goods-producing industries created 31,000 positions, the report said.

By company size, businesses employing between 50 and 499 workers added 54,000 positions.
Base pay increased 3.2% from a year earlier, while gross pay rose 4.7%, ADP said.
"After a three-month slowdown, job creation rebounded and pay growth remained solid," ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said.
The report comes ahead of Friday's September employment figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which cover both private and public sector employment.
Economists expect nonfarm payrolls to increase by 84,000, following August's gain of 162,000, with the unemployment rate forecast to remain at 4.1%.

Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles

Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles
Ukrinform reports this, citing HUR’s post on Facebook.
The data have been published on the War&Sanctions portal.
“Pantsir” is a family of Russian self-propelled short-range anti-aircraft gun-and-missile systems designed to provide air defense for important areas and individual military and industrial facilities.
Russia also uses these systems to strengthen air defense at low and extremely low altitudes and to protect against mass attacks involving air-launched weapons. Since 2023, the Russians have been installing Pantsir systems on rooftops in Moscow. This year, another modification of the system, the Pantsir-SMD-E, was spotted there. Unlike earlier variants, it uses smaller TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles instead of automatic cannons.
Previously, the HUR published information on more than 50 companies involved in producing the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun-and-missile system.
Now, data on another 23 companies involved in producing 95Ya6 missiles have been disclosed. The 95Ya6 is the main medium-range missile used by various Pantsir modifications.
A key role in developing these missiles is played by the Academician Shipunov Instrument Design Bureau, the main developer and manufacturer of 95Ya6 missiles. The company is already known for its involvement in producing weapons for the Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided projectiles and cannons for Su-family fighter aircraft.
At the same time, about one-third of the companies whose information was published today are not under sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition.
They include:
Komponent plant – a manufacturer of proximity target sensors for 95Ya6 missiles;
Sergo Ordzhonikidze Saratov Electrotechnical Plant – manufactures and supplies emission and power-supply units for these missiles;
Tambov Elektropribor plant – a manufacturer of steering units for 95Ya6 missiles.
The HUR emphasizes that, to effectively weaken Russia’s military potential, it is important to coordinate restrictions against companies involved in the production of the full range of Russian weapons, rather than offensive systems alone.
Air defense capabilities, including Pantsir systems, protect Russian enterprises that manufacture cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as Russian troop formations during offensive and defensive operations in Ukraine and other important facilities in Russia.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the HUR has released data on 14 banks, financial intermediaries and payment systems that enable Russia to conduct international transactions while circumventing sanctions restrictions.

European preference in defence is a 'luxury' debate, NATO chief tells Euronews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:30:14 UTC
00:30:14 KST

NATO chief Mark Rutte told Euronews the European preference debate is a "luxury" since neither Europe nor the US can meet the growing demand for defence products and the industry should ramp up its capacity.
A Brussels debate over a European preference in defence contracts ignores a basic problem: Europe's defence industry cannot produce enough, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told Euronews on Wednesday.
"The problem is not: do you buy in Europe or do you buy it in the United States? The problem is: can you buy? The money is there. But the defense industrial base in Europe is underdeveloped. It is not producing enough," Rutte said at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels on Wednesday.
In recent months, the EU has debated whether to favour European-made products in public defence contracts, deeply dividing France, which wants a strict preference, and Germany, which favours a more open approach towards NATO allies.
Rutte, who said he comes from a free-market tradition, called the debate misplaced because neither European nor American factories can meet surging demand.
"It's always better if you have these free markets functioning as open and independent as possible. But at the moment, I think it is a discussion of luxury, whether you buy European or American, because we cannot buy on both sides. There's not enough production," he said.
He urged industry to invest to meet long-term demand and to innovate to develop state-of-the-art products.
"European companies like Thales are investing in the US. US companies are investing in Europe. It is a transatlantic defence industrial base that is working as one, and that's exactly as it should be," Rutte continued.
He cited Ukraine's urgent need for anti-ballistic missile interceptors, which neither the Franco-Italian SAMP/T nor US-made Patriot systems can be produced in sufficient numbers to supply.
"There is enough money for everybody. And there will be a defence dividend coming from this, because all these investments will also lead to societal returns, not only in the defence output and the defence industrial base, but also innovation and everything else," Rutte added.

Russia ramps up disinformation attacks on French media ahead of 2027 Presidential race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:29:40 UTC
00:29:40 KST

Russia ramps up disinformation attacks on French media ahead of 2027 Presidential race
Pro-Russian influence operations have caused a surge of 850% in fake news stories mimicking real media brands, according to a report published this week by disinformation specialist, NewsGuard. Out of the 15 most imitated news outlets, eight are French – including FRANCE 24.
Issued on:
The Russian disinformation operations that emerged at the start of the war in Ukraine have ramped up in the past year, with fake news articles and reports hijacking trusted media brands, to undermine public trust and deceive AI systems, a NewsGuard report released on Monday found.
Specialists from the US media watchdog found that three pro-Russian influence operations were the source of 950 fake news stories that mimicked 163 “supposedly trusted news brands” in 21 countries.
Among the 15 most imitated media brands were eight French outlets, including FRANCE 24, which saw its brand coopted by fake news stories 34 times over 12 months.
“It's no surprise that France, which is one of the biggest contributors of aid to Ukraine, is being specifically targeted,” said Chine Labbé, Europe editor at NewsGuard.
“We know that every time there is a show of diplomatic support for Ukraine – whether it's a speech by Emmanuel Macron, or a trip to Kyiv – disinformation campaigns follow within the same day.”
And ahead of the 2027 Presidential elections, France seems evermore in the crosshairs of pro-Russian actors.
Three presidential candidates who have pledged unwavering support for Ukraine – Raphaël Glucksmann, Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe – have all recently been the subject of fake news stories linked to pro-Russian groups.
Read moreRussia ramps up disinformation war as French presidential elections draw nearer
Europe on the front line
There are multiple objectives for Moscow’s information war according to NewsGuard, which compiled the report with the Ukrainian agency, Center for Countering Disinformation, French government agency Viginum, and anonymous research group, Antibot4Navalny.
These include discrediting support for Ukraine, undermining the reputation of Western leaders, stoking tensions within European democracies and disrupting electoral processes.
Year-on-year, the report found there had been an 850 percent increase in fake news stories mimicking known media brands – rising from 44 in the first half of 2025 to 421 in the first half of 2026.
“The explosion of this phenomenon may mean that the Russians see it as an effective tactic for eroding Western citizens' trust in the media – or at the very least, that there is significant potential to be tapped at little cost,” said Labbé.
“These days, it costs nothing to create a fake news site using AI and generate a lot of content.”
The report found pro-Kremlin influence campaigns had imitated media from global news outlets such as the BBC and CNN, to local news sites such as Ukraine’s Kyiv Independent and France’s La Montagne.
But European media outlets were the main target for this form of hybrid warfare linked to the Russian government under operations known as Matriochka, Storm-1516 and Doppelganger.
The most imitated outlet by far was Euronews, a multilingual platform based in France, which was the target for 82 fake articles between March 2023 and September 2026.
An example from 2026 was published shortly before Hungary’s parliamentary elections, which resulted in pro-Russian former prime minister Viktor Orban being removed from power.
It falsely claimed that pro-European candidate and current Prime Minister, Peter Magyar, called US President Donald Trump a “senile grandpa”, and that he wanted to end agreements between their two countries.
The other seven French news outlets among the 15 most targeted include Libération, Charlie Hebdo, BFM, FRANCE 24, Le Figaro, Le Parisien and Agence France-Presse (AFP).
“In every case, the Russian campaigns hijack the brands’ logos and layouts, sometimes creating a new site using a URL similar to the authentic one, making it difficult for the typical user to discern that it is counterfeit,” wrote NewsGuard. “The stories often include invented quotes from actual subject experts.”
“Leveraging a trusted media brand makes it possible to produce more credible fake news,” added Labbé. “But the long-term goal isn't to make you believe this or that piece of information. Their aim is to sow doubt in all our institutions.”
Read moreRussian interference in Armenia: A nation tested by disinformation
“It could damage trust, not only in our media, but in all media,” Cécile Mégie, Director of Editorial Strategies and Partnerships at France Médias Monde (FMM), which includes FRANCE 24 and RFI, told NewsGuard.
“It’s creating a climate of doubt about everything… The challenge is to navigate this climate and to show we are trustworthy media.”
Influencing AI
Disseminating disinformation on an industrial scale requires an army of fake social media accounts and pro-Kremlin media outlets that NewsGuard identifies as "the Pravda network", also known as Portal Kombat.
Made up of 280 websites that publish articles from pro-Russian outlets, Newsguard estimates that Pravda published approximately 6.3 million articles spreading 115 false claims in 2025.
One of the network’s stories published in 12 languages appeared to be from French news site Le Point. It falsely reported in 2026 that 20,000 Ukrainian soldiers had been evacuated to France for medical reasons where they had then deserted the army to join criminal gangs.
Read moreHybrid warfare: The threat of Russia looms over the Mediterranean
Official figures show that a little over 200 Ukrainians were transferred to French hospitals between February 2022 and April 2025, most of whom were war-wounded or children with serious medical conditions.
But the flood of fake news was enough to convince Google’s AI tool that the story could be real.
When questioned, the tech giant’s AI chatbot sourced fake articles supposedly from Le Point to claim that “thousands” of Ukrainian soldiers had received medical care in France.
“That's one of Matriochka's goals: to whitewash the Russian narrative by getting picked up by other media outlets or finding its way into chatbot responses,” said Labbé.
Read moreAI chatbot responses polluted by pro-Russian disinformation
Google defended its AI tool to NewsGuard, saying it had been unable to reproduce responses that referenced the fake news story.
“We have a high bar for our AI features in Search, and we invest significantly in the quality of responses,” a Google spokesperson said.
Yet another disinformation tactic aims to “overwhelm fact-checkers” themselves, using email campaigns to bombard journalists with fake reports, urging them to investigate their claims.
The goal – according to a 2025 Vigium report, is that fake stories will get picked up and gain traction.
Even if fake stories don’t go viral, they can still erode the overall quality of online news. “We need to be careful about how we address certain narratives,” said Labbé.
“We should treat fake news stories that don’t go viral differently from those that generate millions of views, but we still must continue to monitor them and document the tactics being used. If we don’t fight back, there’s a risk that AI tools will be influenced and citizens will be misinformed.”

Macron backs Spain over Ceuta migration crisis and urges firm EU action

Sánchez and Macron back cooperation between Spain and France and call for greater EU unity on migration, economic and geopolitical issues, despite the Spanish Senate's rejection of the bilateral Friendship Treaty.
The Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez and French president Emmanuel Macron highlighted the close relationship between their two countries and urged greater European unity to confront key migratory, economic and geopolitical challenges.
The joint press conference at the Moncloa Palace was also marked by the Spanish Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Friendship between Spain and France.
Sánchez apologised to Macron for the Upper House's no vote and promised that parliament would approve an agreement of this kind before the end of the current term. "All I can do is apologise," the Spanish premier said of Tuesday's rejection, insisting that the treaty would be adopted again to reaffirm the "sense of brotherhood" between the two countries.
The Treaty of Friendship, signed by Sánchez and Macron in Barcelona in January 2023, had already been endorsed by the lower house of parliament and ratified by France. However, the Senate voted it down on Tuesday, with 142 votes against from the PP and Vox, compared with 106 in favour and one abstention.
The rejection came six days after the Constitutional Court ruled unanimously, on 23 September, that the text was compatible with the Spanish constitution. One of the main flashpoints is a clause allowing a member of the French government to take part in meetings of the Spanish cabinet, and vice versa. Madrid and Paris exchanged letters clarifying that such participation would fall outside regular meetings of the Council of Ministers, but the PP has maintained its objections.
The parliamentary procedure still offers ways to resolve the stand-off between the two chambers. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares accused the PP of "sabotaging" the agreement, while the conservatives insist their stance does not call into question France's strategic importance as a neighbour, ally and European partner.
Sánchez stresses cooperation between Madrid and Paris
During his remarks, Sánchez thanked Macron for France's "solidarity" with Spain during the "difficult days" of the Ceuta migration crisis and pointed to the cooperation between the two countries in various emergency situations.
"Together we have fought a thousand and one battles in a Europe that has faced multiple crises," the prime minister said, citing as examples the joint efforts to secure the EU's Next Generation recovery funds and their collaboration during last summer's wildfires.
Sánchez acknowledged that Spain and France have had their differences, but underlined that both governments have always sought to reach agreements. In this regard, he pointed to a "very strong bond" between the two countries in defending the European project.
Macron likewise stressed the historic ties between France and Spain, recalling that their peoples have "always fought side by side". The French president also highlighted the close bilateral cooperation in areas such as the economy, defence and energy interconnection.
Sánchez responds to Vivas and defends contact with Ceuta's government
Asked about the testimony given by Ceuta's president, Juan Jesús Vivas, before the National Court, Sánchez said that although he was not aware of the precise content of the questioning, there had been constant communication between the central government and the regional executive ahead of the mass arrival of migrants.
"There was constant communication with him and with his government," Sánchez said, explaining that in the days before the incident three-way meetings were held between the central government, the Autonomous City of Ceuta and the government's regional delegation. The prime minister insisted these were not isolated contacts. "There was not one or two, but many exchanges," he said.
Sánchez also argued that no one, including Ceuta's own authorities, could have foreseen the scale of the arrivals that eventually took place. "No one anticipated, neither did they, that we might see a mass influx like the one that occurred on 30 and 31 July," he said.
On a possible visit by the King and Queen of Spain to the autonomous city, Sánchez said there would be an official announcement in due course, but declined to give a date. "You will see when the time comes," he added.
By contrast, Macron stressed that Spain had been "the victim of a multiple attack" and expressed surprise at the reaction of some European countries which, he said, failed to show solidarity with Madrid despite having demanded such support themselves during similar migration episodes. His comments were a thinly veiled reference to Italy and the government of Giorgia Meloni.
Macron calls for balance between solidarity and responsibility on migration
The Ceuta crisis featured prominently in Macron's address. The French president voiced his country's solidarity with Spain and argued that the European pact on migration and asylum must strike the right balance.
"The balance between solidarity and responsibility is very important," Macron said, calling for "robust solutions" to protect the borders, but always within the framework of EU law and in full respect of the Union's values.
Spain and France urge greater ambition for Europe
The two leaders also agreed on the need to strengthen the European project. Sánchez called for a "far more ambitious" EU budget, while Macron argued that the bloc's finances will be crucial in meeting future challenges.
The French president also emphasised the need for EU member states to maintain a common line on trade relations with China. "If we are not united as Europeans, we have no chance of succeeding," he warned.
Sánchez urged deeper European cooperation on security and called for "more transparency" around algorithms and "more control" over fake accounts on social media. He also argued for new mechanisms to shield member states from possible "foreign interference in electoral processes".
Defending multilateralism and a rules-based international order
On foreign policy, Sánchez stressed that Spain and France share a "global vocation" and hold similar positions on a number of crises, including the war in Iran and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Both governments back a two-state solution.
"In the face of the law of the strongest and the fascination with authoritarianism, Spain and France will always stand up for multilateralism and a rules-based international order," Sánchez said.
The Spaniard argued that cooperation between the two countries stems both from their principles and from the interests. "A world without rules is a more insecure world for our citizens," he added.
Macron likewise underlined the need for a common European stance and praised coordination between Paris and Madrid in defending sovereignty, peace and international stability.
Macron's visit has thus served to publicly reinforce the alliance between Spain and France, despite the political strains surrounding the Treaty of Friendship. Both governments have stressed the need to maintain close cooperation and a coordinated position on the main challenges facing Spain, France and the European Union as a whole.

‘He persuaded us’: Labour ministers moved by Andy Burnham’s emotional conference speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:28:45 UTC
00:28:45 KST

The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in Liverpool’s Baltic Triangle, headlined with a set by the noughties girlband Sugababes. As Labour activists and ministers belted out the lyrics under pink spotlights, it was hard not to draw some parallels with the party’s recent history.
There have been painful lineup changes and a lot of internal division, but this week onstage in Liverpool the originals are back together and they only played the hits. The fans can’t get enough.
Burnham’s own show on the main stage had the conference hall in raptures not because of Brexit or social care but because of the display of raw emotion after the tightly choreographed repression of the last six years. He may as well have walked across the stage with his feet crunching over the debris of shattered Ming vases.
The speech combined plans that had been forming inside Burnham’s head for the last decade as well as seat-of-his-pants political instinct. On the morning of the conference, the prime minister took off early for a morning jog and then returned to make final amendments. Even moments before he went on stage, he was still rewriting, aides said. About a quarter of the speech was entirely ad-libbed.
When Burnham was rehearsing the speech, aides said, he knew he was going to cry when he got to the paragraph about his late father – he never managed to get through any of the practice runs without tears.
But the long pause as he composed himself was the most emotional he had been. Several ministers said they themselves had been moved to tears, including Ed Miliband, who had recently lost his mother, as well as Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley, who are Burnham’s closest friends in government and the architects of his ascendancy.
After his speech, Burnham gathered all his ministers for a private pep talk. He said he knew they would not agree with everything, but – with the aura of a general sending his troops into battle – he told them to “get out there” and fight for it. He said he would not send them out with “a pea-shooter” – they needed proper weapons for the fight ahead and he promised he would provide them.
In the hallway outside the conference hall, minister after minister spoke with voices quivering with emotion. “This is all I have ever wanted,” one said.
The bar for speeches from political leaders has been low for the past decade or more. It is rare for clips to be anything more than a soundbite for social media and then a long shopping list of statistics and achievements. Burnham’s was the first time many MPs can recall a speech that was pure political argument.
And there was much in the speech that in normal times would have been a recipe for rebellion: Brexit, the triple lock, electoral reform and the lingering question marks over growth and defence.
“I found parts of the speech challenging, if I’m honest,” one cabinet minister admitted. “It contained things I had always thought we should never touch or an argument about public control which I would previously have said was too backward-looking. But in the room I agreed with every word because he persuaded us, he made an argument and made me question myself. It was a quite extraordinary thing.”
Even within the cabinet, there are those who grimace at the idea of electoral reform. “But you know, he believes in it, and I’m going to swallow it,” said one.
Burnham called his cabinet ministers in for a last-minute meeting just before the speech, where he laid out his private arguments and took their comments and feedback. “I feel almost embarrassed admitting this, but that has never happened before with any other leader,” one said.
On the sidelines of the conference, when cabinet ministers are at their most candid, they sometimes talk as if they have been through a kind of collective trauma – and the Burnham ascendancy has given them the release they need to confess how hard they have found the last two years. There are close new friendships and alliances forged in the coup, which defy previous factional lines.
“There’s the management-speak slogan: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast.’ Well, this is proof positive,” one cabinet minister said. “The past two years were utterly miserable, almost every single thing we achieved was poisoned by petty fighting. Every meeting was a choreographed exercise in pointlessness. Now we are discussing ideas and politics among colleagues who respect and like each other. I look back and I am so overwhelmed with relief that we did this.”
Another cabinet minister said: “I wasted so much of my own bandwidth fighting over the most puerile things, or defending my own staff who were being made miserable. Keir [Starmer] never dared to take it on.”
Even veterans of the Starmer years said they found themselves persuaded despite themselves. “Feels like there’s something quite psychologically profound about daring to take on the triple lock and finding that the planes don’t fall from the skies,” Starmer’s former strategy director Paul Ovenden posted.
Darren Jones, the ousted chief secretary who has made himself the face of the awkward squad, was also quick to lavish praise. “[The speech] told the story of his politics and the type of Britain he wants to build,” he said. “He told us we’d be in no doubt what his priorities are for the country, and he was right.”
Burnham will not welcome the comparison, but the closest recent one is how it felt at the Conservative party conference in the pre-disgrace Boris Johnson years: an electric electoral prospect who can genuinely reach across the political spectrum, hypnotising his doubters by the sheer force of his personality.
But this prime minister has no hint of the sleaze or incompetence that was always in the shadows for Johnson. If it comes, Burnham’s downfall will probably be his own voracious appetite for political risk – but that could also be the making of his premiership.

What happened on diverted Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?
Israel’s prime minister said one of the pilots stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane. The cause of the incident has not been confirmed, however.
A flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was diverted to Saudi Arabia after issuing a distress signal in what appeared to be a hijacking attempt on Wednesday.
The Flydubai flight FZ1073 was diverted as it flew from Dubai to Tel Aviv through Jordanian airspace, prompting Israel to deploy warplanes, the Reuters news agency reported.

- list 3 of 3Flydubai flight to Israel diverted after attack on pilot
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the pilots had stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane. He added that Israel was preparing for other “potential threats” after the incident.
Flydubai said an altercation had occurred on the flight deck and that all passengers were safe and accounted for. The plane was secured by on-duty crew travelling onboard, it added.
“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a Flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”
At Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, officials said both the plane’s captain and first officer were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries, according to a statement from the Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, carried by the Saudi state-run Al Ekhbariya television.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia later identified the injured captain as Indian national Smit Machchhar. The embassy said he was receiving treatment at a hospital in Tabuk and was reported to be in stable condition, adding that it was in contact with his family and Saudi authorities.
The UAE has become a popular holiday destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalised ties in 2020. Here’s what we know about what happened.
What happened?
Footage taken onboard the plane appears to show the injured pilot lying on the cabin floor with several stab wounds, and a passenger with a bloody wound to the head.
In another video, passengers weep and cry out in distress as the aircraft shakes.
Yasmin Abukasis, the mother of one of the passengers onboard, said her daughter Miriam thought she was going to die. “The plane started to lose control,” she told journalists at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport, before other pilots onboard took control of the aircraft.
Flight tracking data indicated the plane descended about 14,000 feet (4,300 metres) in less than 30 seconds about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai. Flightradar24 said on X that an initial general emergency signal designated by code 7700 was issued at about 05:31 GMT and was later changed to another emergency signal with code 7500 declaring “unlawful interference”.
Passenger Dalia Shpigel told Israeli newspaper Haaretz that some people seated towards the front of the plane broke into the cockpit after the plane began to descend and they realised something was wrong.
“An hour before landing, we felt that there was no control over the plane, that it was starting to jump,” she said. “The guys saw that the plane had begun to dive and broke into the cockpit.”
Netanyahu said he later spoke to one of the Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit and overpowered one of the pilots who was reportedly trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems.
“I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage,” Netanyahu said in a statement. “They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster.”
Passenger Yitzhak Lieber, reportedly one of the men who overpowered the co-pilot, sent a video to his family from the plane, international media reported. In it, he says: “There is a pilot who was seriously injured, they’ve evacuated him. We overpowered the terrorist and he is tied up.”
The mostly Israeli passengers were later flown to Tel Aviv on a replacement flight, Tabuk airport confirmed.
The Times of Israel reported that Netanyahu was at Ben Gurion’s Terminal 1 building to greet passengers when the replacement flight landed shortly before 4pm GMT. Families were waiting in a designated area set up for them in the domestic arrivals hall while security officials prepared to interview them.

What do we know about what caused the incident?
The motive of the apparent attack was not immediately clear. Netanyahu said Saudi authorities were interrogating the pilot accused of carrying out the attack.
Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz said preliminary information indicated the attacker intended to crash the plane, killing everyone onboard, calling the incident an “attempted jihadist terror attack”.
An Israeli official who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity identified the attacker as an Omani national.
Israel does not have formal diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia or Oman, maintaining a policy of occasional dialogue through informal channels. Muscat has chosen not to join other countries in the region in normalising ties with Israel over Palestinian rights. Saudi Arabia has made normalisation of Israeli ties conditional on Israel’s acceptance of a Palestinian state.
Israel is days away from marking the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and which triggered Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 75,000 Palestinians – mostly women and children – including about 1,400 since a United States-brokered “ceasefire” supposedly took effect in October 2025.
Was a second Flydubai flight diverted?
No. A second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, was erroneously reported in Hebrew media to have turned around, according to The Times of Israel.
The news outlet added that the mistake appeared to have been due to a glitch on flight-tracking sites.
The plane did not issue any emergency signal, and it was reported to be on its course to Tel Aviv without disruptions.
What has the response been?
Reuters reported that Netanyahu has ordered authorities to “ramp up” security on Israeli carriers and non-Israeli carriers, citing a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid claimed Netanyahu’s political allies had attempted to pass off the incident as the fulfilment of warnings a day earlier about a possible attack on Israel ahead of its legislative election scheduled for October 27.
“The warning about activity abroad is specific, has been in place for more than two years, and has nothing to do with planes or anything resembling what happened this morning,” Lapid wrote on X.
Speaking of Netanyahu, Lapid said: “He’s trying to hitch a pathetic ride on heroic Israelis who prevented a disaster that he (once again) wasn’t prepared for.”

China Focus: Beijing deploys 400 mln parasitic wasps in biological control effort targeting invasive fall webworm
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:25:45 CST
00:25:45 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Beijing is fighting an invasive pest with an army of natural enemies. Since Monday, the Chinese capital has been releasing another 400 million parasitic wasps to control a surge of fall webworms.
These wasps, known scientifically as Chouioia cunea Yang, are dominant parasitic natural enemies of the pest and safe for humans and livestock. "Earlier this year alone, Beijing unleashed nearly 700 million of them," said Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry and also the discoverer of the wasp.
The fall webworm, a major invasive pest native to North America, produces three generations a year, each passing through four life stages, namely egg, larva, pupa and adult. Beijing is currently in the peak damage period of third-generation fall webworm larvae, with a surge of mature larvae set to descend from trees to pupate, Yang said.
The fall webworm can damage more than 300 plant species. In the capital, over 200 species of trees, fruit trees, flowers and crops are under threat, with ash, mulberry and plane trees among its favorite targets. The pest only damages plants -- neither its larvae nor adults are toxic or harmful to humans, the expert added.
In response to residents' reports that fall webworms have been noticeably more numerous in Beijing this year compared with previous years, Yang Sihan, with the Beijing municipal landscape and greenery resource protection center, attributed the increase mainly to warmer winters and frequent summer rainfall.
Warmer winters in recent years have pushed up the survival rate of the pest's overwintering pupae. "Our five-year survey of overwintering populations in some areas shows that the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3 percent in 2023 to 84.2 percent this year," Yang noted, adding that frequent rainfall in Beijing this summer also hampered pest control operations.
Experts explained that the difficulty of controlling the fall webworm is directly tied to the pest's own characteristics and the practical challenges involved.
The fall webworm has an extremely strong reproductive capacity. A single female moth lays an average of 300 to 600 eggs, and up to 2,000 under favorable conditions. Even a small number of surviving insects can allow the population to rebound rapidly. Moreover, the fall webworm showed pronounced generation overlap this year, with multiple life stages present at the same time.
Urban operational conditions also pose challenges. Narrow spaces, tall trees with dense canopies, and the limited range of some ground sprayers can all reduce the effectiveness of pest control.
Despite these challenges, local authorities have rolled out a coordinated response combining early warning and control measures.
According to Yang Sihan, almost 3,000 monitoring sites have been set up across the city under a grid-based management system. Based on pest patterns, meteorological data and expert consultation, officials issue rolling long-, medium- and short-term warnings to guide precise action.
On the control front, beyond releasing parasitic wasps for biological control, crews manually remove larval webs and wrap corrugated paper and non-woven fabric around tree trunks to trap mature larvae descending to pupate.
Traps and insect-killing lamps are also deployed to trap and kill adult moths, thereby breaking the reproductive cycle. In addition, authorities use high-efficiency, low-toxicity, eco-friendly pesticides and carry out ground spraying at staggered times.
The Beijing Municipal Forestry and Parks Bureau is calling on residents to help control this pest.
The bureau advised residents to clear away dead branches, fallen leaves and clutter around their homes to remove places where larvae can pupate. It also suggested cutting off infested branches and leaves when larval webs are spotted, and disposing of them in sealed bags. Mature larvae on tree trunks or the ground, notably, can simply be crushed underfoot.
Meanwhile, anyone who notices chewed leaves, webs or mature larvae on trees in public areas can call the 12345 citizen hotline or report it to their local landscaping and greening department, the bureau added. ■

Ukraine Needs 20mm F-16 Ammo to Down Russian Jet Drones

Ukraine wants to purchase tens of hundreds of thousands of 20-millimeter rounds for its F-16 fighter aircraft to shoot down Russia’s increasingly deployed jet-powered attack drones.
Kyiv is negotiating with several European countries and ammunition manufacturers about potential supplies, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Sept. 30, citing people familiar with the discussions.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ammunition would be fired from the F-16’s built-in cannon, offering Ukraine a potentially cheaper and more widely available alternative to using scarce air-to-air missiles against each Russian drone.
According to Bloomberg, destroying one drone may require approximately 150 rounds. At the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 such rounds per day.
Cheaper option against Russian drones
Ukraine has used AIM-9 Sidewinder and AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles launched from F-16s to intercept Russian aerial targets. These guided missiles are considerably more expensive than cannon ammunition and are also needed by ground-based air defense systems.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots are already using their aircraft’s 20-millimeter cannons against jet-powered drones when other intercept options were unavailable.
The F-16 carries an internally mounted M61A1 Vulcan six-barrel rotary cannon that fires 6,000 rounds per minute. Using it allows pilots to preserve guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets.
Each aircraft carries 500 usable rounds of semi-armor piercing, high-explosives, incendiary (SAPHEI) PGU-28 20mm cartridges.
Pentagon Commits Nearly All $400M in Ukraine Aid a Day Before Deadline
In employing the gun against airborne targets, pilots usually fire half-second bursts which puts out 50 exploding bullets in each brief trigger squeeze. And the trigger is positioned in the same place as it is when shooting a firearm – under your right index finger.
The tactic nevertheless requires pilots to approach drones at relatively close range. Shahed drones are approximately 1/10 the size of an average fighter, which at maximum range for the typical gunshot of 4,000 feet slant range, the target is about 2 milliradians or about the size of the smallest item in the heads-up display (HUD) which is a dot, or about the size of a decimal or period on this page.
Falling debris from destroyed drones and overspray from the natural dispersion of projectiles that don’t hit the target may also endanger people and property within the Vulcan’s ground projected elliptical footprint when intercepts take place over populated areas.
Bloomberg reported that global supplies of 20-millimeter ammunition are more plentiful than stocks of Patriot and Western air-to-air missiles, potentially allowing Kyiv to obtain the rounds more quickly.
Russia expands jet-powered drone attacks
Russia has rapidly increased its use of jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than conventional propeller-driven Shaheds and are more difficult for mobile fire groups and existing interceptor drones to destroy.
According to Ukrainian Air Force, Russian launches of jet-powered drones rose from around 350 in June to approximately 2,850 in August.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched more than 100 drones on Tuesday, including 29 jet-powered models. Ukrainian forces intercepted 18 of the faster drones, he said.
Ukraine is simultaneously developing high-speed interceptor drones and other domestic systems to counter the new threat. Zelensky said on Tuesday that officials had selected the first prototypes of a dedicated countermeasure and established deadlines, financing requirements and planned production volumes.
Kyiv has also received urgent deliveries of F-16 ammunition from Belgium, Spain and other partners. Belgium has agreed to transfer three additional F-16 fighters to Ukraine by the end of 2026.
“As Russia escalates its attacks every day, we need to add more capabilities to shoot down aerial targets and protect people,” Zelensky said.
