GENEVA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China called on the international community to establish a just, equitable, and inclusive global human rights governance system guided by the Global Governance Initiative on Wednesday.
Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, made the remarks while delivering a joint statement entitled "Improving International Human Rights Governance," on behalf of 71 countries at the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council at the Palais des Nations.
The Global Governance Initiative, proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 1, 2025, has received support and positive responses from numerous countries and international organizations.
Jia noted in this joint statement that the international landscape is undergoing profound changes amid a complex and turbulent environment, while global human rights governance is facing profound adjustments.
He said that China puts forward four proposals:
First, adopt a people-centered approach. It is up to the people of each country to assess and improve their own human rights situation, so as to stay true to the original purpose of human rights governance and meet the people's needs.
Second, uphold sovereign equality. All countries should participate, make decisions and benefit on an equal footing. Greater attention should be paid to the voices of the Global South. We advocate fairness, objectivity and non-selectivity, and call for dialogue and cooperation based on mutual respect.
Third, uphold fairness and justice. We oppose the politicization and instrumentalization of human rights, take a holistic approach to all categories of human rights, advance human rights reform in a prudent manner, and support multilateral human rights institutions and experts in discharging their mandates objectively and impartially.
Fourth, uphold the international rule of law. We champion the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, ensure the equal and consistent application of international law and international rules, and oppose double standards, interference in the internal affairs of other countries under the pretext of human rights, and imposition of one's own standards on others.
The joint statement is based on the platform of The Group of Friends of Global Governance in Geneva, officially launched on Feb. 27, 2026, at the Palais des Nations. ■

Thailand's economy broadly stable in August: central bank

00:25:13 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's economy remained broadly unchanged in August on a monthly basis, as higher private investment and a slight rise in private consumption offset declines in manufacturing output and service-sector activity, the central bank said on Wednesday.
According to the Bank of Thailand, merchandise exports excluding gold held steady at a high level, dipping 0.1 percent in August from a month earlier, supported by the global technology and artificial intelligence (AI) cycle.
Electronics exports decreased, reflecting lower shipments of computer parts and electronic integrated circuits and components. Automotive exports also dropped, while exports of petroleum and agricultural products increased, the central bank said in a statement.
Inbound tourists rose 1.8 percent from the previous month, mainly driven by higher arrivals from China, partly due to stronger travel demand during the summer school holiday period, the central bank's assistant governor, Chayawadee Chai-anant, said.
Despite that, tourism receipts remained relatively stable as the average length of stay for foreign tourists shortened, reflecting the recovery of long-haul flights to levels close to those seen before the outbreak of the Middle East conflict, Chayawadee told a news conference.
On domestic demand, private investment rose 2.2 percent month-on-month, boosted by higher investment in machinery and equipment and supported by the global technology cycle and investment in data centers, Chayawadee said.
Private consumption picked up 0.4 percent from a month earlier, fueled by higher spending on services, notably hotels and restaurants, in line with increased foreign arrivals, while spending on durable goods also continued to grow, she noted.
Looking ahead, the central bank expects the Thai economy to recover, though unevenly across sectors, with key growth drivers being exports and private investment, which benefit from the global electronics and AI cycle.
Meanwhile, household consumption is supported by government stimulus measures and improving labor income prospects, consistent with the rebound in tourism and higher agricultural commodity prices, the central bank said.
It added that geopolitical conflicts and international trade protectionist policies, alongside the impact of flooding and El Nino weather conditions, were among the key factors to monitor. ■

Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:24:18 UTC
00:24:18 KST

Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
Ukraine’s NATO-donated F-16 fleet is out of commission more often than it engages Russian drones, The Wall Street Journal has claimed.
The American-produced fighter jets were touted as the latest “gamechanger” weapon in Kiev’s conflict with Russia, a tool that will help “achieve goals outside of Ukraine,” as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said when the first batch was set to arrive in the summer of 2024.
However, a key EU member in the European-led scheme cannot keep up with necessary maintenance of the fleet, according to the newspaper.
What is the F-16 initiative?
The plan was launched in 2023, as Ukraine’s fleet of Soviet-built military aircraft was dwindling. Pro-Kiev propaganda implied that the US-made multirole jets would help Ukrainian forces challenge Russia’s air dominance over the front line. But it was hardly a secret that they would be kept far away from Russian SAMs and fighter jets and only engage long-range drones and cruise missiles.
Donor nations announced they were prepared to spend years training Ukrainian pilots, refurbishing the aircraft they were willing to spare, and happily signing deals for modern replacements to bolster their own militaries – the F-16 initiative was effectively a NATO-backed pyramid scheme allowing everyone to spend big and upgrade their air forces.
Ukraine has since received about 40 jets, roughly half of what the donors pledged, and lost several of them during combat missions, reportedly after corners were cut for expediency during training courses. It is now facing winter with an acute shortage of air defense systems.
What’s the problem?
Belgium’s Sabena Aerospace Engineering, awarded a $235.5 million contract for maintenance of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet, is not keeping up with the demand, according to the Wall Street Journal editorial board.
An inspection that normally takes two to six weeks lasts “as long as 40 weeks in Belgium,” retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery said. Another Western source said more than half of Ukrainian jets are now in maintenance limbo, with the rest set to become grounded by the end of the year.
Was the issue unexpected?
Media reports saying that the Ukrainian F-16 fleet is being overworked surfaced as early as July, as Kiev’s shortage of ground-launched interceptor missiles became more acute. There were also indicators pointing to a bottleneck in Belgium.
In April, the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation reported that not one of the six F-16s that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store pledged to Ukraine in 2023 had been delivered. Four of them were not airworthy to begin with, but the two others were previously used to train Ukrainian pilots in Denmark.
The six jets were stuck at a Sabena workshop in Belgium due to “significant capacity problems,” the report said.
Is Ukraine getting more jets?
There were delays in deliveries as well.
Belgium promised in 2024 to transfer 30 aircraft set to be phased out by its air force, which was expecting F-35 replacements. Then-Defense Minister Ludivine Dedonder said Ukraine would start receiving the old jets “as soon as the F-35s arrive on Belgian soil,” but no transfers have been reported since.
Most of the aircraft that Kiev did get reportedly came from the Netherlands and Denmark, the co-leaders of the F-16 initiative.
Why does Ukraine have air defense problems?
A shortage of Western weapons partially caused Ukraine’s current situation.
When this summer Vladimir Zelensky announced a 40-day “pressure campaign” of long-rage strikes on refineries, civilian ships, and commercial warehouses, his team reportedly hoped that images of smoke-plumes stretching over big Russian cities would support his bid to receive more Patriot missile interceptors from the limited US stockpile.
If true, the plan backfired. NATO nations are scrambling to provide what Kiev wants, while the economic damage caused by Russian retaliation is mounting. And Ukraine already has a $27 billion military budget hole that European donors are struggling to fill.
Ukrainian forces previously learned that Western arms gifts come with caveats. Donated NATO artillery systems lacked interoperability and were described as a “zoo” by troops. Much-hyped NATO battle tanks turned out to be mostly useless in drone-driven warfare and had to be kept away from the front line.
Can Ukraine come up with alternatives?
Zelensky puts on a brave face talking about the dire situation. Last week he claimed Ukraine had successfully tested four new interceptor drones designed to shoot down faster-moving jet UAVs – the kind of targets the WSJ claimed F-16s are well-suited to take down.
But an earlier Reuters report said trials in July “did not go to plan” as the prototypes lost control and “crashed into nearby fields and forests.”
Ukrainian opposition lawmaker Sergey Rakhmanin, who sits on the national defense committee, has said Kiev missed Russia’s rapid development of jet kamikaze drones. He said Ukrainian interceptors cost up to $100,000 apiece and that scaling up production would require too much time, even if funding becomes available.

====================================================================================================

Readings in Korean Confucian Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:23:00 UTC
00:23:00 KST

When I first held Ivanhoe and Wang’s Readings in Korean Confucian Philosophy in my hands and leafed through it, I immediately regretted retiring from teaching a couple of months earlier. I had taught Korean cultural history for decades but, since most of my students couldn’t read Korean or Classical Chinese, I couldn’t include substantial excerpts from the writings of Korean Confucian philosophers among the primary sources I asked them to read. Now that I was no longer teaching undergraduates, I had finally found a book with material I could have assigned. Moreover, the excerpts translated are short enough (with the exception of a lengthy translation at the end of Dasan’s reflections on Mencius) that undergraduates wouldn’t be frightened by them.
Making it even more useful for students, the book opens with a concise survey of the history of Neo-Confucianism on the Korean peninsula, focusing on the eight individuals who provide the material translated for this work. I am disappointed that the introduction doesn’t discuss the earlier history of Confucianism in Korea. However, I realize that this is probably because the earlier versions of Confucianism in Korea were not particularly philosophical. Instead, they were more concerned with government administration, history, and literature. Nevertheless, this book should have been called Readings in Korean Neo-Confucian Philosophy, since only that more philosophical version of Confucianism is covered in these pages.
Ivanhoe and Wang chose to translate excerpts from the writings of eight individuals important in shaping Korean Neo-Confucianism over the five-plus centuries of Joseon (1392-1910). The first two, Jeong Dojeon (1342-1398) and Gwon Geun (1352-1409), were major figures in the introduction of Neo-Confucianism to Korea in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. The next two, Seo Gyeongdeok (1489-1546) and Yi Eonjeok (1491-1553), helped solidify Neo-Confucianism’s presence on Korean soil by delving deeply into its core principles as articulated earlier in China. The third group consists of two of the most important philosophers in all of Joseon’s history, Yi Hwang (1501-1570) and Yi I (1536-1584). Both men are often given credit for Korean-izing Neo-Confucianism in the 16th century by focusing attention on issues which Chinese Confucians had not paid as much attention to, such as the role of emotions in stimulating behavior. Finally, the last group, Jeong Jedu (1649-1736) and Jeong Yakyong (1762-1836), were active in the second half of Joseon. They are known for pushing the boundaries of Neo-Confucian philosophy in Korea, promoting approaches which, though still undeniably Confucian, departed significantly from the mainstream.
The translations in this anthology are readable and, by and large, faithful to the original texts. However, I would have liked to have seen a better indication in the translations of key terms that Confucianism is more about doing than being, more about what happens or is done than about what is, and more about interactions than about solitary existence.[1] One example of a somewhat misleading translation is “sincerity”. In English, that term suggests an absence of deceit or hypocrisy. But the Chinese character translated here as “sincerity” (seong/cheng) means much more than that. It refers to acting in a selfless manner, doing what one is supposed to do according to the role one is playing in the situation one finds oneself in, without trying to gain some personal advantage or follow one’s personal predilections. Because “sincerity” is such an important term in the revered classic The Doctrine of the Mean, it appears in the writings of all eight men featured in this anthology. Gwon Geun, when explaining Neo-Confucianism to his students, told them that sincerity encompasses the different ways human beings act appropriately, saying it referred to the “actual cycle of operations” of major human virtues (55). Readers should have been reminded of that active sense of sincerity when that term reappears in this book.
“Pattern” (i/li) is another problematic translation. It does mean pattern, but it is more dynamic than that translation alone suggests. It refers to normative patterns, which both define and direct appropriate actions in interactive situations. I wish Ivanhoe and Wang had been more explicit about the normative and directive nature of “pattern” and had also signaled in the way they translated that key term that it always refers to at least potential interactions. As Gwon Geon explained, “Pattern is the public-spirited Way (i.e., not some private or personal point of view)” (8). Way is their translation of Dao, which, as Ivanhoe and Wang well know, means the proper way to behave. Unfortunately, their decision to stick to the standard way of rendering those key Neo-Confucian concepts in English means that their translations do not adequately reflect the behavioral implications of these core Neo-Confucian terms.
Those are not their only translation choices which fail to reflect the dynamism I would have liked to have seen. For example, in a poem by Yi Eonjeok, “i ryun” is translated as “the unvarying standard” (136). This is an incomplete translation. “I ryun” means “the unvarying ethical standards”, the fundamental guidelines for human interactions. Similarly, they translate Yi I as defining human nature as “humaneness, righteousness, rites, wisdom, and trustworthiness” (191). Since those five terms refers to different ways of acting appropriately, they should have been translated as verbal phrases rather than as nouns. Yi I was saying that human nature is the potential for acting in humane, righteous, polite, wise, and trustworthy manners.
Two key terms, terms which appear multiple times throughout this text, are eum and yang (C. yin and yang), which Ivanhoe and Wang wisely left untranslated. However, it would have helped readers unfamiliar with Confucian ways of thinking if they had explained the eum and yang are not things. They are instead complementary ways of interacting, with eum referring to the less active and yang to the more active. That meaning is implied in the statement by the Chinese Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi (1130-1200) cited by Yi Hwang: “The Supreme Ultimate moves and produces yang, is still and produces eum” (139).
These quibbles of mine do not mean that I disagree with their translation choices overall. In fact, I may borrow for my own work their “reverential attention” for gyeong (C. jing) and “sympathetic concern” for seo (C. shu). Nor does my preference for more action-oriented translations mean that I would be uncomfortable assigning this to undergraduates. Far from it. I like the wide range of material included, from poetry and letters to philosophical essays and civil service exam policy questions. And I was pleased to see that they even include such visual aids to understanding Neo-Confucianism as the “Chart of the Human Heart-mind and the Heart-mind of the Way” (195).
However, it would have been helpful to those more familiar with Western philosophy than with traditional East Asian philosophy if the translators had pointed out in their introduction how philosophy was done differently in East Asia. Epistemology, ontology, and formal logic were not of much concern. Instead, Confucian philosophers were more concerned with questions of ethics, of how we should behave and how we can discipline ourselves to behave the way we should behave. Even their cosmology, if we can call it that, was more about the fundamental processes, not the fundamental things, which constitute the universe. Even the Confucian description of how the universe came to be is not intended to be chronological. Instead, it is intended to show how everything is related to everything else, that everything has its roots in the stillness behind motion.
The translators could also have let their readers know that much Korean Confucian philosophizing consisted of interpretations of earlier Confucian works, primarily the ancient Chinese Classics, as well as the writings of the Song dynasty (960-1279) scholars in China who systemized Neo-Confucianism. That is implied when they identify the Chinese sources drawn upon by the writers they translate. As can be seen in the translations, Korean Neo-Confucian philosophers interacted with earlier Chinese texts when they laid out their philosophical arguments. It is important, if we want to understand why they say what they say, to know who and what they are relating to. That is why naming their sources is helpful.
That said, I would have preferred to see the names of those Chinese philosophers cited here provided in the romanization of the Chinese pronunciation of their names rather than the Korean pronunciation. Many people who will avail themselves of the translations in this anthology will be more familiar with Chinese Confucianism than with Korean Confucianism and therefore will be puzzled when they encounter the name Ju Hui, whom they would more easily recognize as Zhu Xi, or the name Jeong Ho, whom they would more easily recognize as Cheng Hao. The translators do provide the Chinese pronunciation of key names and terms in parentheses after the first use of the Korean romanization, but readers may skip around among the various translated selections and may therefore miss seeing the more familiar Chinese way of pronouncing those names and terms.
Nevertheless, the pluses of this book far outweigh any minuses. There is much readers can learn from this first-of-its-kind collection of translations of selections from the writings of Korea’s most important Neo-Confucian philosophers. One theme careful readers will notice running through these selections is tension over where li (“pattern”) can be found. Jeong Jedu insists that li operates only within the human heart-mind. Li may tell us how to interact with the external world, but it is not found in the external world. That may be because, for Jeong, li stimulates and directs moral behavior and only human beings can be moral (239-244). Yi Hwang, on the other hand, insists that li exists within everything, human or otherwise. For Yi Hwang, though li and the matter which coagulates into things need to be analytically distinguished, material objects cannot take the shape they have or operate the way they do without their own li (139-142). Yi agrees with Jeong that li is normative, but he disagrees on whether it needs consciousness to operate. Yi argued that the unconscious li in things resonates with the li in our heart-minds and tells us how to interact with them. This view that li is everywhere became the dominant position in Chosŏn, as we can see in Jeong Yakyong’s insistence that “Dogs have the pattern of dogs. Oxen have the patterns of oxen. There clearly are not in me” (327).
It is important to know where to look for li since it is only by identifying the li applicable in a particular situation that we can act appropriately. Philosophy, both in the East and the West, is the search for knowledge. But what does knowledge mean to Korean Confucians? Knowledge for them is primarily knowledge of li, of knowing how to act. This is not epistemology. It is not questioning how we know but discussing how we ensure that our knowledge is an accurate guide to appropriate behavior.
Once we know how we should act, Neo-Confucians insist we have to act that way. It is clear in the selections in this anthology that Neo-Confucianism is an ethical philosophy. It is all about learning how to act appropriately and then disciplining ourselves to act appropriately. What does acting appropriately mean to a Neo-Confucian thinker? It means acting selflessly, putting the common good ahead of any personal benefit or advantage. To ensure you do that, you have to minimize your selfish thoughts and emotions (329-330).
This practical ethical emphasis makes Korean Confucianism quite different from the way philosophy is often practiced in modern philosophy departments in the West.[2] That should be obvious to anyone who reads through the selections in this book. Despite what seem at times to be metaphysical debates, the question of how to act appropriately was always central to their discussions. The glimpses of Korean Confucian thought contained in this book reveal to those unfamiliar with traditional Korean philosophy how its issues and its approaches to solving those issues constitute a philosophical tradition which should become better known in the West. Ivanhoe and Wang have done the field a great service by making that possible.
REFERENCES
Roger T. Ames. Confucian Role Ethics: A Vocabulary. Hong Kong: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 2011.
Halla Kim, “Korean Philosophy Today: Retrospect and Prospect,” Journal of Confucian Philosophy and Culture 40 (2023): 5-29.
[1] For an analysis of Confucianism as primarily action- and interaction-oriented, see Roger T. Ames. Confucian Role Ethics: A Vocabulary. Hong Kong: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 2011.
[2] A good discussion of what makes Korean philosophy Korean can be found in Halla Kim, “Korean Philosophy Today: Retrospect and Prospect,” Journal of Confucian Philosophy and Culture 40 (2023): 5-29.

US appeals court halts Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in two centuries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:22:56 UTC
00:22:56 KST

US appeals court halts Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in two centuries
- A US appeals court halted the execution of Christa Pike, Tennessee's first female execution in over 200 years, to review her claims of childhood sexual abuse.
- Pike was convicted for a brutal 1995 murder committed as a teenager; her clemency petition citing trauma and mental illness was denied by Governor Bill Lee.
- Her case has attracted international attention, with human rights experts and trauma specialists urging commutation due to the potential psychological harm of lethal injection.
AI generated
NASHVILLE, Tennessee – A US appeals court on Sept 30 halted the execution of death row inmate Christa Pike in Tennessee, less than two hours before she was scheduled to become the first woman that state has put to death in more than 200 years.
The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals ordered a “short stay of execution” to give it time to weigh Pike’s claim that her allegations of childhood sexual abuse were not adequately considered during her sentencing. The court did not provide a specific timeframe.
Pike, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee, would be the only person in the modern era of US capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
The Tennessee attorney-general’s office immediately asked the US Supreme Court to vacate the stay order.
The Supreme Court on Sept 29 rejected an 11th-hour bid for a stay of execution, which is set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
The grisly nature of the slaying, which involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram on the victim’s chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir of the carnage, drew intense media coverage at the time.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted the following year of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, appeared as a witness for the prosecution and received probation.
Currently the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, Pike was also convicted in August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an assault on another inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In a 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, her lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including two rapes at ages 11 and 17. And they cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Teen who committed murder ‘no longer exists’
Her lawyers also pointed to evidence that Pike’s mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote in response to Lee’s denial of clemency. “Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.”
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in support of the execution.
Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. Before Sept 30, Tennessee had executed 17 people.
Pike’s case has drawn international attention, with a group of United Nations human rights experts issuing a recent statement calling for commutation of her death sentence.
Sexual violence and trauma experts have also spoken out on her behalf, arguing that the procedures surrounding lethal injection would likely cause Pike to experience severe, traumatic flashbacks of child sexual abuse and rape, adding to the cruelty and anguish of her death.
Tennessee prison officials in May aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for a lethal injection. REUTERS

Photos: Kashmir’s 600-year-old Wazwan wedding feast adapts to modern life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:22:52 UTC
00:22:52 KST

In Pictures
Photos: Kashmir’s 600-year-old Wazwan wedding feast adapts to modern life
Wazwan, a multicourse mutton feast, reflects Kashmiri cultural roots with recipes dating back to the 14th century.
As autumn approaches, the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb echoes across courtyards and back lanes in Kashmir, where cooks prepare Wazwan – a lavish, multi-course mutton feast that remains central to traditional wedding celebrations.
Wazwan arrived in the valley from Central Asia in the 14th century, when rulers brought skilled chefs along with the carpet and shawl weavers that later defined the region’s craft heritage.
Today, the feast is both a marker of social status and a powerful symbol of Kashmiri identity.
Among its guardians is 74-year-old Ghulam Nabi Baba, a veteran Wazwan chef who traces his lineage to those early migrants. His forefathers settled in Srinagar’s old city as part of a community of cooks known as Wazpora.
“There were only seven mutton dishes at that time. Over the centuries we added more, and now there are around 20,” Baba said.
He explained how the number of dishes and the amount of meat often reflect a family’s wealth.
“Forty years ago in Delina [a village in north Kashmir] I cooked 4,500kg (9,920 pounds) of meat. That was a very big wedding. Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200kg (440 pounds),” he added.
Despite the expanding menu, the core techniques have changed little. Lightly spiced meat is still pounded by hand before being simmered slowly over wood fires – a labour-intensive process Baba has followed since joining his father as a cook at 15.
But the pressures of modern life are reshaping the tradition. Baba’s son has chosen to open a restaurant rather than work weddings, saying the round-the-clock demands are too exhausting.
He believes he is still carrying forward the family’s centuries-old culinary legacy – just in a different setting, as Wazwan adapts to contemporary tastes and lifestyles.

TABUK, Saudi Arabia – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sept 30 that the pilot of a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight had tried to crash the plane and kill its passengers, after the aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Passengers gave a similar account of the incident on board, describing a fight for control after the plane suddenly plummeted, losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.
Flydubai said all the passengers – of whom 166 out of 174 were Israeli, according to media reports – were safe, adding that reasons for the altercation were unknown.
“During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board,” Netanyahu said in a video message.
He said he spoke to an Israeli passenger who broke into the cockpit as the plane started to plunge and fought the pilot who was trying to bring down the aircraft.
“I salute these heroes, who showed extraordinary resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives; they prevented a major disaster.”
The flight was rerouted to Tabuk Airport “at 9.45am (2.45pm, Singapore time) and its captain and co-pilot were found to have injuries and were transported to hospital”, a statement from the company operating the airport said.
‘Out of control’
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was “pretty much out of control” after one of the pilots tried to stab the other while they were flying over Jordan en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
“So the co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.
“It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said, adding that a doctor on board provided first aid.

Like a ‘roller coaster’
Describing the flight’s sudden plunge, passenger Almog Italie told AFP it was like “we were having very big turbulence, but there was no turbulence”, adding that it was like riding a “roller coaster”.
According to data from Flightradar24, the aircraft suddenly dropped from nearly 34,000 feet at 3.21pm (Singapore time) to less than 17,000 feet a minute later.
But there was no “hysteria” among passengers, Italie noted, even as fighting erupted near the cockpit.
“The other passengers from the front took over control,” he told AFP via video call from Saudi Arabia.
Neither the airline nor the authorities of the countries involved provided details of what happened on board or the pilots’ nationalities, but some Israeli media said one was Omani and the other Emirati.
Israel’s Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military had scrambled fighter jets after fears of a possible hijacking.
In a video from inside the plane that was reposted by Israeli social media users, one passenger – blood dripping from an open wound on his head – pleaded for assistance and said they were descending into Saudi Arabia, with which Israel has no formal ties.
“We are here during an attack on the plane. We just subdued the terrorists and are preparing to land,” the man said.
“Anyone who can hear me, we need help.”
Bloodied T-shirt
Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the authorities were investigating whether or not one of the pilots had attempted a possible suicide by trying to crash the plane, with the other pilot apparently intervening to prevent the crash.
An AFP correspondent in Tabuk, where the plane landed, saw heavy security near the airport, with several police vehicles and an ambulance parked at the terminal.

Jürgen Habermas: Public Intellectual and Engaged Critical Theorist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:21:00 UTC
00:21:00 KST

Peter Verovšek’s compendious, deeply researched, and engaging study of Jürgen Habermas’s “moonlighting career” as a public intellectual appears at a poignantly appropriate time. Habermas’s death in March of 2026, at the age of 96, brought to a close an intellectual career virtually without parallel in modern history. Habermas was all of 24 when he published an essay criticizing Martin Heidegger’s unreconstructed valuation of National Socialism, “Mit Heidegger gegen Heidegger denken” [“Thinking with Heidegger Against Heidegger”] in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, a large-circulation national daily newspaper, in July of 1953. His last public-facing essay, defending the familiar cause of a unified Europe in the face of the collapse of the United States’s alliances under the Trump Administration, “Von hier an müssen wir alleine weitergehen” [“From Here We’ll Need to Go It Alone”], appeared in the Suddeutsche Zeiting, another major German newspaper, in November of 2025. That is a public role spanning close to three-quarters of a century.
Habermas’s fame as a public intellectual in the Federal Republic of Germany’s intellectual and political life never entirely reached American shores, where his status as a philosopher, critical theorist, and inheritor of the complex legacy of the Frankfurt School largely determined his reception. But in Germany, no fewer than four post-war generations were born and grew up with the certainty that Habermas would weigh in on the dynamics of German political culture, the legacies of National Socialism, the shifting currents of national identity, and the role of the Federal Republic in a broader “post-national” project of European unification, independently of his philosophical work. His fame as a public figure in Germany was such that he was routinely seen as Germany’s public philosopher, the “conscience of the Federal Republic”, a sort of national institution of one.
That remarkable fame was not unmixed. For decades, grumbling about Habermas’s influence on German (and European) public life provoked resentment, complaints of hegemony, of Eurocentrism and apologetics for the global liberal order, of staying too long. It’s also undeniable that, over the course of the last decade, as European and global political developments have steadily eroded the bases of post-national democracy that Habermas spent a lifetime defending, his dominance began to appear to many to be not just outdated but politically unjustifiable. That impression was powerfully deepened by one of his last public interventions, his decision to co-sign a public statement from the Normative Orders research center at Frankfurt University declaring solidarity with Israel in the aftermath of Hamas’s October 7 attack and Israel’s genocidally lethal response. Even for many of his colleagues, the statement (which offered no solidarity for Palestinian civilian victims and asserted that “Despite all the concern for the fate of the Palestinian population […] the standards of judgment slip completely when genocidal intentions are attributed to Israeli action”, an assertion that was broadly interpreted as support for continued Israeli attacks. In the weeks and months following Habermas’s death, multiple attacks from variously-motivated academics, with varying levels of competence, charged Habermas with a range of intellectual crimes, including complicity in mass murder.
Do these criticisms, as clumsy, and ill-willed as they often have been, have a point? Did modern Europe’s greatest public intellectual outlive his time? Was an uncharacteristically clumsy defense of Israel’s indefensible actions evidence of waning powers of political judgment? Or was this in microcosm a glimpse of a deeper set of problems and shortcomings with Habermas’s thought—one that would prompt a correspondingly deep reassessment both of Habermas’s philosophical legacy and his career as a public intellectual?
Answering this question adequately would require at least two endeavors, both weighty. First, we would need to understand far better the full sweep of Habermas’s political interventions, in order to see their unifying themes, their persistent problematics, their development over seventy years. Second, and still harder, we would have to understand far better the complicated relationship between Habermas’s philosophical texts and his public-facing interventions in the (primarily German) public sphere.
Regarding the first of these tasks, an exhaustive review and analysis of the full scope of Habermas’s work as a public intellectual, the book marks a significant scholarly advance. Peter Verovšek’s extensive archival research for this book unearths dozens of Habermas’s earliest works, beginning when he was still a university student attempting to make a living as a free-lance journalist in the brand-new Federal Republic.
Given Habermas’s indelible status as “der Philosoph”, reading his review of an experimental theater production or his musings on “the Musical Style of Film” can be jarring. Yet what emerges from this fascinating reconstruction of the origins of Habermas’s engagement in the embryonic political and cultural public sphere of the brand-new Federal Republic is how completely these short essays and reviews, even ones that bear only marginal political relevance, already conform with the core commitments that Habermas would never once depart from over the next seventy years. Like it or not, emerging from the moral catastrophe of global war and genocide, citizens of the Federal Republic took on an exceptional and historically specific responsibility to develop a democratic political culture out of the ashes of the worst government in recorded history, and in the near-total absence of popular embrace of the values of democratic procedure and democratic life.
For Habermas, all Germans had assumed a solemn moral injunction to keep alive the memory of the victims of their collective moral catastrophe by the practice of rigorous self-criticism regarding which national traditions, which sources of shared identity, and what forms of collective memory would be permissible, and which not. Hence everything in post-war German culture and society was profoundly political, in a deeply moral sense of democratic life. A shared duty imposed itself in both deontic and consequentialist forms: Given their unique position, Germans were obligated to do justice to the memory of Germany’s victims, and to do everything possible to construct a form of German democracy built upon the “universalistic value orientations” embodied in the nascent postwar regime of international human rights as a proactive bulwark against a slide back into the attitudes and practices that made National Socialism possible.
This highly moralized vision of post-disaster political culture explains much of the resentment, perhaps even the exhaustion, that Habermas’s politics could provoke in generations far removed from the “zero hour” of 1945; the grumbling feeling that Germany’s conscience had morphed into Germany’s over-active superego. Habermas however never wavered. Verovšek’s book is particularly masterful in reconstructing how the extended public use of reason of Habermas’s innumerable essays, speeches, opinion pieces, interviews, and other occasional writings stretched from the 1950s, through the student movement of the 1960s, the unsettled encounter with radical politics in the “German Autumn” of the late 1970s, the so-called “Historians Debate” of the mid-1980s, German reunification in the beginning of the 1990s, Germany’s complicated role in the faltering project of European legal and political unification in the early 2000s, and the specters of resurgent nationalism, unbridled technology, democratic backsliding, and the return of international war in Europe in the last years of his life.
Of course, there is more to evaluating the success of Habermas’s life work as a public intellectual than registering its nearly incredible volume and duration. Virtually all of the Enlightenment norms of deliberative democracy, the public use of reason, and “post-national” forms of political identity appear now in full retreat. Even Germany, in most regards a last European redoubt of democratic governance, shows worrying signs of stress in the rise of the far-right AfD party, resurgent nationalism, hostility toward migrants, and a healthy dose of Euro-skepticism. Did Habermas end up outliving the historical window where his political vision could survive?
Verovšek offers a careful, judicious, and guardedly optimistic response to this question. It simply cannot be disputed that the last fifteen years (at least) have seen a string of defeats for the norms that Habermas spent his public life defending. But in response to the triumphalist tone of his critics who see in his public life little more than an apologetics for Enlightenment “liberalism” and the status quo, Verovšek’s reconstruction reminds us that at virtually no point since 1945 was there any guarantee that Germany would succeed in creating a stable democratic form of collective self-rule, no taken-for-granted path toward emerging as the core of a stable democratic Europe. It did not happen by accident and could well have gone much differently, and much worse. Democracy in the post-war Federal Republic had to be made, not found. And Habermas was not just devoted to protecting and promoting a German democratic public sphere. Although he himself would never put it this way, he was personally instrumental in constructing it.
That fact—that Habermas was simultaneously defending, building, and theorizing about a work-in-progress public sphere—lies at the center of the second task mentioned above: coming to a better understanding of the complex relation between Habermas’s philosophical work and his political interventions. This is the central task of Verovšek’s book. It is also devilishly difficult.
For Verovšek, the framework for assessing the relation between theory and practical interventions rests on twin assumptions, which he both ascribes to Habermas himself and also uses as organizing principles for handling the enormous materials analyzed in the book. First, the “separation thesis”, takes seriously Habermas’s own insistence that his academic and public writings not be conflated with one another; that they arise from distinct positions of expertise and authority and differ markedly in their intended audience and effect. The “theoretical continuity thesis” balances this separation thesis with the claim that, notwithstanding the differences between theory and political practice, Habermas’s intellectual works are always and entirely consistent with the philosophical theory, hence the foundational claim that Habermas’s political writing should itself be taken as an indispensable part of the larger corpus.
Taken together the separation and continuity theses seem unproblematic—it would be odd indeed if a thinker as consistent and focused as Habermas were to find himself writing his way into a contradiction between philosophical and political positions. And the dual theses function well as a lens by which Verovšek shows how Habermas’s many political interventions interact with the developing theories of communicative action, the discourse model of participatory democracy, and the all-affected principle as a weak foundation for democratic and legal legitimacy. Among the book’s many strengths is the patience and care with which Verovšek teases out the philosophical commitments that generate Habermas’s political stances on, for instance, German national consciousness and memory politics, the dynamics of European unification, or the risk that unregulated media technologies pose for the future of a halfway-functional political public sphere.
At the same time, Verovšek’s approach does encounter some headwinds in making its case for raising the significance of Habermas’s political work. Much of those headwinds come from Habermas himself, who in interviews and essays has consistently and repeatedly downplayed the importance of his work as a public intellectual, regarding it as a mere “Nebenberuf”—a moonlighting sideline—compared to his theoretical writings. Part of this low estimation no doubt comes down to Habermas’s personal tendency toward self-deprecation. A further explanation lies in Habermas’s acute sensitivity regarding the status of the German philosopher as an elite spiritual/political shepherd, a role he experienced firsthand in his own university days in the encounter with unreformed Nazis among the German professorate.
But I wonder if there is not an even deeper reason that the separation and continuity theses in tandem may not quite capture the complexity of the relation between Habermas’s philosophy and political interventions. Verovšek is surely correct in observing that these two do not simply run along parallel and compatible tracks, but interact with one another to a degree that may be difficult to reconstruct. That interaction is probably best understood as dialectical, in the unsensational sense that interaction leaves neither unchanged, and that incompleteness or gaps in one can sometimes best be revealed by its contact with the other. Habermas was, after all, the chief theorist of the very same national political public sphere in which he spent seventy years not simply as one participant among many (despite his own humility) but among its chief architects, defenders, and contributors. And yet it takes a bit of effort to recall that the two most influential of Habermas’s theoretical works—Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere from 1962, and Theory of Communicative Action from 1981—both ended with dire diagnoses and predictions regarding the health and future of a functional public sphere. Both books saw the public sphere buckling under the weight of instrumental political and economic systems that by their very nature were not oriented toward intersubjective communication. The very transformation that Habermas had in mind in his first book on the public sphere was one of profound and possibly irreversible dysfunction. In the little-read second volume of the Theory of Communicative Action, Habermas’s penetrating diagnosis of the pathologies of political life has since been boiled down to the formula of the “inner colonization of the lifeworld”, a slogan that tends to elide the gravity of the crisis Habermas identified.
What this means is that the “theoretical continuity thesis” may need to reckon with the performative contradiction between a critical philosophy diagnosing the impending extinction of the very same public sphere, whose continued existence was in some significant part his own creation, and which was a functional necessity for his work as a public intellectual. The holistic correctness of the theory’s diagnostic appears to be in tension with the core assumptions of the political interventions—the possibility of the latter presuppose the falseness, or at least incompleteness, of the former.
But from what third position can this contradiction be comprehended? Habermas, for his part, resolutely refused to acknowledge one, leaving his own views on the relation between his theory and practice conspicuously underdetermined. Perhaps his reticence regarding the importance of his political work may register his own awareness of this and of the lack of resources to think through a theory-practice relationship consistently, without the risk of falling back into the lofty Hegelian transcendentalism he so loathed.
Whatever we may make of this problem, what is depressingly clear is the startlingly low quality of public political debate over Habermas’s legacy in the months since his death. Many interventions, even by trained philosophers, read more like Insta or X mini-rants than mature efforts to understand and convince. Inadvertently, they support the direst of his predictions of the fate of the political public sphere. It also puts into sharp contrast what we have lost in Habermas’s passing. The ideal of domination-free communication, so often derided as “unrealistically” utopian, was always for Habermas a counterfactual whose role in public discourse was most readily evident only in its absence. The conclusion of Verovšek’s book, discussing the shallowness of the online critiques of Habermas’s endorsement of the Normative Orders statement on Gaza, Israel, and the risks of violent anti-Semitism in Germany, is astute and insightful in its analysis of so many of these critiques, driven by likes and shares, many of them crudely mendacious and openly instrumental, as though a zombie version of the political public sphere, where political and economic imperatives jerk the limbs of a now-dead lifeworld, are all that is left. An authentic open debate regarding that statement, Habermas’s participation in it, and what that participation may or may not say about Habermas’s larger legacy, is badly needed. Given the decline of the public sphere that Habermas himself diagnosed, however, such a debate cannot be expected.

People switching to Novo's Wegovy pill from obesity injections kept losing weight in real-world study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:19:01 UTC
00:19:01 KST

People who switched from obesity injections to Novo's new Wegovy pill continued to lose weight after three months, according to an analysis of real-world data the company presented on Wednesday.
Real-world studies evaluate associations and can't determine causality. But the results suggest that the Wegovy pill may improve upon the initial weight loss people experience on blockbuster injections rather than simply maintain it. It also suggests that patients may not need to take weekly shots like Wegovy and Zepbound forever, and can instead opt for more convenient treatments such as Novo's pill.
Novo's analysis used data from Ro's telehealth platform on 194 patients with obesity or who were overweight, around 56% of whom were female. Half started on Novo's Wegovy injection and the rest initially took Eli Lilly's shot Zepbound.
Patients who switched from an injection to the Wegovy pill and stayed on treatment for three months lost roughly 4% of their weight, or an additional 8.8 pounds, on average. That's based on an average starting weight of around 221 pounds before taking the pill, Novo said.
Of those participants, 2 in 5 achieved 5% or more weight loss three months after switching to the pill. Meanwhile, the share of people with a body mass index at or above 30 decreased by more than 21% three months after switching to oral Wegovy. A BMI of 30 shifts a person from the overweight category into obesity.
"We have the unique benefit that, in the market, the subcutaneous Wegovy can now be interchanged with a tablet of Wegovy, and the patient can expect the same tolerability profile, the same safety profile, and actually a little bit more weight loss, which is what a lot of them want," Martin Holst Lange, Novo's chief scientific officer, said in an interview.
Among patients with available data, around 82% reported at least one improvement during treatment with the pill. That includes almost 70% who reported better-fitting clothes and around 51% who said they pursued healthier eating.
Around 75% of patients in the analysis said they were satisfied with the switch to a pill, according to Novo.
"I think we are seeing a shift where we, maybe just a year ago, we actually thought that the vast majority of patients who wanted treatment for obesity were happy with a subcutaneous treatment," Lange said. "We see that picture differently now. We clearly see a preference for orals."
He pointed to people who travel a lot and don't want to think about refrigerating their injections.
It is among the first real-world evidence of weight loss outcomes among patients switching from blockbuster injections, particularly Novo's Wegovy shot and Lilly's rival Zepbound, to the new pill. But the study's limitations include variable timing and completeness of the data collected during routine telehealth care, self-reported data being subject to bias and results "not being generalizable to the broader population," Novo said.
In partnership with Novo, Ro said it's focused on learning from real-world data on its patients that can be used by other stakeholders in the healthcare industry.
"The future of healthcare is personal, and you can't get there without the data," said Zachariah Reitano, Ro co-founder and CEO. "Medicine is very good at answering 'does this work on average.' It's terrible at answering 'what works for you.' That's the gap we can bridge."
"We obsess over what enables patients and providers to achieve the best outcomes for every patient," he added. "Why do some patients respond better than others? What is the optimal titration schedule for each patient? What are the best long term maintenance techniques?"
The figures are also one of several new datasets Novo is unveiling this week on its obesity and diabetes pipeline at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy.
CagriSema study
Also on Wednesday, Novo announced that its experimental next-generation obesity drug CagriSema reduced "food noise" — persistent thoughts about food — and showed benefits in organ and bone health. That's based on results from a yearlong functional magnetic resonance imaging study, which is a noninvasive method to measure brain activity during specific tasks.
CagriSema is a combination of Novo's semaglutide — the active ingredient in Wegovy — and a drug called cagrilintide that targets amylin. CagriSema is expected to launch early next year, followed by standalone cagrilintide and a higher-dose version of CagriSema in 2028.
In the study, Novo said CagriSema changed how the brain reacted to tempting, high-calorie foods in areas linked to cravings, pleasure and self-control in people with obesity or who were overweight.
"The signal in the brain changes in a way that actually is associated with improved quality of life," said Lange.
The company added that CagriSema reduced harmful fat around abdominal organs, including in the liver and pancreas, in adults with Type 2 diabetes. Early findings also suggest that patients' bone health was maintained despite substantial weight loss, Novo noted.
The drugmaker said the findings suggest CagriSema may address underlying factors of obesity and diabetes in the brain and multiple organs and tissues, rather than only impacting weight and blood sugar levels.

Turkish court orders access ban on popular news portal over 'LGBTQ+ propaganda'
ANKARA, Sept 30 - A Turkish court has ordered access to the website and social media accounts of independent news portal T24 to be blocked over content deemed "LGBT propaganda", the Justice Ministry said on Wednesday.
Dozens of people were jailed earlier this month under an investigation targeting LGBTQ+ groups in Turkey, dubbed "My Family is Safe", which the government says is aimed at protecting children and family values.
As part of the investigation, Istanbul's 1st Criminal Court of Peace ordered the blocking of T24's website and social media accounts after authorities found that the outlet had produced 118 pieces of content over the past year deemed to constitute "LGBT propaganda", the ministry said in a statement.
The decision was sent to Turkey's Cyber Security Presidency for implementation.
T24 said it had not yet received official notification of the access ban and would appeal once it did.
Turkish authorities have already blocked access to websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ associations, activists and independent media outlets as part of the investigation, including the X account of Amnesty International's Turkey branch.
The crackdown has drawn criticism from rights groups and European officials. The European Union has expressed concern over the arrests and the blocking of websites and social media accounts and called on Ankara to uphold freedom of expression and media freedom.
Human Rights Watch has said the crackdown threatens fundamental rights and the rule of law and called on authorities to end the targeting of LGBTQ+ groups and activists. REUTERS

Pentagon Orders Israeli SMASH Anti-Drone Sights to Protect Military Bases

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:17:49 UTC
00:17:49 KST

The Pentagon has ordered SMASH anti-drone rifle sights from Israeli company Smart Shooter to protect military bases and other critical facilities in the United States and abroad.
The three-year agreement, worth up to $150 million, was signed by Joint Interagency Task Force JIATF-401, Defence Blog reported.
The contract covers the supply of SMASH equipment, software and updates, as well as training and technical support.
The agreement was concluded under an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity arrangement, meaning that specific quantities, prices and delivery schedules will be determined through individual orders.
SMASH is an intelligent fire-control system designed to automatically acquire and track targets, including unmanned aerial vehicles and enemy personnel. The sight is mounted on the standard Picatinny rail of an assault rifle.
The system can track targets up to 250 meters away.
The sight supports three operating modes: a daytime mode using a holographic sight, a night mode with an image displayed on a screen, and a standard mode that allows firing through mechanical sights.
A single battery charge provides up to 72 hours of operation.
The SMASH family includes several versions:
The new order supports JIATF-401’s “Domestic Shield” program, which is aimed at protecting service members, military bases, and other critical facilities from small UAVs.
This is Smart Shooter’s second contract from JIATF-401, following an agreement announced in March 2026. According to the company, thousands of SMASH systems are already in use by U.S. Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps units.
In addition to the United States, SMASH anti-drone rifle sights are used by the Israeli military, the British Army, and other NATO countries. In particular, Germany uses them together with electronic warfare systems to protect critical facilities. The Japan Self-Defense Forces have also recently begun using these sighting systems to engage UAVs more effectively.

Many Swiss men want part-time work, but few take the plunge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:16:59 UTC
00:16:59 KST

Many Swiss men desire, but decline, part-time work
The proportion of men working part-time has doubled in Switzerland since 2000, according to a University of Zurich study supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF). But many are also discouraged from reducing their hours, largely by social norms.
In Switzerland, around 40% of the working population works part-time, a figure that puts the country second among the 38 countries of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), just behind the Netherlands.
According to the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), nearly six in ten working women in Switzerland were in part-time employment in 2025, compared with just over 20% of men.
Sociologists Jan Müller from the University of Zurich and Youngjoo Cha, a professor at Indiana University in the United States, have examined the factors influencing this choice among men. The researchers analysed data collected between 2004 and 2020.
The study, published at the end of July in the journal Community, Work and Family, reveals that few men opt for part-time work in professions marked by a culture of “male breadwinners” or “devotion to work”.
But more men are going part-time in sectors where there is greater support for work-life balance. This trend is particularly evident amongst doctors. In this profession, the research team observed an increase in the number of men transitioning to part-time work.
Swiss buck the trend
The proportion of men working part-time in Switzerland has doubled since 2000, rising from around 10% to over 20%. The average for OECD countries has risen only slightly over the same period, from 8% to just under 13%. Within the European Union (EU), fewer than one in ten men work part-time on average.
More
Why can’t men make part-time work?
According to the study, Swiss culture is conducive to part-time work. With a total of nearly 42 weekly working hours for a full-time employee, the country exceeds the OECD average. Reducing hours is thus an attractive option, especially as high wages make this choice more financially viable, according to Jan Müller.
The legal framework also plays a role. “By international standards, Swiss law offers relatively strong protection for part-time workers,” Müller said. “Contracts are often just as secure as those for full-time workers, which is not the case everywhere.”
In Scandinavian countries, society is “organised so that both parents can work part-time”, Müller added. “In Switzerland, the trend is more towards a system where women remain in part-time roles, but men are starting to follow suit.”
Nearly one in ten men working full-time would like to reduce their working hours. However, few of them actually follow up on this wish, the study shows. “Only 10% of those with a preference for part-time work while working full-time actually take the step of reducing their working hours,” said Müller.
The researcher highlights the limitations of this study, which focuses solely on men who were initially working full-time. Furthermore, it is constrained by the amount of reliable data covering the period.

Passengers from the flight later boarded a replacement plane that was coordinated by the airport and Flydubai and landed at their original destination of Tel Aviv Wednesday evening.

Fed’s preferred gauge showed core inflation at 3.0% in August, much lighter than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:14:57 UTC
00:14:57 KST

Consumer prices posted a smaller-than-expected increase in August from a year ago, according to the Federal Reserve's primary inflation gauge, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday.
The personal consumption expenditures price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, putting the 12-month gain at 3.4%. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for increases of 0.3% and 3.7%, respectively.
Excluding food and energy, PCE posted a 0.2% climb that put the annual core level at 3%. The respective forecasts were for 0.3% and 3.3%.
Though the Fed officially follows the headline PCE number, officials generally consider core a better gauge of longer-term trends.
While the annual increases were less than expected, they came as the Bureau of Economic Analysis changed the way it computes several components of the index. The BEA adjusted methodology for how it measures prices for legal services, software and computer accessories and portfolio management.
The revisions lowered the core July PCE level by 0.36 percentage point.
Stock market futures gained ground following the report while Treasury yields were negative. Traders priced in less of a chance of a Fed rate hike in October, pushing the next expected increase to December.
"This is good news for investors worried about the recent surge in bond yields, and it bolsters the case for not hiking in October," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "However, it's also relatively old data at this point that doesn't reflect this month's surge in diesel prices."
The report also showed that personal income rose 0.2% while spending increased 0.9%, against the respective consensus for 0.4% and 0.8%.
Inflation still high, GDP revised up
Both PCE levels are still considerably higher than the central bank's 2% target, raising the possibility that the Fed will follow up its September interest rate hike with another increase at either of its remaining meetings this year — in October or, more likely, December.
"Even after major methodological revisions, PCE inflation is still running hot however you cut it," said Sonu Varghese, global macro strategist at Carson Group. "The economy is running hot, policy remains easy, and the Fed's challenge is figuring out how much restraint is needed. That's a tailwind for stocks as we move into Q4."
Energy costs were the primary culprit for the price rise in August, though multiple other sectors also showed gains. Gasoline jumped 4.4% and transportation services accelerated by 1.4%. Energy goods and services climbed 2.3%.
Goods and services prices both posted 0.3% increases.
"The PCE Inflation data – the Federal Reserve's favorite – show no progress in August on inflation," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "And it's inevitable that September will be higher. Meanwhile, American consumers are feeling the squeeze."
In other economic news Wednesday, the Commerce Department reported that gross domestic product increased at a 2.2% annualized rate in the second quarter, according to the final of three estimates. That was up sharply from the prior estimate of 1.5% and reflected greater contributions from consumer and government spending as well as investment.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, a metric Fed officials watch closely to gauge underlying demand in the economy, increased 4.6%, an upward revision of 0.4 percentage point.
Inflation measures for the April-through-June period also were slightly lower, with headline PCE prices rising 5% and core at 3.3%, each 0.3 percentage point below the prior estimate.
For the Fed, the various economic signals have posed a quandary.
Policymakers typically can look through price spikes brought on by exogenous factors such as tariffs and the kind of supply shocks driven by the war with Iran. However, the persistence of the price increases, coupled with the unknowns of the artificial intelligence breakout, have posed challenges to traditional modes of thinking.
Markets had been pricing in a strong possibility that the Fed would follow its quarter percentage point September hike with another move in October. However, comments Tuesday from influential New York Fed President John Williams tempered those expectations, and the data Wednesday further dimmed the outlook for an October move.
"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," Williams said in a speech, comments that almost immediately triggered an adjustment in expectations.
Williams added that he still thinks another hike "may be appropriate late this year," leading markets to price out the next increase to December.

An investigation into Dutch media coverage of weight loss drugs that led to several outlets being fined for breaching advertising laws was prompted by a complaint from a rival manufacturer, NRC reports.
Newspapers including NRC, the Telegraaf, the Volkskrant and AD were sanctioned by the health inspectorate IGJ in August, when it ruled that articles about medicines such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were too positive.
NRC said its lawyers had discovered that the IGJ acted after being asked to enforce the Medicines Act, which bans advertising of prescription drugs, by Goodlife, which manufacturers the slimming drug Mysimba.
One of Goodlife’s objections was that the artlcles in NRC and the Volkskrant were unbalanced because of the “complete absence of references to Mysimba in the majority of media reports”.
The Dutch Medicines Act was passed in 1992 to protect public health by banning commercial companies from advertising drugs that are only available on prescription. In many countries drugs such as Ozempic are used for weight loss, but doctors in the Netherlands are only allowed to prescribe them for diabetes.
Commercial battle
Lucas Brouwers, deputy editor of NRC, said: “Apparently the IGJ did not chance upon the articles in NRC itself, but was pointed towards them by a company that sells a rival slimming medicine.
“We are very concerned that the media are being dragged into a commercial battle through the inspectorate.”
Volkskrant editor Pieter Klok said if the fines were upheld, it would make it almost imposslble for health reporters to write about developments in medical treatment.
“This makes it even worse,” he said. “I already had major objections on principle, but now it is becoming very arbitrary. The IGJ must not allow itself to be used by competing parties.”
Maartenm Kok, medical director of Goodlife, told NRC that reporting on obesity treatments in the Dutch media “gave a one-sided and incomplete picture in which only a limited number of medicines were repeatedly and overwhelmingly positively highlighted.“
Nieuwsuur threatened
DPG Media and Mediahuis, the owners of the newspaper titles, are appealing against the fines.
Goodlife also asked the IGJ to investigate TV current affairs show Nieuwsuur after it broadcast a four-part series into the effects of medicines such as Ozempic that work by simulating the effect of the natural hormone GLP-1, which tells the brain the stomach is full.
The company threatened to seek an injunction against the programme after reporter Lune van der Meulen rejected its demand to include Mysimba in the series, but dropped the action after she said on air she had been contacted by a distributor.

Lulworth firing times
Details of road closures and live firing for Lulworth ranges.
Documents
Details
Mupe Bay warning: stay clear of the north half of the beach at Mupe Bay. Due to the possibility of rock fall, for safety you are strongly advised to observe warning signs in the area.
Do not enter the danger area when the range is in use, this is a danger to life. Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.
The monthly firing times also include information on road closures in the surrounding areas.
Grange Hill road closure
From February 2020 military training will take place in the Creech Car Park area four times over the year. This means that Grange Hill, the road between Creech and Steeple, will be closed to the public when ranges are active. Exact dates will be published in the monthly firing times programme.

Bank of Russia to address new budgetary policy parameters when updating macro forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:14:42 UTC
00:14:42 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia is going to cater for new parameters of the budgetary policy when preparing an updated midterm macroeconomic forecast, the regulator said in its draft Monetary Policy Guidelines for 2027-2029.
"The Bank of Russia assumes in the base-case scenario that the primary structural deficit will gradually contract from 2% of GDP in 2026 to 1% of GDP in 2027 and 0.5% of GDP in 2028, with the zero level to be reached in 2029," the regulator noted.
"According to new budget projections, the path of the primary structural deficit during the two coming years is slightly lower than assumptions in the July baseline forecast of the Bank of Russia. With all other things being equal, it means a slightly lower contribution of the budgetary policy to the total demand than it was anticipated in July," the regulator said.
The Central Bank will take into account new parameters of the budgetary policy when updating the midterm macroeconomic forecast to be released on October 23 of this year, it added.

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Russian Presidential Commissioner for Children’s Rights Maria Lvova-Belova discussed family reunions in Russia, Ukraine, and third countries with visiting Pope’s Special Envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi on Wednesday.
"Met with Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi. The topic of family reunions which we are handling on instructions from Russian President Vladimir Putin was central," the Russian ombudswoman wrote on Max channel.
Lvova-Belova recalled that over the past four years 32 children from 24 families have reunited with their relatives in Russia and another 145 children reunited with 118 families in Ukraine and third countries with assistance from her office.
Separately, Lvova-Belova continued, she told the cardinal about the situation with children in regions targeted by Ukrainian attacks. "We discussed further cooperation in the interests of children and their families. We are carrying out the work consistently, in the format of a bilateral group, with assistance from Russian Foreign Ministry officials," Lvova-Belova added.

‘No way they can beat us’: Rutte rebuffs Russian nuclear threats to NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:13:21 UTC
00:13:21 KST

BRUSSELS — NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday issued a strong rebuke to Russia after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening nuclear escalation over NATO activity near its border.
"We had to reply and make clear to [Russia] that NATO is a defensive alliance ... and stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats because it's not helpful," Rutte said at a security summit in Brussels. "NATO is so much stronger than Russia is, so there's no way they can ever beat us."
"The best way to deal with this is to have a little bit of calm," he added. "That's the message: calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going — that's how we deal with it."
Advertisement
Rutte's unusually strong remarks underscore the growing tensions between Moscow and NATO countries as hybrid attacks and Russian-linked sabotage proliferate across Europe.
In recent days, Russia's embassy in Belgium sent NATO a note alleging the alliance was displaying "reckless and irresponsible" behavior near its Kaliningrad exclave, following alliance exercises involving several reconnaissance planes, ground forces and fighter jets near the region, which is between Poland and Lithuania, last month.
"We have emphasised that Russia possesses the necessary means to repel any potential aggression and is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country," the embassy wrote on social media.
In its letter to NATO, Moscow explicitly mentions the use of its nuclear arsenal and issues specific threats to hit allied territory, according to one NATO diplomat briefed on the letter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.
NATO has sent a note back to Russian officials in response, the alliance's spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed.
"We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia," she said in a statement. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Advertisement
Inside NATO, some allies are dismissing the threat. "Our reading is that they want to intimidate allied public opinion so that allies stop supporting [Ukraine], while, at the same time, presenting NATO as the one that would be responsible for an eventual escalation," said the same NATO diplomat cited above. "Textbook Russian propaganda."
"Russia always accelerates when it's the most guilty or when [it] loses," said a second alliance diplomat. "So they are cornered now and they transfer the blame on NATO."
Russia's embassy to Belgium didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russia says European arms factories supplying Ukraine are potential military targets for Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia says European arms factories supplying Ukraine are potential military targets for Moscow
MOSCOW, Sept 30 - Factories in Europe producing arms for Ukraine are legitimate and potential military targets for Russia, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Wednesday.
Zakharova told a press briefing that European countries were directly involved in the conflict through their military support for Ukraine, adding that such activity delayed a resolution to the war.
She was responding to a question about Poland's apparent readiness to host a factory producing Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine. NATO and many European countries say they will continue to do everything they can to support Ukraine and help it push back Russian forces and shoot down drones and missiles.
"Weapons factories in European countries that produce arms for Ukraine are potential military targets for Russia, and one should not assume that military factories outside Ukrainian territory which produce weapons for the Kyiv regime will be safe. Anyone who thinks so is mistaken," said Zakharova.
“European countries are directly involved in the Ukrainian conflict. They are not merely providing aid. By opening arms factories and joint ventures, they are fully involved. And this only delays a resolution to the conflict rather than bringing it closer, as some forces in Europe think or imagine,” she added. REUTERS
