Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streak| Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:55:28 UTC
23:55:28 KST

A number of people have admitted to tears during Andy Burnham’s Labour party conference speech, and most of them mean when he talked about his father, who died very recently. But then there were a few (not me) who welled up when he announced a commission on electoral reform. It was just the sheer shock of it: that we may finally have a prime minister who will follow through on his own long-held beliefs and remain loyal to his long-term support base, even if it makes him avoidable enemies and, medium-term, destroys Labour’s only-trodden path to victory. It felt a bit like slipping through time, and I couldn’t even tell you to when (definitely not the 1990s).
Burnham’s support for proportional representation has always been extremely unusual for a Labour politician. To this day, he ascribes that to his experience of winning an election as mayor of Greater Manchester on a supplementary votes system, where people get to choose a first- and second-preference candidate. He said that campaigning under that system “finally aligned the conversation on the door with what people want from politics, which is about problem-solving first and foremost, not about point-scoring”. He went a bit further this morning, asking Nick Robinson on the Today programme: “Can we really watch a party with less than 30% walk into Downing Street?”
Plainly, he was talking about the spectre of a Reform government, and it’s that very context that makes this already difficult constitutional conversation even more vexed. Back in May, the all-party parliamentary group for fair elections held a meeting to discuss the aftermath of the local elections. It feels like a long time ago, and furthermore, so different in atmosphere as to be irrelevant to the prime minister, but 2020s politics are defined by their switchblade turns. In the matter of constitutional reform, the overriding priority has to be to build a system that’s fair across a range of imaginable scenarios, not just the one in front of you.
The locals delivered great results for Reform, and satisfactory ones for the Liberal Democrats, which reflected the realities of a first-past-the-post (FPTP) system – first, it rewards the winner, and second, it rewards geographical concentration. Labour walked away from the 2024 general election with 63% of the seats on 34% of the votes, the largest overrepresentation ever. The Greens have spent years commanding the fervent support of a geographically diffuse but not insignificant minority, with almost nothing to show for it in parliamentary terms.
The distortions of FPTP have been well-known for years, but historically they were only ever discussed in terms of the barrier to entry they presented to insurgent parties, and the democratic deficit they constituted to any voter who didn’t live in a marginal seat, which is to say the majority of voters. So the counter-arguments were that, for all its flaws, by keeping out insurgents, the traditional voting system kept out extremists: and who wouldn’t sacrifice a little bit (or a huge amount) of democracy, for the sake of steadiness?
Stability was the first myth to fall, when it transpired, over the past 10 years, that you can keep on returning one of two main parties as reliably as you like, and they will have no problem confecting so much intra-party turmoil that you might as well have voted for the Monster Raving Loony party. The efficacy of FPTP in keeping out extremists, meanwhile, was – like a stock market bubble – true until it wasn’t. Once politics has fragmented, the system rewards short bursts of popularity with potentially very long periods of power. That has a toxic effect on the supposedly sober heads of the political centre who, once they see extreme, often bigoted, positions pay off in the polls, steer straight towards them. The best prophylactic against extremism is not a gamified voting system but some political backbone. Undoubtedly in response to all that, public attitudes to proportional representation have changed enormously, hitting an all-time high of 60% support last year. In 2011 it was 27%.
To return to that meeting in May, there was one more finding from the local elections: once you start to lose, under FPTP, you lose calamitously. So the obvious solution, to a room full of already fully committed constitutional reformer MPs, was for the next prime minister to change the system, right? Psephologists John Curtice and Prof Tim Bale sounded the warning: you can’t change the rules just because you’re losing. The point was so self-evident, from such trusted sources, that all the air seemed to leave the room. But four months on, Labour is ahead in the polls, Reform’s support is tailing off and seems to have further to fall. Far more importantly, this week Burnham showed himself prepared to have a thorny, inconvenient debate that wouldn’t necessarily even serve his political interests, and even if it did, would certainly disperse his power, because he believes in his cause and does so persuasively. So he doesn’t look like he’s losing.
- 
  Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

ATESH Partisans Disrupt Donetsk–Melitopol Railway Used to Supply Russian Forces
Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH said its agents disabled three railway control cabinets along the Donetsk–Melitopol railway line, disrupting infrastructure used to support Russian military logistics in temporarily occupied territories.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

According to ATESH, the operation was conducted to mark the fourth anniversary of the movement’s founding. The facility reportedly housed various unmanned aerial vehicles, including hexacopter drones used by Russian forces for battlefield and logistics operations.

Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:55:21 UTC
23:55:21 KST

A Ukrainian ground robot drove toward the front, reached the water in its path, and kept going, swimming across with ammunition and food aboard and no soldier at risk. It ran the first logistics mission with an amphibious ground robot, covering more than 40 kilometers over land and water to resupply positions, the Defense Ministry said.
Water is one of the front's quiet chokepoints: rivers, canals, and marshes that stop ground robots and force risky detours, and that air resupply cannot always solve. The amphibious robot drives like a normal ground vehicle, then switches to swimming in seconds, letting one machine cross terrain that halts the rest.
It is the latest of Ukraine's battlefield-robot firsts, which this year have included air-dropping robots behind Russian lines.
Water stops the others
The robot was developed through Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed defense-innovation cluster, which links developers with the military and government.
The one such robot gains additional capabilities to carry out missions across different terrains.
For this operation, the system was refined over several months in close cooperation with the military, taking into account real tasks, operational experience, and the specifics of frontline terrain. The Brave1 defense innovation cluster provided grant support for the system, helping bring the solution to practical use.
The ministry says it is "expanding the capabilities of robotic systems" so soldiers have more tools for the fight.
Robots with grenade launchers
Earlier, Ukraine employed a new tactic during its major Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk Oblast. During the 3rd Army Corps' offensive, fighters from the world's first experimental unit of unmanned ground-strike vehicles, "NC13", upgraded their kamikaze ground drones with grenade launchers.
During the operation, UGVs equipped with two Bullspike grenade launchers attacked Russian positions, then detonated directly inside their shelters. The occupiers believed they were being attacked by an entire assault group. In reality, they were being torn apart by robots from the 3rd Assault Corps.

Russia’s War Against Ukraine Runs on Credit as Moscow’s Debt Hits 24-Year Record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:55:14 UTC
23:55:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s War Against Ukraine Runs on Credit as Moscow’s Debt Hits 24-Year Record
Russia is preparing to drive government debt to its highest level in more than two decades as the Kremlin increasingly turns to borrowing to cover widening budget deficits and another surge in military spending.
Under the government’s draft budget, Moscow plans a sharp increase in domestic borrowing over the next several years as defense spending rises to levels unseen since the Soviet era, according to budget documents reported by The Moscow Times on September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s Finance Ministry plans to sell trillions of rubles in government bonds annually, with borrowing continuing to rise through 2029.
The result, according to ministry projections, will be a steady increase in state debt from roughly 19.9% of GDP in 2026 to 21.7% next year and 24.1% by the end of the three-year budget period.
That would be Russia’s highest debt-to-GDP level since 2002.
While that ratio remains relatively modest compared with many large Western economies, the speed of the increase is significant for a country that spent much of the 2000s aggressively paying down its sovereign debt with revenues from high oil prices.
During the first years of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, Moscow relied heavily on its National Wealth Fund to cover spending gaps. As those liquid reserves have diminished, borrowing has become increasingly important.
Finance Ministry estimates indicate that state debt increased by roughly $227 billion between 2024 and 2026.
The Central Bank is also playing a larger role in keeping that borrowing machine functioning.
“Without support from the Central Bank, it is impossible to finance the budget deficit even this year,” economist Sergei Aleksashenko said.
Russian banks have increasingly received central-bank liquidity through repo operations backed by government bonds. The volume of those operations has risen by roughly $30 billion since the beginning of the year, reaching about $72 billion by September 30.
The debt itself is also becoming increasingly expensive to service. Interest payments are projected to reach $55 billion next year, then climb to $64.5 billion in 2028 and more than $68 billion in 2029.
By that point, around 10.6% of Russia’s entire federal budget could be consumed simply by servicing debt, compared with roughly 4.4% before the full-scale invasion. Reuters reported that debt-service costs are already projected to account for 9.4% of spending in 2027.
The driving force behind the borrowing surge is military expenditure.
Russia plans to allocate $205 billion to national defense in 2027, roughly 35% of total federal spending and 27% more than previously planned. Total defense expenditure over the next three years is expected to reach around $600 billion.
Earlier, CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that Russia’s economy could collapse in a Soviet-style crisis if the war continues.
A senior diplomat familiar with the CIA’s briefing to Western partner services after Ratcliffe’s late-August visit to Moscow told FAZ that the intelligence assessment was the trip’s central purpose. “Russia is losing the war,” the diplomat said, describing the US assessment as conclusive.

Ukraine Turns Wartime Military-Tech Experience Into New High-Tech Export Drive
Ukraine plans to turn its wartime military technology and digital resilience experience into a broader high-tech export push, with the US among the prospective partners.
This was reported by Reuters on September 30, based on an interview with Ukraine's Minister for Digital Transformation, Oksana Ferchuk.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ferchuk told the agency that Kyiv aims to use its expertise in military technologies and digital innovation, including AI, to sharply increase high-tech exports in the coming years.
"We are ready to cooperate and consult other states in this experience," Ferchuk stated, according to Reuters.
The minister explained that Ukraine is exploring cooperation agreements with the US, other countries and international institutions, drawing on its record of keeping state digital services running during the war, now in its fifth year.
Reuters noted that Ferchuk traveled to Washington this week to meet US economic, cybersecurity and telecommunications officials, as well as senior World Bank leaders. She is pitching the US, the European Union and other partners on cooperation projects in the digital sphere.
She also disclosed that Ukraine is moving data centers and infrastructure underground after an increase in Russian strikes on such facilities in recent months. Ferchuk acknowledged the destruction of infrastructure at dozens of telecom and data center locations, yet described the country's digital services as "alive and running."
Built-in redundancies across locations and cloud providers have kept them functioning, she emphasized. The attacks had been painful, she indicated, but had not significantly disrupted services.
Ferchuk previously oversaw digital transformation at the defense ministry. Reuters described Ukraine as a test bed for the newest weaponry, already helping other countries build their drone defenses.
According to the report, cheaper products and quicker innovation have allowed Kyiv to disrupt the generally slower-moving global military technology sector.
The minister argued that the same approach could work in civilian fields, with AI incorporated along the way. She warned that companies or countries that skip investment in Ukraine risk missing the transformation of new sectors.
Ferchuk added that she had already met World Bank officials in Kyiv, who showed strong interest in Ukrainian digital tools, including platforms for education, telecommunications and social services. Further discussions with the bank were planned for this week, Reuters reported.
Earlier, on July 22, Ukraine and the US signed a bilateral statement of intent establishing a framework for the temporary export of Ukrainian unmanned systems for testing by the Pentagon.
By July 31, F-Drones had delivered the first 2,000 F10 FPV drones under the $1 billion Drone Dominance Program, making the F10 the first Ukrainian drone authorized for export to the US under the initiative.
A broader drone-defense agreement was ready for signing as of September 23, though it had not yet been finalized.

The European Commission (EC) proposed to create an integrated independent communication system for civil defense agencies of all the EU member-countries for seamless communication in emergencies even when conventional mobile communication systems will be out of operation, EC said.

Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN. What is behind it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:53:57 UTC
23:53:57 KST

Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN. What is behind it?
Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN again, two years after severing diplomatic ties with Kiev over a rebel ambush that killed dozens of Malian soldiers and allied Russian forces.
Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop told the UN General Assembly on Monday that Ukraine was aiding armed groups in the Sahel and urged the international community to respond.
Why has Mali raised the accusation again?
Diop’s remarks follow a series of coordinated militant raids in Mali and new reports of Ukrainian assistance with drone operations. Pointing to attacks on April 25 and July 4, he said they exposed a “dangerous connection” between jihadists and separatist rebels, and accused Kiev of aiding forces that threaten his country’s territorial integrity.
“Ukraine is just the visible part of the iceberg,” he said, claiming the violence was part of a wider effort to destabilize the Sahel states and obstruct their break with former colonial influence.
The April offensive by the Al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) struck several cities and killed Malian Defense Minister Sadio Camara. Mali’s army said it repelled assaults on military sites and key infrastructure with support from Russia’s Africa Corps, killing more than 200 militants.
Malian Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maiga described the offensive as an attempt to seize power. The Russian Defense Ministry acknowledged the assault, saying it amounted to an attempted coup and claimed that the attackers had received training involving Ukrainian and European mercenary instructors.
How did the dispute with Ukraine begin?
In July 2024, Tuareg rebels ambushed Malian troops and Wagner Group contractors near Tinzaouaten, close to the Algerian border. Ukrainian military intelligence spokesman Andrey Yusov later said the rebels had received “necessary information” that enabled the operation, adding that “there will be a continuation.”
Yuriy Pyvovarov, then Ukraine’s ambassador to Senegal, shared Yusov’s interview on Facebook, writing, “The work will continue. There will certainly be other results.” Senegal summoned him over the post, while Mali cited the remarks as evidence of Kiev’s involvement, and severed diplomatic ties.
What has been reported about Ukrainian involvement since then?
Le Monde reported in 2024 that Ukrainian intelligence had taught Tuareg rebels to build and operate explosive drones, citing sources close to the group. This month, CNN interviewed Ukrainian personnel who said about 15 specialists were assisting the FLA with unmanned aircraft. One described remotely directing rebel drone missions.
Fousseynou Ouattara, vice president of the defense commission of Mali’s transitional council, told TASS in July that authorities had identified fighters who had received drone training in Ukraine. Malian outlet Bamada also reported that soldiers recovered a drone bearing Ukrainian writing and documents allegedly linked to Ukrainian intelligence during operations against JNIM.
What has Ukraine said?
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has rejected the Sahel states’ terrorism allegations, describing them as “groundless and untrue” and calling Mali’s decision to sever ties “hasty.” In August 2024, it said Bamako had provided no evidence of Ukrainian involvement in the Tinzaouaten attack. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency also referred CNN to earlier official remarks when approached for comment on its September report of Ukrainian drone specialists assisting rebels in Mali.
Is Mali alone in making the accusation?
Niger and Burkina Faso have also accused Ukraine of supporting armed groups. The three Alliance of Sahel States (AES) members filed a complaint with the UN Security Council in August 2024.
During a televised interview on Sunday reviewing his four years in office, Burkina Faso’s interim President Ibrahim Traore said he had placed Ukraine on his country’s “map of enemies.” Speaking about what he described as attempts to destabilize Mali and Niger, he warned these were “only the beginning.” He cited Pyvovarov’s comment, saying the diplomat had “clearly stated that they were involved” in supporting armed groups in the Sahel.
What does Moscow say?
Russia backs the Sahel states’ accusations. Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused Kiev of “state terrorism” against countries in the region, citing reports of serving Ukrainian troops joining attacks alongside armed groups. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova previously said Kiev was opening a “second front” against Russia in Africa by supporting militants in countries friendly to Moscow.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko told TASS on July 17 that Ukrainian instructors trained in drone warfare were embedded with Islamist militants in Mali. He also alleged Ukrainian involvement in attacks on Russian interests in Libya and support for paramilitary forces in Sudan, extending Moscow’s accusations beyond the Sahel.
Why have the Sahel states turned to Russia?
Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso ended defense ties with France, accusing it of failing to contain the insurgency and interfering in their affairs. They have strengthened counterterrorism cooperation with Russia.
Nearly 49,000 people have been killed in violence linked to militant Islamist groups in the Sahel since 2022, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies said in August.
Mali and Russia signed a military cooperation agreement in June 2019. Bamako sought Russian private military assistance in 2021. Wagner was replaced by Russia’s Defense Ministry-run Africa Corps in June 2025. The corps operates at African governments’ official request, Lavrov said last month.
At the UN on Monday, Diop said the AES remained open to partnerships respecting its members’ sovereignty. “We do not accept dictates; rather, we seek sincere and healthy cooperation,” he said.

Tsahkna linked the removal of Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list to France’s position.

Report: Estonian e-commerce among the top in Europe  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:52:52 UTC
23:52:52 KST

TALLINN - According to the 2026 European E-commerce Report, European e-commerce is still growing, but the pace has slowed. Estonia stands out in the report on several fronts: its e-commerce turnover per capita reached 4,252 euros in 2025, the second-highest result among European countries.
European B2C e-commerce turnover was 911 billion euros in 2025, a 7 percent increase from the previous year. For 2026, turnover is projected to grow to 961 billion euros, a 5 percent increase. Adjusted for inflation, real growth last year was 4 percent. Western Europe remains the largest market, accounting for 57 percent of European e-commerce turnover. However, the markets in Southern and Eastern Europe are experiencing the fastest growth.
For Estonian companies, 97 percent of online sales came through their own websites or apps, the highest figure in Europe. "Estonia's result shows that our e-commerce sector is mature, with companies having built strong, independent sales channels. At the same time, the low use of marketplaces means many businesses have not yet capitalized on the opportunity to reach new customers outside Estonia. Cross-border sales represent the next significant growth area," Tõnu Väät, head of the Estonian E-commerce Association, said in a press release.
In 2025, 93 percent of Europeans used the internet, a figure projected to rise to 95 percent by 2026. Last year, 75 percent of Europeans aged 16-74 made purchases online, compared to 68 percent in 2021.
According to the report, efficiency and customer experience are becoming more crucial in mature markets. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in customer service, marketing, personalization, pricing, and analytics. In the future, agentive AI may start handling a larger share of the purchasing process on behalf of the consumer.
Consumers have become more price-sensitive, comparing prices more frequently, seeking cheaper alternatives, and placing greater importance on used goods and cross-border purchases. Payments and logistics are also evolving rapidly, with advancements in mobile payments, digital wallets, instant payments, buy-now-pay-later services, and the proliferation of parcel lockers and pick-up points.
"The era of rapid growth in mature markets is over, and success now hinges on efficiency. Artificial intelligence helps companies improve their service, pricing, and customer understanding. At the same time, we must ensure that regulations do not become overly burdensome for small merchants and that we compete with non-European platforms on a level playing field," Väät added.
The Estonian E-commerce Association is an umbrella organization with over 530 member companies. The association also issues the "Secure Shopping" trustmark.

A request has also been made to revise the Cabinet of Ministers’ regulations on the minimum monthly wage and special allowances for healthcare workers, as well as to introduce a mechanism for regular wage reviews.
Under the Cabinet of Ministers’ regulations on the minimum monthly wage and special allowances for healthcare workers, the minimum monthly wage set for nursing aides and medical assistants is EUR 863, which is EUR 43 higher than the minimum wage planned for 2027, while the minimum monthly wage set for nurses is EUR 1,189. LVSADA notes that without a commensurate increase in healthcare workers’ salaries, the labor shortage in the sector will worsen.

The draft does not specify the actual amount of funding to be allocated, notes LVSADA.

If NATO collectively decides to do so and there is a need, nuclear weapons could be deployed in Latvia - Rinkevics  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:52:36 UTC
23:52:36 KST

RIGA - If NATO collectively decides and there is a need to do so, nuclear weapons could be deployed in Latvia, Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics told members of the press today.
The Lithuanian Seimas voted this month in a first reading to support the repeal of the constitutional ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory. Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction or foreign military bases may not be located on Lithuanian territory.
Rinkevics emphasized that the Latvian Constitution does not contain such a ban. "We have no legally established obstacles in our laws to the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia," said the president.
He explained that in 2003, as Latvia was preparing to join NATO, each member state had confirmed that it would not impose any restrictions on the full implementation of NATO’s collective security mechanisms, including participation in the nuclear deterrence system. "If the need arises and if such a collective NATO decision is made, nuclear weapons will be deployed in Latvia," Rinkevics stated.
At the same time, he emphasized that no specific negotiations regarding the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia are currently underway.
Commenting on the United Kingdom’s offer of nuclear umbrella to the member states of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF)-the Baltic states, the Nordic countries, and the Netherlands- Rinkevics argued that without nuclear deterrence, several conventional wars would have long since broken out in Europe. The use of nuclear weapons is a last resort, but they deter aggressors from unpredictable or large-scale actions, Rinkevics noted.
The politician pointed out that the United Kingdom is already part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence system and that Latvia is currently under the NATO nuclear umbrella provided by the United States and the United Kingdom, but as a member of JEF, Latvia views all additional security measures and elements positively. "We understand that this is still part of NATO’s overall policy," the president said.
As reported, the United Kingdom has offered a "nuclear umbrella" to members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) military partnership (the Baltic states, Nordics countries and the Netherlands) as part of a wider defence agreement.
The umbrella is a security guarantee by a nuclear-armed state to protect a non-nuclear ally.
The offer was confirmed during a visit by General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of the UK’s Naval Staff, to Finland on Monday, where he met with MP Heikki Autto (NCP), chair of parliament’s defence committee.
It is believed that the JEF member countries will sign an agreement at a meeting in Oslo in November.
The deal would mean a separate nuclear umbrella outside of Nato’s extended deterrence strategy offered by the US, UK and France to all non-nuclear member states within the alliance.
"Finland is under the nuclear umbrella. It is guaranteed by our submarines, which are patrolling the Atlantic right now," Jenkins said.
JEF is a coalition of ten like-minded countries-Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, the United Kingdom, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, and Sweden - that comprises high-readiness forces capable of responding rapidly to crises in the high north and Northern Europe.
The coalition was established in 2014 on the initiative of the United Kingdom in response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Finland and Sweden joined the JEF in 2017, even before these countries were admitted to NATO. The JEF is now considered a first-response force that complements NATO.

RTU ranked among world's top 1,000 universities  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:52:27 UTC
23:52:27 KST

RIGA - Riga Technical University (RTU) has been ranked among the world's top 1,000 universities, according to data from the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026.
Over the past year, RTU has risen from the 1,001st-1,200th range to the 801st-1,000th range. The university’s score has improved in all five evaluated categories.
The other Latvian universities included in the ranking are not ranked higher than 1,001st place. The University of Latvia (LU) has maintained its position in the 1,001st-1,200th range, while Riga Stradins University (RSU) has moved up to 1,201st-1,400th range. The Latvian University of Life Sciences and Technologies (LBTU) is ranked below 2,001st place.
The universities have shown improvements in several categories. RSU and LU have seen their rankings rise in four categories. Meanwhile, LBTU’s scores have improved in three categories - research environment, research quality, and international outlook - but have dropped in the categories of teaching and industry collaboration.
The universities’ performance was rated highest in the international outlook category, where the score of each university is its highest across all categories. RTU and RSU performed best in this category, scoring 71.2 and 66.8 points, respectively. All four universities saw their scores improve in this category.
A total of 2,297 universities were evaluated in this year’s ranking. Oxford University received the highest overall rating, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in second place, while Princeton University and Stanford University tied for third.

The minister emphasized the need to share information and work together with allies to de-escalate tensions, while remaining prepared for any Russian provocations.
Meanwhile, Braze noted that Russia is also attempting to undermine support for Ukraine through such actions. She said that Russia is unable to achieve its military objectives and is therefore trying to undermine support for Ukraine from Europe, the United States, and other countries.
Braze emphasized that the incidents occurring in various countries should not be viewed as coincidental, but rather as deliberate actions that are part of Russia’s strategy and must be taken very seriously.
Tsahkna emphasized that it is important to maintain support for Ukraine, especially as winter approaches. He noted that Estonia will host a conference on Ukraine’s reconstruction, and that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has asked that all formats of political cooperation be utilized to prepare for the conference and achieve practical results.
Tsahkna also noted that measures must be taken to ensure that Russian grain is not transported through the Baltic states. He noted that a couple of weeks ago, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) called on the Baltic states to take action and implement countermeasures. According to Tsahkna, the Estonian government will decide tomorrow on a ban on transporting Russian grain through Estonia.

There, the victim was prevented from moving freely or leaving the premises. The man suffered several hours of physical violence, including being beaten with various objects.

In the forest, he was subjected to repeated physical violence, after which the alleged perpetrators abandoned him there.
Two men, born in 2001 and 2007, were arrested on September 23 in connection with the incident. During searches at the suspects’ residences, law enforcement officers found and seized substances believed to be narcotics. The suspected drugs have been submitted for forensic tests.
On September 24, the two suspects were remanded in custody as a security measure by a court order.
Criminal proceedings for kidnapping in an organized group have been initiated in connection with the incident. Such a crime is punishable by a prison term of three to 12 years, with or without confiscation of property, and with or without probationary supervision for up to three years.
Both suspects had previously come to the attention of law enforcement in connection with offenses committed under the influence of intoxicating substances.

At present, Latvia has no evidence that Russia might directly invade any of NATO member states - Rinkevics  - The Baltic Times
Unknown

RIGA - Although there is much talk in many quarters about a possible direct Russian invasion of one of the NATO member states, Latvia currently has no such indications or facts that would prove that, President Edgars Rinkevics told reporters today after a meeting with Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List).
The politician noted that it was confirmed yesterday in Estonia that the fire at the defense industry company Milrem Robotics in Tallinn last month was an act of sabotage orchestrated by Russian special services. Similar reports of sabotage carried out by Russia have also emerged in other countries, the president noted.
Rinkevics did not deny that there may come a time when someone actually loses their life in such incidents. "That, of course, is a completely different situation," the politician remarked.
The president emphasized that the public has long been informed that various provocations and cyberattacks can occur, have already occurred, and will continue to occur in Latvia, and that the responsible authorities are treating this very seriously and with a high degree of responsibility. Public involvement is crucial in this regard, Rinkevics noted. He urged the public to report anything suspicious, which, among other things, could be related to Russian provocations, to the relevant authorities.
Rinkevics assessed that Russia currently has two objectives regarding Latvia. The first is to prevent Latvia from providing assistance to Ukraine - something Latvia has no intention of doing, while the second is to create a sense of insecurity and panic among the public and within the country as a whole.
The president noted that, in his discussions with leaders of other countries, he has observed that understanding of Russia’s objectives is also beginning to take hold elsewhere.
Rinkevics does not consider the statement made by Egils Zviedrs, director of the Constitution Protection Bureau (SAB), in an interview with LETA, that Russia, unable to defeat Ukraine, is raising the stakes in Europe, and that civilian casualties cannot be ruled out, is anything radically new. "We have already called on people and warned them to be prepared - without excessive panic, but with great vigilance," the official said.
Kulbergs, for his part, emphasized that Latvia understands very well what to expect from Russia, and understands it much better than many countries in the West. That is why Latvia is investing in security, especially along the border, concentrating its capabilities, and spending enormous resources on defense and internal affairs, the prime minister noted, adding that Latvia does so to a much greater extent than many other European partners who are less informed about Russia.
He asserted that Russia currently lacks the conventional capabilities for another large-scale military operation, but at the same time, we must understand and be prepared for provocations. "There is no need to be alarmed, but we must be vigilant," the prime minister said.
As reported, Zviedris noted in an interview with LETA that SAB has been warning about an escalation of Russia’s unconventional military operations since early spring. Specifically, Russia is unable to achieve its stated goal - victory in the war against Ukraine, and is therefore escalating the situation in Europe, given the support Western countries are providing to Ukraine.
This escalation includes hybrid threats such as cyberattacks and acts of physical sabotage, as well as information warfare. Russia is escalating the situation because it has failed to reduce Western support for Ukraine or to secure a relaxation of sanctions, Zviedris explained.
Consequently, we are seeing incidents such as drones filled with explosives at Leipzig Airport and acts of sabotage on railway lines in European countries. "Russia is raising the stakes, and unfortunately, we cannot rule out civilian casualties either," emphasized the director of Latvia’s special services.
Zviedris pointed out that so far in Europe, Russia has not carried out only false-flag operations, as everything else has already happened. He reminded that in Latvia there have been acts of desecration of monuments and the arson attack on the Museum of the Occupation, while in Lithuania there have been attacks on Russian opposition figures living there. Meanwhile, recent warnings by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk about Russian threats were directly related to false-flag operations. Similarly, there was a recent Russian attack on a Ukrainian passenger train just two kilometers from the Polish border, Zviedris noted.
"Consequently, Tusk warned of Russian attacks near the borders of NATO countries. Such statements serve as a warning to Russia that we are monitoring its activities near our national borders and will not tolerate them," added the director of SAB.
Zviedris noted that Latvia has requested the deployment of four NATO fighter jets here during the Saeima elections, a request to which Germany has agreed. This step was taken to rule out any possible provocations, such as the appearance of an unidentified flying object in Latvian airspace, which could subsequently spark speculation about the legitimacy of the election process.
"So the Russian threat is real, and since the aggressor has been unable to achieve its goals in Ukraine, the stakes are being raised," Zviedris added.

LONDON, September 30. /TASS/. The average price of diesel in the UK has surpassed the psychological milestone of 2 pounds ($2.66) per liter for the first time in history, according to calculations by Sky News.

More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:51:08 UTC
23:51:08 KST

Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information.
More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology.
The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue.
Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months.
Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027.
David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes. I am not happy about Palantir’s involvement with the IDF in Gaza and ICE in America.”
On Wednesday, the human rights group Amnesty International and patient campaign group, Just Treatment, parked a van styled like a shot-up Palestinian ambulance outside Palantir’s London HQ in a stunt that asked: “Why should a company linked to Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system have any place in ours?”
Protesters have also raised concerns, acknowledged by the NHS England chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health from the Palantir-powered platform may not be as significant as has been claimed.
Palantir says the FDP, which is designed to connect sprawling health service data on topics ranging from surgery schedules to discharge planning, is helping to cut waiting lists and frees up beds. Louis Mosley, the company’s executive vice-president for UK and Europe, has accused people who disagree with that assessment of suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”.
A spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”
Mosley has said its technology was used for locating hostages, not military targeting, in Gaza, although when challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza, the company’s chief executive, Alex Karp, replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
The formal objections to the FDP using personal data cite article 21 of the UK General Data Protection Regulation and express concern that “the involvement of Palantir undermines my personal trust in NHS data confidentiality”. Palantir said its patient data could only be handled according to the NHS’s instructions and remained in the UK.
Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, a not-for-profit that coordinated the data objections, said: “The scale of this public backlash should be a huge wake-up call for the government.”
A spokesperson for NHS England said: “All NHS organisations remain in control of their data within the FDP, with suppliers unable to access it for their own purposes, and we will respond to the objection requests in line with data protection law.”
The 44,000 objectors have also asked that the NHS halts processing of their data through the Palantir platform while their main request is assessed.

Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat from Delaware, reported on 29 September, a day before the end of the financial year, that the Pentagon has obligated 99.8% of the US$400 million that Congress had allocated for aid to Ukraine.
Source: The Washington Sun, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda
Quote from Coons: "The fact that they are finally doing it, like on the last possible day, tells you everything you need to know about that relationship. They don't brief us on time. They don't follow the law, and the partnership is struggling."
Details: The funds were obligated before the end of the financial year on Wednesday 30 September. The department has obligated US$307 million and plans to commit the remaining US$93 million by the 30 September deadline.
The Pentagon's plan includes US$200 million for weapons, ammunition and explosives, US$99.9 million for vehicles, spare parts and equipment, and US$100 million for services such as transporting military equipment.
Background:
- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the allocation of US$400 million in military aid to Ukraine, which Congress had already approved, back in June 2026. Representatives from both parties had been pressing the Pentagon for months to release the funds.
- Recently, the Trump administration made legally binding commitments to spend almost all of the US$400 million in military aid to Ukraine that Congress approved at the end of 2025. However, the package will not include missiles for Patriot systems.

Mounting pressure on Iran could lead to attack on Israel, ex-national security council head warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:50:19 UTC
23:50:19 KST

Former national security council head Meir Ben-Shabbat warned that mounting pressure on Iran could still push Tehran toward a direct attack on Israel, while arguing that a future agreement between Washington and Tehran could provide the Iranian regime with a strategic lifeline, he told Maariv in a Wednesday interview.
Ben-Shabbat, who was among the architects of the Abraham Accords, said the Iranian regime remained under severe pressure but had not yet reached a point of desperation.
“First, regarding Iran’s situation: despite the challenging reality it faces, the impression is that the regime in Tehran still does not have its back against the wall. In medical terms, its condition is serious but not critical.
The Iranians are probably counting on the American willingness to reach an agreement, continue to exist, and save them if they reach the edge of the abyss. In any event, Israel must always be prepared on the assumption that at a certain point in time, which will not necessarily be possible to predict, Iran will consider attacking it,” he said.
Ben-Shabbat also warned that a US agreement with Iran could have serious strategic consequences regardless of whether it formally restricted Israel’s freedom of action.
“Israel’s freedom of action to defend itself against an existential threat is a matter about which there is no dispute. The consequences of an agreement with Iran are very severe even if they do not have an effect on Israel’s freedom of action," he said.
"Any agreement with the Iranians, even if it meets the parameters set by the American administration, will ultimately be a lifeline for the regime in Tehran; it will finance its recovery and preserve the dangers from it."
"This clear and unequivocal position was voiced a few days ago by Gen. Jack Keane, who served as vice chief of staff of the US Army and received the Presidential Medal from Trump. He precisely defined the strategic trap placed before the American president and recommended making the creation of conditions that put the Iranian regime on a path to collapse a goal. Any additional word is unnecessary.”
Iran has been waging a campaign against Europe 'for some time'
Asked whether an attempted attack on RAF Fairford, if linked to Iran or one of its proxies, would indicate that Tehran was expanding its campaign against the West into Europe, Ben-Shabbat said Iran had already been waging such a campaign for some time.
“Iran has been waging a campaign against Europe for some time. I remind you that Iran has already attacked European bases: Iranian UAVs, apparently launched from Lebanon by Hezbollah, directly struck the British Air Force base at Akrotiri in Cyprus.
"The confrontation between Iran and European countries is admittedly not being conducted as a frontal conventional war, but it certainly exists as a multidimensional hybrid campaign combining warfare in the ‘gray zone,’ terrorism through proxies, cyberattacks, and economic influence. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in June 2025 that Israel ‘is doing the dirty work for all of us’ in reference to the campaign against Iran. He was right then, and his words are also correct today.”
Asked whether Israelis and Jews abroad should prepare for an increase in attempts to target them amid rising pressure on Iran, Ben-Shabbat replied: “The system and the citizens must assume so.”
Netanyahu's visit to the UAE tightens important relationship
Ben-Shabbat also addressed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reported secret visit to the United Arab Emirates, saying coordination with Abu Dhabi was particularly important given the possibility of either military escalation with Iran or a diplomatic agreement.
“I remind you that we are in the midst of the confrontation with Iran, with on the one hand – a possibility of military escalation, and on the other hand – a possibility of a diplomatic arrangement. A common position and alignment by Israel and the Emirates are things that require discussion and coordination.”
On the possibility of expanding the Abraham Accords, including through Saudi normalization, Ben-Shabbat said the current regional uncertainty reduced the chances of a breakthrough.
“In general, the chances of this during periods of uncertainty, election campaigns or fighting, are not high. Israel’s value as a security and technological-economic partner is clear. Israeli's interest in expanding the agreements is clear, but it must come from Israeli strength. Under no circumstances should we court them or pay compensation.”
When will the Hezbollah conflict be over?
Turning to Lebanon, Ben-Shabbat said Hezbollah had suffered a strategic blow but that the campaign against the group was far from over.
“The pager operation and the Israeli attack that followed it two years ago were a turning point in the war between Israel and Hezbollah, which led to the elimination of the person who had ruled southern Lebanon and the Shi’ite terrorist organization for 40 years, cut off Iran’s strongest and most important proxy arm that it had in the region, enabled the collapse of the Assad regime and the shattering of the perception of Syria as Iran’s backyard, and created significant shock waves in the Middle East.
“Above and below the surface, the signs of the change that occurred can be seen in every field: Hezbollah lost the control it had over the territory and the line of villages along the border with Israel, it also lost commanders, fighters, infrastructure, and strategic assets; and beyond that, its status in the Lebanese arena.
"Naim Qassem is finding it difficult to step into Nasrallah’s shoes and fill the military, political, or social vacuum he left behind. Lebanese voices expressing deep frustration over the heavy price of Hezbollah’s war, which is not necessarily Lebanon’s war, are growing, and alongside all of these – the Lebanese government, despite its weakness, is trying to establish a new order.
“The Lebanese-American researcher and commentator Hussein Abd al-Hussein determined in an article he published recently that Hezbollah suffered a strategic defeat but refuses to acknowledge it. From Israel’s point of view, these are significant achievements, but the work is not complete and it is too early for summaries.
"All the players in the system understand that the way Iran emerges from the current confrontation will directly shape Hezbollah’s power, status, and future policy. Therefore, Israel must tighten its control over the areas it has defined, maintain a continuous offensive initiative, block every attempt at renewed force buildup, and not ease the pressure on the enemy’s throat for even a moment.”
Israel continues to strive to destroy Hamas
Ben-Shabbat rejected the idea that Israel had shifted from seeking to destroy Hamas to merely weakening the organization.
“I am not aware of a change in the goals of the war regarding Gaza, and in my opinion there is no room for such a change. Determination, patience, and persistence are the key to success. Israel must complete the task until the military and governing capabilities of the Hamas organization in the Strip are completely eliminated, the territory is completely demilitarized, and there is Israeli security control.
"From the perspective of the State of Israel, it is not enough to settle only for removing the security threat; it should have an interest in the area in which the cruel monster that carried out the October 7 massacre grew, becoming eternal testimony to the prices that anyone who thinks in the future about attacking Israel will pay.”
Asked about European measures targeting goods from the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, and their possible economic impact on Palestinians, Ben-Shabbat said he did not have the exact figures but accused some international actors of prioritizing pressure on Israeli settlements over Palestinian economic welfare.
“I am not familiar with the precise economic data, but among some of the players in the international system, the desire to harm the settlement enterprise in Judea and Samaria outweighs the interest in ensuring the economic well-being of the Palestinians there. This is another expression of the double standard and hypocrisy on their part.”
Turkey: A growing power in the Middle East
Ben-Shabbat also focused on Turkey, which he described as a growing regional power taking advantage of changes in Syria, Africa, and the eastern Mediterranean.
“The Greek defense minister, Nikos Dendias, said a few months ago: ‘If we ask the United States and Turkey how they see the future of the world and the region in ten years, we will receive two completely opposite answers – and that is the whole story.’ His words capture the abyss between the American vision and Erdogan’s ambitions for the Middle East and the international system.
“More than any other country, Turkey knows how to exploit global great-power competition and the changes in the Middle East in order to establish its status as a dominant regional power. It dances at every wedding and collects diplomatic brokerage fees from all the players. Following the collapse of the Assad regime and the forced withdrawal of the Iranian military presence, Turkey became the dominant player in Syria. From local territorial control in northern Syria, it moved to exercising broad influence across the entire country.
“Syria is only part of Erdogan’s broader vision of ‘neo-Ottomanism.’ He seeks to restore Turkey to the status of a regional superpower and expand its influence far beyond its official borders. The implementation of this concept was recently evident in the signing of the ‘Mecca Joint Defense Agreement’ with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, but even before that, in its efforts to open intercontinental trade corridors, in its deep involvement in Africa, and in the adoption of the ‘Blue Homeland’ doctrine (Mavi Vatan), which expresses its ambitions in the eastern Mediterranean.
“When these trends are added to Erdogan’s overt hostility toward Israel, it is difficult to ignore the potential for friction and strategic confrontation with him, and this is even without mentioning the Palestinian issue and his support for Hamas. Turkey continues today as well to host senior members of the Hamas leadership on its territory and is conducting a legal and information campaign accusing Israel of war crimes.
“And despite all this, Turkey is not Iran: it is a member of NATO, Erdogan has a close relationship with Trump, and relations with Israel, despite the deep crisis, are still not severed. Precisely in order to prevent this rivalry from turning into a military confrontation, Israel acted correctly when it clarified its red lines in Syria and in general.
“In addition, Israel is also acting correctly when it deepens and expands its security relations with Greece and Cyprus, and also when it enters Africa, into strategic areas that Turkey has its eyes on. In my opinion, beyond all these actions, Israel needs to lead an international move to declare the global Muslim Brotherhood organization an illegal organization, and it must also act systematically to push the Turks out of operating in Jerusalem or in connection with it. With determination, but not necessarily demonstratively.”

South Africa lodges fresh diplomatic protest against US ambassador
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:49:20 UTC
23:49:20 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
South Africa lodged a diplomatic protest with the US ambassador to Pretoria after he criticized the government in media interviews, according to local media on Wednesday.
The Department of International Relations and Cooperation delivered the demarche to US Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III on Tuesday, reported News24, a Cape Town-based news outlet, citing a US government official and other unidentified sources.
Bozell has repeatedly accused President Cyril Ramaphosa of failing to adequately address five demands presented by the White House as conditions for easing diplomatic tensions between the two countries, according to News24.
South Africa has rejected the demands as interference in its domestic affairs, saying its policies seek to address the legacy of apartheid, which left the Black majority economically disadvantaged.
Bozell was first summoned in March over his remarks about the controversial anti-apartheid-era “Kill the Boer” chant, whose lyrics call for killing a “Boer,” a term historically associated with Afrikaner farmers.
The latest protest comes amid deteriorating relations between South Africa and the US since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump has criticized Pretoria’s land and Black economic empowerment policies.
The US is seeking exemptions for American companies from Black economic empowerment rules, an end to land expropriation without compensation and government condemnation of the “Kill the Boer” chant.
It also wants Pretoria to address farm killings and not oppose Trump’s program to grant refugee status to white Afrikaners who say they face racial persecution.
Bozell also warned of further escalation after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions targeting South African officials.

Qatar and UAE back Ethiopian government as fighting spreads beyond Tigray
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:47:38 UTC
23:47:38 KST

Fighting has displaced an estimated 150,000 people, drawing responses from Qatar and the UAE as Ethiopia and its neighbours trade accusations.
Qatar has condemned what it called the military escalation against Ethiopia’s federal forces, while the United Arab Emirates has voiced support for the Ethiopian government amid renewed fighting in the country’s north.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said the fighting threatened Ethiopia’s unity and sovereignty and the stability of the wider Horn of Africa.
It called for an immediate end to the fighting, protection for civilians and respect for the Pretoria Peace Agreement between Tigray and Ethiopia.
The Qatari statement did not name the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) or the new alliance of armed groups fighting the federal government. Qatar said its “full support” was for efforts to reduce tensions and resolve disputes through dialogue.
The UAE condemned what it described as attacks by the TPLF and its armed allies on federal forces, as well as the seizure of airports in Tigray and the spread of fighting into neighbouring Afar and Amhara.
UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan said his country stood in “full solidarity with the government and people” of Ethiopia. He also rejected attempts to change the country’s constitutional order through force.
Fighting spreads beyond Tigray
The statements followed the most serious fighting in northern Ethiopia since the agreement ended the 2020–2022 war, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.
Tigrayan forces seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire last week, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the region.
The TPLF says it is fighting defensively after federal forces attacked Tigray using drones, artillery and ground troops. The federal government accuses the group of launching a planned offensive.
Tigrayan forces captured Erebti in Afar over the weekend. On Monday, pro-government forces said they had taken control of Alamata, an important supply town around 120 kilometres south of Tigray’s capital, Mekelle.
A drone also struck the headquarters of Tigrai TV in Mekelle on Sunday. Journalists said they had left the building after hearing an earlier explosion. No casualties were reported, and the federal government did not comment on the strike.
Médecins Sans Frontières said the number of wounded people treated at hospitals in Korem and Alamata rose to more than 420 between 22-25 September. More than 300 wounded people arrived at Suhul Hospital last week.
The Afar Pastoralist Development Association estimates that around 150,000 people have been displaced by the fighting.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “gravely concerned” by the seizure of the three airports and the spread of hostilities beyond Tigray.
He urged all sides to stop the fighting, protect civilians, allow aid groups to reach those in need and return to talks under the peace agreement.
Ethiopia and its neighbours exchange accusations
Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting armed groups fighting the government. He did not provide evidence for the accusations.
Sudan’s army rejected the allegation and accused Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used to support Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
Egypt’s Foreign Ministry did not name Ethiopia directly but dismissed suggestions that Cairo interfered in other countries as baseless. Spokesperson Nader Zaki said Egypt respected the sovereignty and territorial integrity of other states.
Eritrea has also denied supporting Ethiopian armed groups and accused Addis Ababa of attempting to shift responsibility for the fighting.
The TPLF joined six other armed groups this month in an alliance that says it wants to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration.

'No ban but also not 24x7': SC on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR ahead of Diwali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:46:23 UTC
23:46:23 KST

"We need to find a solution by which we can give a specified time," the SC bench said.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said it would not impose a blanket ban on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR, but would also not permit fireworks throughout the day, saying a balance had to be struck between public health concerns and people’s sentiments.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale said the court would consider allowing firecrackers only during specified hours."We will make it very clear. Neither we are going to agree for total ban, nor are we going to allow them to do it (fireworks) for 24 hours a day. Total ban will affect sentiments. And allowing them throughout the day will have huge impact on every other living being including the old, sick and children," the bench orally observed, as quoted by PTI."We need to find a solution by which we can give a specified time," it added.The observations came during a hearing in which the Centre proposed a limited relaxation for a category of next-generation joined green crackers developed with technical inputs from the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI).Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati submitted a note saying the court could consider permitting the specified green crackers subject to conditions on their manufacture, chemical composition, noise levels and emissions.
According to the note, only duly licensed manufacturers would be allowed to produce the crackers. They would also have to meet the prescribed noise limit of 125 dB(AI)/145 dB(C) peak and could not contain banned chemicals.The proposed crackers are linked or joined fireworks formulated with reduced quantities of barium salts, with the aim of lowering emissions. The proposal is based on the category recommended by CSIR-NEERI and would be subject to applicable safety, noise and emission standards.
The bench further said it would consider the issue concerning the use of barium in firecrackers on October 15.The court's latest observations come ahead of Diwali and follow its earlier orders regulating the manufacture, sale and use of firecrackers in Delhi and the National Capital Region.Last year, the Supreme Court allowed the sale and use of green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR subject to conditions, including restrictions on when they could be used.The court had said their use would be limited to specified hours on the days before Diwali and on Diwali itself, as part of measures aimed at balancing festival-related celebrations with concerns over air pollution and public health.

TEKNOFEST fuels confidence revolution to defeat 'we cannot do it' mindset: Bayraktar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:46:11 UTC
23:46:11 KST

Selcuk Bayraktar, chairman of the board of trustees of the Türkiye Technology Team Foundation (T3 Foundation) and chairman of the TEKNOFEST board, described the festival as “a confidence revolution” challenging the mindset that says “we cannot do it”.
“TEKNOFEST is a confidence revolution. It is a rebellion against the mentality that says, ‘We cannot do it.’ It is an objection to imitation and learned helplessness,” Bayraktar said in his opening address on Wednesday at TEKNOFEST Southeast.
Türkiye’s premier aviation, space and technology festival TEKNOFEST opened its doors to visitors on Wednesday in the southeastern province of Sanliurfa.
TEKNOFEST Southeast, a leg of the event held in southeastern Türkiye, brings together tech enthusiasts, young investors and thousands of visitors for various shows, exhibitions and the finals of technology competitions across 14 categories from Wednesday through October 4.
Describing Sanliurfa as “the zero point of history,” Bayraktar said it was among the lands where humanity transitioned to settled life, developed agriculture and laid the foundations of civilisation.
‘More than 1.6 million young people applied’
Holding its 15th festival since its launch in 2018, Bayraktar said the TEKNOFEST “seedling we planted in 2018 has today turned into a major technology movement.”
He said young people from all 81 provinces of Türkiye and 97 countries were participating in the festival, adding that more than 730,000 teams and over 1.6 million young people had applied to technology competitions in 62 categories.
“These are not just numbers. They are Türkiye’s changing story,” Bayraktar said.
He highlighted the participation of young people from southeastern Türkiye, saying children in the region were learning artificial intelligence and robotics at DENEYAP Technology Workshops.
Referring to the region’s hot climate, Bayraktar said: “When we came to Urfa, we understood something else. If a system works smoothly at noon in the Urfa heat, it will work anywhere in the world, and even in space.”
‘National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky’
Bayraktar said confidence strengthens production, production strengthens technology, and technology creates the foundation for independence.
“That is why the National Technology Initiative exists,” he said.
“The National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky. It is in the fields, factories, laboratories, hospitals, workshops and universities.”
He said the initiative aims to turn ideas into economic value, dreams into production, projects into employment and technology into prosperity for Türkiye.
“Our goal is high technology, domestic production and value-added exports,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to build an entrepreneurship ecosystem that will strengthen our country’s full independence, led by the TEKNOFEST generation.”
Agricultural technologies in focus
Bayraktar also highlighted the strategic importance of agricultural production, saying food had become a more critical issue than ever.
“We can no longer view agriculture simply as a traditional sector. Agriculture must become one of the high-technology fields of the future,” he said.
He pointed to next-generation national agricultural technologies, AI-supported solutions, genetic science, efficiency and sustainable production as areas of focus.
“As the solutions developed by young people meet these fertile lands, our future will become stronger and more prosperous,” he said.
Bringing science together with conscience
Bayraktar also addressed the rapid transformation driven by artificial intelligence, saying the technology could accelerate learning and research but should be viewed as a tool that expands human potential rather than a guide that replaces human judgment.
“Technology is a tool. It is the human who determines its direction and must make the final decision,” he said.
“Our aim is not merely to develop technology, but to determine what kind of spirit and direction we will give it,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to use technology for the benefit of humanity. We want to bring science together with conscience, intelligence with morality, and power with justice.”

How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:45:43 UTC
23:45:43 KST

It was billed as one of the largest real-estate events in Europe, attracting as many as 15,000 people ranging from investment firms to developers. But as the District trade show and summit got under way last week in Madrid, housing campaigners from 140 organisations across the globe turned up, intent on holding their own “counter-summit” to push back against the idea of housing as a financial asset.
Many of the campaigners arrived in the Spanish capital as Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair, was being evicted from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. As anger over the eviction gave way to days of protests and an encampment in the heart of Madrid, the presence of campaigners from Italy to Ireland was a poignant reminder of the global dimension of the crisis.
The eviction underscored how brutal access to housing had become for so many around the world, said Teresa Mamede, a housing campaigner from Lisbon who travelled to Madrid for the counter-summit. “Nobody among us is safe from having this happen to them.”
The Guardian has long reported on the depth of the housing crisis across Europe. Within the EU, prices soared by 53% between 2010 and 2024, according to Eurostat, while rents increased 25% over the same period.
Not all countries have been hit equally; while Vienna remains a bright spot for its ample stock of public housing that has tempered rental costs, Estonia has seen rents surge 208% in the same time period, while Ireland and Hungary have seen increases of more than 100%.
Some of the soaring costs can be chalked up to the “ever-intensifying social experiment” playing out in Europe, research fellow Tim White noted last year, as officials see whether the machinations of finance capitalism can deliver on the fundamental need for housing. “The evidence now seems overwhelming: no.”
Instead, vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected by the market’s shortcomings, while others warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse,” Jaume Collboni, the mayor of Barcelona, told me last year.
Voters in Berlin, however, recently opted for another path. In a city where rents had climbed nearly 70% in the past decade, a quarter of voters backed the leftwing party Die Linke in this month’s state elections, making it Berlin’s strongest party. The strategy behind their success was far from rocket science, said Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir. “Because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue [of housing] unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.”
‘This is just getting started’
Some have sought shared solutions to the shared crisis. At the Madrid counter-summit, campaigners launched a pan-European alliance to demand indefinite rental contracts and rent control across the continent.
Earlier this month, dozens of organisations launched the European Citizens’ Initiative, calling on people to sign their petition for EU-level measures to protect tenants, curb speculation and convert empty buildings into homes. “In every European country, in every major survey, and across all age groups, housing emerges as the number one concern of citizens,” the initiative notes. “We see and feel it every day: workers who can no longer afford the city they build, young people who cannot leave their parents’ home, tenants pushed out of their neighbourhoods after renovation, empty buildings while people sleep on the street.”
In Spain, where the days-long encampment in Madrid has led to similar camps in cities such as Barcelona, Seville and Palma de Mallorca, the protests have already begun to have an impact.
Maricarmen, the evicted octogenarian, will be allowed to return to her apartment, it was confirmed on Tuesday. Her rent will remain around the €500 a month she had paid for years – significantly less than the €2,650 the investment firm that owns her apartment had initially demanded.
This week the Spanish government also said it had approved two housing decrees that include reforms such as a ban on evictions until 2030, and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. But these measures will now have to win approval in the country’s fractured parliament.
What exactly comes next for the housing movement that has gripped Spain in recent days is anyone’s guess. With the spectre of general elections looming and the Socialist-led coalition scrambling to shore up its base of progressive voters, campaigners have spotted a singular opportunity to tackle an issue that Spaniards have long ranked as one of the country’s biggest problems.
“The coming days will be crucial,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said on Tuesday as it called for further protests this weekend. “A historic window of opportunity has opened to reverse decades of the commodification of housing. That is why we need to step up the pressure.”
Or, as the Málaga Tenants’ Union put it in an online post: “This is just getting started.”

Unconditional jail demanded for attacks on emergency workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:44:44 UTC
23:44:44 KST

Unconditional jail demanded for attacks on emergency workers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
People who attack emergency workers, including police officers, paramedics and train staff, will face an unconditional prison sentence from Thursday, under new rules from the public prosecution service (OM).
Prosecutors will no longer settle such cases with a fine or community service, and every suspect will have to appear in court, the OM said on Wednesday. The rules will apply to offences committed from October 1.
It sets fixed sentencing guidelines for three offences: public violence, assault, and attempted serious assault. An attempt to seriously assault an emergency worker without a weapon and without causing injury, for example, will carry a demand of 3 months in prison.
Justice minister David van Weel told MPs that a similar attack on a member of the public would usually lead to a demand for 80 hours community service, broadcaster NOS reported.
Besides emergency workers, the rules cover security staff, sports referees, public transport workers, teachers, judges, lawyers, politicians and council staff. They also apply to attacks on journalists.
“The impact of this violence on society is huge, but unfortunately we are not seeing it decline,” Lisan Wösten, the OM’s national lead on the issue, said in a statement.
Pressure from MPs
 MPs called for tougher sentences early this year after police and firefighters were attacked at New Year, with officers in some places lured into ambushes. “I fully support that approach,” Van Weel wrote in his letter to parliament, according to NOS.
Police officers faced almost 13,000 violent incidents in 2025, and the force’s national lead on the issue, Corry van Breda, has called for heavier sentences.
Since 2006, prosecutors have been able to seek sentences 200% higher for attacks on people in public roles. However, research by the justice ministry’s research centre WODC found this was rarely applied in practice.
The new rules remain a starting point from which prosecutors and judges can still exercise discretion according to the circumstances of a case.
A separate proposal to ban community service for these attacks altogether was criticised last year by the Council of State and judges, who said it would limit their room to weigh individual circumstances.

Unknown
