Sanctions lifted from oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:03:34 UTC
23:03:34 KST

Sanctions lifted from oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
After four and a half years of almost all of Russia’s billionaires being under sanctions, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman have become the first major figures to successfully get themselves removed from the EU’s red list. Meanwhile, Brussels’ restrictions against the rest of the Russian oligarchs and officials it has targeted were extended for three years — the longest single extension so far.
- Hungary has sought the lifting of sanctions on Usmanov since 2022, following a personal request from Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. After this year’s change of government in Budapest, Slovakian PM Robert Fico became Usmanov’s main political ally. But his political weight alone was not enough to get the oligarch off the list. The key factor in finally freeing Usmanov from restrictions was an unexpected intervention from France.
- Usmanov, who was explicitly named a “pro-Kremlin oligarch” in Feb. 2022, is one of Russia’s wealthiest businessmen after amassing a fortune in the 1990s in mining and metals. He owns 49% of USM, a Russian investment group that controls Metalloinvest, the country’s largest iron ore producer, as well as telecoms giant Megafon.
- Usmanov was able to wield influence in Paris thanks to his connections across other ex-Soviet countries — specifically a longstanding friendship with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. In exchange for French support to remove sanctions on Usmanov, Aliyev promised to release two French businessmen jailed in Baku — Martin Ryan, sentenced to 10 years on espionage charges in March 2026, and Anass Derraz, jailed for 12 years in a bribery case. A former aide to Emmanuel Macron was implicated in the Derraz case. In the end, only Ryan was released.
- When it emerged that Usmanov might escape sanctions, Luxembourg followed the French lead and announced that it would demand an end to sanctions on Mikhail Fridman, who had similarly been pressing for years to be taken off the list and filed a €16-billion lawsuit against the government.
- Fridman is a Russian business veteran who also made his riches in the chaotic 1990s. His Alfa Group included leading Russian bank Alfa Bank, the country’s top retailer X5 and the prominent Vimpelcom mobile phone operator. In 2010, Alfa Group made more than $8 billion from the sale of 25% of oil company TNK-ВР to state-owned Rosneft. Fridman and his partners used that money to buy up international assets, consolidating them under the LetterOne holding. The billionaire himself moved to London but fell under British and European sanctions in 2022.
- For now, the removal of sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman is the exception, not the rule. The European Council extended sanctions against 3,000 other Russian individuals and businesses for a previously unimaginable three years (before, there was debate inside the EU about whether to extend sanctions for six or 12 months).
- Now both Russian oligarchs can travel freely in Europe, manage their unblocked assets, including bank accounts, villas, yachts and aircraft, and do business inside the EU. Fridman, for example, can reclaim his stake in Luxembourg-registered LetterOne, which controls the portfolio of international assets acquired with his partners over the decades. Both men remain under American and British sanctions.
Why the world should care
Blacklisting oligarchs has arguably been the most pointless of the West's sanctions initiatives in practical terms. If anything, it has helped Vladimir Putin's regime by rallying the oligarchs around the Kremlin and trapping their capital inside Russia. It might have made sense to offer the oligarchs a way out of sanctions in exchange for doing something useful, such as condemning the aggression or helping Ukraine. But Usmanov and Fridman have now been delisted for nothing, and for the rest, that window has closed, at least until 2029.
France’s willingness to undermine the EU’s agreed sanctions policy in favor of its own specific interests risks further dividing European sanctions policy — something the Kremlin has long hoped for, bet on and tried to engineer. Other EU states will now be far less willing to vote for sanctions that run counter to their own national interests. For instance, Greece and Malta do not like sanctions targeting the maritime transport of Russian oil, and central European countries have interests in Russian gas.

In Georgia, a drunk Russian urinated from a balcony onto café patrons and shouted "Glory to Russia"; he will be deported
Kyiv • UNN
A Tbilisi court sentenced a Russian citizen to 15 days of arrest for hooliganism. After that, he will be deported and banned from entering Georgia for three years.
A scandal involving a Russian citizen has erupted in Georgia. On the grounds of the Monolith Green City residential complex in Tbilisi’s Ortachala district, an intoxicated Russian-speaking man urinated directly from a balcony onto visitors to a café located below. Eyewitness Teona Golodze reported the incident on social media and posted a video recording of it on TikTok. Later, the Tbilisi City Court sentenced the Russian to 15 days of administrative detention for disorderly conduct, UNN reports, citing "News of Georgia" and TV Pirveli.
What happened?
According to Golodze, the incident occurred on the grounds of the Monolith Green City residential complex in Tbilisi’s Ortachala district. When the people sitting below began recording what was happening on their phones and telling him off, the troublemaker responded by shouting "Glory to Russia."
The visitors immediately called the police. The footage shows the intoxicated man, already in the courtyard in the presence of police, trying to justify his behavior with an unusual argument—he claimed he had acted that way because "the bathroom was occupied." At the same time, he complained that the café had supposedly placed chairs and tables downstairs "illegally."
Meanwhile, Golodze noted, the detainee called acquaintances, asking for help and assuring them that his problems with the police had arisen solely because of the slogan "Glory to Russia."
Although the act of urinating itself was not captured on video, Golodze’s account is generally corroborated by the participants’ conversations.
According to the video’s author, the offender was detained administratively. She said that after the court proceedings, he would be deported from the country.
What do Georgian law enforcement authorities say?
Georgia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs confirmed to TV Pirveli that a Russian citizen had been detained administratively.
Proceedings are being conducted under Articles 166 (petty hooliganism) and 171 of Georgia’s Code of Administrative Offenses. The latter article covers acts that offend human dignity and public morality in public places, as well as blatant disrespect for accepted standards of conduct that creates a humiliating or offensive environment (including relieving physiological needs in public places).
What did the Georgian court decide?
The Tbilisi City Court sentenced Russian citizen Alexander Popov to 15 days of administrative detention for urinating from a balcony, while intoxicated, onto café visitors.
The man was found guilty of petty hooliganism and acts that offend human dignity and public morality (Articles 166 and 171 of Georgia’s Code of Administrative Offenses). According to reports, Popov fully admitted his guilt at the hearing.
"I regret what I did, and, of course, it will never happen again," the Russian said.
According to the ruling, immediately after the end of the troublemaker’s detention, he will be deported from the country and barred from entering Georgia for three years.
The incident occurred on the grounds of the Monolith Green City residential complex in Tbilisi’s Ortachala district. Eyewitness Teona Golodze posted a video of the incident on TikTok. The footage captures the troublemaker shouting "Glory to Russia" at people in response to their remarks.
The detainee tried to justify his actions to police officers by saying that "the bathroom was occupied" in the apartment, while the café itself had supposedly installed tables in the courtyard "illegally."
Context
In July, a serious conflict occurred at the Agarani Estate hotel in Kakheti between participants in a Georgian wedding and Russian-speaking female tourists, as a result of which the groom’s brother struck one of them in the eye.
Initially, the sides presented radically different versions: the tourists claimed they had been attacked because they were speaking Russian, while Georgia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs said that the women themselves had provoked the guests—they had shouted insults from the balcony and doused the musical equipment with water. Information circulated on social media that the wedding had been doused from the balcony not with water but with urine; however, official sources did not confirm this.
Both incidents have added fuel to the already heated debate over attitudes toward Russians in Georgia—a country whose two regions are under Russian occupation. While the government’s opponents are demanding tougher action to stop provocations, representatives of the ruling "Georgian Dream" party warn of the danger of "manifestations of Russophobia."

Female Gazan PLC candidate to 'Post': I want a say in the decisions shaping my life - interview

23:02:02 KST

At just 29, Hiyam Taha has already spent years challenging expectations of what a Palestinian woman can do. From earning the trust of a community initially uncomfortable with a woman dispensing medicine to breaking into the male-dominated world of sports, the pharmacist has now set her sights on politics.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday from Hamas-controlled territory in the Gaza Strip, Taha explained why she broke through strict gender expectations a third time to enter politics, why she aligned herself with Masar Jadid (New Path) and what she thinks needs to change for the Palestinian people to have a more prosperous future.
Taha is a licensed pharmacist, a member of the Palestinian Pharmacists Association, and works in the medical humanitarian field. She has witnessed firsthand the “collapsing” healthcare system and its impact on Palestinian civilians.
“As a healthcare professional, you witness firsthand how fragile the healthcare system has become. Patients are struggling to find basic medications, clinics are being undersourced, and the healthcare system is completely collapsing…” she said.
“I struggled to find a place in society as a healthcare professional in Gaza. It’s very hard to prove yourself. I wanted more. I wanted my voice to participate in decision-making because, as a young woman, I have been living through the consequences of political decisions. How about I get a say in that? I want to be a part of this, and if I am going to open the door a little wider for women to see the light in Gaza, then I’m willing to take on the difficulties.”
Taha says Gaza communities fractured, and scattered families need rebuilding
After being displaced five times during the Israel-Hamas War, Taha has watched communities fracture, and families scatter. Some of the patients she spent years building relationships with, including those who initially resisted being treated by a woman, have moved on.
She had earned their trust, sometimes calling them in her own time to discuss their medication schedules, only to have to start over again and again from tents and humanitarian facilities struggling to keep up with demand.
Taha didn’t assign blame for the reality she has lived through, but rather said she felt a responsibility to speak for those dealing with the consequences of decisions made by political leadership detached from reality in the group.
“I want to be the voice of those people, especially patients and young people like myself who have no one speaking on their behalf. I wanted to be their voice, and that was the reason I entered politics and ran for the Legislative Council,” she said.
After privately studying politics while running her own business, organizing boxing classes for women and continuing her work in the medical field, Taha felt compelled to join New Path, which she said was one of the few political spaces where she could find a place as a young person and as a woman in a field dominated by men who have held power for decades.
New Path President Samer Sinijlawi has frequently spoken to and written in the Post about the need to include fresh voices in politics, especially among young people who have inherited the disasters of its leadership.
A fierce critic of Abbas, Sinijlawi told the Post on Monday that he wants to “open political and economic life to a new generation. Women and young people must become decision-makers, not simply symbolic participants. Public appointments should be based on competence rather than loyalty or connections, while education, healthcare, and economic policy must be redesigned to improve people’s daily lives and create real opportunities.”
For Taha, who said she had to fight most of her life for a seat at the table, being handed such an opportunity has been an empowering experience and an opportunity that every Palestinian should be presented with, regardless of their gender.
Taha's vision of democracy and peace
Asked about her and New Path’s vision for what comes next, she said it was important to spread a “democratic cultural atmosphere” and to end the conflict with Israel with a two-state solution based on the 1967 lines.
“Those are things no other parties are talking about in a clear way. We want this to happen. We want negotiations to happen. We want us to be responsible for the negotiation for the first time, not as observers, and not to let mediators interfere with our decision-making,” she said. “We want this for us as Palestinians to happen, and that's the difference between New Path and other parties.”
New Path is focused on communicating to Palestinians “that if you want to have the life and the future you deserve as a young Palestinian, you have to think smartly, and you have to think to expand your horizon, and to know that negotiations will lead you to the future you want,” she continued.
The November elections for the Palestinians Legislative Council present a long-delayed chance for Palestinian statehood, she continued. The upcoming elections will allow Palestinians access to a legitimate authority and state institutions with oversight that can be held accountable by the people.
She insisted that even if the vote couldn’t solve every issue impacting Palestinian society, the economy, education, healthcare and conflict, it will be the “first step that we Palestinians should take, at least to have a legitimate authority that Palestinians could hold accountable afterward.”
She also spoke about needing to shift the image of Palestinians in the global arena from victims and charity cases to capable individuals both willing and able to manage their own affairs.
“We’re just normal citizens who want to live peacefully without interference. If we want to live peacefully, we want to have a future. I want my kids to be in a safe zone. I want to have a say in decisions because if your political decisions are the reason I’m living through these circumstances and consequences, why don’t you let me have a say in that, or let me participate in changing that? If your decisions affect my life directly, then I want to be a part of changing this,” she continued.
Living in a tent as a woman, without the protection of walls or doors that lock, in a territory where speaking to an Israeli is illegal, Taha’s safety is tied to the elections going ahead in November, even if taking part is a gamble. She has witnessed people living without private bathrooms or basic sanitation, and she is risking everything to help Palestinians return to a normal life after years of living in squalor.
In her concluding remarks to the Post, Taha emphasized how critical it is for Gazans to return to their homes, where they can finally sleep with both eyes closed.

EPPO Indicts Two Polish Nationals in €100 Million Electronics VAT Fraud Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:02:00 UTC
23:02:00 KST

The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Katowice has indicted two Polish nationals alleging that they were part of a cross-border VAT fraud and money laundering scheme involving more than 100 million euros ($113.58 million) in fraudulent invoices. The indictment is the first to stem from "Operation Escape Room," a broader investigation targeting an electronic device trading ring operating across Austria, Belgium, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Poland.
According to prosecutors, the network used hundreds of shell companies and fake invoices to conceal transactions, evade VAT, and claim illegal tax reimbursements. In addition to the fraudulent invoices in Poland, the scheme caused an estimated 47 million euros ($53.39 million) in unpaid VAT damage in Belgium and 22 million euros ($24.99 million) in the Netherlands. If convicted, the defendants face between seven and a half and 25 years in prison.

U.S. troops leave Iraq, but future of Iran-backed militias remains uncertain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:01:54 UTC
23:01:54 KST

U.S. troops leave Iraq, but future of Iran-backed militias remains uncertain
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The last U.S. military personnel stationed in Iraq departed Wednesday, ending a 12-year mission against the extremist group Islamic State.
- The Iraqi government hailed the withdrawal as a milestone for the nation’s sovereignty.
- Militias aligned with Iran remain a force in Iraq, raising concerns about their future role in the country.
BEIRUT — America opened its “forever war” in Iraq more than 23 years ago with “Shock and Awe.” It ended it on Wednesday with little of either, even as the legacy of that conflict — which saw Iraq endure sectarian bloodbaths, civil war and an insurgency that made Baghdad the car bomb capital of the world — continues to cast its shadow on the country today.
President Trump, summing up the U.S. role in Iraq as “a very expensive excursion into Hell,” said, “This day is a victory for the United States, a victory for Iraq.... We’re getting the hell out of there.”
It was the second time U.S. forces have pulled out of Iraq. The first withdrawal took place in 2011, capping the occupation that began in 2003 and toppled Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein, and which resulted in Iraqi deaths that number 110,000 to four times greater and the loss of about 4,500 U.S. service members.
But three years later, Islamic State jihadis scythed through wide swaths of Iraq, scooping up U.S.-supplied materiel — as Iraqi troops literally ran away — and seizing control of nearly a third of the country. The U.S., this time at the Iraqi government’s request, led a coalition in a campaign — named Inherent Resolve — that by 2017 had destroyed Islamic State’s caliphate and driven most of its fighters into Syria. Since then, Iraqi forces have fought Islamic State remnants engaged in a low-level insurgency around the country’s remote areas.
President Trump railed against “forever wars,” but with hostilities increasing and negotiations at a standstill, there appears no easy exit from the war he launched on Iran.
Most U.S. and coalition forces, which numbered around 2,500, began leaving Iraq in October 2025, so that by Wednesday all that was left to withdraw were a few hundred service members stationed in Irbil air base in northern Iraq, once the operational hub of Inherent Resolve.
“Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, in a statement.
“Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces,” he said, referring to Islamic State by an acronym for its former name, Islamic State of Iraq and Syria.
Central Command said the anti-ISIS mission would continue, with the coalition now headquartered in Jordan.
“As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and Coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise,” Cooper said.
Iran fired missiles into Jordan last week, killing three American service members. Jordan’s growing role in the war is prompting uncomfortable conversations for the desert nation’s leaders.
The agreement to end the U.S. presence in Iraq was forged by President Biden in 2024 but was continued by Trump, who had made aversion to foreign entanglements — he called the Iraq war “the worst single mistake ever made in the history of our country” — a centerpiece of his presidential campaigns.
On Wednesday, Trump launched into a broadside on Biden. He compared the United States’ uneventful withdrawal from Iraq to the chaos that marked its pullout from Afghanistan in 2021, which saw the U.S. leave behind tens of thousands of Afghans who had worked with American forces, and abandon much of its materiel.
Trump said he directed the military to safeguard U.S. supplies and equipment. “I said I want every screw taken,” the president said. “I said if there’s a screw lying on the ground, take it, if there’s a canvas tent, take it.”
Seemingly responding to polls showing most Americans oppose the war with Iran, Trump said that the fighting there had gone on for six months with only 18 service members killed.
“By the way 18 is too many, but [the Iranians] lost 4,500, we lost 18, and we have — very soon you’ll see, things happening very soon — but we have a nation that’s been virtually destroyed,” he said.
In a notice published Wednesday in the Federal Register, the State Department said it was amending its International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR, so that Syria no longer was among the nations subject to approvals needed for the sale of U.S. weapons and munitions.
Iraq’s government also marked the moment, announcing a four-day holiday it called “Sovereignty Days” and holding a military parade in Baghdad’s streets.
Speaking at a closed-door ceremony in Baghdad, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi hailed the moment as “a new phase” defined by “Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, unity of decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
All of those elements are likely to be tested as never before in the coming weeks, as Iraq walks a diplomatic tightrope between Washington and Tehran, its two top allies, now locked in a war that shows no sign of abating.
Iran over the years of U.S. occupation built considerable influence in Iraq, nurturing militias there since 2003.
Those factions, which also fought against Islamic State, have embedded themselves into the fabric of the Iraqi state and are now an official part of Iraq’s armed forces. They also wield financial power and are linked to political parties that have long clamored for U.S. forces to leave.
Since the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, the militias have escalated their years-long harassment campaign of U.S. forces in Iraq, lobbing rockets and drones on American bases and facilities. Saudi Arabia also accused them of an attack that shut down its east-west pipeline, a charge the militias deny.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has pushed Iraq to curb Iranian influence in Iraq and has pressured Al-Zaidi to force the militias to disband or disarm.
On Wednesday, militias portrayed the U.S. withdrawal as a victory of their own making, organizing a parade through Baghdad, with crowds raising the factions’ flags and pictures of slain Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei to martial music.
At the parade, Jaafar Husseini, a military spokesman for Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful militia that works closely with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said it was the Iraqi resistance that “took up arms against the occupiers, risked their lives and bore the burden of defeating the American occupation for the sake of faith and homeland.”
He added that the factions were not bound by any timetable or agreement mentioned by the government or other political parties.
Trump is set to extend the Qatar camp housing more than 1,000 Afghans who helped the U.S. war effort
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to sign off on a diplomatic note to Qatar extending for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Wednesday at the end of the U.S. budget year, according to two U.S. officials familiar with the matter.
Kurdish leaders in Iraq’s Kurdistan region also have reason to fear the militias. In recent months, Iran-allied factions have attacked the bases of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in northern Iraq. A previous confrontation in 2017 between those militias and Iraqi Kurdish forces, known as the peshmerga, ended with the Kurds having to back down.
Another concern for the Kurdish regional government is how the U.S. withdrawal strips the Kurds of air defenses, which had helped intercept more than 1,000 drone and ballistic missile attacks on the region during the U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” said a statement from the region’s Peshmerga Ministry.
Other Iraqis wonder whether the U.S. withdrawal will trigger a repeat of 2014, when Iraqi forces melted away in disarray.
Al-Zaidi had set Wednesday as a deadline for militias to surrender their weapons, but has since postponed it to June 2027. It is unclear whether the government can adhere to that deadline, especially with the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran still ongoing.
“So long as Iran is at war, it will continue operationally working with these groups in Iraq, and there’s nothing that the Iraqi government can do about it at the moment, and they’re not going to give up their weapons,” said Renad Mansour, an Iraq analyst at the London-based Chatham House think tank.
Mansour noted that in 2008 the Iraqi government tried and failed to rein in militias, even when the U.S. presence and support was near its peak.
“How is this fragmented government with no U.S. support going to be able to fight these groups?” he asked.
A senior U.S. official said Wednesday that Washington has been “clear with Iraq that it is critical that they retain their sovereignty and prevent attacks from within its borders by Iranian-backed militias.” The official added that the United States “fully supports disarmament and transfer of arms to the central government.”
Times staff writer Ana Ceballos in Washington contributed to this report.

Arab media reactions to flydubai hijacking attempt mixed between cautious, sensational
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:01:33 UTC
23:01:33 KST

The incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv received widespread coverage in Arab media shortly after it occurred, but the tone and details of the reports varied significantly between outlets in the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf region and those operating elsewhere in the Arab world.
While media outlets associated with Dubai and Abu Dhabi initially used cautious wording and repeated the airline’s official statement, other Arab outlets quickly reported a serious altercation between the pilots and allegations that one of them attempted to take control of the aircraft and possibly cause it to crash.
Emirati media outlets largely stuck to the airline’s official account. Gulf News reported that the aircraft, which was traveling to Tel Aviv, "experienced an incident during the flight," changed its route, and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. The newspaper emphasized that all passengers were safe and that the airline was cooperating with authorities.
Only later did the report mention that, according to Flightradar24 data, the aircraft initially transmitted emergency code 7700 and later briefly transmitted code 7500, which is used in cases of unlawful interference or suspected hijacking. The report also stressed that the reason for the transmission had not been verified.
Khaleej Times, Al Bayan, Al Khaleej, and Al Emarat Al Youm took a similar approach. The outlets closely followed flydubai’s statement, reporting that the aircraft "was exposed to an incident" or an "unexpected incident" during the flight, landed safely in Saudi Arabia, and that all passengers were in good condition.
Initial coverage did not push attempted hijacking, suicide reports
None of these initial reports confirmed claims of a suicide attempt, an effort to crash the aircraft, or a terror incident.
Saudi Arabia’s Al Arabiya initially took a similarly cautious approach, highlighting comments from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s spokesperson that the incident was not a hijacking. The network focused on addressing concerns raised after the aircraft transmitted code 7500.
Outside official and institutional Gulf media, however, the reporting quickly became more dramatic.
The newspaper Al-Quds Al-Arabi published a headline about a "fight between pilots that put Israel on alert," reporting that the hijacking signal was apparently activated during a confrontation between the two pilots. The newspaper added that Israel scrambled fighter jets and that Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held urgent security consultations.
Al-Araby Al-Jadeed went further in its updated report, saying that alongside the account of a cockpit altercation, there were also reports of an "alleged suicide attempt" by one of the pilots. The outlet stressed that the investigation was still ongoing and that the claims had not been officially confirmed by the airline or Saudi authorities.
Some Arab media outlets cite Israeli sources, push dramatic reporting
The most dramatic reports came from Arab media outlets citing Israeli sources.
An Al Jazeera report said that Israeli security officials had grown increasingly suspicious that one of the pilots attempted to take control of the aircraft and crash it, while the other pilot attempted to stop him. According to the same report, Israel at one point did not rule out the possibility that the incident was a terror event and waited for the results of the investigation in Saudi Arabia.
RT Arabic, which is Russian state-controlled, reported the more dramatic version of events. The Russian outlet reported that, according to Israeli reports, one of the pilots attempted to commit suicide and that the confrontation in the cockpit led to the activation of emergency codes and a change in the aircraft’s route. However, it also clarified that the claim was based on Israeli media reports and sources, rather than an official statement from flydubai or Saudi authorities.
In the first hours of Arab media coverage, a clear divide emerged. Media outlets in the UAE sought to limit speculation, emphasize the safe landing, and closely follow the airline’s official wording.
As reports spread beyond Dubai, additional and increasingly serious claims emerged, beginning with reports of a fight between the pilots, followed by allegations of an attempted takeover, and later claims that one pilot intentionally attempted to crash the aircraft.
Flydubai and Saudi authorities have not officially confirmed the latest versions of events, which should be treated as claims under investigation.

Turkish firm Karmod showcases mobile armored cabins at Teknofest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:01:29 UTC
23:01:29 KST

Sibel Morrow
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Turkish modular buildings manufacturer Karmod is displaying its newly developed mobile armored cabins and bullet-resistant ballistic door and window systems at Teknofest in southeastern Türkiye.
The aviation, space and technology festival opened at Sanliurfa GAP Airport and will run through Oct. 4. Anadolu Agency is the event’s global communications partner.
Karmod’s exhibit includes mobile armored cabins designed for locations requiring enhanced security, along with ballistic doors and windows developed by the company.
Karmod General Manager Zekai Kucuk said the company has diversified its range of security cabins to include armored structures.
“We have a flexible production infrastructure that allows us to develop solutions tailored to specific security requirements,” he said.
Kucuk noted that the company recently added a 28-square-meter, single-body bullet-resistant armored cabin to its product range and was completing tests on a 55-square-meter modular structure designed primarily for export.
The larger model would be the first domestically produced armored structure of its size in Türkiye with a demountable design, he added.
The company’s mobile armored cabin was developed for outdoor security posts and is mounted on a trailer system, allowing it to be moved between locations.
Kucuk said the cabin could be used at military posts and across large military compounds where mobile security infrastructure is required.
Karmod also manufactures ballistic doors, windows and armored barriers. Its cabins can be equipped with observation windows, firing ports, night lighting systems and alarm sirens, the company said.
“We manufacture armored cabins for both operational and commercial locations requiring high levels of security,” Kucuk said.
He said the structures could be used at government buildings, embassies and consulates, military facilities, police and military posts, banks and corporate headquarters.

‘We’re in charge of the flight now’: Passenger describes fight for flydubai cabin - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:01:24 UTC
23:01:24 KST

While other Israeli passengers fought the attacker near the cockpit, he was trying to get two additional pilots to move. The aircraft was diving, he said. The men who could fly it had frozen.
“I had to shake them to get them to move to the front and take control of the plane, because it was diving.”
The Israeli passenger described those moments to me during several hours of WhatsApp correspondence on Wednesday. He was still in Saudi Arabia, where his flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had made an emergency landing. By his account, he had been part of the group that intervened at the front of the aircraft.
When we first made contact, he wanted to correct the reporting.
“I think the newspapers are reporting things that aren’t true,” he wrote. He asked me to send him what we knew so he could tell me what was wrong.
Attacker stabs pilot, passengers restrain hijacker with charger cables
I offered to call. He said he felt uncomfortable speaking with soldiers around him. We continued by message, on and off through the afternoon. I told him I would protect his identity.
He began with a pilot attacking another pilot. There was a small knife, he said, and repeated stabbing. The attacker was trying to force the wounded man out of the cockpit. The wounded pilot was resisting.
I asked how the cockpit door had opened. He said the attacker was trying to push the other pilot out, apparently to take control alone. Israeli passengers sitting near the front rushed toward the struggle.
Flydubai confirmed that flight FZ1073 landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and that all passengers were safe and accounted for. The detailed sequence the passenger described, including the identities and roles of the crew members, has not been independently verified.
He was precise about his own involvement. Others had physically fought the attacker. He had concentrated on getting the additional pilots to the cockpit and finding something to restrain the man the passengers were trying to subdue.
According to his account, they pulled the attacker out and got the other pilots inside. One took control of the aircraft; the other took longer to recover from the shock.
I wanted to understand who these additional pilots were. Had they happened to be traveling on the flight? He said both worked for flydubai and had been assigned to be there. His understanding was that the airline carried additional pilots on flights to Israel. That arrangement still requires confirmation.
He called his own role “combat support,” adding a smiley face to the message.
They needed restraints.
“What did you use?” I asked.
“Charging cables.”
“In the desert, every thorn is a flower,” he added.
Israeli dentist treats wounded pilot
He also described an Israeli dentist treating the wounded pilot. He said the pilot was gravely injured and credited the dentist with saving his life. The pilot’s medical condition could not be independently established.
Throughout our exchange, the passenger called the attacker a terrorist. He was angry that anyone doubted what, to him, had been obvious. When I asked what supported that conclusion, he described the repeated stabbing and the effort to force the other pilot out of the cockpit.
On a particular claim circulating about the incident, he gave a firm answer. I asked whether he had heard the attacker shout “Allahu akbar,” Arabic for “God is greatest.”
“I was standing right next to the cockpit and didn’t hear it, and others who were with me didn’t hear it either,” he wrote.
“None of us heard it.”
His conviction about the attack was clear. Its motive remained unconfirmed in the material available for this account.
As we continued corresponding, he described what had happened after the landing. Saudi doctors were attending to children and passengers who were panicking. Food had been provided.
“How are the Saudis?” I asked.
“Very nice,” he replied. “Very understanding.”
A senior Saudi figure had approached the Israeli dentist, he said, congratulated him for saving the pilot, and thanked him. Then the Saudi took the dentist’s hand and walked with him.
The passenger tried to explain the gesture to me. Holding hands, he wrote, was a local expression of warmth.
A few minutes later, I asked how he was doing.
He said he had yet to absorb what had happened. During the emergency, he had felt detached and kept carrying out tasks. He thought it would hit him when he landed in Israel.
Then he began telling me about the children. The flight was full of families returning from vacations, he said.
“There were terrible screams from children who didn’t want to die.”
One of the men fighting the attacker had a daughter on the flight.
“One girl whose father was fighting the terrorist screamed that she didn’t want him to die,” he wrote.
“That was the only moment when I stopped and thought about my own children.”

-  Denmark. 
In the ranking of European countries' passports, Ukraine is 37th.
This new ranking, Euronews notes, compares passport strength based on how many destinations travelers can visit without a visa, with an electronic travel authorization (ETA), or by obtaining a visa on arrival. The ranking also measured the number of destinations for which passport holders must obtain a visa before entry.
Spain, recognized as the strongest European passport for visa-free travel and ranking third overall, received a mobility score of 174. Spanish travelers have visa-free access to 121 countries, while another 42 countries can be visited with a visa on arrival. However, an ETA is required for 11 countries, and holders also need a visa to enter 24 countries.
Meanwhile, Luxembourg received a mobility score of 173. Ranking fifth in the world, holders of these passports can travel to 122 countries without a visa, while another 41 countries can be reached with a visa on arrival. An ETA is required to visit 10 countries, and a visa is required for 25.
Belgium and France rank sixth, each with a mobility score of 173. Holders of their passports can visit 121 countries visa-free and 41 countries with a visa on arrival. Although an ETA is required for 11 countries, visas are required for 25.
Also receiving a mobility score of 173, six European countries share seventh place: Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden. Holders of these six countries' passports can travel to 120 destinations without a visa, 42 with a visa on arrival, and need an ETA for 11 countries, while visas are required for 25 countries.
Travelers from Ukraine, whose mobility is rated at 142 points, can visit 87 countries without a visa, 8 countries with an electronic travel authorization (ETA), and 47 countries by obtaining a visa on arrival.
A total of 186 countries are assessed in the ranking. Afghanistan is in last place.

Iran's nuclear program remains shrouded in mystery as the regime debates ditching non-proliferation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

What is Iran's nuclear endgame?
September 30, 2026
Iran's nuclear program has entered one of the most critical periods in its history.
Questions over Tehran's stockpile of uranium enriched to 60% and the International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) declining oversight of Iranian nuclear facilities have only deepened the uncertainty. Yet signs of diplomacy remain.
In an interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told US broadcaster Fox News that Tehran is prepared to dilute its enriched uranium stockpile and submit its nuclear program for international inspection, provided a comprehensive agreement is reached within the framework of international law and the landmark Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
Conflicting statements from Iran
However, in contrast to Pezeshkian's diplomatic rhetoric, statements from military and political figures in Tehran point in a different direction.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that US and Israeli actions had created grounds for Iran to withdraw from the NPT, while stressing that no decision had yet been made, according to Press TV, the Iranian government's main English-language satellite TV channel.
On September 19, British newspaper The Daily Telegraph, citing satellite imagery, reported that Iran was actively constructing new facilities and rebuilding damaged ones.
These sites include "Taleghan 2" at the Parchin complex southeast of Tehran and a complex burrowed under what is known as Pickaxe Mountain near Iran's nuclear facility in Natanz.
Both sites were previously targeted in airstrikes during the US-Israel war with Iran, which the Pentagon dubbed Operation Epic Fury and Israel called Operation Roaring Lion.
Their reported reconstruction has fueled speculation that equipment and enriched uranium may have been moved deeper underground.
Washington has maintained a firm stance. Speaking at the UN General Assembly on September 22, US President Donald Trump said: "I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
Can diplomacy still work?
Access to military sites and the scope of IAEA inspections have long been among the most contentious issues related to Iran's nuclear program.
The 2015 nuclear agreement known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) imposed significant restrictions on Iran, in exchange for sanctions relief, to prevent it from developing nuclear weapons.
However, provisions for the inspection of military sites drew persistent criticism from opponents in Washington, criticism that contributed to the US withdrawal from the JCPOA under Donald Trump in 2018.
John Bolton, former US national security adviser and former US ambassador to the UN, told DW that diplomatic efforts and past agreements on Iran's nuclear program are merely a "cover for an unalterable strategy pursued by Tehran."
Arguing that Iran's weapons program was "never" truly halted, Bolton pointed to what he described as the limitations of international institutions, adding that "the IAEA never had access to Iran's military bases, where critical components related to weaponization take place."
When asked about the legal implications of a potential Iranian withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty, Bolton argued that Iran has been in violation of the NPT for more than three decades, meaning a formal withdrawal would make little practical difference.
"The only long-term path to achieving peace and security in the Middle East," Bolton emphasized, "is the overthrow of the regime in Tehran."
War steels Tehran's nuclear resolve
Amid the US-Israel war with Iran and the subsequent changes in Tehran's command structure after the death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, fresh developments have emerged.
The IAEA Board of Governors referred Iran to the UN Security Council on September 9 over alleged breaches of its non-proliferation obligations.
Meanwhile, the 60-day period for technical talks with the United States under the so-called Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, which extended a ceasefire between the two sides, expired in mid-August.
Damon Golriz, a political analyst and lecturer at The Hague University of Applied Sciences, argues that, contrary to Donald Trump's view of his legacy in dismantling Iran's nuclear capabilities, a nuclear-armed Iran would ultimately prove to be "the greatest foreign policy legacy of Donald Trump's presidency."
Reflecting on the military developments of 2026 and the killing of Khamenei in an Israeli air strike, Golriz said: "In February 2026 Tehran faced an existential war."
"The campaign entombed its nuclear facilities and decapitated its key weapons scientists, along with at least five tiers of Iran's top military and security establishment," Golriz added.
"Israel's killing of the supreme leader settled a fundamental security question: Has Ayatollah Khamenei as the main constraint on Iran's nuclear bomb become obsolete?"
Golriz suggests that it was specifically the audacity shown in the targeting of Iran's leadership that upended the country's national security thinking, thereby "strengthening calls to reassess its nuclear doctrine."
Testing Tehran's religious rhetoric on nukes
The official religious decree, or fatwa, banning the production and stockpiling of nuclear weapons has long been a cornerstone of Tehran's diplomatic rhetoric in claiming its nuclear program is peaceful.
First cited by Iranian officials in the mid-2000s, the fatwa was reaffirmed by Khamenei in 2019, when he said producing and stockpiling nuclear weapons was forbidden.
However, amid political developments in Tehran and Mojtaba Khamenei's silence on reaffirming this fatwa since becoming the new supreme leader, questions have been raised whether this religious red line remains intact or has given way to new security considerations.
Tim Bosch, CEO of the Birdwatcher Group and a former senior intelligence officer with the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD), pointed to the significance of this silence alongside rhetoric from military figures in Tehran.
Bosch told DW that there is no definitive proof of a formal change in Tehran's nuclear doctrine.
"However, those opposed to acquiring nuclear weapons in Tehran are now far weaker, and given Mojtaba Khamenei's silence in reiterating his father's fatwa, this observation carries significant weight," he said.
In December 2024, the IAEA assessed that Iran was the only country without a nuclear bomb to posses uranium enriched to 60%, while warning Tehran was "dramatically accelerating" enrichment. A purity of 90% is needed to produce nuclear weapons.
However, with the IAEA barred from inspections, it is anyone's guess as to how far along Iran currently is.
"If the world's nuclear watchdog cannot observe enriched uranium, no intelligence agency can honestly claim to know whether Iran has made the final decision to build a bomb," Bosch said.
"Those who claim with absolute certainty that 'they have made their decision' are either bluffing or mostly advancing their own political agendas: hardliners in Iran on one side, and hardliners in Israel and the United States on the other," he added.
Edited by: Keith Walker

‘Deceptive discounts’ on energy contracts banned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:00:57 UTC
23:00:57 KST

Starting from 1 October, energy suppliers will no longer be permitted to offer ‘deceptive discounts’ on energy contracts. Suppliers will also no longer be allowed to amend their contracts in the middle of the month and give these contracts an identical the same name. The changes have been confirmed by the federal energy regulator, CREG.
Deceptive discounts are substantial introductory discounts on electricity and natural gas contracts. They are factored into price comparison tools, which often means these contracts appear to be the most favourable option in a price comparison.
However, these discounts are often subject to strict conditions. For example, customers must remain on the same energy contract for one or two years before the amount is deducted
From 1 October, this will no longer be permitted. Discounts must apply from the very first kilowatt-hour and remain in force for the entire duration of the contract.
Suppliers of natural gas and electricity are also no longer permitted to change the pricing terms of a particular product for new contracts in the middle of the month whilst retaining the same product name. This is intended to prevent confusion amongst customers.

‘Of course I’m the underdog’: the British former spin doctor trying to turn California red
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

Steve Hilton stands almost no chance of becoming California’s next governor, but that isn’t stopping him from campaigning as though he was just one step away from pulling off the impossible.
The former Downing Street political adviser and Fox News host refuses to be daunted by the rancid political environment for Republican candidates this year, or by opinion polls that tell him he is lagging 20 percentage points or more behind his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra.
Instead, as he barnstorms the state in an effort to rally the Republican faithful and win over as many Democrats and independents as he can find, he is following a full-throated people-versus-the-powerful script and pumping out what he hopes will be crowd-pleasing policy proposals as fast as he can come up with them.
Abolish the department of motor vehicles, he suggested a couple of weeks ago. Cut the price of gas to $3 a gallon. Start a new business school in working-class East Los Angeles. Set up a competition among California’s 58 counties to build 10 brand-new cities from the ground up.
Many of these ideas dovetail with the argument Hilton has made from the day he started running, that California has been driven to the brink of ruin by 16 years of Democratic party control over every statewide office. “Enough is enough,” as his campaign slogan says.
But they also mark a return to his roots as a prolific and occasionally unpredictable political ideas man, known during his time working for the British Conservative party for spitting out proposals while wandering barefoot through the corridors of power.
‘Un-pigeonhole-able’?
Policy has been one of the few throughlines in Hilton’s unconventional political journey from one side of the Atlantic to the other. He’s been a restaurant owner and business consultant as well as a senior adviser in the coalition government led by David Cameron in the 2010s. He came to California largely because his wife, Rachel Whetstone, established herself as a big tech public relations guru in Silicon Valley.
For many years, Whetstone was considered the power in the couple, while he wrote a couple of policy books – about “positive populism” and putting a human face on government – and used his connections in the conservative movement to land his Fox News show. Seizing the chance to try to resuscitate a largely moribund California Republican party came only much later.
Hilton prides himself on being “un-pigeonhole-able” and thinks of his campaign style as some combination of three startlingly different recent presidential candidates – Bernie Sanders, for his unwavering commitment to lift up struggling people; the Kentucky senator Rand Paul, for his fondness for libertarian free-market solutions; and John Kasich, the former governor of Ohio, for his “happy warrior” campaigning style.
Many of his ideas come straight out of the Republican playbook, accounting for the mistrust he inspires in many Democratic voters. He wants to set up a California version of Doge, Elon Musk’s so-called department of government efficiency that took a hatchet to federal agencies in the opening months of Trump’s second presidency. He wants to kill several environmental regulations, including a plan to introduce more energy-efficient vehicle tires over the next decade. (Hilton calls the energy commissioner who came up with the idea a “tire-rant”).
He also wants to cancel big, expensive public works projects starting with the long-delayed high-speed train from San Francisco to Los Angeles, which Hilton, in common with other Republicans, calls “the bullshit train to nowhere”.
Many of his other proposals, though, are harder to define: a plan to eliminate state taxes on the first $150,000 of income, which echoes similar proposals from some of Becerra’s more progressive Democratic primary challengers; the business school plan, which would offer free tuition to lower-income students; or a plan to turn the highway patrol into a full-fledged statewide police investigation force “liberated” from the DMV that currently finances it.
Still, Hilton is a savvy and appealing communicator, with a keen understanding of what frustrates and infuriates ordinary Californians. He acknowledges that his more outlandish ideas are unlikely to win this or any other election. But he believes they tell voters he is a pragmatic, independent thinker who, in an age of extremes and polarized political discourse, can talk to anyone, negotiate with anyone, and can entertain any good idea as long as it makes people’s lives easier and lifts the burden of government inefficiency and bloat.
He knows that California voters of all political persuasions are frustrated by the daily struggle of keeping up with soaring food and gas prices and looking for solutions to an array of social ills from homelessness to dwindling access to healthcare. It’s a big part of the reason why he led the polls for much of the primary campaign and ended up a close second behind Becerra in a crowded field.
“I’m not ideological,” he likes to say. “I’m not tribal.”
The ‘T’ problem
A major problem for him, though, is that he belongs to a party in thrall to “the president whose name begins with T”, as Hilton calls him – a leader whose name is particularly toxic in California, where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a two-to-one margin, and, this year, is dragging down Republican candidates across the country.
That has greatly complicated his quest to convince Californians that, by shrinking the size of the state government and slashing what he sees as over-burdensome regulations on small businesses, he can make the state more affordable for ordinary people. However encouraging it was to win close to 25% of the primary vote in June, building up another 25% of the vote in the general election has proven daunting.
And Hilton knows it. “Of course I’m the underdog,” he said. “Of course it’s an uphill battle. People are out of the habit of voting Republican. Still, I see a narrow but real path to victory. I see winning.”
Often, Hilton finds himself walking a fine line between indulging California’s Trump diehards, a vital part of his base, and broadening his appeal. He has made clear he doesn’t want Donald Trump or any other national Republican figure to campaign for him. He has distanced himself from Trump’s complaints of a “rigged system” and sees no need to restrict mail-in voting. But he has talked in the past of being friends with half of Trump’s cabinet and earned Trump’s endorsement during the primary, making it difficult to put much distance between himself and the man in the Oval Office.
When facing crowds of the Republican faithful, as he did during the primaries and continues to do at town halls up and down the state, his non-tribal bona fides are quickly tested by supporters eager to talk about Democrats stealing elections, conspiring to take away gun rights, and unjustly prosecuting insurrectionists who attacked the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.
At a recent event in San Gabriel, in the eastern Los Angeles suburbs, Hilton did nothing to discourage such talk. Rather, he milked several applause lines by promising to be a champion for such supporters once he was in office. “I’ve never said anything I don’t believe,” he explained in an interview shortly before the event. “I just don’t say everything that I believe.”
Away from the Maga faithful, Hilton has made the case that California’s problems have far more to do with the Democrats than with the occupant of the Oval Office. “You don’t have to like Trump. You don’t have to become a Republican,” he wrote in an unusual full-page advertisement that ran in the Los Angeles Times and the San Francisco Chronicle in July. “You just have to ask yourself: does it make sense to vote the same way and expect a different result?”
On the campaign trail, Hilton likes to point out that California sees more people moving to other states each year than it receives in new residents. This trend goes back to Schwarzenegger’s governorship, and has not, in most years, led to an overall decline in the state population because international migrants have made up the shortfall. Still, Hilton has woven it into his stump speech. “In the time Gavin Newsom has been governor, millions have moved out of the greatest state in the greatest nation on earth. That’s a terrible indictment,” he says. “Are they fleeing Trump? I don’t think so. Most of them are fleeing to states run by Republicans.”
The voters Hilton hopes will be most open to such lines of argument are those he sees suffering most acutely from California’s affordability crisis – working-class, non-college educated, many of them Latino. From the early days of his primary campaign, he has sat down with small groups and listened to them talking about the tax and regulatory burdens on their businesses, or the high cost of running a car or truck, or the struggle to find high-quality public schools in non-affluent parts of the state.
Such small-scale campaigning goes against received wisdom in California, where consultants of both parties have traditionally relied on television and internet advertising in the belief that a state of 39 million people is too big to reach any other way. Still, Hilton is betting that by talking to voters who don’t normally get to interact with candidates, he can spread the word that he is personable, willing to listen, and eager to help improve people’s lives.
A race to the finish
Hilton knows his idiosyncratic mix of styles exposes him to mockery, if not actual satire – his shoot-from-the-hip policy ideas were memorably parodied on the British TV show The Thick of It. He recalled, for example, an episode of his Fox News show when he insisted on promoting the distinctly un-Republican virtues of home nursing visits to promote perinatal health. “It was a low-rated segment,” he said.
But Hilton also has faith in his ability to connect to voters – the British accent probably helps – and his talent for a pithy phrase. He can be devastating, for example, when talking about Becerra, who he calls an “empty suit” embodying the very worst of Democratic party complacency.
“The level of disrespect for the process is actually shocking,” Hilton said. “Clearly he assumes he’s just going to coast to victory on the back of the Democratic machine … We keep inviting him to engage with us in different ways, but he keeps citing schedule conflicts. What are these conflicts? He’s not scheduling anything.”
Becerra did eventually agree to one debate with Hilton, set for Wednesday. In response to Hilton’s criticisms, Becerra spokesperson Jonathan Underland said: “Steve is desperate to land his dream job as a talking head on the Fox propaganda network. That’s why he can’t stop saying Xavier Becerra’s name.”
It remains to be seen if the debate can shake some of the Becerra camp’s confidence, but for now Hilton is on track to do worse than Gavin Newsom’s barely remembered Republican challenger from 2022, Brian Dahle, who lost by 18 points. A recent poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showed even independents favoring Becerra by close to a 20-point margin.
Hilton, though, is refusing to let these numbers bother him as the race enters its final frenetic stretch and his campaign stops become shorter and more intense. On a recent Saturday, Hilton dropped into an Orthodox synagogue in Beverly Hills, where he sported a tallit and a kipa to address a congregation of Iranian Jews for a brisk 10 minutes. On his next stop, 35 miles to the east, he poured exactly one beer and served up one table’s worth of taco plates at a family-owned Mexican restaurant in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains.
He has learned to spit out his message in small bites, asking a group of tattooed truckers at the Mexican restaurant how they would like it if their annual vehicle registration fee was capped at $73 (part of his DMV abolition plan), then telling a gaggle of Republican women in stars-and-stripes shirts that they needed to copy Democratic get-out-the-vote techniques instead of complaining about the other side cheating.
“This election is not about who you hate in Washington,” Hilton pleaded in his Trump-distancing ad in July, “it’s about what you love here.” His supporters keep telling him he has to win because their livelihoods depend on it. But, so far, the wider California electorate believes the race is indeed about who they hate in Washington – and nothing Hilton does or says seems to be changing their minds.

Removing Confederate monuments did not measurably change racial bias, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:00:35 UTC
23:00:35 KST

A recent investigation into whether the presence or removal of Confederate monuments affects racial prejudice found no evidence that these statues cause changes in people’s biases. The findings suggest that while these monuments are deeply tied to historical inequalities, simply being exposed to them does not directly alter subconscious or conscious racial attitudes, and there is no evidence that removing them from public squares does either. The research was published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin.
Confederate monuments are statues and memorials erected to honor the pro-slavery Southern states that seceded during the American Civil War. In recent years, many communities have debated whether to remove these statues, viewing them as symbols of white supremacy that continue to harm marginalized groups. Psychologists often distinguish between two types of prejudice that such environments might influence. Explicit bias involves conscious beliefs and feelings about a racial group, while implicit bias involves subconscious, automatic associations that people might not even realize they hold.
Previous research suggested that implicit bias is driven by local environments and historical oppression. For instance, a 2019 study found that white residents in Southern counties with historically higher rates of slavery still display stronger implicit racial bias today. The idea that changes in community environments can shift people’s biases is supported by other research. For example, a separate 2019 study found that antigay bias declined roughly twice as fast after states legalized same-sex marriage, suggesting that changes in public institutions can shift community attitudes.
The new research, led by Maximilian A. Primbs of Radboud University, was designed to test whether this idea applies to Confederate symbols to see if their physical presence or removal actually changes residents’ racial biases. Primbs told PsyPost that his motivation stemmed from the cultural climate a few years ago. “I had previously done research on the 2020 Black Lives Matter movement and discussions about Confederate monuments and what to do with them were widespread in 2020/2021,” he explained.
“These discussions eventually reached Europe, which had its own subsequent reckoning with colonial monuments,” Primbs continued. “Monuments were being graffitied, removed, or in one case even thrown in a river. I want to contribute to these debates by investigating some of the effects of these monuments.”
His 2024 study, covered by PsyPost, indicated that the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests led to a rapid, immediate decrease in implicit racial bias among white Americans, though this reduction was temporary. These patterns are consistent with the Bias of Crowds model, proposed in 2017, which holds that physical and social cues in an area constantly activate stereotypes, shaping the prejudices of the people living there.
To investigate the impact of Confederate monuments, the researchers conducted four distinct studies. The first study analyzed a massive dataset from the Project Implicit database, comparing it with records of Confederate monuments from the Southern Poverty Law Center. The sample included up to 1.75 million white participants across the United States. The scientists looked at geographic areas such as counties and commuting zones, tracking whether areas with monuments had higher aggregate levels of bias, adjusting for variables like population density and the proportion of Black residents.
The authors tracked changes in bias around the time specific monuments were taken down, looking for immediate or delayed drops in prejudice. The results did not show any reliable shifts in implicit or explicit racial bias following a monument’s removal. While there were some minor correlations between the number of monuments and bias levels, the results were inconsistent and sometimes even pointed in the opposite direction of what the theory predicted. The data provided no evidence that taking a statue down caused a change in the local community’s racial attitudes.
Notably, these results conflict with a 2019 study by two of the current paper’s co-authors, Heidi A. Vuletich and B. Keith Payne, which found that college campuses displaying Confederate monuments had higher average implicit bias among students. The researchers suggest three possible explanations for the discrepancy: the earlier result might have been a false positive, the correlation might have reflected an unmeasured third factor, or college campuses might simply operate differently than wider communities.
“We very strongly expected to find effects of Confederate monuments,” Primbs noted. “Many prior studies have found that historical inequalities like slavery, sundown towns, or the Ku Klux Klan shaped social and cultural norms and structures within geographical regions in ways that caused biased attitudes to persist over generations.”
“Confederate monuments are a physical manifestation of these White Supremacist beliefs, and therefore should have shown a similar link,” he added. “To me, this suggests that perhaps social and cultural environments are more important in determining racial biases than physical environments.”
Because observational data can be influenced by many outside factors, the scientists designed a second study to test the effect in a controlled laboratory setting. They recruited 1,161 white participants and 416 Black participants for an online experiment. Half of the participants were randomly assigned to read an educational text explaining the racist history and symbolism of the Confederacy.
After reading the text, this group took an Implicit Association Test with images of Confederate monuments displayed in the background. This test measures the speed at which a person associates positive or negative words with Black or White faces, serving as a standard metric for subconscious prejudice. The control group simply took a standard version of the test.
The researchers found no statistically significant differences in implicit or explicit bias between the group exposed to the monuments and the control group, for both white and Black participants. Further statistical analyses, known as equivalence tests, confirmed that any potential effect of the monuments was smaller than a conventionally small effect size, indicating that exposure does not meaningfully alter bias.
A third study utilized a different measure of subconscious prejudice called the Affect Misattribution Procedure. In this task, participants briefly see a photo of a Black or White face, followed immediately by an abstract painting that they must rate as pleasant or unpleasant. The idea is that feelings about the face subtly influence judgments about the painting. In a sample of 537 participants, those who viewed a slideshow of Confederate monuments and described their associations with them showed no statistically significant differences in bias compared to a control group.
To see if these laboratory findings held up in the real world, the researchers conducted a final field experiment in Tilburg, a city in the Netherlands. Instead of Confederate monuments, they used a local colonial monument, a 1926 statue showing the Catholic missionary Peerke Donders standing over a kneeling Black man from colonial Suriname, which critics say reflects colonial racial hierarchies. The scientists approached 174 white Dutch pedestrians passing by either the colonial monument or a visually similar control monument and asked them to fill out a survey measuring their conscious racial biases and policy preferences.
Half of the participants were given an informational text explaining the colonial monument’s historical meaning before answering the questions. Similar to the previous experiments, neither the physical presence of the monument nor the provided historical context altered the participants’ explicit racial attitudes. Whether people were standing in front of the colonial statue or a statue of the Virgin Mary, their self-reported feelings about minority groups remained similar.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. The lack of an effect on psychological bias does not mean that monuments are harmless or lack historical importance. “I’d like to make clear that Confederate monuments not affecting racial bias does not mean that Confederate monuments do not have negative effects,” Primbs said, noting that prior research indicates these statues are often perceived as markers of inequality by Black Americans and have been linked to anti-Black hate crimes.
The authors suggest that the transmission of bias might rely more on interpersonal interactions, community norms, and social behaviors than on isolated physical structures. People might absorb prejudice by observing how others act and speak rather than by walking past a monument.
“Confederate monuments are a physical reminder of historical inequality, a built structure commemorating past evil committed,” Primbs said. “Yet, simply removing the monuments had no effects on racial bias. The key takeaway for a lay person might be that undoing past wrongs is not as simple as removing a monument.”
“Discrimination has become deeply entrenched in societal systems, and to tackle it successfully we need to make changes to the system,” he continued.
Future research might explore other environmental cues that are more socially active or frequently discussed to see what actually sustains regional biases. “This research is part of a research line that highlights the historical origins of present-day racial attitudes,” Primbs noted.
“We’re currently pursuing further research that examines how these historical inequalities shape present-day behaviors, for example by affecting how Black and White people interact and share space,” he concluded.
The study, “On Confederate Monuments, Their Removal and Racial Bias,” was authored by Maximilian A. Primbs, Nicolas Sommet, Gijsbert Bijlstra, B. Keith Payne, Ruddy Faure, Tessa A. M. Lansu, Rob W. Holland, Amanda B. Diekman, and Heidi A. Vuletich.

====================================================================================================

Do parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couch | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

Is this the sketch my father would have wanted? Not something I have previously given much thought to. He died 15 years before I even started this job. But my guess is that it is. He was the loveliest of men who only ever wanted for me what I wanted for me. He was stupidly proud of even my most forgettable successes. I still see him in my dreams, cheering me on. He’d almost certainly be embarrassed, but secretly pleased, to find himself in the first paragraph.
But that’s enough about my father issues. Time now to talk about Andy Burnham’s. In his emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech on Tuesday – I can’t tell you how refreshing it is to have a politician other than Nigel Farage say exactly what he thinks and believes – Andy told us he wanted to build the country his father would have wanted. It was almost a debt of honour. Burnham was very precise. This was not his vision. This wasn’t the country he wanted to build. It was the one his dad had wanted. Andy was merely a conduit, channelling Roy, who died earlier this month.
So come Wednesday morning, on the traditional post-speech media round, the BBC’s Nick Robinson had clearly designated himself a latter-day Sigmund Freud for Burnham’s Today programme interview. You get the picture: Andy on the couch, Nick sitting just behind his right shoulder, firmly out of view. Never let the therapist get in the way of the subconscious. Only Robinson can’t take the silences. Some analysts pride themselves on a 50-minute session where nothing is said. That’s when the real psychotherapeutic work gets done. Apparently. A nice earner if you can get it.
There was no time to bother with the niceties. Nick specialises more in speed therapy. Done and dusted inside 20 minutes. From nought to catharsis. There was no “How are you feeling? Is there anything you need to talk about today?” Instead, he cut straight to the chase. And why not? Everyone knows that all patients are merely mainlining their parents. Everything can be traced back to childhood.
Andy clearly doesn’t hold with the Philip Larkin “They fuck you up” doctrine. He only got good stuff from his dad. Or maybe the good stuff is all that he cares to remember. Siggy Robbo missed a trick there. Surely your father would be telling you not to be so nostalgic, he said, but Burnham was adamant. Roy would have stuck to his roots of quiet patriotism. Nick tried another tack. The funeral was taking place on Friday. Was he on an emotional rollercoaster? Andy conceded that he could be. But rollercoasters were his happy place.
This could be habit-forming. Maybe it’s an approach we should take with all our party leaders. Rather than seeing them as players on a global stage with the capacity to make our lives infinitely worse, we should be more understanding. Treat them as patients in need of treatment. After all, you’ve surely got to be a dangerously unbalanced narcissist to even imagine you can run a country. Desire for office should act as a disqualification on health grounds. Some politicians would probably get an automatic upgrade from narcissist to sociopath. Donald Trump and Boris Johnson come immediately to mind.
Think also of Keir Starmer, Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch. Keir clearly had a tricky relationship with his dad. One where there was a lot that went unsaid. So maybe we shouldn’t blame him for never being able to articulate what he felt. Then there’s Nige. Has he inherited a hatred for all immigrants, or is he reacting against his parents? Maybe they took in refugees and forced the seven-year-old Nige to play with them against his will. And where did he get his pathological need for money, no matter how questionable the source? Did his parents squander his inheritance on gifts to charity? As for Kemi, where to start? I’ve never seen a politician so full of loathing. Could that be down to a Larkin-like childhood?
With the therapy over, Siggy briefly turned to the substance of the speech. All the big-ticket policies were for after the next election. What was going to happen in the next three years? Andy shrugged. He was a straight-talking guy. There wasn’t much he could do. Energy bills were going up faster than he could offer rebates. He couldn’t stop the wars around the world. The cost of debt was out of his hands. The Tories could say they would cut welfare, but nothing much would change. We needed to be patient. Things would get better. Just so long as Labour won in 2029.
Social care, the triple lock, Brexit and electoral reform. These were the real engines that would transform the country and reconnect voters with politics. Instruments of trust. How that would happen would be for others to decide. Single market, customs union, rejoin. All were on the table. Let’s just hope the far right haven’t taken over the EU by the time it happens. A national care service. Not ideal – some people would still lose their homes – but better than what was currently on offer. Just don’t forget: Andy was merely a channel of peace. In a rare turnabout, Nick thanked Burnham for the therapy session. The bank transfer would follow.
Over in the main hall, the conference proper was dying on its arse. You could hear the exhibition stands being dismantled as Yvette Cooper, Lucy Powell and others made the last few speeches to polite applause. We ended as all Labour conferences ended – with renditions of The Red Flag and Jerusalem – and then it was a dash for the exits. Not that there was a scrum. Most people had already left.
But it was always going to be this way when the main event had taken place the previous afternoon. This had been the Andy Burnham show. And delegates couldn’t have been happier. The Labour party had rediscovered its soul. Its belief. A leader who could go toe-to-toe with the other parties. Maybe this was also the sketch that Andy Burnham’s father would have wanted.
