The question Netanyahu must answer: What did he know before October 7? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

On June 29, 1973, Sen. Howard Baker (R-Tennessee), the vice chair of the Senate Watergate Committee, asked White House Counsel John Dean a question that began the final unraveling of Richard Nixon’s presidency.
“What did the president know, and when did he know it?”
Benjamin Netanyahu was living in the United States at the time, studying architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and he very likely watched the hearings on television, like the rest of us. He knows that it was the cover-up that destroyed a presidency.
As Israelis prepare to go to the polls later this month, they are asking the same thing about their prime minister. What did he know, and when did he know about the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led assault that left some 1,200 dead in Israel, thousands more injured, and 251 people taken hostage?
Why is he working so hard to prevent an independent commission of inquiry, the Israeli equivalent of the bipartisan Watergate investigation, from examining the events leading up to that horrific day?
This has become a central issue in the October 27 Israeli elections, especially since Haaretz revealed that Netanyahu was personally warned by the leader of the United Arab Emirates of a possible Hamas attack about 10 days before it occurred.
Netanyahu secretly flew to the UAE Sunday to ask President Mohamed bin Zayed to back up publicly his insistence there had been no such advance warning. As of this writing, that hasn’t happened.
Other news outlets have added even more revelations.
The Atlantic, The Wall Street Journal, and Haaretz have reported that Egypt’s intelligence chief Abbas Kamel secretly went to Israel 11 days before October 7 to warn Netanyahu, after previous efforts about the volatile situation in Gaza had gone unheeded.
Haaretz broke the original story. It revealed that bin Zayed phoned Netanyahu in late September to warn him that Hamas was planning a major attack, but apparently offered no specific details of time and place.
Yoav Galant, then the defense minister, said Netanyahu never informed him or the IDF chief of staff of these warnings, and that they learned of them only recently from media reports.
According to The New York Times, Netanyahu did not pass the warnings on to security chiefs. He had earlier rejected their alerts of a Hamas threat, and their suggestions that Israel target Hamas leaders who were fomenting West Bank violence, the Times noted.
Netanyahu believed another conflict with Hamas at that time could sabotage US and Israeli efforts to normalize diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia. That turned out to be prophetic. It subsequently came out that one reason behind Hamas’s timing was to derail the Saudi move, which is what happened.
Haaretz also said that “a former senior Palestinian official” told Israeli intelligence weeks before the attack that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar asked him to let Israel know he was planning to “cause an earthquake… in the prisons due to the prisoner issue.”
Intelligence officials may have misread Sinwar’s “earthquake” message, thinking it was related to the case of an Israeli kidnapped and held in Iraq, not the larger assault, reported i24 Israel news. “In retrospect,” i24 added, “it was Sinwar’s way of extracting additional benefits from Israel while postponing the attack he had planned.”
Israeli and Egyptian intelligence officials are reported to have told the prime minister in September that they had separately learned that Qatar was also funding Hamas’s military wing prior to October 7.
Netanyahu dismissed that information as well, calling it “a collection of recycled lies” and insisted that the money was for humanitarian purposes, as Qatar was saying, even as it was funding the terror group’s military wing.
Qatar, those generous folks who gifted US President Donald Trump with a $400 million jetliner, had been funding Hamas’s military wing for several years while Washington and Jerusalem turned a blind eye for their own political purposes.
Hubris and deception helped pave the road to the tragic failure to prevent a massacre and a war that has led to the deaths of tens of thousands, more than twice that number injured, over 2.2 million displaced, a widespread health crisis, and the massive destruction of Gaza’s homes and infrastructure, not to mention the unprecedented plunge in Israel’s international standing.
Israeli leadership fooled by Hamas
Israeli leaders were the target of a sophisticated Hamas ploy to fool them into believing that the terrorist group was more interested in governing than making war. Qatar was helping sell that message, and Netanyahu apparently bought it, allowing Doha to send millions of dollars to Gaza.
Netanyahu was more focused instead on threats from Iran and Hezbollah, and feeding the friction between Hamas and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank.
That internecine warfare was his key to making certain there would never be a Palestinian state, at least not on his watch. With the two largest Palestinian factions at war with each other, Israeli leaders had an excuse not to pursue a deal with them, especially if that could lead to statehood.
The opposition’s demand for an independent Gaza inquiry is a central issue in this campaign. Netanyahu and his allies insist none of these meetings or warnings ever took place, and have persistently sought to point the blame at security and intelligence officials.
What did Netanyahu know about Hamas’s war plans, when did he know it, and why is he so frightened of the truth coming out?
The Israeli people need and deserve to know. So do the rest of us. This prime minister’s conduct of the Gaza war has done enormous damage to Israel’s standing around the world – witness last week’s walkout at the United Nations General Assembly – and particularly in the United States, in the once solidly supporting Democratic party and across the Jewish community.
As one who lived through the Watergate saga, he should know the cover-up only magnifies the damage already done. This cover-up can do for his legacy what it did for Nixon’s.
A commission of inquiry won’t repair that, but it is an essential first step toward healing the nation at home and abroad.
The writer is a Washington-based journalist, consultant, lobbyist, and former legislative director at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Another Tu-95 Is Gone—and Russia Can’t Build New Ones. Here’s How Many May Be Left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:59:58 UTC
22:59:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Another Tu-95 Is Gone—and Russia Can’t Build New Ones. Here’s How Many May Be Left
A Russian Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed shortly after taking off from Ukrainka air base in the Amur region on September 29—an exceptionally rare loss involving an aircraft Moscow stopped producing decades ago and still relies on to launch long-range cruise missiles against Ukraine.
According to Defense Express, the last comparable loss of a Tu-95MS occurred 11 years ago, in 2015.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian sources have not officially disclosed the cause of the latest crash, although reports circulating inside Russia claim three of the bomber’s four engines failed shortly after takeoff.
Six of the seven crew members were killed, while one survived.
It remains unclear why the aircraft was flying. Defense Express suggested the bomber may have been relocating from Ukrainka to another Russian airfield farther west or northwest, although a training mission also remains possible.
The 2015 crash bears a similarity. That Tu-95MS also suffered the failure of three engines during a flight from Ukrainka. All seven crew members attempted to bail out, with five surviving and two killed.
For an even earlier Tu-95-family accident with no survivors, Defense Express points back more than four decades. In February 1985, a Tu-95RTs crashed over the South China Sea during a mission from Cam Ranh, killing its crew.
But the significance of the September 29 crash goes far beyond its rarity.
Russia no longer manufactures Tu-95MS bombers. The surviving aircraft are Soviet-built machines that Moscow can overhaul and modernize, but every airframe destroyed represents a loss that cannot simply be replaced by ordering another bomber from a production line.
That makes the size of the remaining fleet increasingly important.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence estimated in late August that Russia had around 38 Tu-95MS and upgraded Tu-95MSM bombers in combat-ready condition, according to Defense Express.
Days later, on August 28, Ukraine’s Security Service struck Engels air base with a MICH 2000 drone, destroying another Tu-95MS.
Adding the September 29 crash would theoretically reduce that combat-ready fleet to roughly 36 aircraft, Defense Express calculated.
The precise number available for missions at any given moment may differ because aircraft regularly undergo repairs and maintenance.
Still, the trend is difficult for Russia to reverse.
The Tu-95MS remains one of Moscow’s principal platforms for launching Kh-101 cruise missiles against Ukraine. Yet the aircraft are aging, production has long since ended, and maintaining the remaining fleet becomes increasingly difficult with every passing year.
Previously, a Russian Tu-22M3 long-range bomber crashed in Russia’s Irkutsk region.
The Russian Defense Ministry confirmed the crash, stating that the aircraft was undergoing a training mission. According to the Russian military, the crew ejected and survived.

US Sanctions 13 Individuals and Companies Tied to Iran Weapons Procurement, Including Russian Firms
The US imposed sanctions on 13 individuals and entities accused of helping Iran procure weapons and military components, Reuters reported on September 29.
The measures targeted people and companies based in Iran, Russia, China, Hong Kong, and Pakistan. Reuters wrote that the sanctions are part of the US President Donald Trump administration’s effort to economically isolate Tehran and pressure it to negotiate an end to the war that began with a US-Israeli strike on Iran on February 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia and Iran have also built a broader military supply network despite Western sanctions. UNITED24 Media previously found that Russia supplied Iran with 24 Mi-28NE attack helicopters and planned deliveries of more than 200 Spartak armored vehicles, supported by training, sanctioned shipping routes, and offshore payments.
“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated.
The Treasury Department described the measures as an attempt to hinder Iran’s ability to rebuild its weapons programs and raise the costs for foreign companies and individuals supporting its procurement networks, Reuters noted.
Among those sanctioned was Seyyed Asghar Alizadeh Tabatabai, a Beijing-based representative of Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics. US officials accused him of coordinating purchases of finished weapons systems and dual-use components in China on Tehran’s behalf.
The sanctions also targeted Iran-based Kavoshcom Asia R and D Group, which Washington accused of procuring electronics for Iran Aircraft Manufacturing Industrial Company. Hong Kong-based EC Mojo Technology and its China-based representative Li Fen were designated for allegedly supporting those procurement efforts, Reuters reported.
Other targets included Waseem Pasha Tajammal, chairman of Pakistan-based defense company Cavalier Group, and Russian aircraft manufacturer Joint Stock Company Experimental Design Bureau Named After A.S. Yakovlev.
Washington also sanctioned Russian shipping company MG-Flot, whose vessels it accused of transporting weapons for the Russian government, as well as Saha Airlines, an Iranian carrier affiliated with the country’s air force, Reuters detailed.
Brett Erickson, managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors, questioned whether the measures would significantly restrict Tehran’s ability to conduct missile and drone operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
“This is optics management for the Trump administration to claim ‘We’re hammering them,’ when the reality is we’re poking them with a toothpick,” Erickson told Reuters.
Recently, Trump signed sweeping new sanctions targeting Russia’s energy, defense, financial, and maritime sectors. The law also allows secondary measures against foreign entities that continue helping Moscow evade restrictions or purchase Russian energy.

Russia’s Newest T-14 Armata Tank Still Hasn’t Seen Combat, but Now It’s Supposed to Shoot Down Drones
Russia’s newest T-14 Armata tank, which has yet to see confirmed combat in Ukraine, is reportedly being upgraded with a 152mm gun that Russian sources claim could give the vehicle a short-range air defense role, potentially allowing it to engage drones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on September 30, Russian sources have reported a package of upgrades for the T-14 Armata, including a new 152mm gun, guided ammunition, a reconnaissance drone, and an updated fire-control system.
The 152mm gun would reportedly be capable of firing Krasnopol guided projectiles. Russian sources cited by Defense Express claim the combination could effectively give the Armata the functionality of a short-range air defense system.
The claims were highlighted by armored vehicle researcher Andrii Tarasenko, who drew attention to the proposed modernization of the platform.
Russian sources also claim the 152mm smoothbore gun has a chrome-lined barrel and could launch Kornet anti-tank guided missiles at ranges of up to 10 kilometers.
The reported modernization package also includes a Pterodactyl reconnaissance drone integrated with the tank, as well as a new fire-control system connected to its onboard electronics.
According to specifications cited by Defense Express, the upgraded Armata would carry 40 rounds, 24 of them in its automatic loading system.
Russian state defense corporation Rostec is also reportedly working on a remotely operated version of the T-14, although no timeline for the project was provided.
Despite the expanding list of reported capabilities, the T-14 has not been confirmed to have participated in combat during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Defense Express noted that the tank has remained absent from frontline operations despite years of Russian announcements surrounding the platform.
The reported 152mm configuration also follows previous Russian attempts to equip tanks with larger-caliber weapons. The experimental T-95 tank was developed with a 152mm gun but never entered serial production.

anrealage wraps dresses in up to 2,000 e-ink panels for color-changing ‘skin’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

anrealage wraps dresses in up to 2,000 e-ink panels for color-changing ‘skin’
kunihiko morinaga's ss27 collection combines e ink, 3d printed scales and kyocera forearth printing at paris fashion week.
ANREALAGE SS27 TURNS E-INK INTO A SECOND SKIN
For Spring/Summer 2027, Anrealage takes the idea of a wardrobe update rather literally. Kunihiko Morinaga’s Skin collection, presented during Paris Fashion Week at the Maison de la Radio et de la Musique, imagines clothing as an outer layer that can shed, mutate and regenerate. Drawing parallels between biological skin and the interchangeable skins of digital avatars, the designer builds the collection around surfaces that refuse to stay visually fixed. The premise feels familiar to anyone who has changed an avatar outfit in seconds; translating that behavior to the physical body is the more complicated part.
The transformation begins relatively quietly. Second-skin bodysuits carry pixelated graphics and trompe-l’œil versions of familiar garments, while overlapping scalloped forms gradually detach from the printed surface and become physical scales. Toray Ultrasuede appears among the materials, alongside translucent elements made with Japanese washi, shifting the collection between fabric, graphic image and something closer to an engineered interface. The layered surfaces reference chromatophores — pigment-changing cells found in living organisms — turning biology into a visual system for clothes designed to behave rather than simply sit there.
3D PRINTED SCALES SHIFT COLOR WITHOUT A SCREEN
That behavior becomes more literal through SEKISAI’s Effective Skin technology. 3D-printed scales are formed and colored so their appearance shifts depending on the viewing angle, producing an optical effect as models move through the space. The pieces of Anrealage do not need a conventional display to appear animated: geometry, surface and motion do most of the work. Ridged skirts amplify the effect by turning the scales outward, somewhere between Op Art and a wearable rendering glitch, while keeping the mechanism resolutely physical.
Then the collection goes electronic. Six armor-like cocktail and evening dresses are covered with between 1,000 and 2,000 individually controlled electronic-paper scales using e-ink technology. Unlike LEDs, the elements do not generate their own light; the electronic paper itself changes color, allowing pigments and patterns to travel across the body before draining back into gray and reassembling into new configurations. Beneath the decorative shell is a dense network of wiring connecting the individual modules, with AI-assisted mapping used to organize the circuitry. Suddenly, embellishment starts looking suspiciously like hardware.
KYOCERA FOREARTH EXTENDS THE FASHION TECHNOLOGY EXPERIMENT
The digital layer sits alongside another, less theatrical technology in the collection: Kyocera’s FOREARTH textile-printing system. The process uses proprietary water-based pigment inks and reduces water consumption associated with conventional textile printing by completing production through printing and drying rather than water-intensive steaming and washing stages. Kyocera states that its system uses 0.02 liters of water per kilogram of fabric, including maintenance, while supporting high-definition printing across materials including cotton, silk, polyester and nylon. For Anrealage, which has collaborated with FOREARTH across several previous collections, printing becomes another way of programming the garment’s surface.
Morinaga closes the loop by bringing back the LED-based digital camouflage explored in the previous season, now flashing through fiery colors in reference to Osamu Tezuka’s Phoenix, a recurring symbol of rebirth throughout Skin. The finale makes the collection’s proposition unusually literal: clothes can behave like a third skin, neither entirely textile nor entirely screen, capable of changing its visual identity without changing the person underneath. After more than two decades of Anrealage experiments with reflection, light, shape and digital effects, the future of fashion here is not another wearable gadget. It is the garment itself becoming the device.
project info:
name: Skin
 designer: Kunihiko Morinaga for Anrealage | @anrealage_official
show direction: Shige Kaneko
 location: Maison de la Radio et de la Musique, Paris, France

Exclusive: Sami Abu Shehadeh on Israeli anti-Arab vote exclusion
Unknown

2026-09-30

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh on Israel's 'dangerous' anti-Arab voter exclusion
Just weeks ahead of Israel’s first national elections in the shadow of the ongoing genocide in Gaza, the Central Elections Committee moved to bar Palestinian political representation from the ballot, singling out Arab political parties and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh for personal disqualification. While petitions against Palestinian lawmakers are nothing new in Israeli politics, this election marked a distinct turning point: Abu Shehadeh’s exclusion was backed not only by the far-right coalition of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Benjamin Netanyahu, but by a broad Zionist consensus extending deep into the self-styled liberal camp, including Yair Golan’s Democrats party.
The case against him rests on a single opinion piece published on 8 October 2023 in Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, The New Arab's Arabic edition, an accusation Abu Shehadeh rejects as a calculated attempt to lower the political ceiling for Palestinian citizens, suppress voter turnout and criminalise dissent over wartime atrocities. Speaking to The New Arab in his hometown of Jaffa, the veteran politician discusses the legal and political battle ahead, the erosion of Israel’s remaining judicial constraints, the role of the Zionist left, and why Balad’s founding vision of a true "state of all its citizens" remains, in his view, the only viable democratic horizon in an era of ethnic supremacy and state violence.
Below is a transcript of the interview, edited for clarity and brevity
Q: The Central Elections Committee's decision to disqualify Arab slates and bar you personally received backing across Zionist parties, from Itamar Ben-Gvir to Yair Golan. What does this broad consensus to exclude you signal to you?
Sami Abu Shehadeh: A week ago, the Central Elections Committee in Israel, which is a political body rather than a professional or judicial panel and is made up of parties represented in the Knesset, decided to disqualify not only me but effectively the entire Arab minority from the upcoming Knesset elections. The Arab minority represents 20% of the population of Israel.
Two Arab political slates are running in these elections. Out of 38 lists contesting the vote, only the Arab parties were disqualified. They were barred without any valid legal basis, simply because we think differently and have distinct political platforms.
Regarding my personal disqualification, they cited an article I wrote on 8 October, claiming it violates Israeli law. But the real issue is electoral mathematics: Netanyahu has run the numbers and is trying to steal the election. Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and the Israeli far right know that higher turnout among Palestinian Arab citizens poses the greatest obstacle to Netanyahu returning as prime minister. That is why five separate petitions were filed against our two slates, targeting the Joint List, Ra'am, myself, my colleague Dr Ofer Cassif and Balad.
The committee demonstrated a clear consensus against the Arab community. The ease with which the decision was taken, and the way Israeli Jewish society reacted to it, show the dangerous situation we are facing.
Q: Unlike other petitions, including Ofer Cassif’s, your disqualification received direct backing from Yair Golan and the Democrats. How do you understand this alignment between the far right and centre-left over a single published article?
SAS: The Zionist consensus stretching from Yair Golan to Itamar Ben-Gvir against me, demanding my exclusion as a representative of Balad and the Arab minority, is extremely revealing. These different Zionist factions are trying to impose a single narrative that allows no dissent. They cannot tolerate voices opposing the war or platforms that speak about genocide, apartheid, occupation, state violence and the ongoing ethnic cleansing of our people in the West Bank. Any voice challenging the official narrative meets unified Zionist opposition.
Consider Yair Golan, who presents himself as the leader of the Zionist left and the Democrats, aligning directly with far-right figure Itamar Ben-Gvir against a political leader whose platform centres on freedom, justice and equality for all. This is why I call it racism. The greatest threat to racism is equality. Because Balad leads the fight for full civic equality in Israel, it is treated as fundamentally illegitimate by a racist establishment.
Q: Would you say the campaign against you is not really about the stated premise, an article published in Al-Araby Al-Jadeed and Arab48 on 8 October 2023, but rather a convenient pretext to silence a prominent Palestinian political voice?
SAS: Since 7 October, the Israeli government has moved aggressively to suppress dissent against the war. In the petition filed against me, Ben-Gvir openly boasts about shutting down free expression and silencing dissenting views. He says so without hesitation. The alarming reality is that Ben-Gvir is not an isolated actor. He is an influential government minister backed by a Knesset majority.
Ben-Gvirism and Kahanism now dominate Israeli political discourse and command a significant share of public opinion. An extreme and openly racist figure has moved from the margins into the political mainstream. Silencing Sami Abu Shehadeh is not simply about me personally; it is an attempt to silence any critical voice exposing Israel's discriminatory policies against Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and within the 1948 borders, where we make up a fifth of the population.
Q: These are the first national elections following the war in Gaza. How do you assess the broader shift in Israeli society and its attitude towards Palestinian citizens within the 1948 borders?
SAS: These elections follow an ongoing genocide. Regrettably, Israeli state institutions and wider society continue to reject any serious scrutiny of the war crimes inflicted on our people in Gaza and the West Bank. The political establishment is trying to impose a single narrative that erases Palestinian reality.
Against this, we take a principled, universal human rights position: we oppose harm to any civilian, Israeli or Palestinian, whether before, on or after 7 October. Yet Israeli discourse focuses solely on its own victimhood, while ignoring the killing of more than 70,000 Palestinians in Gaza, the majority women, children and infants, more than 100,000 injured, the destruction of entire cities and the displacement of tens of thousands in the West Bank amid daily settler attacks.
While we categorically condemn violence against civilians on 7 October, we equally condemn the war crimes committed against Palestinians before, during and since. Our platform remains rooted in universal human rights, justice and equality. Neither Balad nor I have ever advocated violence or armed struggle; our programme is entirely political and democratic.
Q: The case against you rests on this single article, with no other evidence presented from decades of public life. Do you believe you are being made a sacrificial lamb to lower the political ceiling and discourage civic participation among Palestinian citizens of Israel?
SAS: What took place in the committee was a kangaroo court. After relentless media incitement against me, without any meaningful opportunity to defend myself in an openly hostile press, the demonisation has reached the point where I fear for my personal safety in public.
Notably, the Attorney General previously acknowledged that nothing in my 8 October article calls for armed struggle. Yet state authorities have offered me up as a sacrificial lamb to appease a far-right movement that relentlessly attacks the judiciary. That does not change the fundamental truth. In 30 years of public life, investigators could not find a single instance of me endorsing violence or armed struggle. That is no accident; it reflects who I am and what Balad stands for as a party committed to international law.
We are living through an absurd reality in which Itamar Ben-Gvir, a figure who has openly called for starvation, mass devastation and ethnic cleansing in Gaza, takes me to court. A politician who incites hatred sits in judgement of a leader calling for an immediate end to the violence, an escape from the cycle of bloodshed and a historic compromise based on equality for both peoples. This is a critical test of what remains of the Supreme Court's judicial independence.
Q: Balad champions the concept of "a state of all its citizens" as the basis for genuine equality and justice. Given the profound rightward shift in Israeli society, is this vision still achievable, or was your disqualification intended to eliminate that political project?
SAS: Balad's central project is genuine civic equality, which poses the greatest ideological challenge to Zionist parties whose foundations depend on ethnic supremacy. They insist on systemic privileges for Jewish citizens over the indigenous population. Balad was established specifically to offer a democratic alternative based on universal rights for everyone, Israelis and Palestinians alike.
It is hardly surprising that racists despise Balad; demanding equality forces them to look in the mirror. Whenever I speak in Europe or North America and explain that our goal is to transform Israel into a state of all its citizens, audiences are astonished. They ask: "How can a country claim to be a democracy while rejecting equal citizenship?" A state that rejects civic equality is inherently at odds with democracy.
Israel clings to the image of a democratic society while systematically enforcing segregation and aggressively targeting the one party committed to genuine equality.
Q: In this climate, does Balad's vision of a state of all its citizens still have practical viability after 7 October and the devastation in Gaza?
SAS: After the staggering war crimes in Gaza, the seizure of land in the West Bank and intensified repression within the 1948 borders, Balad's vision is more urgent than ever. In this dark period, our historical responsibility is to keep alive a beacon at the end of the tunnel.
We must prevent both Palestinians and Israelis from surrendering to despair, because abandoning hope means resigning ourselves to an endless cycle of bloodshed and vengeance. War is a political choice, just as peace is a political choice. We have a duty to preserve an alternative horizon for future generations.
Q: Turning to the Supreme Court: it has historically overturned Central Elections Committee bans, but its composition has shifted significantly to the right. Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg also broke with a 23-year precedent by voting for your disqualification. Given these dynamics, is your appeal a genuine legal petition or also a political attempt to expose the court's limitations?
SAS: Supreme Court justices do not operate in a vacuum; they are subject to societal pressures and the prevailing political climate. If the court functions as a genuinely independent legal institution and adheres strictly to jurisprudence, there are no legal grounds to disqualify me, Dr Ofer Cassif or the Arab slates.
The central question is whether Ben-Gvirism has completely captured the judiciary, just as it has captured law enforcement and government ministries. If the court has succumbed to that ideology, we need to confront that reality openly. I cannot accept being deprived of the right to defend myself simply because the forum itself has become fundamentally compromised.
We are appealing to the Supreme Court to force a choice: will it permit a legitimate platform centred on democratic equality, or will it align the state's legal framework with the demands of the extreme right? I have nothing to hide. Even under the most adverse interpretation of my writing, disagreement with the ideas expressed in an article does not constitute legal grounds to ban an elected political leader.
Q: Did the backing of the Zionist left, specifically Yair Golan and the Democrats, give the court political cover to uphold your ban by signalling that your disqualification falls within a broader political consensus?
SAS: Yair Golan’s position was entirely predictable. During this war, he made public statements supporting the denial of essential supplies to civilians in Gaza. Given that record, his position here is hardly surprising.
The real issue is whether the Supreme Court has the integrity to assess my case strictly on its legal merits, insulated from political considerations. Upholding this ban would extinguish what little democratic space remains. To bar an experienced political representative over one article, while allowing figures like Ben-Gvir, who openly preach expulsion and devastation, to run unchecked, is indefensible by any objective legal standard.
Q: Should the Supreme Court ultimately uphold the ban, what are your immediate political and organisational plans ahead of election day?
SAS: We will never allow Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, the court or any other establishment force to dictate the political leadership of the Palestinian Arab community in Israel.
If the disqualification stands, I will do everything I can to ensure the Joint List's success. Netanyahu’s primary objective is to suppress turnout in our community and guarantee the return of his coalition. We will do the opposite: mobilise our voters, maximise participation and prevent this extreme-right bloc from retaining power. Once the election is over, we will conduct a thorough assessment of our long-term political strategy.

The lawyer of Junaid Hafeez, a Fullbright scholar imprisoned for 13 years in a Pakistani jail, tells DW he is hopeful for his release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Will Pakistan scholar facing death for blasphemy be freed?
September 30, 2026
Junaid Hafeez, a former university lecturer and Fullbright scholar was thrown in prison 13 years ago under Pakistan's strict blasphemy laws for comments he allegedly made on Facebook. After a trial that spanned years, a court in 2019 sentenced him to death.
Last week, a high court in Lahore began hearing Hafeez's appeal, raising hopes his conviction could be overturned.
"I want to see my son free and back home. We are fighting a very difficult battle," Junaid Hafeez's father, Hafeez-un-Naseer, told DW.
Naseer said he met with his son in prison last Thursday through a glass window, speaking to him by phone.
"This case has taken everything from us," he said.
Saif-ul-Malook, a lawyer representing Hafeez, said the academic has read thousands of books during his years in prison.
"He is an intellectual. His health is fine, but he is frustrated inside the jail," Malook told DW. "I am hopeful that under this bench, he will be released."
Who is Junaid Hafeez?
Before his arrest, Hafeez was a Fulbright scholar and had studied in the United States. He later returned to Pakistan and began working as a lecturer in English literature at Bahauddin Zakariya University in the city of Multan.
Human rights groups say that shortly after he began working there as a graduate student in 2011, he found himself targeted by an Islamist student group who took issue with what they considered Hafeez's "liberal" teaching.
Hafeez was arrested on March 13, 2013, accused of using a fake Facebook profile to insult the Prophet Muhammad in a closed group called "So-Called Liberals of Pakistan."
His father has said he was set up by the Islamists on campus, who wanted to get one of their own into an open position at the university.
What are the details of the blasphemy case?
His trial began in 2014. Because of security concerns, legal proceedings were later moved to Multan Central Jail, and were repeatedly delayed until he was sentenced to death by a trial court in Multan. Hafeez challenged the verdict in 2020, and his appeal has yet to be decided.
The Lahore High Court heard Hafeez's appeal on September 22 before a two-member bench. The judges issued notices to the prosecution and the complainant and asked for arguments on the electronic evidence being relied upon in the case. This includes Facebook material attributed to Hafeez.
"Lahore High Court judges have generally been reluctant to hear blasphemy appeals. This time, Justice Sadiq Mahmud Khurram is on the bench. Let's see how he approaches the case. In my experience, there is prejudice against the accused at every stage," Malook said.
Pakistan's blasphemy laws in focus
Hafiz Ehtisham Ahmed, an Islamabad-based Islamic activist, told DW he thinks the court should uphold the blasphemy conviction, arguing abolishing the laws could "encourage disrespect for religion."
"There is international pressure on Pakistan to change these laws. If Hafeez is acquitted, it would raise serious questions about the justice system," Ahmed said.
Strict blasphemy laws in Muslim-majority Pakistan have been widely condemned internationally for their arbitrary applicaiton and the potential for abuse of power.
Pakistani policy analyst Raza Rumi said that judges are under intense pressure when handling blasphemy cases.
"Acquittals or even procedural decisions can trigger threats and public backlash, contributing to delays and caution in handling such cases," Rumi told DW.
Security has been a major issue throughout the proceedings.
"Human rights groups have documented threats against judges, lawyers, and prosecutors in blasphemy cases. Concerns over their safety can affect both the pace of proceedings and judicial independence," Rumi added.
At least seven judges were transferred during the trial. Hafeez's first lawyer, Rashid Rehman, was shot dead in his Multan office in May 2014. He had reportedly received threats in connection with the case.
What are the chances for Hafeez's appeal?
Hafeez can still be released if the Lahore High Court overturns his conviction. But that will depend on the judges' assessment of the evidence and the arguments made during the appeal. A death sentence imposed by a trial court does not become final without scrutiny by the high court.
For Hafeez, the question now is how quickly the Lahore High Court can hear and decide his appeal after years of delays. The next hearing is due on October 10, but it is unclear how long it will take the court to decide.
"We wish that one night we could go to sleep and wake up to find our son free and back home," said father Naseer.
"I still remember the pain we have endured over all these years since my son was falsely accused. Thirteen years have taken so much from our family, but we have never stopped hoping that one day Junaid will walk free," Naseer added.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called for the blasphemy conviction to be overturned. In a February press statement, HRW called for Hafeez's release, adding he has been kept in solitary confinement since June 2014.
"If his appeal is rejected, Junaid's mother will not survive it. His father can barely walk. The whole family has been destroyed. If released, I believe Junaid will become an internationally recognized intellectual, lecturing at leading universities," said lawyer Malook.
"We hope that Hafeez's remaining life will not be wasted in the prison on the death row and [that his] case will be finally concluded and he will be acquitted," Malookadded.

====================================================================================================

Everything Netanyahu does is to stay out of jail: The Bibi Files’ director
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:58:14 UTC
22:58:14 KST

- ‘It’s sort of almost like a monkey on his back, and people forget that he’s motivated to stay out of jail, and everything he does comes back to that,’ Alexis Bloom tells Anadolu
- Bloom says film struggled to secure mainstream US distribution despite Academy Award shortlist, international screenings
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s every political move is shaped by his ongoing corruption trial and his desire to avoid jail, according to Alexis Bloom, director of the documentary The Bibi Files.
“The main message of the documentary is that this man who is leading Israel to the bottom of the sea has a very serious legal case,” Bloom told Anadolu ahead of a screening of the film at the European Parliament in Brussels.
“It’s sort of almost like a monkey on his back, and people forget that he’s motivated to stay out of jail, and everything he does comes back to that,” she said.
Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases. He has denied wrongdoing and pleaded not guilty. His trial, which began in 2020, remains ongoing.
Bloom said she wants audiences to look beyond the rapidly changing daily news cycle and consider Netanyahu’s legal troubles as part of the broader context surrounding his political decisions.
“I would just say, in the daily reporting of deaths and riots and settlements and all the very intense news that happens day to day, take a breath and step back and remember the big picture,” she said.
The Bibi Files is built around leaked footage of police interrogations of Netanyahu, his wife Sara, his son Yair and people in their political and personal circles.
Producer Alex Gibney received more than 1,000 hours of leaked interrogation material before approaching Bloom to direct the documentary, which also involved interviews with insiders willing to speak about Netanyahu.
For Bloom, the film, which premiered in 2024, is an example of how cinema can turn complex political and legal issues into a story that audiences can experience on a more immediate and personal level.
Difficult journey to audiences
The film itself has faced obstacles reaching audiences.
The day before its screening at the Toronto International Film Festival, lawyers representing Netanyahu sought an injunction from an Israeli court to prevent publication of the interrogation footage.
The court rejected the request and the screening went ahead.
The film has also faced restrictions in Israel because of privacy laws, while it has been distributed and screened internationally.
However, Bloom said the difficulties continued beyond Israel, particularly in the United States.
"It was very difficult to release this film in America, and some newspapers didn't even want to review it," she explained.
"We did not get mainstream distribution, even though we were shortlisted for an Academy Award, and it broadcast all over Europe. An American mainstream streamer didn't want to take us on, so it was difficult to get it out there," the director added.
The film has received strong critical attention internationally. Rotten Tomatoes currently lists it with a 95% critics’ score.
‘People are moved by art’
For Bloom, the documentary also illustrates the ability of art to engage audiences with political and social questions in ways conventional political discourse often cannot.
“I think that people are moved by art, and it’s very important for art to engage them,” Bloom said.
“I think art is political. That’s my instinct.”
Political issues, she said, are frequently presented through legal documents, official statements, speeches and daily news reports, but cinema can create a different form of engagement.
The ability of art to move audiences is not separate from its political significance, she added.
"If we want to make political changes, we have to engage people not just with dry old literature, or slogans or kind of bureaucratic means. It has to be through art. It has to be through music. It has to be through everything," she said.
'You cannot stop thousands of cinemas'
Despite distribution hurdles, the film is finding another route to audiences through cinemas.
The documentary is preparing for a major theatrical release in Italy, with screenings planned in around 130 cinemas, accompanied by a live event.
"People want to see what's happening in Israel and want to know what are the corruption allegations against Netanyahu," Italian distributor and journalist Giulia Innocenzi told Anadolu.
She said some screenings had already sold out and expressed hope that the response would encourage more cinemas to show the documentary.
"But not all of them want to screen this movie because, of course, Netanyahu is very powerful, and it's a political issue," Innocenzi said.
She also recalled attempts to block the film’s screening.
"Bibi Files was not screened in Israel because of violation of privacy policy, but also Netanyahu tried to block this movie before the Toronto Film Festival," Innocenzi noted.
She argued that cinema can offer political expression more room than traditional media because attempts to restrict one outlet do not necessarily prevent audiences from accessing a film elsewhere.
“You can try to stop one media stream. You can try to stop a TV channel, but you cannot stop thousands of cinemas,” she said.

Spain orders probe after rights group alleges troops abused migrants in Ceuta

Spain orders probe after rights group alleges troops abused migrants in Ceuta
MADRID, Sept 29 - Spain's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday it had alerted prosecutors to an Amnesty International report alleging the military tortured or mistreated migrants in Ceuta, and ordered an internal probe into whether any personnel were to blame.
The rights group accused members of Spain's armed forces of torture and other cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment of migrants stranded in the North African enclave after over 72,000 crossed the border from Morocco in late July.
Though most of the migrants later went back, at least 10,000 remain in the tiny Spanish enclave in North Africa, straining local resources and fuelling tensions.
Amnesty International Spain Director Esteban Beltran told Reuters the group had documented 22 cases of torture and abuse by military personnel. In what he said appeared to be a pattern, troops had pursued, beaten and humiliated migrants, including women and unaccompanied children, in nighttime operations.
Amnesty said photographs and videos it reviewed were consistent with allegations of excessive force, including images of hooded personnel striking migrants and spraying their faces with irritants before pushing them across the border.
"In view of the report made public by Amnesty International, it has been agreed to send the report to the prosecutor's office and the duty court in Ceuta, and to instruct the Operations Command to investigate and clarify any possible individual responsibilities," the Defence Ministry said.
Amnesty's Beltran welcomed the move but said it should have come sooner, calling for an exhaustive investigation and the suspension of any military personnel implicated.
"These individuals cannot remain in their duties for a single minute longer, at least as a precautionary measure, until responsibilities are determined," he said.
Amnesty also called for improved humanitarian assistance for migrants still sleeping rough in Ceuta.
"This situation has worried us greatly. They are living in deplorable conditions," Beltran said. REUTERS

Sweden should apologise for injustices against Sami people, commission says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:57:48 UTC
22:57:48 KST

Sweden should apologise for injustices against Sami people, commission says
STOCKHOLM, Sept 30 - The Swedish government should apologise to the indigenous Sami people for past injustices and Sami interests should be given stronger consideration against mining and wind power projects, a government-appointed commission said on Wednesday.
An estimated 80,000 to 100,000 Sami live in the northern lands of Sweden, Finland, Norway and Russia, where reindeer herding over vast areas has been the cornerstone of their culture and livelihood.
The government-appointed Truth Commission said that the Swedish state had unilaterally taken ownership of large parts of Sami land, especially during the 18th and 19th centuries.
"The indigenous Sami people today face major challenges in preserving and developing their culture as a direct consequence of the Swedish state's past and present policies," the Truth Commission wrote in the report published on the government webpage.
The commission's findings add Sweden to a list of Nordic countries confronting their treatment of the Sami. Norway, which is home to around 50,000 Sami people, officially apologised in 2024, and a Finnish commission called for redress in 2025.
The report said Sami communities had been forcibly displaced as far back as the 17th century. The commission urged the government to "acknowledge the historical wrongs, abuses, and violations ... and the harm this has caused the Sami people".
The Swedish parliament recognised the Sami as an indigenous people in 1977, but relations with the state have often been contentious. In recent years, they have clashed with authorities over mining and wind power projects the Sami feel impact their reindeer herding.
The commission said the government should strengthen the land use rights status for reindeer herding. The Sami reindeer herding areas cover around a third of Sweden, bigger than the total area of England. REUTERS

Farage spoils for a Brexit brawl with Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:55:45 UTC

Nigel Farage speaks at a press conference during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 4, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
LIVERPOOL, England — Nigel Farage will use a speech in a Brexit-backing Labour heartland to start the fightback after Andy Burnham reignited Britain’s EU debate.
The Reform UK leader — a key architect of Brexit — will make a “major speech” in Doncaster on Thursday to rail against the Labour prime minister opening the door to a possible return to the bloc, a senior Reform official told POLITICO.
Burnham used his first Labour conference as leader, in Liverpool on Tuesday, to snip three political livewires in British politics, including proposing a change to the “triple lock” protecting the state pension and electoral reform.
Advertisement
Farage is spoiling to address all these fault-lines on Thursday.
“He will talk about Burnham wanting to take us into the Euro, return us to freedom of movement with 500 million people and losing the ability to nationalize key industries,” said the Reform official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the pending speech in Doncaster.
The Yorkshire city voted 69% in favor of leaving the EU in the 2016 referendum, making it one of the most pro-Brexit areas in the U.K. One of its MPs is Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
Burnham has reopened the debate in Labour and beyond by saying he will canvass opinion on several options for Britain’s future arrangement with Brussels and set them out around the time of a EU-U.K. summit later this year.
Those options, he has said, could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or “go all the way,” which Reform is interpreting as scrapping the Pound in favor of the Euro. Burnham has not made that specific pledge, and Labour resisted Britain joining the single currency when it was introduced.
Farage is meanwhile planning to argue that EU re-entry would curb the ability of British governments to nationalize key industries — a play by the Reform leader that upends the traditional left-right debate in British politics. Burnham has put emphasis on bringing back “public control” of privatized utilities rather than public ownership, but Farage has changed tack from his Thatcherite credentials to express support for nationalization in some sectors.
Advertisement
So far most of Farage’s criticism of Burnham’s speech has centered on accusing Labour of “going after pensioners” on the triple lock.
But his stance on the PM announcing a commission to investigate overhauling Britain’s first-past-the-post electoral system will be one to watch.
The current voting system makes it incredibly hard for insurgent parties, like Reform, to get a foothold in Parliament. But after a certain polling threshold is crossed it rewards parties with vast numbers of seats on proportionally little of the vote.
Farage has long been in favor of changing this system — but his party has recently attacked Labour’s reversion to a more proportional voting system in mayoral races as being an “establishment stitch-up.”

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking. The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference.
The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes. Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the flydubai pilots stabbed his fellow pilot and intended to crash the plane. He added that one of the passengers on the flight managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they “neutralised” the attacking pilot.
Netanyahu described it as “an extremely severe security incident”. Other officials, including defence minister Israel Katz, have called it an attempted terrorist attack. Netanyahu thanked the passengers and crew who helped to stop the attack, saying they “showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage”.
An Israeli official has identified the attacker as an Omani national, Reuters is reporting. The co-pilot of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv is believed to have stabbed the captain in a possible attempted “terror attack”.
The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli officials said had between 160 and 180 passengers on board, transmitted a general emergency signal about two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was “pretty much out of control” when the alleged stabbing took place over Jordan on the flight’s path from Dubai to Tel Aviv. “The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.
The plane again transmitted the initial general emergency signal before later landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport. Tabuk airport said the plane landed at 9.45am local time and that both pilots were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries.
A second flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed safely at its destination after the tracking data website Flightradar24 initially showed the plane diverting back towards the UAE. Flight FZ1081 was later shown to be on its way to Israel, where it landed in Tel Aviv this afternoon.

A key piece of information from the FlyDubai flight is that someone in the cockpit transmitted emergency codes.
Pilots use four-digit ‘squawk codes’ to broadcast their position for air traffic control. These are used for routine flight but also in emergency situations.
Aircraft trackers at Flight Radar say the FlyDubai plane transmitted both emergency and hijack signals.
The plane transmitted a 7700 squawk code that means emergency. It also transmitted a 7500 squawk code, which can mean a hijacking.
These codes have to be manually entered from the cockpit.

“Our aim is not merely to develop technology, but to determine what kind of spirit and direction we will give it,” Bayraktar said.

He noted that asset recovery and the expansion of international cooperation have been integrated into Russia’s national anti-money laundering (AML) framework and designated as a strategic priority by President Vladimir Putin. Consequently, the regulatory framework and law enforcement practices are being upgraded to dismantle the channels used to siphon criminal proceeds out of the country.
The Prosecutor General's Office plays a leading role in spearheading these recovery efforts. Since 2020, it has hosted an interagency task force combining the resources of 17 authorities and organizations. Its mandate involves resolving bottlenecks in specific cases, developing methodological guidelines, and drafting proposals to refine legal frameworks and international cooperation.
"At the same time, it must be acknowledged that executing existing procedures faces various complexities in most jurisdictions," the head of the supervisory agency concluded.

Tartu Folk festival returns November 12–15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

Tartu Folk festival returns November 12–15
The 11th international folklore festival Tartu Folk will take place in Tartu, bringing together folklore communities from Estonia and from the Baltic and Nordic countries.
Tartu Folk brings together the folklore communities of Tartumaa and Europe to create new friendships, share knowledge and keep alive the song, dance and instrumental music heritage and folk‑costume traditions of different regions. The festival focuses on interaction between people, making music together, dancing and sharing tradition with both participants and the audience.
This year's most distant guests arrive from 1,900 kilometres away, from the Faroe Islands. The youth association Ung í Dansi belongs under the folk‑dance organisation Sláið Ring and deals with keeping old circle dances alive, accompanied by fairy‑tale‑like ballads.
From Lithuania, the youth group Dolija of Vilnius Žvėrynas Gymnasium arrives at the festival; it stands out for strong awareness of tradition in both music and dance and has participated in Tartu Folk before. Latvia is represented by one of the country's oldest folklore communities, Skandinieki, led by the musician Julgī Stalte, who has Livonian roots.
The festival also introduces the cultural landscape of Estonia's islands. This year the festival includes the Muhu folklore group Uijee, awarded the title of folklore group of the year. The folklore club Maatasa, the organiser of the festival, performs traditional songs, dances and instrumental tunes of South Estonia.
The festival begins on Thursday, late in the evening of 12 November, with folk songs on the bank of the Emajõgi River.
On Friday, 13 November, community parties take place in Tartu and Tartumaa, where the festival's guest groups and local traditional‑culture collectives perform. At the Tartu community party, young traditional musicians from Tartu and South Estonia meet this year.
On Saturday, 14 November, the main day of Tartu Folk takes place at the Vanemuine Concert Hall. At the gala concert, the festival's guest groups perform, with presentations inspired by the traditional songs, dances and instrumental tunes of their home regions.
While folklore communities present their tradition as authentically as possible, the folk‑dance groups participating in the gala show how tradition has inspired contemporary choreographers and musicians. The choreographers' works are performed by the folk‑dance ensemble Tarbatu of the Estonian University of Life Sciences, the folk‑dance group Vassakule of the Defense Forces Academy, and the folk‑dance group Pistandi of the Tartu Applied Health Sciences University.
After the gala concert, an international dance club follows, where it is possible to learn traditional dances of the Faroe Islands, Lithuania, Latvia, and Muhu and South Estonia according to the instructions of the main performers. Communities from across Estonia are also visiting, and one can dance, for example, to the Näppepildurid from Tapa or to the Tartu Udmurt ensemble Jumšan Gur; dances of the northern coast are introduced by the dance society Pikne.
At the café stage, small ensembles of traditional musicians can be heard at the same time, among them Susanna Viktoria and Tuvimärulihärrad. The evening ends with an ethno‑disco, led this year by Eveliina and Mitja Pilke from Finland.
On Sunday, 15 November, the festival's final concert takes place under the bridge area of the Estonian National Museum. Performing are the festival's main guests Ung í Dansi from the Faroe Islands, Skandinieki from Latvia, Dolija from Lithuania, Uijee from Muhu and Maatasa from Tartu.
The theme of this year's final concert is mythological beings, through whom the supernatural characters of different peoples and the stories connected with them are introduced. The concert is hosted by Tuule Pihlap and Kaarel Pogga.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Argo Ideon

Epstein case

Children Are Back in School. Measles Is, Too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:50:07 UTC
22:50:07 KST

This fall in the U.S., as kids settle into a new school year, measles is spreading at a level not seen in 35 years. Children have died. And in just the past month, 10 children have been infected in an outbreak linked to a single daycare in Georgia. Far too many students are entering classrooms vulnerable to a highly contagious and dangerous virus.
Yet there has been relative silence from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the agency where I once served as a senior leader, about measles. CDC’s back-to-school messages on X have advised families about sleep, physical activity, healthy lunches, and bullying. All are important. But one message emphasized in prior years at the start of school is noticeably absent and can now be found only in CDC’s online archives: Get your child up to date on routine vaccinations. During the country’s largest measles resurgence in decades, that should be the nation’s most urgent back-to-school message.
CDC’s reticence extends beyond social media. Four measles-associated deaths reported by Pennsylvania were initially absent from the agency’s national dashboard. In late August, CDC posted two of the Pennsylvania deaths, then added an asterisk and language that it was reviewing additional information. The deaths were later removed without a clear explanation. Now two deaths are reported on CDC’s dashboard as of September 28 without identifying the states. This is not transparency; it is silence at a moment when families need clear, accurate information to protect their children.
Why are these deaths being left off the official tally? There’s a disagreement between federal and state officials over how to count measles deaths—even though Pennsylvania investigated each death and reported them to CDC through the established nationally notifiable disease surveillance system that has been used by state and local health departments across the country for years. In late August, when officials from Pennsylvania announced the first two deaths there, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), even questioned if the deaths were fabricated. But Pennsylvania’s definition of a measles-associated death ensures that deaths unrelated to underlying measles infection are not counted.
Leaders at HHS and CDC have said they are working to clearly define measles deaths and that it will update its counts as reviews are complete. But the agency has not explained which deaths they are currently counting, how these decisions are being made, why the data reporting system used by states was changed, and how they will account for the secondary infections and other complications caused by measles.Two former leaders of the National Center for Health Statistics have called this out publicly, writing in STAT that these changes will delay reporting and add to public confusion about the severity of measles.
An important question to ask is whether shifting explanations and new disease-classification systems are clarifying the outbreak or miring it in confusion and making it easier to minimize. A single measles case can expose dozens of classmates, teachers, and siblings, as well as infants too young to be vaccinated. Federal officials should be using their platforms to prevent the next case and not debating the numbers.
Meanwhile, the big picture is being missed: We know how to prevent this.
After the last significant measles surge in the late 1980s, the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that all kids receive a second dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine at age four to six. One dose is approximately 93% effective against measles; two doses are approximately 97% effective. But national MMR coverage among kindergartners fell again during the 2025-2026 school year, and approximately 280,000 kindergartners attended school without documentation that they had completed the MMR series. Vaccine exemptions in 24 states exceeded 5%, meaning these communities no longer have the 95% adequate protection to keep measles from spreading.
The impact extends beyond the child who becomes sick. When an unvaccinated student is exposed to measles, they will often be required to stay at home for at least 21 days. That means missed academics, missed social interactions, and missed work for parents. In addition to the impact on a child and their family, each case of measles costs the public-health system on average $58,600 to respond to, including the cost of contact tracing and quarantines. And measles isn’t over when the rash goes away. It can result in “immune amnesia,” meaning kids are more likely to get other infections over the next two to three years, and approximately one in 10,000 people who recovered from measles will die years later from the rare brain disease subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
Amid the recent deadly outbreaks of measles, our federal health leaders have too often paired a lukewarm recommendation to vaccinate with insinuations and incorrect information about vaccine ingredients, fetal tissue, or waning immunity. The same week families needed clarity about a growing outbreak, Kennedy addressed a conference hosted by Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization he once led.
In response to the outbreak, Pennsylvania has opened up nearly 150 pop-up vaccination clinics in homes and community centers, engaged health systems and local clinics across the state, requested federal support for additional vaccinations, developed a dashboard showing community transmission by county, and worked with coroners to investigate deaths. This is boots-on-the-ground public health.
Our federal health leaders should reinforce that work rather than cast doubt on it, giving parents and schools clear guidance and reporting cases consistently and transparently. Data and definitions matter, but we cannot lose sight of the people who are behind each of these data points. Each case number represents someone who became sick, and behind each death is a grieving family and a life that deserves to be counted. Now that children are back in school, our responsibility is both simple and urgent: to use the tools we know work to keep this preventable disease out of the classroom.

Marti Soosaar: A green exit from the deadlock in Estonian politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Marti Soosaar: A green exit from the deadlock in Estonian politics
Estonia needs a political force that combines individual freedom and economic prosperity with a firm commitment to protecting the environment, writes Marti Soosaar.
Sensible people in Estonia and elsewhere in the world are looking with concern at the triumph and proliferation of conservative populism. The closer elections come, the more people's faces sour after a look at the polling results.
In Estonia, too, the main question seems to be whether the next prime minister will be named Mihhail or Urmas (Center Party head Mihhail Kõlvart or Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu – ed.). Behind them, an increasingly vociferous Martin Helme [EKRE] smells an opportunity to return to the post of minister and "make heads roll." Listening to talk of reversing marriage equality, burning oil shale and the like is about as unpleasant as sitting next to an aggressively ranting non-citizen on the tram.
Who will deliver us from this mess? The Parempoolsed?
Let us do some ratings calculations. EKRE, Isamaa and Center have 50 sets, Reform and SDE 40 and Parempoolsed 11. If the latter become the kingmaker in parliament, which is entirely possible, we will find ourselves in a situation where the government will be ensuring the timber sector's "security of supply," or in the words of timber industrialist Jaak Nigul, harvesting another billion euros from Estonian forests. A few bank accounts would grow, while most people would be left with nothing but tree stumps to look at.
The Greens stand opposed to such developments. Selling a kidney so you could continue binge-drinking with your friends for another week might seem like a good idea through the haze of a hangover after a months-long bender, but it is generally advisable to sober up completely before making decisions of this magnitude. We will have need of our world's best living environment.
We're talking about economic growth as if it could make us happy. Growth is good, but who draws real happiness from it? Let us, instead, center debate around happy people, a brilliant living environment, good mental and physical health. These are the things we should be talking about, instead of spending our days wondering why the economy grew by 2 percent and not 3.
What will improve if Eesti 200 and Greens join forces? The idea that Eesti 200 could be a far greener party is nothing new. Züleyxa Izmailova, a former member of both Eesti 200 and the Greens, fought toward that goal with some success. Eesti 200 was at a crossroads then and made what we believe was the wrong choice, but the measure of a good politician is not whether they make mistakes, it's whether they learn from them.
The Greens have been widely criticized for both ignoring other important topics in society and talking about them. In a sense, we've painted ourselves into a green corner and are pondering how to get out. Clearly, we, too, need major change to move forward. We need to correct our own mistakes and once again take part in the public debate.
Eesti 200 talked about having a long plan ahead of the 2023 elections. But a single election cycle is not a long plan. Mistakes were clearly made when the long plan started and a price has been paid in the polls.
However, any truly long-term plan is also a green plan. That said, green topics tend to be a nice-to-have for people. Everyone is green in words, but making ends meet and security always comes before the environment.
The new party must take this into account because the party and its politics are, after all, for the people of Estonia and no one else. We protect nature because people cannot survive without it and because no other party will do it. Our task is to show how a good life and environmental protection are inextricably linked and that green solutions exist for all the problems that matter to people.
We invite people to join us who want individual freedoms to be protected in Estonia and want us to remain free. Free not only from Russian troops, but free in our thinking as well. People who understand that without protecting our living environment, our future is bleak. Those who want Estonians to be enterprising and prosperous and to fulfill their talents for their own benefit and that of society, but who do not want that prosperity to come at the expense of our living environment.
There are a million other ways to do business than cutting down every tree. We welcome everyone who sees Estonia's future as free and green.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Kremlin dismisses Atlantic US-Russia swap claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:49:41 UTC
22:49:41 KST

Kremlin dismisses Atlantic US-Russia swap claim
The Kremlin has categorically denied that Moscow and Washington discussed a plan whereby sanctions targeting Russia could be eased in return for the release of US nationals imprisoned in Russia.
Presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday responded to a question about an article in the Atlantic citing anonymous sources that claimed the administration of US President Donald Trump was considering relaxing some economic restrictions if Moscow would release individuals Washington considers unjustly imprisoned.
“The issue was not discussed in those terms and could not have been, because we categorically reject the notion that there are any political prisoners in Russia and consider framing the issue in this way entirely inappropriate,” Peskov told journalists.
Russian and US special services continue regular contacts concerning various prisoner exchanges, he added.
According to The Atlantic, the proposal was advanced by White House envoy John Coale and approved by Trump for exploration several months ago. The initiative, the outlet's sources speculate, could have reportedly allowed Washington to broaden its engagement with Moscow beyond negotiations over Ukraine and pursue deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals and other commodities.
Trump’s envoys have been exploring ways to revive economic ties with Russia but have so far viewed at least a partial ceasefire in Ukraine as a prerequisite, the outlet wrote on Tuesday.
Washington and Moscow have separately discussed potential economic cooperation. Following talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow earlier this month, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said the sides had discussed possible “major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects.”
The Atlantic also claimed that Washington is seeking to arrange lower-level talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine as early as next month, could focus on a limited ceasefire covering energy infrastructure, potentially in the UAE.
Moscow has repeatedly said it opposes a temporary truce that would allow Ukraine to regroup and rearm, insisting that hostilities can end only through a comprehensive settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict. Peskov was not asked to respond to the claim.
Speaking at the UN Security Council last week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow would not agree to pause military operation because such a step could be used by Ukraine’s European backers to supply Kiev with more weapons.
The prospect of renewing US-Russian business ties before the Ukraine conflict is resolved has been sharply criticized by Vladimir Zelensky, who told The Atlantic he would try to “block” any sanctions relief for Moscow before hostilities end.

Royal Run 2027 sells out more than 100,000 spots in under three hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:48:40 UTC
22:48:40 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Egypt, UN envoy discuss Libya's political roadmap, elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:48:00 UTC
22:48:00 KST

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and UN envoy to Libya Hanna Tetteh have discussed the latest political and security developments in Libya and efforts to advance the political process and hold elections.
Abdelatty received Tetteh in Cairo to discuss developments in Libya and efforts to advance the political process within the framework of the UN roadmap, the Egyptian foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
Abdelatty expressed Egypt's support for UN efforts to reach a "comprehensive Libyan-Libyan political settlement," stressing that the political process should remain "Libyan-owned and led."
He emphasised the importance of pushing for presidential and parliamentary elections to be held simultaneously, ending transitional periods and unifying Libya's state institutions.
The Egyptian minister also stressed the need to respect Libya's unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Resolving Libya’s political crisis
Egypt is one of the parties to the Tripartite Mechanism of Libya's Neighbouring States, which also includes Tunisia and Algeria.
The Tripartite Consultation Mechanism on Libya was launched in 2017 and suspended in 2019 before resuming in May 2025, when the foreign ministers of the three countries held a consultative meeting in Cairo. The mechanism aims to contribute to resolving the political crisis in neighbouring Libya.
For her part, Tetteh briefed Abdelatty on developments in implementing the roadmap in Libya, according to the statement.
She also reviewed ongoing steps to address outstanding issues related to the constitutional and legal framework governing elections, it added.
Libya has faced political division between two governments since 2022: the internationally recognised administration of Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibeh in Tripoli and a government led by Osama Hammad based in Benghazi and supported by the eastern-based parliament.
UN-led efforts to hold national elections remain stalled, prolonging the oil-rich country's decade-long conflict and instability.
