BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: United List – is the “Kulbergs effect” working?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

Author: Ilona Bērziņa
Just a few months ago, the United List (AS) was one of the opposition forces in the 14th Saeima, associated more with heated parliamentary disputes, the Rail Baltica parliamentary inquiry and criticism of Evika Siliņa’s government. Now the situation is completely different. AS representative Andris Kulbergs heads the Cabinet, while the United List is the clear leader in the polls.
In the latest SKDS poll, conducted from the 4th to the 16th of September among 2,035 Latvian citizens, 14.4% of all respondents said they were ready to vote for the United List. This was the highest result among the parties. Sovereign Power/Young Latvians ranked second with 9.4%, while Latvia First was third with 9.2%.
Compared with August, support for AS has declined slightly, but the party has retained first place. The September poll by Latvijas Fakti paints a similar picture. AS received the support of 15.9% of all respondents, compared with 15.6% in August. Among voters who had already made their choice, support for AS reached 23.8%.
This strongly resembles the position New Unity found itself in before the 14th Saeima election. In the final SKDS poll before that election, New Unity had around 20–23% support among respondents who had named a specific choice. The Factum Interactive poll conducted from the 15th to the 20th of September showed a very similar level of support – around 21–24%.
There is another similarity:
both political alliances largely have their prime ministers to thank for their strong voter support.
In New Unity’s case, it was Krišjānis Kariņš, who took on the task of forming his first government under highly complicated circumstances and successfully steered it through the waves of the pandemic. In the case of AS, it is Andris Kulbergs, who was not afraid to take the helm of the government for a very short period – just four months – and whose sharp rhetoric appears to resonate with voters.
SKDS polls showed a sharp increase in support for the United List following the formation of Kulbergs’ government: from 6.8% in April and May to 9.8% in June. In the pre-election period, this makes it possible to speak of a clearly visible “Kulbergs effect”. Whether this story will end in a similar way to the “Kariņš effect” remains to be seen.
A look at the alliance’s history
Officially, the political alliance consists of the Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions and the Liepāja Party.
The alliance was also formed with the participation of non-partisan professionals brought together by Uldis Pīlēns in the United List of Latvia association, which was later renamed Latvia’s Restart and is now headed by Andris Kulbergs.
One of AS’s distinctive features is that it brings together people and organisations with very different political backgrounds: the Green Party, which left ZZS because of its cooperation with Aivars Lembergs’ For Latvia and Ventspils, representatives of regional politics, members of Liepāja’s political elite, people from the business community and non-partisan professionals.
In the 2022 election to the 14th Saeima, AS received 11.01% of the vote and 15 seats, becoming the third most popular electoral list. Its strongest support came from Liepāja and South Kurzeme. The parliamentary group later shrank to 12 MPs.
Uldis Pīlēns, without whom AS would most likely not be what it is today, has been both the alliance’s candidate for prime minister and its candidate for President of Latvia. He now publicly acknowledges that he has relatively little involvement with the United List, while stressing that he has not severed ties with the alliance and believes AS is a political force capable of surviving in the long term.
Pīlēns, however, is not among the candidates on the AS electoral lists.
Electoral list leaders and their track records
AS is running under number seven, and each of the five electoral districts is headed by a politician already well known to the public.
In Riga, the list is headed by Andris Kulbergs, the current Prime Minister and AS candidate for the post after the election. Before entering politics, he was known as a representative of the automotive industry. In the Saeima, he became particularly prominent as chairman of the parliamentary inquiry into the problems surrounding Rail Baltica and later a commission investigating costs at Rīgas siltums.
In Vidzeme, the list is headed by Edvards Smiltēns, chairman of the Latvian Association of Regions, former Speaker of the Saeima, current Justice Minister and one of the two co-chairmen of the AS board.
In Latgale, the number one candidate is Juris Viļums, an MP in the 11th, 12th and 14th Saeima and head of the AS parliamentary group, with longstanding ties to Latgale. He founded Latgolys Saeima and is a member and one of the founders of the Latgolys Studentu centrs association, now known as Volūda. Former President Raimonds Vējonis is number two on the Latgale list.
In Kurzeme, the list is headed by Māris Kučinskis, a former Prime Minister who also served as Interior Minister during the 14th Saeima and is one of AS’s most experienced politicians.
In Zemgale, the number one candidate is Edgars Tavars, chairman of the Latvian Green Party, co-chairman of the AS board and current Minister for Smart Administration and Regional Development.
The second and third positions on the electoral lists also include a number of familiar names, among them Raimonds Bergmanis, Ingmārs Līdaka, Linda Matisone, Inga Priede, Edgars Putra, Aiva Vīksna and doctor Andris Skride.
What does AS promise?
The United List’s election programme is relatively broad, but economic policy, security and public administration clearly dominate.
On security, the alliance promises to expand the State Defence Service, strengthen the capabilities of the National Guard, complete the eastern border defence line, develop drone and counter-drone technologies, establish a network of shelters, and strengthen the police, Border Guard and State Fire and Rescue Service.
In public finances, the goal is to achieve a balanced base budget within four years. AS also promises to establish a Latvian Development Fund to manage state assets and to review the Rail Baltica project, reducing it to the “minimum viable” scope.
On the economy, AS promises a more stable tax system, a 10% micro-enterprise tax rate for individuals, a reduction in personal income tax on capital gains to 17%, retention of the current corporate income tax regime, less bureaucracy and a state-guaranteed housing construction programme in the regions.
In healthcare, the alliance proposes a state health insurance model under which funding would follow the patient even if they chose a certified private healthcare provider. It also proposes a unified appointment system, transforming the National Health Service into a fund and gradually reducing co-payments for children, seniors and patients with chronic illnesses.
For the regions, AS promises a new municipal financing model, road funding from vehicle taxes, development of ports and special economic zones, and equal EU area-based payments for farmers. Families would be offered housing grants and guarantees, while returning emigrants would receive a special tax regime for four years.
On energy, AS wants to review the implementation of the European Green Deal, examine the use of small modular nuclear reactors and simultaneously develop renewable energy. In foreign policy, the programme declares clear support for NATO, the EU and Ukraine.
Four months at the helm of government
Kulbergs formed his government as a short-term “government of action”. Even while the coalition was being formed, its partners stressed that they would focus primarily on tasks that could still be completed during the remaining term of the 14th Saeima.
AS also secured a highly influential set of positions: the prime minister’s office, the Finance Ministry under Māris Kučinskis, the Justice Ministry under Edvards Smiltēns and the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development under Edgars Tavars.
One of the most visible changes in governance was an attempt to divide ministers’ work into specific tasks that could be reviewed on a regular basis.
However, creating a “short list” did not go particularly smoothly, and it eventually evolved into a government action plan containing 150 measures, with another 35 tasks to be implemented if additional funding could be found without negatively affecting the budget.
Of the 150 measures, 37 relate to budget stabilisation and spending efficiency, 34 to security and foreign affairs, and 21 to reducing bureaucracy and improving the efficiency of public administration.
By mid-August, seven of the ministers’ priority tasks had been fully completed, while results had been achieved on 26 priority measures overall. The remaining measures had been launched and were still being implemented.
A government with a short “shelf life”
Kulbergs’ government was formed only a few months before the 15th Saeima election, and during the debate on approving his Cabinet, Kulbergs himself said that the election result would provide the true assessment of the government’s performance. Judging by the polling figures at the end of September, voters appear satisfied so far.
Unlike Krišjānis Kariņš’ second government or Evika Siliņa’s government, the Kulbergs Cabinet has not had several years before the election to build up a record of achievements.
Four months is enough to demonstrate a leadership style, priorities and initial decisions, as well as to appeal to the public with sharp rhetoric and tough criticism, but it is too short a period to reliably assess the long-term results of many reforms.
What could strengthen AS’s pre-election position…
The first factor is the prime minister’s office. Following the formation of the Kulbergs government, the party’s polling numbers rose significantly. His advantage in pre-election communication is that he can speak not only about what AS would like to do, but also about what the government is currently doing.
The second factor is the alliance’s regional infrastructure. AS is not simply a project of Riga-based politicians. The Latvian Association of Regions, the Green Party and the Liepāja Party have municipal politicians across many regions, while a large proportion of the candidates are connected with municipalities, regional institutions, agriculture and local businesses.
The third factor is the concentration of experienced politicians. Kučinskis is a former prime minister, Vējonis a former President and defence minister, Smiltēns a former Speaker of the Saeima, and Bergmanis a former defence minister.
This allows AS to project an image of experienced professionals with considerable experience in government. In other words, here is the new “adult in the room”.
…and what could make things more difficult
AS is not a single ideologically homogeneous party, but rather a combination of three parties and non-partisan figures. The Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions, the Liepāja Party and the Latvia’s Restart group of professionals all have different political histories and their own regional interests.
During the current Saeima term, the alliance has also lost several MPs, with its parliamentary group shrinking from its original 15 seats to 12. Putting together a joint electoral list is one thing; keeping a unified political organisation together for four years is another.
Another factor is the short lifespan of the Kulbergs government. As AS itself stresses in its programme, four months is not enough to resolve problems that have accumulated over many years.
The party therefore has the prime minister’s office, but still has relatively few results of its own government work on which to base a longer-term assessment.
Who is the AS voter?
The latest publicly available September polling data do not provide a full socio-demographic breakdown that would make it possible to say precisely that the typical AS voter belongs to a particular age, income or education group. However, previous election results, the party’s structure, its candidates and its programme point to several potential segments of the AS electorate.
The first is regional voters. AS already enjoyed particularly strong support in Liepāja and South Kurzeme in 2022, while the municipal networks of the Latvian Association of Regions and the Green Party provide the alliance with recognisable figures in Vidzeme and Zemgale as well.
The second group consists of centrist or moderately conservative voters who want neither distinctly left-wing nor radically populist politics and who prioritise security, business, efficient public administration and regional interests.
The third group is interested in improving the business and economic environment. Since the days of Pīlēns, AS rhetoric has prominently featured the language of “professionals”, “crisis management”, productivity, investment, reducing bureaucracy and making public administration more efficient. The economic proposals are also among the most detailed sections of the party’s programme for the 15th Saeima election.
A fourth potential group consists of people who previously voted for ZZS, New Unity or regional lists but who, for one reason or another, are now looking for an economically pragmatic and simultaneously Euro-Atlantic alternative.

By mid-August, seven of the ministers’ priority tasks had been fully completed, while results had been achieved on 26 priority measures overall. The remaining measures had been launched and were still being implemented.
A government with a short “shelf life”
Kulbergs’ government was formed only a few months before the 15th Saeima election, and during the debate on approving his Cabinet, Kulbergs himself said that the election result would provide the true assessment of the government’s performance. Judging by the polling figures at the end of September, voters appear satisfied so far.
Unlike Krišjānis Kariņš’ second government or Evika Siliņa’s government, the Kulbergs Cabinet has not had several years before the election to build up a record of achievements.
Four months is enough to demonstrate a leadership style, priorities and initial decisions, as well as to appeal to the public with sharp rhetoric and tough criticism, but it is too short a period to reliably assess the long-term results of many reforms.
What could strengthen AS’s pre-election position…
The first factor is the prime minister’s office. Following the formation of the Kulbergs government, the party’s polling numbers rose significantly. His advantage in pre-election communication is that he can speak not only about what AS would like to do, but also about what the government is currently doing.
The second factor is the alliance’s regional infrastructure. AS is not simply a project of Riga-based politicians. The Latvian Association of Regions, the Green Party and the Liepāja Party have municipal politicians across many regions, while a large proportion of the candidates are connected with municipalities, regional institutions, agriculture and local businesses.
The third factor is the concentration of experienced politicians. Kučinskis is a former prime minister, Vējonis a former President and defence minister, Smiltēns a former Speaker of the Saeima, and Bergmanis a former defence minister.
This allows AS to project an image of experienced professionals with considerable experience in government. In other words, here is the new “adult in the room”.
…and what could make things more difficult
AS is not a single ideologically homogeneous party, but rather a combination of three parties and non-partisan figures. The Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions, the Liepāja Party and the Latvia’s Restart group of professionals all have different political histories and their own regional interests.
During the current Saeima term, the alliance has also lost several MPs, with its parliamentary group shrinking from its original 15 seats to 12. Putting together a joint electoral list is one thing; keeping a unified political organisation together for four years is another.
Another factor is the short lifespan of the Kulbergs government. As AS itself stresses in its programme, four months is not enough to resolve problems that have accumulated over many years.
The party therefore has the prime minister’s office, but still has relatively few results of its own government work on which to base a longer-term assessment.
Who is the AS voter?
The latest publicly available September polling data do not provide a full socio-demographic breakdown that would make it possible to say precisely that the typical AS voter belongs to a particular age, income or education group. However, previous election results, the party’s structure, its candidates and its programme point to several potential segments of the AS electorate.
The first is regional voters. AS already enjoyed particularly strong support in Liepāja and South Kurzeme in 2022, while the municipal networks of the Latvian Association of Regions and the Green Party provide the alliance with recognisable figures in Vidzeme and Zemgale as well.
The second group consists of centrist or moderately conservative voters who want neither distinctly left-wing nor radically populist politics and who prioritise security, business, efficient public administration and regional interests.
The third group is interested in improving the business and economic environment. Since the days of Pīlēns, AS rhetoric has prominently featured the language of “professionals”, “crisis management”, productivity, investment, reducing bureaucracy and making public administration more efficient. The economic proposals are also among the most detailed sections of the party’s programme for the 15th Saeima election.
A fourth potential group consists of people who previously voted for ZZS, New Unity or regional lists but who, for one reason or another, are now looking for an economically pragmatic and simultaneously Euro-Atlantic alternative.

MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese ‘front company’ stealing research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:41 UTC
22:00:41 KST

MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).
MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.
“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”
The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.
“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”
Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.
Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.
“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.
“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.
He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.
The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec.
The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.
The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.

Weight-loss drug semaglutide alters reward-seeking behavior in healthy mice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:33 UTC
22:00:33 KST

A new small study in healthy mice reveals that the popular weight-loss drug semaglutide alters behavior and brain activity related to reward and stress. Researchers found that daily doses of the drug changed how animals pursued natural rewards and reacted to stressful situations, while also shifting electrical patterns in a central reward circuit. The findings were published in the journal Molecular Brain.
Semaglutide is a medication widely used to treat diabetes and obesity. The medication is frequently recognized by brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. It mimics a naturally occurring hormone called GLP-1, which regulates appetite and blood sugar. Recently, scientists have begun exploring whether the drug might also treat addiction by dampening the brain’s response to cravings.
Most prior research has focused on animal models with obesity or diabetes. To understand the drug’s baseline effects on a typical nervous system, researchers Alejo Mosqueira, Sanaz Ansarifar, and their colleagues at Aarhus University investigated how semaglutide impacts the behavior and brain waves of healthy mice. The research team specifically looked at the nucleus accumbens, a region deep in the brain that plays a primary role in processing motivation, pleasure, and reward.
The researchers first designed a behavioral experiment using healthy adult male mice. They divided the animals into two main treatment groups to test different dosing schedules. One group received a weekly injection of semaglutide for eight weeks, which mirrors how the drug is prescribed to human patients. The second group received daily injections to account for the faster metabolism of mice and to observe any short-term behavioral changes.
Following the injection periods, the researchers ran the mice through a battery of tests designed to measure movement, anxiety, and reward-seeking habits. They monitored the animals’ food intake, water consumption, and body weight throughout the process to track general physiological health. Both the daily and weekly groups experienced substantial weight loss, alongside noticeable reductions in eating and drinking. The researchers ran statistical analyses to confirm that the weight loss itself was not responsible for the altered behavior.
When assessing behavior, the researchers found changes exclusively in the daily injection group. In an open field test used to measure general movement and anxiety, the daily-dosed mice displayed an increase in jumping against the walls of the testing box. The researchers interpret this as an increased attempt to escape the enclosure. In a separate marble burying test used to measure repetitive actions, the differences between the treated and untreated mice were not statistically significant.
The team also used a nestlet shredding test, providing the mice with a cotton nesting material to see how much they would tear it apart. Mice given daily semaglutide shredded far less of the material than the control group. This reduction suggests a shift in how the animals explore their environment or a potential increase in underlying anxiety.
To evaluate reward-seeking behavior without relying on food, the researchers used a scent-based test. Healthy male mice naturally seek out the smell of female mouse urine, which acts as a rewarding social cue. The semaglutide-treated mice spent much less time sniffing the female urine than the untreated mice. This drop in interest indicates a suppression of natural reward-seeking drives.
Finally, the researchers placed the mice in small containers of water for a forced swimming test, which is commonly used to measure stress coping and depressive-like states. Mice treated with daily semaglutide spent less time floating motionless and more time actively swimming compared to the control group. This behavior often suggests improved stress resilience or an antidepressant-like effect.
In a separate experiment, Mosqueira and Ansarifar’s team examined how a single dose of semaglutide affects neural activity. They anesthetized a small group of healthy mice and inserted microscopic electrodes into the nucleus accumbens. The researchers recorded the animals’ baseline brain waves for 30 minutes, injected the drug, and then recorded for another hour.
The researchers focused on local field potentials, which are the collective electrical signals generated by large groups of neurons firing together. They analyzed different speeds of brain waves, breaking the signals down into slower rhythms known as delta, theta, and alpha waves. These specific wave patterns are heavily involved in how the brain anticipates and responds to rewards, making them a useful target for understanding motivation.
Following the semaglutide injection, the rhythmic electrical activity in the nucleus accumbens shifted. The dominant frequencies of the delta, theta, and alpha waves became slightly faster. At the same time, the physical strength or amplitude of these slow waves decreased. The researchers note that a reduction in delta and theta wave strength aligns with a dampened reward anticipation system.
The study relies on a relatively small number of animals, and the behavioral changes only appeared under the daily dosing schedule. The weekly injection group lost weight but did not exhibit the same behavioral shifts. This discrepancy suggests that the frequency of the dose heavily influences the behavioral outcomes in healthy animals.
The brain wave recordings took place while the mice were under anesthesia, which fundamentally alters normal electrical activity in the brain. The behavioral tests, conversely, involved awake animals taking the drug over multiple days. Because of these differing conditions, the electrical changes cannot be directly linked to the behavioral shifts.
Future research will need to record brain activity in awake, freely moving animals over longer periods. Measuring these electrical signals while mice are actively making choices could clarify exactly how semaglutide changes motivation. Testing different dosages may also help determine whether these effects apply broadly across different treatment regimens.
The study, “Semaglutide alters behaviour and nucleus accumbens oscillatory activity in healthy mice,” was authored by Alejo Mosqueira, Sanaz Ansarifar, Sadegh Nabavi, and Andrea Moreno.

Romania’s parliament rejected Siegfried Mureșan’s attempt to form a government Wednesday, deepening a crisis that began when the coalition collapsed in May.
President Nicușor Dan, an independent moderate, proposed MEP Mureșan for the job — but lawmakers in Bucharest refused to back his candidacy in a crunch vote Wednesday.
It is the second time parliament has formally voted down Dan’s nominee — Mureșan failed to win backing from the Social Democratic Party (PSD), receiving just 182 of the 233 votes needed for a majority — and under Romania’s constitution, that means a snap election is now a possibility.
Advertisement
“We tried to offer the country stability, but we cannot do so as long as the Socialists irresponsibly join forces with extremists while continuing to pretend that they are pro-European,” Mureșan said after the vote. “It is now the president’s responsibility to act. He can either call a snap election or propose a new prime minister,” he added.
Dan said he would hold more talks with party leaders and nominate a new candidate for prime minister on Monday.
He does not want to dissolve parliament for a national vote that would likely benefit the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) party, which is currently ahead in the polls. He wants the feuding political leaders to put aside their differences and make a deal to support a new coalition.
“I ask the parties to organize their internal meetings during this time and to come up with solutions this time which can pass,” Dan said. “I want to assure Romanians and our partners that we will keep the pro-Western direction and that we will respect the financial commitments we have made.”
On the European Union’s eastern border, Romania is a key NATO member and home to one of the alliance’s biggest military bases. The country of 19 million people has played an important role in supporting Ukraine and has come under pressure from Russia as a result.
The current political crisis blew up in the spring when the PSD joined forces with AUR to bring down Liberal Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan’s coalition, in protest at his leadership and deep spending cuts intended to bring a ballooning budget deficit under control.
In the months since, the president has nominated three people to replace Bolojan — one pulled out before going to parliament to seek majority support from lawmakers, and two have now been formally rejected in parliamentary votes.
George Simion, the AUR leader who ran against Dan for the presidency last year, posted on X: “Another government proposed by Nicușor Dan has FAILED to secure the vote of the Romanian Parliament. We have not betrayed Romanian people, and we will not betray them!”
Advertisement
Romania has suffered a succession of democratic crises in recent years, including corruption scandals and a canceled presidential election in 2024 following allegations of a massive foreign influence operation.
Ultranationalist Călin Georgescu, who was leading the 2024 presidential race before it was annulled, is now in detention facing fraud charges, among other accusations.
Last year, Simion promised to make Georgescu prime minister if he won the presidency and is now demanding his ally’s release from custody as a price for supporting any new coalition. “We will not vote for any other proposal until he is released from prison. FREEDOM,” Simion posted.
AUR is by far the most popular party in Romania, according to polls, and would stand to make major gains if a new election were to be called.
Dan’s position has long been that he does not want to put at risk Romania’s pro-Western orientation by handing power to Simion, who has opposed support for Ukraine and is severely critical of EU leadership in Brussels.
But even some of Dan’s allies now think an unprecedented snap election should be considered.
Advertisement
Before Wednesday’s vote, Mureșan himself said a new general election should not be ruled out. “Early elections are not desirable, but keeping Romania in a prolonged political crisis out of fear of snap polls does not offer stability to citizens or confidence to investors who want to create jobs in Romania,” he said.
The Save Romania Union (USR) party, which Dan founded though has since left, backed Mureșan for prime minister. But after losing the vote, USR leader Dominic Fritz called for fresh elections. “The time has come to return to the people’s vote,” he said.

Berlin is a city filled with history, creativity and energy, from street art on the Berlin Wall to cycling through its leafy streets. In this episode, Lilly Douse discovers what brings Germany’s capital to life.
Berlin welcomed over 12 million guests in 2025 and recorded almost 30 million overnight stays. Many visitors come for the famous landmarks, but hidden among them are distinctive areas with plenty to explore.

Few have shaped the city recent history more than the Berlin Wall. Constructed in 1961 and brought down in 1989, it divided the city for 28 years. Today, a long stretch of the wall remains, covered in graffiti and street art.

In West Berlin, the Wilmina Hotel, a former women’s prison, offers guests the chance to stay in an unusual historic building. With iron window bars and long corridors, the former world war two prison took 10 years to renovate.
Cycling with Sascha Möllering of Berlin by Bike, Lilly visits Mauerpark, a green space with a divided history. Their route continues to Zionskirche, a Christian church closely linked to East Germany’s communist past.
For visitors wandering through Berlin on foot, by boat or by bike, there is always something unique to experience.

Exhaling may speed up reaction times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Exhaling may speed up reaction times
The finding could be linked to how brain waves sync with our breathing
A sprinter’s first task is to react to the starting pistol. Now, a button-clicking experiment suggests that how quickly people respond to a cue may depend in part on whether they’re breathing in or out.
Volunteers’ reaction times were faster when they exhaled or held their breath compared with when they inhaled, researchers report September 28 in iScience.
Ken Paller and Erika Yamazaki, then both cognitive neuroscientists at Northwestern University, made their discovery while studying breathing patterns to find treatments for sleep apnea. Yamazaki graduated from her PhD earlier this year.
Paller and Yamazaki determined how sleepy 35 volunteers were with a simple reaction-time test. The volunteers were tasked with clicking a button when an on-screen red square turned yellow.
Yamazaki realized that, because the volunteers’ breathing was recorded through short tubes in the nose throughout the task, the researchers could also check whether inhaling or exhaling influenced reaction times.
Reaction times were, on average, 41 milliseconds faster during exhalation than during inhalation. This finding held regardless of how sleepy or alert the volunteers were.
That might not sound like a huge difference, but Noah Lyles won the 2024 Olympic men’s 100-meter final by five thousandths of a second. Those 41 milliseconds would have made the difference between Lyles winning and finishing fourth.
But the relationship between breath and brain appears to be complex. A 2016 study found that reaction times were faster during inhalation than exhalation in tests of recall and facial recognition. But these tasks differed from the hair-trigger change Paller and Yamazaki studied. Those tasks required more cognitive processing, Paller says, because they required the participants to judge whether, for example, a face look fearful or surprised, rather than waiting for a simple cue. “That may or may not have the same relationship with respiration.”
The mechanism behind these findings isn’t clear, although Paller points to studies, like the one from 2016, that suggest our breath is synced to the ebb and flow of our brain waves.
In a race decided by thousandths of a second, every factor matters, even a single breath.

What will it take to end the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:57:11 UTC
21:57:11 KST

Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is currently facing the largest and deadliest Ebola disease outbreak in its history. The outbreak is unfolding in eastern DRC amid a decades-long humanitarian crisis marked by conflict, violence, displacement, food insecurity, and multiple overlapping health emergencies. These conditions make it much harder to stop the outbreak, which continues to spread at an alarming rate.
More than 8,000 people have been confirmed to have contracted Ebola, while at least 3,900 have died from the disease.
Stopping the spread of Ebola disease requires multiple coordinated actions to be carried out at the same time. The response must include finding people suspected to have the disease, safely isolating them and transferring them for care, tracing contacts who may have been exposed, preventing infection in health facilities and in communities, and working closely with affected communities to build trust, share information about the disease, and encourage people to seek care early.
Focusing on just one area is not enough. No matter how difficult they may be to implement, all these actions are essential and rely on each other to end the outbreak.
Surveillance
Epidemiological surveillance means collecting, gathering and analysing key information to understand how an outbreak is evolving and where the disease is spreading. It helps those responding to an outbreak see how quickly it is spreading and where more action is needed to stop it. By tracking this information over time, health teams can spot warning signs that the outbreak may be spreading to new areas, respond faster, and adapt the response as the situation changes. This includes tracking test results, suspected and confirmed cases, and people who may have been exposed to the disease through contact with an infected person.
Infection prevention and control
Infection prevention and control (IPC) refers to the measures used to stop Ebola disease from spreading, especially within healthcare facilities. Because Ebola disease is spread through contact with infected bodily fluids, preventing exposure is critical. In treatment centres and hospitals, IPC begins as soon as a person arrives: anyone suspected of having Ebola disease is identified quickly, separated from others, and isolated while awaiting test results. Patients with confirmed Ebola disease are then cared for in dedicated areas to reduce the risk of transmission.
IPC depends on strict protocols to protect healthcare workers and other patients. Staff wear full personal protective equipment (PPE) and are specially trained to put it on and remove it safely. It also includes safe blood collection, careful disposal of needles and contaminated waste, routine cleaning and disinfection of beds and equipment, and clear ways for patients, staff, family, and equipment to move within the facility.
Water, sanitation and hygiene
Water, sanitation, and hygiene (sometimes abbreviated to WASH or WatSan) plays an important part of wider IPC efforts, helping to prevent the spread of Ebola disease.
 
In Ebola treatment centres (ETCs), WASH teams regularly clean rooms, beds, toilets, floors, and shared spaces, because bodily fluids can carry the virus. They do this using strict cleaning procedures with soap, water, and chlorine.
WASH also means making sure there is enough water for cleaning, laundry, disinfection, handwashing, and safe wastewater disposal. It helps patients that have survived Ebola disease return home safely by making sure they can wash, change into clean clothes, and disinfect their belongings before leaving the treatment centre. WASH teams also clean ambulances and homes of infected patients, and help carry out safe burials, since the body of someone who has died from Ebola can still spread the disease.
Community engagement
Communities play a crucial role in ending Ebola disease outbreaks. Working in partnership with community leaders helps to ensure that correct information about the disease is shared within affected communities. It also helps people adapt their behaviour to keep themselves and their families safe and seek care when needed. This also builds trust in the broader response.
Community-based surveillance – community members gathering information from within their communities – is also key to make sure we understand how the outbreak is spreading.
Patient care
Patient care is a key part of the Ebola response. It involves caring for people with the disease in a safe and respectful way, giving them the best possible chance of recovery while reducing the risk of infecting others.
Although there is currently no specific cure or vaccine for Bundibugyo virus – which is driving the current outbreak – early supportive care can still save lives. Patients can receive treatment for symptoms such as pain, fever, vomiting, and diarrhoea, which includes fluids, food, rest, and treatment for other illnesses, such as malaria.
Patient care also helps build trust. When people know that treatment centres offer safe, dignified care, they are more likely to seek help early. This helps health teams detect cases sooner, start treatment more quickly, and reduce further spread of the disease.
Bringing care closer to affected communities, including through isolation centres linked to existing health facilities, is especially important. It improves access, helps families stay connected, and strengthens other essential health services at the same time.

U.S. Marine Corps to test electric seaglider in the field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:56:28 UTC
21:56:28 KST

- REGENT Craft said the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab added $5 million to their Seaglider partnership, bringing its total value to $19.25 million.
- Phase IV includes six deliverables focused on demonstrating the full-scale Viceroy prototype in operationally relevant environments and command-and-control integration.
The U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab has added $5 million to its work with REGENT Craft on the Seaglider, an electric craft that skims just above the water, bringing the total value of the partnership to $19.25 million, the Rhode Island company said on Sept. 30.
The new money funds a fourth phase with six deliverables. REGENT says they center on showing what the full-scale Viceroy Seaglider prototype can do in conditions closer to real operations, and on command-and-control work covering how the craft would be tasked, tracked and coordinated alongside other military assets. The company did not give a timeline for the phase or say where the demonstrations will take place.
The partnership has grown in steps. A $4.75 million first and second phase tested whether the concept was technically feasible, and a $9.5 million third phase paid for demonstrations of the full-scale prototype. REGENT says that phase has now been completed, including flight.
“What started as a feasibility question has become a real operational program, and that trajectory says a lot about where this technology is headed,” said Billy Thalheimer, co-founder and CEO of REGENT.
A Seaglider floats in port like a boat, rises onto a hydrofoil as it picks up speed, and then lifts off to fly within one wingspan of the surface. Flying that low uses a cushion of air trapped between the wing and the water, known as ground effect, which cuts drag and lets a battery-powered craft carry useful loads over longer distances.
REGENT says the Viceroy will fly at up to 290 km/h (180 mph) on routes of up to 290 km (180 miles). Because it takes off and lands on water, it does not need a runway, and it can be recharged from shore or from a ship. The company also says the craft’s low flight path keeps it under radar coverage while its electric motors give off little heat, though those claims have not been independently tested in public.
The Viceroy prototype flew in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island, on Sept. 2, a step REGENT called a key milestone in its test campaign. The company is also testing Squire, a smaller autonomous Seaglider.
For the U.S. Marine Corps, the draw is logistics. REGENT pitches the craft as a way to move troops and equipment quickly between islands and ships without relying on airfields or ports, the kind of dispersed operations the U.S. Marine Corps has been planning for in the Pacific.
“This next phase of our MCWL partnership is about putting the technology in the hands of the warfighter so they can fully realize the advantages Seagliders bring to the forward-operating areas,” said Becky Russo, REGENT’s director of defense mission integration.
REGENT says it has secured more than $340 million in funding commitments from investors, including Lockheed Martin and Japan Airlines, and has civilian orders on six continents.

From MH370 to Germanwings: the chilling history of suspected pilot-suicide crashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:55:35 UTC
21:55:35 KST

Reports Wednesday of drama aboard a flyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, in which one pilot is suspected of stabbing his colleague and attempting to seize the aircraft, have revived one of civil aviation’s deepest fears: the possibility that the person entrusted with hundreds of lives could deliberately turn an aircraft into a weapon or a vehicle for suicide.
Such cases are statistically extremely rare, but aviation history shows they are not unprecedented. Investigators and airlines have often been reluctant to conclude definitively that a pilot deliberately killed passengers along with himself, particularly when motive cannot be proved. Yet a series of disasters, from the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 to the Germanwings crash in the French Alps, has repeatedly raised precisely that possibility.
Aviation’s greatest mystery: Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370
The most famous and enduring mystery in modern aviation began on March 8, 2014, when a Malaysia Airlines Boeing 777 disappeared while flying from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing with 239 passengers and crew aboard.
Hundreds of millions of dollars were spent on vast searches across the Indian Ocean, but the aircraft has never been recovered in full. Only scattered pieces of wreckage were later found after washing ashore along the coast of East Africa.
Numerous theories have been proposed, ranging from catastrophic mechanical failure to hijacking and terrorism. Over the years, however, some aviation investigators and experts have increasingly argued that veteran captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah may have deliberately diverted and crashed the aircraft.
According to those theories, Shah remained in control until the aircraft’s final moments and may have been the only person aboard still conscious. Experts have suggested that cabin pressurization may have been disabled, incapacitating passengers and crew, while the younger co-pilot, Fariq Abdul Hamid, was also somehow prevented from intervening.
Investigators also found that Shah had practiced a route over the southern Indian Ocean on his home flight simulator. During the real flight, the aircraft’s communications systems were disabled and the plane changed course, flying along boundaries between Malaysian and Thai airspace in a manner some experts believe was intended to reduce the chances of detection.
Analysis of the flight path has also led to speculation that the aircraft banked over Penang, Shah’s hometown, in what some have described as a possible final farewell. Reports later focused on difficulties in his personal life and his strong political support for an opposition leader who had been imprisoned, but no definitive motive has ever been established.
Germanwings Flight 9525: A deliberate descent into the Alps
If MH370 remains shrouded in uncertainty, the circumstances surrounding Germanwings Flight 9525 in March 2015 were far clearer.
German co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, 27, was alone in the cockpit after the captain stepped out during a flight from Barcelona to Düsseldorf. Investigators found that Lubitz locked the reinforced cockpit door and refused to let the captain return.
For roughly 10 minutes, cockpit recordings captured the captain pounding on the door and attempting to force his way back inside as Lubitz reset the autopilot from a cruising altitude of about 11,500 meters to just 30 meters and directed the Airbus toward the French Alps.
The aircraft struck the mountainside, killing all 150 passengers and crew.
The cockpit voice recorder captured Lubitz breathing steadily until impact. The investigation later exposed serious questions over medical oversight. Lubitz had a history of severe depression that had interrupted his pilot training in 2008. In the months before the crash, he experienced vision problems, searched online for information about suicide and feared losing his job.
Two weeks before the fatal flight, a doctor had reportedly recommended psychiatric hospitalization. Because of medical confidentiality and Lubitz’s failure to inform his employer, Lufthansa, the information did not reach the airline and he continued flying.
The disaster prompted major changes across the industry, including widespread adoption of rules requiring two people to remain in the cockpit at all times, although some of those measures were later revised.
China Eastern Flight MU5735 and the near-vertical dive
Seven years after Germanwings, the crash of China Eastern Airlines Flight MU5735 revived similar suspicions.
In March 2022, the Boeing 737-800 was flying domestically from Kunming to Guangzhou with 132 passengers and crew when it suddenly entered an extreme, almost vertical dive from roughly 29,000 feet.
Less than two minutes later, the aircraft struck mountainous terrain in Guangxi, leaving a deep crater. No one survived.
Video from local security cameras showed the aircraft plunging almost nose-first toward the ground, immediately raising questions over whether the crash could have been caused by an ordinary technical malfunction.
According to reports citing U.S. officials involved in examining the flight recorders, control inputs appeared to have been deliberately made from the cockpit, forcing the aircraft into the dive.
Chinese authorities did not publish a final report formally declaring the crash a suicide. International reports later focused on one member of the cockpit crew, a former captain who had been demoted to co-pilot and was said to have suffered financial losses and serious personal and professional distress. The precise cause, however, has not been officially established as deliberate pilot action.
‘What did you do, shut off the engines?’: EgyptAir Flight 990
Another deeply disputed case occurred in October 1999, when EgyptAir Flight 990 crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Massachusetts shortly after leaving New York’s JFK Airport.
All 217 passengers and crew were killed.
U.S. investigators concluded that relief first officer Gameel al-Batouti waited until the captain had left the cockpit, disconnected the autopilot, reduced engine power and pushed the Boeing 767 into a steep dive.
Cockpit recordings captured the captain returning and asking in alarm what had happened and whether the engines had been shut down. Al-Batouti was heard repeatedly saying that he was placing his trust in God.
American investigators concluded that al-Batouti’s control inputs caused the crash but stopped short of formally declaring that he intended to kill himself, saying his motives could not be determined.
Egyptian officials rejected the suicide theory and maintained for years that mechanical failure was responsible.
SilkAir Flight 185 and the Mozambique cockpit lockout
Similar disagreement followed the December 1997 crash of SilkAir Flight 185.
The Boeing 737 was traveling from Jakarta to Singapore when it plunged into a river in Indonesia at extremely high speed, killing all 104 people aboard.
A U.S. investigation concluded that the flight recorders had been deliberately disconnected and that the crash was the result of intentional actions by the captain, who was reportedly facing heavy financial losses of more than $1 million as well as disciplinary problems at work.
Indonesian authorities, however, did not formally classify the crash as suicide, leaving the case officially unresolved.
A similar sequence unfolded in November 2013 aboard a Mozambique Airlines flight bound for Angola.
The aircraft crashed in northern Namibia, killing 33 people. Investigators found that the captain had taken advantage of the co-pilot’s absence, locked himself inside the cockpit, ignored attempts to re-enter and disregarded aircraft warnings before directing the plane toward the ground.
Later reports said the captain had been undergoing serious personal and family difficulties, including marital problems and the death of his son about a year earlier.
Earlier cases: Royal Air Maroc and Japan Airlines
Suspected or confirmed deliberate crashes long predate the modern era of reinforced cockpit doors.
In August 1994, a Royal Air Maroc passenger aircraft crashed in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains shortly after taking off from Agadir, killing all 44 passengers and crew. Investigators concluded that the pilot had deliberately disconnected flight systems and directed the aircraft toward the ground.
In February 1982, a Japan Airlines flight crashed into Tokyo Bay while approaching Haneda Airport, killing 24 of the 174 people aboard.
Investigators found that the captain, who had serious psychiatric problems, deliberately activated reverse thrust during the approach in an attempt to crash the aircraft. The co-pilot and flight engineer physically struggled with him in the cockpit and tried to pull back on the controls, preventing an even greater loss of life.
The Qantas pilot who fought the urge to shut down his engines
Not every case ended in catastrophe.
One troubling case later reported by the Sydney Morning Herald involved a Qantas pilot who continued flying passenger aircraft for years despite telling colleagues about suicidal thoughts.
The pilot later said that during a flight to Singapore he experienced an overpowering urge to shut down the aircraft’s engines and had to use his left hand to physically restrain his right hand as it moved toward the controls.
He left the cockpit until the episode passed and later returned to his seat.
Despite telling colleagues and being assessed by several doctors, he was initially considered fit to continue flying. He eventually retired in 1982 and was later diagnosed with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety and depression.
The case highlighted one of aviation medicine’s most difficult dilemmas: how to identify a dangerous psychological crisis in a profession where pilots may fear that admitting symptoms could end their careers.
A study by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration found that pilot suicide was exceptionally rare, accounting for about 0.3% of the fatal aviation accidents it examined between 2003 and 2012. The eight cases identified involved small private aircraft rather than commercial passenger flights.
The report nevertheless stressed that deliberate crashes are unusually difficult to predict and prevent, and that the true number may be undercounted because suicidal intent is often impossible to prove without clear evidence.

Solovetsky Monastery restoration to preserve traces of British shelling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:55:00 UTC
21:55:00 KST

ARKHANGELSK, September 30. /TASS/. Traces of shelling off British ships on the Solovetsky Monastery in 1854 during the Crimean War will be marked and preserved during the fortress walls' restoration, the Foundation for Conservation and Development of the Solovetsky Archipelago (Solovki) told TASS.
"One of the most important tasks that has emerged during the restoration is to preserve evidence of historical events of the Crimean War of 1854 - the traces of shelling by the British artillery. In the passage between the Pryadilnaya (Spinning Mill) Tower to the Belaya (White) Tower, we can see traces of damage to brickwork and boulders by metal cores. The restorers face the task to mark the places to where the cores have fallen, to identify them, and to preserve them under the restoration process, leaving the traces for future generations."
At the height of the Crimean War, on July 6, 1854, the Brisk and the Miranda British warships approached the Solovetsky Monastery. The British fired several warning shots, which the monastery perceived as the beginning of hostilities. The return salvo's core from the Solovetsky walls hit the English ship, damaging it quite badly. The squadron commander demanded the garrison surrendered, but the Solovetsky abbot refused to obey.
The intense shelling of the monastery continued for several hours in a row. The British ships rained down about 2,000 cannonballs and bombs on the monastery. However, the sheer superiority of the British in weapons and ammunition proved powerless before the defenders' courage and the fortress walls' power. The monastery's inhabitants resisted skillfully, forcing the British ships to retreat from the archipelago. The fortress walls still have traces of the attack: in the passage between the Pryadilnaya (Spinning Mill) Tower to the Belaya (White) Tower, there are traces of damage to brickwork and boulders by metal cores.
The Solovetsky Monastery restoration is due to be completed in 2029 - by the 600th anniversary of the first monastic settlement on Solovki. The boulder-brick masonry system is a specific feature of the Solovetsky Fortress. The main walls and towers are made of boulders of various sizes, while the structural details - the upper loopholes, the curtain walls' pillars and parapets, arches in the aisles, and vaulted lintels in cannon loopholes - are made of brick. The brickwork features white lime mortar. The used gray-blue natural stone, red brick and white mortar give a bright, unusual and rich color to the walls.
The Solovetsky Monastery is a unique monument of the Russian North, founded in the 15th century. In 1992, UNESCO put the monastery on its World Heritage List.

Quote from NATO: "None of NATO's exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation. We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Background:
- Lithuania previously described Russia's new threats concerning Kaliningrad as psychological pressure.
- Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski believes NATO should step up military exercises near Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast.

Upanishads to Mahabharata: NCERT explains roots of national, SC mottos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:53:39 UTC
21:53:39 KST

The NCERT has introduced a groundbreaking Class IX social science textbook that bridges modern principles of governance with ancient Indian wisdom.
New Delhi: NCERT’s new Class IX social science textbook traces India’s national motto, “Satyameva Jayate”, to the Mundaka Upanishad and the Supreme Court’s “Yato Dharmastato Jayah” to the Mahabharata, linking modern institutions to ancient texts. The lesson presents these connections as expressions of the values and responsibilities that should guide governance in a democracy.“Understanding Society: India and Beyond”, Part 2, became available on Tuesday, September 29, nearly six months into the academic session. Part 1 came out in June. The six-chapter volume, which TOI reported on Wednesday, spans history, geography, political science and economics under the National Education Policy 2020 and National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023.The chapter “Governance and Public Policy” translates the national motto as “Truth alone triumphs” and the Supreme Court’s motto as “Where there is Dharma (righteous duty), there is victory”. It places these alongside the Sengol and Gandhi’s conception of Ram Rajya.These references are “not just symbolic or superficial”, the book says, but express institutional values and the responsibility to ensure good governance.
It contrasts the national motto with “Heaven’s Light, Our Guide”, used by the British Order of the Star of India. The chapter acknowledges that colonial institutions persisted after Independence, but says India’s leaders framed the Constitution in keeping with India’s own values and ideals.The Sengol is described as a “cultural marker of rulership and good governance”, with a tradition dating back more than 1,000 years to the Cholas. Prime Minister Narendra Modi installed it near the Lok Sabha Speaker’s chair in the new Parliament building on May 28, 2023.The textbook recounts Jawaharlal Nehru receiving the sceptre from Tamil Nadu’s Adheenam saints at Independence. Modi had described it as a symbol of the transfer of power. Congress disputed this in 2023, saying there was no documentary evidence that Mountbatten, C Rajagopalachari or Nehru had described it in those terms.Gandhi’s Ram Rajya is presented as an ideal rooted in probity, transparency, compassion and welfare. The chapter links it to the Ramayana and 16th-century Ramcharitmanas, calling it “one of the best examples of good governance and a good collective life”. It discusses Rajdharma as the ruler’s duty to protect people and uphold righteousness.
“Good governance was measured not only by the ruler’s authority but by the peace, prosperity, justice, and well-being in society,” it says. The chapter also draws on Kautilya’s Arthashastra to place the ruler’s happiness in the happiness of the people.The chapter also identifies seven features of good governance: responsiveness, transparency, participation, rule of law, accountability, effectiveness and inclusiveness.It stresses citizens’ rights, equality before the law and access to public services, while assigning responsibilities to government, citizens, the media, civil society and the private sector in achieving public welfare.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

German state pledges stronger economic ties with Türkiye

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:52:14 UTC
21:52:14 KST

The prime minister of Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia state has vowed to build on longstanding economic ties with Türkiye and further strengthen cooperation.
Hendrik Wust made the remarks at the Türkiye-North Rhine-Westphalia Business Forum in Istanbul on Wednesday.
The event was jointly organised by Türkiye’s Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) and Germany’s trade agency NRW.Global Business.
“For decades now, people, ideas, and investment have moved in both directions. Especially now, as international trade barriers increase and supply chains are under pressure, reliable connections are more valuable than ever.
“Our aim is to build on these strong ties and strengthen our cooperation even further.”
He said the state government had agreed on a fast-track visa process for Turkish businesspeople to overcome lengthy processing times that hinder essential face-to-face cooperation.
Wust backed efforts to modernise the 30-year-old European Customs Union and update EU industrial policy to reflect the current structure of global supply chains.
He described the Turkish economy as an indispensable part of the European value chain.
He noted that Türkiye stood out as a top player in foreign direct investment and ranked as the state’s third-largest trading partner.
More than one in three Turkish-owned companies in Germany are based in North Rhine-Westphalia, totalling about 1,300 businesses, he said.
Wust also highlighted Türkiye’s large onshore wind market and investment in power generation and transmission infrastructure, saying energy prices and security were crucial to North Rhine-Westphalia’s heavy and energy-intensive industry.
“We see that Türkiye has one of Europe’s largest onshore wind markets,” he said.
He said new memorandums of understanding signed at the forum could create future partnerships and further strengthen economic and geopolitical ties.
Focus on implementing agreements
Serap Guler, a state minister at the German Federal Foreign Office, reaffirmed Berlin’s commitment to expanding economic cooperation with Türkiye and integrating Turkish industry into European supply chains.
Guler highlighted that around 8,600 German companies currently operate in Türkiye, creating more than 100,000 direct jobs.
She noted that geopolitical tensions and supply chain risks threaten competitiveness, emphasising that both nations must focus on implementing agreements reached during the German-Turkish Foreign Ministers’ Strategic Dialogue held in May.
Unlocking the full economic potential of nearly 540 million people across the EU and Türkiye requires modernising the Customs Union, the minister said.
She stressed the need to remove tariff and non-tariff trade barriers, rely on rule-of-law instruments, and ensure Türkiye applies the agreement to all EU member states.
Guler stated that Germany strongly advocates in Brussels for a “Made with Europe” approach under the EU Industrial Accelerator Act to include key partners like Türkiye.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held another situation assessment with senior defense and aviation officials Wednesday following the incident aboard a flyDubai flight bound for Israel that was diverted to Saudi Arabia after the Omani co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash the aircraft.
A rescue aircraft dispatched by flyDubai landed in Saudi Arabia, and the Israeli passengers stranded in the kingdom began preparing to board for the return flight to Israel.
“They’re starting to put us on the plane,” one passenger told ynet.
The flight is expected to land at Ben Gurion Airport between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. However, some passengers refused to board the flyDubai aircraft, saying they were afraid to fly with the airline following the incident.
Meanwhile, Israeli investigators are increasingly assessing that the co-pilot planned to crash the aircraft in order to kill the Israelis onboard.
An initial investigation has raised the possibility that the Emirati pilot who prevented the co-pilot from crashing the plane, with help from some of the Israeli passengers, used an emergency axe kept in the cockpit and intended for breaking a window.
According to that possibility, the pilot struck or stabbed the co-pilot with the axe while attempting to overpower him.
Investigators have apparently ruled out an earlier suggestion that the co-pilot had managed to bring an axe aboard the aircraft, since flight crews undergo strict security screening before boarding.
However, investigators are also examining the opposite possibility: that the co-pilot, who is suspected of planning the attack, used the axe against the pilot who tried to stop him.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev, meanwhile, asked Netanyahu to immediately suspend flyDubai flights to Israel until the circumstances of the incident are clarified.
Regev said flyDubai had violated the aviation agreement between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, which she said permits only pilots from countries that maintain diplomatic relations with Israel to land in the country.

Regev is also demanding that Israeli airlines be immediately allowed to resume flights to Dubai with Israeli security screening. Israeli carriers are currently barred from flying to Dubai because of a dispute over security requirements.
The incident also had an immediate economic impact. Shares in Israeli airlines El Al and Israir jumped about 7% and more than 9%, respectively, on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
The emerging assessment that the flyDubai incident may have been an attempted terrorist attack could lead more Israeli passengers to favor Israeli carriers, which employ Israeli pilots, many of them former Air Force personnel, and operate under a stringent security system partly funded by the state.

Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:49:01 UTC
21:49:01 KST

Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- King's College London
- Summary:
- A review of more than 265,000 people found that cannabis use was associated with higher rates of both committing violence and becoming a victim of it. The researchers say the link is significant but does not prove cannabis itself is the cause.
- Share:
A large review led by researchers at King's College London has found that people who use cannabis are more likely both to commit violent acts and to experience violence themselves.
Researchers from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) combined data from 63 studies involving more than 265,000 people. They analyzed the general population separately from people receiving psychiatric care.
What the Review Examined
The researchers used the World Health Organization's broad definition of violence, which includes physical, sexual and psychological violence toward another person, both inside and outside intimate relationships.
They also separated self-reported violence from cases that resulted in criminal convictions. When individual studies measured several forms of violence, the researchers focused on the most serious type reported. The findings were published in Psychological Medicine.
Dr. Marta Di Forti, co-author of the study from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) at King's College London, and South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust, said:
"As a clinician, I've seen how heavy cannabis use can be a factor in violence. We've been cautious for a long time about how far we could go in describing this link, but a review of this size lets us speak with more confidence about the risks, while being careful not to stigmatize people who use cannabis more broadly."
Cannabis Use and Victimization
The review also found that people who used cannabis were about one and a half times as likely to become victims of violence. This association was stronger among women than among men.
Professor Sir Robin Murray, senior author of the study from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London, said:
"In the general population, people who used cannabis were around twice as likely to have committed a violent act as those who didn't; for those in psychiatric care, cannabis users were around two and a half times as likely to be violent as other psychiatric patients who didn't use cannabis. The link held in studies that followed people over time, though it was smaller than in studies that looked at a single point in time. For violence that led to a criminal conviction, people who used cannabis were three to four times as likely to have been convicted.
"As cannabis becomes more commercialized and legalized around the world, the conversation about its risks has focused mostly on the person using it. This review shows that violence, both committing it and experiencing it, needs to be part of that conversation too."
Implications for Mental Health and Public Health
Based on the findings, the researchers say mental health services should routinely ask about cannabis use when evaluating a person's risk of violence. They also argue that public health information about cannabis should include the possible connection with violence.
However, the researchers emphasize that the review identifies an association and does not prove that cannabis directly causes violence. Cannabis use often occurs alongside other factors that can also increase the risk of violent behavior or victimization, including alcohol use, other drug use and difficult social circumstances.
Important Limitations
Only a small number of the studies measured how much cannabis people used or how often they used it. The findings involving criminal convictions were also based on a relatively limited number of studies.
Most of the research was conducted before high potency cannabis became common. The researchers suggest that daily use of today's more potent cannabis products could potentially be associated with stronger effects.
The study was supported by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre: Maudsley and the Medical Research Council (MR/T007818/1). The views expressed are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care.
Story Source:
Materials provided by King's College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Giulia Trotta, Victoria Rodriguez, Paolo Marino, Meklit Gurmesa, Edoardo Spinazzola, Zhikun Li, Luis Alameda, Marta Di Forti, Robin Murray, Evangelos Vassos. Cannabis use is associated with increased risk of violence: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychological Medicine, 2026; 56 DOI: 10.1017/S0033291726105856

Against the backdrop of setbacks in the Chinese market, BMW is preparing steps to improve profitability — what it will do

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:48:37 EEST
