Homicides fall as organised crime grows more profitable – and networked
Homicide rates are falling across much of the world, but organised crime is on the rise in many regions as criminal networks diversify into trafficking, migrant smuggling, and the exploitation of natural resources, a new UN report launched on Wednesday revealed.
The study, Crime and Justice in a Changing World, by the UN Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute (UNICRI), was presented on Wednesday at the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in Abu Dhabi.
Drawing on nine regional studies, it finds that homicides fell from 5.9 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 5.2 in 2023 and are projected to decrease by 25 per cent between 2015 and 2030 under current trends.
Regional disparities
However, rates remain high in Latin America and the Caribbean and sub-Saharan Africa – which together account for roughly two thirds of all homicide victims worldwide – and are frequently driven by organised crime, gangs and transnational criminal groups.
The report says the two trends are not contradictory but reflect a shift in where criminal profit is generated: away from localised predation and towards transnational markets, digital victimisation and the exploitation of licit trade and supply chains.
Criminal networks are increasingly intertwined with legitimate economies, the report finds.
In Latin America, cartels that began in drug trafficking have expanded into agriculture, mining, fishing and wildlife, while Europol has assessed that nearly one fifth of criminal networks in Europe operate across multiple criminal markets.
In parts of Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, criminal groups operating from special economic zones traffic thousands of people and run cyberfraud schemes, including romance-investment fraud and crypto scams.
Check our UN News stories and original reporting on Asia’s ‘scam farms’ here
In Cambodia, estimates of illicit proceeds from cybercrime and illegal gambling range from $12.5 billion to $19 billion a year – as much as 60 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Technology has lowered the barriers to entry, with generative AI and “cybercrime-as-a-service” models meaning criminal capability no longer necessarily depends on organisational sophistication.
A 2025 survey of 42 countries cited in the report found that 57 per cent of adults worldwide had experienced a scam and 23 per cent had lost money in the previous 12 months.
Tougher responses
Justice systems are responding under considerable strain, the report says, with many increasingly shaped by concerns around security and State control rather than the rule of law and human rights.
It points to militarised policing, more punitive approaches to prisons and the lowering of the minimum age of criminal responsibility in parts of Oceania, East Asia and Latin America – often in tension with evidence on what reduces crime.
Meanwhile, States are adopting surveillance and AI technologies faster than the rules needed to govern them.
The report also highlights successes, noting that Brazilian megacity São Paulo’s sustained decline in homicides since the early 2000s has been linked to data-driven policing, firearms restrictions and municipal prevention measures.
Five avenues
The study suggests five areas for further research, engagement and transregional coordination:
- how emerging criminal models spread from one region to another
- when and where different kinds of crime overlap and feed each other
- long term effects on crime levels and what happens to trust in institutions
- effects of increasingly transactional cooperation, versus lasting partnerships
- how a multipolar world changes the way institutions work

World News in Brief: Storm clouds over Gaza, deadly obstacles face Mexican women rights defenders, Latvia booze ban proves lifesaver
UN teams are racing to protect families in Gaza from the coming rainy season, but restricted access to land and shortages of critical supplies are hampering the effort, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Wednesday.
Since Monday, partners have assessed three possible sites for temporary shelters for people choosing to leave flood-prone areas or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
They are also examining more than 450 existing displacement sites at high risk of flooding – home to about a fifth of Gaza’s population.
Land and access
Explosive ordnance must be cleared from the new sites before voluntary relocation can happen at scale, Mr. Dujarric said, along with levelling sandy ground and installing drainage, water and lighting.
“The main obstacle is restrictions on access to 65 per cent of Gaza’s land”, he said, adding that the remaining 35 per cent is already overcrowded.
More Israeli approvals are needed to import machinery, spare parts and engine oil, while funding for fuel and shelter is also urgently required.
Meanwhile, health partners are training local medical staff to manage non-communicable diseases, but medicine shortages are limiting early detection and treatment.
“Life-threatening gaps remain in specialized cancer care, including shortages of essential chemotherapy and radiotherapy supplies.”
Women searching for Mexico’s disappeared face deadly violence
Women searching for people forcibly disappeared in Mexico continue to face deadly violence and often themselves become victims, independent UN human rights experts warned on Wednesday, urging the State to protect them.
Recent attacks in Sinaloa highlight the risks. On 29 August, human rights defender Elisa Altagracia Bonilla was reported disappeared, and Alma Rosa Rojo Medina, founder of the collective Voces Unidas por la Vida, was attacked alongside her daughter and two children.
On 1 September, members of the collective Corazones Unidos por una Misma Causa were struck by a vehicle during a peaceful demonstration in Mazatlán.
The same collective has been repeatedly targeted: one member, Rubí Gómez-Tagle, was murdered this year, and another, María de los Ángeles Valenzuela, disappeared in October 2025.
Government missing in action
“The work of these women constitutes a fundamental extension of their rights, the right to truth, justice and reparations…They are carrying out a task that is primarily the State’s responsibility. The State must fully assume this responsibility and not shift the burden onto the families,” the experts said.
The violence occurs amid near-total impunity, they added, calling it “a tragic example of the State’s failure to fulfil its obligations to protect human rights defenders”.
The independent experts – who are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work – welcomed the General Assembly’s decision to designate 19 December the International Day in Recognition of Women Searchers for Disappeared Persons, and urged Mexico to publicly recognise the importance of these women’s work.
They have previously raised their concerns with the Government, including in an April 2026 letter about the killing of Ms. Gómez-Tagle, to which it replied.
New alcohol policy gives booze the boot in Latvia
To Latvia finally, where simple public health measures to reduce alcohol consumption have been linked to a “significant decline in deaths”, just months after they took effect.
According to the UN World Health Organization (WHO), deaths that were wholly attributable to heavy drinking decreased by 27 per cent, after the new restrictions came into effect.
Mortality from alcohol poisoning, liver disease and acute pancreatitis that are all associated with regular drinking “fell significantly”, WHO noted, after evaluating data submitted by the Latvian health authorities.
‘Alcohol is everywhere’
Karina Zalite, head of WHO’s Country Office in Latvia, welcomed the Government’s measures to make alcohol less available, including reducing times when it can be bought, ending instant deliveries when it is purchased online and restricting promotions and sales in gambling venues:
“Alcohol is everywhere in our lives,” she noted.
“It’s at celebrations, in sport, at the checkout counters and stores. It’s easy to forget what it really is, an addictive substance and one linked to at least seven types of cancer.”
According to WHO, cancers associated with drinking include bowel cancer and breast cancer. Alcohol use is responsible for approximately 800,000 deaths across Europe every year.

House Speaker Mike Johnson stumping and fundraising for California GOP congressional candidates
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- House Speaker Mike Johnson is heading to California’s Central Valley and Inland Empire to campaign and raise money for Republicans in midterm contests.
- The California trip is part of Johnson’s plans to campaign in 22 states in an effort to help Republicans retain control of the House before the Nov. 3 election.
- California will play a pivotal role in determining the control of Congress.
House Speaker Mike Johnson plans to visit California on Wednesday to stump and fundraise for Republican candidates in a state that could determine control of the U.S. House of Representatives during President Trump’s final two years in office.
Johnson (R-La.) plans to visit the Central Valley and the Inland Empire, a sign of the importance of California congressional contests in the November midterm election.
David Wasserman, a congressional forecaster for the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, said that Johnson is attempting to mitigate the aftermath of Proposition 50, the redrawing of California’s congressional districts that voters approved in November in response to Trump’s efforts to tilt districts in his favor elsewhere in the nation, notably Texas.
“If it weren’t for Republican efforts to redraw Texas, Proposition 50 wouldn’t have seen the light of day,” said Wasserman, who predicts Democrats will win control of the House, and said that Republicans would have a better chance at holding more seats if they hadn’t prompted the redistricting fight.
Redrawing congressional districts typically happens once a decade after the U.S. Census, and in California, voters in 2010 decided to hand the power of crafting the state’s districts to an independent commission. After Trump pushed Texas to redraw its congressional boundaries to increase GOP representation in Congress last year, California Democrats responded by persuading voters to reshape its districts to favor Democrats, who already dominate the state’s 52-member congressional delegation.
“California Republicans are on the verge of extinction because of the White House action,” Wasserman said.
In Chowchilla, Johnson is scheduled to hold a fundraiser and a rally in support of former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln, who is trying to topple Rep. Adam Gray (D-Merced) in one of the most competitive congressional races in the nation. He is expected to be joined by Republican National Committee chairman Joe Gruters, California Republican Party Chair Corrin Rankin and Congress members from Texas and Michigan.
Johnson is also holding a get-out-the-vote event in support of Rep. David Valadao (R-Hanford), a longtime Democratic target given the voter makeup of his Central Valley district; and an evening fundraiser in Riverside for Jim Desmond, a member of the San Diego County Board of Supervisors who is running in the district being vacated by longtime Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Vista).
Issa decided to retire after his congressional district was redrawn because of Proposition 50. He has endorsed Desmond to represent the new district, which spans San Diego and Riverside counties.
The California trip is part of Johnson’s plans to campaign in 22 states in an effort to help Republicans retain control of the House before the Nov. 3 election.
Despite California’s sapphire tilt — registered Democratic voters outnumber Republicans nearly 2 to 1 — the state’s residents are often the largest donors to politicians on both sides of the aisle. Democrats headed here in coming days include gubernatorial candidates Amy Acton of Ohio, Deb Haaland of New Mexico and Gina Hinojosa of Texas.
Trump sent followers a fundraising appeal Tuesday focused on Democrats’ ability to win control of Congress, which would upend his agenda during his final two years in office.
“I’ve never asked for sympathy. I’ve never asked this country to feel sorry for me. I’ve never asked for anything,” he said in the email. “That changes today. With less than 45 days until midterm elections, the left is ready to put the final nail in my coffin.”
Christian Martinez, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, pointed to the pivotal role California will play in determining control of Congress.
“California’s House races will decide whether working families keep fighters like David Valadao, James Gallagher, Kevin Lincoln, and Jim Desmond or get more of the same from Democrats who raised costs, left the border wide open, and made communities less safe,” Martinez said. “Californians are done paying more, waiting longer, and living with less safety so corrupt Sacramento and Washington Democrats can protect their socialist agenda.”
Anna Elsasser, a spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, shot back that the policies and beliefs of Desmond, Lincoln and Valadao have deeply harmed California families, alluding to high gas prices and the cost of living.
“That’s why Mike Johnson is swooping in to try and save their fledgling campaigns. Voters won’t forget who sold them out to hand massive tax breaks to billionaires and wealthy corporations by gutting healthcare and food assistance, championing chaotic tariffs, and refusing to rein in a costly war that has sent gas prices soaring,” she said. “Californians are ready for change, not another two years of Mike Johnson and D.C. Republicans’ status quo.”

Could a new global panel defuse inequality’s ‘ticking time bomb’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Could a new global panel defuse inequality’s ‘ticking time bomb’?
What if the world tackled inequality with the same kind of scientific firepower it has brought to the climate crisis?
That is the thinking behind a proposal gaining support from world leaders and experts to establish a new ‘International Panel on Inequality’, an independent body that would bring together evidence on the causes and consequences of widening disparities and help governments understand what can be done about them.
The initiative was in the spotlight in New York on 23 September, at an event on the margins of the UN General Assembly’s high-level week, convened by Brazil, Norway, South Africa and Spain.
In remarks delivered by Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, UN Secretary-General António Guterres cast the challenge in stark terms, warning of deepening concentrations of wealth and power and the risks they pose to societies and the international system.
“Sustainable Development Goal 10 calls on us to reduce inequality within and among nations. And yet we see breathtaking levels of income and wealth inequality, with the richest 10 per cent of the world’s population now owning 75 per cent of all wealth,” Mr. Guterres said.
When technology widens the divide
For the Secretary-General, the concern is not simply the scale of inequality today, but how quickly it could deepen.
He warned that the rapid development of frontier technologies could make existing disparities considerably worse, particularly if their wealth and power remain concentrated in only a few hands.
“The breakneck emergence of frontier technology – and the concentration of this technology’s wealth and power in a tiny number of hands – could unleash global inequality at a scale far beyond anything that we have seen,” he said.
The consequences, he warned, reach beyond household incomes and individual opportunity. Unchecked inequality could undermine democratic institutions and deepen the imbalance of power between countries.
“A world where only a few powerful countries can exert control over global security and the global economic architecture is a ticking time bomb,” he said.
An IPCC for inequality?
According to the UN chief, the proposed International Panel on Inequality would seek to place independent, science-based evidence at the heart of the global response.
It would bring together experts to analyse the scale, causes and consequences of inequality and identify practical policy choices available to governments.
Those options could include greater investment in education, health, social protection and decent work; fairer taxation; stronger international cooperation on development finance, trade and investment; reform of the global financial architecture; and more effective enforcement of rules governing corporations and high-net-worth individuals operating across borders.
Gender equality would be central to the Panel’s work, alongside efforts to ensure that technologies such as artificial intelligence are accessible to, and governed by, all countries.
“This proposed Panel can deepen our understanding of the problem – and the policy and political choices that we need to address it,” the Secretary-General said.
‘A collective threat’
Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stiglitz, who chairs the founding committee behind the initiative, argued that inequality should be treated as a global challenge requiring the same depth of scientific analysis that climate change has received.
“Inequality within and between nations is a collective threat to the functioning of our economies and their ability to support human dignity,” he said, stressing that its effects extend well beyond economics to politics, societies and the environment.
The model is the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, which provides the comparison at the heart of the initiative.
Mr. Stiglitz said the proposed inequality panel would similarly provide an independent body of experts able to “assess, synthesize, and present trusted knowledge and analysis” on the causes and consequences of inequality and possible policy responses.
But he also stressed the importance of giving such a body a multilateral foundation and legitimacy. The founding committee, he said, supports establishing the Panel through a UN resolution.
From proposal to UN resolution
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley gave the proposal strong backing at the meeting, looking ahead to the possibility of action by the General Assembly.
For Ms. Mottley, tackling inequality goes to the heart of whether the international community can fulfil the promises made to people through the United Nations.
“I'd like to thank Brazil, Norway, South Africa, and Spain for convening this session that allows us to be able to tee up a resolution that I suspect will become a groundbreaking resolution for this body, recognizing that if we want to be able to guarantee the promise of the UN charter to our citizens across the world, it will be impossible for us to do without ensuring that we address this fundamental issue of income inequality,” said Ms. Mottley.

Somali families face renewed violence amid worsening hunger crisis
Children have been killed and injured in fresh fighting in Baidoa, in Somalia’s South West State, where families were already facing severe hunger and other overlapping crises.
A health facility has also been damaged, according to the UN Children’s Fund, UNICEF, and other humanitarian agencies.
In the past few weeks, clashes have broken out in Baidoa, the state’s largest city, between Government forces and fighters loyal to the former regional president, who was ousted in March.
The army has been seeking to maintain control of the city, which it seized earlier this year. Hostilities flared on Monday, according to news reports, after thousands of local fighters entered Baidoa that morning.
“Children are once again bearing the heaviest burden of violence,” said the UN Children’s Fund, UNICEF, expressing deep concern about the escalation.
“UNICEF calls on all parties to protect children from harm, ensure the protection of schools, and health facilities, and allow safe and unhindered humanitarian access.”
Decades of humanitarian crisis
This recent development occurs against the backdrop of an already severe humanitarian crisis.
Somalia has been experiencing decades of food security crisis driven by recurring cycles of conflict, mass displacement, global trade disruptions and extreme climate shocks like severe droughts and flooding.
Across Somalia, two million children are acutely or severely malnourished, making Somalia one of the world’s biggest malnutrition crises, say UN agencies.
In Baidoa alone, 26,000 people face catastrophic food insecurity, the highest level on the hunger scale, putting them at risk of famine.
The stronger-than-ever El Niño weather pattern is expected to deepen the crisis by intensifying the October-December rainy season.
Overlapping crises
Families on the ground have been torn apart by these overlapping crises, said the UN World Food Programme (WFP).
Hawo’s family is one of them.
Some days we eat just once a day
First, a mortar hit their family home in Baidoa, killing her father. Then her brother died during the fighting. She was forced to flee to Mogadishu with her daughter and now lives there with her aunt.
“Even with my aunt’s support I have been struggling, but sometimes it is really bad,” she said. “Some days we eat just once a day.”
Her daughter Farhiya became listless, losing her appetite and shedding weight.
A neighbour recommended she visit the Weido clinic, but the clinic is turning women and children away due to lack of resources.
“I hope I can get the support I need for my child to recover,” Hawo said, as aid workers worry things will only get worse.
Aid drying up
WFP, which provides the backbone of the overall food aid response in Somalia, is also increasingly strained in the face of mass humanitarian aid funding cuts.
From reaching more than four million people monthly a few years ago, its food assistance can only support just over 670,000 today.
“In 2022, when Somalia was experiencing its longest drought in 40 years, timely and generous funding helped scale up assistance to avert famine,” explained Hameed Nuru, WFP Country Director in Somalia.
“Today, severe funding shortfalls mean we are only reaching a fraction of those in need, forcing us to make painful choices about who receives assistance and who does not,” he said.

Who gets to shape AI? UN debate centres on power, trust and inclusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Who gets to shape AI? UN debate centres on power, trust and inclusion
Artificial Intelligence or AI – and the technology behind it – is moving fast. The question being asked across the world is who gets a seat at the table deciding how it's used and who gets to benefit.
When global leaders gathered at the UN during High-Level Week at the organization’s headquarters in New York, AI emerged as an issue which both unified and divided nations.
Although they largely agree there are significant upsides to AI, they are split on the risks, who writes the rules, and how to stop entire countries from being left behind.
UN News reviewed some of the key speeches made during the UN General Debate to get a sense of the challenges and benefits that nations are focused on.
As UN Secretary-General António Guterres put it: “AI is indeed a game changer — with enormous promise to advance medicine, accelerate scientific discovery, expand opportunity, and improve lives.”
Innovation vs safeguards
Countries seemed focused on finding the right balance: How can we push the positive aspects of AI technology forward without opening the door to disaster at the hands of rogue agents?
President of the General Assembly Khalilur Rahman put it plainly: “AI can be a powerful accelerator of human progress; therefore, we must not close the door to innovation.”
But he also flagged the potential harms; job losses and deepening digital divides while calling for guardrails grounded in science, not fear.
Switzerland struck a similar note, warning that regulation needs to build trust without choking off AI's benefits. Japan zeroed in on cooperation over frontier AI safety.
Saudi Arabia leaned into ethics and responsible use. Singapore backed testing, trust-building and cross-border incident reporting, while flagging the dangers of increasingly autonomous systems.
Mr. Guterres framed the challenge starkly: “The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability: Capability without oversight. Decision-making without transparency.”
People not processors
Once the policy talk is stripped away, most countries are asking: what does this mean for daily life?
The UK talked up faster cancer diagnoses, economic renewal and better public services. India went further, describing AI as a ground-breaking development tool: “We view AI as a transformational driver, for human empowerment, economic prosperity and population-scale problem solving.”
The UK also focused on the potential disruptions. “But we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, and a multiplier of risk.”
The solution? Keep humans, specifically, elected ones, in charge: “Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance. They must be taken by elected governments who serve working people.”
These concerns reflect a broader debate over whether AI will shrink or deepen inequality.
Who writes the rules?
Another recurring question was whether countries will merely use AI or help shape its future.
South Africa was direct: Africa needs a hand in writing those rules, tying it to research, youth and economic transformation. Switzerland agreed that real participation means shaping governance, not just getting access.
India pushed for sovereignty: "We believe in the right of each nation, to shape its eco-system, with the development of its own models, and deployment strategies, consistent with its national goals and priorities."
Meanwhile, China focused on ensuring that technological advances are shared broadly rather than concentrated among a few countries or societies.
“We should take a people centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide and promote development that is universally beneficial.”
Singapore went further still, floating the idea of a future UN framework convention and a dedicated international AI institution, with everyone, not just the frontrunners, at the table.
The UN has already started bringing countries together to discuss the issues raised by AI including establishing an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and holding a Global Dialogue on AI Governance
The real currency: Power and access
The concentration of data, computing power and influence remains a significant worry for many nations.
Brazil flagged the outsized sway of big tech companies. France raised the risk of dependence on either dominant States or a handful of private firms.
Developing countries want to play a bigger role in digital development, urging more access to increased computing power, technical know-how, infrastructure, and a significant say in setting standards.
China tied this to the digital divide, South Africa to participation in research and governance, Saudi Arabia to capacity-building institutions and Switzerland to skills and infrastructure support.
The takeaway: The future of AI may be as much about access as it is about regulation.
Keeping humans in the loop
Security concerns emerged through plenty of speeches.
- France flagged risks around defence, cybersecurity and space.
- Japan pointed to information integrity and increasingly powerful frontier systems.
- Türkiye called for an international legal framework.
- Ukraine warned that the more capable this technology gets, the more urgent the search for peace becomes.
- Singapore added its voice to worries about autonomous weapons and the loss of human control.
So, how much global oversight?
While many nations favour the idea of cooperation, finding common ground on how far it should go, remains problematic.
Russia backed UN-centred rulemaking with universal buy-in. Türkiye pushed for work on a UN convention on AI. The UK called for global principles and standards, and said AI will be a headline issue when it takes the G20 presidency.
The UN chief went furthest, laying out concrete proposals including stronger safeguards, independent oversight, a new risk-management architecture: “But because this affects us all, global coordination is indispensable,” he told the General Assembly.
Not all sovereign governments are convinced tighter controls are the answer. The United States offered the sharpest counterpoint, treating AI dominance as a strategic and economic imperative.
President Donald Trump argued for an alternative vision: "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. Many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the Internet itself."

China Focus: Scholars explore how Confucian wisdom illuminates challenges in AI age
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:59:03 CST
20:59:03 KST

JINAN, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Standing before a virtual image of Confucius, Jonah Dunch posed a question that the ancient Chinese thinker could hardly have imagined: In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), what would he make of the development of society and rapid advance of technology?
Dunch, a Canadian Yenching Scholar from the 2025 cohort at Peking University, was not alone in asking how an ancient intellectual tradition might speak to a fast-changing technological world.
Questions like Dunch's were among those explored as hundreds of guests from around the world gathered for the 12th Nishan Forum on World Civilizations from Sept. 28 to 29, held in the Nishan area of Qufu, east China's Shandong Province, where Confucius is believed to have been born more than 2,500 years ago.
Themed "Civilization, Order and Justice," the forum covered a broad range of issues concerning humanity's future. With AI emerging as a recurring subject, there are queries not only with regard to how technology should be governed, but also what values should guide its development and what place human beings should occupy in an increasingly intelligent physical world.
AI is being integrated into production and everyday life at an unprecedented pace, while posing new challenges for global governance. Some participants said the world is at a critical juncture for building institutions to govern technology, as technological risks rise alongside a growing willingness to cooperate internationally, even amid intensifying competition among major powers.
Xue Lan, dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, said global AI governance is being hampered by fragmented mechanisms, diverging approaches among major countries and an inadequate supply of safety governance.
Amid accelerating global changes, rising unilateralism and protectionism, and the intertwining of civilizational divides and technological barriers, how to coexist and how to cooperate have become shared concerns. At Nishan, participants looked to ancient traditions for perspectives on confronting such global challenges.
For Dimitra Amarantidou, associate professor at the Advanced Institute for Confucian Studies of Shandong University, the value of the Analects of Confucius, like that of classical texts from other traditions, lies not in providing ready-made answers to today's problems, but in helping people rethink the questions themselves.
"Confucius cannot answer the question of how to regulate AI agents who turn rogue," she said. "He may not have an answer to that question, but I think he can help us reformulate the question and say, for example: What is humanity? What does it mean to be human?"
"His focus is on ren -- on humaneness. So he connects humanity with goodness," Amarantidou said. "He helps us keep that in mind: when we are considering these questions, keep the humans at the center."
The discussion of Confucian thought at Nishan also went beyond AI, touching on how traditional ideas continue to find expression in contemporary concepts and practices.
For Eduardo Daniel Oviedo, principal research fellow at the Argentine National Council for Scientific and Technical Research and professor at the National University of Rosario, understanding China's traditional culture, particularly Confucianism, is important to understanding the ideas behind the country's foreign policy.
"China's four global initiatives, the Belt and Road Initiative and the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity all have certain connections with Confucian thought," said Oviedo.
As participants discussed how to respond to the multiple challenges facing the international community, another theme came repeatedly to the fore: dialogue.
Suos Yara, chairman of the Commission on Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Information of Cambodia's National Assembly, said the Nishan forum provides a platform for turning broad principles of civilization, order and justice into meaningful dialogue and for exploring how people can work together to build a shared future.
Jin Minqing, director of the Institute of Contemporary China Studies under the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), called for rejecting notions of civilizational superiority and civilizational conflict, and for respecting the historical traditions, values and development paths of different civilizations.
He also called for following the principle of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits in global governance, building consensus on rules through mutual respect among civilizations, upholding the common values of humanity -- peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy and freedom -- and promoting a community with a shared future for humanity, as well as common development and lasting peace and prosperity.
The significance of the forum indicates that dialogue lies not in eliminating differences, but in enabling different civilizations to listen to one another. Since it was first held in 2010, the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations has developed into an important platform for implementing the Global Civilization Initiative and promoting exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations.
"Great civilizations can transcend time and borders and engage in dialogue with all humanity," Syed Yousaf Raza Gilani, chairman of the Senate of Pakistan, said in a video address at the opening ceremony, describing Confucius as a thinker who transcends his era.
"The most enduring bridges are not built only with bricks and steel, but with knowledge, friendship and people's hearts," Gilani added. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday welcomed people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to offer opinions and suggestions on the solution to the Taiwan question under the "one country, two systems" framework.
Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a media conference in response to a question about recent discussions on the "two systems" solution to the Taiwan question.
Zhang said that peaceful reunification and "one country, two systems" remain the basic policy for resolving the Taiwan question and the best way to achieve national reunification, serving the interests of compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Strait and the Chinese nation as a whole.
"The reunification of the motherland is an unstoppable historical trend," she noted.
The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Zhang said that an increasing number of people in Taiwan have begun discussing the specific content of the solution.
They are also envisioning prospects for a better future following reunification and considering the major opportunities reunification would bring to Taiwan's social and economic development, as well as the tangible benefits it would bring to the people of Taiwan, she added.
"We welcome compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to pool their wisdom and contribute more opinions and suggestions on the solution," Zhang said.
She called on people on both sides to work together to create the historic achievement of national reunification and share in the great glory of national rejuvenation. ■

News Analysis: Britain ramps up youth support amid subdued economic conditions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:32 CST
20:58:32 KST

LONDON, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Britain is rolling out a series of measures in employment, housing and services to boost support for young people faced with mounting challenges amid subdued economic conditions.
"Politicians fail to give people, young people, the support they need as they grow up in a tougher world and then threaten them in their 20s that they will strip away what they are left with," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a speech to the Labour Party Conference 2026 on Tuesday.
He promised to guarantee in-work support, as well as support for those who are out of work and losing confidence and connection.
The prime minister said he would rebuild a system of comprehensive education with parity between academic and technical pathways, open up homeownership to those who are not backed by their parents, and offer mental health support for the younger generation.
Unemployment is recognized as a serious challenge for young people in Britain, with nearly 1 million people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training (NEET) in the second quarter of 2026, official data shows.
The government has launched a range of youth employment support, including the Jobs Guarantee scheme which has been backed by over 400 employers and offers a direct route into work for eligible young people. A new work experience program also offers hands-on experience with retailers.
On Monday, the Chancellor announced a new package to help people into work, education and training. The government will use the National Wealth Fund to create and support a further 130,000 jobs across Britain by 2030, across sectors including artificial intelligence (AI), technology, defense and clean energy.
Funding will be expanded by 100 million pounds (about 133 million U.S. dollars) to all 14 existing Mayoral Strategic Authorities with directly elected mayors, to help provide local apprenticeship services across England from Spring 2027.
A total of 15 million pounds (about 20 million dollars) a year of additional funding will also be spent to restore the Union Learning Fund in England, helping people develop new skills, progress at work and adapt as technology changes the workplace.
"So many young people cast adrift by a school system built for some, not all, overly focused on the university route and not enough on technical education," Burnham told the Labour Party conference. He proposed good quality pathways for all from 14, a 45-day work placement between 16 and 18, and an apprenticeship at 18.
"I also want to get back to a Britain where young people starting out are able to buy a home like my mum and dad did. Like I did," he added at the speech.
A new equity loan scheme -- Your First Home -- will be confirmed at next month's Budget to support more people into homeownership, according to a statement on the official website of the British government.
This is expected to support 2.5 percent deposits, backed by 20 percent government-backed equity loans, for prospective first-time buyers purchasing a new-build property from a developer signed up to the scheme, the statement said, adding that people will be able to access equity loans with an initial interest free period.
To offer specialized support outside of home and school, the government also launched a drive to support the training and employment of 1,000 new youth workers last week.
"It comes as the government makes the largest investment into youth services in a generation following a drop of local authority spending of 73 percent between 2010 and 2023, which led to the loss of vital youth worker roles and youth services across England," according to a statement on the British government website.
The youth workers will work with children aged 11 plus, within community spaces, and through outreach. The goal is to ensure that the most vulnerable young people have access to support, including those at highest risk of becoming NEETs.
The specialist youth workers will collaborate with multi-agency teams across education and training, health and crime prevention to support young people to engage in a range of activities, including sport, arts, mentoring and wider youth services.
Meanwhile, a 450-million-pound (about 599 million dollars) program is also set to increase the number of youth facilities, build, improve and expand spaces for young people to connect, while funding more youth work and enriching in-person activities. ■

Asian Games | Double gold for China on 1st medal day of canoe slalom

Unknown Publisher

20:58:30 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept 30 (Xinhua) -- China won both titles on the first medal day of canoe slalom at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday.
Hu Zhaoshan won the men's single kayak final with a penalty-free run of 91.41 seconds, beating Japan's Yuuki Tanaka by 1.46 seconds.
Kazakhstan's Alexandr Korobov took bronze in 94.48 seconds.
Hu, who had ranked second in both the heats and semifinals, delivered his best result in the final to secure gold.
"I had a bit of trouble between gates 15 and 16 in the tricky middle section, but making mistakes isn't the end of the world - you just have to do your best to make up for them and then focus on performing to the best of your ability," Hu said.
Born in 2004, Hu won China's national championship title in 2025 before taking silver at the National Games. He said that runner-up finish had prompted him to target a strong performance at the Asian Games.
"Now that I've won gold here, I hope to prove myself at the Olympics," he said.
Huang Juan then retained her women's single canoe title with a total time of 114.84 seconds, including a two-second penalty for touching a gate.
Thailand's Atcharaporn Duanglawa finished 11.01 seconds behind to claim silver, picking up four penalty seconds for touching two gates.
Kazakhstan's Anastassiya Ananyeva recorded a faster paddling time than Duanglawa but incurred six penalty seconds, leaving her third in 127.32.
Japan's Aki Yazawa, the only paddler to complete the women's final without penalties, finished fourth in 128.25, missing bronze by 0.93 seconds.
Huang, who won the title at the Hangzhou Asian Games and reached the semifinals at the 2024 Paris Olympics to record China's best Olympic result in the event, said she had focused on improving her semifinal time.
"I performed at the level I expected today," she said. "My aim was to go a bit faster than in the semifinal, and I managed it."
China's canoe slalom team leader Zhang Peng described the Asian Games as a mid-term test in the squad's preparations for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"Once you step down from the podium, everything starts from zero," he said. ■

Chinese business chamber voices concern over reported EU "301" trade instrument
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:24 CST
20:58:24 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) on Wednesday voiced concern over reports that some European Union (EU) member states are pushing for a new EU "301" trade instrument, warning that such a unilateral measure could raise questions over its compatibility with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
In a statement, the chamber said the proposed instrument, if introduced, could risk "weaponizing trade policy" and disrupt China-EU and global trade, while adding uncertainty to global industrial and supply chains.
The CCCEU said unilateral trade measures will not address structural challenges facing European industry, including high energy costs, insufficient investment and the need to strengthen innovation.
European industry has also experienced the negative impact of similar unilateral trade measures. International trade instruments should not become subject to a "race to the bottom," nor should unilateral measures replace multilateral rules, the chamber said, calling for the WTO-based multilateral trading system to be upheld.
The CCCEU said China and the EU are maintaining intensive communication under their Trade and Investment Consultation mechanism and called on European stakeholders to use existing dialogue channels to address differences and concerns.
It also urged the EU and its member states to maintain a fair, equitable, transparent and predictable business environment and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of companies, including Chinese firms.
The chamber said it stands ready to strengthen communication and cooperation with European stakeholders and contribute to an open and stable business environment and China-EU economic and trade cooperation.
The statement came amid reports that some EU member states are urging the European Commission to accelerate work on an instrument modeled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act, which allows Washington to investigate and respond to what it considers unfair foreign trade practices. ■

OSAKA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China took an early lead but lost 2-1 to South Korea in the men's football semifinals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, missing out on a place in the final.
China reached the Asian Games men's football semifinals for the first time in 28 years. Under head coach Antonio Puche, the Chinese side advanced from the "group of death" with one win and two draws before beating Thailand 3-0 in the quarterfinals.

China started with its familiar 5-3-2 formation and looked to threaten on the counter-attack, while South Korea sought to create chances from the flanks and set pieces.
China broke the deadlock in the 22nd minute when Mao Weijie sent a lofted through ball to Wang Yudong, who controlled it with his chest before calmly finishing one-on-one.
South Korea equalized in the 33rd minute after a corner reached Lee Young-jun at the far post. His header hit the post and bounced into the net despite Li Hao's attempt to save it.
After the break, China pushed higher and created several opportunities, but South Korea remained dangerous on the counter-attack. Mao was forced off with an injury in the 66th minute.
South Korea completed the comeback in the 82nd minute when Eom Ji-sung broke forward and crossed to the far post, where Bae Jun-ho headed home to make it 2-1.
In the closing minutes, Zhang Yuning's shot inside the box was blocked by a South Korean defender, prompting China's players to appeal for a handball. The referee waved play on, while Puche was booked for protesting the decision.
China had seven shots, three on target, and 55 percent possession, compared with South Korea's eight shots, six on target and 45 percent possession.
"We played an excellent game. Against a South Korean team with many outstanding players playing at a European level, the whole team showed a very high level," said Puche. "I'm naturally disappointed and saddened by the result. But I'm extremely proud and happy with this team."
China will play the loser of the other semifinal between Japan and Uzbekistan in the men's football bronze-medal match on Saturday. ■

Brown bears kill 162 head of livestock in northern Mongolia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:13 CST
20:58:13 KST

ULAN BATOR, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- At least 86 brown bear sightings have been reported in residential areas of Selenge province in northern Mongolia since the beginning of spring, with the animals killing and eating 162 head of livestock, the provincial department of environment said Wednesday.
"These figures are based on reports submitted by nomadic herders. We cannot rule out the possibility that there have been additional incidents that have not been reported or registered," the department said.
In recent months, there have been multiple reports of bears being spotted in or near residential areas in several provinces across Mongolia. In particular, several bear sightings have been reported in the capital, Ulan Bator, in recent days, prompting authorities to urge the public to remain vigilant and take precautions to protect themselves and others from potential risks.
Experts said encounters between bears and livestock, as well as bear sightings in residential areas, have increased in recent years. They cited several contributing factors, including climate change, food shortages in bears' natural habitats, the overexploitation of natural resources, and forest fires. ■

Norwegian ministers grilled in parliament over Epstein ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:58:12 UTC
20:58:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Norwegian ministers, including 1993 Oslo Accords creators, grilled in parliament over Epstein ties
Norway's prime minister denied Wednesday an "unhealthy culture" among the country's diplomats, as current and former ministers addressed a hearing over ties between late US convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and senior Norwegian officials.
The hearings come against the backdrop of the foreign ministry's payment of more than 130 million kroner ($13.5 million at the current exchange rate) to the International Peace Institute (IPI) between 1997 and 2018, a think tank headed by Norway's Terje Rod-Larsen from 2005 to 2020.
"There is no reason to speak of an unhealthy culture at a large organisation just because of what one or several people may have done," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store told the Storting's standing committee on scrutiny and constitutional affairs.
"You can't tar everyone with the same brush," said the Labour leader, who was called to address the committee about his years as foreign minister from 2005-2012.
The Epstein files have shed light on ties between the US financier and Rod-Larsen and his diplomat wife Mona Juul, the architects of the 1993 Oslo Accords who are now under investigation in Norway—she for "aggravated corruption" and he for "complicity in aggravated corruption".
The couple denies any wrongdoing.
In total, 11 officials who have held the positions of foreign minister or development aid minister since 2005, will address the committee Wednesday and Thursday.
'Accountability failures'
In addition to Rod-Larsen and Juul, the Epstein documents have highlighted ties between the sex offender, who died in prison in 2019, and Thorbjorn Jagland, a former prime minister, foreign minister, secretary general of the Council of Europe and chair of the Nobel Peace Prize Committee.
Epstein also had ties with former foreign minister Borge Brende.
Jagland is also under investigation on suspicion of "aggravated corruption", but is not among the officials summoned by parliament because he was foreign minister prior to 2005 and because parliament wants to avoid interfering with the police investigation.
Brende, who resigned in February as president of the World Economic Forum, was to be heard on Wednesday.
"The Epstein documents raise serious questions about abuse of office, a culture of accountability failures, and poor management of development aid funds," said Jonas Andersen Sayed, a member of the committee.
"The issue concerns public trust in the entire system. It is essential that all the facts are brought to light, that accountability is established, and that the necessary reforms are implemented," he said.
The hearings themselves will not result in any sanctions.
Parliament has also set up an independent inquiry tasked with a much broader examination of the case, which is due to submit its final report by 31 January 2028.

Asian Games | China pockets 3 golds in track cycling, breaking two Asian records
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:08 CST
20:58:08 KST

Gold medalists team China celebrate during the awarding ceremony for the women's team pursuit final of cycling track at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Izu of Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China swept all three gold medals on offer in track cycling at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, winning the women's, men's team pursuits and women's keirin, with Asian records set in both team pursuit events.
In the women's team pursuit final, China quickly established a lead and extended its advantage to more than two seconds midway through the race. The Chinese quartet crossed the finish line in 4:08.818 to win gold in an Asian record time.
Host Japan took silver in 4:10.424, while South Korea claimed bronze after catching Uzbekistan in the bronze medal race.
"We were very united and rode steadily. Everyone gave their all and pushed beyond their limits, delivering our best performance," said Chinese rider Chen Ning.
Teammate Wang Xiaoyue said the team had set a clear goal of breaking the record and winning gold before the race.
"Now that we have achieved our goal, it not only validates the results of our training but also gives us confidence and motivation for the competitions ahead," Wang said.
The men's team pursuit final also saw a showdown between China and defending champion Japan. China clocked 3:47.621 to break the Asian record and beat Japan to the gold medal.
South Korea came from behind to beat Kazakhstan in the bronze medal race.
"We had originally planned to go for first place in the qualifying round, but a mistake left us slightly behind Japan and we failed to meet our expectations," said Pei Zhengyu, who is making his Asian Games debut.
"But we adjusted our mindset in time and successfully broke the Games record in the first round, steadily improving our times. By crossing the finish line first in today's final, we also achieved our goal of breaking the Asian record," Pei said.
In the women's keirin final, Yuan Liying produced a powerful late surge to overtake her rivals and claim gold. Her Chinese teammate Wang Lijuan took silver, while Malaysia's Nurul Izzah Izzati Mohd Asri won bronze.
"This gold medal is an affirmation of my individual ability," Yuan said. "The keirin is a rapidly changing event, and there is no fixed tactic. All I can do is give my best, maintain my rhythm and respond positively to every change in the race."
"I feel very honored to stand on the podium alongside my teammate," she added.
The women's Madison, men's omnium and men's sprint finals will take place on Thursday. ■

No more radio silence: EU plans cross-border lifeline for emergency services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:51:15 UTC
20:51:15 KST

When disaster strikes near a border, police and firefighters can lose contact the moment they cross it. Brussels wants a 5G network, backed by satellites, to change that by 2036.
The EU put forward plans for a new bloc-wide communication system on Wednesday that would allow police, firefighters and other national emergency services to better coordinate during cross-border crises.
Currently, first responders across the 27-country European Union mostly rely on radio to communicate, but secure channels normally stop working at national borders, hampering international operations, Brussels says.
"When crisis strikes, our first responders must be able to communicate instantly across agencies, across borders, across Europe," said the EU's commissioner for internal affairs Magnus Brunner.
The proposed "EU Critical Communication System" would see nations move their emergency comms from radio to broadband technology such as 5G — something Brussels says most are already planning to do.
The EU would then ensure national systems can talk to each other by coordinating exchanges through a central hub and set up a monitoring centre to track cyber security risks and support member countries.
Under the plan, EU satellites will serve as back-up were land-bound systems to fail, as might occur during a blackout.
Using broadband rather than radio will enable responders to share video, messages and geolocation in real-time, normally using a smartphone, although the EU plan does not envisage the adoption of any specific device.
EU officials listed wildfires, counter-terrorism operations, drone threats and search-and-rescue efforts in the Mediterranean as examples of instances where the tech could prove decisive.
Military forces would also be able to use the system, if they so wished.
Brunner cited as an example the challenges met during the massive wildfire this summer in Belgium's High Fens nature reserve bordering Germany.
"The moment a first responder had to cross the border, their radio actually stopped working," he said.
In another case, he pointed to a shooting in the Netherlands, which took place just 200 metres (655 feet) from Belgium, that triggered a cross-border police chase "where every minute counted".
But under the current system, the Dutch operational centre in Maastricht could not directly alert its counterparts in Liege, on the Belgian side — and therefore officers on the street.
The commission said the critical components underpinning the system will be developed by European companies.
EU officials speaking on condition of anonymity listed Airbus, Italy's Leonardo and Austria's Frequentis among the companies that had participated in a pilot.
The satellite back-up could be provided by an EU satellite constellation project currently under development known as Iris², they added.
Brussels would like the system to be fully operational by 2036. The plan needs to be approved by member states and the European Parliament.

Reporter's Notebook: Tourists visit northern Israel as sense of normalcy returns to kibbutzim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:50:28 UTC
20:50:28 KST

On the road between Kibbutz Dan and Kibbutz HaGoshrim, there is a clump of large cement blocks, stacked like one might stack Lego. They are in a field near Kibbutz Dafna. They appear to be one of the many fortifications added or improved in this region after October 7, when there was fear of a mass Hezbollah attack.
Today the cement-block fort is a gathering place for kids, climbing on it and playing.
This is a symbol of how Northern Israel has changed. This area at the northern end of the Huleh valley forms a kind of large basin that is surrounded by hills and mountains.
On one side is the ridgeline over Kiryat Shmona. On the other side are the feet of Mount Hermon, which rises up into the clouds, its summit shrouded obscured. Today Israel controls that summit. It was seized on December 8, 2024 when the Assad regime collapsed.
Israel also controls Mount Dov which sits just below the Hermon.
Residents returned to northern Israel after November 2024 ceasefire
In 2024 this area was a warzone. Most of the residents had been evacuated, including the entire city of Kiryat Shmona. Hezbollah missiles and drones were frequently falling in the valley. Israeli artillery was responding. However, until September 2024 Israel held off an a ground offensive against Hezbollah. Then, after triggering the exploding pagers, the IDF began a limited ground offensive against Hezbollah. There was a ceasefire in November 2024.
It’s hard to remember now how forsaken this place was during the war. Communities such as Metula, north of Kiryat Shmona, were not only a ghost town, but many homes were struck by Hezbollah. The only people in this area mostly consisted of members of local security teams. There were personnel drawn from the local communities who were then given arms and kitted out and recruited back into service so that they could receive proper support from the state to defend their communities. Many of them adopted an esprit de corps, with matching logos on their green shirts, and spray-painted logos and symbols all around the valley. The message to the enemy was that this area was protected. However, it didn’t feel protected to visitors. Everyone knew that Hezbollah’s large rockets could fall here quickly and kill.
On July 27, 2024 a Hezbollah rocket fell in the Druze town of Majdal Shams in the Golan and killed 12 children near a soccer field. This massacre was an example of the deadly threat. Today that threat appears greatly reduced.
Kibbutzim are flooded with visitors over Sukkot
I drove up to Kibbutz Dafna on September 29. Founded in 1939 as one of the many “tower and stockade” communities built by Zionist pioneers, today it has around 1,000 residents. It sits on the Dan river, which is more like a stream that snakes through this area.
The community is simple like many of these kibbutzim up here. The people are friendly. There is a museum devoted to chocolate. A hotel chain called Melonot Metailim or Travel Hotels has a site here. There is a pool. The Kibbutz was crowded with visitors during Sukkot. It is an example of how tourists have returned to the north. People discussed what to do this week. Rafting on the Jordan river? Visiting Kiryat Shmona? Hiking in the Golan. At nearby Kibbutz Amir, the excellent Italian restaurant Loulou was full in the evening.
Hezbollah can no longer set up camp on Mount Dov
It has a feeling of a return to “normal” before October 7. There is a sense now that one can drive where they want. A hike on Ayun stream, near Metula, for instance is one option. Before October 7 this area was on the Lebanese border and there were large signs put up by Hezbollah.
There were Hezbollah flags and a picture of Al Aqsa Mosque and a Palestinian flag on the other side of the border. The message from Hezbollah is that it can do what it wants. The UN used to be seen across the border, doing its usual nothing to stop Hezbollah.
Today that has changed. The enemy is gone, pushed north by the IDF. Homes of Lebanese on the other side of the border have been flattened. Hezbollah positioned eviscerated. The Hezbollah flags and signs are gone. Israel now controls both sides of the border. No longer can Hezbollah set up “tents” in Mount Dov as it used to. Before October 7 there was fear that a clash over the Hezbollah tent provocation would lead to war. Now the war has come.
The feeling of war is still clear here. At night helicopters fly in the distance, the echo of their motors reverberating back and forth across the valley. There are explosions and what sounds like artillery fire. At night sound travels further, and this valley is like a giant auditorium. The explosions could be in Syria or the artillery could be practicing in the Golan. Or it could be controlled demolition of Hezbollah sites in Lebanon. What is clear is that although the war is now somewhere else, it is still ever present.
Threats remain despite return to normalcy
On September 29 the Syrian government detained a terror cell in the Yarmouk Basin which is between the Golan and the Kingdom of Jordan. That means that there are still threats. Israel has also been detaining Syrian civilians and there are concerns about where Israel’s actions in Syria will lead. However, for the masses of visitors who have returned here, to once again turn the north into an area of hiking and sport, it is clear that a feeling of peace and normalcy is at hand.
The Kibbutzim here have known war for 90 years since their founding in the 1930s. This whole area at the time was under threat during the Arab revolt. Zionist pioneer Joseph Trumpeldor was killed in 1921 at Tel Hai, two miles from Dafna. After the War of Independence the area came under fire from Syria and later from Palestinians in Lebanon in the 1970s and then from Hezbollah in the 1980s and 1990s.
They built large bunkers underground, covered in the dark volcanic rock that is common here. The bunkers look like porcupines now, all over the landscape. They are remnants of a different war. Today the communities have modern fortified rooms, attached to many of the small homes. Many of these are new, since October 7. New ones have been added outside. Like the fortified positions along the road, now turned into places for kids to play, these are symbols of the changing landscape from war to peace.

Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev urges European dialogue with Russia to avert nuclear attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:50:17 UTC
20:50:17 KST

"We always need to think about the worst-case scenario," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said at the Euronews' Defence Summit, warning of the risk of a Russian nuclear attack if tensions with Europe escalate.
The European Union should engage diplomatically with Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end and avert a devastating nuclear attack, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.
Russia controls the world's largest nuclear arsenal, with an estimated 4,400 stockpiled warheads, of which 1,796 are strategically deployed.
Radev also criticised Europe's continued deliveries of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine, which he dismissed as a failed "peace by force" strategy.
"There is a limit to just delivering weapons and supporting, because the final peace set-up will be done by diplomacy, not by delivering weapons. So our call is to listen more to each other, to open the lines of communication," Radev said on Wednesday.
"The problem is that no one is raising the question about nuclear risk. Does it exist? Maybe not, I don't know, but this is a risk," he went on.
"We always need to think about the worst-case scenario. Are we prepared for this? Does anybody speak about risk assessment? Does it exist at all? Because we have been trying to achieve a conventional victory over the biggest nuclear power."
Radev referred to the recent statement by Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, who said a war between Russia and Europe would be "completely different" and "very short", a comment seen as an implicit nuclear threat.
This week, Moscow sent NATO a document threatening to "use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" to defend its territory from the alliance, according to Reuters.
Radev rejected "this type of speaking" from the Kremlin but urged his fellow European leaders to consider where an escalation might lead.
Tensions have been rising as Moscow ramps up its hybrid attacks against European countries in an attempt to instil societal fear and deter military support for Ukraine.
"There is a nuclear card," the Bulgarian premier said, noting Russia would be prone to play it if weakened or cornered.
"We need to have this into account. We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation."
Since his election earlier this year, Radev has been in the minority that advocates closer diplomatic engagement with Russia to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Austria have also pushed for dialogue.
Others, however, argue that the Kremlin has little interest in meaningful negotiations and continues to insist on maximalist demands. A short meeting last week between the German foreign minister and Lavrov in New York ended up in bitter recriminations.
The White House's attempts to achieve a temporary ceasefire have all failed. Russia has blocked the Black Sea and launched non-stop airstrikes on Ukrainian cities instead.
Radev seemed undeterred by this track record and insisted Europe should rebalance its "military, economic and diplomatic instruments" in favour of the last strand.
He also pushed back against the label "pro-Russian" that has been attached to his government, which this year vetoed sanctions against Patriarch Kirill.
"The war in Ukraine challenged our critical thinking and realistic approach," he said.
"It challenged our ability to assess the strategic centre of gravity of the opponent. It challenged most of all our ability to design feasible political objectives and to translate them into a sound military strategy and to define a desired end state," he added.
"We have not exhausted the power of diplomacy, and we need to do and to speak more."

Regev moves to halt flydubai flights over pilot's suspected Omani background, source tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:50:13 UTC
20:50:13 KST

Transportation Minister Miri Regev on Wednesday has requested that the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) halt all flights by the airline flydubai entering and exiting the country following the suspected attempted hijacking of a commercial passenger aircraft flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, a source in the ministry confirmed to The Jerusalem Post.
According to the source, Regev’s decision was made after unverified reports indicating that the co-pilot suspected of hijacking the plane may have been of Omani origin. Israeli sources later corroborated to the Post that the suspected hijacker is believed to be of Omani nationality, according to initial investigations.
Flydubai’s agreement to operate in Israel explicitly states that all pilots must be from countries that have normalized relations with Israel, which does not include Oman.
“This is a clear breach of the agreement,” the source stated, “and the Shin Bet must look into this.”
The Post has learned that the Mossad, Shin Bet, IDF, and Transport Ministry have opened a joint probe into the incident, focusing on whether there was any indication of an attack prior to the flight, and how an Omani pilot would have been permitted to fly the aircraft.
Terminal 1 opens waiting and information area for family
Following her announcement, Regev also directed the Israel Airports Authority to open a waiting and information area for the families of everyone on the diverted flydubai flight located in Terminal 1's arrivals hall.
"Family members who wish to come to Ben-Gurion Airport are invited to go to the designated area in Terminal 1, where they will be able to wait and receive information and updates as developments unfold. Representatives of the Israel Airports Authority will be on site and will assist the families as needed," the IAI stated.
IAF says it is prepared for scenarios like that of flydubai attempted hijacking
Later on Wednesday, the IAF released a statement noting its continuous preparation to "confront a range of aerial threats and prevent incursions into Israeli airspace."
"The defense of Israel’s skies is based on maintaining a continuous aerial situational picture, keeping forces on alert, and maintaining the ability to scramble and deploy aircraft at short notice," the Air Force said, noting that "various scenarios are routinely drilled in order to enable early detection, rapid response, and real-time decision-making."
One such scenario includes preparation for "unusual incidents involving civilian aircraft en route to Israel, including preventing the possibility of an airborne terrorist attack," the statement read, which includes any flight that "deviates from its planned flight path, fails to respond to radio calls, transmits a distress signal, experiences a technical malfunction, or when a medical emergency involving a passenger requires an emergency landing."
The IAF added that, in such an incident, "Israeli airspace may be closed and fighter jets scrambled to identify and escort the civilian aircraft."
State Comptroller notes 2024 report recommending aviation security evaluation
Israel's State Comptroller's Office also issued a statement following the flydubai incident, referencing a report that the comptroller published in 2024 examining the security of international civil aviation to and from Israel.
"The State Comptroller’s Office recommends that the National Security Council conduct a staff review...to examine all aspects of international civil aviation security in Israel — flights departing Israel, Israeli aviation abroad, and incoming foreign aviation — as well as the relevance of government and security cabinet decisions on the issue, some of which date back to the 1970s," read the report
The State Comptroller report from 2024 further recommended that, "upon completion of the review, the National Security Council advise the prime minister and the security cabinet on how responsibility for the issue should be regulated and how resources should be allocated in a way that ensures a comprehensive approach."
“The State Comptroller’s Office recommends that the prime minister, transportation minister, and finance minister address the issue and formulate a comprehensive policy on aviation security.”
Yonah Jeremy Bob and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

6 ‘eminent persons’ to weigh ban on European far-right party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:49:38 UTC
20:49:38 KST

6 ‘eminent persons’ to weigh ban on European far-right party
A one-time MEP candidate, experts affiliated to political think tanks, and former Commission heavyweights are tasked with advising whether to pull the plug on European political parties.
MEP Alexander Sell delivers a speech during a commemoration of the 30th anniversary of the Srebrenica genocide at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on July 7, 2025. | Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA
BRUSSELS — Six people appointed by the EU institutions will start discussing on Thursday whether the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations should be banned as a European party and lose funding, according to an internal note seen by POLITICO.
The Committee of Independent Eminent Persons is tasked with advising the watchdog for EU political parties — the Authority for European Political Parties and Foundations — on alleged breaches of European values.
Committee members were selected through a combination of political horse-trading, EU countries pushing their candidates, and European Commission officials selecting former peers — raising eyebrows among the parties and foundations they are now expected to scrutinize.
Advertisement
“We hope that the Committee of Independent Eminent Persons will exercise the legally required neutrality, even though people with clear political affiliations … have been appointed,” said Alexander Sell, vice president of the Europe of Sovereign Nations, and the president of its foundation. The ESN is the European home of the Alternative for Germany party.
“In a true democracy, party representatives should not be involved in decisions regarding the funding of their political rivals,” Sell said.
In July, the European Parliament green-lighted the process to deregister and defund ESN after the authority alleged breaches of EU values, including anti-immigration, antisemitic and anti-LGBT rhetoric, as first reported by POLITICO.
The ESN party is a separate legal entity from the ESN political group in the European Parliament, which is home to 27 MEPs. Political groups are parliamentary factions, while parties are broader alliances of national parties that are funded through the EU budget. The ESN political group doesn’t face sanctions.
The committee will have two months to issue an opinion once it gets all the documentation, and then the authority will make a final decision.
Choosing the eminent members
From the Council side, only two candidates were put forward by individual member states, said an EU official, granted anonymity to speak freely about the selection process: German professor of European law Pia Lange and Lithuania’s Linas Kontrimas, who ran to be an MEP in 2019 for a party affiliated with the European Conservatives and Reformists.
Advertisement
The Commission’s secretariat-general put forward former commissioner Martine Reicherts and former Commission Secretary-General Alexander Italianer, who is now also working as an EU affairs adviser at a law firm.
After a political deal in the European Parliament between the conservatives and social democrats, EU lawmakers appointed Luca Vanoni, a professor who specializes in law and religion, and who has been a visiting professor at the Viktor Orbán-linked think tank MCC. They also chose Anna Pacześniak, who sits on the Scientific Council of the European Social Democrats’ Foundation (FEPS).
Spokespeople and officials from the three institutions insisted that all the appointments were in line with the rules, as the law only forbids sitting EU officials, commissioners and MEPs from being committee members. In the case of Pacześniak, the law only forbids current or former employees of political foundations from being committee members but leaves ample room for people who have other types of affiliation.
The rules also do not call for any cooling-off period before taking a committee role, according to the Parliament’s press services.
Pacześniak said her work at FEPS does not involve any remuneration. “FEPS’s practice is to invite to this group people who can critically analyze the current political situation, and not only those who share social-democratic opinions,” she said.
Kontrimas, who ran to be an MEP on the list of the Lithuanian Farmers and Green Union, told POLITICO that in 2019 he was invited to run as an independent candidate. “I did not belong to the party and do not belong to it now,” he said.
Advertisement
Italianer said the consultancy he works for applies “strict rules to avoid conflicts of interest in accepting assignments.”
In the case of Council and Commission, their nominees had to sign a declaration vowing not to have any conflict of interest. In Parliament, nominees “are required to provide the information necessary to assess their eligibility and independence,” the press service said.
Members do not get paid for their participation in the committee, but expenses are reimbursed.

Unknown

2026-09-30
11:48:59 UTC
20:48:59 KST

A medical rehabilitation center for Ukrainian rescuers purchased 24 tons of supposed therapeutic mud that was actually ordinary sludge taken from a pond, investigators said on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
The procurement cost nearly Hr. 1 million (about $24,000), while the losses to the state budget exceeded Hr.600,000 (about $14,400), according to the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI).

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Four people have been notified of suspicion: the acting head and chief nurse of the State Emergency Service rehabilitation center in Odesa, as well as the director and a manager of a private company involved in the procurement.
‘Ordinary mud of unknown origin’
Investigators allege that the center’s two officials worked with representatives of private companies to arrange the purchase of 24 tons of therapeutic mud.
Official documents stated that the center had received the full quantity of material and that it met the required quality standards.
In reality, the supplier allegedly delivered what the SBI described as “ordinary mud of unknown origin.” The Odesa Regional Prosecutor’s Office said the material was pond sludge rather than certified therapeutic mud.
The alleged substitution was concealed through invoices and other documents containing false information. Those records were then used to authorize the transfer of public money to the supplier.
It was not immediately clear whether the sludge had already been used in rehabilitation procedures or whether investigators had identified any harm to patients.
