NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:34:31 UTC
20:34:31 KST

NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.
- Share:
A new study suggests that Jezero Crater's mysterious "Margin Unit" records a far more complicated history of water than scientists expected, involving ancient lakes, groundwater, and later hydrothermal activity.
When NASA's Perseverance rover arrived at the inner rim of Mars' Jezero Crater in September 2023, researchers expected to encounter sedimentary rocks along what was once the shoreline of a Martian lake. Such rocks form as layers of material accumulate over long periods of time. On Earth, sedimentary rocks made from clay and silt can be especially valuable because they are capable of preserving evidence of ancient microbial life.
Scientists were also interested in the area because Mars orbiters had detected strong signatures of carbonate minerals there. On Earth, carbonates commonly develop in shallow lakes and oceans, including environments that can support life.
Instead of the expected sedimentary deposits, Perseverance encountered igneous rock. These rocks can form when magma cools underground or when volcanic material solidifies at the surface. Because the minerals inside igneous rocks can preserve information about the conditions present when they formed, they can provide exceptionally detailed geological records.
In the Margin Unit, those rocks revealed an unexpectedly complicated history. The evidence indicates that they interacted with water on at least three separate occasions, and each episode changed their chemistry and physical appearance in different ways. The findings were published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.
SuperCam Reveals Mars' Hidden Water History
Much of this evidence came from SuperCam, an instrument mounted high on Perseverance's mast. SuperCam can identify the mineral composition of geological features by analyzing the light they reflect.
When mission scientists identify a promising target, they can direct SuperCam to fire its laser from as far as 21 feet (6.5 meters) away. The laser creates a small burst of plasma, and the spectrum of that plasma reveals the chemical makeup of the rock. Using this technique, Perseverance has studied more than 185 bedrock targets across the Margin Unit.
"Before we arrived at the Margin Unit, the main hypothesis -- derived from orbital observations -- was that the carbonate seen from orbit formed from interaction with the lake that existed in Jezero Crater," said Candice Bedford, a research scientist at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana, and the study's lead author. "But now we know that this location became a sort of crossroads for aqueous systems. The Margin Unit findings are important because Jezero Crater sits inside one of the largest exposures of carbonate on Mars, so what we learn here reaches well beyond this crater."
Ancient Magma Beneath Jezero Crater
Perseverance examined the Margin Unit over approximately 870 feet (265 meters) of elevation. At the higher parts of the area, the rover encountered coarse, crystalline rock rich in olivine. These rocks showed almost no evidence of having been altered by water.
Olivine contains magnesium and iron. The researchers concluded that this olivine-rich unit originally formed inside a mass of magma deep beneath the Martian surface. The magma cooled slowly enough for large mineral grains to develop. Much later, erosion removed the material above it and exposed the rock at the surface.
The situation was very different farther down the Margin Unit, near the ancient lakebed. There, the olivine appears heavily altered. Its grains are fractured, and silica fills spaces between them.
Carbonate and silica are especially interesting to scientists searching for signs of ancient habitability. On Earth, when water reacts with olivine, the process can produce hydrogen that certain microbes can use as an energy source. The same reactions can also create carbonate and silica, minerals that are capable of preserving traces left behind by past microbial activity.
Three Separate Encounters With Water
Researchers can reconstruct the order in which water altered the Margin Unit, although they cannot yet determine exactly when each episode happened.
The first known episode involved groundwater rich in carbon dioxide. As this water moved through the rock, it reacted with olivine and produced carbonate inside fractures at lower elevations. Over time, erosion removed some of the softer surrounding material, leaving the harder carbonate-filled fractures standing out as ridges.
A second period of water activity may have been connected to the ancient lake that once filled Jezero Crater.
"Some of the Margin Unit rocks also contain silica," said Eleni Ravanis, a planetary scientist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa and a coauthor of the study. "Turning olivine into carbonate can leave silica behind, and we see more of that silica in rocks that sat below the water line."
Hot Water Came Later
A third and later episode appears to have involved heated water moving underground.
At one site in the eastern Margin Unit, Perseverance found mineral veins roughly 10 inches (25 centimeters) thick. These veins contain minerals including calcium sulfate and fluorite.
The presence of fluorite provides an important clue about the conditions that produced them. Fluorite commonly forms when hot water circulates through volcanic rock, indicating that Jezero Crater experienced a later period of heated groundwater activity after the earlier interactions with groundwater and the lake.
Together, the observations show that the Margin Unit was not shaped by a single lake environment. Instead, it became a meeting point for several different water systems that altered the same rocks at different stages of Mars' history.
"If there is one thing I have learned after 10 years working with Mars rovers, it is that Mars constantly throws surprises at you," said Bedford. "It is very rare that things are as we expect them to be from orbital data. I hope this work helps reshape how scientists view the history of water in Jezero Crater and across Mars. Ultimately, I hope it helps planetary scientists reconstruct the changing climate and habitability of early Mars."
Story Source:
Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Candice C. Bedford, Eleni Ravanis, Roger C. Wiens, Elise Clavé, Julene Aramendia, Juan Manuel Madariaga, Eleanor Moreland, Stephanie Connell, Alexander Jones, Briony Horgan, Olivier Forni, Bradley Garczynski, Susanne Schröder, Kenneth Williford, Linda Kah, Kathryn Stack, Lucia Mandon, Agnés Cousin, Pierre Beck, Erwin Dehouck, Clément Royer, Adrian Brown. Lake- and groundwater-associated alteration of the olivine-rich Margin unit in Jezero crater, Mars. Communications Earth, 2026; 7 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-03997-9

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Russians started booking tours "at the very last second" to safeguard themselves from contingencies, Maya Lomidze, the Executive Director of the Association of Tour Operators of Russia (ATOR), said during a press conference at TASS.
"Tour operators say that our bookings are not just last-minute, but last-second. Accordingly, all the sales are structured in a way to maintain the price. There is no point in waiting for special offers," she said.
The expert noted that consumer behavior has changed in Russia. Tourists closely monitor market conditions and the global situation. One more trend of the past summer was the demand for organized tours with accommodation in guest houses or unrated hotels, the expert said.

EU plans gradual single-market access for candidate countries: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:33:22 UTC
20:33:22 KST

Melike Pala
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
The European Union is preparing to offer candidate countries gradual access to its single market and research programs before full membership, according to a draft European Commission proposal obtained by news outlet Politico.
The proposal envisages the “gradual integration” of candidate countries into the EU’s single market, including closer trade links and participation in research, innovation and industrial programs, as they work toward full membership, Politico reported Wednesday.
“The single market is the first priority for economic convergence,” the draft review says, adding that earlier integration could strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies.
The document proposes deeper participation where candidate countries demonstrate regulatory alignment and sufficient enforcement capacity, particularly in areas that support preparations for EU accession and serve shared economic and strategic interests.
Under the proposed framework, countries would also be expected to align more closely with EU foreign and security policies.
Access could be limited or withdrawn if countries fail to meet the required conditions, including democratic reforms and alignment with the bloc’s strategic interests.
The European Commission is also considering wider use of qualified majority voting in areas currently subject to unanimity.
The draft says the risk of delays or blockages could increase as EU membership expands.
It also refers to so-called “passerelle clauses,” which can allow certain decisions to shift from unanimity to majority voting without formally amending the EU treaties.
Such mechanisms could potentially be used in areas including sanctions, responses to human rights crises and the deployment of civilian missions.
However, activating the clauses themselves requires unanimous approval from EU member states.
EU leaders are due to discuss enlargement and the bloc’s future institutional arrangements at a summit in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.

US ambassador inaugurates planned Polish-American Centre at Kraków’s Kościuszko Mound
Unknown

The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, has launched a planned new Polish-American Centre to be established in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city. Rose symbolically laid a cornerstone for the new facility and announced a $150,000 (577,000 zloty) grant to restore and preserve the site.
The centre, whose website describes it as a “home for all Polish-American initiatives in Poland”, will be established alongside the famous mound in Kraków created in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko, a hero of both the Polish and American struggles for independence in the 18th century.

“This is a tremendous opportunity for me, on behalf of President Donald Trump and the American people, to celebrate what I consider the most important relationship the United States has with Europe today,” said Rose at the ceremony on Monday.
“America is fortunate to have many, many good friends around the world. But we have no better friend in Europe,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF.
Together with Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska, the speaker of Poland’s Senate, he laid a cornerstone for the new centre and announced the $150,000 grant, which comes from the Ambassadors’ Fund for Cultural Preservation, a programme run by the US State Department.
“Tadeusz Kościuszko is a symbol of the historical bond between Poland and the USA,” declared Kidawa-Błońska. “There is no better place for the Polish-American Centre than Kraków and the mound commemorating a hero of both nations.”

Kościuszko’s Mound was established in Kraków in 1823, following the pattern of two prehistoric mounds that already existed in the city. It honours Kościuszko, a military officer who had fought against Russian rule over Poland and in the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War.
Construction of the new Polish-American Centre is being supported by the Kościuszko Mound Committee in Kraków in partnership with USA250PL, the platform for celebrations in Poland of this year’s 250th anniversary of the American Declaration of Independence.
The Kościuszko Mound Committee has long been engaged in efforts to preserve the mound against partial collapses caused by heavy rain. Polish hydraulics manufacturer PONAR Wadowice is also listed as a partner of the new centre.
The facility says it “will serve as a living symbol of friendship, understanding, and transatlantic cooperation”, providing “a welcoming space for dialogue, creativity, and exchange”. The centre will house event spaces, conference rooms, and offices.
In June, the centre acted as a patron of a United States–Central and Eastern Europe Connection Weekend at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. Next year it plans a commemoration of the Battle of Saratoga, where Kościuszko designed fortifications that contributed to the American victory.
Poland has long looked to the United States for support and as an example during its struggle for independence over the last two centuries, including during the period of partitions in the 19th century, the reestablishment of the Polish state after the First World War, and during the later decades of communist rule.
Since the fall of communism, the US has become Warsaw’s most important security partner – including establishing its first permanent military garrison, named Fort Kościuszko, in Poland in 2023.
The US has opened its first military garrison in Poland, and its first anywhere on NATO's eastern flank.
"This is a historic moment," says Poland's defence minister. "We have been striving for years for this word 'permanent' and it has now become fact" https://t.co/knJEcqv4MB

Last week, President Donald Trump, in a virtual address to the Polish-American Congress (an entity unrelated to the new centre in Kraków), praised his Polish counterpart Karol Nawrocki, a close Trump ally, and described himself as a “great friend of the people of Poland”.
Shortly before that, Nawrocki had expressed confidence that a planned new US military base in Poland would soon be confirmed, and suggested that it would be named Fort Trump.

G20 should be used to address fragmentation of global trade — Reshetnikov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:31:39 UTC
20:31:39 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Dialogue within the G20 can serve as an effective tool for addressing the risks of fragmentation in international trade and preserving the effectiveness of the multilateral trading system based on WTO rules, Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov wrote in his column "G20 Trade Crossroads: Where Countries Meet or Part Ways?" for US magazine Newsweek.
"The G20 forum has repeatedly demonstrated its relevance in preserving the stability of world trade: during the global crisis of 2008-2009 and following the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, when economic turbulence triggered a chain reaction of protectionist measures around the world. The G20 dialogue helped mitigate these trends. We therefore hope that, once again, we will be able to make effective use of this forum to address the risks of fragmentation in international trade and preserve the effectiveness of the multilateral trading system based on WTO rules," he wrote.
The minister stressed that, in this context, the efforts of the United States, which was instrumental in establishing the G20 and currently holds its presidency, to refocus attention on addressing key global challenges deserve high praise.
"However, this raises a question: do all four topics put forward for discussion this year truly represent the most pressing challenges, the failure to address which poses a central threat to global trade? Take the issue of trade in goods produced with forced labor as an example. No one can deny the importance of joint international efforts to combat forced labor, its ramifications and root causes. However, from the perspective of the challenges the international trade faces today, this particular topic does not seem to contribute much to the restoration of the mutual trust, conducive and seamless environment for our businesses worldwide or elimination of unjustified trade barriers," Reshetnikov stressed.
He expressed hope that existing trade disagreements "would not taint what needs to be done to eradicate this heinous human rights violation."
The Russian minister also pointed to the problem of global excess production capacity and overproduction.
Excess production capacity
"This concept is rather debatable - a country possessing certain comparative advantages will produce more than it consumes and will, consequently, export the surplus. This is perfectly normal and, indeed, underpins international trade as a whole. The real question, however, is whether such an excess of production over domestic consumption stems from genuine competitive advantages or is the result of distortions of competition," Reshetnikov wrote.
The Russian economic development minister believes that, in addition to large-scale industrial subsidies widely used by economies that traditionally declare their commitment to a market-based model, there is a whole range of practices that distort competition and create unjustified advantages for domestic exporters. These include tariffs and various non-tariff restrictions that guarantee demand for domestic suppliers. Export controls, restrictions on technology transfers, and the dominance of transnational corporations can lead to monopolization in individual industries, ultimately resulting in a critical level of excess production capacity, he said.

Macron called for faster European Commission investigations, stronger trade defense instruments and requirements ensuring imports meet the same standards imposed on European producers.
On energy, he warned that decarbonization had not eliminated Europe’s vulnerabilities.
“Today, we remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. We can clearly see this with what is happening in the Strait of Hormuz, which poses a problem for our economic models. Even countries that have made substantial progress in decarbonisation, such as Spain and France, each following its own path, still have these dependencies.”
He called for stronger electricity interconnections and greater investment in artificial intelligence, quantum technology and defense.
“We Europeans have more savings than the Americans. Those savings go into our banks and insurance companies. Because we introduced extremely restrictive rules following a financial crisis that originated with American market participants, we overregulated our banks and insurers.”
Macron urged easing financial rules to channel savings into investment, alongside a stronger EU budget and deeper integration of the single market.

Meta shields billions in taxes by classifying AI data centers as experimental models: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:27:57 UTC
20:27:57 KST

Yasin Gungor
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US tech company Meta exploited a federal research tax credit to shield billions of dollars from corporate taxes by classifying its artificial intelligence data centers as experimental pilot models, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
Meta told the Internal Revenue Service that its AI data centers were a “giant experiment that could fail,” the newspaper reported, citing four people familiar with the company’s operations. The maneuver trimmed nearly $4 billion from Meta’s 2025 tax bill, making it the largest beneficiary among publicly traded companies, according to IRS filings.
The strategy relies on a provision dating to the 1980s that was intended to spur innovation by allowing tax credits for supplies used in research rather than standard business operations. People familiar with the matter said Meta began classifying commercially proven processors, including chips bought from Nvidia, as experimental supplies when they were used in artificial intelligence facilities.
Meta defended the practice, saying it invested $200 billion in research over five years, including $57 billion last year.
“Like other companies that invest at this scale, we use the tax incentives Congress established decades ago to encourage this type of domestic investment,” the company said.

Russia Expands Drone Launch Hub as Geran-5 Drones Dominate Attacks on Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:27:18 UTC
20:27:18 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Expands Drone Launch Hub as Geran-5 Drones Dominate Attacks on Kyiv
Russia has continued expanding the Tsymbulova drone base in the Oryol region, adding new launch infrastructure, shelters, and storage facilities over the past four weeks, an OSINT channel Strategic Aviation reported on September 29.
Satellite imagery shows a new area southeast of the existing launch positions with eight dome-shaped shelters for jet-powered drones and an additional launcher. Strategic Aviation reported that paved areas have also been prepared for eight more shelters and two additional launchers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s Geran drones are domestically produced derivatives of Iran’s Shahed attack drones, while newer variants increasingly use jet propulsion.
The Geran-3 was developed from the jet-powered Shahed-238, while the newer Geran-5 is linked to Iran’s Karrar design and can reach far higher speeds than propeller-driven Shaheds. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how these jet-powered variants are becoming harder for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
Six garages for strike drones that were still under construction in early September have now been completed. Another 14 garages have appeared along the access road, the OSINT channel noted.
The facility’s protective infrastructure has also been reinforced. Strategic Aviation reported that several above-ground shelters were converted into underground structures, while additional defensive measures are being installed around launch areas.
Construction has also expanded near existing Geran-5 launchers, with space prepared for six additional launch positions. Towers under construction nearby could be used for anti-drone netting or communications, the channel said.
Strategic Aviation assessed that the expansion is already affecting the composition of Russian drone attacks on Kyiv. The channel estimated that Geran-5 drones now account for roughly 75% of the drones launched toward the Ukrainian capital, compared with about 10% a month earlier.
Further construction is visible in the northeastern section of the site, where heavy equipment is operating on previously unused land. The channel assessed that new storage facilities may be under construction there.
The expansion has also reduced the number of drones left outdoors. Strategic Aviation reported that nearly 100 drones were visible outdoors at the end of summer, while the latest imagery shows fewer than a dozen.
Recently, Russian drones struck civilian sites in Ukraine’s Odesa region, including an animal shelter in Velykodolynske, where three dogs and 10 cats were killed. The attack also damaged residential buildings, warehouses, a gymnasium, a dormitory, and vehicles.

Fire Point Says Its 850-Km FP-9 Ballistic Missile Is Entering the Final Stretch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:27:11 UTC
20:27:11 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Fire Point Says Its 850-Km FP-9 Ballistic Missile Is Entering the Final Stretch
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point plans to complete development of its FP-9 ballistic missile, designed for a range of up to 850 kilometers, by the end of fall 2026, while its shorter-range FP-7 has already entered the codification process.
Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh outlined the company’s progress in an interview with entrepreneur and blogger Andrii Fedoriv published on September 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Terekh said Fire Point has been working on its ballistic missile program for less than two years—a timeline she contrasted with traditional development cycles that can stretch for decades.
“Similar developments have never taken less than 15 years,” she said.
Fire Point is developing two ballistic missiles simultaneously, with both projects now approaching their final stages.
“The short-range ballistic missile is, you could say, already ready. That is, it is going through the codification process,” Terekh said.
She confirmed that the weapon in question is the FP-7, with a range of up to 300 kilometers, or roughly 185 miles.
The second missile is significantly more ambitious.
“The long-range one is 850 kilometers. You could also say that it is in the final stage. But the final stage still means a series of tests,” Terekh said.
Asked when a Ukrainian ballistic missile could reach Moscow, Terekh said Fire Point already has a target timeline.
“We plan to do this by the end of autumn. Specifically, the long-range ballistic missile that should be able to reach Moscow,” she said.
Terekh stressed that Fire Point does not select targets for the weapon. Operational targeting decisions belong exclusively to Ukraine’s Armed Forces. She added, however, that personally she would “very much like it to be Moscow.”
The pace of development has come with an enormous price tag. According to Terekh, Fire Point has invested approximately $200 million in the FP-7 program alone.
“Development of our first ballistic missile, the FP-7, is approximately $200 million that we spent on R&D and preparation for initial production,” she said.
The larger FP-9 will require even greater investment. Terekh attributed the costs to highly specialized engineering teams, repeated testing, expensive materials and the need to develop critical technologies and components internally.
Many of those components cannot simply be purchased internationally because their export is tightly restricted—or because, in some cases, commercially available equivalents do not exist.
“Ballistic missiles mean hundreds of millions of dollars in R&D,” Terekh said.
Only a relatively small group of countries possesses indigenous ballistic missile capabilities, she added.
Earlier, Terekh revealed that Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile completed about 15 test launches and is now undergoing Defense Ministry certification, putting it on track for its first combat use as early as this fall.

Russia Loses 2,090 Troops in 24 Hours, Highest Reported Daily Toll of Full-Scale War
Russian forces recorded their highest reported daily casualty total since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 2,090 troops killed or wounded over a 24-hour period, according to UK Defence Intelligence on September 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Citing figures from Ukraine’s General Staff for September 28, UK intelligence said the reported losses marked the highest single-day total since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Three previous daily totals exceeding 2,000 Russian casualties were recorded in 2024. The fourth-highest figure, 1,960 troops killed or wounded, was recorded on September 16, 2026.
“The casualty rate has remained high since the summer, highly likely as Russia maintains its intensity in the fortress belt region, particularly in the vicinity of the Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropillia,” the intelligence added.
The latest figures add to Russia’s mounting personnel losses throughout the war. Ukraine’s General Staff has separately estimated total Russian military losses at approximately 1.5 million personnel, describing the figure as the country’s highest losses in a single war since World War II.
According to the General Staff, the total exceeds the combined losses sustained by Soviet and Russian forces in wars and armed conflicts since the second half of the 20th century. It estimated that Russia’s losses in Ukraine are roughly 100 times those suffered by the Soviet Union during the war in Afghanistan and 125 times Russia’s officially acknowledged losses in the First and Second Chechen wars.
Separate reports have also pointed to internal problems within Russian military units. Documents obtained by Cyber-ATESH detail combat losses, widespread unauthorized absences, suicides, and serious disciplinary issues within Russia’s 127th Motor Rifle Division.
When assessed alongside battlefield reports and independent Russian investigations, the documents suggest that the division’s official casualty records may significantly lag behind losses documented at the front, while some of its units appear to be facing broader problems with morale and command.

Russian Forces Seize Ukrainian Food Aid From Civilians in Temporarily Occupied Oleshky
Russian forces in temporarily occupied Oleshky are confiscating food dropped by Ukrainian drones for residents, according to Tetiana Hasanenko, chief of the Oleshky Municipal Military Administration, in an interview with Ukrinform published September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian forces have conducted multiple drone deliveries of humanitarian supplies to the trapped civilian population. The most recent operation delivered approximately four tons of food to residents across the city before Russian forces began seizing the aid.

Beyond confiscations, Russian forces continue to detain and abduct residents.

Russian forces have systematized the blockade of Oleshky since early 2024, with civilians facing severe shortages of food, water, medicine, electricity, and gas.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported in June that no official food deliveries had reached the city since late May.
Ukrainian drone operations represent one of the few channels through which humanitarian aid now reaches the roughly 2,000 remaining residents, down from a pre-war population exceeding 24,000.

Kremlin denies Russia has political prisoners as Trump weighs sanctions relief for releases

EU to propose opening the single market to accession candidates, but there is a condition - Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:25:19 EEST
20:25:19 KST

EU to propose opening the single market to accession candidates, but there is a condition - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
The European Commission proposes gradually integrating candidate countries into the EU single market. Access will depend on reforms and support for the bloc's goals.
The European Union will open its vast economy to countries awaiting accession, provided that they agree to stand together with the bloc against hostile states and industrial competitors. Politico reports this, citing a draft proposal by the European Commission, writes UNN.
Details
Candidate countries, some of which have been waiting for EU membership for decades, will be offered unprecedented "gradual integration" into the EU single market, including frictionless trade and access to research programs while their applications are being processed, according to the draft plan.
"The single market is the foremost priority for economic convergence," the review of the "pre-enlargement" policy on the benefits to be offered to candidate countries states.
"Early integration will open opportunities for Union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependence. The European Commission will identify where proven regulatory compliance and enforcement capacity allow deeper participation in research, innovation and industrial cooperation, as well as broader market access. Priority should be given to opportunities that support preparations for accession and meet shared economic and strategic needs," the draft says.
The review, conducted by von der Leyen's chief adviser, Alexandre Adam — a former aide to French President Emmanuel Macron — will radically change the EU's approach to neighboring countries, the publication notes. Currently, almost all economic benefits of closer cooperation are reserved for members, but no new country has joined since Croatia in 2013.
As part of the package of measures by Alexandre Adam, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro will reportedly be offered "road maps" aimed at accelerating the accession process in the coming years. Other countries, such as North Macedonia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Turkey, have faced delays in the process — concerns are growing that they may become disengaged or gravitate toward Russia or China, the publication writes.
Under the European Commission's plan, the economic benefits offered to candidate countries will depend on their support for the EU's foreign policy objectives, while access to the single market will depend on whether they share key technologies with hostile states and trade competitors.
"As industrial and market integration deepens, participation in sensitive sectors should be accompanied by cooperation on investment screening, export controls, sanctions enforcement and the protection of sensitive technologies," the document states.
"The assessment of access should take into account strategic alignment, critical dependencies and the ability to manage risks to infrastructure and supply chains. If these conditions are not met, the scope of participation should be adjusted in accordance with the relevant instrument," the draft says.
The sectors being considered for closer cooperation include semiconductors, quantum technologies, biotechnology, artificial intelligence and space.
According to the review, the ultimate goal for candidate countries should be to become full members of the EU. "However, accession takes time: candidate countries must undergo a rigorous, merit-based process and carry out far-reaching and lengthy reforms," it states.
"This time should be fully used strategically both to prepare the Union for enlargement and to deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest," the document states.
However, the benefits will depend on whether countries make their contribution. "If these commitments are not fulfilled, participation must remain reversible. Access should be suspended or revoked where justified," the proposal warns.
Adam’s report, which is due to be presented to senior officials on October 6, when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen returns from the Western Balkans, will propose new conditions for those joining the bloc to ensure that they do not backslide on democracy and the rule of law.
"The accession process must establish more than mere legal compliance," it says. "Institutions must work in practice, and reforms must be enduring. Therefore, monitoring, incentivisation and enforcement must form a continuous structure extending beyond accession."
But the EU will also change to accommodate broader membership, moving far beyond the club of wealthy Western European democracies as it was originally conceived. The bloc could change its rules to be less vulnerable to the whims of individual members, the review concludes, without the need to reopen the EU’s fundamental articles of law and potentially trigger national referendums across the bloc.
"The European Commission supports changes to the Treaties where necessary, but believes that measures already available under the Treaties should be used now," the conclusion says. Among the options under consideration is a step that would allow more decisions to be adopted by a qualified majority of member countries.
"Qualified majority voting is already the general rule under the Treaties, but unanimity remains in several strategically important areas. As membership grows, the risk of delay or blockage is likely to increase," the document says.
So-called passerelle clauses, which allow decisions to be taken by majority vote rather than unanimously, could be used to facilitate the adoption of sanctions, respond to human rights crises and deploy civilian missions in conflict zones, the review says. However, these clauses require the unanimous support of member countries to be activated.
Leaders from across the EU will be asked to give their views on discussions about how to bring new members into the bloc — and what to offer those still waiting — at a two-day summit in Brussels starting on October 15.

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. The G20 plays a unique role in the multilateral trading system by developing ideas and shaping the framework for future multilateral agreements, including those to be considered by forums such as the WTO. This is particularly important at a time when the international community faces an erosion of mutual trust, Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov wrote in his column "G20 Trade Crossroads: Where Countries Meet or Part Ways?" for US magazine Newsweek.

These ideas and proposals are discussed in an open and informal dialogue. This is particularly important at a time when the erosion of mutual trust has become one of the key challenges facing the international community," Reshetnikov stressed.

EU climate agency warns of rapid Arctic changes, record marine heat waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:24:18 UTC
20:24:18 KST

Melike Pala
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
The Arctic is undergoing rapid changes as marine heat waves reach record levels in European seas, according to a new report released on Wednesday by the European Union's Copernicus Marine Service.
Rising ocean temperatures are driving significant changes across the world's seas, with consequences for marine ecosystems, coastal communities and economies, according to the report.
The report identified the Arctic as one of the regions experiencing the sharpest changes.
Arctic sea ice extent declined by about 490,000 square kilometers per decade between 1979 and 2025, an area nearly the size of Spain, according to the report.
The decline in sea ice has contributed to increased wind and wave activity, leaving around 60% of Arctic coastal infrastructure vulnerable to erosion and rising sea levels, it said.
The report also highlighted exceptionally high temperatures in European regional seas.
The Mediterranean and Black Sea experienced record marine heat waves in 2024, with temperatures more than 4.6C (40.2F) above normal.
Global sea levels have also continued to rise, with the average rate reaching about 4.2 millimeters per year since 2012.

Exclusive: Ukraine's partners could access new tech to counter jet-powered drones, Budanov tells Euronews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:23:07 UTC
20:23:07 KST

Countries with existing drone cooperation agreements with Kyiv could negotiate access to Ukraine’s latest technology for countering Russia’s new jet-powered drones, Kyrylo Budanov told Euronews.
Ukraine is already using its new interceptor technology in combat and is now racing to scale up production before the hardest part of the winter, according to Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
Budanov told Euronews in an exclusive interview that the technology is intercepting Russian jet-powered drones in most cases, but that producing it on a large enough scale remains the main challenge.
The technology could also become available to countries that have already established drone partnerships with Ukraine under agreements known as “Drone Deals.”
Ukraine has signed such agreements with a growing number of partners, including EU countries Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, the Netherlands and Denmark. The deals provide a framework for cooperation including joint production, technology transfer and the exchange of military expertise.
The agreements were developed as Ukraine rapidly expanded its own drone industry and its use of relatively inexpensive interceptor drones against Russia’s conventional Shahed-type attack drones.
But Russia has also been adapting.
Moscow has increasingly deployed jet-powered attack drones capable of reaching speeds of up to 500 km/h, significantly faster than the previous generation of Ukrainian interceptor drones, which could reach around 300 km/h.
The speed advantage meant those interceptors could no longer reliably reach the new Russian drones, forcing Ukrainian forces in some cases to use more expensive and scarce air-defence missiles against them.
Ukraine has since accelerated the development of faster interceptors specifically designed to counter the new threat.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine has become highly effective at intercepting conventional Shahed-type drones, with rates of around 90% or higher during some attacks.
The newer jet-powered variants remain considerably more difficult: Zelenskyy has put their interception rate at 57% earlier this week.
It is this newer generation of Ukrainian interceptor technology that could now potentially become part of the country’s existing partnerships.
“This isn’t about any specific product. It’s in principle about cooperation between countries on similar products,” Budanov told Euronews.
Asked specifically whether Ukraine’s latest technologies, including interceptors for jet-powered drones, could become part of its agreements with European countries, Budanov said:
“Anyone who has made such agreements with us has the right, so to speak, to continue negotiations on specific products.”
Budanov said he believes Ukraine can reach the necessary level of production before the hardest part of the coming winter.
The urgency of that race is already clear on the ground.
Euronews gained exclusive access to an air-defence positions protecting the Kyiv region, where soldiers described how Russia’s faster drones are sharply reducing the time available to detect and engage incoming threats.
When a jet-powered drone is heading towards Kyiv, they said, crews can sometimes have just 10-15 seconds to react.
The relentless pace of the attacks is also taking its toll. Some soldiers told Euronews they had been sleeping for as little as an hour and a half per day in recent days as repeated waves of Russian drones kept air-defence units on alert.
Pavlo Tsugunov, an anti-aircraft battery commander, said the speed and altitude of the latest Russian drones had made them significantly harder for existing systems to engage.
“They are flying higher and faster,” Tsugunov told Euronews. “And for the most part, the systems we have cannot engage these targets.”
The jet-powered drones are adding another layer of pressure to Ukraine’s already stretched air defences, which are simultaneously facing shortages of interceptors capable of stopping Russian ballistic missiles.

Saudi Arabia's Tabuk airport, where the plane eventually landed safely, said that both pilots had been hospitalized after sustaining injuries. Neither the airport or the purported Israeli passenger identified the attacker.
Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Saudi Arabia as it flew over Jordanian airspace, transmitting a general emergency signal and then another emergency signal that indicated possible unlawful interference, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli media said had around 150 Israeli passengers on board, then again transmitted the initial general emergency signal before later landing at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, the website said.
The aircraft's data appeared to show that it had suddenly and rapidly descended by nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal, Flightradar24 said. It was not immediately clear who transmitted the emergency signals.
Israeli media published conflicting reports on the incident, with some outlets reporting that a pilot had tried to crash the passenger plane in an alleged attempted suicide attempt.
Some Israeli media outlets identified the pilots as Omani and Emirati nationals, while others said they were Russian and Ukrainian.
The incident triggered national security consultations in Israel, which has no official diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed.
In a statement, the Israeli prime minister's office said the situation was "under control" and that all measures were being taken to bring the Israeli passengers back to Israel.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday met with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during a a rare visit to the Gulf country. Israel and the UAE have forged close security, military and economic ties since establishing diplomatic ties in 2020.
Earlier this year, Israel provided the UAE with Iron Dome air-defense systems and Israeli personnel to operate them, helping defend against Iranian attacks launched in retaliation for Israeli and U.S. strikes on Iran.
The UAE is yet to comment on the incident, while the Dubai-owned airline has only said that the flight experienced an "incident" and diverted to Tabuk, where it landed safely, and that all passengers were safe and accounted for.
Yasmin Abukasis said her daughter Miriam, who was among the passengers on the flight, had told her that she had heard screaming and that a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor, and that there was blood everywhere.
Israeli media published a photo purportedly taken from inside the plane, which appeared to show a passenger's blood-soaked shirt. Reuters could not immediately verify the image.
Flydubai operates daily return flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv, a route that is popular among Israeli nationals. The flight path normally uses airspace over Saudi Arabia and Jordan.
It is not the first time a flight between Israel and the UAE has landed in Saudi Arabia. A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Riyadh in September 2025 due to a medical incident, Israeli media reported at the time.

Burundi to take third-country deportees from US

Unknown Publisher

Burundi to take third-country deportees from US
BUJUMBURA, Sept 30 - Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under President Donald Trump's hardline immigration policy.
However, Bujumbura will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said Nancy Ninette Mutoni, spokesperson for President Evariste Ndayishimiye.
Tuesday's announcement gave no details of numbers, timing, or financial details.
Washington has sent so-called third-country deportees to some half a dozen African nations under opaque deals that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of dollars.
In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.
Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, living conditions and integration into local communities. "Receiving them requires serious planning — where they will stay, what they will eat and how they will live alongside the local population," she said.
"If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law will be respected," she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added.
The US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available. REUTERS

Passenger on Flydubai flight: 'The pilot was stabbed, we saw blood, we thought we wouldn't make it out alive'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:22:22 UTC
20:22:22 KST

Passenger on Flydubai flight: 'The pilot was stabbed, we saw blood, we thought we wouldn't make it out alive'
Miriam, a passenger on the Flydubai flight FZ1073 that was diverted this morning recounts: “We heard screams from the cockpit, we saw large amounts of blood, and the plane lost control”
Chilling testimonies continue to arrive from FlyDubai flight FZ1073 that was diverted Wednesday morning for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, following a serious incident that occurred in the cockpit.
In a phone interview on i24NEWS' sister Hebrew Channel, Miriam, one of the passengers on the plane, together with her mother Yasmin, who was waiting for her at Ben Gurion Airport, described the moments of terror.
"We heard screams, we saw large amounts of blood"
Miriam, who was speaking on the phone while waiting in the airport area in Saudi Arabia, recounted the difficult moments: "About an hour or two before landing, we just started to hear screams from the plane. Someone started screaming... We just heard screams, and they opened the cockpit and saw large amounts of blood, from someone who had simply tried to murder the pilot and stabbed him with a pocketknife. Then the plane lost control."
According to her, the plane completely lost control for several minutes: "We felt that this was it; we were about to crash. I was already screaming 'Shema Yisrael' and saying, 'I can't die, I'm my mother's only daughter, I can't do this to my mom.'"
Miriam says Israeli passengers were the ones who took control of the situation: “Those who ultimately took control of the incident here were Israelis from the plane, who simply neutralized the terrorist. There was also a nurse here, and a doctor who provided first aid to the pilot. And thank God, there were several pilots on the plane, and they sort of took control of the plane, and in the end we made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.”
"We don't know yet if it is a terrorist."
When asked directly whether it was indeed a terrorist who boarded the plane, Miriam replied cautiously: "We don't know yet. There is speculation that it might be someone from the flight crew. We really don't know. At least, I don't know." Regarding how the attacker was subdued, she said: "I believe it was with their own hands; I wasn't in the cockpit."
Miriam also described the situation on the ground after the landing: "Everyone here is traumatized, in a panic. We just landed in Saudi Arabia, they're giving first aid to the pilot who was injured, I don't know what his condition is, but I understand it's not good, and we're waiting to see what they'll do with us here."
Later in the conversation, she updated that police officers and doctors had entered the area and that they asked the passengers to sit down, and that there were rumors about being transferred to an alternative plane for a flight to Israel. "We were all sure that we wouldn't get out of here alive," she said. "I don't know if it would be from a crash, or from a terrorist, or from a murderous attack."
At a later stage in the conversation, Miriam described the severity of the incident: "It's just as it sounds, it's a terrorist attack in the middle of a flight. That's what it was. And those moments, it's more than just moments; it's several whole minutes and even close to ten or fifteen minutes where we felt we wouldn't make it out of there alive."
The mother, who lost her son on October 7, waited at Ben Gurion Airport.
Miriam's mother, Yasmin, arrived at Ben Gurion Airport to wait for her daughter, who was returning from an 11-month trip in the East ahead of her brother's memorial service.
Yasmin described the moments when she received the news: "I got to the airport to wait for my daughter, who had been traveling in the East for 11 months. She was coming ahead of her brother's memorial service. We were all excited, and then I heard from one of the women here that there was a delay with the Dubai flight… Just then, my daughter called. They told me, ‘No, no, she’s landed.’ Then Miriam said to me: ‘Mom, you have no idea what we went through. Our plane almost crashed.’”
Yasmin revealed that she lost her son, Itamar Abuksis, in battle on October 7th: "I lost my son on October 7th. He fell in Kisufim. A sweet Golani soldier... His name was Itamar Abuksis. And we have a memorial service on Sunday, God willing. And that’s the reason Miriam stopped the trip and is coming back. And suddenly I hear something like this, and I say, ‘Oh my God, this can’t be.’ My whole body is covered in goosebumps; even now I’m under internal stress, and I say, oh my God, what a miracle that it ended this way and not otherwise. But what she went through. That’s a terrifying fear."
"We said 'Shema Yisrael'"
Yasmin also described the details of the story as her daughter told her on the phone: "She told me that they heard screams from the cockpit and a call for help, and Israeli guys there pulled themselves together, ran to him, caught the attacker, and tied him up on the floor. At that point, the plane lost its balance, and they were sure they were crashing. She told me, 'We started shouting Shema Yisrael. I asked God to give me strength because I can't not come home.'"
"I am grateful that it ended this way."
Yasmin summed up her feelings: "Now they are waiting in Saudi Arabia. They don't know what will happen. There are ambulances and police forces that arrived at the scene; they asked if anyone needed medical help. First of all, I am grateful that it ended this way, thank God, and not otherwise, that everyone is healthy. I hope that the pilot is as well. And she said there were two other volunteers, pilots, which was also a miracle, that they managed to help and take control."
At the end of the conversation, Yasmin described the therapy dog that is with her, who joined the family after Itamar’s death: “We brought her after Itamar was killed. Her name is Prana. Prana means life energy in Hindi. My son was full of life. Life was taken from him, and from us; a serious vitality. He was the eldest of six siblings, and we must bring in new life energy.”
As previously reported, the incident began when a passenger plane, a Boeing 737 MAX with over 150 passengers on board, made a sharp U-turn while crossing the skies of northern Saudi Arabia. Simultaneously with the activation of a distress signal by the pilot, an unusual deceleration in flight speed was recorded; the aircraft disappeared from civilian tracking systems, and all radio contact with control towers was lost. This chain of events raised serious concerns of a hijacking and led to the scrambling of Israeli Air Force fighter jets.
Ultimately, contact with the cockpit was reestablished, and an initial assessment indicated that the commotion had erupted as a result of a fight that was not nationalist in nature. Israeli airspace returned to normal operations, and the fighter jets were instructed to return to their base.

Fresh Israeli strikes on Gaza killed at least 6 Palestinians Wednesday, marking continuous violation of a U.S.-mediated cease-fire in the territory.
Gaza's civil defense agency and a hospital said an Israeli airstrike targeting a minibus killed five people and wounded 14 others in in Gaza City, while an earlier airstrike on an apartment elsewhere in the city killed a woman.
Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesperson for the civil defense said there were "five martyrs and 20 wounded, including a number of children and women ... as a result of an Israeli airstrike that targeted a passenger bus in Tel al-Hawa."

Gaza City's al-Shifa hospital confirmed that five bodies and several wounded people had arrived at the medical facility "following an Israeli airstrike that targeted a vehicle near the destroyed cabinet headquarters in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood."
The Israeli military did not immediately comment on either of the reported strikes.
Israel alleges Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of an October cease-fire and has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks.
Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal.

Finnish news agency STT faces "shocking" threat of closure
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:21:44 EEST
20:21:44 KST

The Finnish News Agency STT has announced a significant restructuring of its business which could ultimately lead to a cessation of its operations after nearly 140 years.
In a press release, the agency noted that the restructure is prompted by long-standing losses in its news and photojounalism units.
The statement added that STT has therefore started restructuring talks with staff representatives — affecting a total of 95 employees, nearly its entire workforce.
Of the 95 employees included in the redundancy talks, some 68 work in news and photography while the remainder are employed in other facets of the business.
STT provides news and photo agency services to dozens of domestic media outlets, including Yle, which owns 1.7 percent of the agency.
Union: "Absolutely shocking news"
Founded in 1887, the Helsinki-based agency is one of the longest-operating news agencies in the world, but it has run into significant financial difficulties in recent years.
In 2018, the Finnish government approved a subsidy of 1.5 million euros for the agency, as it was struggling from a gradual loss of clients.
Last year, STT's largest shareholder, Sanoma Media Finland, announced plans to significantly reduce its use of the agency's news and photo services, or possibly end them altogether — leading to a restructuring round and casting further doubt over the agency's future.
"However, adjustment targets were not, in practice, achieved — costs are still higher than revenues. Another round of change would inevitably be ahead, and we do not believe we can offer customers an adequate level of service with a smaller operation than the current one," STT's CEO Kimmo Laaksonen wrote in Wednesday's press release.
In a separate statement released shortly after STT's announcement on Wednesday, Finland's journalism union Journalistiliitto called the move "shocking".
"The shutdown of STT is absolutely shocking news given the current security situation, in which attempts to influence information are an everyday occurrence, and Finland should be strengthening — rather than weakening — the structures of reliable information distribution," union chair Marjaana Varmavuori wrote.
The union's statement called for action, in particular from the Finnish state, to keep STT operational.
"In the worst case scenario, the collapse of STT could trigger a domino effect, in which other news outlets sooner or later also go under," Varmavuori added.
Government suspends funding plans
The Finnish Ministry of Transport and Communications also issued a statement in the wake of STT's announcement, noting that preparations for the state to provide funding to the agency will be suspended until further notice.
The government of Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) had previously stated that it was seeking to ensure the continuity of STT's operations by providing a state subsidy of just over one million euros.
Transport and Communications Minister Lulu Ranne (Finns) noted that STT's financial and operational challenges have been known for a long time, so the restructuring announcement did not come as a surprise.
"It is a pity that STT's long-standing operations are at risk of ending. However, it appears that STT has not been able to respond to the changes in the media industry," Minister Ranne wrote in the ministry's press release.

Ukrainian fighter who returned from Scotland to serve killed in action two days before his 21st birthday

Source: the BBC
Details: Arkadii had begun studying at university abroad, but eventually returned to Ukraine to defend his country.
After Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, the boy's family fled the war and found a new home in the Scottish region of Dumfries and Galloway. There, he attended secondary school and even completed one year at the University of Edinburgh.
However, he had to interrupt his university studies after deciding to return to his homeland and join the army. Arkadii, who used the alias Arka, served as a combat medic and drone operator. He was wounded several times in combat.
On 22 September 2026, the family learned that Arkadii had been killed on 18 September while carrying out a combat mission. He was due to celebrate his 21st birthday two days later.
His mother, Liudmyla, said he was "funny, bright, very charismatic and full of life" and an "incredibly loving brother".
"Ukraine was the country he loved more than anything. As the war continued, I could see him becoming more serious. He followed everything that was happening in Ukraine very closely and felt that he could not simply continue his normal life while other Ukrainians were defending the country where he was born," she said.
His mother added that she is immensely proud of her son.
Quote from Liudmyla: "The hardest thing for me is knowing that I will never again see his living face, hear his voice or hold him. I also grieve for the future he was meant to have – his dreams, his family one day, the children he might have had.
I want people to remember not simply that another young soldier died in Ukraine, but that Arkadii was a whole person, deeply loved, with a family, a childhood, a future and dreams.
He was our son, our pride, and I want his name and his life to be remembered."
Details: Peter Kormylo, archivist at the Ukrainian Prisoner of War chapel in Lockerbie, which Arkadii attended, said the entire community was saddened by his death. The clergyman described him as a "very pleasant young man" who was determined to return to Ukraine and fight.
Quote from Peter: "All I can say about the boy is, having met him on a few occasions, he was a very courteous young man and quite a serious young man. The last time I remember him being at the chapel I found him, when everyone had gone, sitting in the chapel writing a couple of what looked like letters – but in actual fact were prayers.
He was a deep thinker and obviously felt the need to do what many Ukrainians are doing and that's fulfill their patriotic duty."
Details: Anthony Tuffery, rector at Arkadii's old school, described him as "a polite, respectful and hardworking young man".
Background: In July 2025, 21-year-old Artem Naliato, who had been adopted by an Italian family at the age of 12, was killed in action.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Penghu Coast Guard on Wednesday intercepted a Chinese fishing boat illegally trawling off the Penghu Islands, the second such vessel caught in the area in a week.

A preliminary inspection found seven Chinese fishers and about 5,000 kilograms of catch aboard, which were dumped back into the sea.
The incident followed the Penghu Coast Guard’s seizure Saturday of another illegal Chinese fishing vessel with six fishers aboard off Mudou Island.
The Coast Guard’s Kinmen-Matsu-Penghu Branch said it operates around the clock to protect national security, public safety, and fishers’ rights. It added that authorities would take legal action against Chinese fishing vessels caught operating illegally in territorial waters.
Meanwhile, the Coast Guard in a statement Tuesday said its Lanyu patrol vessel has been closely monitoring the movements of Chinese coast guard vessels 2503, the Zhujiajian, and 1401, the Chongming.
Chinese coast guard spokesperson Jiang Lue (姜略) announced Tuesday that the Zhujiajian-led fleet would conduct a “routine law enforcement patrol” in the waters east of Taiwan.
The two ships were located about 97 nautical miles northeast of Green Island and 146 nautical miles east of Lanyu on Wednesday, the Coast Guard said.

Taipei has been expanding smoke-free areas in stages. Xiangti Avenue Plaza in Xinyi District has been smoke-free, except for designated smoking zones, since 2016.
The city government said a survey conducted after smoke-free measures were introduced in Ximending found that 96% of respondents supported the policy, while 93.1% were satisfied with its implementation.

The ministry noted that the exercise includes M1A2T tanks, the Taiwan Tactical Network, the OneWeb backup communications system, and drones.

The Army Training and Education Command will oversee both brigades as they put their full capacity to the test.
Lin said the exercise is the Army's annual brigade-level tactical inspection. He added that units train in sustained operations under immersive settings to ensure combat readiness.
Deployment begins on Oct. 14, with the 564th moving north to probe defenses set up by the 269th. The aim is to test troops' situational awareness during defense and offense.
Both forces will engage each other from Oct. 15–23 to evaluate tactical criteria including firepower support and coordination, drone applications, and special forces deployment. He added that the extension will continue non-stop on a 24-hour basis to strengthen soldiers' will and operational endurance.
Lin said the Army will establish a joint operations command center, with the Armed Forces Reserve Command sending liaison officers to coordinate resources for logistics support. Commissioned officers will judge action performance and use reviews to improve future exercises.

====================================================================================================

Spain publishes sweeping housing decree as protests continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:19:45 UTC
20:19:45 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Spain published a sweeping housing decree Wednesday introducing new protections for tenants and restrictions on property investors, as housing protests continued in Madrid and Malaga and political parties prepared for a decisive parliamentary vote Friday.
The decree, published in Spain’s Official State Gazette, will enter into force Thursday and includes 20 articles covering measures on evictions, rents, taxation and affordable housing.
Among its most significant provisions is one targeting so-called “vulture funds.” The decree restricts companies and other entities whose business includes acquiring real estate from purchasing homes for less than 70% of their appraised market value until the end of 2028, with exemptions including for social and affordable housing.
It also provides for the suspension through 2030 of certain evictions involving vulnerable people without alternative housing and introduces tighter regulation of temporary and room rentals.
Temporary rental contracts will require a genuine and demonstrable reason for their temporary nature, while repeated or unjustifiably long temporary contracts can be treated as ordinary residential leases. For room rentals, the combined rent charged for individual rooms cannot exceed the amount that could be charged for renting the property as a whole.
Rent increases will face additional limits through the end of 2027. When rent is already above the applicable reference-price ceiling, no increase will be allowed, while in other cases increases may not exceed 2% without a new agreement between the landlord and tenant.
A second decree, expected to be published Thursday, contains a separate measure providing for the automatic renewal of rental contracts.
According to El Pais, landlords who decide not to renew a lease after the mandatory rental period would generally be required to compensate tenants with at least 12 months’ rent, with exceptions including cases in which the owner needs the home for themselves or certain family members.
Both decrees are due to face an extraordinary ratification vote in parliament Friday.
The measures come amid days of housing protests. Demonstrators spent a fourth night camped in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol, where the protest grew after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who had lived in her home for more than 70 years.
A parallel camp continued Wednesday in Malaga’s Plaza de la Constitucion, where around 50 people in roughly 25 tents spent the night. Organizers are also preparing a housing demonstration in the southern city Saturday.
The government still faces uncertainty over whether parliament will ratify the decrees Friday. A similar housing decree was rejected by lawmakers in April, when Congress voted 177-166 against validating it.
Opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo said his conservative Popular Party would vote against both decrees, calling the package a “trap.”
“Don’t count on me to rip off anyone,” he said, arguing that the government should instead focus on building more housing.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard spokesman Gen. Hossein Mohebbi speaks during a news conference in Tehran, Iran, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U.S. president’s war in the Middle East has failed.
The message was laid out on Sept. 29 in a 25-page open letter to the American public, calling on U.S. voters to oppose Washington’s support for Israel and its involvement in overseas conflicts.
The letter also argued that Iran and the United States could coexist if Washington were to fundamentally alter its foreign policy toward Tehran.
It accused Trump of deliberately obscuring what it described as the “peaceful nature” of Iran’s nuclear program, which Israel regards as an existential threat, while also downplaying the effectiveness of Tehran’s blockade of Gulf oil shipments.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said he did not expect the letter to prompt any change in the U.S. administration’s conduct just weeks before the elections, but suggested that its message could nevertheless reach American voters.
Mohebbi said that the only way for the war in Iran to end is for Washington to admit defeat and leave.
Later, in remarks to The Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and take to the streets and protest Trump’s policies to denounce what he called the U.S. government’s warmongering policies.
He accused the United States of using Iran’s nuclear program as a ruse to “plunder Iran’s wealth” and to turn the country “back into a colony.”
Meanwhile, Iranian authorities said on Sept. 29 they received the official U.S. response to their proposal to end the Middle East war, days after rejected the plan.

Subsidies of CHF1.3 million

Rasul Medal announces shortlist of nominees for second edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:16:25 UTC
20:16:25 KST

Rasul Medal announces shortlist of nominees for second edition
TEHRAN - The initial list of nominees for the second edition of the Rasul (PBUH) Medal, which is presented alongside the Mustafa (PBUH) Prize to young scientists from the Islamic world under the age of 40, has been finalized.
The shortlist comprises four nominees in engineering sciences, four in mathematics, four in computer science, eight in biological and medical sciences, two in chemistry, and two in physics. The award ceremony for the final winners is scheduled to be held in December.
The initial list considered for the Rasul (PBUH) Medal included more than 100,000 candidates across seven scientific fields. The biological and medical sciences category accounted for 55,878 candidates, followed by 4,675 in physics, 7,897 in chemistry, 1,965 in mathematics, 5,589 in computer science, and 26,377 in engineering sciences. In addition, 14 candidates in the field of nanotechnology met the required criteria to be included in the initial list.
Following a review of the outcomes of previous meetings, the judging panel selected the nominees for the shortlist. Accordingly, four nominees were selected in engineering sciences, four in basic sciences, four in mathematics, four in computer science, and eight in biological and medical sciences.
Under the regulations governing the medal, the Rasul (PBUH) Medal secretariat issued a call last December for scientists under the age of 40 residing in Islamic countries. Scientific institutions and prominent scientists had until January 20, 2026, to submit nominations for the medal.
Symbol of scientific excellence
In order to appreciate prominent scientists and provide the ground for scientific cooperation and development worldwide, the Mustafa Prize was established in 2012 as a symbol of scientific excellence at the international level.
The Mustafa Prize, a top science and technology award, is granted biennially to the top researchers and scientists of the Islamic world in three categories: “Life and Medical Science and Technology”, “Information and Communication Science and Technology”, and “Basic and Engineering Sciences”.
The Prize is granted to works deemed to have improved human life, have made tangible and cutting-edge innovations on the boundaries of science, or have presented new scientific methodology.
Ali Akbar Salehi, the head of the scientific working group of the Mustafa Prize, said in August that the scientists targeted by the award include both Muslim and non-Muslim researchers living in Islamic countries, as well as Muslim scientists residing and working in non-Islamic countries.
“Therefore, it is in this context and from this perspective that we use the term ‘scientists of the Islamic world.’ We aim to identify and introduce talented scientists who are not widely known—not necessarily unknown in absolute terms, but relatively unknown to our own community—and bring their achievements to greater public attention, enabling these scientists to gain greater visibility on the global scientific map,” he said.
He added that, for example, among the 22 scientists who have received the prize to date, laureates have come from Bangladesh, Pakistan, India, Turkey, and Singapore.
“This demonstrates that geography should not be a barrier to the recognition of scientists, and the Mustafa Prize is precisely committed to advancing this goal,” he said.
“One of the objectives of the Mustafa Prize Foundation is to establish a scientific network. The goal is not merely to introduce the prize laureates, but also to connect scientists, enabling them to be identified while creating an environment conducive to synergy, collaboration and mutual scientific exchange.”
He went on to say that the foundation has adopted various mechanisms and initiatives to achieve this objective, many of which are known by their Latin acronyms in connection with the Islamic world.
These include the Science and Technology Exchange Program (STEP). The STEP initiative comprises several components, including STEPOL, which focuses on science, technology and innovation policymaking.
In addition, the foundation organizes “Seasonal Schools,” which are held at different times of the year and focus on specific scientific topics, bringing together experts and individuals interested in gaining knowledge in those fields.
Another initiative is the Faculty Mobility in Islamic Countries (FAMIC) program, which aims to facilitate the mobility and exchange of university faculty members among Islamic countries, with the Mustafa Prize Foundation serving as a facilitator. For example, this year, following an open call and despite the circumstances and developments that arose, two of the 42 applicants were selected to attend a program at a university in Pakistan.
He further noted that another initiative is the Young Scientists Fellowship Program (YSFP), which provides scholarships and financial support to young scientists and researchers from Islamic countries, enabling them to travel to scientific and research centers for training and skills development.
The foundation also operates a scientific observatory that monitors emerging frontiers of knowledge and major scientific developments worldwide. The observatory’s activities also result in the publication of specialized reports and publications on scientific developments.
Mehmet Toner, professor of biomedical engineering at Harvard University from Turkey; Vahab Mirrokni, adjunct associate professor at the Courant Institute at New York University from Iran; and Mohammad K. Nazeeruddin, professor of chemistry at the EPFL, and Sion Campus, from India, were the winners of the 6th Mustafa Prize in 2024.
