Germany's Left Party vows to resist Volkswagen plant’s shift to Israel arms production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:16:18 UTC
20:16:18 KST

- Peace campaigner Andreas Seifert warns Rafael cooperation and possible exports from Osnabruck plant to Israel violates Germany’s international obligations, its own arms-export rules
- Critics say Osnabruck has long been the 'City of Peace,' but deal risks that reputation by tying Volkswagen’s car plant to Israel’s sta
 
 Germany’s opposition Left Party said it would fight politically and publicly against Volkswagen’s plans to repurpose a car factory as a production site for Israeli weapons.
“We will stand against this development politically and publicly,” Thorben Peters, co-chair of the Left Party in Lower Saxony state, told Anadolu.
“We demand full transparency about the agreements, oppose the shift from civilian industry to arms production, and will work with employees and unions to advance a civilian industrial policy.”
Volkswagen announced in early September that it was selling the Osnabruck plant to the state of Lower Saxony and Tel Aviv-based investor Aurelius Capital.
An initial project with Israel’s Rafael defense company was presented as the plant's first industrial anchor.
The Left Party has rejected Volkswagen’s claim that selling the factory and shifting it to defense production was the only way to save jobs.
“Employees are being told they have to choose between unemployment and arms production. We do not accept that false alternative.
“Good industrial policy creates civilian jobs. It does not make peace depend on the next arms order.”
 
Volkswagen’s controversial plans
Volkswagen confirmed in March that it was talking to several defense contractors about the Osnabruck site after deciding to phase out car-making there by summer 2027.
Plans for cooperation with Israel’s state-owned defense firm drew months of protest from local peace groups, opposition politicians and parts of the labor movement.
In July, Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund, Volkswagen’s third-largest shareholder, blocked the initial proposal, according to German media reports.
Volkswagen’s management then advanced a new ownership structure that took the carmaker out of a direct partnership with Rafael.
Under the September terms, Aurelius would take a majority stake and Lower Saxony a minority stake, with Rafael remaining the industrial partner rather than the buyer.
Peters called that partnership “especially problematic,” noting that Rafael is a central supplier to the Israeli armed forces.
“Against the background of serious accusations of war crimes and other violations of international humanitarian law against the Israeli government and its military conduct in the Gaza Strip, this partnership sends a devastating political signal,” he said.
International courts and the UN have opened proceedings over Israel’s brutal war in Gaza.
Gaza’s Health Ministry, in figures also cited by the UN, says more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including more than 32,000 women and children.
The International Court of Justice has been hearing South Africa’s genocidal case against Israel, while the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity commited in Gaza.
Peters warned that Lower Saxony should not enter a joint enterprise with a state-owned Israeli arms firm while those accusations stood.
“Anyone who binds themselves so closely, politically and economically, to a company that equips the Israeli armed forces also bears political responsibility for that,” he said.
 
Peace groups reject shift to arms production
According to local media reports, the project involves manufacturing support components for the Iron Dome missile defense system.
Activists have highlighted that the latest move goes against Osnabruck’s “City of Peace” identity, rooted in its role in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Those agreements ended the Thirty Years’ War and helped shape modern international law.
Among the most vocal groups is Action Outcry – Stop the Arms Trade.
The group’s coordinator, Andreas Seifert, told Anadolu that it takes a critical view of all German arms exports and rejects shipments to crisis regions or to states accused of violating human rights.
“In our view, the transformation of the Volkswagen plant in Osnabruck from a civilian automotive factory into an arms manufacturing facility must be rejected, as it will foreseeably lead to involvement in the export of military goods,” he said. 
“This is not a sustainable model for the plant or the city.”
Seifert said the group also objected to the choice of partner.
“We are also deeply concerned that the chosen partner for this project, the Israeli defense company Rafael, supplies weapons and military equipment for Israel’s war in Gaza,” he said.
He added that Action Outcry has long argued that arms shipments to Israel amid the war in Gaza, the occupation of the West Bank and the war with Iran violate Germany’s international obligations and its own arms-export restrictions.
Seifert also criticized state support for the project.
“In our view, Germany’s share of responsibility for the crimes committed by the Israeli military (IDF) in Gaza must be clarified, and appropriate consequences must follow,” he said.
“Given these considerations, partnering with an Israeli arms company — and supporting it with state funds — is simply unacceptable.”

Unknown Publisher

The Kremlin on Wednesday dismissed press reports that it was discussing the release of political prisoners in exchange for easing U.S. sanctions.
Earlier, The Atlantic reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had “signed on” to White House special envoy John Coale’s initiative to pull back sanctions gradually if Moscow would agree to free Russian political prisoners.
Coale has spearheaded a similar arrangement with neighboring Belarus, a close Russian ally, where President Alexander Lukashenko has pardoned hundreds of prisoners for sanctions relief.
The White House envoy is now reportedly hoping to turn that strategy toward Moscow in order to break the deadlock in U.S.-Russian relations and “help advance the cause of peace.”
However, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists on Wednesday that U.S. and Russian officials have not discussed the idea.
“In this formulation, the issue was not discussed and could not be discussed because we categorically deny the existence of any political prisoners,” Peskov said during a daily briefing.
Nobel Peace Prize-winning rights group Memorial currently recognizes 1,826 people as political prisoners in Russia.
Peskov described the framing of The Atlantic’s report as “completely inappropriate.”
The spokesman did acknowledge, however, that Russian and U.S. intelligence services remain in regular contact regarding prisoner exchanges.
Russia and the U.S. have carried out two prisoner swaps since Trump took office in January 2025.
Earlier this week, the White House nominated Coale to serve as its special envoy for hostage affairs.
Coale, a lawyer who previously represented Americans released during the 1979 Iran hostage crisis, was officially appointed to the Belarus role in November, though he had negotiated prisoner releases before that as deputy Ukraine envoy.

Secondary sanctions caused rapid contraction of Iranian aviation

Iranian carriers have often struggled to meet their financial obligations and maintain their fleets due to decades of financial sanctions and difficulties receiving aircraft parts.

With electoral deadlock possible, anti-Netanyahu bloc targets control of Knesset after election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:12:52 UTC
20:12:52 KST

Less than a month before the general election, with most polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc, parties are already preparing for the first battle after the vote: control of the Knesset.
The anti-Netanyahu bloc is working to coordinate a parliamentary move to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana immediately after the election. The aim is to take control of the legislature during the period before a new government is formed, including in a scenario in which Israel heads to another election.
Following Saturday night’s meeting between Gadi Eisenkot, Avigdor Liberman, Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, joint working groups were established to draft the principles of a possible government and determine which steps should be taken immediately after the election. One of those teams is now working to coordinate the effort to replace Ohana.
Likud leaders and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, meanwhile, have held consultations on possible countermeasures. Their goal is to delay any replacement of Ohana until a new government is formed, allowing Likud to retain control of the Knesset during the interim period.
Under Israeli law, the incumbent Knesset speaker can remain in office during the transition, and the election of a new speaker must take place no later than the formation of the new government. In practice, that could allow Ohana to remain in the post for as long as two months.
But a 2020 Supreme Court ruling involving then-speaker Yuli Edelstein established that if 61 lawmakers demand a vote on appointing a new speaker, the vote must be held immediately, even before a government is formed.
The anti-Netanyahu bloc views replacing the speaker as a parliamentary move rather than the formation of a government, and therefore intends to coordinate it with the Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List. MK Ahmad Tibi has already said in an interview that he would support replacing Ohana with a candidate backed by the anti-Netanyahu bloc.
Electing a new Knesset speaker before a government is formed would give the bloc control over the legislative agenda and influence over which bills are brought to a vote.
That could become particularly significant if coalition talks fail and another election is called. A new speaker could seek to advance legislation backed by the bloc, including a law establishing a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre and legislation limiting a prime minister to two terms.
Passing such laws, however, would still require a parliamentary majority that may not exist. Replacing the speaker is considered a procedural parliamentary step, while some lawmakers who support that move could still oppose advancing contentious legislation during a transition period.
Figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc involved in the discussions told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth that “if necessary, replacing the Knesset speaker will be the anti-Netanyahu bloc’s way of testing the possibility of forming a minority government if there is no clear result, while gauging the public’s response.”

Details of Flemish multi-year budget emerge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:12:48 UTC
20:12:48 KST

Flemish Prime Minister Matthias Diependaele (Flemish nationalist N-VA) has unveiled the details of the Flemish government’s budget accord.
Diependaele stressed that difficult choices had been made by the three coalition partners that share a common but also at times diverging vision.
The budgetary operation is the toughest budgetary exercise ever for a Flemish Government. Diependaele provided figures in his September Statement to the Flemish parliament. “In concrete terms, this round of cuts will amount to nearly 2 billion euros in 2027 and ultimately to 3 billion euros in 2029.”
“3 billion euros, of which 1.2 billion is made in the public administration and in subsidies: that is unprecedented for a Flemish government.”
The Flemish PM emphasised that the budget is also a balanced one. “That provides long-term certainty. Sound public finances are a necessary condition for a thriving Flanders.”
What's the substance?
The PM noted there will be no cuts in education: “Education is the cornerstone of our future prosperity,” was his message.
The Flemish government should no longer outsource tasks it can carry out itself. Staff regulations in the Flemish civil service are being modernised.
Additional savings are also being made in the ministerial departments. In total, this amounts to more than 1 million euros annually.
But the Flemish government is maintaining its level of investment.
“We are also investing in extra care and additional capacity,” Diependaele emphasises. “Youth support, care for the elderly, support for people with disabilities and mental health care will also be further strengthened.”
A balanced budget
The agreement provides for a balanced budget until 2029.
To achieve this balance, 3 billion euros must be cut from the budget over the coming years. To realise this, reforms and savings totalling 3 billion euros have been finalised.
In total, more than 1.2 billion euros will be saved on public expenditure: this includes subsidies (500 million euros) and savings within the civil service (over 700 million euros).
Reforms
The price of service vouchers, the ‘dienstencheques’, will rise from 10 to 12 euros. Anyone purchasing more than 175 service vouchers per year will pay 13 euros per voucher from the 176th voucher onwards.
Registration fees, a tax on property purchases, will be increased from 2 to 3 per cent. This applies to all properties, not just those costing more than 500,000 euros (as was initially planned).
The Growth Allowance, which combines the former child allowance and other financial family support, will continue to be paid up to the age of 23 (currently up to 25) for students still living at home. The exception whereby parents of children who are not continuing their studies are entitled to the Growth Allowance until the child reaches the age of 19 is being abolished.
The birth grant of 1,310.75 euros that parents receive on the birth of their children would only be paid on the birth of their first child.
Some of the reductions in inheritance tax are being postponed until 2029. Inheritance tax on small and medium-sized estates will, however, be reduced: by 160 million euros by the end of the legislative term. The exact details of this reduction will be discussed over the coming years.
Savings
More than 500 million euros in subsidies are set to be cut. Each minister will have to make cuts within their respective areas of responsibility. With regard to cultural subsidies, savings will include cuts in museums and archives.
More than 700 million euros will be saved within the civil service. Around 180 million euros will come from savings on civil service staff, partly by making changes to civil service regulations.
Flemish civil servants will lose two paid public holidays: 2 November (All Souls’ Day) and 15 November (King’s Day). These are paid public holidays in the civil service that are rarely, if ever, observed in other sectors.
Savings are also being made at local authority level. The figure is expected to reach 240 million euros by 2029, mainly through lower indexation of funds from the Municipal Fund.
Transport operator De Lijn will receive less money than previously promised: the promised 50 million euros will be halved to an additional 25 million euros.
Cuts are also planned on support for SMEs, including the subsidies that companies receive to train staff within their organisations.
VRT must make additional savings worth 10 million euros; Media platform VRT MAX may introduce a paid service
Flemish public broadcaster VRT must make an additional 10 million euros in savings over the coming years according to a press release from Flemish Media Minister Cieltje Van Achter (Flemish nationalist N-VA).
The Flemish Government has instructed the public broadcaster to make clear choices in this regard, to place greater emphasis on local programmes and no longer to award exclusive contracts to on-screen personalities.
These savings come in addition to the 16 million euros that the VRT was already required to save between 2026 and 2031.
At the same time, the broadcaster is permitted to “develop a paid subscription service or other forms of a tiered distribution model in addition to the free VRT MAX”.

Iran submits two proposals to ISO for nanotechnology standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:12:27 UTC
20:12:27 KST

Iran submits two proposals to ISO for nanotechnology standards
TEHRAN – Iran has put forward two proposals to the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) aimed at developing international standards in the field of nanotechnology.
The first proposal focuses on establishing standards for silica aerogel-based thermal insulation coatings containing nanomaterials, with an emphasis on defining their properties as well as methods for measurement and performance evaluation.
Owing to their nanoporous structure and excellent thermal insulation properties, silica aerogels have attracted considerable attention as promising materials for advanced thermal insulation coatings. The establishment of an international standard could provide a clear and consistent framework for assessing and comparing the performance of such products.
The second suggestion concentrates on graphene-based materials for electrochemical energy storage. The standard will provide a basis for evaluating and comparing the performance of graphene-based materials in energy storage systems, a field which has gained increasing importance with the development of advanced battery and supercapacitor technologies.
The proposals will be discussed at the ISO/TC 229 Technical Committee meeting on Nanotechnology, which is scheduled to be held in Mexico from October 19 to 23, 2026. Iranian representatives will attend the meeting online.
The country has played an active role in proposing international standards; it is placed fourth following the US, South Korea, and Japan. So far, some13 international nanotechnology standards have been developed at Iran’s proposal, Mehr news agency reported.
Nanotech progress in Iran beyond just a scientific achievement
With over 430 companies operating in the nanotechnology sector, and more than 1,960 nanotech products receiving nanoscale certificates, the advancement of the nanotechnology sector in the country proves to be more than just a scientific achievement.
Relying on domestic capacity, nanotechnology in Iran is not merely measured by scientific rankings and published articles, but products that have been manufactured and entered the industry and the market, IRNA reported.
The total sale of these products amounts to over 970 trillion rials (about 554 million dollars), indicating that the scientific achievement has become an economic and industrial capacity.
Nanotechnology in the country is a typical example of a successful development of a tech ecosystem. From the very beginning, a long-term roadmap was developed to strengthen all aspects of the technology development chain, from education and research to commercialization and market development.
Over the past years, the role of Nano headquarters has not been limited to macro-policy-making, but has included fostering coordination among universities, research institutes, industries, knowledge-based companies, and supporting institutions.
Establishing a strategic technological laboratory network, developing standards for the evaluation of Nano products, supporting start-up companies, and designing industrial programs are among the factors that help transfer nanotechnology from laboratories to the country’s industries.
Despite the 12-day war in June 2025 and the recent 40-day war, 230 products received nanoscale certificates in the past Iranian calendar year (March 2025-March 2026), surpassing the targeted number.
Last year, the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy and the headquarters for nanotechnology planned to obtain nanoscale certificates for 190 products (one product per working day). Still, the figure increased by 40, reaching 230. Currently, the total number of nanotechnology products with a nanoscale certificate has increased to 1965, IRNA reported.
The highest number of products that received nanoscale certificates was recorded respectively in the provinces of Tehran, Fars, and Mazandaran, with 64, 48, and 24 products, respectively.
The provinces of Zanjan (32 products), Qom (17), Markazi (16), Qazvin (11), and Isfahan (7) are placed next.
Out of 230 products, Industrial supplies had the largest share with 72 products. Energy, oil, and related industries accounted for 41, Chemicals for 36, and Pharmaceutical and Health for 26 products.

The bloc’s top diplomat also met with Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa.
The 27-nation bloc has launched a new chapter with Syria since Assad’s fall, with EU chief Ursula von der Leyen telling Sharaa in January that Europe would “do everything it can” to support Syria’s recovery.
The country is trying to rebuild, reboot its economy and attract investment after more than 13 years of conflict that killed more than half a million people and ravaged the country’s infrastructure and industry.
Kallas noted that the EU “is already providing 620 million euros for recovery, humanitarian needs and strengthening institutions.”

UK growth revised up to 0.5%: What drove the stronger figures?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:11:29 UTC
20:11:29 KST

Stronger services growth drove the upward revision to second-quarter GDP growth, as the UK battles high borrowing costs, inflationary pressures and a cooling labour market.
Britain's economy grew more than initially estimated in the second quarter, revised data from the country's statistics agency, the Office for National Statistics (ONS), showed on Wednesday, offering a boost to Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of next month's annual budget update.
The UK's quarterly GDP growth came in at 0.5% in the second quarter, revised up slightly from the 0.4% reported previously.
The figure still marked a slowdown from the 0.6% expansion recorded in the first quarter.
The upward revision was mainly driven by stronger figures for professional, scientific and technical services, following updated business survey data. Services output grew by 0.6%, compared with the previously estimated 0.5%.
"Stronger services growth in the latest quarter means the economy is now slightly larger than previously estimated," ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said in a statement.
Advertising, scientific research, legal services and computer programming were among the main drivers of services growth. Construction also expanded by 0.8%, while production output fell by 0.1%.
Household finances improved as real household disposable income per head rose by 1.0%, after falling by 0.8% in the first quarter.
"Growth has come in marginally better than initially expected, but it remains difficult to come by as households and businesses contend with high borrowing costs, inflationary pressures and a cooling labour market," said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.
He noted that since the second quarter, "the outlook has become more uncertain" following a recent surge in energy prices and borrowing costs.
The UK economy is facing increasing pressure as inflation has been rising and government bond yields have reached multi-decade highs this month.
Chancellor John Healey, who will unveil the budget on 28 October, has pledged to maintain strict fiscal discipline.
According to Carter, tax rises or similar measures in the budget could undermine the emerging positive trends supporting economic growth.
"Ultimately, the Budget will be the first real test of whether the Chancellor can square fiscal discipline with the need to support growth," Carter said, adding that "markets will be looking for a credible plan, and are unlikely to give the government much benefit of the doubt".

Severe funding cuts could leave nearly 8.3 mln without vital assistance: UNHCR
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:11:00 CST
20:11:00 KST

GENEVA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people risk losing vital assistance due to "continued severe funding cuts," the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) warned on Tuesday.
"UNHCR's ability to protect and assist refugees, internally displaced people and stateless people is being eroded by a sustained and worsening funding shortfall," said the agency in a recent report.
Available funding fell 24 percent from 5.2 billion U.S. dollars in 2024 to 3.9 billion dollars in 2025. By the end of July 2026, UNHCR had received only 32 percent of the 8.5 billion dollars it needed for the year, leaving a funding gap of 5.8 billion dollars, the agency said.
The number of people under UNHCR's mandate is projected to rise to 131.2 million by the end of 2026, it added.
"Protection cannot be reduced indefinitely without systems collapsing. Below a certain threshold, services do not simply reach fewer people; they can stop functioning altogether, leaving those most at risk without the protection they need," said Dominique Hyde, UNHCR's director of external relations.
Citing several countries under strain, the agency said 319,000 refugees in Chad face registration delays, while 200,000 women and girls risk losing access to safe spaces and prevention programs and around 233,000 children could lose child protection services.
In Ethiopia, child protection coverage in some areas has fallen by as much as 85 percent. In Sudan, tens of thousands of survivors of sexual violence and children at serious risk could lose access to critical protection services.
Faced with sharply declining resources, the agency said it had undertaken significant and difficult reforms, including cutting its workforce by 33 percent in 2025, closing offices in 140 locations worldwide and discontinuing operations in 15 countries compared with 2024. Yet the prolonged funding shortfall is now affecting even UNHCR's highest-priority protection and solutions work, it said. ■

Laos aims to boost students' literacy

VIENTIANE, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Laos' Ministry of Education and Sports has launched new research to identify factors that promote Lao language skills and literacy among primary school students, particularly those who do not speak Lao as their primary language at home.
The study, with support from the Australian government through the Basic Education Quality and Access in Laos (BEQUAL) program, will track students' learning development over the course of a school year and examine how teaching methods, classroom environments, instructional materials, and other factors contribute to their progress. It will also explore ways to help teachers better address the needs of students from diverse linguistic backgrounds.
Strong language and literacy skills in primary school provide an important foundation for future learning, the local Pasaxon newspaper reported on Wednesday.
The research aims to help ensure that children who begin school with limited Lao language proficiency can participate fully in classroom activities, improve their academic performance, remain engaged in their education, and reduce the risk of early school dropout.
The findings are expected to inform future curriculum development, improvements to teaching and learning materials, teacher professional development, and supplementary Lao language lessons using speaking-practice materials.
The research will also support Laos' broader education priorities, including the 6+3+3 curriculum reform, curriculum and instructional-material improvements, and continuous professional development for teachers. ■

Scientists urge urgent research into Antarctic basin with 3-4m sea-level rise potential
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:10:21 CST
20:10:21 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Scientists have called for urgent research into East Antarctica's Wilkes Subglacial Basin, a vast ice-filled region key to predicting future sea-level rise and containing enough ice to raise global mean sea levels by an estimated 3 to 4 meters.
A review published Wednesday in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment found that major gaps in observations meant scientists could not confidently predict how rapidly the region could change or what climate thresholds might trigger large-scale retreat, according to a statement from Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).
"The Wilkes Subglacial Basin is arguably the last unexplored place in Antarctica," said lead author UTAS Professor Matt King, chief investigator at the Australian Center for Excellence in Antarctic Science (ACEAS).
The Wilkes Subglacial Basin spans about 1,400 by 400 km, with much of its bedrock more than 2,000 meters below sea level, making its ice sheet vulnerable to ocean-driven melting and self-sustaining retreat, researchers said.
"Warm seawater increasingly coming in contact with and melting the ice sheet from below could lead to accelerated and potentially unstoppable ice loss on a massive scale. It's all downhill from there," said co-author Zhao Chen from the Australian Antarctic Program Partnership and ACEAS.
This process, known as marine ice-sheet instability, has long been a concern in parts of West Antarctica. Researchers now recognize that major regions of East Antarctica share similar characteristics.
Evidence from geological records suggests the basin, located largely within Australia's Antarctic Territory, has undergone substantial retreat during past warm periods, raising concerns about its response to future climate change.
The review, co-authored by researchers from countries including Australia, New Zealand, the United States, Britain and China, called for urgent efforts to map the region, improve ocean and ice-sheet observations, and reduce uncertainty about future climate and sea-level impacts. ■

====================================================================================================

Chinese-European joint satellite SMILE releases first science images, data
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:10:19 CST
20:10:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer (SMILE), a joint Chinese-European satellite, released its first batch of scientific images and data on Wednesday, as it entered regular science operations.
These images include the first continuous panoramic image of the northern lights, showing their fine structure over long periods. Another image reveals the glowing remains of a star that exploded about 160,000 light-years away. The satellite also collected the first high-resolution measurements of magnetic fields and ions in Earth's very high orbit.
Scientists say these early results are very promising. The data will help researchers better understand how the sun's activity affects Earth's space environment.
SMILE was launched on May 19 from French Guiana. After roughly a month of orbital adjustments, it reached its working orbit on June 20. All instruments were switched on and operated normally. Calibration was then completed and SMILE began collecting valid data.
The SMILE mission is the first mission-level, all-round, in-depth collaborative space science exploration project between China and Europe, aiming to reveal the mysteries of the interaction between the solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere.
The newly released images and data were gathered by the four scientific instruments aboard the satellite.
SMILE carries the world's first spaceborne soft X-ray imager (SXI), which can turn the previously "invisible" magnetospheric boundary into images. It also carries an ultraviolet auroral imager (UVI), a light ion analyzer (LIA) and a magnetometer (MAG).
Together, these instruments allow simultaneous global-scale imaging of how the magnetosphere changes while also measuring solar wind conditions directly at the satellite. This gives scientists an unprecedented tool for studying space weather events such as magnetic storms and substorms.
Originating from a cooperative initiative jointly launched by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the European Space Agency in 2015, the SMILE project has established an equal, mutually beneficial and complementary mechanism for cooperation.
China was fully responsible for satellite platform development, telemetry and control, ground support, and the construction of science application systems, and led the development of the UVI, LIA and MAG payloads. The European side was responsible for the payload module and SXI development, and provided the launch vehicle, launch site, and active-phase telemetry and control support. ■

Feature: Centuries-old Chinese Wu Opera wins new fans in Berlin
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:10:03 CST
20:10:03 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Before setting off on a two-week trip to China in about a month, Petra Lehmann had not expected to get such a vivid glimpse of traditional Chinese culture so close to home.
On Tuesday evening, Lehmann, chairwoman of the German-Chinese Friendship Association in Ludwigsfelde, watched intently as performers brought the centuries-old tradition of Wu Opera to life on stage at Urania Berlin.
"When they jump, you can hardly hear a sound. It is as if they were flying," Lehmann told Xinhua.
Having previously seen only brief excerpts of similar Chinese performances, she said the evening gave her a much fuller impression of the art form and made her eager to learn more during her upcoming trip to China.
Lehmann was among more than 800 spectators who packed the theater for a performance by the Zhejiang Wu Opera Troupe from east China's Zhejiang Province. The show featured a range of classic pieces, drawing repeated rounds of applause from the audience.
Wu Opera, also known as Jinhua Opera, originated during China's Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) and has a history spanning more than 500 years. As one of Zhejiang's major regional operatic genres, Wu Opera has been listed as a national intangible cultural heritage of China.
The evening opened with the "Nine-Section Dragon," a folk performance featuring a long, brightly colored "dragon" carried by a team of performers. They ran, jumped, rolled and spun across the stage, making the "dragon" twist, rise and dive through the air in fast, carefully coordinated movements.
The program went on to showcase other forms of traditional Chinese stage art. One of the highlights was face-changing, a technique in which a performer appears to switch from one colorful mask to another in the blink of an eye.
Bringing the evening to a close was "Monkey King Thrice Beats the White-Bone Demon," based on a well-known episode from the Chinese classic "Journey to the West." In the story, the Monkey King sees through the tricks of a demon who repeatedly changes her appearance to fool his companions.
On stage, the actors told the story through powerful singing, fast-paced fight scenes, acrobatics and expressive movements, making it easy to follow even for viewers who did not understand Chinese opera.
The event was jointly organized by the Chinese Cultural Center in Berlin and the Zhejiang Wu Opera Troupe, with support from Bank of China Frankfurt Branch. When the show ended, the audience rose to its feet and applauded as the actors returned for their final bows.
He Wenbo, deputy director of the Chinese Cultural Center in Berlin, said that through classic stories, vivid movement and expressive performance, the show crossed language barriers, offered local audiences a window into Chinese storytelling, and created a meaningful moment of cultural exchange.
"I don't speak Chinese, but I could still follow the story and feel the emotion," Berlin resident Sarah Keller told Xinhua. "I came here knowing very little about Wu Opera, but now I'd love to see more." ■

AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:09:52 UTC
20:09:52 KST

A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.
Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.
But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.
The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.
Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.
The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.
The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.
The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.
At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.
Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.
TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”
In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.
With reporting by Agence France-Presse

Viruses run rampant across Havana as water, power fails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:08:02 UTC
20:08:02 KST

Viruses run rampant across Havana as water, power fails
HAVANA, Sept 30 - Cuban housewife Yuamilka Hechavarria was asleep last Tuesday when water rushed into the cistern of the crumbling tenement where she lives in old Havana.
She jumped from bed, scrambling in the darkness of a blackout to top off a bucketful before the tap went dry. It was the first time her building had seen water in two months.
This scenario plays out in neighborhoods across Cuba's capital of Havana daily, where power outages exacerbated by a US oil blockade have crippled the already crumbling infrastructure that supplies water to the city's nearly two million people. Many regularly go without running water for days or weeks.
Hygiene is among the first casualties of the situation, explains Hechavarria, a healthcare worker, who for weeks had been forced to buy water from street vendors or scavenge it from nearby broken pipes.
Diarrhea has run rampant throughout her building, she says, as tenants struggle to keep even tiny apartments clean.
“There's no one in this building who hasn't gotten sick," said Hechavarria, adding that she too was recovering from a recent bout of fever and diarrhea.
Officials in both the United States and Cuba have begun to sound the alarm.
Health authorities in Cuba have warned in recent days of the spread of viruses, including a strain of viral hepatitis, as power and water increasingly fail. And a US health alert earlier this month warned travelers and residents of a "significant increase in diarrheal illness across Cuba, associated with the continuing degradation of the water and energy infrastructure."
Since the US imposed a fuel blockade in January, blackouts across Havana now regularly surpass 24 hours, hampering refrigeration and further crippling antiquated water infrastructure of which nearly 90% depends on electric-powered pumps, according to Cuba's National Institute of Hydraulic Resources.
Around 3.5 million people, or just under half the island's population, now suffer from water shortages, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs has said.
NO ESCAPE FROM NEW REALITY
Hechavarria's home — a poorly ventilated, one-room hovel she shares with her 7-year-old son and husband — would make any doctor cringe, despite her best efforts to maintain order and hygiene.
Thirty families live in similarly cramped quarters in the same small two-story building.
A recent power surge damaged her refrigerator, leaving her without a way to conserve food. She uses it instead to store medicine, beans, and rice.
Plates litter her kitchen counter and sink. She reuses dirty dish water to clean the floor or flush the toilet. She uses soap only when she can afford it.
Her husband, meanwhile, is responsible for pushing a homemade handcart fitted with two large barrels at least once weekly to a pipe that juts from the wall of a local school.
If classes are in session and there is power, the school fires an electric pump that allows water to flow from the pipe into an alleyway.
On a recent weekday morning, neighbor Andres Jimenez, a 76-year-old retired metal worker, had arrived at the spot just as the power went out. Only a trickle of water remained.
"If there's no power, they don't run the pump," he said.
Concerns over hygiene would have to wait, he added.
Nurse Maria Elena Parlado, who lives nearby and works in a clinic in the neighborhood, said there is no escaping the new reality.
"Look around us," she said, pointing to a roadside trash heap beside a small stream of sewage running along the sidewalk.
Even the clinic where she treats local residents for fast-spreading viral outbreaks is without water, she said.
"Between one patient and another I should be washing my hands, but sometimes I can't." REUTERS

PRESS REVIEW – Wednesday, September 30: The Cornell University gang rape investigation reopens. But first: students and prisoners protest in Iran "in a rare show of dissent". Journalist Evan Gershkovich speaks about his 16 months in a Russian prison. Bonus: what can we do to be less lonely? Finally, Fat Bear Week has chosen its winner.
Radio Free Europe reports that "in a rare show of dissent amid crackdown, Iranian university students stage protest". They are rallying against the country's hijab law, calling for the release of some of their classmates who have been imprisoned and speaking out about the poor living conditions on campus. The paper says that protests in Iran have been rare after the mass crackdown in January, when thousands of people were killed according to human rights groups. Iran Wire reports that inmates from 66 prisons across Iran are also protesting. The campaign is called "No to executions Tuesdays" and consists of weekly hunger strikes protesting the death penalty and demanding its abolition.
Next, The New York Times interviews Evan Gershkovich, the Wall Street Journal reporter who was imprisoned in Russia for 16 months. He was released after a US-Russian prisoner swap in 2024. The article is called "The Russian prison Gershkovich carried home". In the interview, he describes the tiny cell he lived in. He could take around six steps in there. He spent his waking hours in anger, panic attacks or crying. He is feeling better now and the nightmares have faded. Gershkovich has published a memoir entitled "This Cursed Beautiful Land" about his experience, but also that of the broader Russian population.
Also: the Cornell University rape investigation has been reopened in response to a lawsuit filed by a woman who says she was raped there in 2024. The New York Times says that her lawsuit brought renewed pressure to reopen the investigation – she is suing seven men, the university, her sorority and the fraternity. The NYT reminds readers that she says she was raped repeatedly over nearly seven hours at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The lawsuit details a series of sexual assaults and how she was pressured into taking drugs.
There have been many text messages tied to the lawsuit. CBS News says it has obtained a video of the fraternity's Snapchat group. At 1:42 am – during the rape – one fraternity guy texted "shop still open?" – like "is the woman still available?" And the answer was "Yeah". The Cut focuses on the journalists who broke the story – student journalists from The Cornell Daily Sun – they've been covering every beat and new development. For the past two weeks, they have been "relentlessly" chasing follow-ups and responses from the university's administration. Earlier, The Cornell Daily Sun published a blistering editorial entitled "Cornell won't, we will" – printing the names of the accused men and blaming the university for its lack of transparency. The Cut says that "throughout it all, the team has approached this case with care and moral clarity".
Bonus: The Atlantic looks at "one reason people are spending so much time alone". The article's central argument is that "inconvenience is the cost of community": we should sometimes do things that we don't want to do – or find irritating – if we want to maintain our relationships.
Finally, The Washington Post looks at Fat Bear Week's winner: a chunky bear named Backpack.

Jai Arrow told 'nothing' about pre-grand final tribute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:06:38 UTC
20:06:38 KST

Jai Arrow says he has been told "nothing" about a tribute awaiting him ahead of Sunday's NRL grand final.
It was widely reported today that Arrow would do a lap of Stadium Australia while a selection of Australian musicians perform Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.
Earlier this year, Arrow retired from the NRL after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).
Speaking to the ABC at this evening's Dally M Awards in Sydney, Arrow said he was unsure of the details of the ceremony.
"[I know] nothing yet, apparently I'm going around … but I don't know anything," Arrow said.
"So it'll be interesting. It won't just be for me, it'll be for everyone fighting MND."
Loading...
Arrow was honoured with the Provan-Summons Medal at the awards night for embodying the spirit of the game, which is measured against the values of respect, honesty, bravery and sportsmanship.
He said the proposed pre-game tribute on Sunday would be an opportunity to continue raising awareness of MND.
"I can use my platform to spread awareness," he said.
Meanwhile, NRL executive chairman Peter V'landys was tight-lipped about the tribute but promised fans they would be "happy and impressed" with the performers selected.
"You'll see, there'll be superstar Australian performers, that's all that we'll say, and everyone will be very happy and impressed with what we've got," he said.
"But it's not about them; it's about Jai, it's about what Jai does; he inspires people.
"We've received a lot of correspondence at the NRL about how his inspiration has made them see their illnesses through."
V'landys also said the league will be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, as well as $1 million to a "fund for underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league".
"If we can lift a lot of other people with Jai's courage and leadership, that's what we're going to do on Sunday night," V'landys said.
The NRL was left without pre-match entertainment for the grand final after talks with Australian artist Tones and I broke down earlier this month.

Russian Attack Forces McDonald’s to Cut Menu Nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:06:07 UTC
20:06:07 KST

McDonald’s has temporarily reduced its menu at all restaurants across Ukraine after a Russian drone attack damaged a warehouse belonging to the company’s logistics partner.
McDonald’s Ukraine announced the decision on Wednesday, Sept. 30, without specifying which products were affected or when its full menu would return.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Due to damage to our logistics partner’s warehouse as a result of a recent drone attack, we are temporarily switching to a reduced menu at all McDonald’s restaurants in Ukraine,” the company said.
Customers can check which dishes are available at a particular restaurant through the McDonald’s mobile app, partner delivery services or directly at the restaurant.
“We thank you for your patience and understanding. Our teams are doing everything possible to continue offering you your favorite dishes every day,” the company added.
Russian drone attacks McDonald’s warehouse
The company’s announcement follows a Russian drone attack on a warehouse used by McDonald’s in Kyiv on Friday, Sept. 25.
Previously President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the facility had been hit during a wider series of Russian attacks on the capital.
“An attack drone against ordinary food,” Zelensky said at the time.
He described the attack as part of Russia’s expanding campaign against civilian infrastructure and foreign companies operating in Ukraine.
Russia Keeps Pounding Kyiv in Daytime After Overnight Strike – Supermarket Hit, Debris Near Embassy
“American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers – all ordinary life is simply a target for Russia,” Zelensky said.
The Sept. 25 attacks killed five people and injured 27 across Kyiv. Four people were killed when a drone hit an office building in the Solomianskyi district, while a 14-year-old boy was killed in a separate attack on a residential building in the Pecherskyi district.
Authorities did not report casualties specifically at the McDonald’s-linked warehouse.
McDonald’s facilities previously damaged
McDonald’s restaurants in Kyiv have also been affected by earlier Russian attacks.
In January 2025, workers at a McDonald’s near the Lukianivska metro station managed to reach a shelter shortly before a Russian missile hit the surrounding area. All employees survived.
A McDonald’s restaurant near Lukianivska was also damaged during Russian attacks in May 2026, with part of its facade melted by the blast.
Despite repeated attacks on its facilities and supply chain, McDonald’s has continued operating restaurants in Ukraine while adapting its menu and logistics to wartime conditions.

Rescue chief: Estonia short of more than 100 firefighters as pay lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:06:00 UTC
20:06:00 KST

Rescue chief: Estonia short of more than 100 firefighters as pay lags
Estonia's rescue service needs around 100 more personnel, its deputy director has said, warning pay remains too low and the shortfall threatens response capacity.
Martin Lambing, the Rescue Board's (Päästeamet) deputy director, said while the service has 34 unfilled positions officially, the real need is over 100
This would allow fully staffing four-person rescue and three-person ordnance disposal teams, he went on.
'Working at the current understaffed levels means crews at certain moments operate with as much as double a standard workload, and with it double the risk, a risk which can also be passed on to the public.
While the rescue service's wage fund received a small increase for next year, this is not a fair rise, Lambing went on.
Under the freshly announced 2027 state budget, firefighters' pay will rise €48 per month to €1,654.
"The pay rise — as far as the cost-of-living component goes — the fact that firefighters got a raise is welcome. But where the dissatisfaction comes in is purely related to the fact that when we look at firefighters' current and future pay and compare it to the average wage and how the average wage is moving, the gap is large and that shortfall keeps growing," Lambing said.
According to Lambing, a fair level for firefighters would be 1.2 times the national average. "That takes into account the risk of the work, the responsibility and the movement towards it. Today this pay and this pay rise certainly do not reduce that gap," he said.
Lambing added firefighters' work and civil protection as a whole are part of national defense, and that if firefighters were to leave their posts it would create a security risk.
"The risk arises simply because these people are highly qualified. They are skilled workers who know how to do this job, and such employees are not easy to find," Lambing said. "When a decision is reached and a person leaves, it is not the case that they go one day and come back the next. And for the rescue system that is a great loss, because they have been through very complex long-term training and if they have also been on the job for years, they are genuinely very competent people."
At the same time, Lambing conceded politicians have not had an easy task finding solutions.
"The Rescue Board, the Ministry of the Interior and also the union — we are actually standing for one goal: to move towards 1.2 times the Estonian average wage. Finding solutions for permanent funding for civil protection and valuing voluntary rescue in the same way — that is a common goal and joint efforts are being made towards it," he went on.
Lambing credited Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200), noting he has fought for firefighters' pay and for crisis preparedness.
Lambing added there are currently 1,700 professional firefighters, augmented by over 3,000 volunteers. Officially while there are 34 unfilled positions, including firefighters and crew leaders with higher-level qualifications to lead complex rescue events, taking a broader context including national defense needs into account, the shortfall is more than 100 personnel, Lambing concluded.

Poland will not boycott G20 summit despite US invitation to Putin

Poland will not boycott G20 summit despite US invitation to Putin
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has criticised the US decision to invite Russian leader Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami, calling it a "bad idea". However, Warsaw will not boycott the meeting.
Source: European Pravda, citing Sikorski in an interview with the Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita
Details: Sikorski dismissed suggestions that Poland should boycott the summit if Putin attends. He said he would take part in the G20 Foreign Ministers' meeting in Atlanta in late October, whether or not Russia's foreign minister was invited.
Quote: "Diplomacy is more complex than it seems and sometimes puts us in uncomfortable situations, but we must be able to handle them."
Details: Sikorski said it was a bad idea to invite Putin, as the Russian leader is banned from entering several countries.
"Putin should not be viewed as a welcome guest as long as he is conducting an aggressive, colonial war against Ukraine," Sikorski added.
In the view of Poland's top diplomat, Trump's decision to invite Putin to the G20 summit indicates that the US president, "as a businessman, believes that in any situation there are solutions where both sides can win."
"This is an ahistorical approach to this war and so far it has yielded no results while, unfortunately, helping to pull Putin out of isolation," the minister added.
Asked whether Poland would thereby be "helping to bring Putin out of isolation by attending the G20," the foreign minister rejected the notion, emphasising that Poland is not the host of the summit.
Sikorski added that a similar dilemma was faced by Andrzej Domański, Minister of Finance and Economy, at the G20 ministerial meeting in Wisconsin. As he noted, they "handled it" there – the Russian minister was absent from the family photo.
The foreign minister was also asked whether Polish President Karol Nawrocki should participate in a "family photo" alongside Putin.
"It seems to me there is room for negotiation here with the American delegation, with the hosts. Especially since other participants – the prime minister of the United Kingdom, the president of France, the prime minister of India – perhaps to a lesser extent, will also not seek such a photograph," Sikorski replied.
Background:
- The Kremlin has not yet confirmed Putin's participation in the G20 summit in Miami scheduled for December 2026.
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul stated that Putin's participation in the G20 meeting could mark the beginning of "serious negotiations" towards ending Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously said that the G20 summit in Miami could serve as a venue for a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the US and Russia.

State Duma speaker certain Biden beat Trump in 2020 through fraud

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. US President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election over Donald Trump through fraud, State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin has said, arguing that, unlike in the United States, democracy in Russia is genuine.
"Our democracy is not contrived, unlike in the West, in the United States. They abandoned genuine elections; they vote by mail, yet there are not even voters’ return addresses. It is nothing but fraud. Trump suffered, and Biden overtook him last time thanks to that fraud," Volodin said at the first plenary session of the 9th State Duma.
Volodin also noted that Biden remains a free man.
"If there were a genuine legal system there, the 'guillotine' would be employed. But they reserve that for the rest of the world, while doing nothing of the sort at home," he added.

Europe lost advantage when rejecting Russian gas, Macron says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:03:44 UTC
20:03:44 KST

MADRID, September 30. /TASS/. Russian gas was one of the fundamental elements of European industry’s competitiveness and Europe itself gave it up, French President Emmanuel Macron said at an economic forum in Madrid.
"We have a problem with competitiveness and innovation. Europe's competitiveness largely relied <...> on inexpensive Russian gas, which triggered a crisis across the entire continent. We severed these supplies, which were key to the competitiveness of our industry, due to [the Ukrainian conflict]. Therefore, there is no more this affordable gas that, so to say, fed Central Europe, which was also the manufacturing core and pulled the rest of our economic sectors along with it," he said.
Europe is currently experiencing a new turn of the energy crisis caused by the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, which has confirmed the European countries' dependence on fossil fuels. He urged in this connection to work toward creating an integrated energy market in Europe and backed fair sharing of the financial burden in major energy projects across the continent. "Let’s stop tormenting ourselves with impossible rules, trying to figure out whether this was produced using nuclear energy, renewable sources, or one thing or another. If it is low-carbon energy produced with us, it is better than if it contains a lot of carbon, and even better than if we import it," Macron added.

This Interview With Raye May Contain Hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:03:06 UTC
20:03:06 KST

It’s been a while since South London singer Raye was a supporting act for another artist. And honestly, she admits, the experience has been humbling at times. With two critically acclaimed studio albums and world tours of her own under her belt, the 28-year-old has racked up countless hours on stage. But opening for pop heavyweight Bruno Mars on his Romantic Tour means she’s facing stadium crowds of around 70,000, a scale that still intimidates her.
This story is part of the 2026 TIME100 Next. Read Anya Taylor-Joy’s tribute to Raye here.
“I think people know ‘Where Is My Husband!’” she tells me on a Zoom call from New Orleans, the 12th stop on her leg of the tour. The hit single has surpassed a billion streams on Spotify since its release a year ago, and she recently performed it at the 2026 MTV VMAs. But that recognition only goes so far when the audience has come to see someone else. “It’s that taste of humility, where you’re like, ‘Right, this person is just staring at me like they are bored out of their mind,’” she says. “But it encourages something within you that’s like, ‘I need to put on a good show for this person!’ It’s quite funny, but also healthy.”
Her determination was forged during years of early-career setbacks that tested her confidence. Raye, born Rachel Agatha Keen, was a teenager when she signed a four-album record deal with Polydor in 2014. She spent the next seven years struggling to release her debut through a label she says stifled her creativity and voice. In the meantime, she wrote songs for global superstars like Beyoncé, Charli XCX, and John Legend while yearning for her own moment in the spotlight.
She reached a breaking point in 2021, making a public plea on social media: “I’ve done everything they asked me, I switched genres, I worked 7 days a week, ask anyone in the music game, they know. I’m done being a polite pop star. I want to make my album now, please that is all I want.” At the time, a Polydor spokesperson said the label was "saddened" by Raye’s posts and had contacted her management team “to discuss and offer [its] full support.” Soon after, Raye was released from her contract and began a new era as an independent artist, co-managed by her parents, Sarah and Paul Keen.
Reflecting on that pivotal moment during an interview on a scorching hot July day in east London, Raye recalls how her pain drove her to speak out. “The catalyst came when I just had no fear of the worst case scenario anymore,” she says. “Genuinely, I had zero expectations. It was spur of the moment and impulsive, and I was very, very, very emotional and very hurt, and in a lot of pain.”
She channeled the trauma of those difficult years into her 2023 debut album, My 21st Century Blues, which has been streamed more than 2 billion times on Spotify. The album’s breakout single, “Escapism,” a raw depiction of a young woman lost in a cycle of avoidance and addiction, went viral on TikTok, fueled by fans’ sped-up versions of the track. Raye embraced the trend, releasing a sped-up rendition of her own. The original reached No. 1 on the U.K. charts nearly three months after its release. A record-breaking six wins at the 2024 Brit Awards, followed by three Grammy nominations later that year, was a sign of her growing global appeal.
The record offered an unflinching look at her struggles with substance abuse and heartache. In one track, "Ice Cream Man," she details the sexual assault she experienced as a young woman in the music industry. The song resonated with audiences worldwide and won the Harry Belafonte Best Song For Social Change Award at this year’s Grammys. “A lot of my first album was very cathartic,” she says. “We touched on some heavy stuff. We were able to create a space of emotion and reckoning.”
If Raye’s first album documented her unraveling, her sophomore record, This Music May Contain Hope, captures her piecing herself back together. The album, which has been shortlisted for a Mercury Prize, covers a whole spectrum of emotion, with hope at its center. Songs titled “I Will Overcome” and “Happier Times Ahead” are infused with powerful affirmations, the kind one might repeat in the mirror before they face the day: “Happier times are coming, alright?/ The sun exists behind the clouds/ It's right there, just hold onto happier times, alright, darling.” That determination and resilience runs through the 17-track record. “In the wild and difficult times the world is in right now, I just wanted to make something that had hope laced in it,” she says. “I knew I needed some, and I knew from playing so many shows that the audiences needed some, too.”
A sense of home also permeates the record. In “Beware.. The South London Lover Boy,” she cheekily warns other women about the smooth-talking, Lime bike-riding “strange creatures” lurking on the streets where she grew up. The humor gives away to heartache in “Nightingale Lane,” a ballad she introduces as documenting the “greatest heartbreak I have ever known.” Named after a road in Balham, South London, the song follows Raye through familiar places that hold memories of a former love.
Earlier this year, Raye and her team placed an unofficial Blue Plaque—which typically denotes a building’s historical link to a notable figure—outside The Nightingale pub, her ex’s favorite drinking spot, to promote the song and make sure “he’ll never forget” what happened. “I thought the pub would've taken it down by now, but [it’s] still up there,” she says, with a laugh. “You’ve just gotta be creative when you're independent and try different things, you know?”
Yet, in the months leading up to the album’s March release, Raye worried about how it would be received. During what she describes as a “silly moment,” the singer even wondered if she had already peaked. Her debut album had set what felt like impossibly high standards and she questioned if she’d “ever have a No. 1 again.” Everything fell into place once she chose “Where Is My Husband!” as the lead track. She had a feeling fellow “single girls” would relate to her frustration with waiting to find a worthy partner, a hunch that turned out to be right. The song topped the U.K. charts in January and became the soundtrack to countless engagement videos and dating chronicles across social media.
The song encapsulates Raye as an artist: an undeniably pop sound, but with a big-band twist and elements of jazz and funk that defy easy categorization. Her refusal to be boxed into a genre was fueled by her experience coming of age in an industry that told her “to pick a sound.” At the TIME photoshoot, early-2000s tracks ring out across the studio until Raye raises a hand and asks for “something else, something jazz.” Soon, Frank Sinatra’s “My Way” fills the room, with Raye adding her own riffs and runs.
This fusion of traditional and contemporary extends to Raye’s live shows. She performs with a big band, but at one point in her set, giant lightbulbs that spell out “RAYE” are tweaked to spell “RAVE.” (A drunk fan pitched her the idea at a festival a few years ago.) “I love having a nightclub segment in my shows and I love jazz,” she says. “Those are two polarizing genres, they're not supposed to be allowed to coexist, but it's really exciting to be able to get on stage and sing ‘Fly Me to the Moon’ with a seven-piece brass section and then go into letting everyone jump and have green lasers. Why not?”
Realizing she could bring all of these impulses together and take control of her own creative direction was a turning point. “A massive part of that has come from just removing any external opinions,” she says. “It's important to have people who can give you a great perspective, but you don't need too many cooks in the kitchen.” By liberating herself of others’ expectations, Raye was able to tune back into the voice that mattered most: her own. “Being able to clear that noise out allowed me to give myself permission to just do what feels right,” she says.
Raye’s close-knit network is with her on set. Her mother is present, as is her teenage sister, Katelyn, who dutifully captures behind-the-scenes photos throughout the day. “She’s got a great eye,” Raye says with pride. Her other sisters, Absolutely and Amma, are emerging musicians in their own right; both feature on her album and have previously joined her on tour. Raye’s grateful for the close bond they share, especially because it hasn’t always been that way. “I navigated a whole journey very distant from my family, and it just wasn't ideal for me,” she says. “This job and career path is so weird, in the most amazing way, but also confusing. We're put on pedestals and I’m treated as ‘Raye the artist.’ If you nurture that too much, you can lose your way. My family really helped ground me.”
Raye has also learned to set clear boundaries in her life. “‘No’ is my favorite word, which is really cool because for my whole life, I'd be like, ‘Okay, yes,’” she recalls. “You’re not a mean person to say ‘no.’ You're not being selfish. You have to really do the work to learn [that].”
The singer is still learning to show herself grace as she navigates life’s complexities in front of an audience. Some days, it’s a harder task than others. “I had a tough gig the other day, where I had a lump in my throat from before I even went on stage,” she says. “You know when you get that lump and it’s just gonna take one little thing to just set you off?” Afterward, Raye apologized for the “bad vibes” in a group chat with her band, who reassured her that being open about her emotions is a good thing. “Some days we’re smiling and some days it’s hard,” she says. “And that day I wanted the ground to swallow me and I wanted to run off the stage, you know? But I told the crowd, ‘I’m having a hard day.’ And I did my best.”
When she’s feeling particularly lost, Raye turns to one of her idols: Aretha Franklin. “I watch that biopic and I’m just so inspired by her story,” she says. “I cry my eyes out and then be like, ‘I’m gonna keep trying.’”
Raye also protects her mental space by limiting her social media time. She doesn’t know the password to her Instagram account, for example. Instead, she approaches her team when she wants to log in for a short amount of time. “Them things can have me scrolling for hours, and then I'll start deep diving and looking at stuff I don't need to be looking at, so it's just better for my head and my heart,” she says.
After a whirlwind few months, Raye is preparing to enter the final year of her 20s and has high hopes for what lies ahead. “I'm excited to see what my 30s are going to teach me,” she says. Career-wise, she’s determined to keep evolving and is set to make her film acting debut in Lineage, an upcoming crime thriller from Top Boy director Yann Demange. She has also teased an upcoming project with Michael B. Jordan, though the details remain under wraps.
Even as she welcomes these new opportunities, music will always take top billing. But a third album will have to wait. “I’m falling in love first!” she quips, before we part ways.
Now, where the hell is that husband?

The October 7 warnings threatening Netanyahu’s Israeli election campaign

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

The October 7 warnings threatening Netanyahu’s Israeli election campaign
Netanyahu faces ongoing pressure over alleged warnings before the Hamas attack as October elections draw near
The controversy over warnings Benjamin Netanyahu is alleged to have received in advance of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks continues to dog the Israeli prime minister ahead of knife-edge elections slated for October 27.
The latest blow to Netanyahu came on Sunday, after a Wall Street Journal report suggested that he had been warned of the attack by Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, who reportedly phoned the prime minister just days before the attack, underscoring previous warnings in September 2023, when he is said to have flown to Israel to warn security officials in person that Hamas was planning an attack.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Netanyahu to sue Haaretz over claims UAE warned him before October 7 attack
- list 2 of 4Benjamin Netanyahu has overseen a genocide: In his telling, he’s a victim
- list 3 of 4UAE confirms Israel PM Netanyahu’s visit to Abu Dhabi
- list 4 of 4Palestine weekly: Israeli politicians vie to look toughest before election
News of Kamel’s warnings follows reports in Israeli and US media earlier this month suggesting that Netanyahu had been warned by United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) in the week before the attack that Hamas’s then-leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning the assault.
Netanyahu has been emphatic in his denials of having received any warning of an attack, and has sued over the claims.
Neither Kamel nor the Egyptian government has commented on the reports. The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said it does not comment on media reports or speculation concerning conversations between government leaders.
Netanyahu has attempted to shift the blame for not being alerted to the attack onto the former head of Israel’s internal security service, Ronen Bar, who announced on Monday that he would sue the prime minister, a longtime political nemesis, for defamation as a result.
Polling suggests that events surrounding the October 7 attacks, which killed 1,139 people in Israel, and questions over responsibility for security failures that preceded them remain important issues for voters ahead of the upcoming parliamentary elections. Continued media coverage has also kept the trauma of the attack at the centre of public debate, more than three years after Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza, killing more than 74,000 Palestinians.
“We know that Egypt’s Chief of Intelligence flew to Israel on September 26 and warned Israel of a … Hamas attack,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “We also know that similar messages came from MBZ.”
“Why they were ignored? That’s the magic of what we call ‘conception’,” he said, referring to ha-conceptzia, the Hebrew term for the underlying assumptions on which Israeli security decisions are often based. “And Israel, not only Netanyahu, believed in the conception that Hamas was deterred and all it wanted was to [push] Israel a little bit to ease the pressure and blockade on Gaza.”
Entrenched politics
Netanyahu’s two main rivals in the race for prime minister have both seized on the alleged warnings.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the Beyachad (Together) alliance, said if the allegations were proven true, Netanyahu “cannot continue to serve in his position for another minute”. Former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party leads Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls by the slenderest of margins, said, “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit.”
The reports do not appear to have had a significant effect on the election polls, but, all the same, the latest revelations in The Wall Street Journal were likely to concern those within Netanyahu’s campaign who had already invested significant time and effort in rebutting the initial round of stories claiming he had been warned by the UAE leader, London-based Israeli academic and media analyst Ayala Panievsky told Al Jazeera.
“However, the opinion polls have been quite stable for years now. I wouldn’t expect a significant portion of Netanyahu voters to break with him over this,” she said. “It could hurt him with voter turnout and excitement among his base, however, which could be significant as the polls seem relatively close.”
Analysts suggested that part of the explanation lay in the Likud party’s and Netanyahu’s longstanding portrayal of themselves as political outsiders under attack from what they were encouraged to see as a hostile political establishment. That narrative may make supporters more inclined to accept the prime minister’s denials and his criticism of the security services and other institutions.
“I think everyone expected [the reports on Netanyahu being given warnings] to be a landmark story, one serious enough to really damage Netanyahu,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg said.
“However, Netanyahu’s rebuttals and threats to sue have given his supporters something to hold on to,” Flaschenberg said. “They’re now free to dismiss the stories as fake, just as the opposition is pushing them. The politics of this really have become that entrenched.”
Years of persecution
However, analysts cautioned that it remains unclear whether acting on any warnings would ultimately have prevented an attack on the scale of October 7. They also pointed to the wider context in Gaza, where years of Israeli restrictions and military actions, widely condemned by rights groups, the United Nations, and a number of states, had contributed to deep grievances and a heightened risk of violence.
“Strategic surprises cannot be prevented,” Bregman continued.
“A determined opponent will eventually inflict on you an October 7. You can delay it. Prevent it temporarily, but you can’t stop it,” he said, “Israel’s next October 7 will come from the West Bank. Not now, but in the future. Maybe in five, 10, 30 years, but it’s inevitable.”

Cristina Etcheberry is helping businesses across Latin America collect recurring payments without friction. Toku, a platform she co-founded in 2020, handles about $8 billion annually for more than 500 corporate customers, including Chevrolet and major insurers like Zurich and MetLife. Toku aims to free businesses from chasing missed bills and matching payment records across disconnected banking systems.
Like technology, the Santiago, Chile native moves fast, decamping to Mexico City less than a week after deciding Toku would enter the country.
In 2025, it raised $48 million in a Series A, the largest ever for a woman-led startup in the region, and Etcheberry has big plans for the platform’s future. In March, Toku launched an AI agent that not only chases payments over WhatsApp, email, or voice, but can also arrange repayment plans—which the company says has reduced unrecoverable debts by up to half.

Every human must contend with the constraints of the body; inside each one a sea of feeling and conflicting identities are sealed. Painter Sasha Gordon reckons with these depths and contradictions by conjuring realms where all facets of being can exist, unguarded and exposed. At 28, she’s had multiple solo exhibitions in major cities—including the captivating “Haze” in New York City in fall 2025—earning acclaim for her mesmerizing figures that are gloriously alive and engaged even when in nightmarish play. Gordon is determined to surface elements of self that society seeks to repress. It makes being in the presence of her work feel like a relief.
Gordon’s portraits feature serene characters that simmer with undertones of violence, rupture, and self-reckoning: two soft-bodied women in a wooden boat in a placid pond, the glowing patch of one of their scalps plucked clean. Pointy crescents of fingernail clippings placed on the tip of a curious tongue. A head held underwater, still as stone, eyes laced with urgency. This is her immense power; to unsettle us from a contained, palatable existence, and embolden us to be in companionship with our shadow selves.
