Ukrainian Drone Autonomy Developer Occam Raises €3.8 Million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:53:02 UTC
19:53:02 KST

The British-Ukrainian defense technology company Occam Industries has raised €3.8 million in investment to develop autonomous drone control software.
Occam Industries discussed the investment with Militarnyi.
Danish venture capital fund North Ventures led the funding round. Finnish Sparkmind and UK-based Grenadyr also participated, while Antler, Tech Horizons, T|Y|R.vc, and Freedom Fund made follow-on investments.
Following the new funding round, Occam Industries’ total investment raised has reached €7 million.
The funds will support research and development, expand the engineering team in Ukraine, scale deployment of the technology by the Ukrainian military, integrate it with new unmanned platforms, and enter defense markets in Europe and other NATO countries.
Occam Industries develops onboard software that enables autonomous operation of unmanned systems using AI and computer vision.
A key feature of the company’s approach is its ability to integrate autonomous capabilities into existing mass-produced unmanned systems without significantly modifying their design or changing the manufacturing process.
The software runs directly on the UAV’s onboard computing module, enabling it to perform specific mission phases without maintaining a constant connection with the operator or relying on satellite navigation signals.
This is intended to maintain system functionality in environments with active electronic warfare (EW) systems and in the event of a loss of the command-and-control link. To integrate these capabilities, the company developed the modular Occam Ludus platform.
“Today, Occam’s technology is already being actively deployed and tested with several Ukrainian manufacturers and military brigades, and feedback from the frontline directly informs the product,” Gui Wainwright, co-founder and CEO of Occam Industries, shared.
The company’s first solution built on the Ludus platform was the Occam Ambush system. It combines autonomous target detection, tracking, and guidance, and is already being integrated into mass-produced FPV drones used in Ukraine.
Using computer vision algorithms, the software can track a designated target and guide the drone without requiring continuous manual control.
Other areas the company is working on include terminal-phase autonomous guidance for interceptor drones, target matching and recognition for strike and reconnaissance missions, mine-laying, and logistics operations.
In February, Occam Industries raised €3 million in a pre-seed round. Following the round, the company underwent field testing as part of Ukraine’s Brave1 defense innovation cluster and moved on to integrating and deploying its technologies in cooperation with Ukrainian drone manufacturers and military units.

Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:51:59 UTC
19:51:59 KST

Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- Arizona State University
- Summary:
- Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.
- Share:
Galaxies can contain hundreds of billions of stars, but every one of those stars begins with cold, dense gas. Large galaxies, including the Milky Way, are surrounded by an enormous reservoir of this material known as the circumgalactic medium, or CGM.
The CGM extends roughly 10-20 times farther than the visible part of a galaxy. Over time, some of this gas can cool, flow inward, gather into dense clouds, and eventually form new stars. Because stars give rise to planets and the conditions necessary for life, the CGM plays an important role in a galaxy's long term evolution.
Yet astronomers have faced a persistent puzzle. If galaxies are surrounded by so much potential star-forming material, why do they not produce far more stars? Something appears to be preventing much of that gas from cooling and falling inward.
Black Hole Jets May Be the Missing Piece
A new study led by astronomers Sanchayeeta Borthakur of Arizona State University (ASU) and Namrata Roy, now at the Raman Research Institute (RRI), offers evidence for one possible answer.
The researchers found that narrow jets of extremely hot plasma launched by supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies can influence gas far beyond the visible galaxy. These jets may disturb the reservoir of material galaxies depend on for future growth, potentially affecting whether they continue producing stars. The findings were published in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.
"This is a pathbreaking result that solves the long-standing mystery of how black holes influence galaxies, their stars, and life as we know it!" said Borthakur, Associate Professor in ASU's School of Earth and Space Exploration. "This work opens a new direction to explore further the intricacies of the connection between the supermassive black holes trillions of miles from where we are to how we came to be here."
Small Objects With Enormous Influence
When a black hole actively consumes gas, it can release tremendous amounts of energy and heat nearby material. Despite their extraordinary power, these black holes are tiny compared with their host galaxies. A supermassive black hole can be roughly comparable in scale to our solar system, while the galaxy around it may contain about 100 billion solar systems.
"The surprising question is: how can something so small energetically impact something so enormous?" said Roy, assistant professor at RRI and former ASU Exploration Prize Postdoctoral Fellow.
The scale of that influence can be difficult to picture. One comparison would be an ant somehow leaving a noticeable mark hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. Astronomers have known that active black holes release immense energy, but exactly how that energy travels across such enormous distances and changes along the way has remained unclear.
The new research provides evidence for how that process may work.
Searching for a Glow Along the Jets
The researchers studied active black holes that produce powerful jets. These narrow streams of hot, rapidly moving plasma can extend well beyond the visible boundaries of their galaxies.
The team searched for signs that the jets were changing the ionization state of gas in the surrounding CGM. In particular, they looked for the faint glow produced by ionized hydrogen.
That signal is too weak to detect clearly around a single galaxy. To overcome that limitation, the researchers combined observations from hundreds of galaxies with active jets. They used data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey together with radio jet measurements from the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey (LoTSS).
By combining measurements taken along the axes of the jets, the team searched for H-alpha, a characteristic signature of ionized hydrogen gas.
Roy, Borthkur and colleagues found that the signal remained weak when observations from every direction around the galaxies were averaged together. Along the radio jets, however, the H-alpha signal became much stronger and easier to detect.
That pattern indicates that the gas is not glowing equally in every direction. Instead, the strongest emission appears along the route traveled by the jet. Rather than behaving like a lamp illuminating everything around it, the jet acts more like a concentrated beam that causes gas to glow along its path.
Black Hole Jets Leave a Distinct Signature
The results suggest that black hole jets affect the gas surrounding galaxies in a highly directional way. Gas becomes more strongly ionized and luminous where the radio jets pass through it.
The researchers also found two regions where the ionized hydrogen glow was particularly bright. One occurs relatively close to the galaxy, where the jet first encounters the CGM. Another appears much farther away, near the outer edge of the CGM, where the jet appears to deposit much of its energy.
Together, these observations reveal how jets can alter or illuminate gas at tremendous distances from a galaxy's center. By changing the surrounding environment, the jets can influence how a galaxy grows and evolves, including whether it continues creating stars or becomes quiescent.
"What excites me most is the scale of the connection," Roy said. "A black hole is incredibly small compared to a galaxy, but its impact can reach hundreds of thousands of light-years, far into the galaxy's outer reaches. The jet carries the energy outward, and the gas lights up along its path.
"As a check, the team also examined a tracer of cooler gas via the absorption signature of magnesium. Unlike the directional glow in H-alpha, Magnesium was more widely distributed isotropically and did not show any connection to the jet direction. This implies that the cool gas component might already exist as a reservoir surrounding the galaxy uniformly on all sides. Yet the jet brightens, heats, and ionizes gas along its own path, lighting up a trail and causing it to glow in H-alpha."
How Black Holes Can Change a Galaxy's Future
The results provide some of the clearest evidence so far that supermassive black holes can influence galaxies far outside their central regions.
By heating, stirring, and disrupting gas throughout the CGM, black hole jets can make it harder for that material to cool and fall back toward the galaxy. Without that incoming supply of cold gas, the galaxy has less fuel available for creating new stars.
In this way, the jets can act as a brake on galaxy growth. Over time, they may help push a galaxy toward a quieter state with much lower levels of star formation.
The black hole, therefore, is doing more than simply "feeding" on matter near the galactic center. Its influence can extend throughout the galaxy's surrounding environment and potentially alter the galaxy's long-term fate.
Direction Was the Key to the Discovery
Earlier studies had searched for similar signals without detecting them. The new findings suggest one reason why.
The H-alpha signature becomes visible only when astronomers examine the gas specifically along the direction of the jets. If researchers had assumed that the CGM behaved the same way in every direction, this effect could easily have remained hidden.
Instead, the results show that the jets ionize hydrogen along their paths, producing a highly directional glow in H-alpha.
The discovery also demonstrates the power of combining large optical and radio surveys such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey and the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey (LoTss). By adding together many individually faint signals, astronomers can reveal patterns that would otherwise be impossible to see.
The findings now provide astronomers and theorists with another way to test how black hole jets interact with galaxies and influence their evolution.
Contributing co-authors include Timothy Heckman at Johns Hopkins University and Tanmay Singh at Arizona State University.
This work is supported by NASA, STScI, and NSF.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Arizona State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Namrata Roy, Sanchayeeta Borthakur, Timothy Heckman, Tanmay Singh. Lighting Up the Circumgalactic Medium: Strong, Jet-aligned Hα Emission around Radio Galaxies. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2026; 1009 (2): L34 DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/ae9cbd

You can now travel between Abu Dhabi and Dubai by train
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:51:37 UTC
19:51:37 KST

Etihad Rail launched the new route on 30 September, with more stations set to open in the coming months.
Etihad Rail has officially launched its route between Abu Dhabi and Dubai, marking the first time the two emirates have been connected by passenger train.
Travellers can now go between the UAE capital and the major tourist hub in just over an hour.
Tickets are priced at AED39 (€9.35) in comfort class, with premium seats coming in at AED109 (€26.13).
Etihad Rail first launched in late June, with trains going from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah, an emirate on the country’s east coast.
The rail network will then be extended further on 30 December, when Al Dhafra, another stop in Abu Dhabi, will open, while Sharjah train station will begin welcoming passengers from 30 March next year.
As the train stations are outside of city centres, Etihad Rail will also offer shuttle services between key points within downtown Abu Dhabi such as the Corniche, Reem Mall, and ADNEC Centre and the Abu Dhabi Mohamed Bin Zayed City Station. These are priced at AED10 (€2.40).
In Dubai, the train station is located at Jumeirah Golf Estates, meaning passengers can then transfer onto the metro. The city is the only place in the UAE that currently has a metro system.
Various other stations are set to open in Abu Dhabi, but commencement dates for these stops are yet to be announced.
Stops include Al Mirfa, which is near the waterfront mangrove destination Al Mugheirah Bay, and Liwa, which is known for its vast desert and its annual motorsports festival held on the dunes each winter.
There is also a stop in Al Sila, right next to the Saudi Arabian border.
The wider Gulf rail network
Plans to connect the Gulf states – the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait – have been proposed, but there are no exact dates on when this project would be realised.
Saudi Arabia is the only other Gulf nation to currently operate passenger trains. The country was part of the Ottoman railway network in the early 20th century, with trains connecting Damascus in Syria to Medina, but this was closed due to the Arab Revolt.
Modern passenger trains now connect cities including Riyadh and Quruyyat, which is near the border with Jordan, and Riyadh and the port city of Dammam. There is also a route between the holy cities of Medina and Mecca.
Metro networks are found in just a few cities in the Gulf, including Riyadh, which opened in 2024, Dubai, which opened in 2009, and Doha, which opened in 2019 ahead of the city hosting the World Cup.
Late last year, Qatar announced that it has signed an agreement with Saudi Arabia to construct a high-speed railway connecting Riyadh and Doha in around two hours. It is set for completion in 2031.

david altrath reveals the timber world inside germany’s motorway chapel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:50:32 UTC
19:50:32 KST

david altrath reveals the timber world inside germany’s motorway chapel
the photographer documents schneider+schumacher’s landmark beside the A45, focusing on its unusual form and relationship with the surrounding landscape.
david altrath photographs germany’s autobahnkirche
David Altrath turns his camera toward the Autobahnkirche Siegerland, a roadside chapel by schneider+schumacher beside the A45 motorway near Wilnsdorf, Germany. His photographic series focuses on the sculptural geometry of the building, tracing the transition from its stark white exterior to the warm, intricate timber structure inside.
Completed in 2013, the chapel was designed as a place for travelers to pause beside the motorway. Its exterior translates the familiar pictogram of a church into a three-dimensional architectural form, with two pointed spires rising above a folded white volume. Altrath photographs this silhouette from close and distant perspectives, isolating its sharp edges, sloping planes and openings against the surroundings.
capturing the chapel’s timber interior
The series shifts toward the material and structural qualities of the building. Inside, a vaulted gridshell made from 66 engineered lumber profiles curves continuously across the walls and ceiling, creating a dense geometric pattern. Altrath’s images draw attention to the repetition of the timber ribs, often framing sections of the structure rather than presenting the interior as a single whole. The photographer also captures how daylight interacts with the gridshell. Small openings across the roof introduce points and strips of natural light, while larger skylights within the spires illuminate the chapel from above. The light picks out individual timber panels, creating changing patterns across the curved surface.
Altrath’s photographs present the Autobahnkirche as a study in geometry, material and light. By moving between its graphic exterior and enveloping timber interior, the series documents the chapel through the architectural details that become most visible when the building is experienced at a slower pace.
project info:
name: Autobahnkirche Siegerland
photographer: David Altrath | @davidaltrath
architect: schneider+schumacher | @schneiderschumacher
location: Wilnsdorf, Germany

British forces leave Iraq as coalition mission ends
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:50:26 BST
19:50:26 KST

British personnel have departed Iraq as the Global Coalition ends its military mission against Daesh in the country, bringing more than a decade of operations under Operation Inherent Resolve to a close, according to the UK Government.
The transition follows an assessment that Iraqi Security Forces and the Kurdish Peshmerga are now able to take primary responsibility for Iraq’s security. Coalition forces, including UK personnel, have left as security arrangements move towards an Iraqi-led model, while Britain plans to continue defence cooperation through a bilateral relationship with Baghdad.
Operation Inherent Resolve was established in 2014 to advise, assist and enable Iraqi partner forces fighting Daesh. The mission operated under the Global Coalition Against Daesh, which brings together 90 partners. Britain’s contribution was delivered through Operation SHADER, under which UK forces provided training, air operations, surveillance and other military support.
Over the past decade, British personnel trained or assisted more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 members of the Kurdish Peshmerga. Training covered infantry skills, weapons maintenance, counter-IED work, medical support and engineering.
The RAF also flew thousands of sorties during the campaign, striking more than 2,300 Daesh targets and providing surveillance and reconnaissance in support of Iraqi ground operations. The Government said Iraqi forces had strengthened security across the country, allowing essential services to return and communities affected by the conflict to recover. The conclusion of the coalition mission in Iraq does not mean the end of Operation SHADER. The Government said Britain would continue its contribution to the wider effort against Daesh and remain involved in work intended to counter the group’s propaganda and reduce the spread of extremist messaging.
The Government said: “We pay tribute to the UK personnel who have played their part in the Global Coalition. Working alongside our global Coalition partners, the UK remains committed to ensuring the global defeat of Daesh and its violent ideology including thorough the continuation of Operation SHADER.”
Future UK-Iraq defence cooperation is expected to concentrate on counter-terrorism, military education, capability development and defence industrial collaboration. Britain said it would continue working with Iraqi partners to establish what it described as an enduring bilateral defence partnership.
The Government added: “Our commitment to Iraq and the wider region remains steadfast. Building on a decade of close cooperation, we look forward to developing an enduring bilateral defence partnership with Iraq.”

He made the remarks in his column "G20 Trade Crossroads: Where Countries Meet or Part Ways?" for US magazine Newsweek.
"The WTO solidified the instruments that countries can legitimately use to respond to the surges in imports and various forms of trade distortions, primarily trade remedies and the disciplines under the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures. The improvement and adaptation of these mechanisms is in our hands. "The G20 is a platform where we need to reach agreements respecting the diversity of views of its members. If, instead, we use this platform for mutual naming and blaming, or put forward solutions that are clearly unacceptable for some of its members from the outset, the G20 risks losing its practical purpose," Reshetnikov stressed.

EU to expand Mediterranean naval mission to target Russia's shadow fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:49:49 UTC
19:49:49 KST

The EU is set to broaden its Mediterranean naval mission to counter Russia's shadow fleet, protect subsea infrastructure and engage in naval diplomacy with Northern African countries.
Brussels is set to expand its naval mission off Libya into a broader Mediterranean security operation targeting Russia's shadow fleet and threats to critical maritime infrastructure.
The mission, codenamed EUNAVFOR MED IRINI, would be extended until 31 March, 2029, under a draft Council decision obtained by Euronews.
Created in 2020 to enforce the United Nations arms embargo on Libya, the operation would take on a wider role monitoring illicit activity, protecting infrastructure and combating migrant smuggling.
Its current mandate expires in March 2027. The draft would extend it for another two years, with a €16.88 million budget, while significantly broadening its scope.
In June, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the operation had changed its rules of engagement and begun boarding ships suspected of belonging to Russia's shadow fleet.
The revised mandate would explicitly make limiting Russia's shadow fleet one of IRINI's tasks. It says the operation should contribute to that effort while respecting the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and other international rules.
The text also places greater emphasis on maritime situational awareness, including the detection and monitoring of illicit activities and threats to EU security and economic interests.
The operation would support efforts to protect critical maritime infrastructure, such as fibre-optic cables and subsea pipelines, and would be able to test and pilot new technologies for maritime protection.
IRINI's existing role includes combating migrant smuggling and human trafficking by helping to disrupt the business model of smuggling and trafficking networks.
The revised text specifies that IRINI will support the "detection and monitoring of migrant smuggling and trafficking networks through intelligence gathering and aerial patrols on the high seas" in its approved area of operations.
Enforcing the UN arms embargo on Libya and measures against the country's illicit oil exports would remain part of the mandate. The operation would also continue providing capacity-building and training for Libyan maritime law-enforcement and search-and-rescue institutions.
The revised mandate also puts greater emphasis on regional maritime-security cooperation. IRINI would act as a platform for cooperation and use naval diplomacy and exercises to explore opportunities beyond Libya with other interested countries, naming Egypt, Tunisia and Lebanon.
EU ambassadors green-lighted the mandate on Wednesday. Formal adoption is expected at the meeting of Economic and Finance Ministers on 9 October, following which it will be published in the EU's official journal.

PACE urges member states to earmark 10% of Ukraine recovery funds for veterans' rehabilitation
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), in a resolution adopted at its session on 29 September, called on member states to allocate at least 10% of their funding earmarked for Ukraine's reconstruction to the rehabilitation and reintegration of veterans.
Source: European Pravda, citing the PACE press service
Quote: "Support for veterans constitutes one of the greatest social challenges facing Ukraine."
Details: The Assembly called on member states to allocate at least 10% of their national funding earmarked for Ukraine's reconstruction to the rehabilitation and social reintegration of veterans and civilians with disabilities.
PACE also called on the Ukrainian authorities, with support from member states, to develop a single transparent mechanism for accessing benefits and services. This would bring together long-term rehabilitation, psychological support, home care, housing adaptations, professional reintegration and accessible infrastructure.
More broadly, PACE called for a comprehensive minimum support package for veterans covering physical and mental health, rehabilitation, employment, education, housing and social protection, including at least three years of enhanced, coordinated support after leaving military service.
It also called on member states to ensure that veterans' rights apply across borders, strengthen support for families and former prisoners of war, and assist Ukraine in consolidating its veterans' support system.
Background:
- Ukraine was previously reported to be planning to raise the issue of Russian compensation in cases before the European Court of Human Rights at the PACE session.
- PACE has also proposed a way to transfer frozen Russian funds to Ukraine on the basis of rulings by the European Court of Human Rights.

Somali waters saw widespread piracy between 2008 and 2018. Piracy declined for several years before re-emerging in late 2023 amid rising security tensions in the region.

Conversation cards 'Tales in Your Back Pocket' picked as Estonia's best museum souvenir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:46:00 UTC
19:46:00 KST

Conversation cards 'Tales in Your Back Pocket' picked as Estonia's best museum souvenir
The Estonian Museum Association announced the winners of the 2026 EMMA Estonian Museum Souvenir Awards at the Estonian National Museum on September 28.
A total of 23 museums submitted 42 products and product lines to this year's competition. Entries ranged from pins and handmade jewelry to board games, seed kits and a bread-baking kit.
"This year's entries showed that a good museum souvenir is not simply an item bearing a museum's logo. The best products convey the museum's story, are practical and well-made and allow visitors to take the museum experience home with them," said Kristi Paatsi, a board member of the Estonian Museum Association and organizer of the EMMA competition. "The jury was particularly pleased to see many smaller and regional museums taking part in the competition, as well as local makers and museum staff themselves being involved in creating the products."
The Estonian Health Museum's "Jutud tagataskust" ("Tales in Your Back Pocket") conversation cards, which won first place and a €1,000 prize, are connected to the exhibition "Hüvasti, noorus!" ("Goodbye, Youth!"). The jury praised the cards' innovative format, distinctive character and professional execution. The conversation cards were created primarily to provide companionship for older people, but in today's social media-centered world, they can help people of any age start and sustain a conversation.
Second place and a €600 prize went to the Estonian Open Air Museum's series of insect brooches, "Eesti Vabaõhumuuseumi kutsumata külalised" ("Uninvited Guests of the Estonian Open Air Museum"). The handmade wooden brooches depict some of the greatest enemies of the Estonian Open Air Museum's prized assets: wood-destroying pests ranging from the deathwatch beetle to the house longhorn beetle. The jury highlighted the souvenirs' strong connection to the museum and distinctive execution. The brooches were hand-painted by Estonian Open Air Museum conservator Marike Laht.
Third place and a €400 prize went to Iisaku Kihelkonna Museum's "tutiviht," a traditional bundled whisk. According to the jury, it is a clever and distinctive souvenir with a strong connection to the museum's permanent exhibition and the potential to appeal to both Estonian and international museum visitors.
The €500 Museum Card (Muuseumikaart) product development prize went to Tallinn City Museum's "Legend Chocolate." QR codes on the chocolate packaging allow customers to listen to Tallinn legends in three languages. The jury praised the product's thoughtful presentation, the involvement of a designer and its inventive approach to connecting a physical souvenir with stories told by the museum.
In addition to the award-winning souvenirs, the jury gave special mention to Kondas Center's handmade "Maasikas ja tigu" ("Strawberry and Snail") board game, TYPA Printing and Paper Art Center's stationery set featuring historic lead type symbols and washed sheep's wool from the Center of Rural Curiosity. The latter was highlighted as a good example of how a museum can give existing material a new and practical use.
According to the jury, the strengths of this year's entries included drawing on museums' identities and stories from their collections, involving local producers and craftspeople and paying attention to reuse. At the same time, the jury urged museums to take a more comprehensive approach to products' visual presentation, packaging and choice of materials: A sustainable product should also come in environmentally friendly packaging.
EMMA is Estonia's biennial museum souvenir competition and has been held since 2009. The competition aims to recognize museums' product development efforts and encourage them to draw on their collections, exhibitions and stories to create new, high-quality and contemporary products.

Belgium Orders NASAMS to Protect Strategic Sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:44:47 UTC
19:44:47 KST

Belgium has ordered medium-range NASAMS air defense systems from Norwegian company Kongsberg to strengthen the protection of its strategically important military and infrastructure sites.
The defense company’s press service reported this.
The contract, worth kr10 billion (approximately €918 million), was signed with the Netherlands Armed Forces’ procurement agency on behalf of Belgium.
“We are very pleased to welcome Belgium to the family of NASAMS nations,” Eirik Lie, President and CEO of KONGSBERG, said.
He noted that acquiring these SAM systems will provide Belgium with reliable nationwide air defense coverage and help strengthen overall European security.
In late February, Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Belgium would receive NASAMS air defense systems, which it plans to deploy to protect the Port of Antwerp, Europe’s second-busiest port.
The government moved to procure the new SAM systems after the country faced numerous incidents of unknown drones flying over strategic sites in 2025.
Drones were also spotted over the Port of Antwerp, nuclear power plants, BASF’s chemical plant, and the Europa container terminal. Following these incidents, in early November, Belgian armed forces personnel were ordered to shoot down any unidentified drones over military bases.
Belgium’s Ministry of Defense reported that the first part of the NASAMS will become operational in 2027. This will allow nearly two-thirds of the port area to be protected.
The NASAMS air defense system consists of a command post, an AN/MPQ-64 Sentinel radar for detection and guidance, launchers carrying six missiles each, and specialized vehicles for reloading and maintenance.
The system’s primary interceptors are AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles, which, depending on the variant, can engage targets at ranges of up to 40 km. The system can also use short-range AIM-9 Sidewinder guided missiles and specialized AMRAAM-ER missiles with an extended range.

Amsterdam urges health minister to rescue crack treatment study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:44:09 UTC
19:44:09 KST

Amsterdam urges health minister to rescue crack treatment study
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The mayor of Amsterdam, Femke Halsema, has called on the government to step in to save an experimental programme to treat crack addicts with a medicine usually prescribed for ADHD.
The inspectorate IGJ has halted production of the medicine, dexamphetamine, at a Dutch hospital as part of an ongoing supervisory procedure.
The IGJ did not name the hospital or say how long the investigation would take, but a spokesman told Dutch News: “We are concerned about the quality of the medicine.”
Amsterdam city council said last week it wanted to start giving the dexamphetamine to people addicted to crack cocaine in an experiment similar to the methadone programme for heroin users.
The probe has been backed by the other three major Dutch cities – Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – after initial research showed it could help ease crack users’ cravings.
Halsema and Alexander Scholtes, alderman responsible for healthcare, said suspending production of the drug would have a devastating impact.
Promising method
They have written to health minister Sophie Hermans urging her to review the IGJ’s decision and come up with a solution to ensure the study can continue.
“What it means is that the only highly promising method for treating these seriously addicted people has gone out of the window,” Scholtes told TV station AT5. “We can’t let that happen.”
The city council said the suspension of production was “unexpected and for reasons that are unclear to us”, but the IGJ said its investigation pre-dated the experimental programme.
A spokesman said the medicine used in the trial was the outcome of 12 years of research and development by the REDUCE project, whose partners include GGD Amsterdam, the city’s health authority, to develop a form of dexamphetamine with long-term effects.
Halesma and Scholtes have asked Hermans to organise a meeting with all parties concerned before November 1 to discuss a solution. “We value the independent position of the IGJ highly and are not impinging on their judgment,” they wrote.
But they added: “Every day we see people in Amsterdam whose lives are being taken over by a serious crack addiction.”
GGD Amsterdam estimates there are between 3,000 and 9,000 crack users in the city, many of whom are homeless or have mental health problems, or both.
The Trimbos institute, which specialises in mental health, and addiction support service Mainline said in a report three years ago that there were around 27,900 problematic crack users in the Netherlands.

Israeli strikes kill eight people in Gaza, medics say
CAIRO - Israeli strikes killed at least eight Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on May 17, health officials said, as ceasefire efforts meant to end fighting between Israel and the Hamas militant group falter.
In the weeks since halting its joint bombing with the US in Iran, Israel has stepped up its attacks in Gaza, where Hamas has been tightening its grip, even as Israeli troops remain in control of more than half the territory.
Medics said an Israeli strike killed one Palestinian near a police post and another at a tent encampment in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip. The Israeli military said it killed a militant who posed an immediate threat to forces in the area.
Separately, Gaza medics said another Israeli airstrike killed at least three people at a community kitchen near Al-Aqsa Hospital in Deir Al-Balah, in the central Gaza area. The Israeli military said the strike targeted a Hamas commander developing anti-tank missiles.
Meanwhile, official medical sources said three Palestinians were killed - one in a shooting incident in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip and two others in an Israeli airstrike near a bakery in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on that incident.
On May 16, the Israeli military said that Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the head of Hamas’ armed wing in Gaza, was killed in what it described as a precise strike on Gaza City on May 15.
Hamas confirmed Haddad’s death but stopped short of threatening revenge.
Hamas commander killed in airstrike
The Israeli military said it had also killed Bahaa Baroud, a Hamas Operations Headquarters commander, in an airstrike on May 16, accusing him of planning multiple imminent attacks against troops and Israeli civilians in recent weeks.
The military said Baroud posed an immediate threat and was targeted in a precise strike, adding that measures were taken beforehand to reduce civilian harm, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.
Gaza health officials said Baroud, along with another person, was killed in the airstrike, which targeted their car in Gaza City.
Israel and Hamas remain deadlocked in indirect talks to advance US President Donald Trump’s post-war plan for Gaza that is meant to end more than two years of fighting with Hamas disarming as Israeli troops withdraw from Gaza.
Some 870 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes since the October ceasefire, according to figures that do not distinguish between combatants and civilians. Four Israeli soldiers were killed by militants during the same period.

We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:41:58 UTC
19:41:58 KST

The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.
Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”.
That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets.
The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks.
The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.
In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.”
But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene.
“In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said.
However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”
A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth.
But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”.
“Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.”
Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.
That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.
“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.
“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

Sound and vision: Creators Olivier Calvert and Jose Luis Agreda on the art of animation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:40:27 UTC
19:40:27 KST

Greece's biggest International Animation Festival, Animasyros, is now firmly ranked among the top events of its kind in Europe. With a programme richer than ever, this year's festival showcased more than 280 films by established and emerging filmmakers from 50 different countries.
Animasyros, one of Europe's major animation festivals, recently wrapped up its 19th consecutive year of celebrations in Ermoupoli, flying the flag for the Greece's biggest International Animation Festival.
Beyond the seven competition sections (International, Student, K.ID.S, AnimaPride, National Competition, TV & Commissioned Films and Feature Films), this year's edition included a special focus on Irish animation, a theme marking 200 years of Ermoupoli, educational workshops, parallel events, international collaborations and the Market, which has now become a key reference point for the entire industry in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Vassilis Karamitssanis, President of the Animasyros International Festival, spoke to Euronews about what the event has achieved so far and what lies ahead next year, when Animasyros celebrates its 20th anniversary:
"In the 18-19 years that Animasyros has been in the spotlight, or that have elapsed since its founding back in 2008, I believe it has become the most important hub for animation in the Mediterranean and in Greece. It places strong emphasis on showcasing Greek and European talent around the world and also aims to highlight new techniques and technologies in the field of animation, which I consider to be the key to a sustainable future for the audiovisual sector in general and for European animation in particular."
Listen up
One of the most prominent guests at this year's edition was the internationally recognised and multi-award-winning sound designerOlivier Calvert.
With a long track record of collaborations with leading directors and organisations, the Montreal-based Canadian creator has shaped the sonic universe of numerous acclaimed productions, including the Oscar-nominated short film The Girl Who Cried Pearls. He was also part of the Oscar-winning sound team for Denis Villeneuve's Arrival.
During the festival, Calvert presented a masterclass devoted to sound as a decisive storytelling tool. The festival paid tribute to his work and screened a selection of films:
"Sound design shapes the overall sound of a film, which means you can work with its sonic environment. It can be realistic – birds, traffic noise, the sea, the waves. But it can also operate on a subconscious level. You can really create tension in a scene by adding other sounds beneath the music or the voice, or by removing sounds," explained Calvert.
"You can build tension that way. It is important, because sound is the filter through which you look at the image. It gives you the emotion with which you perceive that image. There is a saying I like very much, which was also the subtitle of my workshop: 'The image is the body, but sound is the soul'."
"For me, it is the whole emotional landscape of the film. It is all the sound, not just the music. Every sound is music in a way, so it contributes to the emotional impact of the film. There is a big difference between fiction films and animation. In live-action films you first create sound for a normal environment. In animation everything is constructed, an entirely new world, so why should the sound be natural, real? In an animated film we do not need the sound to be realistic. So yes, we can create a completely different world, a unique world. A new universe to discover, both in terms of image and in terms of sound.
"Sometimes I get involved very early in the creative process, especially with directors I have already worked with. They now bring me in at a very early stage, because we can shape the film using sound as a storytelling device. You can tell a story purely with images and you can tell a story purely with sounds. So the challenge is to build a story through the collaboration between images and sounds. That is where I can help the director achieve this. I am something like an artistic director for sound," added Calvert.
"I dare to take on the role of adviser for them. As soon as I am hired for a film, we start to discuss ideas around it. And we work together with the composer. I am not a composer. That is why I always collaborate with someone else on the sound, who is the composer. This trio (director, composer and sound designer) is very important. For me the soundtrack of a film is a whole. There is the music on the one hand and the sound effects on the other. Everything goes together, so it is a major collaboration between director, composer and sound designer. Yes, there is great synergy between the three."
Cross-border collaborations
This year's festival opened with the Greek premiere of Decorado by Goya-winning Spanish creator Alberto Vásquez (Unicorn Wars, Birdboy: The Forgotten Children), with the support of the Embassy of Spain in Greece and the Cervantes Institute. The film, which received the Paul Grimault award at this year's Annecy animation festival, recalls The Truman Show in animated form.
It is an existential black comedy about the absurdity of modern life and the control that others seek to impose on us, featuring the director's trademark macabre visual style, which combines innocence and dark humour with a dystopian contemporary reality.
José Luis Ágreda, the film's creative director spoke to Euronews about the project: "Decorado, the film we presented here at Animasyros, is a parable, a dark parable about our society and the way in which each of us, every individual, feels within it. The film is also about how society or, more specifically, companies try to dehumanise people.
"The story is about a man without a job for whom everything seems strange. He does not perceive things as reality because they have nothing to do with him. There is humour and these funny animal characters," said Ágreda_. "But when the viewer enters the world of the film, they realise that it is a dystopia, a universe that becomes ever darker. And they understand that it concerns them, as it reflects today's world. This was our way of getting audiences to think about what is happening around us today."_
"The animation style we use has many references to classic Disney cartoons. I mean classic American animation. But we give it a different twist, so that viewers do not immediately recognise it, while at the same time realising that there is something strange. It is as if we have a very happy world, like the society they try to sell us, but inside it there is something rotten. So we try to work with these characters and this kind of environment, yet we create odd colours, unusual combinations of colours. In the end, people feel: 'OK, this is a nightmare, not a dream'."
"What happens to the hero, Arnold, is very similar to what we experience on social media. You feel that you are at the centre of attention and of everything, but you are not. Everything around you is constructed, fake, not real. That is because we live in a society that stays with appearance and not with being. This is the idea behind our film: that we are on a stage, on a set, where we play a role while ignoring what is really happening around us. We do not realise that everything around us is fabricated. This gives us the impression that everything is perfect. The result? We do not deal with the great problems of our society."
The Awards
The Grand Prize of the International Competition at the 19th Animasyros was awarded to Please by Anna Mantzaris, while the prize in the Greek Competition went to Konstantinos Demis for The Dog.
In the Student Competition, the award was won by Gauze, a film about Palestine created by a team of five students from GOBELINS Paris, Noran Fikri Alezabi, Nicholas Arujah, Xinyue Ma, Yulin YUE and Xiaonan Zhou.
In the Television and Commissioned Films category, the prize went to Saltwater by Eilidh Nicoll from the United Kingdom.
The Animapride competition section features films with LGBTQI+ content and showcases creativity, queer expression and acceptance. The jury awarded its prize to Eyeliner by Aisha Boujilouli. The first prize in the K.ID.S category was given to The Eagle and the Kinglet by Paul Jadoul from the Czech Republic.
The Audience Award at Animasyros was collected by Martin Lund's Unstoppable, a subversive and emotional, humourous adventure film.

Are Russian ‘Iva’ MANPADS Chinese Knock-Offs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:40:15 UTC
19:40:15 KST

A report on the Russian Rossiya 1 television channel on Monday, Sept. 28, was intended to show soldiers from a mobile fire group of the 51st Air Defense Division in Rostov.
It included an interview with an operator demonstrating a shoulder-launched man-portable air defense system (MANPADS) weapon. The soldier referred to it as the “Iva” – Russian for willow.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Milbloggers and other open-source analysts began to question the origin of the weapon.
They argued that the launcher didn’t share the characteristics of other Russian systems such as the Igla or Verba – other words used for willow.
Chinese, Iranian, or a hybrid?
The milblogger Dead District, posting on X on Monday, suggested the weapon was an Iranian Misagh-2, while other military analysts disagreed.
The US military issues site The War Zone (TWZ) and Ukraine’s Militarnyi compared the launcher with existing Chinese and Iranian designs and concluded that it more closely resembled the Chinese QW-18/QW-18A or QW-19 series of MANPADS, rather than Iran’s Misagh-2 or 3 – derivatives of the Chinese launchers.
The Swiss analytic site MiGFlug, citing TWZ, offered other possibilities for the weapon’s origin: a system bought directly from China, perhaps for evaluation; an Iranian-built derivative; a Russian copy of one or other design; or, unlikely but possible, a North Korean weapon.
The arguments were further complicated by another suggestion from the Defence Blog military issues site which said that Pakistan’s Anza-2 MANPADS is also thought to be based on a Chinese design.
Russia Keeps Pounding Kyiv in Daytime After Overnight Strike – Supermarket Hit, Debris Near Embassy
Previously, in July, Reuters reported that China was expected to transfer several hundred MANPADS to Iran as part of an arms deal.
China has been accused of being involved in the illegal global trade in shoulder launched surface-to-air missiles (SAM), as summarized in the 2022 report by the Small Arms Survey.
Why would Russia need foreign MANPADS?
It is logical for mobile fire groups in the Rostov region, which shares a border with Ukraine and frequently faces drone attacks, to deploy MANPADS.
The presence of an apparently foreign MANPADS system, assuming it is something more than a publicity stunt or has been simply provided for evaluation, raises the question as to why?
Russia inherited the capability to build its own MANPADS from Soviet times and has exported them all over the world. It could be that stocks of MANPADS, along with other weapons systems, have been denuded by the war in Ukraine.
Examples of Moscow addressing shortages since the 2022 full-scale invasion through expedient measures include taking 50-year-old tanks out of mothballs to replace frontline losses and cannibalizing Russia’s RM-48U training missiles, combining their components with parts from air-defense missiles and foreign electronics to supplement its ballistic missile capabilities.
In the meantime, the weapon experts will continue to investigate the origin of the “Iva” system which will then enable them to technically assess its potential in the role for which it is being used in Rostov.

Can we vaccinate people against scams? Researchers are testing new ways to fight online fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:40:06 UTC
19:40:06 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Earlier this month six men were extradited from South Africa for allegedly conning more than 100 U.S. women out of more than $6 million. According to the FBI, the men were members of a large organized crime ring that sometimes crafted and maintained elaborate romantic relationships to defraud their targets.
The idea of someone using romance to con you isn’t new; it’s practically a tale as old as time. But the Internet made it possible to implement these schemes from the other side of the globe. Thanks to the ubiquitous nature of online socializing and dating, it no longer sounds inherently fishy to fall for someone you’ve yet to meet in person.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Fangzhou Wang is an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of Texas at Arlington who studies online financial crimes. She says that now AI is the latest technological advance that’s making romance cons harder to spot—and easier to scale.
Thank you so much for coming on to talk with us today.
Fangzhou Wang: Thank you for inviting me.
Feltman: So how did you get interested in studying romance scams?
Wang: So initially when I get into the field of online scams, so my research actually broadly focuses on online financial crimes and how technology actually creates new opportunities for the offenders to target and exploit the victims in cyberspace. And over time, my work has somehow expanded from what I study in the Ph.D. into, you know, online scam more generally, particularly, you know, [the] human side of those scams. So how scammers actually use persuasion, trust and deception to influence people’s decisions. So this kind of, you know, progression of my research, you know, naturally lead me to online romance scam because this is very interesting scam and how people actually tricking the victims on dating apps, where in the same time financial exploitations is oftentimes built around this kind of, you know, interpersonal, loving relationships.
And more recently, I have also studied, you know, a little bit regarding to the aftermath of the scam, where you have money mules, money launderers and, you know, broader networks that actually help move those illicit funds. And in more recent years, I began to focus in on, you know, how online scam or online financial crime impacting, you know, different populations, specifically elderly population, which could be one of the most vulnerable populations in the societies.
So that is how my research actually progressed, you know, moving from online financial crime, online scam, to romance scam and, more recently to, like, money mules or scams against elderly populations and ultimately, you know, of course, leading me to understanding a more broader, you know, psycho-eco systems that may impact the victims and also the societies as general.
Feltman: Well, to take a step back, could you tell our listeners, a little bit about what kind of scams are, are out there these days that you’re studying?
Wang: Well, the current scam I’m currently studying is, of course, the first one is online romance scam, and the second one I focus most heavily on is going to be the Bitcoin scam, meaning that, how scammers actually utilizing Bitcoins or broader, you know, cryptocurrency systems to elicit, you know, fund from the victims, and how those scams can potentially impacting both the victims and societies.
And aside from the general online scams, I have been also studying, you know, a little bit regarding to cyberstalking and also cyberbullying as well, especially those against teenagers and also minors. And in addition, with regarding to a more broader, you know, abusive nature of cyberspace potentially, I also study a little bit regarding to “sextortion” and also a little bit regarding to, you know, how image-based sexual abuse can potentially be penetrated online and against, you know, different victims from different age groups.
Feltman: Could you give us some examples of common romance scams that we’ve been seeing lately?
Wang: Well, lately, ’cause, you know, online romance scam in general, you know, the scammers are trying to use fake identities to persuade the victims into giving up their monies by building a trusted relationships in the firsthand. So that is a very common online romance scam that we have been knowing in the societies. But however, in recent years, I wanna say online romance scam has been industrialized in a more Bitcoin or investment-based trusted scams that [are] happening online. Specifically, when the scammers are building trust with you first, and then the scammers are enticing you or luring you to go on fraudulent investment platforms where the scammers will tell the victims that, “oh, we need to build a wonderful future together. And in order to do so, we need to do the investment, or we need to invest on these platforms and accumulate our assets all together.” But in return, the victims will find out the scammers are actually building up the fake platforms by themselves to lure the victims to invest on. So in the end of the day, the victims are actually just investing their own money by putting the money just directly into the scammers’ pockets. So that is how the romance scam are gradually developing from simply just using persuasive cues into the scammers are industrialized their operations by building, like, an entrepreneur around their operations by, you know, luring the victims into the investment apps before, you know, they actually exploiting them voluntarily in some ways.
Feltman: So we’re not talking about, you know, somebody messaging you online and talking you into sending them some amount of money. We’re talking about, you know, big operations where they’re forming, in some cases, really, like, long-term online relationships with you. You know, there’s an entire operation then funneling you into giving them money in what seems like a business decision.
Wang: Exactly. I wanna more emphasize the online romance scam nowadays is developing more like an organized crime or more likely to be a white-collar crime, if you wanna say it more generally. So instead of just a petty crimes that impacting only a smaller portion of the victims, but, you know, the victims around the globe are impacted by this kind of scam. And we do not know exactly where majority of the scammers are coming from, but we just know they stay anonymized, they stay organized, they stay in a group and trying to get into as many victims’ mind as they can or even their bank account.
Feltman: So how do you go about studying romance scams?
Wang: So one area of my work actually examine how romance scam operates, so that is going to be the one central things I’m currently studying on. So I have been studying, you know, scam communications and offender strategies to understand how scammers actually use staged processes to construct identities, initiate, you know, relationships, build trust, and eventually, you know, transition into what I called a financial request or financial crisis. So this, kind of, help us to think about, you know, romance scam as a staged processes instead of just like one single deceptive messages, and then the victims just give out money. So it’s not like this way.
And most recently, I have been studying, you know, how we can actually prevent romance scam before the victimization even occurs. So one of my most recent projects [is] actually trying to dive further into the persuasion strategies used by the scammers, how the persuasion actually works into enticing the victims to fall into those crises. So the basic idea is very similar to a vaccine, if I use this example. So instead of, you know, simply telling people how scam actually exist, so we expose potential users or potential victims to weakened example of the persuasive strategies of the scammers that they could potentially be using during the scamming process and explain how those strategies actually work. So the goal is, of course, to cut the connection or cut the persuasion cues in the first place before the victims fall into the bigger traps. So the goal is, of course, to help people to recognize that or resist to those techniques when they encounter in a real relationships.
Some of my recent works also examine, you know, the role of AI in those scams, especially generative AIs. So they can potentially make it easier for the scammers to produce, you know, convincing messages—because nowadays, if we get a chance to interview an offenders in cyberspace, they’d probably be like, “We won’t be [writing] those prescam scripts by ourselves. We use generative AI to generate realistic images to target more people in the societies.” So, and they also use AI to generate those images and identities.
And of course, at the same time, our research also [asks] whether people can be trained or recognize manipulation regardless of whether deceptive content was created by [a] human or AI and which type of cue is more persuasive to the potential victims or the general crowd.
Feltman: What are your findings, tell us, about how people can avoid these scams and spot them?
Wang: Well, I wanna say, all of my research that I just described in the previous questions, they are all in progress. But what is actually surprising me is, you know, how difficult it can be to translate, you know, general scam awareness into actual resistance. Because people, when they hear about online scam or romance scam, they may even be able to list, right, those clear and obvious warning signs. But recognizing a red flag in those [in the] abstract is very different than actually being able to tell them in the actual conversations when they are having [them] with the scammers. And somehow, even though with those awareness already preexisted in their mind, they can still be very susceptible to those persuasions. So this is one reasons that, you know, a lot of scam awareness, so-called trainings, can be less effective than they actually think they can [be]. Because a lot of time, you know, the scammers, they will read our papers as well. So they will adapt their strategies as well, simultaneously, when our researchers and our societies begin to progressing against those scams. So that is one central findings of my research.
And another interesting one, from my prevention research, is that, you know, simply creating a sense of threat or fear does not necessarily appear to be the most important mechanism for protecting people—because we do not want to, you know, entice a fear from the victims without actually telling them what the scam is actually about. [This] does not reduce their online activities or sometimes may have more adverse effects on how they actually talk to people online. So what seems especially important for me is that developing people’s motivation and ability to resist the persuasion is more important than enticing just, you know, the simple fear—because that kind of mentality suggests prevention messages should go beyond just saying, “Romance scam are dangerous,” right? So they should teach people what manipulation and persuasion looks like in the actual conversations and what to do when they actually encounter those red flags.
Feltman: And what are some of the red flags that people should be looking out for?
Wang: From a researcher’s standpoint, I think, the first one is not going to be the broken grammar again—because, a lot of [the] time, when people are saying, “Oh, the scammers are using a broken English, or they are using a fragmented sentencing when they are chatting with you, it’s the sign of a scammer,” [but] nowadays scammers are now, they are using AI to generate, you know, sentences. So of course, the grammar is gonna be great. It’s awesome. It’s just like a native, speakers when talking to the victims.
But I wanna say the most important sign I want everyone to notice [is the] use of images and the videos—because you want the person talking to you online [to] show their behavior is consistent, meaning that the images and the videos needs to be always consistent, telling the stories. But, however, it’s very hard in today’s world as well because the deepfakes can always help the scammers to create whatever images and videos they want to create, even in a consistent ways. So although I wanna say it is a red flag, but in some other ways it’s, you know, the scammers, if they really invest into the scam, they probably can overcome this challenge as well.
And the third red flag I wanna mention is whether they will have a video chat or voice chat with you in a live settings. This is a common red flag that I always recommend people to do when they are trying to, you know, talking to strangers online, especially for a prolonged period of times. But, however, [on the] other hand, things always come with double-edged sword, right? Because with the deepfakes and AIs, the scammers can just embed a deepfake, um, software into their video chatting platforms, and then they can change their face, change their voice. So I wanna say, overall, in general, it’s just very hard to actually, like, completely eliminate the opportunities to encounter scams online, especially on the dating apps.
So I wanna say: always have somebody around you, so you can always talk, talk to them when you see anything [that] might be raising your red flags. Do not keep yourself in a bubble without talking to your friends or your families or your classmates, right? So always let people around you, like, really care about you. Tell them what is going on in these conversations, what’s actually raising your suspicions, and they might be the perfect individual that can help you to tell if it is a scam or give you more advice on how to talk to strangers on the platforms. So that’s my suggestions.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, and it sounds like, unfortunately we’re at a point technologically where no matter how real the relationship feels and no matter how much evidence you think you’ve acquired that it’s real, maybe if someone you’ve only ever spoken to virtually asks you for money, that should just always be a red flag, unfortunately. Maybe in the 1 percent of situations where that is someone who genuinely loves you asking for money, maybe they just need to be let down. [Laughs.]
Wang: Exactly. Another thing I think [is] it is also very important that the prevention does not always place [the] responsibility on the victims’ families alone. The dating apps, the social media companies, financial institutions, and the law enforcement also have important roles to play. So we should not simply just asking the victims, “How you can become better at detecting scam by yourselves online?” but ask, you know, how the platforms or how the general societies can make those scams harder to carry out in the first place.
Feltman: Absolutely. Well, thank you so much for coming on to, uh, talk to us about this.
Wang: Thank you so much for inviting me.

Europe's car industry is most at risk from its reliance on a handful of countries for chips and critical materials, according to a new report which warns that going electric is pitting carmakers against AI and data centres for the same supplies.
Europe's carmakers rely on a narrow group of countries, suppliers and processing hubs for the chips, magnets and metals their vehicles need, and that dependence is the biggest supply-chain risk facing automotive manufacturing in the bloc, a new study found.
The analysis, carried out by the Czech and German arms of consultancy EY at the request of the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) and published on Tuesday, scored ten critical materials and components against six factors that could constrain supply.
Concentration of supply scored highest, at 4.6 on a five-point scale.
Five inputs stood out as the most vulnerable: semiconductors, silicon, tungsten, neodymium-iron-boron magnets used in electric motors and wiring harnesses, the cable bundles that connect a car's electrical systems.
The industry has felt the risk before.
Chinese curbs on rare-earth exports shut several European production lines last year, according to suppliers' association CLEPA, while a supply crisis at chipmaker Nexperia prompted ACEA to warn of potential "significant disruption to European vehicle manufacturing" last October.
For six of the ten inputs, the riskiest stage is refining and processing the minerals rather than extraction.
China dominates rare-earth refining and magnet production as well as gallium and germanium processing, while Taiwan and South Korea are major chipmaking hubs.
"Europe's main challenge is not only access to raw materials. More critical are the shortages of processing capacity, qualified suppliers and specialised expertise," said Zdeněk Dušek, automotive consulting partner at EY Czech Republic.
"These capabilities cannot be built within one or two years," Dušek added.
Competing with AI
Electrification sharpens the problem.
Electric cars need fewer conventional parts but more semiconductors, power electronics and critical materials, putting carmakers in competition with AI, data centres, defence and clean energy for the same supplies.
The shift to electric vehicles increases competition with other industries for the same critical materials and components by about 15%, the study estimates.
Carmakers are often small customers in these markets, accounting for 17% of end demand for semiconductors and just 3% for gallium, a metal used in power electronics and radar.
Increased competition and concentrated supply chains are pushing prices higher. Gallium, for instance, has risen more than elevenfold in price since 2016, from about $197 to around $2,269 per kilogram, amid growing demand fuelled in part by AI development.
"Carmakers are increasingly competing for these supplies with other industries, such as manufacturers of chips for artificial intelligence," said Martina Nimčová, a manager in business consulting at EY Czech Republic.
Self-driving ambitions add to the pressure, as autonomous functions increase reliance on chips, sensors, gallium and germanium, the study notes.
For instance, Volkswagen partnered with Uber to deploy a fleet of autonomous, all-electric "ID. Buzz AD" microvans, with rides on the Uber platform planned to begin in Los Angeles in late 2026 before scaling to thousands of vehicles.
Meanwhile, Stellantis aims to start producing robotaxis for Uber in 2028 using Nvidia's self-driving technology.
No quick fix
The study outlines four scenarios in which disruptions around the world could leave European carmakers short of vital supplies: disruption to electronics supplies from Taiwan, resource nationalism in Asia, strained trade corridors in the Americas and instability along Africa's mineral export routes.
Logistics is the common thread, and even a short interruption can halt just-in-time production lines, as the 2021-2022 chip shortage showed.
"Expanding capacity for the most critical inputs often takes more than five years," Dušek explained, adding that the advantage goes "not to those with the best strategy on paper, but to those who act earlier and can scale capacity more quickly."
Full self-sufficiency is not realistic, the study concludes.
Instead, it urges Europe to speed up permitting and qualification, target investment at the tightest bottlenecks, diversify suppliers and logistics routes, monitor supply chains more closely and give private investors long-term demand certainty.
"This isn't just risk management. It's about safeguarding Europe's industrial strength," said Sigrid de Vries, ACEA's director general.
With new capacity measured in years, the study's message is that the time to act is before the next shortage, not during it.
