Israel's Lobby: How pro-Israel groups influence US politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:03:53 UTC
19:03:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Who shapes America's Israel policy? Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick examine the power of Israel's Lobby
In late August, Jonathan Pollard, a former US Navy intelligence analyst convicted of spying for Israel in the mid-1980s and subsequently jailed for 30 years, announced that he would run in Israel's forthcoming October election as a member of the new right-wing Israel First party.
Pollard's return to public life follows his release from parole restrictions in November 2020. A month later, the US-born former spy left Newark Airport for Tel Aviv aboard a Boeing 737 owned by Israeli-American billionaire Miriam Adelson, who is said to be worth $33.9 billion and has donated more than $200 million to the Republican Party.
On arrival at Ben Gurion Airport, Pollard received a hero's welcome and was greeted by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israel's Lobby, published in mid-August, opens with this episode. Written by two Jewish Americans — investigative journalist Eli Clifton and political scientist Ian Lustick — the book uses Pollard's return to Israel as an entry point into a much broader examination of the networks of money, politics and influence that shape US policy towards Israel.
The authors note that Pollard has since used his celebrity status to promote and champion one of Israel's most controversial politicians, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
"Pollard is a great entry point to begin a conversation about the influence of Israel's lobby in the United States," Clifton tells The New Arab.
"A spy being lifted out of the country on a billionaire's private jet sounds like a scene from a John le Carré novel. But this took place with open transparency, in the full glare of the world’s media."
So how does Israel — a country with a population of just 10 million and a landmass that is roughly the same size as the state of New Jersey — exercise so much influence in Washington?
This question is addressed several times in Israel's Lobby. Both authors define the lobby as "a loose coalition of individuals and organisations that actively work to shape US foreign policy in a pro-Israel direction."
They also stress the lobby's historical ties to Christian evangelicals and other streams within American politics, including US trade unions and the neoconservative movement.
"The Israel lobby has access to our campaign finance system here in America," Clifton, also a cofounder of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, explains.
"Other countries do not have that. Israel's lobby, by contrast, has an enormous influence over our politicians. This has serious implications for both our national security and our elections in the United States," he adds.
"Money is a major source of the lobby's influence and power,” Lustick tells The New Arab.
He recently experienced the lobby's censoring tactics firsthand while promoting his co-authored book in a church in suburban Philadelphia to a group called The Jewish Justice Collective.
"The church was subjected to demands from lobby representatives requesting the event be cancelled," Lustick explains.
"The lobby is constantly trying to prevent truthful views about Israel from being discussed in public."
A wave of repression
Both authors say the lobby's ascendancy in recent years has produced "a wave of repression and a constriction in the free-speech rights of Americans, unmatched since the anti-communist hysteria of the McCarthy period" in the 1950s.
They speak about some of the lobby's most powerful organisations, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
In the 2022 tax year, AIPAC's primary fundraising vehicle, the American Israel Education Foundation (AIEF), had revenues of approximately $69.9 million and held assets worth over $186 million.
Today, most of AIPAC's resources are directed to influencing the voting patterns of US senators and members of Congress on matters pertaining to Israel.
The topics vary. In July 2023, for instance, Congress passed a resolution pledging continuing aid for Israel and declaring that the country was "neither racist nor an apartheid state."
"AIPAC is unquestionably the most successful foreign policy lobby in the United States," says Lustick, who served as the State Department's expert on Israel-Palestine affairs during the Carter administration (1977 to 1981).
The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) is another powerful group within Israel’s Lobby.
The organisation was founded in New York more than a century ago to combat anti-semitism and other forms of racism and bigotry.
Today, however, the ADL has redefined definitions of anti-semitism, say Clifton and Lustick. Presently, any criticism of the Israeli military or the Israeli government is being documented by the ADL as "anti-semitic incidents."
Both authors cite numerous examples of this information being used to shape public discourse about Israel across the United States.
In May 2023, the Biden White House issued the US National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism. This relied almost solely on data produced in the ADL annual audits, both authors explain.
In September 2025, the Trump administration did the same. On the latter occasion, the State Department organised a briefing for journalists on anti-semitism in America that relied entirely on the ADL's 2024 audit.
Clifton and Lustick claim these numbers were manipulated to dramatise a torrent of anti-semitism. The session opened with ADL statistics showing 9,354 antisemitic incidents in 2024, "the highest on record."
Citing ADL sources, the journalists were told that Jews "account for 2 percent of the US population but were the target of nearly 70 percent of religiously motivated hate crimes in 2024."
"The ADL is presently measuring things that were not previously defined as anti-semitism, such as protests against Israel," says Lustick.
"This is a shameless way to promote the false idea that a tsunami of anti-semitism has erupted in the United States because of October 7."
An anti-semitism witch hunt
Both authors describe this manipulation of statistics as "an anti-semitism witch hunt."
They say Israel's lobby uses "false, hoax-like, strange accusations of anti-semitism to try to suppress all serious debate about Israel."
Clifton and Lustick cite The Adam and Gila Milstein Family Foundation as a "prime example of the anti-semitism witch-hunt that Israel's lobby is presently engaged in."
In August 2025, the Milstein Family Foundation widely distributed an article originally published by Adam Milstein in The Jerusalem Post that attacked Zohran Mamdani, then a leading candidate in New York City's mayoral election.
The article referred to Mamdani as an "Islamo-leftist" who "refuses to acknowledge Israel's right to exist as a Jewish state," and as aligned with "anti-semitic incitement and terror."
Lustick describes The Milstein Family Foundation as "aggressive and far right."
He tells The New Arab, "They try to smear all critics of Israeli policy in American politics as anti-semites. They also find ways to suppress free discussion on university campuses across the United States about American policy in the Middle East."
Clifton and Lustick claim "the overwhelming majority of Jewish Americans do not prioritise Israel's well-being or interests."
And yet, Israel's lobby is consistently attempting to tell another story.
"The day-to-day messaging coming out from the social media channels of organisations like AIPAC and ADL essentially endorses the anti-semitic trope that all Jewish Americans, and all Jews, hold dual loyalties to Israel," Clifton explains. "But it's simply not true."
Lustick claims there has been a noticeable change at the "grassroots level" of Jewish institutions across the United States whenever the topic of Israel is raised, especially inside synagogues in recent years.
"Previously, it was to be expected that on major Jewish holidays there were lots of social, educational and cultural events that celebrated Israel," the political scientist explains.
"But now, in most non-Orthodox American synagogues, talking about Israel has become a very delicate and controversial issue. The rabbis avoid the topic. It's just too hot to handle, and there are now too many divisions within the Jewish community."
JP O’Malley is a cultural critic, journalist and writer. He writes regularly about books, geopolitics, history, film, arts and culture for various publications, including the Sunday Independent, The Irish Examiner, The New World, The Age and New Eastern Europe

Passportless mess

Unknown Publisher

‘He is, in simple terms, a man who destroys everything.’
In this entertaining short documentary from the Czech filmmaker Maja Penčič, truth and myth collide in the figure of Zoran, a former resident of a block of flats in Belgrade, Serbia, whose larger-than-life personality and convoluted biography have left behind accounts that can’t be reconciled. Penčič sets out to find Zoran, or at least to understand who he was, by surveying the people who claim to have known him at different stages of his life. Throughout, a rotating cast of acquaintances characterise him as everything from ‘warm’, ‘intelligent’ and ‘exceptional’ to someone who ‘never feels shame’ to, quite simply, ‘a dick’. The home-video aesthetic lends the proceedings an intimacy and a faintly surreal quality that evokes the imperfections of memory. The film never settles on a single version of events, instead watching the details rearrange themselves around a few fixed points, until what is left is less a man than a cautionary tale.

"At this time, Russians continue to attack our cities. We urge citizens to stay in safe places during air raid alerts and the threat of shelling," he added.

Insects play critical role in ecosystems beyond just providing food, new research shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study.
The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals.
Nearly three-quarters of terrestrial and freshwater vertebrates eat invertebrates, according to the paper, with insects frequently making up a large portion of their diets.
However, their relationship goes beyond predator and prey.
The paper, led by Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, documents dozens of less obvious ways vertebrates depend on the estimated 14m to 30m species of insects found around the world.
Chimpanzees, for example, have been recorded applying insects to treat open wounds, while more than 200 bird species use ants to remove parasites or maintain feathers. Other birds build nests near wasps or other stinging insects, in a likely effort to gain protection from predators.
Insects also provide shelter, the study notes. Birds, reptiles and mammals use termite mounds and ant nests, which can offer stable temperatures and humidity. White-throated round-eared bats, for instance, excavate cavities in termite mounds and use them as roosts.
Other insects act as sanitation workers. Dung beetles remove animal waste and can make dung drier and more aerated, in turn reducing parasite survival, according to the study. Meanwhile, moths living in some bird nests consume feces, feathers and other debris. The review notes that insects have performed similar functions for millions of years, citing evidence of beetles feeding on feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period, which lasted from about 145m to 66m years ago.
Other insect-vertebrate relationships include beetles removing ectoparasites from rodents and snakes feeding on firefly larvae to obtain defensive toxins, as well as antbirds using live crickets during courtship.
Mutually beneficial relationships also occur across the insect-vertebrate realm, with sloths relying on moths to deposit nitrogen in their fur and spur algal growth, which the sloths then eat. Sloths then descend from trees once a month to defecate on the ground, providing substrate in which moths lay eggs.
According to the study, such overlooked relationships could become increasingly important as insect communities evolve. Although the extent of insect declines varies across habitats and regions, the review says that “widespread and considerable disruption” of insect communities is “inevitable” as land use changes.
Grames called the study a “wake-up call for anyone concerned about the biodiversity crisis”.
“We need to pay attention to insects and make their conservation a top priority, because conserving insects will benefit all the other species that rely on them. Insects are so much more than just food for vertebrates like birds and bats – they create and maintain habitat, provide protection to other species, help with reducing diseases and removing waste, and so many other ecosystem services that we, and other species, rely on. They really are the unsung heroes of the natural world,” she added.
Grames also pointed to the critical role insects play in addressing the climate crisis, saying: “About 12% of the global carbon forest stock is leaf litter and dead wood, and insects are responsible for decomposing about 30% of it. So even though insects are small, their activities influence global carbon cycles. Insects also help with forest regeneration by dispersing seeds into areas where other, large – seed dispersers have disappeared. Pollination and seed dispersal, both of which are done by insects, are two of the biggest limitations in forest regeneration.”
Similarly, Rob Cooke, senior ecologist at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology and a co-author of the study, highlighted the broader ecological implications of insect declines, saying: “Widespread insect declines globally are likely to have far-reaching effects on wildlife. Beyond reducing an essential food source, losses of insects risk changing ecosystems, disrupting pollination and seed dispersal, weakening sanitation, and altering the many interactions that help ecosystems function.”
The consequences for vertebrates remain difficult to predict due to the lack of studies on insect-vertebrate relationships. The study notes that “the lack of systematic descriptions of trophic and non-trophic interactions, hampered by an ongoing decline of natural history research”, makes it difficult to understand how changes in insect biodiversity affect other species.
For co-author Chris Elphick, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut, understanding the diverse roles that insects play across vertebrates’ lives is essential for designing effective conservation strategies.
“If you want to have vertebrates, then you’ve got to be thinking about insect conservation, and we don’t do that nearly enough,” Elphick said.

From mass raids to quiet crackdown: a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

When federal agents fatally shot the US citizen protesters Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January during the nation’s largest immigration-enforcement operation ever, it marked a turning point for the second Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.
Donald Trump in his second term had sparked outrage and huge protests with federal immigration officers descending en masse on one Democratic-run city after another in what some leaders called militarized “invasions”. Los Angeles, Chicago, Charlotte, New Orleans, then Minneapolis saw lines of masked and armored officers swaggering into town to conduct street arrests, ambushes of day workers waiting in Home Depot car parks for hire, and neighborhood sweeps. Adults and kids were whisked off to detention and protests met with aggressive deployment of chemical spray, teargas, fists and batons. The killings in Minneapolis were the culmination of what appeared to many to be a federal shock force increasingly out of control while being defended by federal leaders – and public opinion broadly turned against this violence.
There was a change of personnel and the administration flagged a switch to a “quieter” approach to immigration enforcement. But while large-scale theatrics on the streets waned, less visible enforcement is no less aggressive on the ground today and continues to ramp up in multiple ways. Here’s a timeline of how the administration’s anti-immigration campaign has evolved in recent months as Trump races to remove millions of people from the US.
2026
26 JanuaryMinneapolis madness leads to a changing of the guard
Greg Bovino and other federal agents in Minneapolis on 13 January 2026, a week after the fatal shooting of Renee Good by an ICE agent. Photograph: Seth Herald/Reuters
Two days after Pretti was killed by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and 19 days after Good had been shot dead by an ICE agent, the US president announces that his “border czar”, Tom Homan, an immigration-enforcement veteran, will deploy to Minnesota, while Gregory Bovino, the border patrol’s confrontational commander-at-large, suddenly stands aside. Bovino was the face and voice on the street of federal aggression; Good, Pretti and ICE watchers were the symbols of the resistance; and Liam Ramos was the image of collateral harm.
The then secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Kristi Noem, at a press conference in New York on 8 January 2026. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA
Kristi Noem becomes the first cabinet secretary fired during the second Trump administration when she loses her leading role at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Noem was tainted with scandals over her close relationship with senior adviser Cory Lewandowski and a $220m advertising campaign starring herself and using a firm with connections to her former staffer. She had also repeated a false narrative that Pretti “brandished” a gun at federal agents and called Renee Good a domestic terrorist. Weeks later, Bovino retires and tells the New York Times: “I wish I’d caught even more illegal aliens.”
Markwayne Mullin at a confirmation hearing for the position of secretary of homeland security in Washington DC on 18 March 2026. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA
Markwayne Mullin, formerly a first-term senator from Oklahoma with “mixed martial arts fighter” on his résumé, is confirmed by the US Senate as the new DHS secretary. At his confirmation hearing, he says about immigration-enforcement officials: “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day.”
Oklahoma police shackle a man at the McIntosh county criminal justice center during an operation with ICE on 3 September 2026. Photograph: Nick Oxford for the Washington Post via Getty Images
The DHS, in its own words, has “supercharged” efforts to work with local and state law enforcement via so-called 287(g) agreements. From January 2025 these deals mushroomed nationwide, from 142 to 2,315, with most modeled as a “taskforce”. They deputize local and state officials to actively enforce immigration laws during regular police work – normally under federal jurisdiction. By spring, this collaboration acts as a force multiplier for arrests, while allowing federal agents to avoid the spotlight as local cops take on more frontline duties. It also makes immigration enforcement harder to spot for protesters.
A family leaves after an immigration court hearing at the Jacob K Javits federal building on 31 July 2026 in New York City. Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty Images
Attorneys and researchers start noticing immigration court dates being scheduled for unusually large groups of people with little to no notice, in what they say is a tactic to increase the number of deportation orders without ever giving someone an individualized hearing. These mass court dates balloon in June, affecting many thousands of people. Many more applicants struggle to find attorneys and prepare their now-rushed cases. Children are a particular target, too, being rushed through hearings as due process is undermined.
After the longest DHS shutdown ever, congressional Republicans use a partisan process to provide the department with an additional $70bn, funding it for the rest of Trump’s second term in a move that critics say undermines accountability. All told, the DHS has received roughly a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding since Trump retook the White House.
Demonstrators rally as the supreme court prepares to hear oral arguments in Mullin v Doe on 29 April 2026. Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
The US supreme court rules in favor of the Trump administration’s bid to strip temporary protected status (TPS) from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians who were legally in the US and protected from deportation. When Trump took office, 17 countries had active TPS designations, which allowed roughly 1.3 million people who were already in the US to live and work legally while it was unsafe for them to return home. But under his second administration, more than a million people who are generally law-abiding and often contribute economically to essential industries with significant labor shortages have already lost their TPS permissions. Now they face imminent risk of deportation to countries as dangerous as Afghanistan, Haiti and South Sudan if they do not qualify or cannot afford to apply for another immigration status. “We’re going after them right now,” Mullin has said of Haitians. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.”
Federal agents patrol the John F Kennedy international airport in New York on 23 March 2026. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA
ICE significantly increases its collaboration with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to detain immigrants with expired visas – many of whom have pending applications for green cards, asylum, employment-based visas, etc – at airports, sometimes near public spaces such as ticket counters or gates. However, the vast majority of arrests continue to occur where they are far less easy to detect and record on camera, such as in people’s homes and cars.
ICE agents detain an individual exiting his immigration court hearing at the Jacob K Javits federal building on 16 July 2026 in New York City. Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty Images
The DHS reports 49,571 immigration arrests, which sets a new monthly record for the second Trump administration, after previously doing so in June. A majority of the people arrested in July have no criminal history. Detentions also increase, with about 66,000 people in custody by the end of the month. Preliminary reports suggest immigration arrests in August have kept pace with July.
A memorial for Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot by ICE agents, on 14 July 2026 in Biddeford, Maine. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images
An ICE officer kills Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 26, in Biddeford, Maine, during a vehicle stop in which Durán was not the intended target, making him the 11th person fatally shot by federal immigration officials both on and off duty during Trump’s second term. The shooting comes days after federal agents similarly killed another immigrant father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston while he was driving his building crew to their job. The DHS briefly pauses most ICE traffic stops until Trump intervenes, posting online: “We CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!” In one 24-hour period, 13 to 14 July, three people die in ICE-involved incidents.
AugustEven more local cops do ICE’s bidding
Federal officials reach the milestone of 1,000 new287(g) agreements since 26 January, expanding collaborations with local law enforcement agencies at an even faster clip than during the second Trump administration’s first year in office.
AugustVisa applications
All visas for people applying to immigrate to the US are paused for an unknown amount of time while officials undergo training around the new “public charge” policies.
Markwayne Mullin announces the success of Operation Rotten Apple, in New York on 1 September 2026. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters
Mullin retroactively announces Operation Rotten Apple, which from 27 July to 29 August quietly rounded up nearly 2,200 immigrants across New York state. The operation is a case study in how aggressive immigration enforcement continues, including in Democratic-led “sanctuary” cities, without the previous theatrics.
A migrant child seeking asylum waits to be processed by the US border patrol in Yuma, Arizona, on 3 May 2022. Photograph: Nicolo Filippo Rosso/Bloomberg via Getty Images
On August 1 the federal government ends its contract providing more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children with legal representation. At the same time, attorneys report that immigration judges are taking a “deport at all costs” approach to their young clients, who suddenly are not receiving the time they need for their pending applications to be adjudicated by other agencies before they are ordered removed from the US. Many of these kids qualify for a green card or other immigration status because they have been abused, abandoned, neglected, trafficked or otherwise severely mistreated, but their applications are often subject to backlogs and quotas that cause delays. In September, the Guardian reveals that Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, has been leading an unprecedented drive across several government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist, and, in some cases, flout federal law.
Taken together, these policy changes are less showy but they have ramped up arrests, detentions and the number of people forced to leave the United States – and put millions more at immediate risk of the same. Many of these people have legal status or ongoing cases for winning or upgrading their legal status, or years of crime-free, honorable life in the US, but are being rounded up, often with little access to due process or attorneys who can help. This latest iteration of Trump’s mass deportation campaign is no longer defined by federal agents patrolling cities with smoke canisters in hand. It’s much more insidious but also more ruthless and effective – and it’s happening everywhere.

Bill Gates predicts AI will kill a billion people – but saying he’s been wrong before is quite the understatement | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:23 UTC
19:00:23 KST

The Bill Gates rehabilitation tour is in full swing. After having his carefully cultivated image tarnished by the revelation of his connection to Jeffrey Epstein, Gates lay low for a while. Now, however, the Microsoft co-founder is once again thrusting himself into the public consciousness, this time with a dire warning about AI. If left unchecked, AI could cause “a billion deaths”, Gates declared in an interview with NBC on Sunday.
Perhaps I should be terrified by this announcement from a man who, for all his sins, knows a thing or two about technology. But I’m sick of hearing about the hypothetical dangers of AI when the technology is being used to kill people today. Gates may not be directly involved in Microsoft any more, but, rather than making prophecies about the future, I’d love to hear what he thinks about the company’s role in the AI-enabled destruction of Gaza.
Another thing I’d like to hear Gates explain is why he reckons anyone should trust his judgment about anything, considering he met with Epstein on several occasions after being introduced to him in 2011. To be clear: that’s three years after the financier pleaded guilty to charges including solicitation of prostitution from a minor. Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, has said he recalled “being aware that Epstein had faced prior legal issues”, but didn’t understand the extent of them. Two minutes of Googling (or Binging) could have made it clear the man was bad news.
The oversight is particularly strange because Gates is obsessed with his public image. His team have a custom-size mannequin on which they test his outfits. The goal, per the Wall Street Journal, is “to depict someone calm and approachable, like Mister Rogers”. Not someone who cavorts with a sex offender.
Ignorance isn’t Gates’ only excuse. He has also said that Epstein “knew a lot of very rich people and [claimed he] could get them to give money to global health”. It seems the 17th richest man in the world didn’t know any wealthy people he could hit up for donations himself and, for the sake of the world’s health, had to lean on a dodgy financier whose funds were obtained in mysterious ways.
I’m not accusing Gates of anything nefarious. But, if we are to take his Epstein excuses at face value, I’m accusing him of being a fool. If we can’t trust his judgment about a man like Epstein, I’m not sure we should trust his proclamations about the future of humanity.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

Inside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west of Scotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs.
It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging.
The coastline here, a metallic grey seen through the bothy’s windows, is dotted with beds of one of the UK’s most biodiverse and carbon-rich habitats, a 9,000-year-old pink seaweed called maerl, two of which are a mile long. This rare, fragile and threatened seaweed produces hard, chalky, coral-like skeletons that provide nurseries for scallops and fish.
Now, 10 years after local people, divers, activists and creel fishers ran a successful campaign to have scallop dredging banned by law in a 600 sq km (150,000 acre) zone now designated a marine protected area (MPA), they say they have already witnessed a dramatic revival of marine life. The transformation of a seabed damaged by decades of dredging has allowed the recovery of scallop populations and ended the fractious territorial battles between the industrial dredge fishing boats and the smaller, more sustainable creel boats, local people say.
The community rowing club and nearby tour operators report increased sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. A large spawning ground for herring, once plentiful here but since overfished, has been spotted nearby and in prawn and lobster creels, or pots, which are laid on the seabed.
Diyanne Ross, 65, the local artist who made the lanterns, is part of the Blue Hope Alliance (BHA), a coalition of groups using citizen science to protect marine ecosystems in the north-west Highlands. She says the community’s achievements in protecting underwater habitats was the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles. It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”
As a child, Ross remembers going out to sea for “boxes” of haddock, ling, pollack and cod – before populations declined. But she has seen recent signs of recovery. “There is more variety of fish being caught here than before,” she says. – anglers are catching haddock and cod.”
Outside on the pier, a hardy angler on holiday from Glasgow who has braved the wind to catch what he can, is rewarded by three fresh mackerel.
The recovery of scallop stocks, says Alasdair Hughson, a scallop diver, Scottish Creel Fishermen’s Federation (SCFF) chair and one of the BHA’s founders, has been “massive” and the seabed transformation like “night to day”. A decade ago, a boat supplying hand-dived scallops to his company, Keltic Seafare, would spend just two weeks in the Summer Isles.
Hughson, whose firm supplies shellfish to UK restaurants, admits his business stands to gain from the dredge ban, but says hand-diving is more sustainable, a claim backed up by research from Open Seas. The marine conservation organisation found low-impact fishing methods, such as diving and creeling, are not only more sustainable than dredging or trawling but that more of the revenue generated stays in the local economy.
Now, the Donna Marie creel boat, skippered by Ullapool-based Gary Lewis, runs to the Summer Isles almost all year. Lewis, who used to have to travel farther, to Skye and the Western Isles, before the dredge ban, says: “It’s not just the catch that’s improved, but the general health of the seabed.”
Central to the weekend-long Maerl-Herring festival celebrations, which includes storytelling, artworks and film, is the public launch of a BHA report spanning a decade of citizen science studies.
Jason Hall-Spencer, a professor of marine biology at Cyprus University of Technology, who wrote the report, says it shows the dredge ban in Wester Ross’s MPA, set up to protect the slow-growing maerl habitats and other marine features, has done its job. It has “protected the maerl to a massive extent” he says.
Author of the Conservation Status of Maerl Habitats in north-west Scotland, partly funded by NatureScot, Hall-Spencer has carbon dated the maerl in the bay as 9,000 years old.
“If scallop dredgers had spent the last 10 years going up and down here, the habitat would be obliterated,” he says. A single pass of heavy towed gear such as that used by scallop dredgers can crush or bury up to 70% of maerl. “The seabed is now incredibly rich. Maerl is a very important habitat, chock full of bivalves which provide food for skates and rays.”
Peter Drake, 73, a retired prawn fisherman from Polbain, a hamlet that is part of Achiltibuie, was part of Sea Change Wester Ross, a campaign group supported by SCFF, which grew into BHA. “It’s good to remember what we have achieved here” says Drake. “There’s already an improvement in fish populations, but it will take time.”
Orfhlaith McDevitt, 25, who has lived here for two-and-a-half years and runs Coigach Community rowing club, says: “People from the club say they see more minke whales, dolphins and porpoises than they did 10 years ago.”
Years before Ocean, David Attenborough’s documentary, sparked outrage by showing footage of scallop dredgers bulldozing the seabed, causing damage that could be seen from space, Sea Change and the SCFF compiled a body of evidence of the devastation scallop dredgers were doing to fishing grounds and seabeds in Wester Ross.
The dossier was presented to Scottish ministers in parliament. In 2016, despite fierce opposition by the dredging lobby, scallop dredging was forbidden by law in the Wester Ross MPA, now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl. Prawn trawling is permitted in designated areas, while hand-diving for scallops and creel fishing by local boats under 150 gross tons, is also permitted.
The maerl’s three-dimensional structure allows high levels of oxygen, essential to scallops, and emits a chemical that attracts them.
But threats to the ecosystem remain: the BHA surveys, also highlighted damaged maerl in some locations – from illegal dredgers and from invasive algal growth that scientists believe could be caused by nutrients from salmon farms.
“We know that salmon farms put more nutrients into the water,” says Sara Nason, a journalist and documentary maker who founded Sea Change, which later became the BHA and organised the Maerl-Herring festival.
The BHA has now launched a three-year project with more than £153,000 of support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional funding from members of the North & West District Salmon Fishery Board, to continue its work.
Elsehere, the battle for Scotland’s sea rages on. The Scottish government, which was criticised in June by the independent watchdog Environmental Standards Scotland for not fulfilling its legal duty to restore and protect the seabed, has launched a public consultation on improving protections for marine habitats and species inside and outside the MPA network.
Theresa Ross, who runs Achiltibuie Stores for the community of about 250 people living along this stretch of coastline, says the MPA is “fully supported” by local people as it “ensures fishing is more sustainable”.
But for a rural coastal community, where the sea supports livelihoods and few jobs exist, there are competing concerns, she says.
“There are more people working on the fish farm here than fishermen,” says Ross, whose husband is one of about six fishers in the village, while her son is one of 10 working on the farms.
“I support the status quo. But the fish farms are full-time jobs, guaranteed employment and well paid,” she says. “They are not weather dependent, like fishing.”
Nevertheless, Nason is one of many who are delighted that the end to dredging has been such a success, describing the protection of the maerl beds as “beyond priceless … We’ve achieved recovery of the whole ecosystem.”

Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

Federal regulators have been urged to stop the broadcast of White House advertisements promoting Donald Trump that critics say amount to government propaganda and violate laws against using public money to promote partisan causes.
Public Citizen, an advocacy group, called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to intervene and block further airing of three ads it said were “designed to boost the image and character of Donald Trump” as part of the Republicans’ campaign for November’s midterm elections.
“Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising,” the organization wrote. “Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads.”
Broadcast stations cannot reject ads from legally qualified political candidates – but Trump is not technically a candidate, although he has urged voters to imagine that he is, on the November ballot.
“Public Citizen strongly urges the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission to direct broadcasters to stop broadcasting these apparently illegal campaign advertisements and calls on individual broadcasters to cease airing the campaign advertisements,” the group wrote in a letter addressed to both agencies.
“It is the greater responsibility of both the FCC [and] FTC and individual broadcasters to keep the airwaves fair and honest and operate in the ‘public interest, convenience, and necessity’.”
The White House has labeled the ads – which began airing last week – “public service announcements” and has responded defiantly to criticism. It has established a webpage arguing for their use.
Axios reported that more ads are set to broadcast, with Trump personally choosing which to use during the campaign for November’s midterms, which most polls suggest the Republicans are on course to lose.
“This is just the beginning,” an administration official told Axios, which reported that the ads are being produced inside the White House.
One is a rerun of a commercial aired by the Trump campaign before the 2024 presidential election and features black-and-white footage of him walking while his voice announces “the final battle”. He pledges to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and “rout the fake news media”.
The only difference from the 2024 ad are the words “paid for the US government”.
Another shows images of the president at various events while he is heard declaring “America will never be a communist country.” It takes place against the soundtrack of a choir signing the song Love Me.
A third advertisement shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump declaring that “the United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.”
The Wall Street Journal reported that the commercials were funded by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which is responsible for immigration enforcement and is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
The DHS came under scrutiny early this year after a $200m advertising campaign that boosted Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary. Noem told a congressional committee that Trump had “signed off on the ads”. Her testimony reportedly infuriated Trump, who subsequently fired her.
The latest Trump ads had aired more than 90 times across nationwide channels, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now and CBS by Sunday evening, the Journal reported. They were run during Saturday Night Live, Fox News Sunday and during several college and NFL football games. Public Citizen said the cost of the three ads already broadcast was estimated at more than $1m.
“Donald Trump is not a candidate for any elective office. The FCC and broadcasters are not constrained by the special rule protecting candidate advertisements.
“Although the White House contends these ads are ‘public service announcements’, and therefore may be paid for with taxpayer dollars, [they do not] meet the standard of a public service announcement. They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program.”
On its website, the White House denounced the criticism as “highly dishonest” and likened the ads to previous public service announcements by previous presidents, dating back to Woodrow Wilson and Franklin D Roosevelt in the first and second world wars, and including the more recent administrations of George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.
“The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” says the statement, under the headline “Presidential public service announcements are nothing new.”
“Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending – at home, at the border, and abroad.”
The Guardian contacted the FCC and FTC for comment.
Brendan Carr, the FCC chair and a close Trump ally, said on Wednesday that the ads fell “within standard practice” without raising “red flags” and did not require the commission’s intervention.

As AI images become common, the threat to elections draws alarm: ‘How will voters know what’s true?’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

An image of Bianca Motley Broom, the mayor of College Park, Georgia, kissing a man – who was not her husband – in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it’s fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people.
“I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.”
Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator.
The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern by legislators, advocates and the public.
A poll taken in mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women.
“The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and co-founder of Women Who Tech.
The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota.
A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”.
Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories.
Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said.
“The public is deeply concerned.”
Fact from fiction
Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic.
“As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI-generated images, fake stories about the candidates, how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?”
Warnock is among a group of Senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media.
The outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input.
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.”
Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation pre-empting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the Senate.
State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry.
Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them.
While legislators in Georgia began debated deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation.
Motley Broom said she believed she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.”
While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said.
“These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … that lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”

royal enfield revolutionizes the electric motorcycle experience with flying flea c6
designboom explores how royal enfield's flying flea c6 merges historic metalwork with connected software for a new generation of city commuters.
ROYAL ENFIELD REIMAGINES CITY TRAVEL WITH ELECTRIC MOTORCYCLE
During Paris Design Week 2026 Royal Enfield invited designboom for a test drive event of the Flying Flea C6 electric motorcycle, presenting its vision of a lightweight, design-driven alternative to conventional motorbikes to Europe. Developed under the sub-brand Flying Flea, the vehicle strips away the complex mechanics, offering an intuitive riding experience that invites a new generation of urban riders to transition from electric bicycles and shared micro-mobility options into the realm of full-fledged electric travel.
‘The idea for the Flying Flea C6 grew directly out of watching people navigate cities on Lime bikes and asking, “Why wouldn’t they love a proper motorcycle?” For us, that’s an essential new audience. It’s a segment that hasn’t been spoken to enough, because no one has given them a compelling reason to make the leap,’ explains Mohit Dhar Jayal, President – Brand and Strategy at Royal Enfield, directly to designboom.
FLYING FLEA HAS LANDED IN EUROPE
As the Flying Flea C6 rolls into European cities from Barcelona, Rome, Berlin and London, its arrival offers more than just a new commuting option — it introduces a vehicle specifically tailored to the dense, evolving geography of modern European capitals. At a compelling price point of 5990 euros, Flying Flea C6 draws from 125 years of production history, Royal Enfield created Flying Flea as an independent, forward-thinking sub-brand dedicated entirely to electric exploration. Developed by a team of over 200 designers and engineers across technical hubs in India and the UK, the Flying Flea C6 reflects a deep investment in original engineering and long-term research. This thoughtful balance of historic legacy and future technology has already earned the vehicle major international recognitions, including the Red Dot Award 2025 in the Design Concept category, the Good Design Award 2025, and the iF Design Award 2026.
Instead of replacing urban culture, the vehicle is designed to blend into it. ‘When you look at cities, you see that they’ve all got old bones, but a new soul,’ notes Dhar Jayal during the Paris event. ‘We use the same principle. Bridging the gap between the old and the new is something we pride ourselves on.’
Future-forward technology paired with timeless design ethos
The physical design of the Flying Flea C6 pays homage to classic 1940s wartime machinery through a modern lens, featuring a forged aluminum front suspension and exoskeleton frame that give the vehicle a striking, sculpted silhouette. At its center, the cooling fins framing the battery twist and turn from dynamic front elements into subtle rear forms, meeting in a central wing-like shape.
The vehicle is available in three carefully considered colorways: Flea Green, a classic tone referencing the original historic model; Storm Black, combining glossy and matte surfaces for urban contrast; and Parachute White, inspired by lightweight parachute textiles and fashion-forward aesthetics.
‘The battery box and the new Parachute White are elements we are particularly proud of,’ shares the Flying Flea design team. ‘There are people within the segment who want something that is even more of a standout — people who look for that extra bit of refinement in aesthetics.’
The human-centered experience is rounded out by a classic round touchscreen, physical joystick controls, an intuitive dial for changing ride feel, and customizable seating setups. Powering the experience is custom connected software that links directly to a companion smartphone app. The system learns rider preferences over time, receives continuous improvements wirelessly, and lets users manage charging routines directly from their phone, plugging seamlessly into standard home wall outlets to make daily charging effortless.

Half of Girls Who Want to Play Sports Never Get the Chance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

For decades, women’s sports were asked to prove themselves. Would people watch? Would fans fill the stands? Would brands invest?
Today, we know the answer. Professional women’s sports leagues like the WNBA and the NWSL are booming.
But as we celebrate what is happening at the highest levels of women’s sports, we should be asking how many girls will never discover what they are capable of because they never got the chance to play.
The sports access gap
According to the Women’s Sports Foundation’s inaugural WSF Sport Report, more than half (54%) of girls ages eight to 18 who have never played organized sports say they want to.
Somewhere among those girls is a child who could discover the sport she loves. A future captain. A coach. An Olympian. Maybe even a champion. Most will never become professional athletes, nor should that determine whether their opportunity mattered. Sports can shape health outcomes, confidence, leadership, and a sense of belonging that lasts well after competition ends.
But none of us can know what sports might unlock in a girl until she gets the opportunity to find out.
As a Women’s Sports Foundation Trustee, I care deeply about what happens long before an athlete reaches the world’s biggest stages. That is why the foundation’s new research feels so important at this moment. Our findings show us where women’s sports are thriving, where barriers remain, and where we need to focus next.
One of the biggest takeaways is the disconnect between girls’ interest and their opportunity to play. Girls want to participate, but too many still are not getting into the game. And the WSF’s report reveals that when they do, families are spending more on their sports than they are on boys’. The question is not whether girls are interested. It is whether we are creating enough opportunities for that interest to become participation.
And getting girls into sports is only the beginning. We have to give them reasons to stay.
The report also points to a belonging gap that is evident among teens. Among the youngest children, 80% of both girls and boys say sports are “for someone like me.” Among teens, girls are less likely than boys to say the same.
Girls do not need to be convinced that sports are for them when they are eight. We need to make sure that, as pressures mount during the teen years, the sports environment does not give them reasons to question whether they still belong.
What opportunity can unlock
I know personally what can happen when a girl gets that first opportunity.
I started running track around 12 years old. There was no grand plan that I would become a professional athlete or an Olympic champion. I was a kid who got the chance to try something, discovered what I was capable of, and had people around me who gave that interest room to grow.
That opportunity ultimately took me to Harvard, where I competed and studied neurobiology and global health, and eventually to the Olympic podium. Along the way, sports helped shape not only the athlete I became, but the person I became and the possibilities I saw for my life beyond the track.
Every girl deserves the opportunity to find out where hers might lead.
No athlete makes that journey alone. Behind every woman competing inside the world’s biggest arenas are years of access, coaching, resources, and people who reinforced that she belonged.
And that path matters at every level. Industry leaders surveyed for the WSF Sport Report overwhelmingly see progress at the professional level. But the picture changes at college, the only part of the pipeline where more say progress has declined than improved.
That contrast should get our attention.
Protecting the path forward
College sports are a critical bridge to professional and Olympic competition. As college athletics undergo historic changes to athlete compensation, revenue sharing, and name, image, and likeness opportunities, decisions being made now will help determine who benefits from this new era.
We cannot celebrate the destination while allowing the road to it to narrow.
And at a moment of such significant change, the WSF Sport Report points to a troubling disconnect around one of the protections that helped make today’s opportunities possible. More than five decades after Title IX helped transform sports for girls and women, 79% of girls surveyed have never heard of it. More than half of their parents haven’t either.
Opportunity can be inherited, but the knowledge of how it was won cannot be assumed. Without that knowledge, how can the next generation protect the rights they may not even know they have?
That lack of awareness is especially striking when nearly half of the industry leaders surveyed for the report identify Title IX rollbacks or weakened enforcement as the greatest threat to continued progress for girls and women in sports.
Our responsibility is not simply to benefit from the doors that have been opened. It is to make sure they remain open, and to open more for the girls coming behind us.
For decades, women athletes were asked to prove that investment in their sports could work. They have. Now, we have the chance to build on that success for the next generation.
That means creating a sports culture where more girls can get in the game, find a place where they belong, understand their rights, and discover where sports might take them.
The greatest legacy of this moment will not only be how far women’s sports have come. It will be how we work together to give more girls the chance to find out how far they can go.

====================================================================================================

Childhood war exposure might shift the neural correlates of attachment-related anxiety and avoidance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

Growing up in a war zone is linked to differences in how a child’s family environment relates to their brain connectivity, a new study suggests. Published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, the research indicates that the link between a child’s attachment-related characteristics and the communication between emotional brain regions differs depending on war-related stress. The findings provide evidence that severe environmental unpredictability is tied to different patterns of neural connectivity, raising the speculative possibility that the developing brain calibrates to its surroundings rather than simply sustaining uniform damage.
Neuroscientists have established that early adversity is linked to altered wiring between emotional hubs and the brain networks responsible for self-control. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that childhood adversity was associated with accelerated decreases in functional connectivity between cortical and subcortical brain regions. These specific neural changes were linked to fewer internalizing symptoms but lower academic performance. Additionally, a 2017 study found that in adult women, a history of childhood stress was linked to altered resting communication between the amygdala and prefrontal regions that regulate emotion.
Building on this foundation, developmental theories predicted that extreme stress recalibrates how attachment and brain systems interact. The authors of a 2011 theoretical paper proposed that harsh, unpredictable environments prompt the developing brain to recalibrate how a child’s stress responses and attachment styles adapt to their surroundings. Applying these ideas to extreme stress, a 2019 study of children growing up near war zones found that chronic adversity is associated with differences in how early caregiving relationships shape empathy-related brain responses.
The new study directly tests this moderation model by examining how a child’s attachment characteristics relate differently to their brain connectivity in the context of war exposure. The research was led by Sarit Roizman and Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus, an associate professor in the Educational Neuroimaging Group at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology. They focused on resting-state functional connectivity, which measures how different brain areas communicate with one another when a person is awake but not focused on a specific task.
“We know that chronic, unpredictable stress in childhood is a major risk factor for later anxiety and mood problems, but we know much less about how it gets ‘under the skin’ in the developing brain,” Horowitz-Kraus told PsyPost. “When the war began on October 7, 2023, our lab was in the middle of an ongoing brain-imaging study of Israeli children. This gave us a rare, if painful, opportunity to compare children scanned during the war with children of similar ages scanned before it.”
“The caregiving environment is the child’s first line of defense against stress, so rather than asking whether war simply makes children’s brains ‘different,’ we asked a more specific question: does living through war change how attachment-related characteristics in the family relate to the brain systems that link thinking and emotion?” she added.
To understand these mechanisms, the researchers recruited 79 children between the ages of 5 and 13. The participants were divided into two groups based on when they were assessed. The war-exposed group included 42 children who lived in Israel and were evaluated between October 2023 and December 2024, during an active period of war. The non-exposed comparison group consisted of 37 children who were assessed prior to the war, between 2021 and August 2023.
All children underwent a resting-state brain scan using magnetic resonance imaging. To help the children stay still in the scanner, they watched abstract visual patterns without sound. Parents completed detailed questionnaires to assess different aspects of the child’s life and behavior. This included a measure of executive functions to track everyday difficulties with memory, organization, and self-control.
Parents also completed a questionnaire assessing attachment-related anxiety, such as worrying about abandonment, and attachment-related avoidance, such as preferring not to share deep feelings. For the war-exposed group, parents filled out a specialized survey tallying the family’s exposure to war-related events. This survey asked how often the family heard air raid sirens, experienced disruptions to their daily routines, or dealt with the absence of a caregiver due to military reserve duty.
The researchers found that the two groups did not differ in their overall levels of attachment-related anxiety or avoidance. Initially, the war-exposed children seemed to have more difficulties with executive functions, but this difference was not statistically significant once the researchers adjusted for nonverbal intelligence and the timing of the assessments. The actual group differences emerged in how the children’s brains were wired in relation to their attachment characteristics.
“War did not produce a single, uniform effect on children,” Horowitz-Kraus noted. “What differed was how attachment related to how the child’s brain is wired, which may have long-term effects.”
In both groups, children showed a range of attachment-related difficulties, but the neural patterns associated with those difficulties differed entirely depending on whether the child was exposed to war. In the war-exposed group, higher levels of attachment anxiety and avoidance were associated with moderately reduced communication between the cingulate cortex and the amygdala, two key structures that process emotional reactions. In the non-exposed group, the exact same attachment difficulties were associated with a different pattern: moderately reduced connectivity between the amygdala and the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory formation.
“What really struck me, which I shouldn’t be surprised about after twenty years of researching this phenomenon, is how behavior is translated into brain function- the anxiety was seen in children’s altered brain function,” Horowitz-Kraus explained. “Within each group, the associations between attachment and emotion-related connectivity were moderate to fairly strong,” she added.
Additionally, the researchers examined communication between large-scale brain networks, such as the default mode network, which is active during internal thought, and the salience network, which detects important emotional or sensory cues. They found indications that the relationship between attachment difficulties and large-scale network communication actually reversed depending on how much war-related exposure a child’s family reported. At lower levels of exposure, attachment difficulties were linked to negative or reduced communication between these networks. At higher levels of exposure, the association flipped, becoming positive. While the overall interaction between exposure and attachment was statistically robust, the specific shifting patterns at each level of exposure did not pass strict statistical thresholds, meaning they should be interpreted with caution.
“This is evidence that should guide further research,” Horowitz-Kraus said. “It cannot be used to diagnose or predict outcomes for any individual child but definitely triggers additional questions related to how different levels of exposure are related to parent-child relations and what the long-term effect would be- we are focusing on these questions these days.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that an individual’s attachment style predicts how their brain’s emotion and cognitive control networks respond to relational experiences and perceived threats. The new results build on this concept, highlighting that extreme environmental stressors like war are tied to complex shifts in how family attachment characteristics and a child’s brain networks relate to one another.
“In other words, similar relational profiles may rest on different brain mechanisms depending on the environment a child is growing up in,” Horowitz-Kraus pointed out. “That matters for how we assess and support children in times of crisis, and it points to caregiver–child relationships and emotional co-regulation as a promising target for support.”
The comparison group, assessed before the official onset of the war, cannot be considered entirely free from stress, as children living in the region may have experienced varying levels of environmental adversity prior to October 2023. Because the two groups were assessed at different time periods, it is difficult to completely separate the effects of war exposure from broader changes that occurred over time.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “Please don’t read this as ‘war damages children’s brains,'” Horowitz-Kraus emphasized. “One speculative possibility is that these patterns reflect the developing brain calibrating to an unpredictable environment rather than a deficit, but our data cannot tell adaptation apart from vulnerability.”
The study design captures a single snapshot in time, meaning it provides evidence for associations but cannot confirm that war exposure directly causes these brain changes. The researchers also relied on parent-reported questionnaires rather than directly observing parent-child interactions or conducting clinical psychological evaluations. The study did not measure symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, or depression in the children or their parents.
It is possible that the mental health of the parents, who were also experiencing the stress of war, influenced both the children’s brain development and the parents’ responses on the questionnaires. “We are also interested to know if some aspect of children’s characteristics can serve as ‘protecting’ factors- helping some children to be less affected by these adverse events,” the researcher noted.
“The most important next step is longitudinal research that follows these children and others over time, to see whether these brain–behavior patterns predict later emotional and cognitive outcomes and how they change as circumstances stabilize,” Horowitz-Kraus said. “Ultimately, we hope this work will inform interventions that strengthen caregiver–child co-regulation to help buffer children against the effects of prolonged stress.”
“This study complements our related work showing that war-related stress is associated with differences in cognitive-control and sensory network connectivity in children,” she added. “I’m deeply grateful to the families who took part in research during such a difficult period, and to the Diane and Guilford Glazer Foundation for funding this work.”
The study, “War-related exposure moderates the association between attachment-related characteristics and cognitive–limbic functional connectivity in children: an fMRI study,” was authored by Sarit Roizman, Rola Farah, Ayelet Elor, Dror Kraus, Mika Rotman, Noga Gal, and Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus.

Abdi says seeking to make Kurdish an official language in Syria

Breadcrumb
Efforts continuing to make Kurdish an official language in Syria, says Abdi
Syrian presidency adviser and former leader of the now-defunct Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi has said efforts were continuing to make Kurdish an official language in the country, stressing that it represented the community’s identity.
Abdi said developing and teaching Kurdish as a mother tongue was a central part of the Kurdish people’s struggle, as debate continues in northeastern Syria over the future of education and the language of instruction amid efforts to integrate educational institutions into the state system.
The issue has taken on added significance following months of fighting between Damascus and the SDF earlier this year, which saw government forces regain control of around two-thirds of the territory previously held by the Kurdish-led group. The SDF was subsequently dissolved in August as Kurdish-administered areas began to be integrated into the Syrian state.
Abdi was appointed an adviser to the Syrian presidency by President Ahmed al-Sharaa following the SDF’s dissolution. Sharaa also signed a decree recognising Kurdish as a "national" language, but this is not the same as making it an official language.
The decree meant that Kurdish could be taught as a subject in Kurdish-majority areas of the country.
Abdi's comments came after classes were suspended at several Kurdish-language schools in northeastern Syria amid demands that all subjects be taught in Kurdish, rather than limiting Kurdish instruction to three lessons a week, according to local teachers.
In a video message, Abdi said "learning in one’s mother tongue is a natural right," noting that significant efforts had been made over the past 14 years to provide education in Kurdish in Syria.
He described Kurdish-language education as a "historic step" and said efforts would continue to make Kurdish an official language in Syria. He also urged families to send their children to schools where Kurdish is taught.
Abdi said "we must continue our education" as northeastern Syria goes through a transitional period, adding that Kurdish-language teaching in preparatory and secondary schools would continue under curricula adopted by the autonomous administration.
Kurdish-language teacher Adel al-Sayed, from Qamishli in Hasakah province, told The New Arab that students he had spoken to preferred all school subjects to be taught in Kurdish, while having no objection to learning other languages, including Arabic.
He said some students who had spent 12 years studying in Kurdish and were preparing to enter university could be particularly affected because they did not speak Arabic fluently. He added that they had welcomed Abdi’s call to continue attending Kurdish-language schools.
Teacher Bahar Bublani, also from Qamishli, said schools across northeastern Syria and the rest of the country began the academic year on 6 September, but classes were suspended at several schools in the Jazira region that use Kurdish as their language of instruction.
She said protests in the region had called for all subjects to be taught in Kurdish rather than limiting instruction to three classes, adding that students and their families remained committed to Kurdish-language education while supporting the teaching of Arabic and other languages.
The future of higher education has also emerged as part of efforts to reorganise educational institutions in the region.
