Press review: EU may tighten Ukraine aid oversight as US, Iran explore nuclear compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. The EU is considering stricter monitoring of aid to Ukraine amid corruption scandals; Washington and Tehran are seeking a nuclear compromise involving sanctions relief; and China supports possible trilateral talks between Putin, Xi, and Trump at the APEC summit. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: EU weighs tighter oversight of Ukraine aid amid corruption scandals and rising costs
The European Union is discussing new mechanisms to track how financial assistance allocated to Ukraine is spent, although its ability to do so is limited, members of the European Parliament told Izvestia. To date, EU countries have provided Kiev with 224.5 bln euros, while part of a new package of 90 bln euros could be released ahead of schedule. Against this backdrop, calls within the bloc for stricter oversight of how the funds are used are intensifying. They have been fueled by corruption scandals in Ukraine, including those involving the energy and defense sectors.
Discussions in Brussels about tightening oversight of how this assistance is spent are intensifying, European Parliament member Fernand Kartheiser told Izvestia. "As far as I know, there has not yet been a public discussion on the issue. However, I suspect that such discussions are taking place. In some EU countries, leading politicians are already openly calling for tighter control over financial flows to Ukraine," the politician stressed.
Brussels already has certain mechanisms for exercising oversight. Under the Ukraine Facility program, payments are tied to Kiev’s implementation of agreed reforms, while the Ukrainian side is required to report on expenditures and the ultimate recipients of the funds.
Brussels has pledged to tighten monitoring of new financial assistance to Kiev, although the effectiveness of such measures has been called into question, Slovak member of the European Parliament Milan Uhrik told Izvestia.
"The European Union is preparing to send tens of billions more for Ukraine’s military needs, while Brussels is promising ever greater oversight of how this money is spent. But European taxpayers have heard these promises before and many simply no longer believe them. More money, more military commitments, and more risks, while the question of accountability remains unresolved," he said.
Further increases in assistance to Kiev are already sparking disagreements within the European Parliament, MEP Petar Volgin said. According to him, European governments should give priority to the security of their own countries rather than continue increasing support for Kiev.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: US, Iran explore nuclear compromise as sanctions remain key bargaining chip
The United States and Iran held another round of indirect negotiations, the second since the start of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. According to US media reports, during the latest contacts, the American side offered Tehran a series of concessions involving sanctions relief and the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad in exchange for concessions on nuclear energy. Sources say the Iranian side showed flexibility during the consultations. Donald Trump, however, has publicly denied that such talks are taking place at all, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes.
According to Axios sources, during the latest contacts, the American side expressed its willingness to ease comprehensive sanctions against Iran and unfreeze its funds abroad in exchange for specific steps by the Islamic Republic to limit its nuclear program. Washington, meanwhile, believes it is negotiating from a position of strength.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continues to grow, while the blockade and sanctions continue to erode Iran’s position, a US source told Axios, adding that the US needs assurances that Iran is serious.
CNN sources confirmed that during consultations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the Iranian delegation signaled that it was "flexible on nuclear issues."
Bloomberg, however, offered a more modest assessment, noting that Tehran and Washington made only limited progress during the indirect negotiations in New York. According to the news agency, Iranian officials privately expressed pessimism about the prospects of reaching an agreement to end the conflict with Washington and restart operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has warned that continued pressure on Iran will only aggravate the situation for its neighbors. "In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either. If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe," Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said.
Izvestia: China backs potential Putin-Xi-Trump talks on global security, regional conflicts
Talks between the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States at the APEC summit would be important for shaping a multipolar world, Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui told Izvestia. The Kremlin confirmed that Vladimir Putin plans to attend the organization’s summit, which will be held in Shenzhen in November. Donald Trump also plans to attend the forum. According to experts, if the opportunity arises, the leaders could discuss the development of a new security architecture as well as regional issues, including the Ukraine conflict and the Taiwan crisis.
According to Zhang Hanhui, Moscow, Beijing, and Washington should coordinate their efforts on economic and security issues, since no single country is capable of resolving global challenges on its own.
"All countries should follow the example set by us, China and Russia, in how to build relations between neighboring countries and between major powers. And we will work together to make our contribution to the development of the economy, the global economy, and to maintaining peace and stability throughout the world," Zhang concluded.
The main focus of potential talks would be the transformation of the global security system and the broader world order, according to Konstantin Blokhin, leading researcher at the Center for Security Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences. Russia, China, and the United States remain the world’s three key players, he told Izvestia. No crisis can be resolved without their participation, something even American analysts recognize.
The leaders could also discuss regional conflicts. According to Blokhin, the Ukraine issue would almost certainly be discussed at the meeting. China could offer its mediation services, although the United States would most likely view such an initiative skeptically. The White House would see China’s active involvement in the peace process as a capitulation on its own part.
Vedomosti: US expands Pentagon role in protecting midterms from foreign interference
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth issued a memorandum overnight on September 29 instructing his department to deploy all the resources of the government to protect election infrastructure from interference by "foreign adversaries." Under the directive, US Cyber Command and combat support forces will concentrate their efforts on identifying and neutralizing foreign interference in US democratic processes. Experts interviewed by Vedomosti argue that greater Pentagon involvement could create organizational problems that Trump might use to attribute election difficulties to foreign actors.
Back in 2016, the US administration of then-Democratic President Barack Obama claimed that Moscow had allegedly interfered in the US election in an effort to support Trump’s candidacy. Now, the Trump administration itself is seeking to highlight concerns about potential threats surrounding the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, which will determine the composition of Congress for the next two years, Vedomosti writes.
Observers and commentators at US media outlets, including CNN, CBS, the Republican-leaning Fox News, The New York Times, and The Wall Street Journal, regard this as a deliberate Trump strategy in light of what they see as the likely election results - according to the Cook Political Report forecast, Republicans could lose both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon is not capable of rigging the election in favor of Republicans, but the department’s increased involvement could create organizational problems, Igor Shkrobtak, senior researcher at the Department of Military and Political Studies at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies told Vedomosti. In his view, President Trump, if necessary, would be able to find someone to blame for any difficulties in conducting the vote, whether Russia, China, North Korea, or Iran.
Trump knows that after the 2026 midterm elections, it will not only become much more difficult for him to carry out his agenda, but the influential positions of his "clan" within the Republican Party will also come under threat, according to Vladimir Vasilyev, chief researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences. The expert considers it likely that Trump could use any available means to "disrupt" the elections, up to and including the imposition of martial law. "The American political system is on the verge of its most serious test," Vasilyev said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Asian coking coal shortage boosts demand for Russian supplies
A growing shortage of metallurgical, or coking, coal in Asian markets is driving greater interest in Russian supplies. According to NEFT Research data as of September 6, Grade Zh coking coal was priced at $176 per metric ton on an FOB Far East basis, meaning the price at the port of shipment, up 2.9% over the week and 32.3% since the beginning of the year. Experts polled by Rossiyskaya Gazeta expect the Asian coking coal market to undergo a structural shift as demand patterns change, with prices for the most sought-after grades potentially increasing 20-30% by 2029.
Alexander Kotov, consulting partner at NEFT Research, told the newspaper he expects that prices for the most sought-after grades of coking coal could rise by 20-30% from current levels through 2029, with the market set to undergo a structural transformation over the next three years as the geography of demand in Asia changes.
The current price increase may be driven by a slowdown in Chinese production due to stringent environmental inspections at mines following the accident at the Liushenyu mine in late May, strong demand from India, and production problems among key exporters in Australia. There, even a slight worsening of weather conditions during the rainy season, which runs from November through February, can disrupt supplies.
Russian metallurgical coal shipments to China are expected to total around 32-34 mln metric tons in 2026, while Russia’s overall exports of all types of coal to China could decline to 80-85 mln metric tons. According to Alexander Kotov, China currently accounts for more than 60% of Russia’s coking coal exports.
Coking coal production in Russia increased by 3.6% in June. In addition to China, the key market, India continues to show strong interest in metallurgical raw materials. According to forecasts, India will increase purchases to 89 mln metric tons by 2027 and 104 mln metric tons by 2030, compared with 76 mln metric tons last year.

Sohlberg sets Central Elections Committee hearing on Likud petition against Fly&Vote initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Central Elections Committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg has set an October 6 hearing on the Likud petition concerning AID Coalition’s Fly&Vote initiative, which helps Israelis living abroad arrange travel to Israel to vote.
In a decision issued Tuesday, Sohlberg ordered the parties to submit additional factual and legal information about the initiative’s activities, the services it offers and the payments it collects.
The additional responses are due by October 4 at 4 p.m. The hearing is scheduled for October 6 at 1 p.m. at the Knesset.
Sohlberg ordered AID Coalition to explain differences between its response to the petition and information published on the Fly&Vote website. It must detail the nature of each service listed on the site, the sequence in which it is provided and whether it is currently being offered.
He also ordered the organization to explain precisely what it called a “donation constituting an advance payment” in its response to the petition.
Sohlberg further instructed Likud and AID Coalition to address whether the CEC chairman has the authority to issue an injunction against a person or corporation outside Israel over activity conducted abroad. The attorney-general was ordered to submit her position on the same question.
AID Coalition aims to preserve 'democratic foundations of the State of Israel'
AID Coalition describes itself as a US-based “non-partisan, non-affiliated” organization whose mission is to strengthen and preserve “the democratic foundations of the State of Israel.” Its website lists projects supporting victims and communities affected by October 7, as well as collaborations with Israeli pro-democracy groups during the protest period before the attack.
Fly&Vote seeks to help Israelis living abroad participate in the October 27 election. The initiative says it helps users check their eligibility to vote, handle passport and documentation issues and find or book flights to Israel. Its website also advertises organized flights from major cities.
AID Coalition says participants bear their own travel costs and that it does not ask how they intend to vote or condition its assistance on their political views.
Likud allege links between AID Coalition and partisan activity
Likud petitioned the CEC earlier this month, naming AID Coalition and several other respondents. They include the Israeli Base nonprofit; three individuals; the Democrats party; the attorney-general; and the State Comptroller’s Office.
Israeli Base’s website describes it as a development of AID Coalition. AID Coalition has separately said that the Israeli organization is an independent and distinct entity.
The petition alleges links among AID Coalition, Israeli Base and political activity intended to weaken support for the Likud. It argues that the services or benefits offered through the initiatives may amount to prohibited election benefits or election bribery and may be subject to election-propaganda and party-financing laws.
The petition also addresses Fly&AID, a separate AID Coalition initiative offering participants a “service grant” of $250 for each day of volunteer activity in Israel, for up to three days.
In his decision, Sohlberg ordered Likud to state whether, following AID Coalition’s response, it agrees to remove the claims concerning Fly&AID. He also asked whether the party agrees to remove Israeli Base, the three individual respondents and the Democrats from the case in light of their responses.
AID Coalition rejected Likud’s allegations.
“We received the Likud’s petition, which seeks to deny Israeli citizens - those who boarded planes to fight on October 7, who pay taxes and are involved in the life of their homeland - the right and duty to take part in determining the future of the State of Israel,” it said.

How Israeli Checkpoints Choke Palestinian Life in the Occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

How Israeli checkpoints suffocate Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank.
Illustration: Hokyoung Kim
The Big Story
Sep 30, 2026 6:00 AM
Lama Rabah
Sabrina Slipchenko
Charles Boutaud
Firas Tawil
Elena DeBre
Choke Points
Lost time. Lost jobs. Lost friends. Lost family. Lost lives. How Israeli checkpoints suffocate Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank.
Illustration: Hokyoung Kim
The Big Story
Sep 30, 2026 6:00 AM
Lama Rabah
Sabrina Slipchenko
Charles Boutaud
Firas Tawil
Elena DeBre
Aref Jaber is on a neighbor's roof, trying to get home.
At 51, he is clambering over a wall into the next backyard, up onto the next roof, along the line of stone houses that stand between him and his own front door. He has no choice. Alleys and side streets in his neighborhood have been sealed with cement blocks and barbed wire, and a single point of access, called Checkpoint 160, is the only way in or out for the 140 families who live there.
But Checkpoint 160 is closed again; Jaber is not sure why. The whim of a soldier, a crash in the scanning system, breaking news in the region—it could be anything.
For the last three years, he says, this has happened at least two days a week. So the community has devised a system of alternative routes. Jaber calls his neighbors to ask if he can come through. They check their windows for soldiers, and then Jaber scales ladders and traverses roofs. “When I finally get home,” he says, “it feels like I’ve achieved something monumental.”
The enclosure of Jaber’s neighborhood is a dense microcosm of what life is becoming across the occupied West Bank—for Palestinians, that is. At the same time that deadly Israeli settler violence robs communities in the West Bank of their land, and amid the genocide in Gaza, Israel has expanded its infrastructures of military control and domination.
Since 2023, Israel’s fragmentation of Palestine, underway for generations, has accelerated. The West Bank has, for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians who live there, ceased to exist as a contiguous territory. According to the most recent UN data from December 2025, at least 925 fixed and temporary checkpoints, metal gates, roadblocks, and earth mounds divide the West Bank. (A Palestinian governmental commission reported this month that the number is now 942.) This fracturing has torn families apart, stifled the economy, and obstructed access to essential services such as hospitals and schools.
Aref Jaber climbs onto the roof of a neighbor's home to get to the street in the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Israel has never publicly listed the checkpoints it operates, their staffing hours, or their closure times. On the ground, Google Maps is practically useless for Palestinians; it is blind to the checkpoints and tries to route drivers onto roads reserved for Israeli-plated cars. Instead, citizens have developed their own ad hoc networks to inform each other of closures.
As far as we know, no organization has used that network—combined with new datasets and on-the-ground reporting—to measure what this does to daily life.
Over 18 months, WIRED, Lighthouse Reports, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ) and the Palestine Reporting Lab investigated the system that has carved the West Bank into cantons and measured what it cost people to move through it.
We analyzed tens of thousands of Telegram messages Palestinians sent to navigate daily checkpoint delays and closures
Working with the Institute for Social and Economic Progress (ISEP), a Palestinian research organization, we polled hundreds of people across the West Bank to find out how checkpoints shape their lives.

The number of movement obstacles in the West Bank rose by more in the past three years than it did over the previous 18.
Obstacles in 2023
Obstacles added 2023-2025
The average West Bank commuter—someone who drives several times a week—loses about an hour and a half each week to additional travel time in an effort to avoid checkpoints. Over the course of a year, that amounts to 77 hours lost.
For some, the delays are far longer. People going from Ramallah to Al-Eizariya, on the edges of Jerusalem, could do so in 27 kilometers/48 minutes. Instead, it's 45 kilometers/100 minutes.
Our data shows that people have to take all sorts of complex routes to avoid checkpoints.
Using the median route taken in our dataset, someone who commutes back and forth four days a week would lose nearly seven hours in additional travel time every week.
Anyone who commutes four days a week from Ramallah to Hebron is robbed of over 12 extra hours of travel time.
One pair of towns, Anabta and Beit Lid, are 8 kilometers apart.
It used to be a 10 minute drive. It now routinely takes 50 minutes each way.
Our data analysis found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent in the aftermath of October 2023, frequently exceeding hours at a time.
Together, Palestinians in the West Bank lose about 30 years every day.
Data can count the checkpoints, clock the closures, and tally the hours lost at the gates. But how does the system upend the life of a single family?
Losing Access to an Education
More than a decade ago, Amal and her family left the US. They moved back to a home in Al-Janiya, where they built a house with a garden, and a mountain view. “Mashallah,” she says of it still. (The names have been changed due to safety concerns.)
By the time the family arrived, Al-Janiya's main entrance had already been closed for over a decade. Israel sealed the eastern road in 2003; it now serves as an entrance to Talmon, an Israeli settlement built on the village's land.
The only way in or out of Al-Janiya that Amal's family has ever used runs west, through the neighboring village of Ras Karkar. Fifteen minutes down that road is her husband's shop in Ramallah.
A little further on, a local university, where her daughter Lina studies software engineering.
With open roads, Lina's commute could be around 12 kilometers/20 minutes.
With the detour because of a checkpoint, it became 32 kilometers/47 minutes.
Amal’s eldest, Dana, went farthest, to another university to study dentistry. She is set to be the first doctor in the family.
Dana's commute should be around 35.5 kilometers/47 minutes. It is now often a 90-minute drive.
AL JANIYA
RAS KARKAR
RAMALLAH
BIRZEIT UNIVERSITY
AL QUDS UNIVERSITY
Every day that Dana and Lina drive to their universities, they each lose about an hour on the circuitous route and at checkpoints. Over the course of an academic year, they have lost about three days each due to the detours.
“You loop and loop and end up at the same point… I swear, I get dizzy… By the time you arrive, you're just sad. You sit there asking yourself: what is this life?” Amal said. "You can take it once. Twice. For a year. Then it crosses some limit and you can’t.”
Thirty percent of people in the West Bank said that checkpoints have prevented them from starting or completing a university education. Most students living outside major cities cross at least one checkpoint on the shortest route to their nearest university.
Last summer, Amal's family decided they couldn’t spend another academic year in Al-Janiya, and they moved near Ramallah. “We grieve leaving our village,” Amal said, “but it’s not really a choice.”
They join more than one in ten people in the West Bank who say they’ve moved to other cities or regions because of checkpoints, along with 31 percent who say they’re considering moving for the same reason.
An Inheritance of Loss
Roads that once tied Palestine together have been closed off again and again, first by militarized borders and barriers, then by permits, and finally by hundreds of checkpoints.
Khalil Tufakji, a Palestinian cartographer and expert on Israeli settlements, has watched Israel assemble this system for decades. The purpose of checkpoints is the fragmentation of space, he said—“every city closes in on itself”—and in this way, the homeland shrinks to a city.
The system that confines Palestinians was built in layers. Under British colonial rule, Palestinian communities were at times subjected to roadblocks, systemic and capricious searches, border barriers, and a system of permits that restricted who could move by vehicle across the territory.
In 1948, in what is known as the “Nakba” or “catastrophe,” Zionist forces expelled more than 750,000 Palestinians from their homes. Hundreds of villages were depopulated or destroyed, and people were driven into exile.
Those who remained were placed under Israeli military rule for the next 18 years, forbidden to work, trade, study, or seek medical care beyond their towns without an Israeli permit.
In 1967, when Israel seized the remaining Palestinian territories, it reconstructed the same permit system there. Palestinians were sorted into categories, the color of an ID card determining who may go where.
In 1988, UN Special Committee reports classified the closing of areas in the occupied territories as collective punishment.
In 1995, the Oslo Process resumed. It was meant to lead to the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state. Instead, it further fragmented Palestinians by dividing the West Bank into administrative islands.
By the early 2000s, this system of closures and permits had become the status quo. In 2002, Israel started building the 713-kilometers-long separation wall, 85 percent of which runs through the West Bank.
And since 2007, Israel has imposed a blockade on Gaza, isolating it from the rest of Palestine.
In the years that followed, the restrictions intensified.

2026
This has meant that every generation of Palestinians since 1948 has inherited a smaller world than the one before it. Grandparents in Jenin, a city in the northern West Bank, tell stories about driving to have lunch in Jerusalem or a weekend in Beirut.
Parents from West Bank towns mention visiting Gaza. Their children remember school trips to Jericho's ancient sites, to an amusement park in Tulkarm and to the zoo in Qalqilya. Most people in the West Bank today have never been to Gaza, according to the ISEP poll. Over 40 percent of respondents said they had never seen the sea, though from high points, in places like Ramallah, you can see it in the distance.
A Palestinian family on the beach of Gaza on August 25, 1997.PHOTOGRAPH: ANTOINE GYORI/GETTY IMAGES
Today, people in the West Bank are living through another period of fragmentation. Three-quarters of those living in the West Bank have close relatives in other governorates. A quarter of parents said their children have never met close relatives who live in other parts of the West Bank. A generation is being locked in: Nearly a third of people under the age of 25 say they’ve never even left their own governorate.
In response to WIRED’s questions, the Israeli Military said, “Decisions regarding the placement of roadblocks, their opening or closing, are made in accordance with operational situation assessments and security considerations alone.” It is a policy that is “continuously adjusted according to the situational assessment on the ground, while balancing the residents’ ability to move freely throughout the area and security needs.”
In a letter addressed to Israel’s Central Command and top military officials, as reported by the newspaper Haaretz in June, the legal adviser to the Israeli military, Colonel Cobi Marcus, advised that the current system of checkpoints and movement obstacles has intensified beyond any legal justification. Haaretz reported he “warned” that since October 2023, the proliferation of movement restrictions, imposed on residents without authorization, may violate basic rights and the principles of international law.
Rema Hammami, an anthropologist at Birzeit University who has researched checkpoints, calls the current situation unprecedented. “Every single community, village, every single Palestinian city is going to be a separate prison. And if there's no pushback on it, they’re just going to keep going forward with it.”
There have been military checkpoints in other parts of the world, like Sri Lanka and Iraq. But Hammami says nowhere compares to the "density, scope, and comprehensiveness” of the system in the West Bank.
A Family Split
Route 60 was part of Reem Yassin’s life for six years. It’s the West Bank's central highway and the main road connecting Ramallah, the West Bank’s political hub, with Nablus, the commercial center of the north.
Yassin was the senior resident anesthesiologist at An-Najah National University Hospital, a leading medical facility in Nablus, which is 45 kilometers away from her home in Ramallah, in the central West Bank.
Yassin says the drive took her around 40 minutes in 2020, when she began her residency—an annoying but manageable commute. After October 2023, the Israeli military erected an additional three checkpoints on the most direct route between Ramallah and Nablus, and she says existing checkpoints began to close far more frequently.
When she gave birth to her first daughter, Yara, she would drop the baby off at her parents house in ’Asirah al-Qibliyah, a village south of Nablus, which meant she had to pass through a different checkpoint, Al-Muraba’ah, off Route 60.
Data analysis shows that since October 2023, Al-Muraba’ah has been one of the most congested checkpoints in the West Bank, often becoming a chokepoint as other routes into Nablus were closed. It would routinely take drivers 20 to 30 minutes to cross, but delays of several hours weren’t uncommon.
To make it work, Yassin would pack the night before, like she was catching a long flight: snacks, a breast pump, clothes for herself and for Yara. She would leave the Ramallah apartment in the dark, before 6 am, to drop Yara in 'Asirah before crossing Al-Muraba’ah.
"I didn't have a life anymore," she says. "I’d go to work and see my daughter for an hour at night. The rest of the time was at the checkpoint." She is one of a third of West Bank parents who say that checkpoints regularly prevent them from seeing their children during their waking hours.
The patterns are unpredictable. One moment, cars pass the checkpoint without much delay; at another, it can take hours. Events that should have little bearing on West Bank mobility can suddenly trigger a lockdown. On June 13 and 14, 2025, when Israel began bombing Iran, about 70 percent of checkpoints were suddenly closed, according to our analysis of Telegram data, an almost 350 percent increase from the week before.
Alexandra Rijke, a cultural geographer who spent years researching checkpoints in the West Bank, calls unpredictability one of the occupation's core mechanisms. Not knowing whether you can go to work or school, or what will get you punished, has a huge impact on people's lives. "Arbitrariness is incredibly violent," she said.
Across the West Bank, the roads between whole regions converge at a handful of checkpoints.
Their closure can divide north from south, force drivers away from their destination before they can turn back toward it, and leave an entire city dependent on a few guarded exits.
The Divide
Every journey we mapped from the southern West Bank toward the center and north narrowed to Wadi an-Nar.
The Divide
When its gates close, it cuts the West Bank in two.

The fastest road from Ramallah toward East Jerusalem and the southern West Bank passes through Jaba checkpoint.

The Enclosure

The Enclosure

Wadi an Nar
Yassin follows a protocol for crossing. Windows down before the soldiers ask. Then the script, which she can recite: "Hand over your ID. Where are you going, where are you coming from, what do you do?" Sometimes the soldier holds his phone up close and takes photos of her face with her ID and license plate. One time, she said, a soldier leaned in through the window: "You're beautiful," he said.
She often saw men pressed face-down against the hoods of their cars, hands behind their backs, the soldiers shouting. Sometimes, on her way back, the same men are still detained.
When asked, nearly two-thirds of people say humiliation or fear most characterize their feeling about checkpoints. Of people stopped at a checkpoint in the last six months, nearly 40 percent said their vehicle was searched by a soldier, and more than 20 percent said they were physically searched. About one in seven said a soldier had pointed a gun toward them.
Eventually, even dropping her daughter off in the morning stopped making sense. Yassin began staying at her parents' house near Nablus most nights. Her husband Montasir stayed in Ramallah and visited on some weekends. He usually left them Saturday morning, before the settler traffic on Route 60 picked up and checkpoints got worse.
As Yara grew older, she began to ask questions. When she opened her eyes in the morning, she’d ask: "Mama, why didn't you take us to Baba?" Then, because she already knew the answer, she’d say, "Is the road closed?"
In the end, the checkpoints proved too great a barrier for Yassin too. The move to her parents’ wasn’t enough. She was still losing hours at the checkpoint. After her second child was born earlier this year, Yassin decided not to go back to work. She extended her maternity leave and was weighing what comes next: a pause, a position closer to home if she can find one, perhaps something abroad. "I can't do it again," she said. Since then, Yassin has left her job at the hospital.
Deadly Delays
In the summer of July 2024, a young man from Reem Yassin’s village was shot by Israeli forces in the leg. The injury itself was not life threatening. But after soldiers held his ambulance at a checkpoint for almost an hour, he entered severe hemorrhagic shock, Yassin recalled.
Yassin, who was completing part of her medical residency at Rafidia Surgical Hospital in Nablus, was the doctor who received him. Recognized immediately by his family, she worked to stabilize him as his blood pressure plunged.
"We almost lost him," Yassin recalls. "We had to keep pumping blood into him." He survived, luckily, but his situation is far from unique: Nearly two-thirds of people in the West Bank say checkpoints have been a barrier to their access to medical care.
Between October 2023 and August 2026, the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) documented 237 access denials and 240 mission delays by Israeli forces. In early 2026, incidents included soldiers detaining a medical crew at the Sarra checkpoint, soldiers throwing an ambulance crew’s keys down a mountainside at Huwwara, and a Palestinian woman in labor being transferred between vehicles across locked gates. (In response to questions on medical delays, the Israeli Military said, “In accordance with international law, the IDF allows freedom of movement for medical vehicles, including ambulances, for the purpose of providing medical treatment and evacuating the wounded.”)
These delays carry fatal consequences. The Red Crescent attributes 25 deaths since 2023 to the obstruction of its medical teams. In July 2026, a Palestinian infant, Ahmad Zaid, died after Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint blocked the vehicle transporting him for more than an hour.
In response, the Red Crescent has begun bringing facilities to the people, building makeshift medical points inside villages since ambulances are now so often delayed and cannot reliably access hospitals. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) also started providing first aid training to medical and nonmedical volunteers so they can respond to urgent medical needs in cases when an ambulance is delayed or stopped at a checkpoint.
Sleeping at the Factory
After October 2023, delay times at checkpoints across Nablus spiked to levels beyond anywhere else in the West Bank. Commuters in Nablus spent an average of nearly an hour and 50 minutes avoiding checkpoints. Ali Haj Ali has worked at Sama Pharmaceuticals, a medicine factory east of Nablus city, for over a decade; now, at 37, he supervises the maintenance of the company’s production lines. When he leaves at the end of his shift at 4:30 pm, he has stopped expecting to reach his home before 8:00 pm, even though it’s only 16 kilometers away.
Some nights, he doesn't get home at all. He sleeps at the factory, in an arrangement Sama built during Covid-19: Two offices hold a bed and a dozen mattresses for whoever can’t make the trip home.
When checkpoints close, Sama’s employees sometimes have to sleep on site.PHOTOGRAPH: Lama Rabah
“My three kids, my wife, my mother, my father, I’d barely see them,” he said. “And forget about seeing friends.” But this is the best job he thinks he can find, so he keeps going.
On a recent afternoon, Ali sat in a room at Sama Pharmaceuticals, along with his colleague, Ohood Khatatbeh. In minutes, they were filling in the details for one another, recounting what they call “Nablus’ checkpoint crisis” in 2024 and 2025. Ali would sometimes reach the checkpoint, sit there for hours, then just turn around and go home.
"Nothing is guaranteed, that's just how it is here. It's like a lottery," Ali said.
Ohood, the factory’s quality assurance manager, is 38 years old, and the mother of three sons. Her town, Beit Furik, is southeast of Nablus. It has a single gate, in or out. Her whole day is dictated by that gate.
The town has had to come up with its own protocol, as Ohood calls it: For every three private cars, one shared taxi gets through. What they cannot control is the pace, interrupted by the soldiers’ change of shifts.
Best case, if the Beit Furik gate is open and traffic is moving freely, the drive home can take 15 minutes. But for a year and a half, it routinely took her more than 5 hours daily. On the worst day, it took 10 hours. In 2024, Ohood's teenage son had finished a final exam in biology at his school in Nablus just before she was finishing her shift. They found each other at the Beit Furik gate at 4:30 pm, in a line that packed the road several cars wide, all heading for the single entrance to a town of almost 16,000.
Ohood and her son waited in line together until 3 am the following morning.
"The regular employee, the one not separated from work by a checkpoint," she said, "would be home, eaten, showered, asleep, and already dreaming, while I'm still at the checkpoint."
Across the West Bank, checkpoints have begun to reshape how businesses like Sama operate. The company has started rejecting highly qualified candidates after assessing the checkpoints they would have to cross to get to work, Ohood said. It’s even started writing it into the job postings, as a requirement: Candidates must live in Nablus. About half of people polled said checkpoints have impacted their or their spouse’s ability to get a job.
In late 2025, Ohood’s one-week-old baby, Aws, came down with jaundice. She and her husband drove him out of town to the hospital. But on the way back, as she remembers it, they found the soldier already closing the gate.
"Go back," the soldier yelled in Arabic from the other side of the gate in Beit Furik.
"Go back where?" her husband asked. "We have a sick child with us."
The soldier raised his rifle and pointed it toward them. "For God's sake," Ohood told her husband, "let's just go back." He tried once more anyway, offering to turn around himself if the soldier would just let Ohood and the baby cross the gate on foot. The soldier lost his temper. "I'll shoot you," he said.
They turned around, the baby crying in their arms, and waited in line for an hour and a half until the soldier opened the gate again.
A Different World
By 2000, Aref Jaber says every road in and out of the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron, named after his family, was sealed with earth mounds and concrete slabs. By 2010, he says, iron gates were installed and checkpoints were manned by soldiers. Three years ago, new closures were installed on the very entrances to people's homes, and iron fencing was wrapped around the gates so no one could squeeze through.
The neighborhood sits between the Ibrahimi Mosque, the settlement outposts in the old city in Hebron, and the Kiryat Arba settlement, and has only one way in or out: a turnstile, an inspection room with digital scanning, a metal gate, and a military watchtower, called Checkpoint 160. It’s “as if we’re entering another country,” Jaber says of crossing it. Except the country on the other side is his own house.
For months after October 2023, Israeli forces imposed a curfew on the neighborhood every night, from 10 to 7 in the morning. Now it's every weekend, Aref said. From Friday afternoon until Sunday morning, the checkpoint is closed. No one in, no one out. Jaber says the people who die on Sundays are lucky, because you can bury them the same day. Die on a Saturday, and there is nothing to be done until the checkpoint opens again.
The Palestinians in the neighborhood need to wait for Israeli approval for things big and small: whether they want to evacuate a patient, hold a funeral, or bring in a canister of cooking gas. Locals cross the checkpoint on foot and climb the hill, carrying the sick, carrying groceries up to the neighborhood, dragging suitcases down toward the checkpoint. Jaber’s 6-year-old grandson should be able to go to the school 50 meters away. But it now sits behind an earth mound wrapped in barbed wire, and reaching it would mean a three-kilometer detour on foot, along settler-dominated roads. Jaber waves at his cousins, who live behind the same earth mound. "They have a whole different life there," he says. "We're in the closed zone."
Houses belonging to Palestinians who have been forced to leave them or use a different entrance by the Israeli Military and Israeli settlers are seen in the Jaber neighborhood of Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Even amid the unrelenting pressure of apartheid, people can still imagine a different life. On January 6, 2026, at around 3:00 pm, a Palestinian driver approached Wadi an-Nar, the checkpoint controlling the only road linking the north of the occupied West Bank to the south since 2000. He noticed something strange. No soldiers stood in the way. The checkpoint was open. He took out his phone, recorded a twenty-second video, and posted it in a local Telegram channel.
Within the hour, the clip spread through the West Bank. Everyone was confused. Did Israel remove its checkpoints? Was this really happening?
At 5:57, admins of the “Road Conditions” Telegram group were joking about crossing checkpoints off their lists.
At 6:10, the admins posted that the soldiers had returned. At 6:12, they said the gates were shut.
There was never an explanation. Some assumed it was a drill for Israeli forces. Others, simply a change of shifts. But for three hours, people allowed themselves to imagine a West Bank without checkpoints. A West Bank you can drive the full length of, 130 kilometers from north to south, in less than two hours.
And for a moment, they inhabited a world where they could plan the next day, the next hour. Where Amal’s daughters would reach their lecture halls in minutes. Where Reem wouldn't have to give up a job to keep her family together. Where Ali would walk through his front door before his son fell asleep. Where Ohood would take her baby to the hospital without a rifle raised at her. Where, perhaps, you just keep driving: to Haifa, to Gaza, anywhere you want.
And Aref Jaber would walk down his own street, past the ladders he no longer needs. He would open his front door, and be home.

Fewer California Republicans approve of Trump, poll says. That could hurt GOP midterm chances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Fewer California Republicans approve of Trump, poll says. That could hurt GOP midterm chances
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
With gas prices topping $6 a gallon and an unpopular war continuing in Iran, President Trump’s approval has slipped with California Republicans — a falloff that could diminish the party’s chances in the state’s few competitive congressional races.
A new poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, co-sponsored by The Times, found that 76% of Republican voters in the state approve of the president’s performance, down from 83% last year.
The president’s approval has softened even among those who still support his performance. Only 44% of Republicans in California said they strongly support Trump’s performance, down from 57% who said the same in August 2025.
That could translate into lower Republican turnout in the state’s few competitive races, said the poll’s director, Mark DiCamillo.
“Republicans are losing some of their enthusiasm in terms of being motivated to vote,” he said.
In addition, the more Trump tries to make the midterm elections about himself — such as the pro-Trump ads recently sponsored and paid for by the government — the more Democrats might be inclined to show up, said G. Cristina Mora, the UC Berkeley institute’s co-director.
“That might actually have a galvanizing effect on voters,” she said.
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing in the race for California governor. Here’s what you need to know about the candidates.
Trump’s sinking support in California mirrors a national decline in the president’s approval, even among Republicans.
The congressional map in the state was already challenging for Republicans after voters last year approved a referendum championed by Gov. Gavin Newsom to redraw districts to be more favorable for Democrats — a response to similar efforts by Republicans in Texas and other states.
In the new map, only four of the state’s 52 districts are currently considered safe Republican districts, while three additional districts are seen as competitive, according to the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan political handicapper.
The remaining 45 districts are seen as either likely or solidly Democratic in a state where Democrats hold a roughly 20% advantage in party registration.
Only one race is considered by Cook to be a true toss-up — California’s 22nd Congressional District in the Central Valley, which is held by Republican Rep. David Valadao.
“We’re looking at the best case scenario for Democrats at this point,” said Erin Covey, Cook’s U.S. House editor.
Valadao, one of only 10 Republicans to vote for Trump’s impeachment in the wake of the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection, faces progressive Democrat Randy Villegas, a political science professor who has the backing of Bernie Sanders. The Vermont senator is joining Villegas this weekend for a rally in Bakersfield.
Valadao first won a seat in Congress in 2012, but was ousted from office during the Democrats’ “blue wave” election in 2018, in which the party gained 40 seats in the House in the first election after Trump took office in 2016. Valadao was able to win back his seat in 2020 and has held it since.
As Californians prepare to elect a new governor in November, the top concern they want the new leader to prioritize is reducing the state’s entrenched high cost of living, according to a new poll.
There has been scant public polling in the race, but a poll conducted in June by a political committee backing Villegas showed the Democrat holding a 4-point lead over Valadao.
Two other congressional districts in the state are listed by Cook as leaning Democratic: 
- California’s 48th Congressional District in Riverside and San Diego counties, now held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who opted to retire rather than seek reelection in the redrawn district.
- California’s 13th Congressional District in the San Joaquin Valley, where Democratic Rep. Adam Gray is trying to fend off a challenge from Republican Kevin Lincoln, the former mayor of Stockton.
Trump’s approval also dipped among Black and Latino voters in the poll. Both groups were part of Trump’s winning coalition in the 2024 presidential election.
The poll also found broad disapproval of two signature Trump administration policies.
It found that 70% of California voters disapprove of Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran, including 1 in 5 Republicans.
Also, 70% of California voters believe that the president’s immigration policies are hurting California’s economy and local businesses, including 1 in 5 Republicans.
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish between Sept. 15 and Sept. 20 and included the opinions of 6,989 registered California voters. The margin of error is plus or minus 1.5 percentage points.

Anthropic says its AI models could manipulate, blackmail and harm humans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Anthropic says its AI models could manipulate, blackmail and harm humans
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns its increasingly autonomous AI models could pose “existential risks to humanity,” with 80 of 261 pages devoted to potential harms such as manipulation and blackmail.
- Revenue surged twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion in 2025, but Anthropic reported an $8-billion operating loss and plans to spend $518 billion on chips and data centers.
- The company is seeking a $2-trillion valuation even as two customers generated nearly a quarter of its revenue and safety concerns cloud the AI sector’s path to profitability.
Anthropic disclosed that its advanced artificial intelligence technology poses “existential risks to humanity” in an initial public offering document.
As the company prepares for the largest listing in history at $2 trillion, its IPO prospectus has been circulated among investors and viewed by Reuters and other news outlets.
This comes after calls for a coordinated slowdown in AI development by Chief Executive Dario Amodei, echoed by rivals OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX’s Elon Musk.
Nearly a third of the prospectus spotlighted “risk factors,” saying that its increasingly autonomous AI models could manipulate, blackmail or behave in unexpected and harmful ways. Less than 50 pages were dedicated to business metrics, while 80 of 261 pages were about potential risks from the technology.
Safety concerns have swelled after a series of cybersecurity incidents in which AI models skirted instructions and hacked companies, deceived humans, created fake identities and broke into government websites during testing.
The leaked prospectus revealed a company whose revenue growth has exploded but has been offset by massive costs for infrastructure investment in chips and data centers.
In 2025, Anthropic’s revenue grew 12-fold to nearly $4.6 billion, while it lost $8 billion on an operating basis, according to Reuters.
Anthropic’s total on-paper loss stood at $42 billion in 2025, and the company plans to spend $518 billion on data centers and chips in the coming years.
The total operating expense was $12.65 billion in 2025. Of this, $7.33 billion went to the computing and cloud capacity used to train and run AI models, a threefold surge from 2024.
Beyond existential risks to humans, the company also highlighted the business risk of being too dependent on a handful of companies for revenue. Nearly a quarter of its revenue came from two customers in 2025, who are not locked into long-term contracts.
Critics are also concerned about creative accounting at play.
For investors, these risk disclosures might make it challenging to evaluate whether or not to back one of the champions of the AI boom.
“It’s not just about the threat AI may pose to humanity. More immediately, it’s about what ‘model misbehavior’ means for whether or not they can scale,” said Trevor Noren of Sage Road Research, an investment research firm. “Retail investors paying attention have every reason to question that path.”
AI bulls believe the massive investments are justified given the unprecedented growth as models evolve from chatbots to competent AI assistants that can take actions on behalf of humans ranging from maintaining your inbox to closing deals for entrepreneurs.
Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on data centers and chips due to the rapid growth it expects in the coming years, according to the prospectus. The company is demanding a $2-trillion valuation, twice what it was valued at in its previous private funding round of $965 billion.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a breakaway faction of researchers from OpenAI who were concerned about safe AI development.
Since then, its astronomical growth, with the release of Claude Code late in 2025, has enabled the company to surpass OpenAI, its chief rival.
OpenAI also confidentially filed for an IPO in June, but Altman has signaled that the company wouldn’t be going ahead with the listing amid mounting safety risks.
This week, OpenAI decided to hold back the release of its new model after a poor showing during safety evaluations.
In the IPO market, SpaceX’s successful $1.7-trillion listing demonstrated investor appetite earlier this year.
“As SpaceX has exemplified, IPOs are now more and more about returning value to private market investors than generating value for public market investors,” Noren said. “Dario Amodei is not Elon Musk. Concern about AI’s path to profitability has escalated significantly since June.”

Hamas, PIJ and Mohammed Dahlan form electoral coalition despite Hamas pledge to cede Gaza rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:59:34 UTC
18:59:34 KST

Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the exiled leader of Fatah’s Democratic Reform Current, Mohammed Dahlan, have formed an electoral alliance to run in the Palestinian Legislative Council elections in November, PIJ Deputy Secretary General Mohammed al-Hindi confirmed to the Associated Press.
The confirmation comes weeks after Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan, told The Jerusalem Post that the UAE-based Palestinian politician was working to unify the factions ahead of the elections.
Al-Hindi claimed the terrorist organization would support “a unified national list” made up of independent figures rather than members of the groups. The PIJ has not historically participated in elections run by the Palestinian Authority, but Al-Hindi claimed the group would “support a national list that is agreed upon.”
Trump’s 20-point plan stipulated that Hamas would have no role in governing Gaza and would disarm. Hamas subsequently agreed to relinquish governance, though implementation of the plan’s disarmament provisions remains contested. Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya, however, affirmed to Al Araby TV earlier this week that the group had planned to run in the November elections.
Coalition would allow Hamas to commit to PLO but retain 'resistance ideology'
Prof. Kobi Michael, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) and the Misgav Institute, previously told the Post that forming a list with Dahlan, and creating a new coalition outside of the official Hamas movement, would allow the group to accept the Palestinian Authority’s terms for running in the election, without giving up the resistance ideology at the core of its belief system.
Candidates are required to commit to the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, as well as its political and national program and relevant international resolutions. The PLO recognizes Israel, something Hamas has historically rejected.
Diliani, who repeated his comments to AP to the Post, did not confirm the reported alliance, though he stopped short of denying it, acknowledging that multiple Palestinian factions are creating a unified list.
“The Nov. 28 election is our first parliamentary vote since 2006. Our list should offer voters qualified public servants and professionals,” said Diliani. “An inclusive electoral list is the most appropriate political vehicle for us to unite in facing these challenges and in protecting our people and our national cause”.
“The Palestinian Authority has failed Gaza and the Palestinian people everywhere. We have initiated efforts that included Hamas, Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, and other factions and independent professionals into rallying around one national recovery and rebuilding program,” he added.
“Our people know the cost of weakened national institutions and a frail leadership,” Diliani concluded. “Our vision returns law, accountability and the ballot box to national decision-making.”
The reported alliance comes after years of tension between Dahlan and Hamas, and Dahlan and the Palestinian Authority. As the first head of the PA’s Preventive Security Service, he spent years battling Hamas and, according to an exclusive report by Vanity Fair, was involved in a Bush administration-backed plot to oust the group from Gaza in 2008.
Dahlan was removed from his position in Khan Yunis, where he was born, following Hamas’s violent takeover of the Gaza Strip. After years of political confrontation, Dahlan also eventually left the West Bank amid allegations from officials within his own Fatah party.
Following a leaked recording in which Dahlan criticized Abbas and his sons, the PA brought a series of allegations against him, including that he had attempted to mount a coup against Abbas, been involved in the circumstances surrounding Yasser Arafat’s death, and embezzled approximately $16 million in public funds.
Despite the apparent years of conflict, Dahlan wrote in a vision statement shared exclusively with the Post last month that “We want our entire relationship to move from an attempt to weaken one another to cooperation in building the homeland and protecting the national project...”

2 tankers hit by unknown projectiles in Strait of Hormuz: Maritime agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:59:12 UTC
18:59:12 KST

Mohammad Sio
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Two oil and liquefied natural gas tankers were struck by unknown projectiles Tuesday while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Wednesday.
 
In a warning, UKMTO said it had received a delayed report of an incident that occurred within the strategic waterway on Tuesday.
 
“A verified source has reported that a crude oil tanker has been struck on the port side by an unknown projectile,” the agency said.
 
In a separate warning, UKMTO said it received a delayed report that a liquefied natural gas tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
 
It classified the incident as an “attack” and urged vessels transiting the area to exercise caution and report any suspicious activity.
 
UKMTO did not identify the vessel or provide details on possible casualties, damage or the origin of the projectile.
 
It also did not identify the destinations, cargoes, owners or flags of either vessel.
 
It said authorities are investigating the incident.
 
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, which comes amid tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy and commodity supplies.
 
Iran's military said Sunday that it intercepted 19 vessels that attempted to transit the strait outside a navigation route designated by Tehran during a two-day period.
 
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major point of contention in negotiations between Tehran and Washington, with both sides maintaining differing positions over control and management of navigation through the waterway.
 
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
 
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway.

US ambassador slams EU's 'Buy European' weapons push as ‘self-interest’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:58:41 UTC
18:58:41 KST

Preference for European-made arms could disrupt the transatlantic defence industrial base and benefit Europe’s "enemies", Ambassador Andrew Puzder warns.
The European Union's push to favour its domestic arms industry risks "alienating allies" and fragmenting the transatlantic defence industrial base, the US's Ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, has told Euronews.
Speaking at Euronews' Defence and Space summit in Brussels on Wednesday, Puzder said: "Only our enemies benefit when we lose focus on making sure we have the most effective weapons, supporting our mutual defence.
"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we’ll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics," he added.
Puzder also said that when lives are at stake, "capability and availability should determine the solution, not geography."
The European Commission and EU states have tabled proposals to favour domestic arm manufacturers in order to reduce European reliance on US-made arms amid signs of fractures in the transatlantic alliance under Donald Trump.
The Pentagon has fiercely opposed the move, despite the US administration heaping pressure on NATO's European allies to become more independent in their self-defence.
Trump's threats to forcibly seize Greenland as well as the dramatic retreat in financial and military support for Ukraine have added momentum to the EU's push to prioritise European-made weapons.
The proposals have nonetheless split member states, with some EU governments warning against over-protectionism, especially given the US's arms manufacturing power.
On Tuesday, NATO’s top military commander Alexus Grynkewich cautioned that “codifying preferences as to where military hardware is made” only benefits Europe's "adversaries", while speaking to the European Parliament’s defence committee.
Puzder praised the Commission for allowing American defence material to be procured for Ukraine as part of the bloc's recent €90 billion loan to Kyiv, saying that the US would lobby for the same provisions in upcoming defence policies.
"We’ll keep having candid conversations. Sometimes we’re going to disagree. Generally, I believe we will agree," Puzder said.
He also said that the EU executive had indicated it had "no intention" of preventing EU member states from using national funds to buy US weapon systems.
"An alliance which faces our adversaries with unity and strength rather than division and self-interest," the ambassador added.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political scientist’s view: What will decide the fate of Latvia’s next coalition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:56:55 UTC
18:56:55 KST

The SKDS poll results published shortly before the election brought no major surprises – the top three remained unchanged (United List 14.4%, Sovereign Power/Young Latvians 9.4%, Latvia First 9.2%), while the overall balance between the political forces also remained largely unchanged. However, shifts in support for individual parties were noticeable: the Progressives fell by 2.6 percentage points and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians by 2.4 points, while the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) gained 2 percentage points and the National Alliance (NA) 1.1 points. What do these poll results tell us just days before the election? BNN asked political scientist Filips Rajevskis, co-founder of Mediju tilts.
“The fate of the next coalition will be decided by the parties hovering somewhere around the five-percent threshold. It is clear which party is the leader, but who it will form a coalition with – that is the big question,” the political scientist said.
Filips Rajevskis also believes the next parliament will be fairly fragmented and will largely resemble the current composition, although the distribution of votes will change.
“We can see that the Union of Greens and Farmers is around the five-percent threshold, and they have been fairly consistent there. New Unity is also at roughly the same level, somewhere around five percent. If we look at projections in terms of seats, the current coalition could end up with more than 50 votes. The big question is how many votes above 50 they would have and whether that would make the current coalition viable. Ultimately, that is up to the voters.”
“If, for example, all the parties in the current coalition cross the 5% threshold but together end up with 52 or 53 seats, then you essentially get something like Evika Siliņa’s government number two, which, with such a narrow majority, is not really capable of functioning effectively.
That could bring very significant changes to the way coalition-building is approached after the election.”
Asked by BNN about recent speculation that the United List could also invite Latvia First (LPV) into the coalition, Rajevskis recalled that the Prime Minister has repeatedly said that Latvia First is a “red line” for his party.
“I am somewhat surprised by such a radical position from the Prime Minister, especially knowing that it will most likely be him who has to form the next coalition. By taking such a position, he immediately puts the Progressives in a much more favourable position, even though I do not think they are his first choice when it comes to forming a coalition.”
“There are many factors that, in the heat of the pre-election campaign, have been elevated to a level that perhaps should have been left for reflection after election day,” Rajevskis said.
Filips Rajevskis agreed with BNN that Latvian politics has repeatedly seen situations where parties say one thing before an election and then do something entirely different afterwards.
“That is exactly the problem.
If we look at the experience with red lines, it has been particularly painful for the Progressives.
They drew a very clear red line against ZZS, saying that under no circumstances would they govern together. Now they are in the same government as ZZS, and they are still being reminded of it.”
“That is a painful experience for any political force. If, all the way until the next election, people keep reminding you that you lied to voters, that is not a good look.”
BNN also asked the political scientist how he views campaign posters that feature, alongside the actual candidates and party leaders, politicians who are not themselves running in the election and who are clearly not going to leave their influential and comfortable positions in Brussels.
Rajevskis acknowledged that this is also not good practice.
“To a large extent, Harmony brought this practice into Latvian politics, with Ušakovs appearing on posters in practically every election even though he himself only ran in municipal elections.
New Unity has also used this for years by putting Dombrovskis on its posters.
I think at some point this will change when they realise that voters no longer fall for it. But as long as it works, the tool will continue to be used.”
The political scientist also stressed the importance of voter turnout.
“If turnout is sufficiently high, it will increase the number of votes needed to cross the five-percent threshold. That will, of course, have a major impact on the result. And then there is another question – how many parties will cross the five-percent threshold. That will determine how many votes and seats will ultimately be needed to form a government.”

Hong Kong route linking Yau Ma Tei and Tseung Kwan O to fully open in December
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

India’s Javelin Deal: The Unending Loop of Procurement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:56:00 UTC
18:56:00 KST

“BIG news! India plans to buy the battle-tested Javelin anti-tank system,” U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor announced on X on August 28, as the Indian Army signed the letter of offer and acceptance (LOA) for the purchase of the missile system through the foreign military sales (FMS) route, also adding that it’s opening the door to “co-production possibilities.” For the Indian Army, it marks 16 years of ups and downs and the long lead time to fill a critical capability gap in anti-tank guided missiles (ATGM), even if only piecemeal.
The Javelin is a versatile, one-man-portable and platform-mounted fire-and-forget anti-tank precision weapon system that is capable of defeating all kinds of armor and fortified positions. It is in service with more than 25 countries, including the U.S. Army and the U.S. Marine Corps.
Following this, Lockheed announced a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) and the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), a partnership between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, for the “co-production of the Javelin All Up Round (AUR) in India.” The MoU will explore establishing a final assembly and integration facility for the Javelin AUR, along with component production capabilities, in India, Lockheed said in a statement.
While the specifics of the LOA haven’t been released yet, the U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification of November 2025 said that India would purchase 100 Javelin rounds and 25 launch units at an estimated cost of $45.7 million.
The entire saga can be viewed through two prisms: the deepening India-U.S. defense cooperation, and India’s rickety military modernization epitomized by the Javelin saga.
The Quest for ATGMs
The nearly 1.3 million-strong Indian Army started looking for a new generation fire-and-forget ATGM in the early 2000s to replace the Konkurs and Milan in service. The overall requirement is for over 40,000 missiles to equip the 382 infantry battalions and 44 mechanized regiments. However, as the indigenous effort by the Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) was delayed, the Army started looking for import options to partly fill the deficiency.
In August 2010, Defense Minister A. K. Antony informed the Indian parliament that his ministry proposed to issue a letter of request to the U.S. government for procurement of the Javelin ATGM along with transfer of technology under their FMS route. After the issue of the letter of request, further procurement-related necessary action will follow, he added.
The Army’s first experience with the Javelin came in 2009 during the bilateral exercise Yudh Abhyas, where the U.S. Army fielded it and so, was under consideration. While it was extensively tested, the deal didn’t move forward due to U.S. technology transfer limitations. This was when the Army moved to acquire the Spike ATGM manufactured by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems of Israel.
The Spike Journey
The Defense Acquisition Council, the highest decision-making body on procurements in the Ministry of Defense, accorded initial approval for procurement of Spike in 2009 for over 8,000 missiles and 300 launchers with technology transfer for their domestic manufacture, a deal worth $500 million. It was approved in October 2014, but the contract negotiations went into a loop over cost and technology transfer.
In fact, in 2016, in anticipation of the deal and to meet the domestic manufacturing requirement, Rafael set up a joint venture with Kalyani Group to manufacture sub-assemblies, with defense public sector firm Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) being the system integrator. The deal was cancelled in January 2018, just ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to India visit, as it was felt that indigenous development was making progress. However, the deal was revived soon after, by the end of 2018, for the purchase of 170 launchers, 4,500 missiles and 15 simulators. This too dragged on for a few years but never came to fruition due to questions being raised over the missile’s performance during the validation trials.
All through this, the Javelin was never fully out of the picture.
After the Balakot air strike in February 2019 in response to the Pulwama terrorist attack and simmering tensions with Pakistan, the Army procured a small number of Spike-LR (long-range) ATGMs under the emergency procurement route sanctioned by the MoD to fill critical deficiencies. The order was for 12 launchers and around 250 missiles. The Army repeated the order for the Spike-LR in 2020 in another round of Emergency Procurement sanctioned after the standoff with China along the disputed border at Ladakh.
Orders were capped at 3 billion Indian rupees, valued at $42 million in 2019. The Spike-LR, a 4th-gen missile with a range of up to 4 kilometers, is a different variant from the one originally tested. This remains the only new generation ATGM inducted by the Indian Army in the whole period.
Given the long and convoluted procurement process, emergency procurement has become the preferred way to fast-track critical procurements.
India-U.S. Defense Industrial Cooperation
The Javelin deal, which emerged out of growing India-U.S. bilateral defense and strategic cooperation, is one of the earliest defense deals between the two countries and the one that dragged on the longest.
Incidentally, the Javelin was also tested in 2024 along with Stryker infantry combat vehicles. However, the performance of the missile was sub-optimal as the lot provided for trials was dated. While the Stryker deal drags on, Operation Sindoor in 2025 reinforced the deficiencies.
The Javelin deal strengthens the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership and also opens discussions on mutually beneficial co-production and additional opportunities to strengthen the defense industrial bases of both countries, a U.S. Embassy statement said. The local manufacture of assemblies and parts of the Javelin fits into the overall deepening of India’s presence in the supply chains of U.S. companies manufacturing components and sub-assemblies.
TASL itself is now a major player in this segment with a series of tie-ups with U.S. defense majors. For instance, with Boeing, it manufactures fuselages, secondary structures and vertical spar boxes for AH-64 Apache attack helicopters, and vertical fins for 737 aircraft; and fixed wings for Lockheed Martin’s C-130J and F-16 aircraft. Such integration of Indian industry over the last two decades has positioned the U.S. as India’s top defense export destination.
While India has significantly increased its defense procurements from the U.S., the effort for co-development and co-production has had no real success to date. The crown jewel of that effort, the license manufacture of the GE-414 jet engine domestically to power the Light Combat Aircraft-Mk2, has been stuck for several years now.
Though small as a system, the Javelin is high in its battlefield impact and will be a step forward in the joint endeavor. That this was announced amid the current turbulence in the India-U.S. relationship showcases the distance travelled by the two countries on the defense and strategic front.
Acquisition of the Javelin too is through the Emergency Procurement route that limits the numbers that can be purchased. The larger requirement of the Indian Army for ATGMs remains unfulfilled.
An ATGM is a critical battlefield weapon whose importance has grown manifold since its utility was underscored in Ukraine and other conflicts. While the Indian armed forces look at niche and emerging technologies, procurement of several other such basic but critical systems are caught in a loop. This merits immediate attention and action even as India keeps Operation Sindoor rolling and prepares for the next round of confrontation with Pakistan.
While development of the indigenous man-portable ATGM by DRDO has made progress, the timelines are still long. Coupled with evolving threats, this Javelin deal is likely the first of many.

Ethiopia's last Jews dream of visa for Israel

Issued on:
Ethiopia has one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world, rumoured to be the descendants of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon in 950 BC. From the 1970s to 1990s, this community known as Beta Israel was persecuted under the Communist regime, and Israel evacuated more than 20,000 Ethiopian Jews in dramatic airlifts known as Operation Solomon and Operation Moses. But a few thousand were left behind.
Thirty years on, these Ethiopian Jews are still waiting to rejoin their friends and family in Israel, and to escape the dire living conditions that the shunned community endures today.
Most have sold their land to be closer to Israeli consulates or the embassy, but have had no certainty over their future for years.

Volodin becomes first State Duma Speaker to serve more than two terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:54:18 UTC
18:54:18 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Vyacheslav Volodin has become the first State Duma Speaker to lead the lower house for more than two consecutive terms. He previously held the post in the seventh and eighth State Duma.
On Wednesday, at the first plenary session of the ninth State Duma, deputies elected Vyacheslav Volodin as house speaker. A total of 406 out of 442 deputies voted in favor of the decision. Volodin was nominated by the United Russia faction. Another 36 deputies voted for Dmitry Novikov, who represents the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF). The Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, and A Just Russia - For Truth did not nominate candidates for the position.
The 9th State Duma speaker thanked his colleagues for their trust and support. "I'll do my best not to let you down," he noted. Volodin emphasized that democracy presupposes the implementation of procedures, norms, and rules. According to him, adhering to these principles will allow Russia’s parliamentary movement to grow and improve the quality and effectiveness of its work.
At the September 28 meeting with the heads of the 9th State Duma factions, Russian President Vladimir Putin supported Volodin’s nomination, noting that during the 8th State Duma, the chairman created a principled and businesslike atmosphere.
Volodin first took the speaker’s seat in 2016 in the 7th State Duma and retained the post in the eighth Duma in 2021. By 2024, he had set the record for the longest tenure as State Duma speaker. Under Gennady Seleznev and Boris Gryzlov - who also led the Duma for two terms each - the lower house's term lasted four years. Consequently, they each held the speaker’s post for a total of approximately eight years: Seleznev from January 1996 to December 2003, and Gryzlov from December 2003 to December 2011.
Sergey Naryshkin, the 6th State Duma speaker, led the house for five years - from December 2011 to October 2016. Ivan Rybkin’s tenure lasted just two years - from January 1994 to January 1996 - as the first the Duma was elected for that specific term.
Volodin served as a State Duma deputy from 1999 to 2011. From October 21, 2010, to December 2011, he served as deputy prime minister and chief of the government staff. From 2011 to 2016, Volodin was first deputy chief of the presidential staff, overseeing the domestic policy directorate and interethnic relations.
