‘I wanted to live’: A Ukrainian orphan’s journey through Russian occupation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:54:07 UTC
18:54:07 KST

‘I wanted to live’: A Ukrainian orphan’s journey through Russian occupation
Denys Kostev says he was forcibly transferred from Kherson in 2022 and coerced into pro-Russian campaigns before finally escaping.
Kyiv, Ukraine – When the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began, Denys Kostev was 18 and living in an orphanage in Kherson. Appalled by the war, he used to film social media videos decrying the invading Russian forces.
But he was soon forcibly transferred to occupied Crimea, and his rhetoric suddenly went in the other direction.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4At least 10 people killed in Russian and Ukrainian attacks
- list 2 of 4Lavrov: Russia’s war in Ukraine will continue ‘through to the end’
- list 3 of 4Russia scales up strikes on Ukraine as largest steelmaker halts operations
- list 4 of 4Russian strikes kill eight, injure dozens across Ukraine
Now in Kyiv four years later, Kostev told Al Jazeera he played the role of a poster child for wartime Russia just to survive.
Sprightly, eloquent and photogenic, he used to attend a theatre club at his orphanage in the southern Ukrainian city, where he lived after his mother’s incarceration and death.
The experience helped him “star” in numerous videos for Russian television networks – because refusing to be filmed meant risking physical assault or being threatened with jail, he said.
“It was useful to play this pro-Russian role,” said Kostev, who, having ultimately escaped Russia, is now preparing to fight for Ukraine. “I wanted to live.”
But surviving did not come easy, he said.
Kostev’s terrifying journey
Tanks rolled into Kherson days after the war began. People suspected of pro-Ukrainian sympathies were rounded up and interrogated. Some were allegedly abused.
In late 2022, while at the orphanage, Kostev also studied in a trade school. But as the war intensified, he and others were relocated to the Luchisty (“Full of Sunshine”) summer camp in Russia-annexed Crimea.
“Every morning, you wake up to the Russian anthem, and every Monday, there’s a celebratory hoisting of the Russian flag,” Kostev said of his time there.
The orphans were isolated, he added.
“They’re without parents, no one to explain what’s right or wrong,” he said. “At a certain point, you begin to repeat pro-Russian narratives.”
At least one teenager Kostev met in the camp enlisted to fight against Kyiv, he said.
Ukraine is working to return allegedly abducted children and collect evidence against individuals suspected of being involved in their capture. More than 2,600 children have returned so far.
The summer camp’s “administration” has not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. Kyiv said that 84 Ukrainian orphans were held there in 2023.
Those who left were among almost 4,000 children forcibly taken from orphanages in Russia-occupied Ukrainian regions, according to Ukrainian rights groups. Kyiv claims that Moscow has herded almost 20,000 Ukrainian minors to Russia to “brainwash” them during the war.
While the Kremlin acknowledges that children are being “re-educated”, it rejects Ukraine’s claims, saying that any children who have been moved were rescued from war zones.
Some of these children lost parents during Russian shelling, and others ended up in “summer camps” after pro-Moscow authorities reportedly convinced their parents to let them go for “safety reasons”.
Ukraine claims that some children were abducted from parents who refused to collaborate with Moscow-installed “administrations” in Russia-occupied areas.
Russian forces and their Ukrainian collaborators have also been accused by Ukrainian rights groups of interrogating and abusing parents – and checking their bodies for pro-Kyiv tattoos or bruises left by recoiling firearms.
‘Deeply disturbing reports’
International rights groups decry the alleged abduction and indoctrination of children as one of the Kremlin’s gravest crimes.
“The physical destruction of this war is visible to everyone, but the campaign to abduct and ‘re-educate’ Ukrainian children as Russian represents something more sinister altogether,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.
“It’s unacceptable,” he said. “There are deeply disturbing reports that Russia is carrying out military indoctrination with a view to use some of these children in the armed forces in their war against Ukraine.”
Some 5,500 young Ukrainians in Russia-occupied areas were sent into Yunarmiya (“Young Army”), a movement that provides military training, according to Ukrainian officials.
The earlier the age, the deeper the transformation of a child’s worldview, according to Svitlana Chunikhina, vice president of the Association of Political Psychologists of Ukraine, a group in Kyiv.
“Children have a flexible psyche; they quickly adapt to a new environment, they mostly trust adults – sometimes involuntarily, but they have no other choice – and take many things for granted,” she said.
That is why they cannot resist Moscow’s narratives, she said.
“But it doesn’t mean that the same will surely happen to all Ukrainian children,” Chunikhina said.
While younger children studied in the camp according to the Russian curriculum, the education system did not appear to have had a thorough, comprehensive programme for teenagers such as Kostev.
Along with his friends, he hung around a Soviet-era compound dotted with cypresses, acacias and evergreen shrubs.
They were not allowed to leave it – but occasionally sneaked out to buy cigarettes and alcohol. Those who were caught drunk were isolated for three days in the hospital and were threatened with prison by the camp’s security chief, a former officer with Ukraine’s special forces who had switched sides, said Kostev, who is now 22.
The idea that the children would “never return to Ukraine” was drummed into them, he said.
In April 2023, after months in camps in Crimea, Kostev was sent back to the occupied southern town of Henichesk – and learned that Russian troops had withdrawn from Kherson seven months earlier.
He enrolled in another trade school and was housed in a squalid, ice-cold dormitory he complained about in a video that went viral.
The next morning, Russia-installed police strip-searched him, claiming he was “spying” for Kyiv and threatened him with jail, he said.
Then he was forced to extol Russia on camera.
In one video, he said he had joined a Kremlin-funded youth movement, wrapped himself in a Russian flag and declared that he wanted to enlist.
But he told Al Jazeera that he was forced and coerced into championing Russia, and had always wanted to leave.
In early 2024, Kostev got in touch with his elder brother and grandmother who had relocated to Germany. He managed to join them and later crossed into Poland, where he spent months awaiting a new Ukrainian passport.
In April, he returned to Ukraine. He said he has attended a military training camp and is now in the early stages of his military career as a drone pilot.
“Wherever you are – home is better,” he said, sitting in a shopping mall in a Kyiv suburb, shortly before air raid sirens forced everyone outside.

Just under two-thirds of Swiss railway stations are accessible to the disabled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:53:00 UTC
18:53:00 KST

Just under two-thirds of Swiss railway stations are accessible to the disabled
Around 65% of railway facilities in Switzerland are either partially or fully accessible to the disabled. Half of all bus stops can be used without restriction by people with disabilities.
The Disability Equality Act requires railway station operators to make their stations accessible by the end of 2023. According to a progress report by the Federal Office of Transport on the current status of implementation, 1,168 of the approximately 1,800 railway stations were accessible as of the end of 2025, with a further 193 due to follow by 2029. As larger stations were the first to undergo structural modernisation, 83% of all passengers can now benefit from accessible stations. This figure is set to rise to 87% by 2029.
Nevertheless, 454 stations still require adaptation, of which 261 will not be upgraded until after 2029, as the report presented to the media on Tuesday showed. The main reasons for the delays are said to be a lack of resources for planning and a shortage of staff, as well as financial constraints. However, under the 2025–2028 service agreement, the federal government has allocated additional funding of CHF250 million.
For around 150 stations where a full refurbishment is deemed disproportionate, permanent alternative measures will be provided, such as assistance from staff, the report added.
Half of bus stops are accessible
The report presented also covered the refurbished bus stops for the first time. There are 25,000 bus stops in Switzerland, or 48,000 kerb edges. Half of these can be used spontaneously by passengers with reduced mobility. At 13% of the kerb edges, independent boarding without additional assistance is guaranteed. At 37%, assistance from driving staff is required, usually through the use of a folding ramp.
Around 42% of kerb-side boarding points cannot be used either independently or with assistance from staff. According to the report, alternative arrangements are essential at these locations. As a rule, a shuttle service is provided to the nearest stop that complies with the Disability Act.
More
A better way to live for the disabled in Switzerland?
Those present gave a positive assessment of the work completed to date. “The inner determination to make real progress is there,” said Transport Minister Albert Rösti to the media. It is not just a matter of fundamentally improving the infrastructure, but also the mobility of people with disabilities, said Centre party parliamentarian Christian Lohr. “Mobility is important for people with disabilities to participate in social life,” he added.
Association plans to take action against delays
Although the statutory deadline under the Disability Act had already expired at the end of 2023, the implementation of accessibility in public transport is slowing down, the umbrella organisation for people with disabilities, Inclusion Handicap, announced on Tuesday. At the round-table discussion chaired by Transport Minister Albert Rösti, no binding commitments were forthcoming from the authorities or public transport operators.
In view of the delays, Inclusion Handicap is calling for the establishment of a task force. This task force should identify obstacles to implementation and funding. “People with disabilities are clearly losing out when it comes to new large-scale projects,” co-president Olga Manfredi was quoted as saying in the press release. There can be no inclusion without accessible public transport.

Japan court rules voice rights protected in AI cloning case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:51:56 UTC
18:51:56 KST

Aamir Latif
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
A Japanese court ruled on Wednesday that voices are protected by publicity rights, similar to portrait rights, in the first such ruling in the country in an artificial intelligence (AI) cloning case, local media reported.
The Tokyo District Court delivered the ruling in a lawsuit filed by famous voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The court, however, dismissed his demand that the operator of TikTok take down videos narrated using artificial intelligence with a voice that he claimed was similar to his own.
Tsuda is best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime "Jujutsu Kaisen."
Currently, Japan does not have any clear laws that stipulate voice rights.
But the Justice Ministry has recently laid out guidelines stating that uploading videos to social media that use voices similar to those of real people and generating revenue from them may constitute a rights violation.
Tsuda filed the lawsuit after an anonymous poster uploaded 188 videos about urban myths, the occult and trivia between July 2024 and Sept. 2025 that were narrated by a voice similar to his.
The account was later deleted in June this year.
An analysis found strong similarities between Tsuda's voice and the AI-generated voice, which the plaintiff said misled viewers.
The operator of TikTok argued the narration employed a "standard male voice" and would not be mistaken for Tsuda, while the poster said the AI was trained using a friend's voice.

A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers urged President Donald Trump on Sept. 29 not to ease sanctions against Russia, amid reports that his administration is considering sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners.
Democratic Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Mike Quigley, along with Republicans Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson, called on the administration to maintain pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers' statement comes as Washington considers using sanctions relief as leverage to encourage Russia to take steps toward ending the war.

"Two weeks ago, Congress passed the most significant Russia sanctions legislation since 2017," they said. "We look forward to the Administration's first round of new sanctions designations ahead of Oct. 18, the first deadline in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act."
The legislation, spearheaded by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and signed by Trump on Sept. 19, authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil.
The U.S. president said on Sept. 22 that he would use the tariff authorities granted by the legislation if necessary to help end Russia's war against Ukraine.
The debate over sanctions relief comes as Russia's economy faces mounting pressure from long-term Western restrictions. Sanctions relief has become one of Moscow's main objectives, while some U.S. officials see easing sanctions as an incentive for Russia to agree to a ceasefire.
The latest push comes as Washington seeks to revive efforts to end the war. Those efforts stalled earlier this year amid Russia's territorial demands and the U.S.-Iran war.
Moscow has continued its attacks against Ukraine while clearly showing no indication that it is prepared to accept a ceasefire or make concessions in negotiations.

Danish economy grew 0.9% in second quarter after sharp upward revision

18:50:12 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Serviceman detained in Ukrainian Armed Forces for “leaking” positions - woman from channel for seeking close relationships was eliciting information

Serviceman detained in Ukrainian Armed Forces for “leaking” positions - woman from channel for seeking close relationships was eliciting information
Kyiv • UNN
The machine gunner passed his female interlocutor the coordinates of units and equipment in the Kramatorsk direction. He was taken into custody.
A serviceman of the Armed Forces of Ukraine was detained for passing information about the location of Ukrainian units and military equipment to a woman he had met online. The Office of the Prosecutor General reported this on September 30, UNN reports.
A serviceman of the Armed Forces of Ukraine who passed information about the location of Ukrainian units and military equipment was detained
Details
"According to the investigation, a machine gunner from one of the brigades of unmanned systems met a woman on Telegram who presented herself as a servicemember of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. They met through a channel for finding romantic relationships. During their communication, the woman gradually elicited information from him about the location of Ukrainian units. In this way, the investigation believes that the serviceman was being used "in the dark" in the interests of the russian special services," the post reads.
According to the OPG, from September 4 to 16, 2026, the man "passed the woman information about the positions of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and marked on electronic maps the geolocations of personnel and equipment, including those of his own formation in the Kramatorsk direction."
"He was exposed on September 19. During the search, a mobile phone used to disseminate this information was seized. The serviceman was charged with the unauthorized dissemination of information about the movement, deployment, and location of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and other military formations (Part 2 of Article 114-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). He is currently in custody," the post reads.
Recall
The SBU exposed an agent of the russian GRU in the Armed Forces of Ukraine in the Kharkiv region who passed the enemy data on the deployment of units. The perpetrator, a 30-year-old man who had been mobilized, collected information about command posts, warehouses, and artillery, and also possessed combat grenades and explosives.

Srebrenica school allegedly threatens penalties over Bosnia and Herzegovina jerseys: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:48:29 UTC
18:48:29 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
A school in Srebrenica allegedly threatened students with penalties for wearing Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team jerseys, daily Dnevni Avaz reported Wednesday.
JU Secondary Center Srebrenica reportedly declared Bosnia and Herzegovina national team jerseys offensive, while students were warned they could face sanctions, including a lower conduct grade, according to parents.
Sanja Mocevic, director of the Srebrenica High School Center in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Republika Srpska entity, reportedly told students not to come to school wearing the national team jerseys in the future.
Murat Tahirovic, president of the Association of Victims and Witnesses of Genocide, responded to the case and sought clarification of the decision.
“If it is true that the student of the Srebrenica High School Center was reprimanded because she came to school in the jersey of the football team of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that the students were then threatened with sanctions for wearing such a jersey, then this is a procedure that is deeply worrying and unacceptable,” he said.
Tahirovic requested a public explanation of the regulations under which the national team jersey was declared unacceptable.
He also called on education authorities in Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina to urgently investigate the case and protect students from discrimination and humiliation.
“Srebrenica is a place of genocide, but it must not be a place where children are taught that Bosnia and Herzegovina is undesirable,” Tahirovic added.
In July 1995, Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN-declared safe area of Srebrenica and systematically killed 8,372 Bosniak men and boys in what international courts, including the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, have recognized as genocide.

Hungarian appeals court cuts German activist's jail term to seven years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:47:56 UTC
18:47:56 KST

Hungarian appeals court cuts German activist's jail term to seven years
BUDAPEST, Sept 30 - A Hungarian appeals court on Wednesday reduced the prison sentence of a German citizen convicted for assaulting suspected far-right sympathisers in Budapest in 2023 to seven years from eight.
The defendant, identified only as Maja T., was among a group of anti-fascist activists who travelled to Hungary to counter a far-right rally. Arrested in Berlin in December 2023, Maja T. was later transferred to Hungary to stand trial. A lower court handed Maja T. an eight-year sentence in February.
• According to the indictment, Maja T. was part of a far-left group that planned to take up an "ideological fight with violent attacks against sympathisers of the extremist right" with the aim of assaulting people with "various instruments capable of causing death."
• The appeals court judge said the sentence was being reduced because for one of the two counts on which Maja T. was convicted, the defendant should be considered an accomplice rather than a co-perpetrator and should not be considered part of an organised criminal group.
• The case drew international attention when Germany's Constitutional Court ruled in February 2025 that it had been unlawful to extradite Maja T., who identifies as non-binary, to Hungary, upholding her argument that the decision violated the European Union's Charter of Fundamental Rights.
• Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who was ousted in an April election, Hungary introduced anti-LGBTQ+ policies, including laws that Brussels says discriminate against people on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.
• Authorities in Hungary have given assurances that non-binary people are not subject to discrimination or violence in prisons there.
• Maja T., who was one of several individuals to go on trial over the attacks, had told the court earlier that the accusations against them were political.
• The first accused in the trial was Italian teacher Ilaria Salis, who was released from house arrest in June 2024 after she was elected a member of the European Parliament. Prosecutors were seeking an 11-year sentence for her. Salis and her family said she was innocent. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Ukraine Finally Has Bipartisan Support in the US. Why Are Ukrainian Consuls Working to Destroy It?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:47:55 UTC
18:47:55 KST

On Sept. 18 US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. Eighty-six senators from both parties voted for it. So did 262 members of the House of Representatives.
When the $60 billion Ukraine aid package passed the House in April 2024, 112 Republicans voted against it. For the Russian Sanction bill this month, seven did.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Seven.
For two years the fear was that a Trump presidency would be a disaster for Ukraine. It hasn’t been. Republicans who once treated Ukraine as a Democratic cause now vote for it. Trump signed the bill into law. Fifty-eight House Democrats defied their own leadership to vote yes.
Four days after the signing, President Zelensky sat down with President Trump in New York and came out saying Trump had made his “final decision”: Ukraine will get licenses to produce Patriot missiles. The missiles that stop Russian ballistic missiles before they hit Ukrainian targets.
It’s been a long time since the news from Washington was this good.
It’s also fragile. Trump promised the Patriot licenses once before, in July, and walked it back. Days after the New York meeting he wouldn’t confirm it to reporters. Nothing is locked in. Every Congressional vote of support has to be protected.
And the biggest threat to it right now isn’t coming from Ukraine’s enemies in Congress. It’s coming from a small group of people who carry the title of Ukrainian consul.
Ukrainian Intel Exposes Russia Helping Iran Target US Forces
Who they are
Ukraine’s honorary consuls in the United States are not diplomats. They are US citizens, though often of Ukrainian background. Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs gives them the title and apparently, very little oversight.
These consuls have been active in meeting with congressmen and speaking to the press to push a policy that Ukraine opposes.
Working against their own government
Ukraine’s official policy toward its citizens abroad fits in two words: come home.
In December 2024 the government created a Ministry of National Unity, and the Prime Minister said its main job would be “the strategy, programs and incentives on how to bring Ukrainians back to live and work in Ukraine.” That work continues today inside the Ministry of Social Policy. Housing help. Jobs. Services for people coming back.
And people are coming back. According to the International Organization for Migration, over 1 million Ukrainians have returned home from abroad since the full-scale invasion. From Poland, from Germany, from the Czech Republic. Under the drones. Because the country needs them.
Meanwhile some of Ukraine’s consuls in the US are lobbying the American government to keep Ukrainians here permanently, and to bring more.
That isn’t Ukraine’s policy. It’s the opposite. So who are they working for?
For the consuls who practice immigration law, the answer isn’t complicated. It’s their business.
What they’re doing with the title
One consul is an immigration lawyer. At a political event for a Republican congressman who had just taken a hard vote to send weapons to Ukraine, she didn’t thank him. She lectured him about immigration and compared the President of the United States to Nazi Germany. Then asked him to review some cases she was working on.
Another consul, a former Republican political operative, asked me to help him reach Senator. Not about air defense. Not about long-range strikes. About one Ukrainian truck driver ICE had picked up. This summer he went to an American newspaper, speaking as Ukraine’s consul, and accused a state highway patrol and ICE of “using deception” to arrest Ukrainian truckers. The highway patrol program belongs to a Republican governor. The Department of Homeland Security is now run by the consul’s own former boss.
Maybe some of those drivers were treated unfairly. Their lawyers can argue that in court. But think about who read that story. A Republican governor and a Republican cabinet secretary opened their home-state paper and found the representative of Ukraine saying their people lie.
What they want
This month the American Coalition for Ukraine sent a policy sheet to Congress titled “Protecting Displaced Ukrainians in the United States.” A group of Ukrainian-American immigration lawyers wrote the document and their organization is co-sponsor of the program. It counts 510,000 Ukrainians living here on temporary status and asks Washington to keep all of them. No exception.
Many Ukrainians were given temporary residency in America in 2022. The lawyers want it extended and made permanent, meaning the temporary refugees never return to Ukraine but become US citizens.
Then it asks for more. Reopen the Uniting for Ukraine program to more new arrivals.
Why this is so dangerous
Ukrainians should understand one thing about American politics. Donald Trump won the presidency twice on one issue above all others: immigration. For a Republican, this is not a policy detail. It is the core of his party.
So when Ukraine’s representatives spend a meeting on green cards, a Republican hears that Ukraine’s priority is not the war. It’s getting its people into America. And when someone speaking for Ukraine compares his President to the Nazis, he stops taking the calls.
This will not win Democrats votes to help Ukraine either. Democrats introduced the Ukrainian Adjustment Act earlier this year. Thirty-two Democrats co-sponsored the bill which was a vote to support Ukrainian refugees as well as political stance against President Trump. Unfortunately, when it came time to vote for the Russian sanctions bill, only 13 of those Democrats were willing to support Ukraine.
Voting against Trump on immigration is an easy vote for a Democrat. Voting for sanctions or weapons is hard. Many representatives are choosing to show their support for Ukraine by supporting refugees. The consuls are helping them do that.
What needs to happen
To the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: An honorary consul speaks in Ukraine’s name. Consuls who use that title to fight against American immigration policy instead of for Ukrainian defense should be removed or silenced. No more meetings with congressmen to talk about their legal cases. No more statements to the press. The lack of an ambassador in Washington is not helping.
To the Government of Ukraine: Say it publicly. Ukraine’s lobbying the United States government to grant Ukrainians refugees permanent residency is a disaster for Ukraine-US relations.
To Ukrainians and Ukrainian-Americans: Write to the American Coalition for Ukraine. Thank them for their work on sanctions. Then ask them to stop lobbying the United States government for more immigration and to take their name off the immigration sheet. One ask. Weapons.
None of this is against the refugees. My family helped resettle more than a dozen Ukrainians in America. The best way to help the refugees is to help Ukraine win the war. Advocating for the refugees is the opposite of advocating for Ukraine. If you want to push for immigration reform, join an immigration advocacy group, not a Ukrainian group.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act is a symbol of bi-partisan support for Ukraine and stepping stone to stronger American-Ukraine relations. Don’t let Ukraine’s own consuls tear it down.

2-MIN READ2-MIN
2
 Listen
A US-led coalition deployed in Iraq more than a decade ago to fight jihadists concluded its mission on Wednesday, a move celebrated by the country’s leaders, but which some fear will embolden pro-Iran armed factions.
Coalition troops deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight Islamic State, which had seized large swathes of territory, committing massacres and forcing thousands of women and children into slavery.
The group was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group’s remnants.
The United States and Iraq agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition’s mission, and its troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the autonomous northern Kurdistan region.

Dubai-Tel Aviv flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after hijack scare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:46:24 UTC
18:46:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Dubai-Tel Aviv flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after suspected hijacking attempt
A commercial flight carrying around 180 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday following a suspected hijacking attempt by one of the pilots.
The aircraft, operated by Emirati airline Flydubai, transmitted an emergency alert two hours into the flight when it plummeted 14,000 feet in less than a minute.
The incident occurred over the Jordan-Saudi border after the copilot, an Omani national, stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the plane, according to Hebrew media reports.
Several Israeli passengers helped the Emirati captain subdue the attacker and prevent the aircraft from crashing.
Israeli fighter jets were scrambled to intercept the aircraft, which safely landed in Tabuk.
Israeli officials are reportedly investigating the incident as a potential terror attack, though the motive remains unclear.
"This morning there was an extremely serious security incident," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement from his office.
"The pilot who carried out the stabbing was arrested and is currently being questioned by the Saudi authorities," he said.
'Stabbings, blood'
Videos of the injured pilot were circulated on social media while passengers described scenes of chaos and panic as the aircraft descended.
"There were screams. Stabbings, stabbings, blood, blood," a passenger named Adam told Israel's Channel 13 News.
"Several Israeli guys took control of the situation, they managed to stabilise the aircraft," he said.
Tabuk Airport said the Emirati captain and the co-pilot were injured and were receiving treatment in hospital.
Another passenger, Miryam Shira Ohayon, said the co-pilot tried to crash the plane and kill everyone on board.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," AFP quoted her as telling reporters by speakerphone.
Flydubai flights suspended
Passengers arrived in Tel Aviv at 1835 local time (1535 GMT) on a Flydubai flight from Tabuk. Israeli media reported that some initially refused to board the aircraft and demanded rescue by an Israeli airline.
Flydubai said the aircraft “experienced an incident while en route”, adding that it landed safely at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport and that all passengers were safe and accounted for.
"The safety and wellbeing of our passengers and crew remain our highest priority," the statement read. "Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available."
Netanyahu said later on Wednesday that all Flydubai flights would be suspended until further notice while the investigation takes place.
Transport Minister Miri Regev had earlier demanded the move and asked the Civil Aviation Authority to investigate whether the UAE violated its agreement with Israel. The bilateral aviation agreement forbids pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel - such as Oman - from landing in the country.

The programme will also involve a TAI Atak helicopter flyover, a demonstration flight by the Turkish Gendarmerie’s Steel Wings aerobatic team, a demonstration by the Baykar Bayraktar TB3 and more.
TEKNOFEST Southeast admission is free, but visitors must register online before entering.
Visitors may enter and exit the event area between 9 am and 7 pm local time.

The U.S. military announced Wednesday it has completed its withdrawal from Iraq – ending a 12-year mission to fight the Daesh terrorist group – after The last troops departed a northern air base under an agreement between Baghdad and Washington.
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds.
Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country's increasing strength and sovereignty.
The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the northern semi-autonomous region. Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought – with little success so far – to disarm.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an "orderly departure" from the air base in Erbil, in northern Iraq's Kurdish-majority region.
"This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS (Daesh) as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region," he said. "It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a "new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making and balanced partnerships with its friends."
He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against Daesh and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight Daesh, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the terrorist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region.
Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in northern Iraq have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish authorities said that the region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
"The departure of the United States from the ... Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern," the statement said.
Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.
"The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that "any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means."

The Voice of Armenia: 100 years of public broadcasting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:45:48 UTC
18:45:48 KST

Wednesday 30 September 2026 12:16
Wednesday, 30 September 2026, 12:16
PHOTO Armenian Public Radio
Font size
The Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) and the Public Radio of Armenia are partners within the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). This year, our Armenian colleagues are celebrating the 100th anniversary of their broadcasting service. To mark the occasion, they have sent the foreign-language services of Radio Bulgaria a special presentation on the history of the broadcaster and its relationship with its audience from 1926 to the present day.
Listen!
If you look at a world map or globe today, you will hardly notice Armenia. Among the world's 194 countries, we rank 138th in terms of area, covering just under 30,000 square kilometres. Only when you zoom in does Armenia come into view. Zoom in further and you can make out a country whose outline resembles the profile of a woman's face. Perhaps that is why we Armenians call our country "Mother Armenia".
But today's conversation is not about Armenia or its historical past. We would like to talk about an event that took place exactly 100 years ago, on 1 September 1926. On that day, the Armenian Radio addressed its listeners over the airwaves for the first time. The historic words were: "Listen! Listen! This is the Yerevan Radio Broadcasting Station speaking."
Regular broadcasts eventually began on 15 June 1927.
From 1929 onwards, programmes were presented for the first time by professional radio announcers.
Today, practically anyone with a smartphone and an internet connection can start a live broadcast from virtually anywhere. Decades ago, however, this was an insurmountable technical challenge even for many specialised institutions equipped with dedicated technology, let alone for individuals.
On 1 May 1934, the editorial team responsible for social and political programmes organised the first-ever live radio report from Yerevan's Lenin Square, today's Republic Square. It was presented by radio announcer Yegishe Hovhannisyan.
The first live sports broadcast took place on 15 September 1937 at Yerevan's Republican Stadium, during a football match between Spartak Yerevan and Dynamo Moscow.
The tragic fate of the Armenian people scattered us Armenians across the world. The time came when Armenian Radio decided to produce and broadcast programmes for our compatriots living abroad as well.
In 1947, the Armenian Radio began preparing programmes for the diaspora. The first such programme was broadcast on 10 September 1947 at 7 p.m. And the first words were: "This is Yerevan, this is Yerevan..."
Yerevan, Armenia
PHOTO Reuters
Alongside all this, public broadcasting has another fundamental mission: preserving our audio heritage. Whether it is called an archive, a phonotheque, or a golden collection, the essence remains the same: safeguarding Armenia's national cultural treasures and passing them on to future generations.
Today, the Amernian Radio phonotheque contains 102,422 audio tapes with a total duration of 12,324 hours. Naturally, these recordings have been digitised, so they can no longer be lost, erased, destroyed by fire or simply disappear. They include music recordings, radio dramas, speeches by prominent figures, addresses and broadcasts, and by no means only in Armenian or exclusively related to Armenia. We also preserve recordings in the languages of many other peoples.
The Public Radio of Armenia has a rich heritage and a wealth of wonderful stories born out of collaborations with prominent Armenian writers, composers and artists.
Another distinctive feature of our broadcaster is that we have four resident musical ensembles. The oldest of them, the Aram Merangulian Honoured Ensemble of Folk Instruments, is also celebrating its 100th anniversary this year. They are joined by the Estrada Symphony Orchestra, the Sayat-Nova Ashugh Ensemble and the Arevik Children's Music Ensemble.
It was precisely the Arevik ensemble that represented Armenia at the Junior Eurovision Song Contest for the first time in 2007, finishing in second place. In 2021, Armenia's Junior Eurovision representative, Maléna, won the competition, and as a result, the following year's contest, in 2022, was held in Armenia.
Incidentally, Armenia also hosted the international Eurovision Young Musicians competition this year, in 2026.
Radio today is no longer simply radio. It is a multimedia platform, a major media holding comprising seven radio programmes, dozens of large and small recording studios, a website and video productions. The website of Radio Armenia is available in twelve languages and features both the languages of Armenia's national minorities and those of the countries in the region.
Today, the Public Radio of Armenia is a full member of the European Broadcasting Union. On this occasion, we would also like to congratulate our four partner broadcasters from Ireland, Croatia, Lithuania and Finland, which are likewise celebrating their centenaries this year.
Wherever you live, whoever you may be, if you ever find yourself in Yerevan, come and visit the Public Radio of Armenia. Right here at the entrance, you will be greeted by our singing statue, from which beautiful, sophisticated Armenian music can be heard every day. Our building, constructed in 1956 and still serving radio and the public to this day, is known as "Radiotun", the Radio House. This is our home. The home of our national culture, our music, literature, spirit and spoken word."
PHOTO Armenian Public Radio
On the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Armenian Radio, we wish our colleagues continued success in their dedicated efforts to promote and preserve the cultural wealth of their country!
Edited by R. Petkova

Philidelphia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:45:16 UTC
18:45:16 KST

Philadelphia seems to attract Google Maps weirdness. The last time I opened a map to verify some local directions, it popped up an image of the Grand Concourse ceiling of the 30th St. Amtrak station, identified as "Philidelphia Train ticket office":
And the Quadrangle, a student residence where I live, always gets identified as weird fragments of nearby stuff — most recently as the (entire?) Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, which is actually a dozen or so (other) buildings in the neighborhood:
In fact "the Quadrangle" is the whole rectangle + triangle, not just the western triangular part, and it contains three designated "College Houses", not just "Riepe". In the past, I used to click the Google Maps "Suggest an edit" button, correcting labels like "Pathology Laboratory" and "Helen's Hair House". But now I just accept the metaphors.
Googlemaps didn’t exist when I lived in Fluff’ya, but it has its share of linguistic anomalies not least of which is the ‘Philly O’ and ‘wooder’ for ‘water’. The linguistics lab was right near Mark’s triangle-quadrangle. My 42-yr-old son was born at HUP and I worked right across the street (as did Victor) in Williams Hall for 7 years. I was standing right there when a cop cursed, tackled and cuffed a crook right next to a cart selling breakfast bacon-egg hoagies, and I knew many a colleague who got mugged if they made the mistake of walking further west than 42nd st.
Here's a theory: There is a small group of fun-loving students who are sending in these weird things to Google as "corrections". Not easy to test, I know…
One can find a few other instances of "Philidelphia" out there, including in google-books-corpus versions of texts you would think would have been professionally proofread before publication. One thing about English orthography is that it's probably even harder to reverse-engineer spelling from pronunciation for reduced vowels than unreduced ones, and the second vowel here is reduced.
The other question, though, is what it's reduced to. Schwa or something else? With one candidate for "something else" being closer to KIT than schwa is, i.e. the one in the second syllable of "roses" for those who distinguish that from "Rosa's." Which of those do I have in Philadelphia? I'm actually not sure now that I'm self-conscious about it. But the non-schwa alternative ("a distinct near-close central unrounded vowel [ɪ̈] (or equivalently [ɨ̞]," to quote wikipedia) might go better with an "i" spelling.
Surely over the decades Labov must have had a grad student or two gather data on exactly which reduced vowel local speakers use here (or what the ratio was, if it varied)? It seemed seasonally appropriate to consult Hall & Oates' "Fall in Philadelphia" (from 1972), and in the chorus when they sing the title in harmony I'm not entirely convinced they're both using the same reduced vowel.
The other source of spelling variation might be "analogy-to-Philip" versus "analogy-to-philanthropic." But do those have different vowels in their respective second syllables? Does it vary by speaker?
Google Maps locates a book store in the middle of an intersection near my suburb's train station. In eight years of crossing that intersection almost every day, I've never seen it. But then again it doesn't show on either the aerial or street view.
I have intruded on Professor Packard's privacy by consulting his online CV to determine exactly which years he was in Philadelphia. And it was after Frank Rizzo was no longer in office and after the Phillies had finally won the World Series, so the golden age was over and the distinctiveness of local speech (which had supposedly once induced Labov to give up a pretty stable job in NYC …) was no doubt already on the wane.

Somali waters saw widespread piracy between 2008 and 2018. Piracy declined for several years before re-emerging in late 2023 amid rising security tensions in the region.

Rae detention center pressure exposes gaps in state migration response

Rae detention center pressure exposes gaps in state migration response
The extra burden on Rae municipality caused by migration pressure may become a symbol of the state's inability to cope with illegal migration, migration expert Kert Valdaru said.
Illegal migrants who entered Estonia and were detained have put pressure on Rae municipality's child protection workers, who must represent people in the local detention center who claim to be minors. Estonia has detained 269 illegal migrants this year, more than seventy of whom said they were minors. Later checks showed that only two were actually under 18.
Valdaru said the situation around the detention center shows how the state shifts its responsibilities onto the municipality without providing enough resources.
Rae municipality's detention center may become a symbol that the state cannot handle migration. I think it is absurd that the detention center is a state institution, but suddenly the municipality is told to go there and take care of things, Valdaru said.
Figuratively speaking, a state high school is built, children arrive in September, and then the state calls the municipality and says, send teachers here to teach. The state must take greater responsibility for dealing with unaccompanied minors in the Rae detention center and provide better resources to the municipality to cover the costs, Valdaru added.
Tartu City Council member Sandra Laur said illegal border crossers place an unreasonable burden on the municipality's social system.
In Rae municipality, these minor cases already make up one-third of child protection specialists' workload. Instead of dealing with our own people, we have to care for and feed them at a time when our own residents are struggling with the cost of living, Laur said.
Narva City Council member and former interior minister Katri Raik noted that the only current detention center is overloaded and under pressure.
We have one detention center in Rae municipality and it is overcrowded. Do we actually need to expand its capacity, Raik asked. The question remains what the municipality's obligation is and whether the state is honest and gentlemanly enough to reimburse the municipality afterward, because hybrid attacks have become part of our daily lives, Raik added.
At the same time, Raik said she does not see expanding the detention center to Narva as a realistic option.
Police and Border Guard Board Deputy Director General Veiko Kommusaar said the state is doing everything it can to curb migration pressure coming from Latvia, but fully closing the Estonia–Latvia border is not a solution.
Our main effort must be at the European Union's external border and in catching smugglers. Closing the border with Latvia would cost €8 million over thirty days and would not solve the migration problem as a whole, Kommusaar said.

Mumbai: Despite the triple shock of below normal monsoon, West Asia conflict pushing up crude and commodity prices and US tariff hurting Indian exports India inc is doing well with the ratio of upgrdes to down grade at a decadal high of 3.2x. According to rating agency ICRA the sound fianncail position of the corporartes is due to extended deleveraging by businesses and bank non-performing assets being at an all time low.ICRA said credit quality remained strong in H1 FY27, with the credit ratio rising to 3.2x from 2.8x a year earlier and 3.1x in FY26, well above the 10-year average of 1.5x. The annualised upgrade rate moderated to 14% from 17%, but downgrades fell to a multi-year low of 4%; defaults stood at 0.04%, with no investment-grade defaults.“Indian corporates enter H2 FY2027 from a position of strength, supported by healthy balance sheets and substantial liquidity buffers,” said K Ravichandran, executive vice-president and chief rating officer, ICRA. He flagged elevated crude prices, deficient monsoon, inflation and US tariff uncertainty as risks, but said strong balance sheets should prevent broad-based credit stress.Power, real estate, auto components, finance and capital goods, together about half of ICRA’s rated portfolio, contributed around 50% of upgrades.
Upgrades mainly reflected stronger businesses and parents, lower project risks, higher scale, improved asset quality and deleveraging.ICRA expects crude prices, a 12% monsoon deficit and weaker reservoir levels to weigh on consumption and agricultural growth. It sees agricultural GVA growth slowing to 1% in FY27 from 3.3%, while retail inflation may average 5% against 2.1% in FY26.
GDP growth is expected to moderate to 7.1% from 7.8% in Q1. Rural-linked and discretionary sectors may slow, while microfinance collections, vehicle-finance AUM growth and fleet-operator asset quality could weaken.ICRA expects any stress to remain granular, supported by healthy corporate balance sheets, bank asset quality and capitalisation. US tariff uncertainty remains an additional risk, particularly for exporters and generic pharmaceuticals.Corporate leverage is at a decade-low 2.0x, with cash covering nearly half of total debt. Policy support, public investment and spending on infrastructure and clean energy should provide further buffers against external shocks.

Alar Karis embarks on farewell whistle-stop tour of neighboring countries
President Alar Karis has set off on a round of official visits to Estonia's nearest neighboring allied countries ahead of leaving office next month.
The head of state is being accompanied by First Lady Sirje Karis on the whistle-stop tour, which takes in Germany, Poland and Sweden, as well as Finland, Latvia and Lithuania.
The purpose is to thank the heads of state in these lands for their close, trusting and friendly cooperation during Karis' term, which started in 2021, and to reaffirm these alliances for the future.
"In my role as head of state, I have learned over the past five years that it is in the most difficult moments that you realize who your friends are and how much trust is worth," President Karis remarked.
"Estonia has been lucky: We are surrounded by countries with which we have far more in common than just geography. We are united by shared values and security, a sense of responsibility for the future of our region, and a warm friendship that has developed over the years. Those values are held by people who know how to listen to one another and whose word you can trust. That is what I would like to express my gratitude for as my time in office comes to an end," the president went on via a press release.
Estonia is linked to all of the countries he will be visiting by close bilateral relations and everyday cooperation within the EU and NATO, as well as the additional links to Finland, Sweden, Latvia and Lithuania via the Nordic-Baltic or NB8 cooperation, which is only growing in significance.
He underscored the role played in Europe's security by each of the countries he is visiting, as well as their contribution to strengthening NATO's eastern flank and their support for Ukraine, as well as the fruitful relations Estonia enjoys with them in the spheres of education, culture and the economy.
"Recent years have shown us just how important it is to have friends and allies by your side with whom you share a common understanding of European security, freedom and a rules-based world order," the president continued. "Russia's aggression against Ukraine has boosted our cooperation even further, and brought the nations of the Baltic Sea region closer together than ever before."
The final round of visits really started at the end of August with an official visit to Latvia, hosted by President Edgars Rinkēvičs. This was followed by the 81st UN General Assembly in New York last week, which the president attended.
The presidential couple have already this week met with Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Mrs Elke Büdenbender in Berlin, followed on the Tuesday by trips to Warsaw, meeting President Karol Tadeusz Nawrocki and Marta Nawrocki, and to Lithuania, where they were received by President Gitanas Nausėda and First Lady Diana Nausėdienė in Vilnius.
Still to come is a visit with President Alexander Stubb and Suzanne Innes-Stub in Helsinki on Thursday evening, rounded off on Friday by a trip across the Baltic to Stockholm, where Alar and Sirje Karis will be hosted by King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia of Sweden.
Alar Karis became head of state in October 2021 and formally hands over the presidency to Ülle Madise on Monday, October 12 this year.
Ülle Madise's replacement as justice chancellor still needs appointing
One aspect of the succession which is being clarified is how the next Chancellor of Justice will be chosen and by whom. Since Madise is the incumbent chancellor, it is not clear yet if she will nominate her successor, or if President Karis will do it ahead of leaving office.
Epp-Mare Kukemelk, spokesperson for the Office of the President, told ERR "The head of state will submit a proposal for a candidate for chancellor of justice to the Riigikogu in the coming weeks".
The Chancellor of Justice is appointed by the Riigikogu at the proposal of the president, for a seven-year term. Madise was several years into her second term when she was elected head of state.
MP Madis Timpson (Reform), who chairs the Riigikogu Legal Affairs Committee, noted it would be wise for the potential nomination to be run past the Riigikogu factions first, though no such discussions have yet taken place between the committee and the president.
Timpson noted there are "certainly quite a few people in Estonia whose knowledge, experience and professional background would enable them to perform the duties of chancellor of justice very well" and stressed the need for political neutrality for that office.
Madise was elected Estonia's next president in the first round of voting at the Riigikogu on September 2.

Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
BRUSSELS – Russia has warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a “dangerous and reckless course” that entailed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict”.
The document said this included the possibility “of Russian strikes against decision-making centres in the alliance’s member states right from the outset of the conflict”.
“Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” said the text, classed as a “non-paper” – diplomatic jargon for an informal document.
In addition to the private warning, Russian embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing NATO of escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad.
Russia also rejected Western allegations that it poses a threat to Europe.
The statements said Russia had no intention of attacking NATO countries but warned that any aggression against Kaliningrad – a heavily militarised Russian territory that is sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania – would be met with the strongest possible response.
The warnings highlight a sharp rise in tension between Russia and European countries, which accuse Moscow of stepping up a “hybrid war” on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
NATO slams ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’
NATO spokeswoman Allison Hart confirmed Russia had sent a non-paper to the alliance but did not disclose its contents.
“We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia. We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine,” she said.
A senior European defence official said: “(This is the) first time since (the) Cold War that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious.”
A NATO diplomat said: “I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible. (It) reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine.” REUTERS

Huang Tzu-chien (黃子謙), vice chair of the union, said the demand for a 5% raise was on par with the level of increase in minimum wage this year. Low pay has led to some employees leaving the company, he told Radio Taiwan International.
The company has about 1,600 employees in Taiwan, nearly 1,000 of whom are union members. Some 96% of the members voted in favor of the strike, which is scheduled to begin Monday and continue through Wednesday.
Ahead of the strike, Shen began an 80-hour hunger strike Tuesday outside the company’s factory in Douliu, Yunlin.
Ministry of Labor spokesperson Chin Shih-ping (金士平) told Radio Taiwan International the ministry supported its lawful exercise of the right to strike and said the union had followed the legally mandated procedures before calling for a strike. The employer may not take adverse action against employees participating in the strike, Chin added.
AGC said it respected the union’s right to express its views in accordance with the law and would continue communicating with its employees, per Public Television Service.
The company said the two sides had agreed during their first negotiation to continue discussions, adding that it had proactively invited the union to a second round of talks on Sept. 24. The negotiation fell through after the union requested a proposal authorized by AGC’s headquarters.

09:40:28 UTC
18:40:28 KST

German company STARK has presented its new unmanned surface vessel (USV), the Vanta 12.
STARK told Militarnyi about the new USV.
The Vanta 12 is designed to conduct reconnaissance and surveillance, electronic warfare (EW), maritime area patrols, and strike missions.
The unmanned surface vessel is 12 meters long, can reach speeds over 40 knots, and has a range of up to 1,200 nautical miles (approximately 2,222 km). Its stated payload capacity is up to two tonnes.
According to the developer, the vessel is designed to remain at sea for several weeks without returning to base.
“Hybrid threats are challenging because they often lack a clear point of onset. Suspicious activity near a cable or energy facility does not necessarily indicate an attack, but it is important to detect such activity in a timely manner, monitor how the situation develops, and respond rapidly. Therefore, persistent maritime presence and surveillance are becoming increasingly important to protect critical infrastructure. Given the growing use of unmanned aerial systems, the ability to conduct electronic warfare at sea is becoming equally important,” Maksym Cherkis, Chief Operating Officer of STARK Ukraine, shared.
The platform uses autonomous navigation and software incorporating AI capabilities. Its modular architecture allows for the integration of various sensor suites, electronic warfare systems, and weapons.
The unmanned platform is controlled using Minerva, a system the company developed to integrate remotely operated systems of different types into a unified command-and-control architecture.
The Vanta 12 is equipped with ten Cascade loitering munitions developed by STARK, which were publicly unveiled at the Eurosatory international defense exhibition in June. The company has also launched the munitions from a maritime platform.
The loitering munition is launched from a dedicated tubular container. The Cascade has a maximum flight range of up to 100 km, a cruising speed of approximately 100 km/h, and a terminal dive speed of up to 220 km/h. Its payload capacity can reach 4.5 kg.
In addition, the Vanta 12 has been integrated with four Sea Venom anti-ship missiles manufactured by MBDA. These lightweight anti-ship missiles were jointly developed by the United Kingdom and France and are designed to engage surface targets, including corvette-class warships.
The Vanta 12’s capabilities were tested in September during the REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal. REPMUS is an annual large-scale exercise and experimentation program focused on robotic and unmanned maritime systems, organized by the Portuguese Navy with the participation of NATO structures and the European Defence Agency.
During REPMUS, the Vanta 12 operated alongside crewed and other unmanned platforms. According to STARK, the vessel conducted simulated combat scenarios, while the Minerva system controlled the platform and launched the Cascade loitering munitions.
STARK is a European defense technology company that develops and manufactures unmanned systems for air and maritime operations, as well as software for their control and management. The company operates in Germany, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Greece, and Sweden.
The Vanta 12 is a further development of STARK’s family of unmanned surface vessels, which also includes smaller platforms. In August, the company delivered the first Seetaube unmanned surface vessel to the German Armed Forces. The vessel was developed on the Vanta platform.
To scale up production of the Vanta family, STARK is partnering with German shipbuilder Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft (FSG). The companies plan to expand the industrial base for manufacturing these platforms in Germany and other European countries.
Militarnyi previously reported on the opening of STARK’s Ukrainian R&D center and the delivery of Virtus strike drones to Ukraine, which had previously undergone testing in combat conditions.

Ukrainian FPV operators struck a Russian T-54 deep behind the lines, releasing footage of the engagement.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces had covered the aging tank with additional protective structures in an attempt to shield it from aerial strikes. The improvised protection did not stop the FPV.
The T-54 traces its origins to the immediate post-World War II period and carries a 100mm main gun, making it one of the oldest mass-produced tank designs Russia has pulled from long-term storage and returned to wartime use.
According to the Skif Griffins, this particular vehicle had traveled an extraordinary distance before reaching the battlefield.
The tank was reportedly brought from storage facilities in Russia’s Far East—almost 9,000 kilometers away.
After surviving decades in reserve and a journey spanning much of Russia, it was ultimately detected in the Russian rear by Ukrainian drone operators and struck by an FPV.
The T-54’s reappearance on the battlefield also shows how deeply Russia has drawn on its armored reserves during the war.
In the decades after the T-54 entered service, the Soviet Union and later Russia fielded successive generations of tanks including the T-72, T-80 and T-90.
Yet vehicles whose basic design dates back to the first years after World War II are again being pulled from storage and sent toward the front. The Skif Griffins argue that the return of such old armor points to continuing pressure on Russia’s stocks of newer tanks and ammunition.

In Pictures
Photos: A journalist is crowned king in Uganda
The death of King Oyo Nyimba in August triggered widespread grief and a succession dispute in Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom.
A journalist has been crowned king of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom, a traditional monarchy plunged into grief and a succession dispute following the death of its “boy king” last month.
Prince Edward Rukidi Nyabongo, long employed as a broadcaster and editor with the state-run Uganda Broadcasting Corporation, took his regnal name after performing night-time rituals before being ushered into the palace.
He was formally unveiled to his subjects on Tuesday in Fort Portal, a town in western Uganda near the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were abolished in the 1960s by a republican president seeking to unify the newly independent country, but were restored in 1993.
While cultural monarchs hold no constitutional powers and are barred from partisan politics, they retain significant influence as custodians of tradition and identity.
Speaking at the ceremony, President Yoweri Museveni urged traditional leaders to promote local languages.
Nyabongo, in a short address, promised to be a unifying figure and told the New Vision newspaper that “heritage must be matched by discipline and hard work”, describing royal descent as a duty rather than an entitlement.
Nyabongo was not high in the line of succession. Elders of the ruling Babiito clan selected him from a pool of eligible princes after King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV died of cancer in August at the age of 34, reportedly without a publicly acknowledged heir.
The queen mother, Best Kemigisa, has challenged the decision, claiming Oyo left a young son whose identity will be revealed “at the right time”. The prospect of a “Baby Oyo” has stirred supporters on social media and raised questions over the legitimacy of Nyabongo’s coronation.
