Pompeii’s 2,000-year-old eruption just gave scientists a better clock for Earth’s past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:37:41 UTC
18:37:41 KST

Pompeii’s 2,000-year-old eruption just gave scientists a better clock for Earth’s past
Pompeii’s devastating eruption is helping scientists put far more precise dates on some of the biggest events in Earth’s history.
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Mount Vesuvius’ famous 79 CE eruption has given scientists a remarkably precise benchmark for dating events deep in Earth’s past. The improved technique could sharpen the timelines of volcanic eruptions, asteroid impacts, extinctions, and other major moments in geological history.
- Share:
Nearly 2,000 years ago, Pliny the Younger documented what he witnessed when Mt. Vesuvius erupted, burying Pompeii and killing his uncle, Pliny the Elder. His account did more than preserve the story of one of history's most famous volcanic disasters. It also recorded enough information about when the eruption occurred to give modern scientists an unusually precise historical reference point for testing volcanic dating techniques.
Researchers from the Berkeley Geochronology Center, UC Berkeley and the University of Padua in Italy now report in Science Advances that this historical benchmark has helped them significantly improve the precision of argon-argon dating. By calibrating the method against the inferred eruption date of Aug. 24, 79 CE, they have strengthened what is already one of the most widely useful tools for determining the ages of rocks and volcanic events.
The advance could help geologists, paleontologists and archaeologists assign more reliable dates to events in Earth's past. That includes eruptions from volcanoes that continue to pose risks to heavily populated regions around Mexico City, Naples and Yogyakarta in Indonesia. The improved calibration could also help researchers verify other dating techniques, including carbon-14 dating of organic materials and uranium-lead dating of rocks that formed billions of years ago early in Earth's history.
A More Precise Clock for Volcanic History
"If you want to put together the eruptive history of a volcano in relatively recent time, precision and accuracy really count," said study leader Paul Renne, a Berkeley professor in residence of earth and planetary science and director of the independent Berkeley Geochronology Center. "The study shows that you can achieve that kind of highly useful precision and accuracy into the historical realm."
Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the correct value, while precision reflects how consistently that measurement can be reproduced. To test the recalibrated method, the researchers examined eight samples of sanidine, a potassium-containing volcanic mineral from Vesuvius.
The argon-argon measurements placed the eruption 1,938 ±13 years before the minerals were analyzed in 2025. Based on the historical evidence preserved in Pliny the Younger's writings, the minerals were actually 1,946 years old. That corresponds to a precision of 0.7% and an accuracy of 0.4%.
"This lets us more precisely infer causality between events in the geologic record, for example a meteor impact structure and a mass extinction," Renne said.
About a decade ago, Renne used argon-argon dating to establish precise ages for a meteor impact, major volcanic eruptions in India and the extinction of the dinosaurs. All three events occurred within a span of only a few tens of thousands of years about 66 million years ago. Those measurements bolstered the idea that the asteroid impact intensified volcanic activity, creating a one-two punch that contributed to the extinction of all non-avian dinosaurs.
Pliny's Date Helps Refine a Radioactive Clock
Graduate student Caroline Hasler also closely examined historical records surrounding the Vesuvius eruption. Her work allowed the team to validate the August 24 date attributed to Pliny the Younger to within two months.
That historical constraint helped researchers improve their measurement of the half-life governing the decay of potassium-40 into argon-40, the process that underlies argon-argon dating. The revised half-life is 12.044 billion years, give or take 0.088 billion, making it twice as precise as the earlier value derived from nuclear physics.
Pumice From Oplontis Provides Better Samples
Renne and his colleagues had already used sanidine from pumice produced during the 79 CE eruption to test argon-argon dating. After their 1997 analysis, they predicted that future work could reduce the uncertainty to less than 1%.
They have now reached that target with the help of improved pumice samples, a more advanced mass spectrometer and updated neutron irradiation methods.
Argon-argon dating is based on the natural radioactive decay of potassium-40 in volcanic rock into argon-40. Argon-40 is generally not present in minerals before an eruption occurs. Researchers expose rock samples to neutrons, converting the non-radioactive potassium isotope potassium-39 into argon-39. They then measure the relative amounts of argon-40 and argon-39. A larger proportion of argon-40 indicates an older sample.
In 1998, co-author Andrea Marzoli of the University of Padua collected new pumice from Oplontis, another Roman settlement buried by the eruption. These samples contained more potassium than those used previously and came from material released during the earliest part of the eruption.
Why the Earliest Pumice Matters
Magma beneath stratovolcanoes such as Vesuvius can separate into layers. Iron and magnesium tend to become concentrated near the bottom of a magma chamber, while more soluble elements such as potassium remain closer to the top.
Because of this structure, potassium-rich magma is generally among the first material expelled during an eruption. It therefore settles near the bottom of the resulting ash and pumice deposits. Marzoli's samples came from these lower deposits, making them particularly valuable for argon-argon dating.
Despite their potential, the samples were placed in storage and remained unanalyzed for decades. Several years ago, graduate students Hasler, Anthony Fuentes and Andy Tholt, working with postdoctoral fellow Jack Carter in Renne's laboratory, proposed returning to Marzoli's nearly 30-year-old material to see whether it could improve upon the 1997 measurements.
The researchers had already published work aimed at reconciling argon-argon dating with uranium-lead dating, the two methods most widely used to determine the ages of rocks. Achieving a more precise calibration of argon-argon dating was an important part of that larger effort.
"They came up with a Bayesian scheme -- published in 2025 -- to intercalibrate these two most important geochronometers that we have, which have not been giving us consistent results over the years," Renne said.
The Vesuvius measurements from 1997 were included in that earlier calibration, but their uncertainties were large enough that they had relatively little influence on the final result. The newly refined Vesuvius measurements carry much greater weight.
"It was really just a combination of better samples, instrumental advantage and a more concerted effort. All of those things came together," Renne added. He credits co-author Bill Cassata with a major role in developing the analytical strategy and data analysis.
Reexamining the Date of the Vesuvius Eruption
Before the team could use the eruption as a dependable benchmark, Hasler needed to address a long-standing disagreement over exactly when Vesuvius erupted.
Some historians have proposed that the eruption occurred later in the fall of 79 CE. Their argument partly rests on a coin recovered from Pompeii that they believe could only have been produced in September.
Hasler compared that coin with other Roman coins from the same period and concluded that it was probably minted before September. The researchers nevertheless allowed for a two-month uncertainty around the eruption date. That uncertainty had little effect on the calibration of the dating technique itself, but it was important when determining the half-life of potassium-40.
Connecting Earth's Different Dating Methods
Renne said the improved accuracy and precision of argon-argon dating should also make it especially useful for calibrating radiocarbon dating. Radiocarbon dating is the dominant technique for establishing the ages of organic materials such as wood when they are younger than about 55,000 years.
"We're hoping to really unify as many geologic dating methods as we can by using the same mathematics, the same Bayesian approach, and just bringing more data, more raw observations into that mix," he said. "But argon-argon dating is always going to be a standard -- it's going to be an important calibrant in that sense."
Along with improving calibration of the argon/argon dating method, Renne said the findings establish a new benchmark for how accurately the technique can determine the ages of relatively recent volcanic eruptions. The results show that argon-argon dating can now reach decadal accuracy for events that occurred within recorded history.
The work was funded by the National Science Foundation (2102788, 2030393), the Ann and Gordon Getty Foundation and the Berkeley Geochronology Center.

Flydubai pilot stabbed in attempt to down Israel-bound plane
Published September 30, 2026last updated September 30, 2026
An Indian pilot was stabbed by his copilot on Wednesday in a failed attempt to crash a Flydubai plane that was bound for Israel.
After he was stabbed, Captain Smit Machchhar opened the cockpit in time for other passengers to intervene and the plane was ultimately able to land safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Israel's defense minister, Israel Katz, said that "an attempted jihadist terror attack" had been thwarted after several passengers subdued the copilot.
Flydubai confirmed that all passengers were safe. It later announced it had suspended flights to and from Israel amid an ongoing investigation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has now ordered authorities to "ramp up" security on both Israeli and non-Israeli carriers following the Flydubai flight incident.
Passengers return to Israel
On Wednesday evening, passengers from the diverted Flydubai flight arrived in Israel on a replacement plane, where numerous relatives were waiting for them.
Netanyahu also met with some of the passengers. A video posted to Netanyahu's X account showed him at the Tel Aviv airport meeting a man called Yaniv Hayoun who still had blood on his shirt after the midflight altercation.
The video described Yaniv as one of the passengers who entered the aircraft's cockpit.
Later, Netanyahu named the Indian pilot who was injured in an altercation with his co-pilot, who allegedly attempted to crash the Flydubai flight.
"My salute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery. Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on social media.
"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar is in stable condition and is being treated in a Tabuk hospital after an emergency landing.
 
Meanwhile, Israeli Foreign Minister said that he spoke with his UAE counterpart Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
"Mutual determination was expressed to strengthen relations between the countries on all levels and to collaborate against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability in the region," Saar wrote on X.
Saar also spoke with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul over the phone.
Wadephul said that he strongly condemned the incident as a serious attack on civil aviation. He added that his thoughts were with those who survived the flight and with those who feared for the lives of their loved ones. Wadephul also said that the circumstances surrounding the incident must be clarified quickly and thoroughly.
Later, US President Donald Trump announced he had discussed the Flydubai flight incident with Netanyahu. Trump said Netanyahu told him an Israeli plumber had helped prevent the aircraft from crashing.
"I did speak to Bibi Netanyahu at length about this event, and it seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot," Trump told reporters.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.
"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.
Later, a Flydubai spokesperson said that the reasons for an altercation that "occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073" remained unknown and were under formal investigation.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts," a spokesperson said in a statement published by the AFP news agency.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 initially showed a second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, diverting back toward Dubai. It later showed the aircraft continuing toward Tel Aviv. There was no immediate explanation for the change.
How far did the plane fall?
The Israeli news portal Ynet reported that the aircraft entered a steep descent and that passengers helped one pilot prevent the other from crashing the plane.
Flight tracking data shows the aircraft suddenly losing around half its altitude as it neared Saudi Arabia's border with Jordan.
The plane dropped from nearly 34,000 feet (10,360 meters) at 05:21 GMT/UTC to below 17,000 feet (5,180 meters) at 05:22 GMT/UTC, according to Flightradar data.
Israel's Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military scrambled fighter jets amid initial fears of a possible hijacking. That possibility was later dismissed, according to the reports.
Israeli minister says 'attempted jihadist terror attack' thwarted
Israeli leaders announced that a "jihadist" pilot had attempted to crash a Flydubai plane carrying mostly Israeli passengers.
In a video message, Netanyahu said that "during the flight... one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board."
He added that passengers and crew subdued the attacker, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where the pilot was arrested.
"I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster," Netanyahu said.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz described the incident as "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was "thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers."
Earlier, Netanyahu's office said he had held consultations over the incident and was monitoring developments.
"The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel," his office said.
An unnamed senior Israeli government official told Channel 12 that a major disaster had been averted.
Meanwhile, Israel's Foreign Ministry informed its diplomats that the incident was "an attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords."
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

Six Flags shuts California roller coaster at centre of lawsuits
LOS ANGELES – Six Flags Entertainment is permanently retiring the X2 roller coaster, which has been the subject of lawsuits alleging that the ride caused brain injuries.
“While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Brian Oerding, the president of the company’s Magic Mountain Park in Valencia, California, said in a statement.
“Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”
The X2 ride opened in 2008 and featured 360-degree rotating seats that flipped riders forward and backward at speeds approaching 76 miles per hour (122kmh).
More than 16 million people have ridden it, according to the company.
More than 100 people have claimed injury, according to the lawsuits.
Six Flags shares were down 4.3% as of 1.45pm in New York (1.45am, Singapore time) on Sept 29.

AI firms set sights on data from bankrupt companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:34:52 UTC
18:34:52 KST

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Artificial intelligence (AI) companies are on the lookout for large data sets from bankrupt firms to train their models, resulting in a new commercial market and a data security crisis in the global tech sector.
US tech giant Google and AI startup Micro1 submitted multimillion-dollar bids to buy internal communications and passenger data from Spirit Airlines, which had filed for bankruptcy.
Suppliers and workers are concerned about the potential leak of sensitive information.
Google bid $10 million for the data set, while Micro1 is willing to pay $12.5 million.
Spirit Airlines sold 27 aging Airbus aircraft for $668 million on Sept. 25 amid financial difficulties.
Some 97.5 million passenger records collected since 1992 are on the sales list, according to court documents filed with the New York Bankruptcy Court.
The database contains 13.7 million email addresses, loyalty program information and data from partner firms.
The package also includes personnel files for more than 175,000 workers and 1.5 million internal communications extracted from various channels like email and Microsoft Teams.
The court will approve the sale at a hearing expected to take place on Wednesday.
Companies selling their data while filing for bankruptcy has become a global business model.
Commercial information like financial data is not covered by data protection laws, leaving the entire process to be governed by contractual agreements, legal experts say.

No, Macron isn't planning to trigger a war with Russia to stay in power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:34:37 UTC
18:34:37 KST

Allegations are circulating online that Macron will put France at war with Russia to postpone elections and stay in power as his second consecutive term comes to an end. However, the country's constitution makes this unfeasible in many ways.
For months now, European leaders and NATO have been raising alarms over a sharp rise in Russian hybrid threats with increasing urgency, calls that have been echoed by French President Emmanuel Macron.
A slew of social media users, however, are alleging he is not expressing his concerns for security purposes, but for his own benefit.
As French presidents cannot serve more than two consecutive terms, Macron will have to hand over the reins of power to his successor following the 2027 presidential election, set to take place next spring.
For this reason, according to several social media posts, Macron is exaggerating the threat and drawing France further into the war between Ukraine and Russia, as a means to justify a potential war with Moscow. The end goal? To cancel or postpone these elections and so stay in power, they claim.
Such posts have garnered thousands of views, and appear to have been fuelled by a meeting that Macron held with presidential hopefuls and party leaders in mid-September to brief them on the current security challenges facing France.
However, this is an unlikely and complicated strategy to implement. To understand why, The Cube, Euronews' verification team, spoke with French constitutional experts.
President cannot declare war
The main factor that pours cold water on these claims is the fact that the president's powers are limited by the constitution. Specifically, it says that they cannot unilaterally declare war.
"The constitution states that the president is the head of the armed forces," Guillaume Tusseau, constitutional law professor at the Sciences Po Law School, told The Cube. "But in this matter, he has to share his power with the government because the army is placed at the disposal of the government and not of the president of the republic."
"Based on Article 35 of the constitution, only parliament can authorise an armed intervention by French armed forces, and the government has to present that to parliament," he added. "So it's not the decision [that can be] formally [made by] the president."
Should a president decide to launch a war without consultation, this would constitute a violation of the constitution, which in turn could trigger impeachment proceedings.
Even if, for example, a country wages a war against France, the constitution still does not stipulate that this would automatically influence the timing of an election.
"The postponing of elections is not automatic at all [in case of a war], and my hunch is that it will be very difficult to [influence the timing]," Tusseau said.
This is because the timeline for elections to take place is clearly detailed in Article 7 of the constitution, which states that elections must be held "no fewer than 20 days and no more than 35 days before" the current president's term ends.
Tusseau noted that the constitution only allows for a limited postponement if one of the candidates dies or is incapacitated a few days before the first round, or between the first and second round.
Additionally, if France were directly under attack, elections could be postponed to guarantee the safety of voters.
"But if we read the constitution, nothing in it allows the president to postpone the elections [for the reasons claimed on social media]," Tusseau said.
Activating Article 16?
One key argument put forward by proponents of the original theory is that Macron would support being at war, as they claim this would allow him to use Article 16 of the constitution, and supposedly allow him to decide to stay in office as he sees fit.
Article 16 does grant the president exceptional powers if the country's institutions, independence and the integrity of its territory or the fulfilment of its international commitments are threatened "in a serious and immediate manner."
However, this still requires consultation with the prime minister, presidents of the assemblies and the Constitutional Council.
Baptiste Charvin, a constitutional lawyer who wrote his comparative law thesis on combating disinformation, explained that this is not the first time people have alluded to the threat of activating Article 16.
"As far as I can recall, it was invoked just before Macron took to the stage to announce the lockdown in 2020, and in 2022 following the outbreak of war in Ukraine," he said.
"The article in question seems to give rise to several misconceptions, and is mainly used to attack the executive, which is often accused of harbouring dictatorial ambitions," he added. "All the more so given that Macron cannot stand for a third term in 2027."
Charvin stressed that a "very high threshold of public calamity" must be reached for Article 16 to be activated. This condition was added during a constitutional amendment, specifically to limit abuses.
Here, he referred to former President Charles de Gaulle activating Article 16 in 1961 to handle the Algiers putsch, a military coup d'état staged by renegade French generals in Algeria.
Tusseau noted a caveat to activating Article 16: it requires the president to protect constitutional values, not amend the constitution.
"The philosophy of the device is that the president can only take legislative and administrative measures, but not constitutional ones, because the constitution establishes the timeframe for elections," he said. "Saying that the president could amend the constitution based on Article 16 is highly dubious for the vast majority of constitutional scholars."
Tusseau added that, while there is no empirical evidence that Macron might be brooding over plans to launch a war and postpone elections, considerations should be made regarding the strength of institutions to protect against abuse.
"Constitutional scholars and citizens must realise that there are weaknesses in our institutions, and, as we saw in Poland, in Hungary, in several constitutional countries, it's always possible to abuse constitutional devices despite careful drafting," he said.

EU considers opening its single market to candidate countries – Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:34:00 EEST
18:34:00 KST

EU considers opening its single market to candidate countries – Politico
Politico has learned that EU candidate countries will be offered unprecedented "gradual integration" into the EU's single market, including frictionless trade and access to research programmes while their applications are being assessed.
Source: a draft European Commission proposal obtained by Politico, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Under the plan, the EU would open its market to candidate countries provided they agree to stand with the EU against hostile states and industrial competitors.
Quote: "Earlier integration would open opportunities for Union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies. The Commission will identify where verified regulatory alignment and enforcement capacity allow deeper participation in research, innovation and industrial cooperation, and wider market access. Priority should go to opportunities that advance accession preparations and meet shared economic and strategic needs."
Details: The review, prepared under the leadership of Alexandre Adam, chief adviser to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, would radically change the EU's approach to the countries in the region. At present, almost all the economic benefits of closer cooperation are reserved for EU members, but no new country has joined the EU since Croatia in 2013.
As part of the review, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro will be offered "roadmaps" designed to accelerate the accession process in the coming years. In other countries, such as North Macedonia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Türkiye, the process is dragging on. Concerns are growing that they could move away from the EU or closer to Russia or China.
Under the Commission's plan, candidate countries will receive economic benefits in proportion to their support for the EU's foreign policy objectives. Access to the single market will also depend on whether they refrain from transferring key technologies to hostile states and trade competitors.
"As industrial and market integration deepens, participation in sensitive sectors must be accompanied by cooperation on investment screening, export controls, sanctions implementation and the protection of sensitive technologies," the review document says.
It notes that market access should take into account strategic alignment, critical dependencies and the ability to manage risks to infrastructure and supply chains.
According to the review, the ultimate goal for candidate countries should be full EU membership, and this period "should be put to full strategic use to both prepare the Union for a larger membership and deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest".
Background:
- The European Commission has postponed until 6 October the presentation of its assessment of how future EU enlargement will affect the EU's key policies and what changes the EU itself may need to accept new member states.
- European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos previously outlined four areas for changes to the EU enlargement process: internal reforms of the EU, strengthened democratic safeguards, gradual integration and transitional measures.

Despite the enemy's efforts to politically isolate Iran, the Iranian delegation had been at the focal attention in New York, Araghchi said, adding that numerous discussions were held with European nations, Persian Gulf littoral states, and other countries, and diplomatic initiatives aimed at breaking the deadlock in foreign policy have been pursued with determination.

Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

'Super Intelligence': Is Trump right to rename AI?
September 30, 2026
What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI).
Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives.
In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.
'AI is not superintelligence'
The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone.
"Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading."
Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence.
Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this."
Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control.
Rebrand won't quell AI fears
"The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. "If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence."
Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States, Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity.
A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence.
Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control.
The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place.
A branding gift to help the AI boom?
Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China.
Yet both Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to.ran tasks they were not meant to.
With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.
"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it's playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."
Superintelligence remains a moving target
While the current AI models keep improving and can already run many tasks on their own, the next step that many labs discuss is AI systems that improve themselves. That's called recursive self-improvement or RSI.
On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.
Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."
In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.
While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.
Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.
At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.
"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

Iran says received US response to its proposal to end the war
Iranian authorities said on Wednesday they received the official US response to their proposal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, state media reported, days after US President Donald Trump rejected the plan.
"At today's cabinet meeting, the American side's proposal was presented to President Masoud Pezeshkian by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi," government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani told the official IRNA news agency, without specifying the content of the reply.
After seven months of since the launch of the US-Israeli war on Iran, indirect talks between the United States and Iran resumed last week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Iran said it has put forward seven conditions for ending hostilities and reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas exports.
The strait lies at the heart of the conflict between the United States and Iran, which began with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic in late February.
Tehran imposed a blockade on Hormuz after the war started, prompting Washington to respond with its own blockade on Iranian ports.
While not all conditions have been made public, Iran is notably demanding a ceasefire across the region, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah has been battling Israeli forces.
It is also demanding the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump rejected the proposal when speaking to the press on Saturday, but Tehran had been awaiting an official response via Qatari mediators.
Fighting has subsided in recent weeks, though Tehran has continued to target ships in the strait.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of the country's military, said on Wednesday that they have been striking small vessels that try to pass through the strait.
"We have been striking ships for quite some time now—specifically the small vessels I mentioned that attempt to pass. We block their passage, yet the US has not retaliated for a while," Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebi told state TV.
The US, meanwhile, has stepped up its economic warfare against Iran, imposing sanctions on Iranian airlines and vowing to take a hard stance against foreign companies that provide them with assistance.

The passengers departed Saudi Arabia for Israel aboard a flydubai replacement aircraft after eight hours on the ground.
Netanyahu quoted a passenger as saying that passengers along with a member of the crew broke into the cockpit after the aircraft “entered a tailspin and began to dive” and found the co-pilot “trying to sabotage the plane’s systems”.

A second set of pilots on board, who were due to replace the first pair, landed the plane.
The aircraft’s flight data showed it suddenly and rapidly descended by nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before a first emergency signal was sent on the morning, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

Yasmin Abukasis said her daughter Miriam, who was among the passengers on the flight, had told her that she had heard screaming and that a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor, and that there was blood everywhere.
Israeli media published a photo purportedly taken from inside the plane, which appeared to show a passenger’s blood-soaked shirt.
Reuters could not immediately verify the image.
Flydubai operates daily return flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv, a route that is popular among Israeli nationals. The flight path normally uses airspace over Saudi Arabia and Jordan.
It is not the first time a flight between Israel and the UAE has landed in Saudi Arabia. A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Riyadh in September 2025 due to a medical incident, Israeli media reported at the time.
In a video purportedly of an Israeli passenger on board the flydubai flight and carried widely by Israeli media, the passenger said one of the pilots was seriously injured and the other was slightly injured, after one of the pilots was stabbed.
Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, said both pilots had been hospitalised after sustaining injuries.
Neither the airport nor the purported Israeli passenger identified the attacker.
Incident comes weeks ahead of Israeli election
The incident heightened security fears in Israel weeks before Israelis vote in the first election since the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023 attacks, with Israel’s security figuring prominently in the campaigning.
Responding to the incident on X, far-right security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir wrote, “Terrorism is a devil with whom no agreement must be reached”.
Israeli media published conflicting reports on the incident, with some outlets reporting that a pilot had tried to crash the passenger plane in an alleged suicide attempt. Some Israeli media outlets identified the pilots as Omani and Emirati nationals, while others said they were Russian and Ukrainian.
“Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Doron Spielman, a Netanyahu spokesperson, told Reuters.
Netanyahu met on Sept 27 with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during a rare visit to the Gulf country. Israel and the UAE have forged close security, military and economic ties since establishing diplomatic ties in 2020.
Earlier this year, Israel provided the UAE with Iron Dome air-defence systems and Israeli personnel to operate them, helping defend against Iranian attacks launched after Israel and the United States began strikes on Iran.
The UAE has yet to comment on the flydubai incident, while the Dubai-owned airline has only said the flight experienced an “incident” and diverted to Tabuk, where it landed safely, and that all passengers were safe and accounted for. REUTERS

Best Mattresses for Kids (2026): Saatva, Birch, Helix, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

The Best Kids’ Mattresses, Put Through the Toddler Test
Featured in this article
Kids, especially toddlers, aren’t mattress reviewers. They don’t wake up and tell you the pressure relief is lacking or that they appreciated the vegan foam and airy woven top. Instead, as a parent, it’s your job to become the observer, paying attention to the little things, like how easily they can climb into bed, whether they stay asleep, if they seem comfortable while moving around, plus how well the mattress can handle inevitable spills, jumping, and tumbling.
For the last few months, my toddler daughter tested each mattress in this guide in her bedroom on a Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. I narrowed down the mattresses tested by looking for beds specifically designed for children and prioritizing a mix of constructions, price points, and features. I paid close attention to everything from how well she slept, how easily she could climb onto the mattress, the edge support for myself during bedtime stories, and how cool each cover felt on a warm summer day. Some mattresses stood out for specific features, while others offered impressive value or the ability to grow with your child. Regardless of the specific accolade, every pick here earned its spot through toddler testing.
Want more mattress-buying advice for every kind of sleeper? Check out our guide to the Best Mattresses, the Best Organic Mattresses, and the Best Mattresses for Side Sleepers.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Also Tested
Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress for $919 (Twin): My biggest complaint with the Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress is, unfortunately, the reason I had to stop testing it. It was just short enough that it didn’t fit in my daughter’s twin bed frame, leaving a solid 8-inch gap between the bottom edge of the mattress and the foot of the bed frame. Every other twin mattress I tested fit the frame without any issues, making the Nolah the odd one out. It’s a bummer, because the mattress otherwise had a lot going for it. It’s got the flippability of many mattresses we tested, and its hybrid design was very comfy, with great edge support. If it’d fit the bed frame properly, I think it would’ve been a contender.
FAQs
What’s the Difference Between a Kids’ Mattress and a Regular Adult Mattress?
Many kids’ mattresses have firmer sleep surfaces for younger children and specific features like flippable designs, waterproof and stain-resistant covers, or reinforced edges that stand up to roughhousing. Kids’ mattresses also typically have a lower profile, which makes it easier and safer for kids to get in and out of bed.
They’re also available in smaller sizes, most commonly twin and full, which are typical for kids’ bedrooms and smaller bed frames. A full-size mattress can make sense for a child who needs more room but still benefits from the features mentioned above. Once your child reaches their teen years or no longer needs these features, an adult mattress may make more sense.
Why Are Many Kids’ Mattresses Flippable?
Many kids’ mattresses are designed to grow with your child. They typically have a firmer side for younger children as they transition from a crib mattress and a softer side for older kids. Being able to adjust firmness by flipping the mattress can save you from replacing it after a few years when your kid’s wants change.
What Do Mattress Certifications Mean?
You’ll probably come across several mattress certifications while shopping. Here’s what the most common ones mean:
- CertiPur-US applies to polyurethane foam and verifies that the foam has been independently tested for emissions, durability, and certain chemicals, including formaldehyde and specific flame retardants.
- GreenGuard Gold certifies that a mattress has been tested for low chemical emissions, known as volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which can cause irritation in the nose, eyes, throat, as well as other ailments.
- Global Organic Latex Standard (GOLS) verifies that latex is responsibly sourced and processed according to environmental and production standards.
- Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) certifies organic textile materials like cotton and wool. It ensures the materials meet strict environmental and manufacturing standards, with no VOC emissions or off-gassing.
We have more info about mattress shopping terms.
Should I Buy a Foam or Hybrid Mattress for My Child?
Foam mattresses are usually lighter and easier to move, which helps when you’re changing sheets or rotating the mattress. Hybrid mattresses combine foam with coils, which can boost pressure relief, edge support, and airflow to help prevent overheating. Neither is inherently better; it comes down to your little one’s needs and what feels most comfortable.
How Long Does a Kids’ Mattress Last?
A quality kids’ mattress should last anywhere from 7 to 10 years, depending on how heavily it’s used. Replace a mattress if you notice sagging, permanent body impressions, or tears. Also, if your child has outgrown the mattress’s size, it’s probably time for a new one.
What Should You Look for in a Mattress?
- Materials: Kids’ mattresses use many of the same materials as adult mattresses. You’ll commonly see memory foam for cushioning, higher-density foam for support, latex for a responsive, bouncy feel, and steel coils for extra support, airflow, and edge support. You’ll also see materials like Tencel, which is a plant-based fiber often used in mattress covers because it’s soft and breathable. Cotton and wool are often found in natural or organic mattresses. When researching mattresses, you might also see materials described with the brand’s proprietary names, whether it's gel-infused memory foam or a stain-resistant treatment. When shopping for and comparing mattresses, look past the marketing name to see what the material actually is and what purpose it serves.
- Firmness: There’s not much strong research or official medical guidance on mattress firmness for children. However, the American Academy of Pediatrics does specify that infants should sleep on a firm, flat mattress to reduce the risk of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID). When it comes time to transition out of the crib and into a “big kid bed,” it stands to reason that a firmer mattress will be more comfortable and familiar to a young child. Mattress firmness for kids of any age is ultimately a matter of preference, not a medical mandate, but we recommend consulting your child’s pediatrician for additional advice.
- Pressure Relief: A mattress that properly supports a child’s weight can help with body development and spinal alignment as they grow. It can also help prevent restless nights and lead to better sleep.
- Edge Support: This refers to how reinforced a mattress’s perimeter is. As a parent who loves reading with my daughter, the last thing I want is for the mattress edge to sink in as I sit next to her. It also helps protect a child from falling out of the bed.
- Shipping, Trial, Warranty: Most online mattresses ship compressed in a box and are delivered directly to your door, and some brands offer in-home delivery and setup. A sleep trial gives you a window to test the mattress at home and return it if it isn’t a good fit. Be sure to pay attention to the fine print, though; some brands charge return or processing fees. The warranty covers manufacturing defects for a set period but typically not normal wear and tear, spills, or damage.
- What Else to Consider: Be sure the mattress fits your child’s bed frame. Also consider the height, especially if the mattress will be used on bunk beds and trundles. If you’re hoping to keep a mattress for several years, a flippable model can offer more flexibility. Also consider the practical stuff: stain-resistant and water-repellent covers can come in handy for inevitable spills or accidents.
Should I Buy a Mattress in a Store or Online?
All of the mattresses I tested for this guide were purchased online, and most were shipped vacuum-sealed in a box. Many come with sleep trials so you can test them at home and return them if they don’t work for you.
Buying online often makes it easier to compare prices, materials, and certifications without driving from store to store. That said, shopping in person lets you get a sense of a mattress’s firmness before committing.
How I Tested
My almost 2-year-old daughter tested each mattress in her own bedroom over several months, sleeping on them in the same Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. Because toddlers don’t provide detailed feedback on things like lumbar support and motion transfer, I took a more observational approach by paying attention to how well she seemed to sleep and how easily she could climb into bed.
I also tested each mattress from a parent’s perspective by sitting on the edges, climbing into the beds for nighttime cuddles, and monitoring things like how easy it was to set up, whether my daughter seemed hot while sleeping/after waking up, how supportive it felt, and how the mattress held up to normal toddler behavior. I also considered each mattress’s construction, materials, and price.
I narrowed down the mattresses by focusing on models designed and marketed for children rather than smaller versions of adult mattresses. I wanted to test a range of price points and constructions, as well as explore features relevant for kids, like flippable designs, stain resistance, and lower heights.

Most major Dutch data centres keep energy usage secret: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:31:59 UTC
18:31:59 KST

Most major Dutch data centres keep energy usage secret: report
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Most data centres in the Netherlands do not make their environmental impact public, which conceals water and electricity usage, according to an investigation by Trouw and Lighthouse Reports.
The Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), which collects data on behalf of the EU, lists only 104 data centres but the industry body Dutch Datacenter Association (DDA) says there were 186 commercial data centres at the end of 2025.
These figures cover data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT capacity, which are required to report their energy and water use, among other things, under the EU’s Energy Efficiency Directive.
The RVO’s list is missing almost half the centres counted by the DDA, and that count does not include the many data centres run in-house by banks, hospitals and other companies. Trouw estimates that public data is available for only around a quarter of large data centres.
Dutch data centre energy 
 Data centres used 5.1 billion kWh of electricity in 2024, or 4.6% of the national total, according to statistics from CBS – a 37% rise on 2021. Figures for 2025 are not yet available.
RVO figures published this summer showed that Microsoft’s largest Dutch data centre alone uses 1% of national electricity, though the power is said to come from renewable sources. Google, which runs two large data centres in the Netherlands, does not publish its figures.
Grid operator TenneT expects data centres to account for 10% to 15% of Dutch electricity use by 2030. Water use is lower, at an estimated 0.1% of the national total.
Aarhus Convention 
 Reporters working with Lighthouse Reports spent a year filing freedom of information requests in all 27 EU member states and with the European Commission. Most were refused, with some countries saying they did not have the data, and others citing commercial confidentiality.
The group has now filed a complaint under the Aarhus Convention, a treaty signed by the EU and all its member states that guarantees public access to environmental information. The complaint is before the convention’s compliance committee, which meets four times a year.
Lighthouse Reports says the Netherlands discloses more than most other EU countries, where reporters met what they called a “wall of silence”.

Polar oceans transformed as warming melts ice habitats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:31:22 UTC
18:31:22 KST

Climate change is increasingly reshaping the polar oceans, with Arctic waters warming rapidly, sea ice shrinking and wildlife losing habitat at both ends of the planet, an annual report said on Sept. 30.
The Copernicus Ocean State Report depicts profound changes across the world’s seas, from record-breaking heatwaves in the Mediterranean and Black seas to shifts in marine ecosystems and increasingly acidic waters.
“The message is very clear. The ocean is changing rapidly,” said Pierre Bahurel, director general of Mercator Ocean International, which runs the European Union’s Copernicus Marine Service.
Some of the more dramatic effects from global warming are taking place in the poles, which occupy around 20 percent of the global ocean surface.
The Arctic’s combined sea surface and sea-ice surface temperature rose 4.2 degrees Celsius between 1982 and 2024, or around 1 degree per decade, according to the 10th annual oceans report.
By comparison, global sea surface temperatures have been increasing by 0.12 degrees per decade.
As temperatures rise, Arctic sea ice has shrunk by nearly half a million square kilometers per decade since 1979, equivalent to losing an area the size of Spain every 10 years.
The retreating ice exposes Arctic coastlines to waves, worsening coastal erosion and raising risks for coastal communities and infrastructure, the report warned.
“The Arctic sea ice has been declining since the early 80s, leaving around 60 percent of coastal infrastructure vulnerable to erosion and sea level rise,” Karina von Schuckmann, director of the oceans report, said in a media briefing.

AI will not defeat humans with deadly virus as theory alone is not enough — scientist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:30:58 UTC
18:30:58 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Artificial intelligence (AI) will not defeat humanity by creating a deadly virus against it because it cannot experimentally verify its theories and calculations, while biological predictions are not always borne out, Nikolay Nikitin, Doctor of Biological Sciences and professor at the Lomonosov Moscow State University Department of Virology, told TASS.
He noted that AI is already helping scientists identify promising compounds for drugs and develop new materials, serving as an auxiliary tool.
"If we are talking about using artificial intelligence to create biological threats and engineer deadly viruses, AI will not defeat humanity. In biology, one can perform as many calculations and make as many predictions as one likes, but until the effect of a virus on a specific cell culture has been studied in a laboratory, this data has no practical value. AI calculations in biology are not always accurate, and AI itself cannot conduct experiments. Therefore, neural networks will not surpass us in this area and will not independently create any biological threats," Nikitin told a TASS correspondent.
In September, US company Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, reported detecting cases in which its AI models were used in potentially dangerous research that could be linked to the development of biological weapons. The company’s report said its safety systems had identified five such cases. In particular, Anthropic obtained data indicating that scientists had attempted to use the neural network to plan experiments to enhance the function of the chikungunya virus, adapt avian flu to mammals, and prepare a grant application on overcoming immune defenses against viruses of the orthopoxvirus genus, which cause smallpox.
After detecting the threats, the users’ accounts were blocked. The company decided not to disclose the countries the researchers were from or the scientific institutions they were affiliated with. The report emphasized that the company "does not claim that [the researchers] intended to cause harm."

South Africa has maintained a willingness to engage in talks, but said that its sovereignty must be respected and that it will not compromise on domestic priorities like addressing historical injustices.

UK’s Burnham says rejoining EU among options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:29:04 UTC
18:29:04 KST

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham waves after he delivered his Leader's Speech during the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, England, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Sept. 30 that Britain should consider options for its future relationship with the European Union, including ultimately rejoining the bloc, as he steps up efforts to rebuild ties with Europe.
Speaking to the BBC after telling the Labour Party’s annual conference that Brexit had “done more harm than good,” Burnham said Britain should examine different models for its long-term relationship with Europe and decide which offered the best path forward.
“We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay,” Burnham told the broadcaster.
“We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union. We could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about single market, or we could go all the way.”
Osborne, a former Conservative finance minister, has argued that Britain should pursue a customs union with the EU, while the Liberal Democrats have called for Britain to rejoin the bloc’s single market.
Burnham said the pros and cons of each option need to be assessed, and the country needs to “be clear about where we want Britain to go in the next decade.”
Britain voted to leave the European Union in 2016, ending more than four decades of membership and triggering years of political upheaval, with successive governments grappling with the economic and diplomatic consequences of that vote.
On Sept. 29, Burnham said he would use a November U.K.-EU summit to outline options for Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc.
Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer in July, has previously said he would like Britain to rejoin the European Union in his lifetime. He has argued that Britain could not afford another decade of uncertainty over the issue.
“I am very clear, and I will say this bluntly: Brexit has caused more harm than good,” he said. “So the question is, what do we do about that?”
Beyond European diplomacy, Burnham addressed mounting public anxiety over a looming winter energy crisis and severe cost-of-living pressures as households face surging utility bills. Acknowledging the acute financial strain on families, the prime minister stressed that his government is exploring potential relief measures, though he warned that public finances remain heavily constrained.
“The question I’ve got is, ‘how many can I afford?’” Burnham said, balancing public relief demands against fiscal discipline.
“What can we do given the state of the public finances? And people wouldn’t thank me for making unfunded payments that then cause pressure on mortgages, and we’ve seen that in the past and we’re not going back there.”
Burnham argued that while short-term financial breathing room is difficult to scale without triggering broader economic risks, structural overhauls are essential to resolving the country’s utility and economic vulnerabilities.
“We will work hard to take that pressure off people’s shoulders,” he added.
“But I would be the first to say it’s hard.”

Injuries and arrests as French high school student protests spread
SAINT-DENIS, France, Sept 30 - Dozens of people have been injured and hundreds arrested, most of them teenagers, officials said, in a wave of French student protests against teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings that on Wednesday spread to more schools across the country.
The demonstrations and blockades, which began last week and coincided on Tuesday with a broader public-sector strike, have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for France, as they spread to 356 high schools and turned more violent.
On Thursday, the government will unveil the country's 2027 budget, which is expected to involve spending cuts aimed at easing pressure on government finances.
In Saint-Denis, a suburb north of Paris, students stood outside the gates of their school near a fire that had been set as police looked on, while in Lyon and Lille television images showed people throwing projectiles at lines of police officers.
"There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told Reuters. She said temperatures in classrooms could swing from sweltering to below freezing, depending on the weather.
SCORES INJURED OR DETAINED
According to the OECD global policy forum, French spending on education was in the middle of the range among member countries and increased between 2015 and 2022, but its share of the budget has slightly decreased.
France's Education Minister Edouard Geffray told reporters that there had been 119 injuries, both among students and school staff, since the beginning of the demonstrations. He added that most of the affected staff were school principals and teachers.
Politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed party, including Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis, have joined the demonstrations.
Other officials and politicians have denounced the party for rhetoric they said was stoking students' anger, while Interior Minister Laurent Nunez accused far-left groups of inciting violence.
"We observed that, in certain places, there were individuals acting as agitators — people who, moreover, moved from one school to another to stir up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence," he said.
Nunez told reporters at a press conference that some 625 people were detained on Wednesday and more than 440 people the day before, most of them minors. Nunez said there were seven incidents in which people threw hydrochloric acid at law enforcement officers.
The government has criticised violence that has broken out at some of the demonstrations but said that difficulties in high schools should be acknowledged and addressed.
"High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash cans set on fire," French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters in Madrid.
Gamze, a 17-year-old student in Saint-Denis, said students in the historically working-class suburb were treated unfairly compared with students elsewhere.
"It's always us ... who are suffering when, in Paris or in the countryside, they're not in such a situation," she said. REUTERS

On 2 April 1964, two days after the coup that overthrew Brazil’s leftwing president João Goulart, US president Lyndon B Johnson was the first foreign head of state to recognise the change of government. ‘Please accept my warmest good wishes on your installation as President of the United States of Brazil’. he wrote to Pascoal Ranieri Mazzilli, speaker of the Chamber of Deputies. Under pressure from the Brazilian military, the Congress had handed Mazzilli the presidency. Fifteen days after the coup Mazzilli was replaced by Field Marshal Humberto Castelo Branco, who installed a military dictatorship at the Planalto Palace in Brasília. With Washington’s blessing, it would last until 1985.
João Goulart had come to power in 1961 with plans to implement agrarian reform and nationalise strategic enterprises in several sectors (oil, energy, mining and telecommunications) that required the expropriation of US companies. He also pursued an independent foreign policy, opening trade with Maoist China in late 1961 and re-establishing diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union (Brazil had severed ties in 1947). The final straw for the US came when Goulart refused to support US policy towards Cuba.
The success of the 1964 coup owed much to the CIA and US Agency for International Development (USAID). During Brazil’s 1962 legislative election, they financed opposition politicians and political organisations, paving the way for military intervention. US ambassador Lincoln Gordon and his military attaché Colonel Vernon A Walters (a personal friend of Branco’s), were also key, monitoring preparations for months before the coup.
All that is now in the past, and since the beginning of the 21st century Brazil has been an emerging power. Already Latin America’s economic leader, it could soon become the world’s biggest agricultural exporter, ahead of the US. The South Pacific's struggle for climate justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:27:22 UTC
18:27:22 KST

‘If we save the Pacific, we will save the world,’ UN secretary-general António Guterres said in Tonga in August 2024. His acknowledgement that the Pacific archipelagos are on the front line of the coming climate disaster gave his remarks to the Pacific Islands Forum Summit a prophetic cast. But they also implied that it was the powerful, and especially industrial, nations that would save them – with the Pacific islanders, once under the yoke of the French, British and American empires, still consigned to the role of victims.
But these islanders have long since stopped waiting for the international community to wake up. The Pacific region is pioneering new ways of thinking about and pursuing climate justice. Its small island states are among the world’s lowest emitters of greenhouse gases (around 0.03%). the main cause of global climate disruption, whose impacts include ever-rising sea levels and worsening environmental disasters. Yet these states suffer the most brutal consequences: increasingly violent and frequent cyclones, prolonged droughts, flash floods, disrupted seasonal cycles, soil salinisation, coastal erosion and the destruction of coral ecosystems. All these phenomena directly affect housing, harvests, access to water and economic resources.
This structural injustice feeds deep anger. How can it be acceptable that peoples whose way of life is still largely based on subsistence farming and modest patterns of consumption developed over centuries of adapting to the environment should be the first victims of an industrial system created far away? Why should the inhabitants of Samoa, Vanuatu, Fiji and Kiribati pay the price for prosperity they have never benefited from? These questions challenge the foundations of the international order and justice itself.

Travelling through southern Albania on horseback in 1809, Lord Byron was so captivated by its mountains scored by rushing streams, its fertile plains and the hospitality of its inhabitants that he would later celebrate its unspoiled natural beauty in his poem Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage: ‘fairest in her features wild / Where nothing polish’d dares pollute her path’. With its strategic position between the Bay of Vlorë and Strait of Otranto (connecting the Adriatic and Ionian), this island became a forward post for the Venetian and later the Ottoman empire. Occupied by Italy and Germany during the second world war, it was a Soviet submarine base from the mid-1950s until 1961, when Albania’s dictator Enver Hoxha severed ties with Moscow.
Across the bay is the Vjosa-Narta protected area, including the Narta lagoon, a stretch of coastline and the mouth of the Vjosa, one of Europe’s last wild rivers. Lying on a major migration route between Africa and Europe, Vjosa-Narta’s lakes, sand dunes, pine forests and beaches attract some 250 species of birds, including pink flamingos and pelicans.

Twenty years ago, I’d joined the cousins in their search for their grandmother’s village near Saratov. Out of a population of 3,000 in the 1980s, barely a dozen people remained on the former collective farm. Though vegetation was slowly reclaiming the village, it still had a mayor, who every morning swept the old Soviet ‘red corner’, a former assembly hall with a parquet floor and a stage where the locals once put on plays.
Every two weeks, a post van made its way up a dirt track to deliver the mail and basic supplies. On our trip, the cousins had reminisced about their Soviet childhood as though it were a lost country. As we drank and laughed, their bond seemed unbreakable.
This spring I heard they’d fallen out, though from phone conversations I couldn’t tell why. Perhaps seeing them in person would change that, I thought. So I flew to Moscow, despite the threat of Ukrainian missiles and drones.
The city didn’t look like the capital of a country brought to its knees by Western sanctions. There was a time when you would hurry through its streets, head down. Now you could linger on its newly widened pavements, admiring the art nouveau façades of buildings you had barely noticed before.
Between 2015 and 2023, the city authorities renovated 14,000 residential blocks and 380 historic buildings. Since 2022 the redeveloped banks of the Moskva have been part of a 15km pedestrian route that goes from the new Moscow City business district past the Kremlin to Sokolniki Park in the northeast.

Settler terror escalates in the West Bank

====================================================================================================

Settler terror escalates in the West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:27:15 UTC
18:27:15 KST

On 3 August some residents of Ramallah were holding a small party for a friend’s son who had recently graduated from high school. The younger ones were dancing in the middle of the hall while the older guests tried to chat over the music. Then the news came in that the Hamayel brothers had been arrested by the Israeli army.
The Hamayels live in a village near Ramallah. Its residents and those of other villages nearby are regularly attacked, and settlers from several ‘outposts’ – one only recently established, a few hundred metres from the brothers’ farm – prevent them from accessing ever-growing areas of their olive and almond groves, springs, water cisterns and grazing lands.
‘Outposts’ are small Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territories, occupied since 1967, which have been established on private or public land without formal approval from the Israeli planning authorities, yet receive logistical support – openly, unofficially or covertly – from state bodies as well as private donors. The drive to establish these outposts has gained considerable momentum since the late 1990s, aiming to hinder the transfer of more West Bank territory to the Palestinian civil authority. According to the Peace Now website (peacenow.org) there are now 390 outposts, compared to 146 settlements officially founded since 1967. As many as 249 have been established in the last four years.
The day before the brothers’ arrest, around a hundred sheep were stolen from one of the Hamayel family’s farms. Fearing that there would be more thefts, the brothers, their father and their brother-in-law returned to the farm to collect cans of olive oil and a few essentials. Immediately, some Israeli Jews, perhaps residents of a nearby outpost, appeared, photographed them and called in soldiers, who arrested the brothers, blindfolded and handcuffed them, and took them away.

The United States' decline is also China's problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:27:14 UTC
18:27:14 KST

The United States' decline is also China's problem

====================================================================================================

The United States' decline is also China's problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:27:14 UTC
18:27:14 KST

Some analyses are like self-portraits: their implicit assumptions reveal most about their authors. This is true of many Western interpretations of what China hopes to get out of the war between the US and Iran. Two experts writing in Foreign Affairs expressed the view that Beijing is ‘keen to exploit the war to sap US power, gain intelligence on US military systems, and erode the US-led order’. Academic Phillips O’Brien asked, ‘Is China going in for the kill?’ and in Le Parisien journalist François Lenglet set out why ‘Beijing will win the Iran war’.
Yet there’s nothing to suggest that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is obsessed with the supposed ambition of supplanting US hegemony. Despite alarmist talk of a geopolitical ‘great replacement’, all the evidence suggests that Beijing is, in fact, more a victim than a cause of the erosion of the ‘US-led order’, an order from which it has greatly benefited.
A form of Chinese imperialism may well exist, but it’s less immediately recognisable than the kind that alarms Western media and politicians: it’s not a desire to see China prevail, but a belief that US supremacy is preferable to chaos. Such an unusual – and temporary – geopolitical inclination would lead Beijing to favour the US retaining its dominance, provided it does not cause too great an upset to the global balances it long guaranteed, or hamper China’s own development.
It’s highly likely that China is pleased that the US failed to secure its promised lightning victory over Iran. In search of a new geopolitics

18:27:10 KST

In 1997 George F Kennan warned that NATO expansion would be ‘the most fateful error of American policy in the entire post-cold-war era’. So the architect of the West’s cold war strategy of containing the Soviet Union was angered and dismayed when the US Senate approved the accession of three former Eastern bloc states – Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic – the following year.
Now, he predicted, ‘the Russians will gradually react quite adversely and it will affect their policies.’ By 1998 Kennan, the first director of policy planning at the State Department and author of an important article in Foreign Affairs recommending that the US confront the Russians with ‘unalterable counterforce at every point where they show signs of encroaching upon the interest of a peaceful and stable world’. had come to believe that the West, having won the cold war, was squandering the possibility of that peaceful and stable world through its aggressive posture.
‘I was particularly bothered by the references to Russia as a country dying to attack Western Europe,’ he told Thomas L Friedman. ‘Don’t people understand? Our differences in the cold war were with the Soviet Communist regime. And now we are turning our backs on the very people who mounted the greatest bloodless revolution in history to remove that Soviet regime’.
Kennan’s warning went unheeded. And, as he had foreseen, the Russians did indeed react ‘quite adversely’ and invaded Ukraine in order, they claimed, to prevent Kyiv from joining NATO. In putting the issue back on the agenda in 2008, and even more directly in 2020-21, NATO members knew Moscow regarded it as a casus belli, as former German chancellor Angela Merkel acknowledged in her memoirs.

'Robbery of the century': Turkey freezes ex-minister's assets as fund crisis grows
Turkish prosecutors have moved to freeze the assets of a top governing party official and former minister who resigned at the weekend over allegations she profited from an investment fund crisis.
In a brief statement late Tuesday, prosecutors said they had sent "a letter concerning the freezing of all assets" of Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, to "all the relevant institutions".
Turkey has been wrestling with the fallout from an investment fund scandal that erupted this month with the collapse of what officials have called a "Ponzi-like" scheme.
Following allegations by Turkey's main opposition Yeni Parti that she and her husband made millions trading in such shares, Kaya, the deputy head of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AKP party, said late Saturday she was resigning.
While admitting nothing, Kaya, who was Turkey's family minister from 2016 to 2018, said she was taking "political responsibility" to ensure that any investigation could be conducted "independently, impartially".
At a news conference earlier Saturday, a Yeni spokesman, Gokhan Gunaydin, said the party was seeking clarification over claims that Kaya invested 63 million lira ($1.3 million) in shares in April and sold them in September, earning a profit of around 1.3 billion lira ($26.5 million).
He also said her husband had allegedly invested 100 million lira and earned back 826 million lira, collectively netting the pair an alleged profit of nearly 2.2 billion lira ($45 million).
Gunaydin said it was "clear" Kaya had received insider information and pledged that the party would unveil more names this week.
'Robbery of the century'
The scandal is expected to dominate the coming agenda in parliament, which formally reopens on Thursday following the summer recess.
"This name is the tip of the iceberg," Yeni leader Ozgur Ozel told a party meeting on Wednesday, describing the scandal as "the robbery of the century".
On Tuesday, Erdogan held a three-hour meeting with economic aides over the fund crisis, after earlier defending his party's record.
"The AK Party is a clean party, just as its name suggests; it is a party true to its name. No one can tarnish this party's purity or stain that cleanliness," he told party cadres.
"Without looking at their own pitch-black records, they even try to give us lessons in morality and political ethics. 'Get lost', I tell them," he said of his political opponents.
The crisis erupted in mid-September when several funds said they were unable to satisfy investor redemption demands, sending Istanbul's main stock exchange tumbling.
A day later, regulators moved to address the crisis by placing into liquidation seven companies that hold 131 investment funds, whose assets are reportedly worth around $17 billion, with the Capital Markets Board (SPK) saying more than 455,000 individual investors were affected.

BUREAU uses color and translucency to reshape 44 sqm lilac apartment in lisbon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
