It's nearing midnight here in Germany, and we're closing our updates for Wednesday. Thank you for joining us.
We'll be back in the morning with the latest news out of Germany.
BMW plans to reduce senior management by 20%
Another German carmaker, BMW, announced that it plans to simplify its organizational structure and rely more heavily on AI to adapt more quickly to changes in the global market.
To achieve this goal, the company plans to eliminate 20% of its "divisions and associated management roles" by mid-2027.
This change will initially affect relatively senior division heads, though its impact will also be felt at lower management levels. However, it is not linked to a large-scale reduction in headcount, according to BMW.
Earlier this year, BMW announced a voluntary redundancy program for all areas except production.
According to company sources, the total global workforce will be reduced by around 8,000, with many jobs likely to be cut in administration as well as in research and development in Germany.
Volkswagen terminates almost all collective wage agreements
German automaker Volkswagen has terminated most of its collective wage agreements in Germany, potentially renewing bitter disputes with employee representatives as the company seeks to cut costs.
Following a meeting with employee representatives in Hanover on Wednesday, the company announced that various provisions in the agreements would need to be adjusted in light of cost pressures.
By terminating the agreements by December 31, 2026, Volkswagen aims to open up room for negotiation. The employment security provisions agreed upon in 2024 and set to last until the end of 2030 will not be affected.
German union leaders have expressed their opposition to Volkswagen, accusing the company of declaring "war" on its staff and threatening strikes in response.
"This is a foul blow against the workforce and once again a shameless attempt to reach into employees' pockets," said IG Metall union official Thorsten Gröger.
Meanwhile, VW works council chair Daniela Cavallo predicted a "bitter dispute at the turn of the year."
Earlier this month, the carmaker and unions reached an agreement to eliminate a total of 100,000 jobs across the entire 10-brand group by the end of the decade. This is the largest restructuring in the history of the global auto industry.
READ: Germany's Deutschlandticket to cost €66.80 from 2027
Germany's nationwide Deutschlandticket will cost €66.80 ($78) per month from January 1, 2027, up from the current €63, transport authorities said on Wednesday.
It is the first price increase to be determined using a new cost-based formula rather than through political negotiations between Germany's federal and state governments.
Click here to read mooe about why the Deutschlandticket is getting more expensive.
'The time for hesitation is over': SPD eyes judicial review of AfD
The center-left Social Democrats (SPD) have just unveiled a series of measures to bolster democracy, including a call for an "immediate" review of whether the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) should be banned.
The draft paper, which DW has seen, says "the time for hesitation is over."
The AfD has emerged as the strongest party in two of three recent regional elections. It is also currently leading national polls at around 27%.
Under Germany’s system of "defensive democracy," political parties can be banned if, according to Article 21 of the Basic Law, they seek to impair or abolish the country’s free democratic basic order, or threaten the existence of the Federal Republic. In previous ban cases, judges has said that proof of an "actively combative, aggressive stance" against democracy is required for a ban to be imposed.
The idea was shaped by the experience of the Nazi era, when Adolf Hitler and the Nazi regime dismantled the Weimar Republic’s democratic system and established a dictatorship.
Fast forward to 2026, and the question of whether the AfD meets the legal criteria for a ban is becoming increasingly prominent among politicians, jurists and other experts.
The SPD draft argues that the AfD "systematically attacks our free society, normalizes racism, and discredits democratic institutions."
Only three constitutional organs can formally apply for a party-ban ruling: the Bundestag, the Bundesrat or the federal government. Whether the AfD is unconstitutional would then ultimately be decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.
The SPD believes there is sufficient support in the Bundesrat to begin examining whether the evidence against the AfD would justify taking the next step.
That distinction is important: an initial review or preparatory process would not itself be a ban proceeding. A formal application would ultimately have to go to the Constitutional Court. The process is expected to take years.
SPD sources are optimistic that the review process could be started by the end of the year. That is the most concrete timeframe I have heard yet, and it’s a clear sign that discussion of an AfD ban is moving from a largely theoretical debate toward a more concrete political and legal process.
A policy turnaround: Germany moves to replenish natural gas reserves
German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has officially called on the energy company Sefe (a state-owned enterprise) to replenish Germany's gas storage facilities, which are already alarmingly low.
A spokesperson for the minister stated that the main reason lies "in the ongoing geopolitical risks." These risks have existed for some time. The tense situation in the Strait of Hormuz has led to drastically higher energy prices on the world market, causing the private sector to hesitate in purchasing supplies for the winter, waiting for prices to drop.
As a result, according to official figures, the overall fill level of all Germany's gas storage facilities stands at 57.6%. That is significantly lower than during comparable periods in recent years.
Nevertheless, Reiche had long hesitated before taking the step she has now taken.
A remark made at the government press conference — that Reiche’s move had now been taken "...in consultation with Chancellor Friedrich Merz" — caught the attention of journalists. That's because the resolute economy minister, who is skeptical of government intervention in the economy in general, has the power to make such a decision on her own.
So speculation was rife: Was she now instructed by the embattled chancellor to now take action? Of course not, government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius was quick to say.
At any rate, the ministry stated that the gas supply for the winter is secure. This is good news for the majority of renters and homeowners in Germany: slightly more than half of all homes are still heated with gas — a fuel that is becoming increasingly expensive.
Police operation targets distribution of neo-Nazi music
Police have searched premises in Germany and several other European countries in an operation targeting the distribution of neo-Nazi music.
Authorities in the northeastern German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania said raids were carried out across Germany, as well as in Estonia, Italy, Poland and the Czech Republic.
Four of the suspects whose premises were searched are accused of membership in a far-right criminal organization that spreads a "National Socialist (Nazi), antisemitic, racist and dehumanizing ideology" by producing and selling music that promoted it.
Eight further suspects targeted by the operation are believed to have committed hate speech offences linked to the audio recordings produced by the alleged criminal organization.
Another 10 people linked to the suspects also had their homes raided.
More than 390 police officers were deployed during the operation, run by state criminal police office in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Unknown Christmas work by Humperdinck discovered
A "Christmas Lullaby" by composer Engelbert Humperdinck (1854-1921) donated by his great-grandson to his birth city of Siegburg has been confirmed to be a previously unknown work.
"For the music world, the find is a sensation," city spokesman Jan Gerull told the DPA news agency.
The one-page manuscript with the work for four-voice male choir was given to the Siegburg city archive by Humperdinck's great-grandson, Lothar Witte, some time ago for its collection related to the composer.
The head of the Musicwerkstatt Siegburg, Christian Ubber, said it had first had to be clarified whether Humperdinck had used and published the work in another context.
"This examination took some time and turned out negative so that it is only now certain that this 'Christmas Lullaby' was really unknown up to now," he said.
According to city spokesman Gerull, the piece, a highly indivualized version of the German Christmas song "Josef lieber, Josef mein," is not easy to sing owing to the composer's sometimes complex style.
But, he said, this had not dampened the enthusiasm.
"Siegburg is looking forward to having the piece performed before Christmas," he said.
Cabinet gives green light to care system reform package
The German Cabinet has put its seal of approval on a draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann on reforming the care system.
The proposed reforms, which will now be put before the parliament, seek to prevent an estimated shortfall of some €8-10 million ($9 million to $11 million) next year.
The reforms were the subject of heated debate between the conservative bloc of Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Linnemann belongs, and its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the junior coalition party the Social Democrats (SPD).
The draft bill builds largely on proposals by former Health Minister Nina Warken, also from the CDU.
No details on the exact content of the bill as it now stands have been released.
Bundeswehr failing to tackle sexual harassment — report
The German armed forces are doing too little to crack down on instances of sexual offenses against women in their ranks, according to public service broadcaster ARD.
This comes as the Bundeswehr is actively seeking to recruit women.
Witnesses and victims of such offenses told the ARD's news magazine REPORT MAINZ that many personnel were scared to report what had happened to them for fear of negative career consequences.
The number of suspected cases of sexual harassment has been rising every year, with 413 reported in 2024 and 472 in 2025, but the number of unreported cases is likely high, according to the ARD.
A spokeswoman from the Defense Ministry told REPORT MAINZ that there had been an "disproportionate rise" in reports of sexual offenses this year.
Women have been permitted to join the Bundeswehr in all capacities for 25 years but still make up just 13.6% of personnel.
The Defense Ministry has, however, rejected the claim by a military historian in the program that the integration of women in the Bundeswehr had so far failed.
Women in the Bundeswehr were "accepted and respected," and there was no "value and rights free space for any group of people" in the German armed forces, it said.
Cabinet debates care reform after uncertainty
The German Cabinet is to discuss the draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann to reform the care system after much heated debate between the coalition partners, the Federal Press Office in Berlin has said.
The reform proposals have highlighted divisions between the bloc of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) with Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and junior coalition partner the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Those divisions made it uncertain up to the last moment whether Wednesday's meeting was to take place.
Police raid Hells Angels sites in Germany and elsewhere
More than 1,000 police officers have launched raids in Germany and other European countries targeting Hells Angels bikers and an associated money-laundering network.
Duisburg police said the officers would execute a number of arrest warrants and confiscate up to €48.6 million ($55.15 million) of illicit funds.
More than 100 locations were to be searched, with 71 people under investigation.
Searches are being carried out in the states of North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg, Berlin and Bavaria, as well as in Belgium, Bulgaria and the Netherlands.
According to police, those under investigation are suspected of "forming a criminal association, predatory and commercial blackmail, gang and commercial fraud and commercial money-laundering."
They are also believed to be behind weapons offenses, physical assault and tax avoidance.
The operation is under the supervision of state prosecutors in Duisburg, with the involvement of the State Office for Combating Financial Criminality in North Rhine-Westphalia (LBF).
Coalition in race to put care reform debate to rest
A package of reforms to Germany's care system put forward by conservative Health Minister Carsten Linnemann remains a source of contention within the coalition.
It remained unclear early on Wednesday whether a planned morning Cabinet meeting to agree on the package called by Linnemann would take place.
The junior coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), opposes any cuts to care services.
Among other things, it has called for a cap on personal contributions to care in retirement homes and financial adjustments to make the division fairer between private and statutory nursing care insurance models.
Both ideas have met with skepticism from Linnemann.
The reform of the system has been made necessary by the growing number of people needing care as the population ages, which has raised costs.
The National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds (GKV), which also represents care insurance institutes, estimates a shortfall of €4.4 billion ($5 billion) this year, and €10 billion in 2027.

According to company sources, the total global workforce will be reduced by around 8,000, with many jobs likely to be cut in administration as well as in research and development in Germany.
Volkswagen terminates almost all collective wage agreements
German automaker Volkswagen has terminated most of its collective wage agreements in Germany, potentially renewing bitter disputes with employee representatives as the company seeks to cut costs.
Following a meeting with employee representatives in Hanover on Wednesday, the company announced that various provisions in the agreements would need to be adjusted in light of cost pressures.
By terminating the agreements by December 31, 2026, Volkswagen aims to open up room for negotiation. The employment security provisions agreed upon in 2024 and set to last until the end of 2030 will not be affected.
German union leaders have expressed their opposition to Volkswagen, accusing the company of declaring "war" on its staff and threatening strikes in response.
"This is a foul blow against the workforce and once again a shameless attempt to reach into employees' pockets," said IG Metall union official Thorsten Gröger.
Meanwhile, VW works council chair Daniela Cavallo predicted a "bitter dispute at the turn of the year."
Earlier this month, the carmaker and unions reached an agreement to eliminate a total of 100,000 jobs across the entire 10-brand group by the end of the decade. This is the largest restructuring in the history of the global auto industry.
READ: Germany's Deutschlandticket to cost €66.80 from 2027
Germany's nationwide Deutschlandticket will cost €66.80 ($78) per month from January 1, 2027, up from the current €63, transport authorities said on Wednesday.
It is the first price increase to be determined using a new cost-based formula rather than through political negotiations between Germany's federal and state governments.
Click here to read mooe about why the Deutschlandticket is getting more expensive.
'The time for hesitation is over': SPD eyes judicial review of AfD
The center-left Social Democrats (SPD) have just unveiled a series of measures to bolster democracy, including a call for an "immediate" review of whether the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) should be banned.
The draft paper, which DW has seen, says "the time for hesitation is over."
The AfD has emerged as the strongest party in two of three recent regional elections. It is also currently leading national polls at around 27%.
Under Germany’s system of "defensive democracy," political parties can be banned if, according to Article 21 of the Basic Law, they seek to impair or abolish the country’s free democratic basic order, or threaten the existence of the Federal Republic. In previous ban cases, judges has said that proof of an "actively combative, aggressive stance" against democracy is required for a ban to be imposed.
The idea was shaped by the experience of the Nazi era, when Adolf Hitler and the Nazi regime dismantled the Weimar Republic’s democratic system and established a dictatorship.
Fast forward to 2026, and the question of whether the AfD meets the legal criteria for a ban is becoming increasingly prominent among politicians, jurists and other experts.
The SPD draft argues that the AfD "systematically attacks our free society, normalizes racism, and discredits democratic institutions."
Only three constitutional organs can formally apply for a party-ban ruling: the Bundestag, the Bundesrat or the federal government. Whether the AfD is unconstitutional would then ultimately be decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.
The SPD believes there is sufficient support in the Bundesrat to begin examining whether the evidence against the AfD would justify taking the next step.
That distinction is important: an initial review or preparatory process would not itself be a ban proceeding. A formal application would ultimately have to go to the Constitutional Court. The process is expected to take years.
SPD sources are optimistic that the review process could be started by the end of the year. That is the most concrete timeframe I have heard yet, and it’s a clear sign that discussion of an AfD ban is moving from a largely theoretical debate toward a more concrete political and legal process.
A policy turnaround: Germany moves to replenish natural gas reserves
German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has officially called on the energy company Sefe (a state-owned enterprise) to replenish Germany's gas storage facilities, which are already alarmingly low.
A spokesperson for the minister stated that the main reason lies "in the ongoing geopolitical risks." These risks have existed for some time. The tense situation in the Strait of Hormuz has led to drastically higher energy prices on the world market, causing the private sector to hesitate in purchasing supplies for the winter, waiting for prices to drop.
As a result, according to official figures, the overall fill level of all Germany's gas storage facilities stands at 57.6%. That is significantly lower than during comparable periods in recent years.
Nevertheless, Reiche had long hesitated before taking the step she has now taken.
A remark made at the government press conference — that Reiche’s move had now been taken "...in consultation with Chancellor Friedrich Merz" — caught the attention of journalists. That's because the resolute economy minister, who is skeptical of government intervention in the economy in general, has the power to make such a decision on her own.
So speculation was rife: Was she now instructed by the embattled chancellor to now take action? Of course not, government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius was quick to say.
At any rate, the ministry stated that the gas supply for the winter is secure. This is good news for the majority of renters and homeowners in Germany: slightly more than half of all homes are still heated with gas — a fuel that is becoming increasingly expensive.
Police operation targets distribution of neo-Nazi music
Police have searched premises in Germany and several other European countries in an operation targeting the distribution of neo-Nazi music.
Authorities in the northeastern German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania said raids were carried out across Germany, as well as in Estonia, Italy, Poland and the Czech Republic.
Four of the suspects whose premises were searched are accused of membership in a far-right criminal organization that spreads a "National Socialist (Nazi), antisemitic, racist and dehumanizing ideology" by producing and selling music that promoted it.
Eight further suspects targeted by the operation are believed to have committed hate speech offences linked to the audio recordings produced by the alleged criminal organization.
Another 10 people linked to the suspects also had their homes raided.
More than 390 police officers were deployed during the operation, run by state criminal police office in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Unknown Christmas work by Humperdinck discovered
A "Christmas Lullaby" by composer Engelbert Humperdinck (1854-1921) donated by his great-grandson to his birth city of Siegburg has been confirmed to be a previously unknown work.
"For the music world, the find is a sensation," city spokesman Jan Gerull told the DPA news agency.
The one-page manuscript with the work for four-voice male choir was given to the Siegburg city archive by Humperdinck's great-grandson, Lothar Witte, some time ago for its collection related to the composer.
The head of the Musicwerkstatt Siegburg, Christian Ubber, said it had first had to be clarified whether Humperdinck had used and published the work in another context.
"This examination took some time and turned out negative so that it is only now certain that this 'Christmas Lullaby' was really unknown up to now," he said.
According to city spokesman Gerull, the piece, a highly indivualized version of the German Christmas song "Josef lieber, Josef mein," is not easy to sing owing to the composer's sometimes complex style.
But, he said, this had not dampened the enthusiasm.
"Siegburg is looking forward to having the piece performed before Christmas," he said.
Cabinet gives green light to care system reform package
The German Cabinet has put its seal of approval on a draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann on reforming the care system.
The proposed reforms, which will now be put before the parliament, seek to prevent an estimated shortfall of some €8-10 million ($9 million to $11 million) next year.
The reforms were the subject of heated debate between the conservative bloc of Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Linnemann belongs, and its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the junior coalition party the Social Democrats (SPD).
The draft bill builds largely on proposals by former Health Minister Nina Warken, also from the CDU.
No details on the exact content of the bill as it now stands have been released.
Bundeswehr failing to tackle sexual harassment — report
The German armed forces are doing too little to crack down on instances of sexual offenses against women in their ranks, according to public service broadcaster ARD.
This comes as the Bundeswehr is actively seeking to recruit women.
Witnesses and victims of such offenses told the ARD's news magazine REPORT MAINZ that many personnel were scared to report what had happened to them for fear of negative career consequences.
The number of suspected cases of sexual harassment has been rising every year, with 413 reported in 2024 and 472 in 2025, but the number of unreported cases is likely high, according to the ARD.
A spokeswoman from the Defense Ministry told REPORT MAINZ that there had been an "disproportionate rise" in reports of sexual offenses this year.
Women have been permitted to join the Bundeswehr in all capacities for 25 years but still make up just 13.6% of personnel.
The Defense Ministry has, however, rejected the claim by a military historian in the program that the integration of women in the Bundeswehr had so far failed.
Women in the Bundeswehr were "accepted and respected," and there was no "value and rights free space for any group of people" in the German armed forces, it said.
Cabinet debates care reform after uncertainty
The German Cabinet is to discuss the draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann to reform the care system after much heated debate between the coalition partners, the Federal Press Office in Berlin has said.
The reform proposals have highlighted divisions between the bloc of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) with Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and junior coalition partner the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Those divisions made it uncertain up to the last moment whether Wednesday's meeting was to take place.
Police raid Hells Angels sites in Germany and elsewhere
More than 1,000 police officers have launched raids in Germany and other European countries targeting Hells Angels bikers and an associated money-laundering network.
Duisburg police said the officers would execute a number of arrest warrants and confiscate up to €48.6 million ($55.15 million) of illicit funds.
More than 100 locations were to be searched, with 71 people under investigation.
Searches are being carried out in the states of North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg, Berlin and Bavaria, as well as in Belgium, Bulgaria and the Netherlands.
According to police, those under investigation are suspected of "forming a criminal association, predatory and commercial blackmail, gang and commercial fraud and commercial money-laundering."
They are also believed to be behind weapons offenses, physical assault and tax avoidance.
The operation is under the supervision of state prosecutors in Duisburg, with the involvement of the State Office for Combating Financial Criminality in North Rhine-Westphalia (LBF).
Coalition in race to put care reform debate to rest
A package of reforms to Germany's care system put forward by conservative Health Minister Carsten Linnemann remains a source of contention within the coalition.
It remained unclear early on Wednesday whether a planned morning Cabinet meeting to agree on the package called by Linnemann would take place.
The junior coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), opposes any cuts to care services.
Among other things, it has called for a cap on personal contributions to care in retirement homes and financial adjustments to make the division fairer between private and statutory nursing care insurance models.
Both ideas have met with skepticism from Linnemann.
The reform of the system has been made necessary by the growing number of people needing care as the population ages, which has raised costs.
The National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds (GKV), which also represents care insurance institutes, estimates a shortfall of €4.4 billion ($5 billion) this year, and €10 billion in 2027.

Russia sends NATO new nuclear threat over Kaliningrad as tensions rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:07:46 UTC
17:07:46 KST

Russia told NATO it would be ready to use nuclear weapons if alliance members attempt to isolate Kaliningrad Oblast, NATO spokesperson Allison Hart told the Kyiv Independent Sept. 30.
The warning came in a Russian non-paper delivered to NATO, which also threatened possible strikes against decision-making centers in NATO member states at the outset of such a conflict. The message adds to renewed Russian nuclear rhetoric toward Europe and warnings over hypothetical military action against the Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea.
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the note said.
It also raised the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
Hart rejected the threats, saying that NATO considers itself a defensive alliance and does not view its military activities as a threat to Russia.
"We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine," she said. "Russia's use of hybrid tactics is a sign of desperation. But we will not be dissuaded from our support to Ukraine."
The Russian Embassy in Ireland issued a similar warning on Sept. 30.
The embassy claimed that the European Union and NATO are increasing military activity along Russia's western border, including through military exercises. It also cited what it called "information" that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad Oblast, without providing evidence or identifying the source of the claim.
Kaliningrad Oblast is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, located between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory.
The embassy also pushed back against warnings from European officials that Moscow could be preparing for a military confrontation with Europe, saying there was no basis for such claims.
It cited Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov as saying that if the West attacks Russia, Moscow would respond with "a completely different war and a very brief one."
Russia has repeatedly used nuclear rhetoric in its confrontation with Western countries over its full-scale war against Ukraine. The U.K. has previously condemned Moscow's nuclear signaling as destabilizing and warned that such rhetoric increases the risk of miscalculation.
Western officials have also raised concerns over what they describe as growing Russian hybrid operations against NATO members, particularly countries on the alliance's eastern flank and those supporting Ukraine.

IDF chief cancels US trip as Israel raises military alert across all fronts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:05:46 UTC
17:05:46 KST

IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has canceled a planned visit to the United States, scheduled for next month, due to the security situation in Israel, ynet has learned.
The trip was to include meetings with the commander of U.S. Central Command and the chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, with talks focused on military cooperation over Iran and other threats. Zamir told his hosts that with the IDF on heightened alert across all fronts, he did not believe it was right to leave Israel and oversee events from abroad.
“You can’t put the military on alert and then fly abroad,” a senior IDF official said. Zamir has raised the military’s readiness level and ordered commanders to remain in their sectors ahead of the Jewish holiday season, which is considered a particularly sensitive period from a security standpoint.
Two active fronts are commanding particular attention. In Gaza, Israel has received a concrete warning that Hamas may attempt to abduct a soldier. Israeli officials believe Hamas is seeking to deter targeted killings by the IDF and Shin Bet while exploiting the sensitive period ahead of elections in the United States and Israel, calculating that political constraints could limit Israel’s ability to respond forcefully.
The second front is the West Bank, where friction between settlers and Palestinians has risen sharply. That tension was evident again in the Palestinian village of Jalud on the night between Monday and Tuesday and could further inflame the area, following deadly terrorist attacks over the past two weeks at a spring near Neve Tzuf and at the Maccabim checkpoint.
Netanyahu: ‘There are signs that ahead of the elections, our enemies will try to attack us’
For Zamir, the combination of the holiday season, events marking three years since Oct. 7 and the upcoming elections makes the coming period especially sensitive. The IDF is therefore preparing not only for known threats, but also for tactical incidents that could quickly spiral into a broader escalation.
Zamir decided to cancel his trip before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Tuesday of a possible attack ahead of the elections. Netanyahu’s remarks, however, went beyond the security picture itself. A warning delivered by the prime minister at an Air Force base, standing beside an F-15, carries particular weight and would ordinarily suggest concrete intelligence of an imminent attack. At the time of writing, it remains unclear whether such intelligence exists, though the assessment could change rapidly as events unfold across the Middle East.
The security situation remains sensitive, though such tensions are not new. In recent months, Israel has come close to escalation on several occasions without Netanyahu publicly warning of the threat.
At present, there is no known concrete threat of an imminent attack on Israel. Rather, security officials see a sensitive period that Israel’s adversaries may seek to exploit. The alert level regarding Iran remains extremely high but unchanged, and the IDF is prepared to resume fighting on short notice.
Iran could still take unusual action during this period, just as it could have previously. The security situation remains fragile, but the underlying threat level has not fundamentally changed.
The IDF General Staff is also mindful that Israel is entering a politically sensitive period. Senior officers stress, however, that the military will not become a political actor and that its decisions will be based solely on professional and operational considerations.

UN Yemen envoy concludes Cairo talks on Yemen escalation, regional repercussions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:05:42 UTC
17:05:42 KST

Ikrame Kouachi
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg concluded a three-day visit to Cairo on Wednesday, holding talks on the military escalation in Yemen and its regional repercussions.
In a statement, Grundberg’s office said the envoy met Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy during the visit.
The talks addressed “the recent escalation in Yemen and its regional repercussions, including in the Red Sea, as well as UN efforts to end the conflict sustainably,” the statement said.
Grundberg expressed his “appreciation for the continued support provided by Egypt and the Arab League to the mediation efforts led by the United Nations,” according to the statement, which provided no further details.
Grundberg arrived in Cairo on Monday as part of UN diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the military situation in Yemen, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Clashes have continued since July between government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, including in Taiz, Lahj, Marib, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda provinces, marking the widest escalation since a relative lull began under an April 2022 truce.
The recent escalation ended the relative calm and displaced around 180,000 people, while thousands fled to Djibouti, according to UN and government figures.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Fighting intensified in September, with the Houthis taking control of several key areas in Al-Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including the strategic city of Mokha, and reaching Mayyun Island overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

From 1 October, anyone visiting the dentist would be well advised to carry their identity card with them. From that date, dentists are obliged to verify their patients’ identities when using the electronic third-party payment scheme, under which the patient pays only their share of the cost.
For adults, this means the Belgian electronic identity card (eID) or electronic foreign nationals’ card; for children, the Kids-ID or ISI+ card.
If the patient does not have their identity card with them, the dentist can also verify their identity in another way, e.g. by using a sticker from the health insurance fund.

Veteran white politician nicknamed 'grandmother' shakes up Johannesburg mayor race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:02:46 UTC
17:02:46 KST

Veteran white politician nicknamed 'grandmother' shakes up Johannesburg mayor race
JOHANNESBURG, Sept 30 - A 75-year-old white politician nicknamed "gogo", meaning grandmother, is running for mayor of Johannesburg in a high-stakes November race that analysts say could reshape South Africa's politics.
Helen Zille, a former mayor of Cape Town and head of the Western Cape province, has campaigned to "fix" Johannesburg with viral videos showing her swimming in potholes and paddling down flooded streets. Her run has put pressure on the African National Congress (ANC), currently leading a coalition in the city, and excited some residents fed up with years of dysfunction.
The race will test whether frustration over poor service delivery can outweigh loyalty to the ANC, still revered by many as the party that ended apartheid. A Zille victory would give her pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) control of South Africa's economic hub and could shift the political landscape ahead of national elections in 2029.
Despite being Africa's richest city, Johannesburg faces chronic power cuts and water shortages, and downtown buildings are sometimes "hijacked" — or taken over — by gangs, which charge people for staying in them. The city has had seven mayors in the last five years.
POOR SERVICES TEST VOTERS' LOYALTY
Car repair shop owner Rashied Najam was won over by the DA after Zille visited his shop and listened to his problems. Officials had neglected repeated pleas to fix a leaking sewage plant nearby, he said.
"Here comes a lady that's my total opposition, Helen Zille, and she meets me and she shakes my hand and hugs me," said Najam. Zille later held a campaign event at his shop.
This is the first time he is planning not to support the ANC, the party of liberation hero Nelson Mandela. "I love them. But they're disappointing," he said.
The ANC's Johannesburg regional chairperson Loyiso Masuku, one of its potential candidates for mayor, acknowledged problems with service delivery and blamed it on the city's rapid growth.
"We're going to be proactive in terms of how we deal with our infrastructure challenges," she said, adding that residents like Najam "do deserve better services".
BEYOND POTHOLES, A RACIAL TEST
Zille said Johannesburg would be much tougher to govern than Cape Town.
"Just getting functional budgeting and allocation working, getting rid of corruption, and focusing on the basics is going to be the big challenge of Joburg," Zille said in an interview.
But the race also taps into South Africa's deep-seated racial divisions, testing whether voters in the mostly Black city are willing to cross those lines three decades after the end of apartheid. The DA is often accused by critics of defending white minority interests, which it denies.
Despite frustrations with its governance, many South Africans "equate the ANC with their Black identity," said political analyst William Gumede.
"We don't yet have enough people who have moved from a voting point of view from the apartheid racial identity barrier... to a new era where they vote based on competition," he said.
"But Johannesburg could actually be where we cross the barrier."
COALITION POLITICS TO DECIDE WINNER
Jacob Seane, 83, a resident of Soweto, a township within Johannesburg, said he had voted for the ANC since the first multiracial elections in 1994 and would never change.
"I think they saw their mistakes and they will fix their mistakes," he said.
Zille said internal DA polling showed her leading with about 40% of votes. An Ipsos poll in September showed the ANC at 31% and the DA at 28%. With no party expected to win outright, the city's government will likely depend on coalition negotiations.
The DA has had a mayor of Johannesburg twice before, but winning the city back would be a major boost ahead of 2029.
Asked about winning votes across racial lines, Zille said: "I just hope that when people get into that ballot box ... the tug of the past isn't too strong." REUTERS

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

17:02:39 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Ukraine could face losses of around $17 billion due to the closure of its Black Sea ports, according to Yulia Mendel, former press secretary to Vladimir Zelensky.
"A long Black Sea blockade, metallurgists say, could cost the country about $17 billion. And there is no strategy from the state on how to work or rebuild. Last year this sector was still 5.5% of GDP. If that industry disappears, what exactly is left to hold the state up?" Mendel wrote on X.
Since July 22, the Greater Odessa ports - Odessa, Chernomorsk and Yuzhny - which handle the bulk of Ukraine’s grain and metal exports, have not received or dispatched a single foreign cargo vessel. The shipping standstill came during the peak of the harvest season. Despite the significantly higher costs of alternative logistics, Ukrainian agricultural producers have been forced to reroute shipments via the Danube River ports of Izmail, Reni, and Ust-Dunaisk, the Romanian port of Constanta, or by road and rail to the western borders. This shift has already caused a logistical collapse at Ukraine's land border crossings.
In early September, TASS calculated that Ukraine’s lost foreign currency revenue from the suspension of commercial shipping through the Greater Odessa ports had already totaled approximately $3.15 billion.

More Than 114,000 Ukrainians Are Missing, Up From 42,000 in Two Years
Eighty-three delegations gathered in Toronto for the Pathways to Peace conference, where the EU announced sanctions against 27 individuals and entities involved in the deportation and indoctrination of Ukrainian children.
Bring Kids Back UA reported on September 29 that representatives of 72 states and 11 international organizations attended the conference, co-hosted by Canada, Norway, and Ukraine. Delegates also heard testimony from Ukrainians who survived Russian occupation and captivity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The EU sanctions target 27 additional individuals and entities involved in the deportation, forcible transfer, "re-education," and indoctrination of Ukrainian children. European Commissioner Dubravka Šuica also confirmed the EU's endorsement of the conference's joint communiqué.
This is a system, and the response to it must be just as systematic.
Maksym Maksymov
Head of Bring Kids Back UA
Maksymov urged participating states to deliver concrete commitments for returning Ukrainian children, civilians, and prisoners of war.
Norway announced approximately $25 million in additional funding for UNICEF and the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Canada also announced new funding for programs supporting survivors, returned civilians, prisoners' families, and children, while Japan backed a Council of Europe initiative focused on Ukrainian children.

Ukrainian authorities know of more than 300 detention sites holding Ukrainians in Russia, Belarus, and occupied territories, while the ICRC has access to none of them.
Ukraine has verified 20,651 cases of deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children as of September 2026. By September 28, 2,650 children had returned home through the Bring Kids Back UA initiative.
The Toronto conference builds on work launched in Montreal in 2024 and complements the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children.
The coalition currently includes 51 members and coordinates diplomatic, humanitarian, legal, and informational efforts to return deported or forcibly transferred Ukrainian children.
Earlier, on September 18, the US president, Donald Trump, signed a law making the forced deportation of Ukrainian children an explicit ground for sanctions against Russia, covering both direct and indirect involvement.
Six days later, Washington announced $27 million to trace, return, and reintegrate Ukrainian children, including $12 million already approved for programs assisting those brought back from Russia and occupied territories.

Three South Korean soldiers were injured in two explosions on September 21 near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone, a heavily fortified border buffer zone between the Koreas that is commonly known as the DMZ.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár reaffirmed their backing for Ukraine’s defense efforts, its European integration path, and a defense spending target of 5% of GDP aligned with NATO goals.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The two foreign ministers described increasing pressure on Moscow as a key shared interest. The statement stated: "Comprehensive strengthening of pressure on Russia, in particular through sanctions, to induce it to end its brutal war of aggression and engage in constructive negotiations with the goal of achieving an immediate ceasefire and a comprehensive, lasting and just peace in Ukraine."
Berlin and Bratislava confirmed their commitment to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders.
The document noted: "Both countries agree to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders on the basis of general principles of international law and not to accept Russia's attempts to forcibly redraw borders through its war of aggression, which violates international law."

Germany and Slovakia agreed to strengthen European energy stability and diversify energy supplies in line with REPowerEU objectives, taking into account the unique needs of individual EU member states.
To enhance defense capabilities, the two countries plan to strengthen the Euro-Atlantic security framework alongside NATO. This includes achieving the agreed 5% of GDP defense spending threshold, mobilizing financial resources for defense operations, and expanding the European defense manufacturing industry.
This agreement was adopted as part of an ongoing bilateral framework initiated in August 2017. Approaching the ten-year mark of this partnership, both foreign ministries agreed to hold regular diplomatic consultations on foreign, security, and European policy matters.
The strategic partnership between Germany and Ukraine led to the launch of a joint initiative for the production of long-range "Deep Strike" drones. During the announcement, defense officials noted that the venture focused on the development of unmanned aerial systems with a range of up to 1,500 kilometers.
The agreement also included the transfer of technology and the establishment of maintenance hubs within Ukraine, which allowed for the systems to be serviced locally. By integrating Ukrainian combat data into the design process, the collaboration aimed to create technology capable of bypassing electronic warfare systems more effectively.

‘We’re afraid of dying’: Brazilian news site will not cover upcoming elections after threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:00:19 UTC
17:00:19 KST

Four years ago, during Brazil’s last presidential election, the tyres were slashed on the pickup truck used for reporting by Tapajós de Fato, an independent journalism website in the Brazilian Amazon.
Days later, a cat’s severed head was left next to the car park, alongside a note bearing the name of one of the site’s founders, Marcos Wesley Pedroso, and a warning that he would be next.
Last July, security cameras outside Pedroso’s house showed cyclists circling the block, whistling and filming his car until, minutes later, another car crashed into it. “I believe they wanted me to come outside so they could ambush me,” said Pedroso.
Police have not identified those responsible or established whether the cases are connected, but Pedroso sees them as part of a wider series of threats linked to Tapajós de Fato’s reporting on environmental and Indigenous rights violations, land disputes, and pesticide contamination in the Amazonian state of Pará.
As a result, the site’s team decided not to cover this year’s elections – which will choose the next president, state governors, members of the lower house and part of the senate, with the first round on 4 October.
“We’re afraid of dying and of putting our families’ safety at risk,” said Pedroso.
He added that the site, whose name refers to the 1,238-mile-long (1,992km) Tapajós River, would remain online and continue covering environmental issues, but would avoid stories about the election.
News of violence around election time is not uncommon: in 2022 a man was struck on the head with a piece of wood after saying he did not support the far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro’s re-election bid.
Journalism and free-expression organisations in Brazil see Tapajós de Fato’s decision, first reported by a network of independent Amazonian media outlets, as a serious example of the consequences of attacks against journalists during the electoral period.
“It reflects the different forms of attempted censorship and silencing that journalists have to face in Brazil,” said Letícia Kleim, legal coordinator at the Brazilian Association of Investigative Journalism.
“Silencing the message by silencing the messenger affects not just their community, but democracy as a whole, which will no longer receive the valuable information they were providing by reporting on the Amazon from within the region.”
Her association is part of a coalition that recorded 4,400 online attacks against journalists, media outlets and the press on X and Instagram between 30 August and 12 September alone, an increase of 67% compared with the previous two weeks.
Because the election campaign was still under way, Kleim said it was not yet possible to know whether there had been more attacks than in the previous election, although she stressed that the context four years ago was particularly hostile because of the then president Bolsonaro, who routinely attacked the media and made threatening remarks to reporters such as: “I’d like to smash your mouth.”
Kleim said: “His government made discrediting the press a priority at times; his family, supporters and politicians close to him embraced that agenda, and many continue with it.”
Bolsonaro is now unable to run because he is under house arrest serving a sentence for attempting a coup after losing the 2022 election, but one of his sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, is in a technical tie in the polls with the incumbent, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
“The possibility of Flávio being elected worries me enormously,” said Pedroso. He said reporting was even more dangerous four years ago, particularly in the Amazon – where Bolsonaro’s anti-environmental and anti-Indigenous policies led to soaring deforestation, a gold rush into Indigenous lands and increased criminal activity.
In 2022, the British journalist Dom Phillips, who reported for the Guardian from Brazil, and the Brazilian Indigenous expert Bruno Pereira were ambushed and killed in the Amazon by men accused of links to a transnational criminal network exploiting an Indigenous territory.
The Amazon-based NGO Comitê Chico Mendes, named after the environmentalist murdered in 1988, issued a statement deploring the threats against Tapajós de Fato: “We cannot normalise an Amazon where fear determines what can and cannot be reported.”
Pedroso said that Tapajós de Fato had decided to make the threats public after years of reporting them to the authorities without any investigation producing results.
“Deciding not to cover the elections was not easy,” he said. “With a great deal of humility and responsibility, I know the role we play in educating and informing many people in the communities around us, but there was no other way. In the end, those are the people who lose out.”

Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid on Wednesday accused the government of playing “cheap politics” at the expense of Israel’s security following the Flydubai plane scare.

Passengers on the plane told Israel’s Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouts from the front of the plane and heard the altercation between the pilots, and that the plane dipped steeply before the emergency landing.
At the time of reporting, all the passengers were on the plane and there was a heavy presence of Saudi security forces around.
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon was quoted by the AFP news agency as saying that the plane was “pretty much out of control” when one of the pilots tried to stab the other while they were flying over Jordan en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
“So the co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone, held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.
“What we understand, according to flight radar tracking, is that two emergency signals were transmitted from the flight – the first was a general emergency signal and the second, a few minutes later, seemed to indicate some kind of unlawful interference on the flight,” Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from Doha, Qatar, said.
“Tracking data also shows that the aircraft plunged nearly 14,000 feet within 30 seconds during the incident – a steep, sharp descent that would have unnerved passengers.”
Later on Wednesday, Flightradar24 temporarily showed a second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverting back to Dubai, but then showed it continuing on its planned route to Israel.
Normalised ties
Flydubai is a low-cost sister carrier of Emirates airline. The UAE has become a popular holiday destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalised ties in 2020.
Flydubai’s fleet relies entirely on variants of the 737, a twin-engine, single-aisle aircraft widely used by airlines around the world. It has nearly 100 planes, including 69 of the Max 8 variant.
The flight originated from Dubai airport, the Middle East’s busiest and the world’s largest in terms of international travel. It handled a record 95.2 million passengers last year.
It is not the first time a flight between Israel and the UAE has landed in Saudi Arabia. A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Riyadh in September 2025 due to a medical incident, the Israeli media reported at the time.
‘Inside threat’ to civil aviation
Philip Baum, the managing director of Green Light Ltd – a training and consultancy firm specialising in inflight security, hijacker and unruly passenger management – said that while it is too early to tell exactly what happened on the Flydubai flight, the incident draws into focus the “insider threat to civil aviation”.
“Regardless of whether or not, it was a terrorist attack or whether it was a heated argument on the flight deck, or indeed, whether it was some mental health breakdown, it illustrates the fact that the insider threat is probably the greatest threat to civil aviation nowadays,” Baum tells Al Jazeera.
“In the post-9/11 era since September 11, 2001, we’ve actually lost more lives on board commercial aircraft as a result of pilot suicide than we have as a result of terrorism. So we really do need to think about who’s at the controls, and how we can prevent the wrong person being at the controls because we’ve got this new enhanced part of the investigation,” he said.

Europe’s energy security has a Black Sea opportunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Last Friday, 25 September, a vessel carrying 90,000 tonnes of Libyan El Sharara crude oil arrived at the port of Kulevi on the Black Sea coast in Georgia. It was the second Libyan delivery for the Kulevi Oil Refinery in less than a month, following the first cargo in August.
Black Sea Petroleum (BSP), a privately owned company based in Georgia, owns and operates the Kulevi Oil Refinery. Operations began in October 2025, and today the refinery processes exclusively non-Russian crude oil. The Libyan deliveries form part of a long-term supply agreement.
BSP’s existing production already offers a basis for supplying European markets with straight-run products, while EURO 5 fuel production is planned by 2029.
Kriti Legend at Kulevi with BSP’s first shipment of Libyan crude oil, 30 August 2026. / via Black Sea Petroleum
Europe’s need for diverse fuel supplies
Europe continues to import fuels used in transport and industry. According to Eurostat, EU net imports in 2024 amounted to 15.7 million tonnes of oil equivalent for gasoil and diesel and 11 million for jet fuel. Both are included in the Kulevi Oil Refinery’s expansion plans.
For Kulevi, the opportunity is to supply EU markets alongside Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, drawing on non-Russian crude and the Black Sea’s shipping connections.
Following the Oil Coordination Group meeting on September 8, 2026, the European Commission reported that higher EU refinery production and alternative international supplies were helping meet demand for diesel and jet fuel. Stocks remained sufficient, but developments in the Middle East and seasonal demand could tighten markets in the weeks and months ahead.
Additional refining capacity connected to maritime trade could give Europe more sources of these fuels. For Kulevi, the opportunity is to supply EU markets alongside Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, drawing on non-Russian crude and the Black Sea’s shipping connections. This would add another route through which international crude supplies can reach Europe as refined products.
An operating refinery connected to the sea
Four pipelines run for three kilometres between the Kulevi Oil Refinery and the nearby port and terminal. They carry crude oil, naphtha, gasoil and fuel oil. The port and terminal are separate facilities owned and operated by SOCAR.
Pipelines connecting the Kulevi Oil Refinery with the nearby SOCAR-owned port and terminal. / via Black Sea Petroleum
Crude arriving by sea or rail can reach the refinery through the terminal. Refined products can move in the other direction for shipment. The two Libyan cargoes show this infrastructure in use, bringing North African crude to the Black Sea for processing.
Black Sea Petroleum has invested €200 million in the Kulevi Oil Refinery to date. A further €650 million is planned by 2029 to expand refining capacity and introduce new fuel production units.
Supply contracts, certificates of origin and shipping records document the crude’s origin and its movement from the supplier to the refinery in Georgia.
The pipeline connection allows the refinery to use the terminal for both incoming crude and outgoing products. Expansion can therefore build on an established route to international markets. Greater refining capacity would increase the volumes handled through that route, while new production units would broaden the types of fuel available.
Investment already under way
Black Sea Petroleum has invested €200 million in the Kulevi Oil Refinery to date. A further €650 million is planned by 2029 to expand refining capacity and introduce new fuel production units.
Processing units and storage tanks at the Kulevi Oil Refinery. / via Black Sea Petroleum
The company plans to raise annual refining capacity from 1.2–1.5 million tonnes to 4.5–5 million tonnes by 2028. Plans also include bringing EURO 5 fuel production units into operation by 2029. The planned product range includes petrol, diesel, jet fuel, liquefied petroleum gas, marine fuel and bitumen.
These products would serve road transport, aviation, shipping and construction. Diesel and jet fuel would also place the expanded refinery in markets where the EU is a net importer. The investment programme is intended to support those exports while also meeting demand in neighbouring countries.
Honeywell refining technology and licensed processes will support the planned expansion, alongside automation and modular processing units. Engineering and construction for the next stages have continued since the first phase opened in October 2025.
BSP has completed 40,000 cubic metres of new storage capacity, with another 40,000 cubic metres nearing completion. This storage will support larger volumes of crude and products as production grows.
Building lasting European relationships
Led by co-founder and chief executive David Potskhveria, Black Sea Petroleum is establishing a Belgian company and plans to open its Brussels office in mid-October. The office will give EU institutions and European business partners a permanent point of contact for discussions about the refinery and its investment plans.
BSP’s European Advisory Council and strategic advisers bring experience in European and international affairs to its work with EU institutions, national authorities and businesses across Member States. They support direct relationships between the company’s team in Georgia and its European counterparts.
BSP welcomes interested partners to visit the Kulevi Oil Refinery, see production first-hand and meet the people responsible for its operations and development.
Last week’s second Libyan delivery provides a concrete starting point for those conversations. The refinery is operating, non-Russian supplies are arriving and investment is continuing. Its development could give Europe an additional source of fuels through an existing Black Sea route, with a company seeking lasting European partnerships.

FlyDubai flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after reported fight between pilots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:59:24 UTC
16:59:24 KST

FlyDubai flight to Israel makes emergency landing, passenger says "co-pilot tried to murder the pilot" and crash jet
A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent attempt by one of the pilots to seize control of the aircraft and crash it, passengers and Israeli officials said.
"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers and other crew members who intervened. The prime minister said he instructed Israel's "security establishment to prepare for potential additional threats."
An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack, which was thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit, overpowered the terrorist, and with their own hands returned control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew that was present," according to a statement.
The plane diverted to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base. No passengers were injured in the incident, but the pilot who was attacked by his fellow crew member reportedly sustained stab wounds, and Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries.
According to Netanyahu, the pilot who carried out the stabbing was placed under arrest and was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities." An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship.
In a social media post, the Israel Foreign Ministry identified the wounded pilot as Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian national. It described him as a "hero" who "fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit."
According to the foreign ministry, Machchhar unlocked the cockpit door to allow passengers and crew to enter and intervene.
"Together, their extraordinary courage saved 174 lives," the foreign ministry said.
The plane landed in Tel Aviv shortly before 8 p.m. local time on Wednesday. People could be heard singing and chanting as the passengers disembarked. Family members came to the airport to celebrate their loved ones' safe return.
One passenger said the plane dropped "very, very sharply suddenly" multiple times before balancing out. Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place over Jordan.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."
"There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," Ohayon said.
Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
One passenger seated at the front of the plane said a "group of young people fought" with the attacker.
The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information. CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.
The Israeli Air Force was first to notice something was wrong, an Israeli official with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News. The air force noticed the flight deviating from its flight path and descending at an alarming rate, the official said. When it tried to contact the plane, it received no response. It then got the emergency alert that specified a hijacking, not just a distress call.
At that point, according to the official, the flight was still several hundred miles from Israeli airspace. However, even 90 seconds or so into the incident, the air force feared a 9/11-style attack, so it immediately made the decision to close Israeli airspace, and seconds after that it scrambled several jets, the official said.
The jets never left Israeli airspace because it became clear that the plane had turned toward Saudi Arabia, and that Saudi Arabia had scrambled its own jets, the official said.
This sequence of events occurred within the span of about two to three minutes, according to the official, and the entire episode lasted about 15 minutes.
A statement from FlyDubai said only that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and that the aircraft "was successfully secured by on-duty FlyDubai crew traveling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely" in Saudi Arabia.
The airline said "all passengers and crew are safe and accounted for," and it confirmed that two replacement aircraft had been deployed to Tabuk to "relieve the passengers and crew," though many Israeli passengers told media outlets they would not reboard a FlyDubai plane.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," the airline said in its statement, urging "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that there were four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship aboard the flight.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.
Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.
Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in a social media post on Wednesday, said "the naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board."
Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in the upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X: "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."
"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also posted about the incident Wednesday, saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."
"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

Taiwan's GlobalWafers August profit rises 145% as wafer market outlook improves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:59:07 UTC
16:59:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — GlobalWafers Co.’s August profit more than doubled, with the silicon wafer industry expected to strengthen as AI and memory chipmakers expand production.
The company reported August revenue of NT$4.76 billion (US$149.6 million), up 7.63% from the same month a year earlier. Profit reached NT$704 million, a 144.98% year-on-year increase, according to CTEE and MoneyDJ.
AI and memory chipmakers are ramping up production, supporting orders for 12-inch products. A new round of price increases under long-term contracts for 2027 is gradually taking shape, further improving the outlook for wafer suppliers.
GlobalWafers' August revenue remained relatively subdued, partly due to a fire at its Novara plant in Italy in July and the traditional summer holiday period in Europe, which typically slows industrial activity. The company said the Novara facility is recovering faster than originally planned after the fire affected part of its back-end production of 8-inch wafers.
Key plant systems have been restored, while the epitaxial wafer process, which was not directly affected by the fire, has resumed. The first batch produced after the fire has already been shipped.
Full production has yet to resume, however, as back-end processes directly affected by the fire are still being rebuilt. Other GlobalWafers providing support are operating at full capacity.
On pricing, GlobalWafers has been negotiating with customers over adjustments for the second half of the year to reflect higher energy, raw material, logistics and overseas manufacturing costs. The size of the adjustments varies by product specifications and customer.
Meanwhile, market prices for 6-inch, 8-inch and 12-inch silicon wafers have been rising, with prices for some 12-inch products already adjusted. GlobalWafers is expected to benefit from high utilization rates at its existing facilities, the gradual recovery of its Novara plant, and higher wafer prices.
The market outlook is supported by a structural supply gap for silicon wafers, the base material used to manufacture semiconductor chips. Made from high-purity silicon, wafers provide the surface on which circuits are formed during chip manufacturing, according to Pocket Securities.
Twelve-inch wafers are widely used for AI servers, high-performance computing and advanced chips. Global monthly demand has reached about 11 million 12-inch wafers, while effective supply remains below 10 million.

====================================================================================================

Chair of Russian opposition party Yabloko charged with “hooliganism” for spoiling his election ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:57:41 UTC
16:57:41 KST

A citation for petty hooliganism was filed against Russian opposition politician Nikolai Rybakov, chair of the Yabloko party, after he wrote slogans on four ballots during elections in St. Petersburg. The Insider identified at least 13 similar cases since 2022 in which a message or drawing on a ballot served as grounds for administrative prosecution. Rybakov became at least the 14th such voter.
Yabloko’s press service reported the petty hooliganism charges against Rybakov on Sept. 29. His case is being heard by the Vyborgsky District Court of St. Petersburg.
On Sept. 20, Rybakov voted at polling station No. 360 in St. Petersburg. None of the four ballots he was given included Yabloko or its candidates. The politician invalidated the ballots by writing “For peace,” “For freedom,” “For a ceasefire agreement,” and “For a life without fear.”
Rybakov had already done something similar in the September 2022 elections. At the time, according to photos published by the party, he wrote “I vote for peace” on his ballot before placing it in the box.
At least five such cases emerged in 2022
Some of the first known cases initiated over writing on ballots emerged during regional elections in September 2022.
In Moscow, Lev Karmanov drew a peace dove and wrote “No to war” on his ballot. Election commission members would not let him put the sheet into the electronic ballot scanner and offered him a new ballot instead while leaving the first one on the administrators’ table. Police detained Karmanov after he left the polling station, and the Chertanovsky District Court ultimately fined him 50,000 rubles ($600) for “discrediting the armed forces” — a ruling later upheld by the Moscow City Court.
The court found the message to be public, since the ballot is handed to commission members and later counted. In the ruling, it was thus stated that Karmanov “publicly displayed” a ballot with the message “No to war.”
That same day, in Veliky Novgorod, police filed a “discrediting” report against Anton Bochanov, who also wrote an antiwar phrase on his ballot before dropping it into a transparent ballot box. According to police, the message ended up facing outward and was visible to commission members and other voters.
In Kirov, a similar citation was filed against Natalia Ryabova, whose ballot bore the messages “Glory to Ukraine” and “Russia will be free,” along with an obscene phrase about Vladimir Putin. Additionally, media outlets reported on another administrative case concerning Moscow polling station No. 1936 in Orekhovo-Borisovo, where a voter left an anti-war slogan on their ballot.
Another case arose in 2022 in Aramil, Sverdlovsk Region, where art teacher Darya Sergeyeva wrote “No to war,” “Glory to Ukraine,” “Put Putin on trial,” and other phrases on her ballot while also drawing a peace dove and the Ukrainian flag. Commission members contacted the police. In November, Sergeyeva was fined 15,000 rubles ($180) for “discrediting the armed forces.”
The Insider found at least five episodes of administrative prosecutions over writing and drawings on ballots in 2022 alone.
Another six cases in 2024
The practice continued in the presidential election in March 2024. St. Petersburg resident Alexandra Chiriatyeva wrote “No to war” in red marker on the back of her ballot, and the Dzerzhinsky District Court charged her with two offenses at once: petty hooliganism and “discrediting the army.” Chiriatyeva was sentenced to eight days of arrest and fined 40,000 rubles ($480). A statement from St. Petersburg’s joint court press service claimed that by writing on the ballot, Chiriatyeva had “damaged state property.”
Another case emerged in Simferopol, where a woman wrote “No to war,” “Against human deaths,” and “Ukraine will win” on her ballot. The Central District Court of Simferopol fined her 40,000 rubles ($480) under the article on “discrediting” the army.
In Podolsk, near Moscow, Maria Alekseyeva was detained over writing on her ballot and charged with the same offense, after which the Podolsk City Court fined her 30,000 rubles ($360).
In Bratsk, Alexander Shokhirev wrote “No to war” and “Glory to Ukraine” on his ballot, photographed it, and then dropped it into a transparent ballot box. The Bratsk City Court found him guilty both of “discrediting” the army and of displaying banned symbols. He was sentenced to 12 days of administrative arrest.
A man from Dubna, Moscow Region, made a social media post featuring a photo of his ballot, which had been spoiled with the caption “No to war.” The Dubna City Court fined him 30,000 rubles ($360) for “discrediting” the army. In his case, the grounds for the charge were not just the message itself but also the posting of the ballot photo online.
Another case occurred during St. Petersburg’s regional elections in September 2024. Election observer Marina Popova dropped a ballot marked “No to war” into the box and was cited under two articles: petty hooliganism and “discrediting” the army. The Kuibyshevsky District Court sentenced Popova to five days of arrest and a 30,000-ruble ($360) fine.
The judge initially sent the citations back to police for revision, noting that the law does not provide for standalone liability for damaging a ballot. The following day, a different judge found Popova guilty after members of the election commission argued at the hearing that the ballot was state property and had been damaged.
In total, The Insider found at least six such episodes in 2024.
In 2026, ballot cases have already led to arrests
Besides Rybakov’s case, at least two more incidents are known from the September 2026 elections.
Stanislav Morozov, a blogger from Penza, posted a video of himself filling out ballots: on one, he wrote an obscene phrase about Vladimir Putin, and on another he crossed out the name United Russia and added a separate obscene message. The Pervomaisky District Court of Penza sentenced him to 14 days of arrest for petty hooliganism — the same article of the administrative code applied to Rybakov. The court’s published materials did not specify which of Morozov’s actions was deemed petty hooliganism.
In Vladimir, Alexander Stepanov wrote on his ballot: “No to war! For peace!” The slogan was noticed after the ballot ended up in a transparent ballot box. The Frunzensky District Court of Vladimir fined Stepanov 30,000 rubles ($360) for “discrediting” the army.
The Insider’s count of 14 such cases since 2022 excludes incidents in which people were only detained but no record of citation could be found, as well as detentions in which the report was filed solely over other actions, such as resisting police.
In at least three previous cases — those of Chiriatyeva, Popova, and Morozov — law enforcement used the same Part 1 of Article 20.1 of the Code of Administrative Offenses on petty hooliganism that is now being applied against Rybakov. The maximum penalty under this article is 15 days of administrative arrest.
Yabloko’s federal party list was removed from the State Duma race on Aug. 10 after internal polling appeared to show support for the anti-war party growing rapidly. Party leaders then urged supporters to invalidate their ballots by marking more than one box. By the start of voting, courts had also removed nearly 30% of Yabloko’s single-mandate candidates, The Insider calculated.
