The number of JOLTS job openings dropped to 7.079 million in August, also below expectations.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.26%, the S&P 500 declined 0.17%, and the Nasdaq was down 0.09% on Tuesday. American indexes opened Wednesday on a positive note.
Meanwhile, European stock markets traded mixed amid geopolitical tensions.
The eurozone’s economic confidence fell 0.5 points month-on-month to 97.9 in September, while the bloc’s consumer confidence declined from minus 15.5 to minus 16.5 points at the same time.
Germany’s public debt hit €2.7 trillion ($3.1 trillion) in the second quarter due to infrastructure, climate and defense spending despite signs of recovery.
EU Energy and Housing Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said the union paid more than €100 billion ($113.5 billion) in additional costs for the same volume of oil and natural gas this year, emphasizing the need to reduce dependence on fossil fuel imports.
Expectations of new tax hikes in the French budget led to a decline in the country’s stock market, which was already under pressure due to debt issues and political deadlock ahead of next year’s presidential election.
The likelihood of tighter Fed policy and rising energy prices in Europe caused the euro/US dollar exchange rate to drop to its lowest level since May 2025 at 1.1312.
Germany's DAX 40 rose 0.1% and Italy's FTSE MIB 30 gained 0.09%, while France's CAC 40 dropped 0.53% and the UK's FTSE 100 fell 0.45% on Tuesday. European indexes opened Wednesday on a mixed trend.
Near Wednesday’s close, Asian equity markets traded mixed as investors remained cautious ahead of US data releases.
Beijing announced new support policies to limit the economic slowdown and said it would assess measures to stabilize its real estate market.

Weak domestic demand and the prolonged stagnation in the Chinese real estate market pressured household and business confidence, while the country focused on exports and industrial production to support growth.

Qatar is intensifying efforts to broker a breakthrough between the United States and Iran and bring an end to their seven-month war, but the latest round of indirect talks has produced little progress. U.S. officials believe the deepening stalemate is increasing the likelihood of renewed military confrontation, with some assessing that President Donald Trump could order a return to major combat operations after the midterm elections, Axios reported. 
Trump again insisted Tuesday that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon and suggested the conflict would ultimately end on Washington’s terms. “They are doing very poorly. I don’t know if they are ready to give up yet. They will give up. This is to stop a nuclear weapon. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon,” he told reporters. 
Iran, meanwhile, accused Washington of being unable to choose between diplomacy and war. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Trump was “trapped in a quagmire in which he can neither negotiate nor fight,” according to Iranian media cited by Axios. 
Despite the increasingly sharp rhetoric, Qatar has not abandoned the diplomatic track. Qatari officials are expected to continue shuttling messages between the sides even as frustration grows in Doha over their refusal to compromise. Qatar previously played a central role in securing the June memorandum of understanding that briefly halted the fighting before the arrangement later unraveled. 
On Monday, Qatari mediators held separate talks with Iranian and U.S. officials. According to Axios, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his team spent several hours discussing a two-page Qatari compromise proposal before Qatari representatives traveled to Washington for talks with Trump administration officials. 
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said Doha was continuing to pass messages between the parties and search for common ground. “We are conveying messages between the sides and working to find common ground in order to reach an agreement,” he said. “Only that will save us all from the consequences of the conflict.”
The Qatari proposal is aimed at bridging the two central disputes separating Washington and Tehran. Iran wants the United States to lift its naval blockade, while the Trump administration is demanding concrete Iranian concessions on the nuclear program. U.S. officials had initially described Monday’s contacts as “positive and constructive” and said Tehran appeared willing to show flexibility on nuclear issues, but by the end of the day there had been no significant movement. 
Talks remain ‘stuck’
“It is stuck,” one source familiar with the talks told Axios. “The Iranians are asking for things the U.S. can’t accept and the U.S. thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise.” Pakistan and Egypt have also urged Tehran to make concessions on its nuclear program, while Iran has insisted it will consider such steps only after Washington returns to the terms of the June memorandum. 
The dispute has also exposed conflicting messages from Washington. U.S. officials told Axios earlier this week that Trump was prepared to offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in exchange for concrete measures to curb Tehran’s nuclear program. Trump later rejected that account on Truth Social, writing that he had offered Iran nothing. 
Preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remains one of Trump’s stated objectives in the war. He has also described weakening Tehran’s ability to threaten neighboring countries as a U.S. goal.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly presented UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan with what an Israeli source described to CNN as new intelligence indicating that Iran has resumed progress on its nuclear program. According to the report, the material included information about new construction at the so-called Pickaxe Mountain site, about 140 miles south of Tehran, which Israel views as a potentially important location in any effort to rebuild Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. The UAE publicly confirmed Netanyahu’s visit, though its official account said the meeting focused on bilateral ties and regional developments. 
Separately, Iranian authorities reported Wednesday that Ali Hemmati and Majid Nikandish, two people detained over anti-government protests earlier this year, had been executed after being convicted in connection with the deaths of four security personnel in Mashhad. Human rights groups had previously listed Nikandish among protesters facing execution, though independent verification of the circumstances surrounding the case remains limited.

Boeing beats Northrop to build U.S. Navy’s sixth-gen jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:19:03 UTC
16:19:03 KST

- The U.S. Navy selected Boeing on Sept. 29 to develop its F/A-XX sixth-generation carrier fighter under a contract valued at more than $20 billion.
- The jet will begin augmenting and eventually replacing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers in the 2030s, the Pentagon said.
The U.S. Navy has picked Boeing to build F/A-XX, its first sixth-generation carrier-based strike fighter, choosing the company over Northrop Grumman and awarding a development contract valued at more than $20 billion.
The U.S. Department of War announced the award on Sept. 29. The contract covers the full-scale development phase and buys multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems and weapons integration testing, the Pentagon said.
The new jet is meant to augment and eventually replace the U.S. Navy’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers beginning in the 2030s, flying from carriers alongside the F-35C. The service released a single artist’s rendering of Boeing’s design on a carrier deck, but Boeing said the aircraft’s technical and programmatic details remain classified under U.S. national security and export laws.
“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform. Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program,” said Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space & Security.
The win gives Boeing both of the U.S. military’s next-generation crewed fighter programs. The U.S. Air Force selected Boeing for the F-47 on March 21, 2025, over Lockheed Martin, and Lockheed was reportedly eliminated from the Navy contest that same month, leaving Boeing and Northrop Grumman as the final two bidders.
“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly. We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs,” said Parker.
Northrop Grumman, which can still challenge the outcome, acknowledged the decision and said it was waiting for more information about the selection, Aviation Week reported. The company had hoped the program would return it to the role of fighter prime contractor, a position it has not held in decades.
Whether one company can carry both fighters at once has been debated since the F-47 decision, with Northrop already building the B-21 bomber for the U.S. Air Force.
“The industrial base concerns among the Pentagon brass have not faded when it comes to both NGAD programs at once. I wonder how much the Boeing win was impacted by this. This will likely be a NAVAIR optimized F-47,” Tyler Rogoway, editor-in-chief of The War Zone, wrote on X.
Boeing points to its St. Louis operation as the answer. The company said construction continues there on a secure manufacturing facility that it describes as the largest in the United States, and which will be part of its all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system.
“Investment in facilities is just one part of the story; we’re also investing in technology and people so that we can deliver for our customers,” Parker added.
St. Louis is also where Boeing builds the jets F/A-XX will replace. On the same day as the fighter award, the U.S. Navy gave Boeing a separate contract worth about $16.7 million to plan and prepare the shutdown of the Super Hornet and Growler production lines.
“I worked with the Trump Admin to bring production of the Navy’s next fighter to MO,” wrote U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt, a Missouri Republican, on X.
The award ends a long stretch of silence and uncertainty around the program. F/A-XX stalled for months after the F-47 decision while funding fluctuated and the U.S. Navy weighed its options, and the Pentagon approved moving ahead with a choice between Boeing and Northrop Grumman in October 2025 without naming a winner. Congress then set aside $897 million for F/A-XX in the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act and required the Pentagon to award a development contract.
The announcement came shortly before the end of the fiscal year, when the funding Congress added for the program was due to expire, Aviation Week also reported.
Unlike the F-47, which received its designation on the day of its award, the Navy fighter is still known only as F/A-XX.

Social minister butts heads with doctors over doctor-patient confidentiality

Social minister butts heads with doctors over doctor-patient confidentiality
The Estonian Medical Association has sent an open letter to Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform), raising concerns that police and other state agencies can access patient records.
Doctors stressed that the doctor-patient relationship is built on trust and that protecting patient confidentiality is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. Patients must be able to share information about their health with a doctor, confident that it will not reach others.
"The current situation, in which police and other state agencies have access to health records, is unacceptable and threatens trust in the entire healthcare system. Patient confidentiality must remain intact even after information is entered into a database," said Neeme Tõnisson, president of the Estonian Medical Association.
The health information system and its administrator, TEHIK, fall under the social affairs minister's authority. The minister is responsible for protecting the data.
The association is calling on Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform) to stop access to health records through government information systems without patients' consent. It says access in exceptions clearly defined by law should require a court order.
"The medical association is breaking through an open door here because a legislative amendment is already being drafted with the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs and will soon go before the government. They know this very well," Joller wrote on social media.
Joller said TEHIK had done nothing wrong, as it had acted and continues to act under current law.
"The Police and Border Guard Board, whose employees sometimes requested health records without sufficient justification, has already changed its practices," she added.
Joller also stressed that no matter how good the systems are, people will always be the weak point. "And here I would also expect the doctors' representative organization to contribute."
Joller said she wanted the association to address healthcare workers who share patients' health information on social media.
The minister said the association should remind its members that sharing patient stories at a conference, training session or elsewhere requires the patient's written consent in a reproducible form. That consent must explain where, when and how the person's information will be used.
She also expects the association to stress to its members that they may not even disclose that a particular person is a particular doctor's patient.
Joller noted that the Data Protection Inspectorate (AKI) has also said patient confidentiality covers all information learned about a person during treatment, not just their diagnosis.
"Disclosing the information requires the patient's consent or a clear legal basis. I have asked AKI to assess the conduct of some doctors to determine whether proceedings should be opened. Why doesn't the medical association do that itself?" Joller wrote.

Royal Navy chief: JEF to create new combat units and get UK nuclear deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:18:00 UTC
16:18:00 KST

Royal Navy chief: JEF to create new combat units and get UK nuclear deterrence
The Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), established to strengthen the security of 10 countries in the Nordic and Baltic region, will form new combat units centered on British military capabilities and nuclear deterrence, Royal Navy chief Gwyn Jenkins said.
The Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a U.K.-led defense cooperation and rapid-response framework for Northern European countries, which also includes the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, will sign an agreement in Oslo in November to establish new combat units, Gen. Gwyn Jenkins of the Royal Marines said in an interview with Finnish newspaper Iltalehti.
According to Jenkins, deploying JEF combat units would not necessarily require NATO's Article 5 to be invoked. The JEF complements NATO and allows its member states to respond rapidly to situations in which a JEF country comes under threat. He said wartime defense plans have already been drawn up for the new units, which should be capable of entering combat immediately if necessary. The plans cover operations by JEF countries' navies, their own national defense requirements and support for NATO's wartime plans.
The navies of JEF countries would form the core of the new units, although their composition and capabilities would depend on the specific mission. Traditional warships and submarines would be supported by military aircraft, helicopters, marines and special forces. Uncrewed systems, including aerial and maritime drones and other autonomous technologies, would also be used extensively. Jenkins described the approach as a hybrid fleet. Britain's state-of-the-art F-35 stealth fighters based aboard its aircraft carriers would be an important part of the JEF's capabilities.
The backbone of the force's military deterrence would be Britain's nuclear weapons, carried aboard British submarines patrolling the Atlantic Ocean. Jenkins said the Royal Navy maintains constant readiness to provide nuclear protection for the Nordic region as well. He stressed that Britain's nuclear deterrent is not only part of NATO's collective defense but also provides the U.K. with a sovereign defense capability.
According to Iltalehti, Britain's nuclear deterrent would in the future also extend through the JEF to all of its member countries, rather than solely through NATO's nuclear defense framework. Jenkins said this should also send a direct message to Moscow.
The Royal Navy chief linked the strengthening of the JEF primarily to Russia's behavior. He said the greatest problem is Moscow's unpredictability, meaning Russia could at some point test European democracies, including by testing NATO's Article 5 in the Baltic or Nordic region.
At the same time, the general stressed that there was no reason to panic. However, that did not mean the JEF or NATO could lapse into complacency; they must also prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Jenkins said the purpose of military preparedness is not to start a war but to prevent one. Deterrence must be sufficiently credible for Moscow to understand that an attack on a JEF or NATO country would be bound to fail. He said this requires maintaining readiness, conducting exercises and sustaining a military presence in the region.
In his interview with Iltalehti, the Royal Navy chief also said the U.K. was prepared to deploy its military capabilities to the Baltic Sea to strengthen Finland's defense. He said keeping sea routes open would be essential. If military support were needed for Finland, the Nordic countries and the Baltic states, functioning links between the Atlantic Ocean and the Baltic Sea would have to be maintained. Jenkins said Britain wants to use its frigates, destroyers and autonomous systems for this purpose and deploy them wherever they are needed in a particular situation.
The agreement to be signed in Oslo in November is expected to give these plans a concrete organizational structure. It should provide further details on how the JEF's collective defense in the Baltic region, the Nordic countries, the North Atlantic and the Arctic will be strengthened.
Finnish expert: This is a big deal
Finnish security expert Henri Vanhanen commented on the announcement that JEF units would be established, saying the move is far more significant for Finland's security than may currently be understood.
"This is not just about new combat units or British nuclear weapons. A framework is now being created in Northern Europe that would allow Britain and a group of Finland's closest partners to take rapid military action in a critical situation, even without NATO. This is a major change," he wrote on social media.
Vanhanen explained that if Russia were ever to seek to test the West, it would benefit from creating as ambiguous a situation as possible — one in which NATO's 32 member states would have to consider exactly what was happening, whether it constituted an attack and how to respond. The JEF, however, makes such a strategy more difficult.
"This would not even require a joint decision by all 10 JEF countries. Britain could, for example, act together with Finland, Sweden and other willing countries. Each country decides for itself how to use its forces," he noted.
With greater military capabilities now set to underpin the framework through the creation of new combat units and the strengthening of capabilities, particularly at sea, this is highly significant for Finland, Vanhanen wrote.
"We depend on the Baltic Sea and connections to the West. Britain, meanwhile, is one of Europe's strongest naval powers, a nuclear-armed state and a country capable of deploying truly significant military force here," the Finnish expert said. "So Britain is not simply promising to support Northern Europe. It is already building, in peacetime, a system through which it could come here to fight if necessary. The more of this that is prepared in advance, the less room there will be for uncertainty when a crisis occurs."
Vanhanen noted that while NATO is the foundation of Finland's defense, it does not make sense to put all its eggs in one basket. The JEF means that, if necessary, the U.K. and other willing countries can also act quickly by reaching agreements among themselves. Russia therefore can no longer count on hesitation within NATO buying it additional time.
"For this reason, I currently consider strengthening the JEF to be one of the most important pillars of Finland's defense," he concluded.
Vanhanen has worked as a researcher at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, focusing on Finnish security and defense policy and Northern European security. He has also worked at Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs, the European Parliament, the U.S. Embassy in Helsinki and the Finnish Parliament. He has worked with the center-right National Coalition Party.

Fight between pilots reportedly triggers hijacking code on Dubai-Tel Aviv flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:17:35 UTC
16:17:35 KST

Mohammad Sio, Ikram Kouachi and Sahin Demir
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
 
A fight between the pilots of a passenger plane flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv reportedly triggered a hijacking code before the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, according to Israeli daily Ynet.
 
“An altercation occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073,” said Flydubai, and said crew members traveling aboard the aircraft managed to secure the plane and divert it safely to Saudi Arabia.
 
The Dubai-based carrier said the flight, which was operating from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion International Airport, landed safely at Tabuk Airport and all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for.
 
Flydubai said the reasons and motives behind the altercation remain unknown and are subject to a formal investigation.
 
“We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts,” it cautioned.
 
The flight was carrying 174 passengers and briefly transmitted a distress signal.
 
Ynet said the aircraft had been scheduled to land at Ben Gurion Airport.
 
The aircraft was operated by Dubai-based carrier Flydubai and was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the incident occurred.
 
According to the report, the code indicating a possible hijacking was activated during the cockpit altercation.
 
The aircraft subsequently landed at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
 
Around 90 minutes after takeoff, while entering Jordanian airspace, the aircraft transmitted code “7700,” the international code for a general emergency, the newspaper said.
 
It subsequently transmitted code “7500,” which is used to indicate unlawful interference with an aircraft, including a possible hijacking.
 
At around the same time, the plane changed course, returned to Saudi airspace and began flying at a low altitude over the kingdom, according to the report.
 
After initially heading south, the aircraft turned west while remaining inside Saudi airspace before landing in the kingdom.
 
Captain, first officer injured
 
Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk said in a statement that its Air Traffic Control Center received a distress call from Flydubai flight FZ1073 at 8.44 am for an emergency landing.
 
It said an emergency was declared at the airport and preparations were made to assist the aircraft, which landed safely.
 
The airport said both the aircraft captain and first officer were injured and transferred to a hospital for necessary medical care.
 
There are conflicting reports over the nationalities of the two officers. Channel 12 said the crew consisted of a Russian pilot and a Ukrainian co-pilot, while Ynet reported that the pilot suspected of attempting to crash the aircraft is of Omani origin and that the second pilot is Emirati.
 
Israeli Channel 12 later said the incident appeared not to be security-related and that authorities were checking whether the distress signal had been activated accidentally because of an argument between the pilot and co-pilot.
 
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have ordered military rescue planes to be sent to Saudi Arabia to bring home Israeli passengers on the Flydubai flight.
 
Flydubai later informed Israeli authorities that a replacement aircraft would be dispatched from Dubai to Saudi Arabia to bring back the Israeli passengers who had been on the flight, Ynet reported.
 
Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport said in a follow-up statement that all passengers departed at 5.40 pm local time (1440GMT) aboard an alternative aircraft provided by the airline.
 
The airport reiterated its commitment to the policies and regulations of Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation, as well as international conventions and treaties concerning the safety of civil air navigation, passengers and crew.
 
The Israel Airports Authority, meanwhile, denied reports that the country’s airspace had been closed during the incident.
 
Senior officials in Israel’s aviation industry said suspicion of a security incident on the Flydubai flight had not yet been ruled out, Ynet reported.
 
According to an initial assessment cited by the officials, one of the pilots allegedly “attempted to cause a crash,” while the other pilot managed to thwart the attempt with the help of Israeli passengers.
 
The Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said the situation was “under control” and that “all means are now being deployed to safely return the Israeli passengers to Israel.”

Vaccines may counter Alzheimer's disease. New position paper explains how
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:16:20 UTC
16:16:20 KST

Ever since the accusation, long since debunked, that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine was associated with autism, vaccination has been going out of style. Vaccines had some rebound after the COVID pandemic began, but anti-vaxxers continue to promote vaccine hesitancy; meanwhile, as resistance proliferates, the United States has reported the highest numbers of measles cases in 35 years.
No credible research argues the case against vaccines, and evidence accrued over generations demonstrates that they reduce the incidence and severity of disease. Yet in recent years, it has become evident that vaccination can protect not only our bodies against the diseases they are designed to foil, but our minds.
Now a position statement in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease by a panel of experts, the "Vaccines for Dementia Study Group," including Chuck Greenblatt of Hebrew University and Richard Lathe of the University of Edinburgh, highlights the evidence between various infections and the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, and the corollary – that vaccination against unrelated diseases can diminish the probability of Alzheimer's disease.
"Hallmark" clumps of abnormal proteins found in the brains of Alzheimer's sufferers weren't the cause of the dementia, as was assumed for decades. They are a byproduct of the brain's fight against infection. And, crucially: "Findings that vaccine recipients are at reduced risk of developing Alzheimer's disease have now been replicated around the world," the statement sums up.
Bow wow how?
Vaccine skepticism may stem from more than personal fear of needles, as suggested by the fact that even inoculating Bowser against rabies is becoming passé. A study of 2,200 American adults found that 37 percent think canine vaccines are unsafe and unnecessary; and a fifth assume they're ineffective.
This is terrible for the pets and their vets. The burgeoning skepticism may also augur ill for our future neurodegenerative disease rates, going by the position statement, which strongly supports the theory of a pathogenic origin for Alzheimer's disease, and the pro-vaxx lifestyle for the greater good of our continuing cognizance.
How could vaccines against other problems prevent Alzheimer's? By causing "immunopotentiation" – strengthening the immune system in general. Do all vaccines cause generalized immunopotentiation? Some do more than others; the anti-tuberculosis shot called BCG and the anti-shingles vaccine Shingrix exhibit heightened potential in reducing the probability of Alzheimer's disease.
The statement does not present new research but summarizes decades of research into Alzheimer's. They stress that so far, links between pathogen infection and dementia, and between vaccination and dementia prevention, are correlational.
"Nevertheless, the consistency of findings across vaccine classes, populations and study designs supports investigation of immunopotentiation as a potential strategy for Alzheimer's disease prevention," it concludes.
Could the results be skewed by "healthy vaccinee bias"? No, which they demonstrate through three recent "natural experiments," which exclude the possibility that people who get vaccinated are merely more healthy and less at risk of dementia." (Natural experiments are where a factor is changed by nature or circumstance, rather than by the investigators themselves.)
All three studies exclude this bias and suggest that shingles and influenza vaccines can protect against dementia.
Note that our pets can develop dementia too. Behavioral changes have been observed in aging cats and dogs, who may become more prone to "accidents" in the house. Maybe this would be worse if the authorities didn't force us to vaccinate our pets on a regular basis.
Plaque and perdition
Alzheimer's specifically is estimated to afflict one in 11 percent of people 65 or older, but its cause remains unclear. It can't even be diagnosed in the living. The verdict remains problematic until autopsy, but doubts are arising even about the classic diagnostic method.
Since 1991, diagnosis of Alzheimer's has relied on postmortem findings of abnormal protein buildup in the brain: neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein) and clumps of amyloid-beta protein.
But there are snags to that diagnostic method. Some people with Alzheimer's have no abnormal proteins, and some elderly people with perfect cognition have brains riddled with plaque. Tests of monoclonal antibodies designed to remove amyloid-beta plaques were not a success, and a panel of world experts concluded that the effects of plaque removal on dementia were "absent or trivial." There have been recent protests about corporate fiddling with statistics to try to show that the clumps cause disease.
All this suggests that protein buildup in the brain isn't the disease: It's the hallmark of a fight against inflammation, likely within the brain itself.
It's become clear that our brains are not the sterile environments we once assumed. They do house some bacteria, fungi and viruses, Lathe and colleagues report separately. The microbes identified in brains appear to be a subset of the gut microbiome. Many others have found similar results, Lathe says, notably the group of Louis Carrasco in Madrid.
Lathe and colleagues in the U.S. have compiled a list of individuals where treatment with antimicrobials apparently reversed the trajectory of dementia, and also found an unusual historical report of a 24-year-old with premature Alzheimer's, apparently as a result of scarlet fever.
Is infection of the brain itself necessary? The critical issue is the inflammation the bug causes, which need not be in the brain, Greenblatt says. But clearly the brain can get infected, for example through the nose; respiratory infection, such as community-acquired pneumonia, correlates with higher dementia rates; also, people with dementia and Parkinson's lose the ability to identify smells.
The heartbreak of brain herpes?
One agent singled out as a possible culprit is herpes simplex, or HSV-1, which heavens knows is common enough. Ruth Itzhaki of the University of Oxford has written that there is "overwhelming evidence" that HSV-1 plays a role in the case of people who also have a certain gene involved in fat metabolism, APOE4 – which is also a known risk for Alzheimer's disease.
Recurring herpes outbreaks cause immunological reactions that may lead to the features Alzheimer's disease, she tells Haaretz. So, herpes may not cause Alzheimer's, but may be associated.
While she suspects herpes may play a major role in our species' dementia problem, the evidence points at many agents - bacteria and fungi, she says, and agrees with the thesis of immunopotentiation to diminish dementia risk. "The facts speak for themselves," she says.
Lathe personally doubts that herpes is a major cause. "Our big study [the Pathobiome] found very little herpes," he explains, adding that if Alzheimer's was caused by herpes viruses, it should be treatable by antiherpetics. Those do work against herpetic encephalitis or neurology; they don't work against Alzheimer's disease, he sums up. What the brain biome project has found so far are "the usual pathogens" – staphylococcus aureus bacteria, candida albicans fungus and the like. Hi guys!
A trivial cost
So the cause of Alzheimer's disease remains obscure, nor is there any cure, despite some claims of drugs that "reverse" the trajectory. There is no question that reducing Alzheimer's incidence would be a boon for the world economy. Vaccines are cheap, typically a few dollars a pop, while the cost of treating the symptoms of Alzheimer's is estimated at about $1.3 trillion a year worldwide, the authors say.
"Even a 10 percent reduction in Alzheimer's disease rates would save $38 billion each year in a single country, the USA," they write, and about £4 billion a year in the United Kingdom. So, vaxxing costs peanuts compared with the financial burden of Alzheimer's, the authors point out; and as the world population continues to grow and age, the burden of care will increase.
There are caveats. Studies detecting diminished Alzheimer's rates among the vaccinated are predominantly observational, the authors caution, but the sheer amount of evidence, activity – going back over a century – weighs against a bias. As early as 1908, it was observed that people, especially children, given the tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin exhibited significantly reduced rates of dying from other infectious diseases. Albert Calmette, the co-inventor of BCG, speculated that BCG somehow conferred "a special aptitude" to resist other infections.
This was prophetic. During the COVID pandemic starting in 2019, it proved that inoculation with BCG administered years before the outbreak correlated with improved COVID outcomes. It is true that the efficacy of protection was inconsistent, but that could reflect different vaccine types used, different susceptibilities of the study participants and differences in a host of other parameters.
The bottom line is that some studies, if not all, found correlation between BCG and a reduction in all-cause mortality.
The anti-TB shot also confers protective effects against a range of conditions including eczema, diabetes, and multiple sclerosis.
At what age? "If you received BCG as a kid and were lucky enough to get booster at 14, you have some chance the effects would last 50 years," Greenblatt answers. "Immunity wanes with age. Most childhood vaccines need boosters. That's why Shingrix [against shingles] is so important, as a booster – the bug has been there all the time; the herpes is just waiting to come out."
You again, herpes. Lathe sums up that vaccination in general seems beneficial to Alzheimer's reduction though some are clearly better. BCG and Shingrix are better, for example.
One paper identifies 45 viral exposures that were "significantly associated with increased risk of neurodegenerative disease."
What have we? Increasing indications that our wellness and vaccine uptake influence the risk of developing Alzheimer's. A recent meta-analysis concluded that adult vaccinations, particularly against with shingles, influenza, pneumonia and the "Tdap" vaccines against tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough, are associated with a lower risk of dementia.
Why not end back with our best friends. The cost of vaccinating Froofroo against rabies runs $10 to $55 a year in the United States. The cost of suspected rabies is her life – there is no cure – and if a rabies suspect digs her fangs into your ankle, anti-rabies shots will cost you hundreds to thousands of dollars. In other words, protection is vastly cheaper and unlike the disease, it isn't life-threatening. That is the very point that the statement makes in the case of Alzheimer's disease as well.

Ian Bremmer: 'We have passed peak Trump in terms of disruption on the global stage'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:15:18 UTC
16:15:18 KST

Ian Bremmer: 'We have passed peak Trump in terms of disruption on the global stage'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Ian Bremmer, the American political scientist, author, and founder and president of Eurasia Group and GZERO Media. According to Bremmer, we may now be entering the autumn of the "Donroe Doctrine" and the MAGA era: an "America First" isolationist approach in which President Donald Trump envisions a return to "greatness" in Gilded Age fashion. But is this the America voters had envisioned?
Yet Bremmer is equally emphatic about something else: "America, of course, is a democracy where the people do express their will." Ultimately, he believes, the political consequences of Trump's second term will be determined by voters. He has argued that Republicans risk losing the House, and possibly the Senate, in the upcoming midterm elections.
For Bremmer, however, the Trump phenomenon is also deeply personal. "President Trump and his administration frequently put themselves above the interests of the country," he says. "And this really has nothing to do with the Republican Party." Trump, he points out, was once a Democrat. In Bremmer's view, this makes the phenomenon distinctly Trumpian, and suggesting that "this pattern will go away after Trump."
Read moreEarly voting begins in US midterms that could see Republicans lose control of Congress
Meanwhile, Trump has mastered what Steve Bannon famously called "flooding the zone": overwhelming the political system with a torrent of executive orders, announcements, and initiatives. But Bremmer cautions against assuming that everything the president declares, or orders, automatically becomes American policy.
"Trump says a lot of things, and he even writes a lot of executive orders," Bremmer observes, "but what ends up being executed and implemented turns out to be a fraction of that."
Courts, Congress, foreign governments, economic interests and, at times, members of Trump's own party have all acted as constraints on what the administration can actually implement.
And yet, beyond the domestic political struggle, Trump's foreign policy is reshaping America's relationship with the world. And while "Trump is deeply unpopular in France, across Europe, in Canada and the UK, he's actually quite popular among most of the Latin American countries".
Read moreEurope and Canada are 'strong, even stronger together', Carney tells European Parliament
Across much of Latin America, there has been a rightward political shift, and Trump's hardline policies have found greater resonance, particularly where questions of security, borders, drugs and instability are immediate and consequential. Venezuela, meanwhile, has become one of the most consequential and controversial expressions of his foreign policy, and a centerpiece of what has come to be called the "Donroe Doctrine," a Trump-era interpretation of the Monroe Doctrine asserting a more forceful American role throughout the Western Hemisphere.
The stakes became particularly stark after the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in a military operation in January 2026. Trump subsequently said the United States would oversee Venezuela during the transition.
At the United Nations General Assembly in September, Trump himself invoked the language of conquest and plunder when speaking about Venezuela and the United States' post-Maduro role. After describing a major oil deal between the United States and Venezuela, he declared: "To the victor belong the spoils."
Read moreIran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
It was precisely this worldview that prompted one of Bremmer's sharpest critiques of Trump, expressed in an interview with Katy Tur on MS NOW during the week of the General Assembly.
"The most consequential thing," Bremmer had argued, "is when President Trump spoke about Venezuela, declaring, 'To the victor goes the spoils,' which is the way he sees Iran. It's the way he sees AI. But it's absolutely antithetical to the reason the United States set up the United Nations after World War II."
He went on to describe Trump's UN speech as "a knife in the creation of that order," arguing that "you couldn't have said something that was more problematic for what the Americans used to stand for on the ashes of the Second World War that we won."
Read moreFact-checking Trump's speech at the United Nations General Assembly
Bremmer contrasts that philosophy with the principle he believes originally shaped the postwar international order: not that victory entitles you to the gains, but that it carries great responsibility: for governance, stability and peace, not only for the United States but for all nations of the world.
So what happens when the country that built the postwar order begins to challenge the principles on which that order rests?

EU Approves 5 Defense Projects Worth $369M, Ukraine Takes Part in 4 of Them

16:15:08 KST

The European Commission has approved the first five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI) worth $369 million, with Ukraine included in four of them.
The projects will strengthen Europe’s defense capabilities by developing key military systems together. Following today’s decision, the defense projects can now move towards funding.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
EDPCI is a funding track within the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP), a $1.7 billion EU-wide initiative to strengthen and modernize Europe’s defense industry. The Commission allocated €325 million ($368.6 million) to support the creation and deployment of EDPCI, a program of large-scale industrial projects that lays the groundwork for member states to collaborate on major defense initiatives.
“The proposal concerns an area of shared competence, in particular the industrial dimension of the Union’s defence readiness. The objectives pursued by the proposal cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States acting alone”, the European Commission wrote in the document.
The industrial projects focus on five priority areas: drones and counter-drone systems, maritime and seabed defense, space, air and missile defense, and strengthening security along the EU’s Eastern Flank, wrote the European Commission on its website. Ukraine is participating in all areas except space.
Project Details
The industrial projects focus on the following key initiatives:
Russia Hits Kyiv With Ballistic Missiles, Killing 2 Women as Child Dies in Wider Region
- Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER): Aims to enable the coordinated development, scaling, and deployment of European unmanned and counter-unmanned systems to address critical capability gaps across member states. The estimated budget is $3.97 billion to $5.68 billion by 2033.
- Integrated Maritime and Seabed Defence (IMSD): Seeks to establish a federated and interoperable European maritime and seabed defense architecture. It is designed to strengthen the EU’s ability to prevent, detect, deter, and respond to threats across the maritime domain. The estimated budget is $48.9 billion to $81.8 billion by 2045.
- EU Federated Integrated Air and Missile Defence (EU-FIAMD): Designed to provide member states with a collective and effective integrated air and missile defense system, including early warning information and command-and-control capabilities. The estimated budget is $62.5 billion to $90.9 billion by 2040.
- Eastern Flank Watch (EFW): A comprehensive multi-domain effort to enhance the security of the EU’s eastern border, ensuring the protection of the entire union and strengthening its defense readiness. The estimated budget is $68.2 billion to $113.6 billion by 2036.
- Space: While Ukraine will not participate in this specific initiative, the project aims to create new market opportunities and reduce the EU’s structural dependence in the space sector. The estimated budget is up to $27.3 billion by 2034.

Groups raise concerns over Taiwan’s Maanshan nuclear plant restart review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:30 UTC
16:13:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Civic groups have called for greater scrutiny and transparency in reviewing the plan to restart the Maanshan Nuclear Power Plant following the Nuclear Safety Commission’s approval of an initial proposal.
The commission said Thursday that it had completed its review of an initial plan to restart the plant in Pingtung, which ceased operations after its operating license expired in May. It added Taiwan Power Company (Taipower) must carry out additional work, including safety inspections, before submitting another report for review.
Thirty-four environmental groups issued a joint statement Tuesday saying the proposal did not contain all the information necessary to determine whether the plant should be restarted. Even if the plant is restored to an operable condition, that would not by itself guarantee the safety of its operations, per CNA.
The decision on whether to restart the plant should not be based solely on its technical feasibility, it should also take into account factors including geology, climate, and natural disasters, the groups said.
The groups called for a broader range of experts to be involved in the review, beyond nuclear specialists, as well as meaningful participation from residents living near the plant. They also asked that the names of the members of the review committee and experts be made public.
The groups include Citizens of the Earth, the Pingtung Environmental Protection Union, and the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance.
At a public hearing on Aug. 1, Li Ken-cheng (李根政), chair of Citizens of the Earth, criticized the lack of public participation in the review process, demanding that the project undergo environmental assessment.
Lin Cheng-yuan (林正原), a researcher at the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance, said at the hearing that the Maanshan plant has been operating for 40 years, increasing the risks associated with aging equipment, and many of its components can no longer be replaced.
The plan submitted for review focuses on whether the plant can return to the condition it was in before its shutdown and does not address whether it would meet current safety standards after being restarted, he added.
In March, Taipower submitted an application to renew the Maanshan plant’s operating license after lawmakers amended the Nuclear Reactor Facilities Regulation Act in May to allow nuclear power plant operators to apply for 20-year license extensions beyond the existing 40-year limit.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) has said the plant could resume operations as early as 2028.

Mack’s hybrid tractor aims to replace U.S. Army’s M915 trucks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:12 UTC
16:13:12 KST

- Mack Defense will display its hybrid-electric Common Tactical Truck line haul tractor prototype at AUSA 2026 in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12-14.
- The U.S. Army program aims to eventually replace about 35,000 heavy tactical vehicles, including platforms such as the M915 Line Haul Tractor.
Mack Defense will display a hybrid-electric heavy tractor it built for the U.S. Army’s Common Tactical Truck program at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12-14.
The truck is Mack’s on-road entry for the program and is designed to replace older highway haulers such as the M915 Line Haul Tractor. The Allentown, Pennsylvania, company said on Sept. 28 that the tractor will be on show at booth No. 7501 at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center.
According to Mack Defense, the Common Tactical Truck effort supports the planned modernization and eventual replacement of about 35,000 vehicles the U.S. Army uses for combat logistics, support and service-support missions.
The line haul tractor is based on Mack’s commercial Granite truck in a 6×4 configuration, meaning three axles with two of them driven. Mack says it is set up for moving heavy loads over long distances on highways and secondary roads. It shares its underlying design with Mack’s other prototypes to keep parts common across the family, which the company says simplifies maintenance and lowers lifetime costs.
All three of Mack’s Common Tactical Truck prototypes use high-voltage hybrid-electric systems. The company says they cut fuel use, allow extended “silent watch” operation with the engine off, and can export electrical power to equipment outside the truck. Mack pitches those features for situations where refueling may be limited and soldiers depend on onboard radios, electronics and possibly small field power grids.
Mack Defense began building the hybrid approach into its entry in late 2023, when it partnered with BAE Systems to integrate BAE’s Gen3 propulsion and accessory power management systems into its prototype.
The tractor also uses drive-by-wire controls, which replace mechanical links with electronic ones. Mack says that setup supports driver-assistance features including collision avoidance, blind-spot detection, driver alerts, anti-lock brakes, traction control and rollover mitigation, and leaves room for autonomous driving later. Other features include a new suspension for rough terrain, predictive maintenance technology meant to reduce unplanned breakdowns, cybersecurity measures, and an open systems architecture intended to make future upgrades easier.
“Our team used its experience in designing and integrating advanced vehicle technologies to build these next-generation trucks,” said David Hartzell, president of Mack Defense. “These upgrades will help provide the Army with safe, innovative, cost-effective, fuel-efficient and next generation tactical vehicles.”
Mack built three prototypes for the program: an on-road tractor, an off-road tractor and a load-handling system truck. The company also submitted designs for a cargo truck with a material handling crane, a wrecker/recovery truck and a tanker.
The company received its prototype agreement on Jan. 27, 2023, when the U.S. Army awarded Other Transaction Authority deals worth $24.25 million combined to four teams: Mack Defense, Navistar Defense, Oshkosh Defense, and a partnership of American Rheinmetall Vehicles and GM Defense. Each team’s prototypes represented its offering for the M915 Line Haul Tractor and M1088 Medium Tractor, the Palletized Load System, and the Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Truck, and the service ran an operational demonstration of the designs in August and September 2024.
When the prototype contracts were awarded, Mack Defense said an initial production contract could cover more than 7,000 trucks valued at over $5.1 billion.
The route to that production contract shifted in January, when the U.S. Army said in a Jan. 21 notice, reported by Janes, that it was re-evaluating its truck replacement plan after reviewing industry responses to requests for information issued in the fall of 2025. Before that pause, the service had planned testing to support a single-vendor award.
On March 19, 2026, the U.S. Army published a commercial solutions opening for the program, moving its acquisition strategy toward readily available commercial products, Inside Defense reported. The solicitation covered six vehicle variants meant to replace the Palletized Load System, the Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Truck and the M915 Line Haul Tractor, and said the Army would not rule out firms that specialize in only one or two variants.
Mack’s announcement does not say whether the company responded to that solicitation, and it gives no production timeline, quantity or contract value.
The company’s booth will also feature three products from its parent, Volvo Group. They include a Prevost H3-45 motorcoach with 56 seats and a Volvo D13 engine, and a Volvo Construction Equipment L120 wheel loader adapted for military use with a fording kit for water up to 1.5 meters (4.9 feet) deep, a split cab to reduce height for transport, and lifting and tie-down points for air freight. A Volvo Penta D16, a 16.1-liter inline six-cylinder off-road diesel engine, completes the display.

Taiwan forum highlights health benefits of regular exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:04 UTC
16:13:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should make regular exercise part of everyday life to promote the health of citizens and to save medical costs, officials said Tuesday (Sept. 22) at an international symposium in Taipei.
During his opening remarks at the symposium, Sports for All Agency Director-General Fang Jui-wen (房瑞文) asked how many people in the audience had exercised that morning. Many in the 500-seat conference room raised their hands.
Fang said the show of hands appeared roughly consistent with Taiwan’s national average but emphasized the need to encourage more people to exercise regularly. According to a survey conducted by his agency, 35.6% of people in Taiwan were classified as regular exercisers.
Taiwan defines regular exercise as exercising at least three times a week for 30 minutes each time, with a heart rate of at least 130 beats per minute or enough exertion to cause sweating and shortness of breath.
Fang said the government hopes to increase the proportion of regular exercisers because physical activity offers a range of health benefits, including a lower risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes and hypertension. He also pointed to evidence linking physical activity to a lower risk of dementia and other health problems.
“We want people to ask, ‘Have you exercised today?’ instead of the common phrase, ‘Have you eaten today?’” Fang said.
He said the symposium was designed to help Taiwan learn from international experience, particularly from Japan and South Korea, where governments have developed programs encouraging people to incorporate physical activity into their daily routines.
The event adopted the phrase “From Now On...” as its theme, encouraging people to begin exercising immediately rather than waiting. Speaking to local media after his remarks, Fang said he hoped the symposium could become an annual event and provide a platform for experts from Taiwan and other countries to exchange ideas on exercise and public health.
Health Promotion Administration Deputy Director-General Lin Li-ru (林莉茹) also emphasized the importance of exercise as Taiwan deals with rapid population aging. Lin said regular physical activity could help people prevent or manage chronic diseases and maintain their health as they age.
“Exercise can prevent illness, and the data shows that it is very important for citizens to exercise,” Lin said. “If everyone gets in the habit of daily exercise, they can learn that exercise is a very important part of good health.”
South Korea’s experience
The symposium’s first speaker was Wook Song, a professor in the Department of Physical Education at Seoul National University. His research interests include exercise physiology, aging, chronic diseases, sarcopenia, and exercise interventions for older adults.
Song said research has increasingly demonstrated the relationship between physical activity and better health outcomes. He cited research indicating that physical activity is associated with a lower risk of death from all causes, as well as benefits related to conditions including diabetes and dementia.
One large study found that people who engaged in moderate-to-vigorous activity had a 31% lower risk of death from all causes than inactive people.
“Physical activity is great medicine, and we do not need to exercise like athletes,” Song said.
He also highlighted the potential benefits of combining aerobic and resistance exercise. Song said resistance training was particularly important as people age because muscle strength and function decline over time.
He discussed sarcopenia, an age-related condition involving the loss of muscle mass and strength or physical function. The WHO included sarcopenia in the International Classification of Diseases in 2016, while South Korea added it to its national disease classification in 2021.
Song said muscle strength generally peaks in early adulthood before declining with age, raising the question of how much of that decline can be prevented or slowed through regular exercise, particularly resistance training.
Governments face an “implementation gap” because although the health benefits of physical activity are widely recognized, many people still do not exercise regularly, Song said. He suggested governments could use incentives, fitness programs, and national campaigns to encourage participation.
South Korea’s National Fitness 100 program, for example, provides physical fitness assessments, exercise counseling, and nationally recognized certificates based on participants’ fitness levels. The program is available to children, adults, and older people through fitness certification centers.
Song also highlighted Seoul’s Wrist Doctor 9988 program, which uses smartphones and wearable devices to encourage residents to increase their physical activity.
The program awards points for activities such as walking, with accumulated points convertible into Seoul Pay credits that can be used at participating businesses. It had 2.55 million participants as of 2025, equivalent to about one-quarter of Seoul’s population. Song said such programs demonstrate how governments can use technology and incentives to make exercise easier to incorporate into everyday life.
The symposium’s broader message was that exercise should not be viewed solely as a recreational activity or something reserved for athletes. Instead, officials and researchers said physical activity can form part of a broader public health strategy aimed at helping people remain healthy and independent as they age.

Taiwan Army seeks NT$11 billion to boost Stinger missile stockpile

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Army has proposed allocating NT$11.03 billion (US$345 million) to replenish its Stinger missile stockpile, shortening the procurement schedule by a year.
According to the Ministry of National Defense’s proposed 2027 budget submitted to the Legislative Yuan, the procurement covers additional ammunition for existing Stinger missile systems, per Liberty Times. The project is separate from a previously budgeted military investment program to acquire man-portable Stinger missiles.
The latest budget classifies the purchase under logistics and maintenance spending for general ammunition procurement and maintenance, rather than as a new weapons acquisition program. The funding is intended to cover missiles purchased from the US, excluding launch systems and vehicle platforms.
The additional missiles are intended to replenish stocks for Taiwan’s existing Avenger mobile air defense systems, Dual Mount Stinger air defense systems, and Apache attack helicopters equipped with air-launched Stinger missiles, Liberty Times reported. The replenishment would strengthen the military’s ability to sustain air defense operations during a potential conflict across the Taiwan Strait.
The procurement was originally scheduled to run from 2026 through 2031, spreading payments over six years. The latest budget moves the completion date up by one year to 2030, shortening the project from six years to five while keeping total funding unchanged.
The proposed budget allocates NT$1 billion each for 2026 and 2027, with the remaining NT$9.03 billion scheduled for 2028 through 2030, according to Liberty Times. That translates to average annual spending of about NT$3.01 billion over the final three years, roughly three times the annual allocations in the initial phase.

HMS Daring has taken on fuel for the first time in years, in the clearest sign yet that the destroyer is close to going back to sea after nearly a decade tied up alongside, according to the ship.
The ship’s own account posted the moment on Tuesday evening, noting she “hasn’t heard this over main broadcast for quite some time” before giving the pipe: “Do you hear there. No smoking, no naked lights, fuelling Ship.” A photograph with it shows a bunkering tanker secured alongside, hoses run across to the destroyer, and a rating on the upper deck watching it happen.
The pipe warns the ship’s company that fuel is going aboard and that ignition sources are banned while it does. Warships take on fuel because they are going somewhere.
Daring has been out of service since April 2017, and we reported last year when she passed 3,000 days alongside. She is now at roughly 3,470 days, or nine years and six months.
The vessel underwent the Power Improvement Project, the replacement of the diesel generators that had left the Type 45 class at risk of losing all power at sea, along with a wider package of refit work. She came back to Portsmouth in early 2023 and has not moved since.
Crewing began ahead of trials, with shakedown expected from around the turn of this year. That would be her first time off the wall since 2017.
The Power Improvement Project has worked through the class ship by ship, with Dauntless completing the same work before her. The intention is to hold the destroyers in service into the 2030s, and a study is now running on whether their out of service dates can be pushed further right.

SBU officers exposed the agent ahead of time and detained her while she was setting up a concealed camera near a Ukrainian Armed Forces soldier's vehicle. During searches, two improvised explosive devices and a mobile phone containing evidence of cooperation with Russian special services were seized from her.
The court found the woman guilty under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.

Nathan Cleary wins first Dally M Medal, Tamika Upton claims third on NRL awards night
Injured Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary has accepted his maiden Dally M Medal from his couch, while Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton took out the NRLW award for the third time in four seasons.
After years of being the consensus best player in the men's game, Cleary finally made it official by romping clear in the Dally M count, securing the award with two rounds remaining and ultimately finishing 14 votes clear — 67 to Braydon Trindall's 53.
- Nick Campton analysis: Cleary has no worlds left to conquer after Dally M victory
Trindall made a late push to cause a major upset before injuring his shoulder in round 24, while the rest of the top five — Dylan Edwards, Haumole Olakau'atu and Scott Drinkwater — failed to poll in round 25, when Cleary got a maximum six votes in a 22-14 win over Melbourne.
Having suffered a gruesome compound fracture of his left leg in the Panthers' preliminary final loss on Sunday, Cleary was not at the awards ceremony on Sydney Harbour, instead accepting the award via video message.
"I want to start by saying how grateful I am for everyone's support the past few days," he said from a couch with his injured leg propped up in a cast.
"I can't thank everyone enough for the messages they've sent through."
He thanked his parents, who he has been living with this year while his house has been being renovated.
He credited his Panthers teammates for making him a "10,000 times" better player, while he also paid tribute to girlfriend Mary Fowler, who is currently playing for Manchester City in England.
"It's tough doing the long distance but she always makes me feel supported and loved. That's all I could ever ask for," he said.
The NRLW count was much closer, with 2022 winner Raecene McGregor pushing Upton to the 11th and final round of the season, but the Broncos gun finished with 31 votes to McGregor's 29.
Upton is preparing to play for her sixth NRLW premiership when the Broncos face the Roosters for a second straight year on Sunday, when the league will honour Jai Arrow after his MND diagnosis earlier this year.
The tribute is set to occur in place of traditional pre-game entertainment after negotiations with Tones and I fell apart.
NRL boss Peter V'landys on Monday promised "surprises" and said on Wednesday night that a number of Australian artists would be part of the tribute, although Arrow said earlier in the night that V'landys had told him "nothing yet".

"We don't do any of this work for these awards but it's special to be recognised."

CIA Chief Reportedly Warned Russia Its Economy Could Collapse Like the Soviet Union

CIA Chief Reportedly Warned Russia Its Economy Could Collapse Like the Soviet Union
CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that Russia’s economy could collapse in a Soviet-style crisis if the war continues, German outlet Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported on September 26.
A senior diplomat familiar with the CIA’s briefing to Western partner services after Ratcliffe’s late-August visit to Moscow told FAZ that the intelligence assessment was the trip’s central purpose. “Russia is losing the war,” the diplomat described the US assessment as concluding.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Earlier reporting had already indicated that Ratcliffe brought Moscow a bleak assessment of Russia’s deteriorating military and economic position, after which the Russian leader Vladimir Putin reportedly canceled a planned meeting with him.
The latest FAZ account provides additional detail on the economic warning delivered during the visit.
According to FAZ, the US assessment distinguished between Russia’s military situation and its longer-term economic position. American intelligence reportedly viewed the battlefield as moving toward a stalemate, while concluding that Russia could not sustain the war economically.
“The economy will collapse, just as the Soviet Union did at the end of the Cold War,” the diplomat told FAZ, describing the assessment presented to Moscow.
The message was also tied directly to US policy toward Ukraine, the report noted. Washington wanted Moscow to understand that the assessment shaped its approach, and that Russia’s position would weaken over time.
Putin therefore should not expect US President Donald Trump eventually to abandon Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to FAZ. The resulting American message to Moscow was straightforward: “Negotiate!”
FAZ reported that the assessment also influenced how some European officials interpreted Washington’s recent diplomacy toward Russia, including Trump’s invitation for Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December.
Russia’s economic strain has also been visible in its construction sector, where bankruptcies rose 41% year over year by early September. Housing demand fell sharply across several regions as developers faced high borrowing costs, inflation, and mounting debt.

Skyrora hot fires scaled-down orbital rocket in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:09:06 BST
16:09:06 KST

Skyrora has completed a 45-second static hot-fire test of a scaled-down version of its Skyrora XL orbital launch vehicle at Machrihanish on the west coast of Scotland, according to the company.
The test vehicle was built to validate subsystems and components similar to those intended for the full-size rocket, and the firing gathered data on the pressurisation system alongside engine characteristics including propellant flow rate and chamber pressure. According to Skyrora, initial data indicates the subsystems operated successfully throughout, and the engineering team is collating and analysing the results before conducting a second test.
Dr Jack James Marlow, the company’s chief operating officer, said: “You don’t build confidence in an orbital launch vehicle by waiting until the finished rocket is on the launchpad. You build it through thousands of decisions, measurements and tests along the way. This scaled-down XL system lets us test and validate the technology, subsystems and components together, understand how they perform and make improvements before scaling up to the full vehicle. Our approach is simple: test, learn, refine and test again, so that when Skyrora XL reaches the pad, we have confidence grounded in evidence.”
The company describes its method as testing early, testing repeatedly and testing systems together before scaling them up, on the basis that problems found at small scale are cheaper and quicker to fix than problems found late. Work will progress through larger and more demanding trials before anything is integrated into the full vehicle.
Skyrora XL is a three-stage rocket designed to carry small satellites into low Earth orbit. The company is headquartered in Scotland and designs, manufactures and tests its vehicles and engines at Cumbernauld, with a wider programme covering the Skylark L suborbital vehicle, propulsion work and additive manufacturing.
In 2025 Skyrora became the first British launch vehicle manufacturer to receive a launch operator licence from the Civil Aviation Authority, permitting a suborbital launch of Skylark L from SaxaVord Spaceport on Unst in Shetland.
Machrihanish, on the Kintyre peninsula, was a Royal Air Force station and a NATO forward operating base during the Cold War, and its runway remains among the longest in Europe. The site has since been taken into community ownership and hosts a range of engineering and aerospace tenants, Skyrora among them.
Domestic launch has been given weight in defence terms that it did not carry a decade ago. Lord Coaker told the House of Lords this week that British national security depends on freedom of action in space, including the ability to protect British and allied space assets, and that investment is going into resilience through the UK Space Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan. Sovereign launch matters to that argument because a satellite replaced quickly after being lost or degraded is worth considerably more than one that has to wait for a slot on somebody else’s rocket.

Nespresso is phasing out its compostable coffee capsules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:07:13 UTC
16:07:13 KST

Nespresso is phasing out its compostable coffee capsules
Nespresso is discontinuing its range of compostable paper capsules, which was introduced just a few years ago.
A spokesperson for the Nestlé subsidiary confirmed press reports when contacted by the AWP news agency. The paper capsules had been launched as a pilot project to offer customers an additional choice. However, feedback highlighted issues relating to their limited shelf life and the overall “product experience”, the company says. Nespresso therefore states that it is now more convinced than ever that aluminium is the best choice for preserving the coffee’s flavour and aroma.
More
Your favourite coffee was probably made by a Swiss machine
In Switzerland, the paper capsules have not yet completely disappeared. They are expected to remain available in some Nespresso boutiques for around a month, depending on when stocks run out. The product had been tested in 14 European markets.
The compostable capsules with 82% paper packaging were launched in 2023, following three years of development. Once the pack of capsules had been opened, Nespresso recommended using them within four weeks. According to the company, the aluminium wrappers, on the other hand, protect the coffee from light, air and moisture for up to a year.
Nespresso does not, however, view this decision as a step backwards in terms of sustainability. According to a life-cycle analysis commissioned by the group, the carbon footprint is virtually identical: for a small cup of espresso, it is 79 grams of CO₂ equivalent with the paper capsule and 81 grams with the aluminium one.
The company now intends to focus more on aluminium recycling, aiming to dispose of the capsules increasingly via standard recycling schemes. In France, 80% of the population can already recycle Nespresso capsules via standard recycling schemes; in Switzerland, the recycling rate stands at 73% and the aim is to increase this further.

Christa’s final night: Tennessee set to execute first woman in 200 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:06:54 UTC
16:06:54 KST

A Tennessee prison is making final preparations for the execution of Christa Pike, who is scheduled to become the first woman put to death by the state in more than 200 years. Pike, now 50, is due to be executed by lethal injection at 3 a.m. Thursday Israel time, after years of delays and legal challenges. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee this week rejected her request for clemency, clearing the way for the sentence to be carried out.
Pike was 18 when she murdered 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer on Jan. 12, 1995. The two were enrolled in a vocational training program in Knoxville along with Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Prosecutors said Pike became convinced Slemmer was interested in Shipp and, driven by jealousy and rage, lured her to a secluded area on the University of Tennessee campus.
There, Pike and Shipp tortured and killed her. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large piece of asphalt, while Shipp carved a pentagram into her body. The crime scene drew particular attention amid the “Satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s, when widespread fears in the United States centered on supposed satanic cults abducting and ritually abusing people, including children.
Pike’s death sentence made her one of the youngest women ever sent to death row in the United States. She has never denied responsibility for Slemmer’s killing, but for years her lawyers and supporters have argued that execution is disproportionate given her age at the time, her later-diagnosed mental illnesses and a childhood marked by neglect and severe sexual abuse, including rapes at ages 11 and 17.
Her current attorney, Stephen Ferrell, has also argued that Pike’s trial lawyers failed during the sentencing phase to present jurors with crucial details about her background or to emphasize her youth. Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. She told police that she had initially intended only to confront Slemmer physically but lost control and killed her.
In her clemency petition, Pike’s lawyers argued that her untreated mental illness left her unable to “hit the brakes.” Pike herself expressed remorse in a statement included in the petition.
“I was an 18-year-old kid and mentally unstable,” she said. “It took me many years just to understand the gravity of what I had done, and even longer to understand how many lives I destroyed. I took someone’s daughter, sister and friend. It makes me sick today to think that I was capable of committing such a crime.”
Ferrell has argued that scientific understanding of adolescent brain development has advanced substantially since Pike was sentenced and that imposing the death penalty on someone who had only recently turned 18 is now exceptionally rare. He has also pointed to the different sentence received by Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the murder and was given life imprisonment with the possibility of parole because of his age.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, 275 people have been executed in the United States in the modern death penalty era for crimes committed between the ages of 18 and 20, but death sentences for defendants in that age group have become increasingly uncommon. Robin M. Maher, the center’s executive director, has said she does not believe a jury hearing Pike’s case today, with evidence of the sexual abuse and neglect she endured, would sentence her to death.
Slemmer’s family sees the case very differently. Her mother, May Martinez, has rejected arguments that Pike should be spared because she was so young when she committed the murder, saying her daughter was denied the chance to grow older at all.
“Not a day goes by, not a minute goes by, that I don’t think about Colleen,” Martinez said. “The holidays are the hardest. Colleen’s birthday was last week. She should have been 51.”
Executions of women remain exceedingly rare in the United States. Only 18 women have been executed since 1976, roughly 1% of all executions during that period. Tennessee last executed a woman in 1820. The most recent woman executed anywhere in the United States was Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman put to death in Missouri in 2023 for a 2003 murder.
In a final attempt to halt Pike’s execution, her lawyers appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing that her post-traumatic stress disorder could cause “severe mental suffering and heightened psychological terror” when she is restrained on a gurney for the lethal injection.
Pike has also asked that only women take part in the execution process, arguing that the presence of men during her final moments could trigger trauma. Tennessee corrections officials said they would try to accommodate at least some of her requests, including having female officers move her from her Nashville prison to a high-security facility during the 24 hours before the execution.
Before Lee rejected her clemency petition, Pike said in a letter to the media that whatever the outcome, she had reached a sense of peace.
“I’m not afraid to die,” she said. “I’m just nervous about the process itself.”

Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv reports hijacking code, loses contact
Aircraft carrying more than 150 passengers descended to suspicious altitude; Israeli fighter jets scrambled
Mohammad Sio
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
ISTANBUL
A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 150 passengers briefly transmitted a code indicating a possible hijacking, descended to what was described as a suspicious altitude and diverted toward Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, according to Israeli media.
Israeli daily Ynet said two Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled following the alert.
The Flydubai aircraft was expected to land in Saudi Arabia shortly after the incident, Ynet reported.
Ynet said sources in Israel reported that it was probably "not a security incident."
Israeli Channel 12 later reported that contact with the aircraft had been lost after reports emerged of a possible hijacking.
A security source cited by Ynet stressed that “there is no confirmed information about a hijacking. The pilot activated a distress signal.”
Following the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz convened an urgent security consultation, according to Ynet.
