Fuel prices above €2 per litre: Who will foot the biggest bill in Portugal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:08:16 UTC
15:08:16 KST

From fishing to agriculture, and from freight to passenger transport, many sectors have felt the impact of sharp fuel price rises in Portugal since the start of the Iran war.
"Any sector that includes road fuels in the [value] chain will face additional costs because prices have been trending upwards in recent months," warned Nuno Figueiredo, spokesperson for DECO PROteste, the Portuguese consumer-rights organisation, at a time when retail prices for these energy products in Portugal are several dozen cents higher than on the day the Iran war began.
Despite the slight relief in fuel prices recorded on Monday, monitoring by the Directorate-General for Energy and Geology (DGEG) shows that on 28 February, when the conflict broke out, the average price of standard diesel and standard 95 octane petrol in mainland Portugal stood at €1.596 and €1.681 per litre respectively.
Almost seven months later, on 27 September, the prices had already risen to €2.219 and €2.113 per litre, in that order. An increase of 62 and 43 cents per litre in each case.
This reality is unfolding against a backdrop of severe disruption on oil markets caused by the conflict being fought by the US and Israel against Iran, which has led to significant damage to energy infrastructure and refineries across the Middle East.
It is also being fuelled by restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, through which around 20% of global oil consumption passed before the war.
Drawing on data from Statistics Portugal (INE) on inflation, the DECO PROteste spokesperson notes that in August the rate accelerated to 3.3%, a rise "almost entirely" explained "by the increase in the price of diesel", according to the institute.
Overall, in the same month, prices for energy products were up 12.2% compared with a year earlier. In this context, Nuno Figueiredo argues that it is possible "to state with confidence that the impact [of high fuel prices] will be felt across almost the whole economy".
Yet, at a time when "almost all of us depend directly or indirectly on fuels", some sectors are feeling the consequences of these increases "more immediately", Figueiredo stressed to Euronews.
In this article, we explain which activities are most exposed to the impact of the high prices being charged at service stations in recent weeks.
From fisheries to agriculture and beyond
Among the sectors where the effects are likely to be most visible in the coming period, fisheries stand out. This is because "the cost of each trip out to sea, with fuel more expensive", will be higher from the outset, meaning it "will be passed on more quickly to the price of the final product", the consumer-rights spokesperson tells Euronews.
The same is expected to happen in agriculture. "Costs build up throughout the whole growing period and then, later on, as a result, they are also reflected in consumers' wallets."
In both cases, "the consumer suffers indirectly from the consequences of fuel prices". Even "indirectly", because of "all the logistics involved" in getting products to customers. "All types of transport associated with industry" and with the movement of goods will, therefore, "also face higher costs", Figueiredo points out.
"So, inevitably, it will be the consumer, as the last link in the chain, who ends up spending more money to buy what they used to buy more cheaply", the DECO PROteste representative concludes.
Indeed, speaking to "Dinheiro Vivo", the National Association of Public Road Hauliers of Goods (ANTRAM) and the Farmers' Confederation of Portugal (CAP) warned that the rise in fuel prices would ultimately be paid by consumers.
And in an interview given at the start of September to Antena 1 radio, when fuel prices had already passed €2 per litre, the director-general of APED - the Portuguese Association of Distribution Companies, Gonçalo Lobo Xavier, also warned that this would "be reflected in the final price of goods" on supermarket shelves.
The effect, however, would not necessarily be immediate or fully passed on, APED insisted, saying that retailers have absorbed part of the rise through "margin reductions" in profits.
The recent impact on the food basket
Despite this backdrop, Figueiredo adds that the basket of 63 essential food items monitored by the consumer-rights organisation registered, in the week between 16 and 23 September, a price drop of €1.86 compared with the previous seven days.
A "contradiction", in Figueiredo's words, because it "ran counter to the upward trend in fuel prices" seen over "three or four consecutive weeks" in the run-up to that analysis.
So how can these figures be explained? "Some products became cheaper and did not have a direct link, or we did not identify a direct link, to fuel prices, otherwise they too would have increased." The country is therefore experiencing a situation in which it is not possible "even to make a forecast" about "what will happen tomorrow", the DECO PROteste spokesperson notes.
Faced with this scenario, Figueiredo urges consumers to "go back to what people used to do and do a big monthly shop", choosing to go to the supermarket "in the weeks when there is a downward trend" in basket prices. The aim is to avoid "weekly fluctuations" that may be damaging for household budgets.
"The best advice is to try to take advantage of periods when prices have fallen, in the case of food in particular, and try to buy a larger quantity of what is needed", the representative says.
Transport? "Electric vehicles will feel it less"
As with freight, the rises in diesel and petrol prices are also likely to be felt in passenger transport. This is particularly true for services that rely "exclusively" on this type of fuel, Figueiredo tells Euronews.
He also points out that "electric vehicles will feel it less", even though "electricity is not, strictly speaking, at the best prices either".
Speaking to Jornal de Negócios, Sónia Ferreira, president of the National Association of Passenger Transport (ANTROP), said on 22 September that higher fuel prices could mean an additional cost of an estimated €35 million for the passenger transport sector in Portugal.
Price rises are also being felt in other sectors
Representatives of other industries have likewise been warning about the consequences that these fuel price increases may have for businesses. One example is the Association of Civil Construction and Public Works Industries (AICCOPN) which, according to the "Jornal Económico", stressed that this trend is particularly damaging for construction, as it is a sector inseparable from the use of heavy machinery and road transport of materials.
Earthmoving contractors in particular took to the streets last week, staging a go-slow protest to draw the government’s attention to the difficulties they are facing.
The organisers pointed out that fuel accounts for almost 70% of the final price charged to clients and that, according to SIC Notícias, the government led by Luís Montenegro has agreed to extend to this sector the support of 10 cents per litre already in place for professional and agricultural diesel.
Meanwhile, AIMMAP – the Association of Metallurgical, Metalworking and Related Industries of Portugal, through its executive vice-president Rafael Campos Pereira, highlighted the cost of road transport as one of its main concerns, reporting that companies operating in the sector are cutting margins in order to remain competitive "in the markets", ECO - Economia Online reports.
Speaking to RTP, the medicines distribution sector has even admitted it may limit daily deliveries, stopping them at weekends, and estimates that the higher operating costs stemming from price rises could leave it facing losses of up to €4 million this year.

Malaysia begins Myanmar repatriations despite warnings from UN and rights groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:05:11 UTC
15:05:11 KST

Malaysia began sending back about 1,500 Myanmar nationals on Tuesday, the government confirmed, as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants and asylum seekers by returning them to the war-torn country.
The group is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens that Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres amid a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.
Both the UN and advocacy organisations voiced concern on Tuesday, saying the group could face a dangerous homecoming in Myanmar, where a civil war has raged since 2021.
Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya people in the first group, and there is worry they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide. The Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the UN.
Many of the Rohingya escaped to Malaysia during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.
On Tuesday afternoon, AFP reporters saw three ships belonging to the Myanmar navy, used in a previous repatriation exercise, departing from Malaysia’s Lumut naval base. The Myanmar nationals were processed at the naval base before boarding dozens of buses which arrived under police escort at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium.
Malaysia’s interior ministry confirmed that the repatriations were under way.
It said it a statement that the repatriation was part of the government’s plan to resolve the “legacy issue” of foreign asylum-seekers in Malaysia – of which it said 95% were from Myanmar.
“This long-standing issue has imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people,” the statement said.
But in Geneva, the UN rights chief, Volker Turk, urged Malaysia to stop the process immediately, saying nobody should be deported to Myanmar, given the severity of the situation on the ground.
“This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses, and where many cruelly face the real risk of more of the same violence again upon their return,” he said in a statement.
“The conditions are far from safe and sustainable, and it is deeply questionable whether any return in these circumstances can be considered truly voluntary.
“The hundreds of thousands who have fled Myanmar in fear for their lives must be protected, and their fundamental human rights to seek asylum and protection abroad properly considered.”
The Malaysian prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya. The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur.
They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state. They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation.
Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.
Last week more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organisations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar.
Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.

Darnytsia’s Kyiv plant was struck three times, on Sept. 23, 26 and 28 respectively. On the latter, attacks also hit two ATB-Market warehouses in the Brovary district, a refrigerated warehouse of JS Company Rud in Zhytomyr, and an OKKO gas station in Kyiv.

For the second consecutive month, Russian forces have engaged in a systematic campaign of air strikes targeting major civilian commercial enterprises across Ukraine in retail, food processing, pharmaceuticals, logistics, and energy.
Strike on Ukraine’s largest drugs manufacturer Darnytsia three times in one week
Darnytsia’s main manufacturing complex in Kyiv was struck for the third time on Sept. 28, following previous strikes on Sept. 23 and Sept. 26. Founded 95 years ago, the company is the leading pharmaceutical company in Ukraine by sales volume in physical units. Every sixth package of medicine on Ukrainian pharmacy shelves is produced by Darnytsia, according to the company’s website. The company manufactures over 180 products, focusing primarily on cardiology, neurology, and effective pain management
While automated air-raid protocols protected staff and resulted in zero casualties, the enterprise withheld operational specifics for national security reasons. “We are not publishing any details about the aftermath of the strike or the condition of the plant. I also ask you not to post photos or videos, describe the damage, or add any details,” Kateryna Zahorii, chair of the Board of Directors at Darnytsia, wrote in her Facebook post.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 29, 2026
Complying with Good Manufacturing Practice standards since 2002, Darnytsia exports its products to over 20 countries worldwide.
According to financial statements registered in YouControl, Darnytsia demonstrated stable top-line revenue alongside changing net financial results over recent years. In 2025, Darnytsia recorded a total revenue of Hr. 4.25 billion ($ 95.1 million), resulting in a net loss of Hr. 1.04 billion ($23.3 million).
Ukraine’s largest food retail ATB again under fire
The escalation against healthcare supply chains coincides with severe damage inflicted on Ukraine’s food distribution networks. On Sept. 28, Russian air strikes struck two food storage warehouses belonging to Ukraine’s largest supermarket chain, ATB-Market, in the Brovary district of Kyiv region, Forbes Ukraine reported citing the retailer’s press service. Founded in 1993 as a small network of six grocery stores in Dnipro, ATB-Market has grown over more than 30 years into Ukraine’s largest national retail chain.
According to the State Emergency Service and Kyiv Regional Military Administration Chief Tymur Tkachenko, the strike ignited major fires and caused a localized ammonia leak, though emergency crews isolated the hazard without civilian threat.
The Brovary attack is the latest in a series of devastating blows to ATB’s logistics network. On Sept. 4, Russian drones destroyed ATB’s distribution hub in Dachne, Odesa region, following three separate summer attacks that wiped out the retailer’s largest logistics center in Dnipro in June and damaged facilities in Kharkiv and Odesa, Forbes Ukraine reported. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, ATB has lost over 110,000 square meters of warehouse space, more than half its total logistics capacity - with four distribution centers destroyed, three heavily damaged, and one under occupation.
In 2026, ATB wrote on its website that it operates over 1,320 stores spanning 352 populated locations across 22 Ukrainian regions and serves over 4 million daily customers.
Drones hit OKKO and ice-cream manufacturer Rud
Ukraine’s prominent ice cream producer Rud suffered a Russian drone attack that completely destroyed a 4,350-square-meter refrigerated warehouse alongside administrative units, specialized loading equipment, and stored finished goods. With over 20 years of experience in the market, JS Company Rud (Zhytomyr Butter Plant) is Ukraine’s ice cream producer and a logistics provider specializing in the storage and delivery of deep-frozen food products, according to its website.
The attack completely destroyed a 4,350-square-meter refrigerated warehouse alongside administrative units, specialized loading equipment, and stored finished goods, according to Interfax-Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Facebook that the plant is located in Zhytomyr region.
State Emergency Service operations deployed 70 firefighters and 19 emergency vehicles to extinguish the resulting blaze, though rescue teams were temporarily forced to pull back to safe areas due to the threat of repeated double-tap strikes.
Meanwhile, leading fuel retailer OKKO confirmed that a Russian attack struck one of its gas stations in Kyiv. Station staff enacted emergency safety protocols, halting fuel dispensation and evacuating customers to bomb shelters without casualties. OKKO’s emergency assessment teams remain on site evaluating structural damages and preparing restoration work.
Operated by PJSC Concern Galnaftogaz, OKKO is one of Ukraine’s premier retail fuel networks, encompassing over 400 filling station complexes nationwide, according to the company’s website. Beyond fuel distribution, the brand operates the country’s largest roadside dining infrastructure, featuring over 20 restaurants under brands such as A la minute, Pasta Mia, and Meiwei, alongside convenient stores at its stations. OKKO also engages in wholesale and retail petroleum sales, product storage, and transportation, supported by an infrastructure of 11 oil depots and 19 stationary and mobile fuel quality control laboratories.

Move to rejoin EU among options for UK, says Burnham
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:04:30 BST
15:04:30 KST

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the European Union.
The prime minister told the BBC a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now" but the UK needed to "consider the options" for its relationship with the EU as "where we are isn't good enough".
It comes after he pledged in his Labour conference speech on Tuesday to explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year.
The move could set up a huge dividing line at the next general election, with the Conservatives accusing Burnham of trying to "reopen old wounds by restarting the battles of the Brexit years".
As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".
In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason, Burnham was challenged over whether he was reopening divisive arguments about rejoining the EU, despite promising not to in May.
In response, the PM said: "No, I'm not proposing that, am I? I am saying that in a context when we're looking at a 10-year plan for Britain, Britain needs to consider the options as to where we will be.
"That is way before you even get to anything that's put before the public, this is about now just looking at what are the broad options for our relationship."
He suggested these options could include staying "exactly as we are", a closer relationship similar to that being discussed by the EU and Canada or rejoining the EU customs union.
However, Burnham stressed that "to leap back to a proposal and a referendum on it wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".
Pressed over whether including an in-out referendum in a future Labour manifesto was a possibility, Burnham said: "Yes, things are possible. I think where we are isn't good enough."

Asked earlier on BBC Radio 4's Today if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, Burnham replied that he wanted to "look at the options".
The PM added that he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now".
French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be "very good news" if the UK wanted to rejoin the EU, while Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said his country would welcome Britain back "with open arms".
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said his party had put forward "concrete plans to boost our economy, strengthen our defences and cut people's taxes by joining the single market and a customs union".
He added: "Talk is cheap. Burnham must stop with all the 'maybes' and get negotiating that better deal for Britain today."
The party's Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said last week there is "no rejoin on the table", adding Britain would effectively be treated as a "fresh entrant state" if it wished to join the bloc again.
Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door".
Tice said: "He says Brexit has done more harm than good but what's done real harm is a Labour government that can't deliver growth, can't control migration and now wants to outsource the job to Brussels."
He added Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".
In his Labour conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham blamed Brexit for a loss of control over both immigration and the economy, telling delegates he did not believe the current relationship was "good enough".
He told activists he wanted to use the rescheduled summit later this year to lay out "different options" for the UK's long-term relationship with Europe.
He promised to "find consensus" on an option to clarify the UK's position, although did not offer further detail of how this would be measured.
In response to Burnham's conference speech, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "Labour cannot pin the blame for their disastrous economic decisions on a vote that happened over a decade ago.
"Besides, they are already dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset."
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "All Andy Burnham offers on repairing our relationship with our biggest trading partner is a promise to keep our options open.
"The Green Party is very clear that we should rejoin the customs union to start reversing the damage, and full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK."

China’s R&D spending hits record 2.8% of GDP, beating OECD average for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:01:56 UTC
15:01:56 KST

China’s R&D spending hits record 2.8% of GDP, beating OECD average for the first time
Beijing plans to double down on basic research, cutting-edge technologies and scientific talent as it strives to achieve tech self-sufficiency
For the first time, China’s spending on research and development as a share of gross domestic product has surpassed the average for Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members – a trend one analyst expects to continue as Beijing seeks to strengthen technological self-reliance amid intensifying global competition.
R&D expenditure exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of GDP, Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun said at a press conference on Tuesday. The OECD average stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, the National Bureau of Statistics reported.
Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the achievement showed how China’s investment in innovation had reached a level comparable to that of developed economies. He expected the share of GDP devoted to R&D to keep rising, with a greater focus on optimising funding allocation and improving research efficiency.
“We must continuously increase the proportion of investment in basic research to build a solid foundation for ‘zero-to-one’ original breakthroughs,” Wang said, while ensuring that “large-scale R&D investments translate more efficiently into industrial competitiveness”.

Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year ‘no better than cheap multivitamin’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year are no better than a £22-a-year multivitamin, according to analysis by the consumer watchdog Which?.
Which? found that many popular supplements that are aimed at women over 45 going through menopause or perimenopause lack meaningful quantities of key nutrients, yet cost 20 times more than standard multivitamins.
The global menopause supplement market is valued at nearly $17bn and is expected to reach $25bn by 2030, as women look for ways to manage a variety of symptoms associated with menopause such as hot flushes, poor sleep and mood swings.
But research by Which? found that none of the supplements it studied contained the correct nutrients in the right doses to support their use for menopause.
Shefalee Loth, a public health nutritionist at Which? who co-led the research, said: “Which? is concerned that the supplements industry has become a wild west and regulators are not doing enough to get a grip on dubious marketing and unchecked quasi-medical claims from firms apparently seeking to cash in on people’s health anxiety and insecurities.”
Calcium and vitamin D are the most important nutrients during perimenopause and menopause as they support bone health as oestrogen levels decline. Maintaining good levels of iron, magnesium and other vitamins and minerals can also help with symptoms.
Nutritionists from Which? examined the active ingredients in 26 popular supplements sold by retailers such as Holland & Barrett, Boots and Amazon and found that a high-quality multivitamin alongside targeted supplements where needed was often cheaper and potentially more effective than a so-called all-in-one menopause blend.
It found that Asda’s A-Z Multivitamins & Minerals, costing 6p a day (£22 a year), contained all essential vitamins plus 200mg of calcium and 100mg of magnesium. In contrast, the most expensive supplement, Love Mushrooms’ Empower, cost £1.33 a day for a two-tablet dose (£485 a year) yet did not contain menopause-specific nutrients such as magnesium and calcium.
Similarly, Wild Nutrition’s Women’s 45+ Daily Multi Nutrient, costing £1.27 a day (£468 a year), contained just 1.5µg of vitamin D, 60mg of calcium and 30mg of magnesium, significantly under NHS recommended daily amounts, Which? found.
The watchdog also found that many menopause supplements’ key nutrients were in doses too low to be beneficial, or they omitted important vitamins and minerals altogether.
The highest-scoring menopause supplement analysed, Vitabiotics’ Menopace Max, cost 93p a day (£340 a year) – more than 15 times the price of Asda’s 6p multivitamin.
The findings follow research by UCL into 201 supplements sold in the UK that found less than half of products contained vitamin D and calcium and the majority of ingredients were not specifically recommended by major menopause societies.
Responding to Which?’s research, Dr Xand van Tulleken, an honorary associate professor at the UCL Institute for Global Health, said: “Every year our annual spending on menopause supplements is hundreds of times more than our spending on menopause research. There is no persuasive evidence that menopause supplements have a significant effect on women’s symptoms, some of them are dangerous, and the pricing and marketing is exploitative and confusing. They are a massive rip-off for consumers who desperately want to be well.”
Martin Last, the director general of the Health Food Manufacturers’ Association, said: “We encourage industry manufacturers to formulate and recommend supplements as required by the many food regulations that apply to food supplements. Many life stages, including the menopause, may create increased nutritional demands on an individual and these may be met by supplementation as an addition to a healthy diet.”
In a statement provided after publication, Holland & Barrett said its own-brand menopause products were “specifically formulated for the nutritional needs associated with this life stage” and that “they contain meaningful, evidence-based levels of key vitamins and minerals and are not simply standard multivitamins with menopause branding”.

Arrestor gear contract to go to Marshall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:02 BST
15:00:02 KST

The Ministry of Defence intends to extend and combine two contracts with Marshall Land Systems covering the aircraft arrestor systems used at British and overseas military airfields, placing the work by direct award on the grounds that no other supplier could do it, the department stated in a transparency notice.
The notice, identifier 2026/S 000-091979, was published on 29 September and gives a contract value of £7.5 million excluding VAT, rising to £9 million with VAT included. The earliest date the contract can be signed is 4 December 2026, with estimated dates running from then to 5 December 2028 and two further one-year options that could carry it to December 2030.
Arrestor gear is what stops a fast jet running off the end of a runway when something goes wrong on landing or during an aborted take-off. According to the notice, the requirement covers a sustained and supported capability delivering a safe, effective and reliable means of preventing runway excursions, supporting the enabling of the Strategic Base, standing commitments and contingent capability in line with Defence Strategic Direction and the RAF Command Plan.
ACCOMM/00087 covers engineering and logistic support to Rotary Hydraulic Arrestor Gear and Portable Hydraulic Arrestor Gear in use in Britain and at overseas bases, while ACCOMM/00035 covers the Arrester Barrier. Both were competitively let, and the department intends to combine them into a single contract as part of a 24-month extension whose value for the extension period alone is put at £5.6 million excluding VAT.
The justification for going direct rests on obsolescence, and according to the notice, the Arrester Barrier System is obsolete and Marshall, as the incumbent, holds the technical understanding of it, the suitably qualified and experienced people, and access to the technical drawings and approved repair instructions from the original equipment manufacturer. A change of supplier, the department states, would deliver services both different from and incompatible with the existing ones, and the age of the equipment means only Marshall holds the necessary know-how and can supply compatible spares, so that going elsewhere would cause disproportionate technical difficulties in operating and maintaining the system.
The extension is being placed under Section 41 of the Procurement Act 2023, relying on the direct award justification at paragraph 7 of Schedule 5, which covers additional services from a single supplier, and the notice is published under the defence and security special regime.
Transparency notices of this type are required before a contracting authority makes a direct award, and exist so that the market can see the intention and the reasoning before the contract is signed rather than afterwards. They can also record a switch from an unsuccessful competitive procedure to a direct award, though nothing in this notice indicates that happened here.
Marshall Land Systems is based at Hangar 22 at Cambridge Airport and is recorded in the notice as not being a small or medium-sized enterprise, which sits oddly with the notice also flagging the requirement as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises. Options attached to the contract cover spares, repairs and post design services, and the contracting authority is Defence Equipment and Support at Abbey Wood, with the requirement run by the Support Capabilities and Commodities Team within the National Armaments Director Group.

Russians seize food supplies dropped to Oleshky residents by Ukrainian military
Tetiana Hasanenko, Head of Oleshky City Military Administration, has stated that Russian occupiers are confiscating food parcels dropped using drones by the Ukrainian military for local residents in Oleshky.
Source: Hasanenko in a comment to Ukrinform
Quote: "This is not the first time the Ukrainian military has dropped food to people in the community using drones, but the most recent operation was the largest aid delivery yet – four tonnes.
Naturally, some received one parcel, some got several, and others received nothing at all.
Regarding whether the Russians are taking these food products away from people – yes, they are.
Furthermore, if the items are not produced in Russia, they immediately ask residents: 'Where did you get this?' They tell them: 'If the Ukrainian Armed Forces are dropping food to you, it means you are collaborating with them.' Meanwhile, the occupiers consider the city to be Russian territory and regard the local residents as Russian citizens who are violating Russian law by cooperating with Ukraine."
Details: According to Hasanenko, residents in the community continue to disappear as a result of abductions by the Russian forces: "People are being taken away; an entire family has disappeared without a trace. We do not know where they are – they were taken to a basement [a torture chamber] and that is all. Whether they are alive or not is unknown."
Background:
- On 19 September, the Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organisations reported a critical humanitarian situation in occupied Oleshky.
- Hasanenko said that food was last officially delivered to Oleshky on 26 May and that there are now cases of families eating dogs. Over 6,000 people, including roughly 200 children, might still remain in Oleshky and the surrounding district.
- Ukrainian forces carried out one of their largest humanitarian aid delivery operations to Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, using drones to transport nearly 4,000 kg of food.
- At the end of March, Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, noted that Oleshky "is not living, but merely surviving".

China's non-manufacturing PMI at 50.2 in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:57:42 CST
14:57:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's non-manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) came in at 50.2 in September, up 1.2 percentage points from August, official data showed Wednesday.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 indicates contraction.
The business activity index for the construction sector rose 3.4 percentage points month on month to 50.3, and the services sector index rose 0.9 percentage points to 50.2, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Among services industries, the indices for telecommunications, broadcasting and satellite transmission services, monetary and financial services, and insurance all stood above 55, well above the boom-bust line. The indices for capital market services and real estate remained below the line.
The new orders index stood at 46.5 in September, up 2.4 percentage points from August, indicating a recovery in market demand. The new orders index for construction rose 3.3 percentage points to 45.7, while services rose 2.2 percentage points to 46.7.
The NBS data also indicated that overall input prices for non-manufacturing business activities continued to rise.
The sales price index rose 1 percentage point from August to 50.3, indicating a recovery in overall sales prices.
The employment index rose 0.5 percentage points month on month to 45.9, pointing to improved hiring conditions.
The business activity expectation index reached 55.5, up 0.5 percentage points from August, indicating stronger confidence among non-manufacturing enterprises in market development. The construction business activity expectation index rose 3.6 percentage points to 55.4, while the services business activity expectation index remained unchanged at 55.5.
Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS, said the non-manufacturing business activity index rebounded noticeably in September and returned to expansion territory.
Huo noted that the services business activity index moved above the boom-bust line, reflecting a recovery in services market activity, while the construction business activity index climbed to its highest level this year, with construction progress accelerating.
Wednesday's NBS data also showed that China's manufacturing PMI stood at 50.1 in September, up 0.3 percentage points from August and back in the expansion zone. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

COLOMBO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's cabinet on Tuesday approved the appointment of a committee to advise the government on efforts to secure the return of Sri Lankan cultural artifacts held overseas, including items taken from the country during the colonial era.
The committee is also expected to facilitate further exchanges with its Dutch counterpart on the return of cultural artifacts.
Sri Lanka carried out the first phase of its cultural heritage restitution process in 2023, when six artifacts held by the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, were officially returned to the country.
The government said Articles 7 and 13 of the UNESCO 1970 Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property provide states with a basis to seek the return of cultural property belonging to them that is held abroad. ■

S. Korea-born twin giant pandas scheduled to return to China in December

Unknown Publisher

This photo released by the Everland theme park on Sept. 30, 2026 shows twin giant pandas Rui Bao and Hui Bao in South Korea. The twin giant pandas, born in South Korea in July 2023 and currently residing at Everland's Panda Second House, are scheduled to return to China in the third week of December, Everland said Wednesday. (Everland/Handout via Xinhua)
SEOUL, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Twin giant pandas Rui Bao and Hui Bao, born in South Korea in July 2023 and currently residing at Everland's Panda Second House, are scheduled to return to China in the third week of December, Everland said Wednesday.
All giant pandas born outside of China should be returned before they reach four years of age, ahead of the onset of their potential breeding years, according to Everland, the resort and leisure division of Samsung C&T.
Everland said it has closely consulted with the Chinese side to ensure an optimal relocation timeline for the twin sisters.
The exact departure date and destination will be finalized considering various factors such as the twins' health, local weather conditions and logistics.
Rui Bao and Hui Bao will enter a mandatory one-month health management and quarantine period ahead of their departure.
Everland said that it will fully prepare for a safe and secure transit while organizing farewell programs for visitors. ■

Ukraine was first to request secrecy over North Korean POW transfer: South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:57:08 UTC
14:57:08 KST

South Korea’s spy agency has said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy likely disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to rally support for greater assistance to Ukraine, while reiterating that Kiev had requested secrecy over the move.
The National Intelligence Service (NIS) gave the assessment during a closed-door briefing to the National Assembly’s intelligence committee on Wednesday, according to lawmakers who attended.
Zelenskyy revealed during his address to the UN General Assembly last week that the captured soldiers had been transferred to South Korea, prompting Seoul to demand an apology over what it said was a breach of a confidentiality agreement.
The NIS said the two countries had understood from the outset that the transfer would remain confidential and that Ukraine had been the first to request secrecy, Yonhap News Agency reported.
Lawmaker Yoo Yeong-ha said the agency believed Zelenskyy’s disclosure was intended to build public support in South Korea for supplying weapons and other assistance to Ukraine. Yoo did not elaborate or say how the intelligence service made its assessment.
South Korea has provided humanitarian aid and other support to Ukraine but has refrained from supplying weapons, in line with its policy of not arming countries actively engaged in conflict.
Seoul awaits apology
Yoo said the intelligence committee was told Ukraine had offered neither an apology nor an expression of regret through official or unofficial channels.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and his office have said the confidentiality agreement was intended to protect the soldiers from dangers they could face if the transfer became public.
A Ukrainian presidential official reportedly denied that such an agreement existed. South Korea’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Ukrainian ambassador on Monday to express strong concern over that denial.
The NIS said the two soldiers arrived in South Korea in mid-September and had no major health problems, according to lawmaker Yun Kun-young, who also attended the briefing.
The agency said that while in Ukraine, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, according to Yun.
South Korean officials have voiced concern for the safety of the soldiers and their relatives in North Korea. Experts said the transfer could also trigger protests from Pyongyang and complicate efforts to restart talks between North Korea and the United States.
North Korea has not publicly commented on the transfer, but has previously accused Seoul of abducting its citizens or luring them to defect.
North Korean troops in Russia
The two soldiers were among thousands sent by North Korea to help Russia repel a Ukrainian incursion into its Kursk border region, as part of expanding military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. North Korea has also supplied Russia with conventional weapons.
Yun said the NIS estimated that around 9,000 North Korean troops were engaged in surveillance operations in Kursk.
He also added that the lawmakers were told Russia has given North Korea weapons technologies to support its military modernisation plans but has been reluctant to transfer cutting-edge technology related to nuclear-powered submarines and intercontinental ballistic missiles.

China's manufacturing PMI at 50.1 in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:57:03 CST
14:57:03 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for China's manufacturing sector stood at 50.1 in September 2026, up 0.3 percentage points from August and back to the expansion zone, official data showed on Wednesday.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 signifies contraction.
The manufacturing sector's business climate improved further in September, with the PMI rising for a second consecutive month, said Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the National Bureau of Statistics.
Among the 21 industries surveyed, 12 reported a PMI above the expansion threshold, four more than the previous month, Huo noted.
The sector saw expansion in both manufacturing output and market demand in September. The production sub-index climbed to 51.7, up 1.3 percentage points from August, while the new orders index was at 50.5, still above the threshold.
Driven by the acceleration in production, enterprises' willingness to purchase strengthened, with the procurement volume index reaching 51.0, an increase of 0.5 percentage points from the previous month, said Huo.
PMI for the equipment manufacturing industry, the high-tech manufacturing industry and the consumer goods industry stood at 51, 52.5 and 50.7, respectively, all remaining in the expansion zone.
Affected by rising international commodity prices and growing demand in some industries, the purchasing price index for major raw materials and the ex-factory price index for manufacturing stood at 60.8 and 54, respectively, up 4.2 percentage points and 3.6 percentage points from the previous month.
PMI for medium-sized and small manufacturing enterprises came in at 49.7 and 48.9, respectively, increases of 0.3 percentage points and 1 percentage point from the previous month, as business activity picked up. ■

S. Korean banks' lending rate rises in August on policy rate hikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:56:59 CST
14:56:59 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- South Korean banks' lending rate rose last month as consecutive policy rate hikes drove up borrowing costs for both households and businesses, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The weighted average rate for new bank loans gained 0.13 percentage points from a month earlier to an annualized rate of 4.40 percent in August, rebounding from a decrease of 0.04 percentage points in July, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
Amid the growing inflationary pressure, the BOK delivered back-to-back rate hikes in July and August, lifting its key interest rate to 3.00 percent from 2.50 percent.
The rate for fresh bank loans to households climbed 0.12 percentage points over the month to 4.76 percent in August, marking the highest since November 2024.
The mortgage loan rate for households swelled 0.18 percentage points to 4.66 percent, and the credit loan rate soared 0.36 percentage points to 6.33 percent.
The mortgage rate has maintained an upward trajectory since May, reaching the highest since November 2022.
The rate for banks' new corporate loans advanced 0.10 percentage points to 4.30 percent in August on a monthly basis.
Lending rate for large companies added 0.03 percentage points to 4.21 percent, and the rate for small and medium enterprises increased 0.16 percentage points to 4.38 percent.
The weighted average rate for new bank deposits stood unchanged at an annualized 3.21 percent in August from a month earlier. ■

Russian attack kills two, wounds four in Kiev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:56:45 UTC
14:56:45 KST

Ukraine's air defences are seen in action during a missile and drone strike on Kyiv amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine early on September 30, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Russian strikes killed four in and around Ukraine’s capital on Sept. 30, the authorities said, in a barrage of attacks which hit the city’s energy infrastructure and cut power.
Heavy explosions rang out across Kiev throughout a night of almost continuous air alerts warning people to take cover in bomb shelters from ballistic and cruise missiles backed up by drones.
Kiev, home to some 3 million people, has faced several nights of sustained aerial barrages, as well as increasing daytime strikes in an escalation of the more than four-and-a-half-year-long war.
In Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it had conducted “a massive missile and drone strike” on Kiev and the surrounding region that targeted the power infrastructure.
Ukraine’s main energy provider DTEK confirmed that the grid was damaged and supplies were affected.
“DTEK’s power engineers managed to quickly restore electricity to 8,000 households,” the company said in a statement, calling it “another difficult night for the capital.”
Strikes on Sept. 30 hit residential buildings and businesses, sparking fires and widespread damage to property and cars, the authorities said.
City mayor Vitali Klitschko said a driver at local utility firm KievTeploEnergo was killed when a warehouse was hit, while two others were killed elsewhere.
The emergency services said a child was found dead under the rubble of a residential building that was destroyed in the wider Kiev region.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shaheds.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Sept. 29 said he was “alarmed” by the scale of the escalating daily attacks in Ukraine and civilian casualties on both sides.

'Divide Hindus for Muslim rule’: BJP invokes British ‘divide and rule’ policy to target Congress over Revanth Reddy remarks

NEW DELHI: The BJP on Wednesday drew a parallel between the British policy of “divide and rule” and what it described as the Congress’ “divide Hindus for Muslim rule” approach, while targeting Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy over his remarks on Lord Ram and Lord Shiva.Also Read | 'Shiva god of poor, Ram of rich': Telangana CM Revanth Reddy's off-the-cuff remark draws BJP's ireBJP MP and party spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi, speaking at a press conference at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi, said, “The Britishers used the concept of divide and rule... Congress’ approach is to divide Hindus for Muslim rule.”
To reinforce his argument, Trivedi claimed that Congress MP and leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi had “deliberately chosen” a Muslim-majority constituency. He was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s former constituency of Wayanad in Keralam, a seat where Muslims account for more than 40% of the electorate and form the majority.The Congress leader currently represents Uttar Pradesh’s Raebareli constituency in the Lok Sabha.
What did Revanth Reddy say
The controversy stems from Revanth Reddy’s remarks at a media conclave in New Delhi on September 28.Responding to a question about the Congress’ weak presence in North India, Reddy said, “We are Dravidians. People here (north) are Aryans. We are devotees of Shiva. These are devotees of Lord Ram. BJP stole Ram. It's an emotion.
It's a sentiment. Why Modi ji does not say Har Har Mahadev. Have BJP people ever said Har Har Mahadev on a stage. They say only Jai Sri Ram. When we say Har Har Mahadev, they don't like it.”“Shiva is the God of the poor, Ram is the God of the rich and the BJP is a party of the rich,” he added.
The remarks predictably drew a sharp response from the BJP, while the Congress defended Reddy, saying that Lord Ram “looks rich” and Lord Shiva “physically looks poor.”"Why should he (CM Revanth Reddy) apologise? I'm defending Revanth Reddy. Look-wise, Lord Ram wears a lot of ornaments. He looks rich, whereas Lord Shiva, with no clothes, physically looks poor. That is the difference. But we have affection for both the Gods, we pray to them, and we wish that both the Gods bless us," Telangana Congress president Mahesh Kumar Goud said.

Tallinn mural plan backfires as graffiti artists tag over works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:55:00 UTC
14:55:00 KST

Tallinn mural plan backfires as graffiti artists tag over works
While Tallinn is utilizing city-commissioned murals to reduce graffiti, street artists have responded by painting over them. The university town of Tartu takes a more conciliatory approach.
A street artist calling themselves "PASR" has tagged several official murals, telling the city, in English, "You will lose this war," prompting a police report and a cleanup.
"PASR" joins "CTAH" in being one of the commonly seen graffiti tags in the capital.
In summer the Tallinn City Government announced six new murals by five artists would be completed over the summer as part of a drive to curb graffiti.
However, the street artist or artists under the name "PASR" opted to paint over the works approved by the city. The alleged reason was that one wall previously covered by PASR artwork had been painted over. In recent months, the tag "PASR" has appeared over several murals approved by the city.
The "You will lose this war!" tag appeared on a wall in Poska tänav in the Kadriorg neighborhood. On a wall on Weizenbergi tänav – the road which leads up to the presidential palace – where the city had commissioned a mural depicting Swan Lake (the nearby park also has a small lake with swans) graffiti appeared stating that using murals to fight graffiti was a very poor idea. In the Poska case, the city had the text painted over.
The situation has come to be something of a vicious cycle as of now: the city commissions a mural, but it soon gets painted over, during the hours of darkness. The city then paints over that fresh graffiti or commissions another mural, but seldom has to wait long before more graffiti tags appear over the latest city-approved artwork.
Manuela Pihlap (Center), head of the Põhja-Tallinn district, called graffiti an issue which has been growing year by year. "It is precisely to make the cityscape a little nicer that we have invited street artists to come and create art openly. We support them and also provide them with materials, but we want to see nicer murals, not squiggles," Pihlap said.
The district government filed a police report the day after a mural in Põhja-Tallinn got painted over. "We hope the police will track down whoever did it. At the moment, we plan to clean the graffiti off the wall and paint it white again, and we are also considering putting some new artwork on the same wall," Pihlap added.
Pihlap said she had spoken with street artists, who expressed surprise that the mural had been painted over. "As far as I understand, the rule in that world is that you do not paint over another artist's work. If you do, you either have to cover the wall completely, or create a better piece. In this case, neither 'rule' was followed," she said.
One street artist, Sirla, who organizes the Stencibility festival, told ERR that Tallinn and Tartu have taken very different approaches. "Tallinn has declared war and has been communicating that it is opposed to graffiti and that official murals are specifically intended to reduce graffiti in the urban environment. Tartu, meanwhile, has taken the position that it supports art in public space and provides funding for new works to be created rather than for old ones to be painted over," Sirla said.
Erge Jõgela, an urban design specialist with Tartu City Government, said the city treats street art as a type of free expression and does not rush to remove works, unless they are obviously obscene, criminal, or in an inappropriate location. The city does not approve or curate works on its street art walls — these emerge spontaneously. "We have taken the position that just as we do not approve works in advance or issue permits for artists to work, we do not remove or suppress distinctive works in reasonable and suitable locations," Jõgela said. The only works Tartu approves in advance are large-scale murals on apartment building façades, most of them created under the SmartEnCity project umbrella.
Jõgela added that Tartu has approved city-owned walls as "donor surfaces" for the Stencibility festival, from which artists choose a "canvas". The city does not know in advance which walls will be used or what will be painted on them. She said cooperation with the festival has been excellent and the trust placed in organizers has not been abused.
While the city government-approved murals in Tallinn and Tartu are placed on public property, homeowners have reported a rise in graffiti on the walls of private properties too.
The identity of many of the most prolific graffiti artists – such as "CTAH", whose work often adorns hard-to-reach places like chimneys and bridges, or "DJ Tiine Rott" (literally "pregnant rat"), is not publicly known.

ADF neutralizes five ballistic missiles, 155 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:52:00 UTC
14:52:00 KST

ADF neutralizes five ballistic missiles, 155 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, September 29, Russian forces attacked with Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Kursk region, Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles launched from Voronezh and Bryansk regions, and 188 attack UAVs, including 86 jet-powered drones, of the Shahed type, as well as Gerbera and Parody decoy drones. The drones were launched from the areas of Orel, Millerovo, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, as well as Hvardiiske and Chauda in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The main direction of the attack was the Kyiv region.
The air assault was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Wednesday, September 30, Ukrainian air defense had shot down or suppressed 160 targets: five Iskander-M/S-400/Zircon/Oniks ballistic missiles and 155 drones.
Hits were recorded at 18 locations.
The attack was ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, two people were killed and four injured in Kyiv as a result of the Russian missile and drone attack on September 30.
A child was killed in Vyshhorod, Kyiv region, as a result of the Russian combined attack, and there were also casualties.

China threatened the EU with a &quot;firm&quot; response to restrictions on businesses
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:51:54 EEST
14:51:54 KST

China threatened the EU with a "firm" response to restrictions on businesses
Kyiv • UNN
Beijing warned of a firm response to restrictions on Chinese businesses or goods. The EU is demanding results in the negotiations by October.
China's Ministry of Commerce issued a resolute warning to the European Union. This came ahead of high-level talks expected to take place in Beijing next week. UNN reports this, citing CNBC.
Details
China will "respond firmly" if the EU imposes restrictions on Chinese businesses or goods, according to a statement by China's Ministry of Commerce published late on Tuesday, September 29.
The ministry said that such actions, while China and the EU are conducting trade negotiations, would "seriously undermine mutual trust" and "derail" the talks.
China and the EU have been conducting trade negotiations since this summer, as Europe seeks to reduce its record trade deficit with China by October. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič warned in an interview with Euronews this week that Beijing must achieve "concrete results" by October or face "tougher measures." He is expected to visit Beijing next week.
Earlier this week, Noah Barkin of the Rhodium Group said that Europe was considering measures to close the bloc to China.
Citing European officials, he said that Germany and France were finalizing a joint document calling on the European Commission to accelerate the development of an instrument that one official described as enabling Brussels to "cut China off from the European market within 24 hours."
Barkin said these measures could be similar to the U.S. approach involving Section 301 tariffs. The statement from China's Ministry of Commerce said this was a reaction to Europe's consideration of "301-type" instruments.
Additional information
Although the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) surpassed the EU in 2020 to become China's largest trading partner in goods, the EU's trade deficit with China is the largest in the world, recently exceeding the U.S. figure. This is according to data from China's customs service obtained through Wind Information.
If services are included, the EU said it was China's largest trading partner, with total trade amounting to 880 billion euros, or nearly $1 trillion, last year.

Seoul suspects Zelenskyy revealed North Korean POW transfer to win arms support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:47:02 UTC
14:47:02 KST

South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war.
South Korea's spy agency believes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of two North Korean POWs to boost public support in South Korea for providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy disclosed last week that his country had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, saying they were "not easy to capture alive."
Hours after Zelenskyy's remarks at the United Nations, South Korea's President Lee Jae-myung expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives from any repercussions in North Korea.
On Monday, Seoul summoned Ukraine's envoy in the South to express "serious concerns" over Kyiv's disclosure of the transfer.
Lawmaker Yoo Yeong-ha said on Wednesday that Seoul's spy agency believes Zelenskyy "may have decided to disclose the transfer" in the hope that it could "generate public support in Seoul for providing Ukraine with weapons and other forms of assistance."
Another lawmaker, Youn Kun-young, said the two POWs arrived in South Korea from Ukraine in mid-September.
They were "in generally good health, with no major health concerns," he said, adding the two's "willingness to come to South Korea was confirmed several times," citing Seoul's spy agency.
Earlier this week, Seoul's foreign ministry said that "as the matter concerns the personal safety of the individuals involved and their families," the two sides, Seoul and Kyiv, had "agreed to handle it confidentially."
Lawmaker Yoo said on Wednesday there was no agreement between the South Korean and Ukrainian leaders to keep the matter confidential, but that diplomatic officials from the two sides had agreed to confidentiality during their communications.
"From the outset of the discussions, the Ukrainian side proactively requested strict confidentiality, citing concerns about the potential impact on future prisoner exchanges (with Russia)," he added.
Ukraine captured the two North Korean soldiers early last year among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow.
One of them told South Korean media he was conscripted aged 17 and had served in a reconnaissance unit.
A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South.
The row also risks complicating Kyiv's requests to Seoul for armaments supplies.
South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war.
Nevertheless, it has been considering requests for defensive weapons, especially since North Korea deployed troops to support Russia in pushing back a surprise Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region in 2024.

Hong Kong urged to boost private housing supply as student demand jumps 45%
Government forecasts annual demand for non-local student housing at 2,310 flats over next decade, 45 per cent higher than last year’s estimate
Hong Kong authorities are facing calls to increase the proportion of private housing in selected districts and work more closely with developers to expand accommodation for non-local students.
The government forecasts annual demand for non-local student housing at 2,310 flats over the next decade, 45 per cent higher than last year’s estimate, according to the latest Long Term Housing Strategy progress report released on Monday.
The Housing Bureau based the figure on an average annual increase of about 7,100 student visas between 2016-17 and 2025-26, noting that roughly 65 per cent of those students did not live in university-provided halls or hostels.

US-led coalition ends mission in Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:46:01 UTC
14:46:01 KST

A US Air Force C-130 Hercules military transport aircraft prepares for takeoff from Camp Victory on the outskirts of Baghdad International Airport on September 29, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Iraq on Sept. 30 announced the end of the U.S.-led international coalition’s mission after more than two decades, marking a transition toward bilateral security relations with coalition member states.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS [ISIL] as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said.
“It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the ISIL, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi hailed the end of the mission as the start of a new chapter.
“A new phase has begun, defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, unity of decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends,” Zaidi said at a ceremony.
He also declared that Oct.1 would be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.
The premier said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against ISIL and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq’s Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish regional government’s Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.

Watch: Massive fire destroys 8 houses, several cowsheds in J&amp;K's Kishtwar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:45:42 UTC
14:45:42 KST

NEW DELHI: A fire that broke out shortly after midnight reduced at least eight houses and several cowsheds to ashes in a remote village in Jammu and Kashmir's Kishtwar district.The fire erupted in a house in Mungli village in the Warwan area and spread rapidly to neighbouring structures. With residents struggling to contain it, earth movers were used to pull down parts of the affected houses and create a gap to prevent the flames from spreading further.
No human casualties were reported in the blaze but reporting suggests that there have been livestock casualties.The exact extent of the livestock loss, however, could not be ascertained as a detailed assessment was not possible during the night, as reported by news agency PTI.The absence of a fire station in Warwan meant fire tenders had to be summoned from Kokernag in south Kashmir's Anantnag district. The firefighting operation continued for several hours before the blaze was brought under control around 4 am.
Officials said the site was being monitored as some areas were still smouldering.The cause of the blaze was also not immediately known.The local administration has begun assessing the damage and the relief needed by affected families.
A relief vehicle is also being arranged from the district headquarters, officials said.The incident comes as authorities regularly warn residents in the remote Warwan region about the risk of fires during winter. Families commonly stockpile dry grass and fodder for their livestock during the season, and officials have advised them to keep such material away from homes and other residential structures.Similar precautions have also been communicated through government and religious institutions in the area.

Apple will sell 6 million iPhone duos in 2026, Counterpoint says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:45:00 UTC
14:45:00 KST

Apple will sell 6 million iPhone duos in 2026, Counterpoint says
SAN FRANCISCO – Apple is set to sell about six million units of the iPhone Duo in 2026, Counterpoint Research said, offering the first estimate for how the company’s inaugural foldable device will fare.
The figure, more typical of the niche foldable segment than Apple’s usual smartphone sales, is contingent on how well the company ramps up production of the new hardware, Counterpoint senior analyst Ivan Lam said. 
Priced at US$1,999 (S$2,554) and set for an October release, the iPhone Duo sits atop the Apple line-up and carries industry-wide hopes for stoking greater interest and sales of foldable phones.
Market researcher IDC estimates foldables will grow 13% to 22.9 million units shipped in 2026 with Apple’s help. Without the iPhone Duo, the segment would have seen a decline, it said.
Introduced alongside the Duo in September, Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro family has had a fast start in China, Counterpoint said. 
The company’s Pro edition smartphones were for the first time released without a corresponding base-model upgrade, steering consumers looking for an upgrade to the pricier models and helping deliver a 12% rise compared to the iPhone 17 Pro’s initial sales. 
That performance bucked a broad downtrend in the world’s largest smartphone market, with Chinese brands taking the brunt of a 17% year-on-year decline across summer 2026, according to the researchers.
That helped Apple grab 33% of China’s highly competitive smartphone arena, an unusual feat when companies like Huawei, Oppo, Vivo and Xiaomi usually have roughly equal shares with Apple. 
But elevated component costs are forcing all phone makers to raise prices and try to make up the shortfall of unit sales in higher revenue per unit. That works in Apple’s favour by narrowing the cost advantage of its rivals.
“Price hikes of over US$200 on many Chinese flagship models may have raised the price anchor, strengthening the iPhone’s relative value proposition,” Lam said. BLOOMBERG

South Korea, North Korea trade blame over explosions that injured 3 South Korean soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:38:59 UTC
14:38:59 KST

South Korea and North Korea traded accusations on Wednesday over two explosions on September 21 near the Military Demarcation Line in the western section of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers.
South Korea strongly demanded that North Korea apologise and take "responsible measures" over the incident and urged Pyongyang to immediately stop its "border-hardening activities," Yonhap News Agency reported.
"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Lt. Gen. Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations at the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), told reporters.
"We make it explicitly clear that North Korea bears full responsibility for any future consequences that may arise," he added.
Seoul claims that North Korean resin antipersonnel mines deliberately planted on the southern side of the Military Demarcation Line were highly likely the cause of the September 21 blasts.
North Korea denied the allegation, accusing South Korea of fabricating the findings and warning of "immediate and merciless" retaliation if its troops are fired upon.
"What should not be overlooked is the fact that the armed gangsters of the ROK are now cooking up the groundless results and 'justifying their conduct' for political and military provocation against the DPRK, openly talking about 'reasonable and corresponding enforcement of measures'," Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said in a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency.
DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name, while ROK stands for the Republic of Korea, South Korea’s official name.
Kim stressed that North Korean soldiers "have never crossed the border" while accusing the South Korean military of threatening its soldiers with warning broadcasts and shots.
"If the ROK military gangsters fire at our soldiers carrying on the permanent project for the southern border, not warning shots, our border units will take immediate and merciless retaliate attack," she said.

Eiffel Tower chief to step down after scandal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:38:55 EEST
14:38:55 KST

Eiffel Tower chief to step down after scandal
Kyiv • UNN
SETE CEO Patrick Branco Ruivo will leave his position at the end of the year following an investigation into an incident involving female employees. The tower was closed due to a strike.
The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower will resign at the end of the year. This came after female employees of the iconic Paris landmark were barred from attending a visit by a Hindu religious organization. UNN reports this, citing AP.
Details
Patrick Branco Ruivo, CEO of Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave his position after an investigation conducted by an independent firm revealed a number of operational violations related to the September 5 visit.
These violations resulted in "female employees being excluded from the visit that day, which is an unacceptable situation," according to a SETE statement dated September 29. Ruivo was appointed at the end of 2018.
The Eiffel Tower, visited by 7 million people annually, was closed on September 7 due to a staff strike in protest against what a union representative called "unacceptable" management directives.
Anger among employees of the 330-meter landmark intensified after management told staff that female employees should not have contact with a delegation from the Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha organization.
The organization, known as BAPS, is a worldwide religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan sect, a branch of Hinduism, the publication writes. It held celebrations to mark the opening of a traditional Hindu stone temple in Paris.
At the time of the incident, BAPS said in a statement to the Associated Press: "This coordination was undertaken solely for reasons of operational courtesy and logistics, to ensure the smooth visit of a large group of people without inconvenience to tower staff or the public. It was never intended as a gender-based request."
Ariel Weil, head of SETE, said Tuesday that he had requested the implementation of measures and training programs promoting gender equality.
Additional information
This is not the first time the 137-year-old tower has been closed because of a strike. In February 2024, it was closed for six days due to striking employees who demanded improved maintenance of the historic landmark and higher wages.

Eesti 200 and Greens consider merger ahead of 2027 vote

Eesti 200 and Greens consider merger ahead of 2027 vote
Riigikogu party Eesti 200 and the Estonian Greens (Rohelised) are considering a merger ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu election, Eesti Ekspress reported.
But the move may not solve either party's central problem: both are polling below the 5-percent threshold needed to win seats, and their combined support would still not be enough. The latest ERR-commissioned Emor poll saw Eesti 200 at 1.9 percent and the Greens at 1.1 percent — a combined 3 percent.
The talks are driven by different needs on each side. Eesti 200, which has 13 Riigikogu seats, has long languished below the threshold and may struggle to find candidates by March. For the Greens, the issue is funding — potential candidates are unable to pay the €946 election deposit themselves, something Eesti 200 may be able to help with.
Party leader and Education Minister Kristina Kallas, according to Eesti Ekspress, "agrees with the statement 'the Greens and Eesti 200 are considering a merger'." Kallas said talks continue and clarity will come by end-October, when the Greens hold a general assembly.
Eesti 200 has met with other parties about potential mergers too. In spring the party met with its former coalition partner, the Social Democrats, though party leader Lauri Läänemets and former minister Piret Hartman soon wrapped up the talks. Eesti 200 also met with the Free Party, which had eight seats at the XIII Riigikogu (2015-2019) but currently has none — those talks drew a blank as well.
More progress has been made with the Greens, who last had Riigikogu seats in 2007-2011, Rasmus Lahtvee, Greens co-chair, and party board chair Marti Soosaar told the paper nothing has been decided, though Soosaar said he likes the merger idea and thought a new party emerging would be viable.
Commercial Register data shows the Greens currently have more members — 705 — than Eesti 200 at 579. The minimum number of members a party can have to remain valid is 500.
The original Eesti Ekspress article is here.
Eesti 200 were founded in 2018, winning their first Riigikogu seats – 14 of them – at the 2023 elections, and finding themselves in office with Reform and, until spring last year, SDE. Eesti 200's rating has tanked since then however, in the wake of donations to Ukraine scandal which engulfed one of its former MPs soon after the election. Another Eesti 200 MP, Züleyxa Izmailova, herself a former Green Party leader, went back to SDE in 2024.
