How Buildner's Iceland Slow Sauna Competition Winners Respond to a Volcanic Landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Buildner has announced the results of the Iceland Slow Sauna architecture competition, developed in partnership with Slow Travel Mývatn. Set beside Þúfa – Private Homestay in the volcanic landscape of Lake Mývatn in northern Iceland, the competition invited architects and designers to create a compact retreat combining a sauna and greenhouse within a single architectural experience. Rooted in the Icelandic tradition of bathing as a ritual of stillness and renewal, the brief asked participants to explore how heat, light, vegetation, and landscape could shape an intimate place of recovery and connection to nature.
Rather than treating the sauna and greenhouse as separate functions, the brief emphasized the transitions between them: hot and cool, dark and bright, enclosed and open. Participants were encouraged to think in terms of atmosphere, ritual, and sensory experience while responding carefully to the exposed climate and volcanic terrain of Mývatn. The project also reflected the values of Slow Travel Mývatn and its founders, Óli and Bianca, whose nearby homestay is centered on authenticity, local materials, and a slower relationship with the landscape.
Across the submissions, recurring themes included reinterpreting Icelandic vernacular forms, restrained material palettes, passive environmental strategies, and carefully framed relationships with the surrounding terrain. Many proposals extended the bathing ritual beyond the sauna itself, using the greenhouse as a space for cultivation, cooling, rest, and contemplation. The strongest projects demonstrated how a modest program could achieve architectural richness through proportion, sequencing, materiality, and the careful calibration of thresholds between contrasting environmental conditions.
The competition was evaluated by an international jury comprising Teoman Ayas of MIMStudios, Louise Braverman of Louise Braverman Architect, Martin Fenlon of Martin Fenlon Architecture, Manuel Irsara of S I R S, Einar Jarmund of Einar Jarmund & Co AS Arkitekter MNAL, Gustav Jerlvall Jeppsson of STRÅ Arkitekter, Sai Luo of LEL DESIGN STUDIO, Gonçalo Marrote of Madeiguincho, Caspar Schols of Studio Caspar Schols, Antonio Yemail Cortés of Yemail Arquitectura, and Edward Birnbaum of Therme Canada. The jury recognized proposals that approached the sauna as a choreographed sequence of experiences, balancing atmosphere and restraint with climatic responsiveness, material clarity, and a strong relationship to the Icelandic landscape.
Buildner's other ongoing competitions include Portugal Long Table Restaurant, which invites participants to transform a former horse barn in northern Portugal into a small-scale restaurant and guest retreat centered on food, gathering, and slow living; New York High Falls Riverfront Market, exploring a new civic market within Rochester's future High Falls State Park, where industrial heritage, public space, and the Genesee River gorge converge; and MICROHOME 2026, the 11th edition of Buildner's small-scale housing competition, developed in partnership with Kingspan and offering a 100,000 EUR prize fund for new approaches to compact living.
Projects:
First Prize Winner + Buildner Student Award
Project title: Linear Ritual
Authors: Prusha Kadir, Joel Jansson, Emil Sandström, Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden
Linear Ritual proposes a compact greenhouse and sauna retreat that extends the existing homestead while responding closely to the volcanic landscape and climate of Lake Mývatn. The project organizes its program as a linear sequence, guiding visitors through arrival, greenhouse, shower, and sauna while gradually shifting temperature, humidity, light, and views. Its form draws from Icelandic vernacular buildings, adapting a steep roof profile to address snow, wind, and rain while creating taller interior volumes where required. Timber construction, simple detailing, and a restrained material palette reinforce the proposal's emphasis on durability and buildability. By combining hospitality, bathing, and food production within a modest footprint, the project establishes a clear spatial ritual in which environmental transitions become central to the building experience.
Second Prize Winner
Project title: Slow Sauna - Descent into Stillness
Authors: Jeremy T Anderson, Pascal Henle, Australia
Slow Sauna - Descent into Stillness proposes a bathing retreat organized around a gradual descent into the Icelandic landscape. Rather than treating the sauna as a standalone object, the project choreographs movement, enclosure, and changing environmental conditions as part of the bathing ritual. A translucent double-skin envelope surrounds a compact inner volume, filtering light, weather, and views while giving the building a softened presence within the volcanic terrain. Circular interior spaces contrast with the rectilinear outer shell, establishing a sequence of concentrated rooms for bathing, washing, and contemplation. The proposal combines a restrained material palette with a modular structural system, balancing atmospheric qualities with a rational construction framework. Through its emphasis on descent, filtered light, and spatial transition, the project frames the sauna as an immersive sequence rather than a singular destination.
Third Prize Winner
Project title: The fourfold ritual
Authors: Marty Ilievski, Clément Vignes, Atelier Fasea, France
The fourfold ritual proposes a compact retreat in which the sauna is understood as a sequence of interconnected elemental experiences rather than a single enclosed room. A timber sauna forms the thermal core of the building and is surrounded by a translucent greenhouse accommodating cooling, relaxation, planting, and circulation within a unified environmental envelope. The project is organized around the interaction of earth, fire, water, and air, using shifts in temperature, humidity, vegetation, and daylight to structure movement through the interior. Drawing on familiar Icelandic vernacular forms, the proposal combines straightforward construction with a layered box-within-a-box organization. The new volume connects to the existing house while maintaining a close relationship with the surrounding volcanic landscape, creating a concise spatial sequence that moves between enclosure and openness, heat and coolness, darkness and natural light.
Buildner Sustainability Award
Project title: Iceland Slow Sauna
Authors: Jordan Paul Scheuermann, United States
Iceland Slow Sauna reinterprets the traditional Icelandic baðstofa as a compact multifunctional retreat integrating sauna, greenhouse, workshop, and recovery spaces within a single architectural volume. Drawing from vernacular forms while incorporating contemporary environmental strategies, the project combines a steeply pitched timber structure with a translucent polycarbonate skin that captures solar heat, shelters vegetation, and creates a thermally buffered environment around the sauna. Its orientation and sectional organization respond to the volcanic landscape, prevailing winds, solar exposure, and the protective qualities of the existing berm. Rather than isolating the sauna as a destination, the proposal links preparation, bathing, cultivation, recovery, and reflection through a sequence of interconnected spaces. The resulting system uses architecture and environmental performance together to establish a broader interpretation of wellness rooted in Iceland's climate, landscape, and building traditions.
Highlighted Submissions
Project title: Towards the Horizon
Authors: Park Juseok, South Korea
Towards the Horizon proposes a sauna and greenhouse as a low, elongated intervention that gradually immerses visitors in Lake Mývatn's volcanic landscape. Rather than reproducing the form of the neighboring guesthouse, the project follows the basalt terrain and uses a gently ascending sequence to bring users progressively closer to the surrounding landscape. Entry, vestibule, shower, sauna, kitchen, greenhouse, and relaxation areas are arranged as a continuous journey in which compression gives way to expansion and darkness transitions toward light. The sauna forms the thermal center of the sequence, while a panoramic opening frames the landscape and the greenhouse provides a bright final space for rest and cultivation. Through its emphasis on changing temperature, brightness, enclosure, and view, the proposal transforms bathing into a gradual spatial ritual moving from heat and intimacy toward openness and nature.
Project title: Spatial Cycles Of Warmth
Authors: Ilira Salihu, Julius Maria Meier, Switzerland
Spatial Cycles Of Warmth proposes a compact timber retreat in which sauna and greenhouse operate as a continuous thermal and spatial system. The project organizes the bathing ritual as a sequence of enclosure and openness, moving from the sheltered entrance through the sauna's intense heat to a bright, climatically balanced greenhouse and relaxation space. Rather than treating the programs as separate rooms, the design uses changing temperature, light, air, and water to structure movement and perception. A low timber frame, raised above the volcanic terrain, establishes a restrained relationship with the landscape, while shingles, planted roof surfaces, and generous glazing respond to Iceland's material and environmental conditions. The greenhouse extends the experience of recovery through planting, daylight, and views, allowing the building to move between warmth and coolness, protection and exposure, before reconnecting visitors with the surrounding landscape.
Project title: RAUÐUR SKÁLI (Red Shelter) Lake Mývatn, North Iceland
Authors: Samuel Kearney Caplice, Patrick Doyle, Ireland
Rauður Skáli proposes an inhabitable environmental sequence that combines sauna, relaxation, greenhouse, and storage functions within a compact modular structure. Organized on a 1 x 1 meter grid, the building uses a lightweight raised timber frame supported on steel ground screws to sit above the uneven volcanic terrain with minimal site disturbance. Movement through the veranda, compressed entry hall, greenhouse, relaxation space, and sauna is choreographed through changing conditions of temperature, humidity, light, and enclosure. The greenhouse acts as both a cultivated space and a luminous threshold, while the elevated sauna frames views toward the surrounding landscape. Red fiber cement cladding, translucent polycarbonate panels, iron-oxide-treated timber, and cedar-lined interiors establish a consistent material language. Through its emphasis on thresholds, adaptability, and atmosphere, the project transforms the sauna into a ritualized journey between exposure and shelter.
Project title: VARMUR CABIN
Authors: Pongsakorn Pongtawevirat, Ratchanon Chalermpao, Nidana Tohnimah, Thanapat Kongdith, ACTIVE SPACE COMPANY LIMITED, Thailand
VARMUR CABIN proposes a compact sauna and greenhouse retreat that combines two distinct functions within a single connected building beside the existing guesthouse. The project separates the greenhouse and sauna externally while linking them through a shared interior zone and serving shelf, allowing the two environments to operate independently while exchanging heat and activity. A translucent polycarbonate greenhouse contrasts with the darker charred-wood sauna volume, while warm timber interiors establish a consistent material language throughout. Residual heat from the sauna is redirected to support greenhouse cultivation, integrating environmental performance into the spatial concept. Elevated above the lava field to preserve surrounding views, the 35-square-meter intervention balances clear zoning, straightforward construction, and a restrained relationship with the existing homestead.
Project title: Thresholds of the Slow Ritual
Authors: Luke Yaeger Mcdonell, United States
Thresholds of the Slow Ritual proposes a sauna and greenhouse retreat organized around a sequence of changing temperatures, atmospheres, and relationships to the surrounding volcanic landscape. The project uses the contrast between a warm timber sauna and a translucent greenhouse to structure a gradual transition between enclosure and openness, with intermediate spaces mediating between the two environments. Its plan responds directly to the existing homestead and site conditions, orienting the sauna toward Lake Mývatn while positioning the greenhouse to receive natural light. Timber framing, wood cladding, and polycarbonate panels establish a simple material palette, while the greenhouse also captures residual heat from the sauna. Through its emphasis on thermal rhythm, spatial thresholds, and landscape views, the proposal turns the bathing routine into a carefully choreographed sequence of preparation, heat, cooling, rest, and contemplation.
Project title: Black Sauna
Authors: Milan Marko M Engström, Benoit Lagarde, France
Black Sauna proposes a retreat organized as a gradual journey between two contrasting sauna environments connected by a greenhouse. The first is conceived as a dark smoke sauna built from stabilized rammed earth using locally sourced volcanic rock, black clay, and sand, creating an enclosed mineral space shaped by shadow, heat, and filtered light. In contrast, the second sauna is built in timber and opens toward the volcanic landscape through a large glazed facade, creating a brighter, more outward-looking environment. Between them, a translucent greenhouse provides a space for cooling, rest, and vegetation, mediating the transition from darkness to light and enclosure to openness. Through its use of local materials, simple construction techniques, and carefully sequenced spaces, the project interprets the sauna as a ritual centered on heat, landscape, memory, and slowness.
Project title: The Return
Authors: Yizhao Li, Rundong Ying, Michelle Wang, United States
The Return proposes a thermal retreat in northern Iceland organized as a sequence of sensory transitions between darkness and light, cold and warmth, enclosure and landscape. Rather than treating the sauna as a single destination, the project choreographs a gradual journey through six experiential stages: invitation, seclusion, purification, immersion, expansion, and regeneration. Curved and rectilinear geometries shape the changing room, shower, pool, sauna, and greenhouse, with each space establishing a distinct relationship to the body and surrounding volcanic terrain. Circular skylights introduce light, mist, and water into the more enclosed spaces, while large openings extend the pool and sauna toward the landscape. The greenhouse completes the sequence as a space for cultivation and gathering, connecting the ritual of bathing with growth, nourishment, and the changing Icelandic environment.

Man arrested in connection with suspected RAF terror plot called police on self - report

One of the suspects in a suspected bomb attack on a Royal Air Force base called the police before the attempt was thwarted, The Times reported on Tuesday evening.
The suspect called 999 almost an hour before a farmer driving home called the police after seeing three vans surrounded by men in balaclavas, according to the report.
The motives of the caller are still under investigation, as the authorities are unsure if the suspect was attempting to sincerely stop the operation or if it was part of the larger plan.
Police are investigating the motives behind the operation itself after no explosive devices were found as part of their investigation, and are considering if the suspects were conducting surveillance, testing security, or trying to send a message to the British government, The Times wrote.
Police said that searches of London properties had been carried out as well as the vehicles at the scene, but while a significant quantity of fuel was found, no explosive devices were present.
UK police defend decision to release suspects on bail
Head of national counter-terrorism policing Laurence Taylor also defended the decision to release the five suspects on bail, which US President Donald Trump had criticized the day before.
"I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I'd like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers," Taylor said.

U2 frontman Bono compares Ben-Gvir comments on Gazans to Nazi leader Heinrich Himmler's rhetoric

U2 frontman Bono compared comments made by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir about residents of Gaza to the rhetoric of Heinrich Himmler, one of the leaders of the Nazi regime and one of the architects of the Holocaust.
In an extensive interview with Rolling Stone magazine published on Monday, marking the band’s 50th anniversary celebrations and ahead of the release of its new album, the Irish musician criticized Ben-Gvir and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he claimed was keeping Ben-Gvir in the government to preserve his coalition majority.
During the interview, conducted by journalist Brian Hiatt, Bono addressed comments Ben-Gvir made about Gaza residents in a conversation with former hostage survivor Rom Braslavski: “There are people there who are not worthy of life. They do not need to live; they are not people either.” Bono compared the rhetoric used by the minister to that of Himmler.
Bono stressed that he continues to support Israel while also supporting the Palestinians’ right to their own state. He addressed the international dispute over whether genocide is taking place in Gaza, saying that the term is a legal one that will ultimately be determined by international courts. However, he expressed bewilderment over the fact that Ben-Gvir continues to serve as a minister in the government.
Later in the interview, Bono spoke about the profound influence Jewish creators and artists have had on his life, worldview, and music. He accused Ben-Gvir of damaging the image of Judaism through his remarks and described the situation as scandalous.
According to Bono, Israel must address the injustices of the Nakba through a political compromise, even if there are parties unwilling to accept it. He added that justice is a fundamental value in Judaism.
Ben-Gvir calls for Gazans to emigrate to Ireland
Ben-Gvir reacted to Bono's interview with an AI music video posted on X/Twitter, labeling it "Gaza to Ireland."
In the video, Gazan children sing to Bono to help them emigrate to Ireland, and tell him to "listen to Ben-Gvir."
The video claims that over 1.5m. people in Gaza want to "start over in a Third state," and tells Bono, "don't preach."
The comments were made against the backdrop of the creation of the song “The Tears of Things,” in which Bono explores Jewish history and the war in Gaza, using the biblical figure of David and Michelangelo’s statue of David.
The song attempts to understand the conflict through the lens of Jewish history. Bono again condemned Hamas’s October 7 attack during the interview.
This is not the first time the singer has criticized the Israeli government. In May 2025, during the Ivor Novello Awards ceremony in London, he called on Israel to move away from Netanyahu and far Right elements, while also demanding that Hamas release the hostages and end the war.
Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

- Taiwan continues talks with the US on arms sales, receiving reassurances that US policy remains unchanged despite pressure from China.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Republican US Senator and Senate Armed Services Committee chairman Roger Wicker said Washington’s security commitments to Taiwan must be upheld, following a meeting on Sept 29 with Alexander Yui, the democratically governed island’s representative to the US.
Four other senators from US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party called on his administration last week to release more than US$15 billion (S$19.17 billion) in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan.
The United States does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.
Washington is bound by the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act to provide Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its own territory, with the means to defend itself.
“As members of Congress, we have a duty to make sure this law is adhered to and that decisions about the defence needs of Taiwan are based on our joint assessment of military necessity,” Wicker said in a statement.
Wicker also said he discussed with Yui what he called the rise of Chinese aggression against the United States’ Indo-Pacific allies.
“In response – and in accordance with the Taiwan Relations Act – Congress has authorised and appropriated a surge in resources to provide Taiwan with enhanced training, security assistance, and arms sales. These authorities must be used for the purposes that Congress intended,” Wicker added.
China has repeatedly called for Taiwan arms sales to end, and in May, following a Beijing trip, Trump said he was keeping a new package worth some US$14 billion in abeyance.
However, after meeting President Xi Jinping in Washington last week, Trump said only that the Chinese leader understood his position on Taiwan.
Wicker urged the US to uphold a precedent when former president Ronald Reagan said Washington would not consult Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan.
Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims and says only the island’s people can decide their future.
Taiwan is in continuous talks with Washington about arms sales and had received reassurances since the summit between Trump and Xi that US policy on Taiwan had not changed, Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said earlier on Sept 29. REUTERS

Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid has accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of “fear-mongering” after the incumbent leader warned that the country’s enemies may attack before next month’s general election.
Lapid, who heads the Yesh Atid party, dismissed the warning after meeting the prime minister on Tuesday.

Air pollution is slowing down marathon runners, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:49:27 UTC
13:49:27 KST

Higher levels of nitrogen dioxide on race day are linked to slower marathon times, particularly among non-elite runners, new research suggests.
Air pollution added minutes to marathon runners' finishing times across six major races, a new study has found.
Runners in the Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, New York City and Tokyo marathons have seen their finishing times affected by air pollution levels on race days in recent years.
Researchers at the University of Leicester analysed more than 2.7 million race performances from some of the most popular World Marathon Majors, which host thousands of athletes every year, across editions held between 2010 and 2024.
“From our analysis of more than two million marathon runners, we observed that levels of nitrogen dioxide were strongly associated with their finishing time,” said James Donaldson, the study’s lead author.
For every microgram-per-cubic-metre (µg/m3) increase in nitrogen dioxide, finishing times were 1.43 minutes slower for men and 1.56 minutes slower for women, the researchers found.
On a high-pollution race day when nitrogen dioxide levels reached 10.3 µg/m³ compared with a low-pollution level of 5.2 µg/m³, finishing times were around seven to eight minutes longer.
The researchers also analysed fine particulate matter — PM2.5 — but found no statistically significant association with finishing times.
The highest median race-day concentration of nitrogen dioxide was recorded in London at 10.9 µg/m³, and the lowest in Berlin at 6.1 µg/m³. The good news, that the situation got better in London.
“Despite the known harms of air pollution, it is important to note that levels of nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 on marathon day in London appear to have fallen substantially since the 2010 event, which is great news for heart health,” said Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, which supported the study.
Non-elite runners hit the hardest
The effect was greater among recreational runners, whose finishing times rose by 2.12 minutes per 1 µg/m³ of nitrogen dioxide, compared with 0.34 minutes for elite runners.
Nitrogen dioxide comes primarily from the burning of fossil fuels by human activities, such as cars, trucks and factories, as well as from natural processes and chemical reactions in the air.
It has been linked to impaired lung function, airway inflammation and adverse cardiovascular responses.
The authors identified several potential explanations for these patterns.
As well as spending longer on the course, slower runners are more likely to train in the same urban areas where marathons are held, accumulating chronic pollution exposure, while elite runners typically prepare in cleaner environments and compete internationally, the authors wrote.
Donaldson also noted that “the physiological adaptations that result from the high-intensity training undertaken by elite athletes may offer some protection against the harmful effects of air pollution”.
“As well as this, the fact remains that exercise is still very beneficial for your cardiovascular health - it can reduce the risk of heart and circulatory diseases by up to 35 per cent,” said Williams, adding that the findings should not put people off running.

Russia strikes energy facilities in Kyiv and nearby areas in prelude to winter assault
Sept 30 - Russian drone and missile attacks hit energy infrastructure in Kyiv and the nearby areas on Wednesday, Ukrainian officials said, a prelude to another winter campaign aimed at wrecking the national energy system.
"Russia has escalated to massive strikes on energy infrastructure," Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said on Telegram, adding that energy facilities had come under attack in other regions as well.
"Since summer, there's barely been a day without an attack on our energy infrastructure. But a combined strike of this scale hasn't happened since the end of last heating season."
Ukraine is preparing for another winter assault on power and heating facilities after last year entire cities were plunged into darkness and cold for days or weeks.
Koretskyi instructed local authorities to check the readiness of backup power systems at critical facilities, and finish installing and connecting them as soon as possible.
FIVE KILLED IN ATTACKS
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that energy infrastructure in the capital and the surrounding region was the main target of the overnight attack that involved nearly 190 drones and ballistic missiles.
Five people, including a child, had been killed across Ukraine, Zelenskiy said.
Power company DTEK did not detail the damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv but said workers had restored supply to 8,000 households.
Russia acknowledged the massive overnight assault, saying it had hit a data centre in the capital supporting Ukraine's armed forces, various power plants in the Kyiv region, an industrial complex in Odesa region, and port infrastructure in Izmail.
The attacks followed weeks of near-constant barrages of jet drones, which Ukraine struggles to shoot down.
Zelenskiy said Ukraine - which is also short of interceptors to down ballistic missiles - had received new air defence support packages in recent days.
Thanking allies for the deliveries, he called for more protection ahead of the winter.
Ukraine's air force said that five missiles and 155 drones had been intercepted in the overnight attack.
DEBRIS AT WESTERN EMBASSY
On Wednesday morning, Kyiv was shrouded in thick fog from the smoke of attacks. Emergency services asked residents to keep windows closed.
Citing preliminary information, Klitschko said debris had been found at a Western embassy in the centre of Kyiv. He did not specify which embassy.
Among neighbouring nations, a drone crossed into Moldova's airspace and exploded near the eastern village of Hirbovet, while European Union and NATO members Romania and Poland both scrambled military jets, the countries said.
Flights at Polish airports Lublin and Rzeszow were temporarily suspended.
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, hitting refineries and online retailers to undermine Moscow's war effort.
One person was killed in drone attacks in Russia's Bryansk region, which borders Ukraine, while a Ukrainian drone attack on the oil-producing Samara region damaged private houses, regional governors said. REUTERS

Hungary's reckoning with Orban's corrupt system picks up speed with high-profile arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:37:00 UTC
13:37:00 KST

Hungary's reckoning with Orban's corrupt system begins
September 30, 2026
One of the new Hungarian government's key pledges was to investigate corruption under Viktor Orban, recover embezzled assets, and hold those responsible accountable. Or, in the words of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, it is time to "liquidate Orban's mafia state." During his election campaign, Magyar had already announced a "program for the road to prison." As prime minister, he launched "Operation Purgatory" at the end of June 2026.
Measured against his fighting talk, little has happened so far. There have been no sweeping purges of the state apparatus, although some government funds flowing to Orban-aligned businessmen have been cut off. Police and prosecutors have summoned a handful of relatively unknown individuals for questioning, and a few people were arrested. The governing majority also established an agency to recover assets, but it is is not yet up and running.
But at the beginning of the week, Hungarians witnessed the first significant development in the promised reckoning with the Orban system. Two prominent lawmakers and former ministers were arrested over corruption allegations.
On Monday, Magyar's Tisza Party parliamentary faction used its two-thirds majority to lift the immunity of two lawmakers from the opposition Orban camp: Balazs Hanko, formerly minister for culture and innovation and a lawmaker from Orban's Fidesz party, and Miklos Sesztak, a former development minister who is now a lawmaker for the small Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP), which has been a Fidesz affiliate since 2010. Both are the subject of corruption investigations.
Illegal party financing, bribery
Balazs Hanko was not among those in Orban's system who enriched themselves on a large scale. But he is seen as a symbol of the common practice under Orban of systematically using public money to fund the ruling party, Orban's network of allies, election campaigns, and propaganda efforts. Specifically, as minister, Hanko allegedly unlawfully allocated around 50 million euros from the National Cultural Fund (NKA), which he oversaw, in 2025 and 2026, including funds intended for election campaign purposes.
The case of Miklos Sesztak is different. He is one of the wealthiest lawmakers in Hungary and has made headlines for more than a decade with his personal corruption scandals — another typical trait of the Orban system. As minister, Sesztak allegedly accepted around €30 million ($34 million) in bribes with an accomplice between 2015 and 2018. The alleged payments involved contracts related to the state-owned Hungarian bus company Volanbusz and the construction sector.
Barricaded in parliament with his family
Sesztak went straight to the prosecutor's office on Monday after his immunity was lifted, where he was taken into pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko took a different route. He arrived at Parliament on Monday morning with his wife and four teenage children and, after his immunity was lifted, said he was waiting for the authorities to make a decision. In practice, it appeared that he was barricading himself inside. Only after Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer formally ordered Hanko in writing that evening to leave the building, and he received a summons from the prosecutor's office, did he finally head for the exit, accompanied by his family and Fidesz lawmakers protesting what they called Magyar's "arbitrary rule."
The entire episode was livestreamed on Viktor Orban's Facebook page. After Hanko said goodbye to his family outside, a misunderstanding occurred. His SUV driver, apparently believing Hanko was already inside the vehicle, drove off without him. Hanko ran after the SUV, and the livestream on Orban's Facebook page then cut out. Later that evening, Hungarian media reported that Hanko had also been placed in pretrial detention.
Prime Minister Magyar's immunity lifted
Earlier that afternoon, Prime Minister Peter Magyar delivered a sharp speech in Parliament on the two cases. His own immunity had also been lifted beforehand — over a case that is classified in the records as theft.
In June 2024, Magyar took a phone from a man who had been filming him without permission at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube, where it was later found. Magyar had explicitly asked for his immunity to be lifted in the case. It is a calculated PR move intended to show that the same standards apply to everyone. But it is also a risky maneuver — if convicted, Magyar could lose his seat in Parliament.
In his parliamentary speech, he offered Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers a stark comparison: "How many hundreds of thousands of phones would you have to throw into the Danube to come close to the trillions allegedly stolen by the Fidesz-KDNP mafia?"
Dispute over Prosecutor General
Magyar has also spoken forcefully about Hungary's justice system. He has praised rank-and-file judicial employees while criticizing the leadership of the prosecutor's office, accusing them of repeatedly covering up corruption cases as "collaborators of the Orban system." At the center of the dispute is a fight over the appointment of a new prosecutor general.
The Tisza faction rejected Zoltan Szathmary, the candidate proposed by President Andras Baka, because his brother works for the Office for Constitutional Protection and, in that role, is a suspect in an ongoing politically sensitive case known as the "Gold Convoy" affair. In March 2026, Viktor Orban ordered the detention of a legal Ukrainian money shipment. The escorts were arrested in dramatic fashion, and cash and gold bars were seized. Orban and other Fidesz politicians indirectly accused Magyar's Tisza Party of receiving funding from Ukraine. Several people involved in the operation are now under investigation for abuse of office. Orban himself is not currently part of the proceedings, but could be in the future.
Hungarians seek a swift reckoning
Although Magyar has formally emphasized the independence of the judiciary, his comments in the current debates have given the impression that he is getting ahead of judicial decisions or becoming too deeply involved. At the same time, expectations among many Hungarians for a swift reckoning are high — and public debate's often return to the topic of how people want to "hear the handcuffs click." A recent poll found that a large majority of Hungarians consider the former Orban order "systemically corrupt" and a "mafia state."
Overall, Magyar and his government face the challenge of balancing the rule of law with public expectations. Many former critics of Orban are also calling for the reckoning with the Orban system to be handled properly. Prominent attorney Gyorgy Magyar, for example, who represented people in numerous human rights and rule-of-law cases under Orban, called for "prudence, patience, calm, discipline, and professionalism" in an interview with the news outlet Hirklikk.
Questions remain about whether "Operation Purgatory" will be merely spectacle, or whether the justice system will investigate corruption cases independently and in keeping with the rule of law.
This article was originally published in German.

Balazs Hanko was not among those in Orban's system who enriched themselves on a large scale. But he is seen as a symbol of the common practice under Orban of systematically using public money to fund the ruling party, Orban's network of allies, election campaigns, and propaganda efforts. Specifically, as minister, Hanko allegedly unlawfully allocated around 50 million euros from the National Cultural Fund (NKA), which he oversaw, in 2025 and 2026, including funds intended for election campaign purposes.
The case of Miklos Sesztak is different. He is one of the wealthiest lawmakers in Hungary and has made headlines for more than a decade with his personal corruption scandals — another typical trait of the Orban system. As minister, Sesztak allegedly accepted around €30 million ($34 million) in bribes with an accomplice between 2015 and 2018. The alleged payments involved contracts related to the state-owned Hungarian bus company Volanbusz and the construction sector.
Barricaded in parliament with his family
Sesztak went straight to the prosecutor's office on Monday after his immunity was lifted, where he was taken into pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko took a different route. He arrived at Parliament on Monday morning with his wife and four teenage children and, after his immunity was lifted, said he was waiting for the authorities to make a decision. In practice, it appeared that he was barricading himself inside. Only after Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer formally ordered Hanko in writing that evening to leave the building, and he received a summons from the prosecutor's office, did he finally head for the exit, accompanied by his family and Fidesz lawmakers protesting what they called Magyar's "arbitrary rule."
The entire episode was livestreamed on Viktor Orban's Facebook page. After Hanko said goodbye to his family outside, a misunderstanding occurred. His SUV driver, apparently believing Hanko was already inside the vehicle, drove off without him. Hanko ran after the SUV, and the livestream on Orban's Facebook page then cut out. Later that evening, Hungarian media reported that Hanko had also been placed in pretrial detention.
Prime Minister Magyar's immunity lifted
Earlier that afternoon, Prime Minister Peter Magyar delivered a sharp speech in Parliament on the two cases. His own immunity had also been lifted beforehand — over a case that is classified in the records as theft.
In June 2024, Magyar took a phone from a man who had been filming him without permission at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube, where it was later found. Magyar had explicitly asked for his immunity to be lifted in the case. It is a calculated PR move intended to show that the same standards apply to everyone. But it is also a risky maneuver — if convicted, Magyar could lose his seat in Parliament.
In his parliamentary speech, he offered Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers a stark comparison: "How many hundreds of thousands of phones would you have to throw into the Danube to come close to the trillions allegedly stolen by the Fidesz-KDNP mafia?"
Dispute over Prosecutor General
Magyar has also spoken forcefully about Hungary's justice system. He has praised rank-and-file judicial employees while criticizing the leadership of the prosecutor's office, accusing them of repeatedly covering up corruption cases as "collaborators of the Orban system." At the center of the dispute is a fight over the appointment of a new prosecutor general.
The Tisza faction rejected Zoltan Szathmary, the candidate proposed by President Andras Baka, because his brother works for the Office for Constitutional Protection and, in that role, is a suspect in an ongoing politically sensitive case known as the "Gold Convoy" affair. In March 2026, Viktor Orban ordered the detention of a legal Ukrainian money shipment. The escorts were arrested in dramatic fashion, and cash and gold bars were seized. Orban and other Fidesz politicians indirectly accused Magyar's Tisza Party of receiving funding from Ukraine. Several people involved in the operation are now under investigation for abuse of office. Orban himself is not currently part of the proceedings, but could be in the future.
Hungarians seek a swift reckoning
Although Magyar has formally emphasized the independence of the judiciary, his comments in the current debates have given the impression that he is getting ahead of judicial decisions or becoming too deeply involved. At the same time, expectations among many Hungarians for a swift reckoning are high — and public debate's often return to the topic of how people want to "hear the handcuffs click." A recent poll found that a large majority of Hungarians consider the former Orban order "systemically corrupt" and a "mafia state."
Overall, Magyar and his government face the challenge of balancing the rule of law with public expectations. Many former critics of Orban are also calling for the reckoning with the Orban system to be handled properly. Prominent attorney Gyorgy Magyar, for example, who represented people in numerous human rights and rule-of-law cases under Orban, called for "prudence, patience, calm, discipline, and professionalism" in an interview with the news outlet Hirklikk.
Questions remain about whether "Operation Purgatory" will be merely spectacle, or whether the justice system will investigate corruption cases independently and in keeping with the rule of law.

Taiwan to offer free flu, COVID-19 vaccinations for eligible groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:35:20 UTC
13:35:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The first phase of this year’s publicly funded flu and COVID-19 vaccinations will begin Thursday as cases of both rise.
The Taiwan Centers for Disease Control announced Tuesday that the first phase of the program will cover 11 groups, including healthcare and disease prevention workers, people aged 65 and above, Indigenous people aged 55 to 64, as well as residents and workers at nursing and long-term care facilities,
For COVID inoculations, children younger than six who have never received a COVID vaccine are eligible. Elementary through high school students and poultry, livestock, and animal disease prevention workers are eligible only for the flu vaccine.
Other priority groups eligible for both vaccines include pregnant women, people with underlying health conditions, parents or caregivers of infants younger than six months, and preschool and childcare workers.
The CDC has procured about 170,000 doses of enhanced influenza vaccine, which will be prioritized for people aged 65 and above receiving care at nursing and long-term care facilities, as well as facility workers, according to a press release.
The second phase of the program will begin Nov. 2, when both vaccines will become available to adults aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic conditions.
Adults aged 18 and older who receive vaccinations can earn health tokens that can be used at places such as convenience stores and sports venues, according to the CDC. Recipients will receive 900 points for a COVID vaccine, 450 for a flu vaccine, and 600 for a pneumococcal vaccine.
This year, about 4,000 clinics and hospitals will provide publicly funded flu and COVID vaccinations. Starting Thursday, people can check nearby providers through local health department websites, the CDC’s VAX MAP or official LINE account, or by calling the 1922 hotline, and make appointments.
The CDC warned flu and COVID transmissions remain at epidemic levels. The latest data showed 138,654 outpatient and emergency visits for influenza-like illness in a single week, about 17% higher than the figure recorded at the end of August.
COVID-related visits totaled 10,502, down about 50% from the end of August but remained at elevated levels following a summer peak.
The CDC urged those eligible to get vaccinated on time and encouraged them to receive both vaccines during the same visit.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan won two silver medals and one bronze on Tuesday at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, with medals coming in men's trap shooting, women's +87-kg kurash, and women's team sprint cycling.
Shooter Yang Kun-pi (楊昆弼) won silver in the men's individual trap after a closely contested final against Kuwait's Khaled Almudhaf. Yang, 23, entered the final after tying the Asian Games record in qualifying and remained in contention for the gold medal until the final shot. He missed his final target, allowing Almudhaf to secure the gold, per UDN.

Following the competition, he told local media that he had improved significantly since the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou.
In the women's trap event, Taiwan's Lin Yi-chun (林怡君) finished sixth and did not advance to the medal positions.
Shih earns silver in kurash

Kurash is a Central Asian wrestling sport in which competitors seek to throw their opponents. Unlike judo, ground techniques are prohibited, and competition is conducted standing.
She previously competed in judo, though she retired after failing to make Taiwan's team for the Hangzhou Asian Games, subsequently working as a judo coach. She returned to combat sport competition this year after switching to kurash, winning silver at the Asian Championships in June before making her Asian Games debut in Nagoya, per UDN
After winning silver, she thanked her mother for encouraging her to return to competition. She said winning a medal at her Asian Games debut felt like completing an item on her bucket list.

In track cycling, Wang Sin-ting (王歆婷), Chen Ching-yun (陳靖云), and Liu Shang-ying (劉尚盈) won bronze in the women's team sprint with a time of 49.061 seconds.
Taiwan finished behind China and Malaysia and edged Japan for the bronze medal. Malaysia recorded 48.566 seconds for silver, while China won gold with 45.370 seconds, per CNA
The bronze was Taiwan's first cycling medal at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. Taiwan did not win a cycling medal at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou.
The three medals on Tuesday brought Taiwan's medal total to 37, including three gold, 10 silver, and 24 bronze medals.

Taiwan researchers find ‘copy-and-paste’ trick behind protein evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:34:55 UTC
13:34:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University researchers have found that proteins can develop similar functions in different species by repeatedly copying and adding the same small sections to their genetic code, CNA reported Wednesday.
The study focused on galectins, proteins that help cells communicate and play a role in the immune system. These proteins can gather into tiny droplet-like clusters inside cells, but humans and zebrafish use different amino acids to achieve the same result.
A team led by Huang Chieh-jung (黃介嶸), a professor at NYCU’s Institute of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, found that proteins do not necessarily need to fine-tune every part of their structure to develop new functions, per UDN. Instead, repeating certain sections can make the proteins better at forming these clusters.
Huang said the process is similar to using the “copy” and “paste” commands on a computer. Rather than making one small part of a protein much stronger, evolution can repeatedly add the same useful section until the protein has enough of it to perform the desired function.
The finding helps explain how different species can independently develop similar biological functions, a process known as convergent evolution. The researchers said the approach also shows how nature can build complex functions from simple, repeated components.
The study was published in EMBO Reports in February. The team said the findings could help scientists design new biomedical materials with specific properties by copying nature’s approach to building proteins.

NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:34:34 UTC
13:34:34 KST

NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Curiosity rover marked 5,000 Martian days by capturing morning and afternoon views that were blended into a striking Mars “postcard.” The panorama shows Curiosity, its tracks, and the enormous landscape surrounding Mount Sharp and Gale Crater.
- Share:
NASA's Curiosity rover has captured a striking new view of Mars as it passed a major mission milestone: 5,000 Martian days on the Red Planet.
While stopped at a sandy ridge nicknamed "Chocolatal," Curiosity used its navigation cameras to photograph the surrounding landscape at two different times of day. The cameras normally capture images in black and white.
The first panorama was recorded on Aug. 30, 2026, at 9:56 a.m. local Mars time, marking the mission's 5,000th Martian day, or sol. A second panorama was taken on Sep. 2, 2026, at 5:39 p.m. local Mars time, during Curiosity's 5,003rd sol.
Morning and Evening Combined Into One Mars View
After the images arrived on Earth, the two panoramas were combined into a single scene. Color was then added as an artistic interpretation, with blue used for the morning view and yellow for the afternoon.
The finished "postcard" follows the style of similar Curiosity images created in the past, including one taken in November 2021.
Several parts of the rover are visible in the foreground. They include Curiosity's cylindrical UHF antenna, which sends data to spacecraft orbiting Mars, along with the finned Multi Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG) at the rear. The MMRTG serves as the rover's nuclear power source.
Curiosity's tracks are also visible extending away across the Martian terrain.
A View Across Gale Crater
The rover is currently exploring the lower foothills of Mount Sharp, a mountain rising 3 miles (5 kilometers) inside Gale Crater. From Curiosity's position, the panorama looks downhill toward the crater floor, while the distant rim of Gale Crater is only faintly visible along the horizon.
Curiosity was built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. JPL operates the mission for NASA's Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of NASA's Mars Exploration Program portfolio.

Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:28:32 UTC
13:28:32 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

For Lyndsay and her son, living with disability in Denmark means planning outings around bathrooms; her “Changing Places” campaign reveals wider barriers to everyday life.
Trying to get back into the job market after a layoff can be confusing and exhausting. An expert shared her advice on the steps you can take to make it easier.
Lena arrived in Denmark as a 9-year-old refugee from Kosovo, attended Danish schools and built a career at some of the country’s biggest companies. She says racist slurs and comments questioning whether she belongs have followed her into adult life. Now she has written a book about identity, discrimination and learning to define herself on her own terms.

September records Denmark’s highest raw electricity prices since December 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:28:09 UTC
13:28:09 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

North Korea denies South's claim, calls DMZ blast a 'farce'
September 30, 2026
North Korea on Wednesday denied a South Korean claim that blamed Pyongyang for a mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that left three South Korean soldiers injured.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, accused Seoul of coming up with false evidence after blaming Pyongyang for last week's explosion.
"It is too low and dirty as befitting the tribes of South Korea," Kim said in a statement carried by state media KCNA.
"Such a farce is by no means new."
What did South Korea say?
After the incident occured, South Korean authorities launched an investigation.
South Korea's Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said on Tuesday that North Korean mines caused the blast and that it would take "corresponding" action. He also said North Korea likely planted mines to fortify the border.
He said the South Korean military "has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages."
The South Korean military has also demanded an apology from North Korea for the explosion.
"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, .... and we strongly urge an apology and responsible measures," an official from Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters.
Violation of the Korean War armistice, says UN Command
The South Korean joint chiefs said South Korean and UN investigators found another North Korean mine Tuesday during a follow-up inspection.
The UN Command said the investigation has "identified an active Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea's) anti-personnel mine on the ROK side of the Military Demarcation Line."
The UNC concluded thatNorth Korea violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War.
The UNC is a US-led multinational military force that oversees the Korean armistice agreement and administers the southern side of the DMZ.

====================================================================================================

Tokyo succumbs to ‘rain fatigue’ after a record 35 consecutive days of showers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:23:15 UTC
13:23:15 KST

Residents of Tokyo awoke to a familiar sound on Wednesday: raindrops splashing against windows and balcony floors.
The Japanese capital has seen a record 35 consecutive days of rain that experts blame on a combination of climate change and El Niño, which has created a prolonged front of high pressure in the Pacific Ocean.
The record rainfall has triggered a sharp rise in the price of vegetables, cast a shadow over tourism and left millions of Tokyoites wondering if they will see sunshine again.
Central Tokyo has been drenched by 629mm (24.8 inches) of rain between the start of September through to Monday this week, nearly three times the normal level, according to the agency.
It experienced just 45.8 hours of sunshine over the same period, the second lowest on record, the Mainichi Shimbun said, while on 14 days the sun did not appear at all.
The weather is affecting people’s physical and mental health, according to Hiromichi Ito, a doctor and director of a clinic in the capital, who told the Sankei Shimbun newspaper that prolonged rain, low atmospheric pressure and high humidity can lead to headaches, dizziness and other symptoms.
While the rain had turned to a light drizzle by late Wednesday morning, more could be on the way, as this year’s El Niño warms the Pacific Ocean, intensifying extreme weather patterns triggered by the climate crisis.
“Autumn rain fronts are staying longer than usual,” Masayuki Kyoda, an official at the Japan meteorological agency (JMA), told Agence France-Presse.
Tokyo’s rainy season usually occurs in June, but there have been regular downpours throughout the summer, causing heavy flooding in parts of the region. Earlier this month, Typhoon Dujuan caused flooding and landslides in neighbouring Chiba prefecture, killing eight people and destroying dozens of homes.
This week, meteorological officials said another typhoon, the 26th of the season, was moving in a north-easterly direction and could brush the Kanto region, where Tokyo is located.
While Kyoda said it was difficult to establish a direct link between climate change and the streak of wet weather in Tokyo – the longest since records began in 1886 – the agency said in a recent report that “global warming was affecting Japan’s weather long-term, including through more precipitation”.
The previous longest period of consecutive rain in Tokyo lasted 33 days between 27 June and 29 July 2019.
The prolonged rainfall has triggered a rise in the price of vegetables, particularly leafy greens, as a result of crop damage in agricultural regions near Tokyo, media reports said, with one supermarket worker in the capital quoted as saying that price of a head of lettuce had more than doubled to ¥450 (£2.17).
Residents also complained of not being able to dry their washing, forcing them to make trips to the local launderette.
The news that the city has not enjoyed a single dry day since 27 August prompted many take to social media to complain of “rain fatigue”.
“This endless rain must be to blame for my low mood,” said one X user. “If you’re feeling worn out, it’s not your fault.”
Yojiro Noda, the lead singer of the band Radwimps, posted to his 1.1 million followers: “Tokyo, a lifetime of rain.”
Another wondered if the city would match the 40 days and 40 nights of rain referenced in the Old Testament.

Morocco's King Mohammed VI appoints Fatima Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:21:51 UTC
13:21:51 KST

Mansouri is only the second woman in the Arab world to hold the office of prime minister. Her established political career has seen her serve as mayor of Marrakesh and member of parliament previously.
Morocco's King Mohammed VI named Urban Planning Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country's prime minister on Tuesday, making the 50-year-old attorney the first woman to hold the office in the Muslim kingdom.
Mansouri, who until her nomination also was the mayor of Marrakech, was tasked with forming a new government, the Royal Palace said in a statement. The announcement came four days after results of parliamentary elections were announced, with Mansouri’s centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, scoring the highest votes.
Mansouri, the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Najla Bouden in Tunisia, is expected to build a coalition in the coming days to form a government. Morocco’s electoral system makes it difficult for a single party to win an absolute majority.
Her government is expected to make billions of dollars in investments linked to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, while seeking to deliver on promises to fight inflation, raise wages and create jobs.
The Moroccan Constitution gives the king, who is the country’s highest authority, the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections.
That was a change successfully pushed by Arab Spring protesters in 2011. Before that, the king could name the prime minister without any such restriction.
Mansouri joined PAM upon its creation in 2008 by Fouad Ali el-Himma, a childhood friend and close adviser to the king.
A law graduate from the University of Montpellier in France, Mansouri became one of the party’s top leaders in 2024. She twice served as mayor of Marrakech and was a member of parliament.
Mansouri is the daughter of the “pasha of Marrakech” Abderrahmane el-Mansouri, a senior local official who was also Morocco’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, headed Marrakech’s bar association and was a major landowner.
She faced accusations of conflict of interest after a group of unidentified hackers claimed she had used her position for personal gain regarding land transactions in Marrakech. Mansouri denied the allegations, called them defamatory and took legal action.
One million of the 15.8 million registered voters in last week’s election voted for the Authenticity and Modernity Party, marking its first win since its creation. The election was the first since the Ceuta migration crisis last July and deadly youth-led protests last year.
After the royal nomination, the focus shifts to the coalition that will form the next government.
PAM has expressed its willingness to work with all parties, but some, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have announced no plans of such collaboration, insisting they will remain in the opposition.

HSBC unveils RedCoin as name of Hong Kong stablecoin for 3.3 million PayMe users
A survey by the lender shows that 74 per cent of customers know at least one use case, but there are also misunderstandings
HSBC on Wednesday named its stablecoin offering HSBC RedCoin, paving the way for Hong Kong’s biggest lender to make the coin available to the more than 3.3 million users of its PayMe app for money transfers, shopping and dining.
When launched before the end of the year, the stablecoin would be offered only through PayMe and HSBC’s Hong Kong mobile banking app, HSBC said.

Person-to-person money transfers ranked second at 53 per cent, while cross-border remittances and merchant payments each stood at 52 per cent.

Merz says Europe faces new opportunities amid unprecedented pressure
The head of the German government made the statement during a speech in Saarlouis at a ceremony marking the opening of streets named after former German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and former French President François Mitterrand, according to Ukrinform.

Coast guard intercepts Iranian dhow, seizes 526 kg narcotics worth over Rs 3,000cr
NEW DELHI: The Indian Coast Guard, in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), seized approximately 526 kg of narcotics from an Iranian dhow in the Arabian Sea west of Lakshadweep, officials said.The Coast Guard said five Pakistani nationals operating the vessel were also detained during the operation carried out near Lakshadweep on September 25, as reported by news agency PTI.The drugs, valued at over Rs 3,000 crore in the international market, were seized after the vessel was intercepted during the operation.The Coast Guard conducted coordinated sea-air surveillance to track the suspicious vessel before launching a hot pursuit and boarding the dhow.The operation was carried out in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) to intercept the vessel. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine, while five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended.The dhow, its crew and the seized drugs were escorted to Mumbai under armed security for joint interrogation and further legal proceedings.The operation was part of coordinated efforts by the Coast Guard and Gujarat ATS to detect and disrupt suspected transnational maritime drug-smuggling networks.
The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled through sea routes. The Coast Guard has previously conducted joint operations with Gujarat ATS and other agencies to intercept vessels suspected of carrying illegal drugs.
In April 2025, the Coast Guard, along with Gujarat ATS, seized 307.5 kg of narcotics off the Gujarat coast, according to the Coast Guard's official record of interdiction cases.Several drug-interdiction operations have been conducted along maritime routes in the Arabian Sea, with agencies relying on intelligence inputs, vessel surveillance and coordination between maritime and land-based enforcement units to identify suspected consignments.The Coast Guard said the latest operation underlined its efforts to strengthen maritime surveillance and prevent illicit activities in India's maritime zones. The seized drugs and apprehended crew were brought to Mumbai for further investigation and legal action.

South Korea doubled down Wednesday on its claim that Ukraine violated a mutual confidentiality agreement over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs), saying Kyiv was the first to request secrecy over the matter.
 
South Korea’s spy agency, the National Intelligence Service (NIS), said the two countries had a shared understanding to keep the transfer confidential from the beginning of the process.

The soldiers were captured in Russia’s Kursk region in early 2025 after being deployed to support Russian forces against Ukrainian troops.

It added that Seoul made no promises of support in return to Kyiv for the transfer of the soldiers.
 
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has slammed Zelenskyy for publicly revealing the transfer and his office has since said that Ukraine breached a nondisclosure agreement aimed at keeping the transfer a secret to protect the soldiers from dangers they could face if their transfer were to be disclosed.
 
A Ukrainian presidential official reportedly denied the existence of a nondisclosure agreement.
 
South Korea's Foreign Ministry summoned the Ukrainian ambassador Monday to express strong concern about the denial and demanded an apology from Kyiv.
 
"There was a nondisclosure agreement through several channels, including phone calls between the two countries' foreign ministers and consultations between our embassy (in Kyiv) and Ukraine's foreign ministry," said the NIS.

China Focus: Innovative applications drive healthy growth of China's private economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:04:38 CST
13:04:38 KST

A robot exhibit from PaXini AI conducts a toy assembling challenge at the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 19, 2026. (Xinhua)
TIANJIN, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- At a private-enterprise investment fair held recently in Tianjin Municipality, north China, two large embodied AI robots furnished with sensors stood center stage, demonstrating how they handle dangerous and repetitive inspections in chemical plants.
Ke Qinlin, who heads the ecosystem collaboration and innovation center at Sevnce Robotics Co., Ltd., said the company has spent the past few years refining its products in real-world settings such as chemical industrial parks and logistics warehouses. In his view, what truly opens up the market is not just a technology, but an ever-growing list of scenarios.
This reflects a national push in China. In November last year, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline to "accelerate the cultivation and openness of scenarios, and promote the large-scale application of new scenarios" -- the first systematic national effort of its kind.
The guideline defines scenarios as specific situations for testing new technologies, products and business models, serving as a bridge between technologies and industries, and between R&D and the market.
It covers emerging sectors such as the digital economy, AI, all-domain unmanned systems, clean energy and ocean development, as well as traditional sectors in transition, including manufacturing, transportation and smart logistics.
The initiative is already taking hold. From AI-powered drugmaking to robot swarms inspecting cross-sea bridges, and from brain-computer interfaces in clinical care to smart management of high-speed drones, China is seeing a steady stream of new applications, as frontline industry needs increasingly serve as proving grounds for new technologies.
For Sevnce Robotics, the scenario list gives it a clearer direction for R&D. Ke said many chemical industrial parks need to constantly screen for hazards. Once such needs are identified, the company can focus its R&D on high-risk, repetitive inspection tasks, making its products better suited to real-world production, whether identifying hazards or reading instrument data.
Sevnce Robotics has already partnered with companies including PetroChina, Sinopec and BASF, as its robots move from standalone products into real-world applications in the energy and chemical sectors.
"The scenario list brings previously fragmented market demand into focus," Ke said. "It gives us greater confidence to expand."
Niu Jianbo, deputy director of the Institute of Modern Management at Nankai University in Tianjin, said opening up scenarios allows private enterprises to "take their technologies to the scenarios and refine their products through real-world use," helping reduce the trial-and-error costs of commercializing innovations and accelerating the shift from concept validation to large-scale application.
Beyond the fair, more private enterprises have embedded scenarios into frontline operations. PaXini AI, an embodied perception company centered on multi-dimensional tactile sensing, has a data collection factory in Tianjin, where a humanoid robot equipped with dexterous hands rapidly performs complex tasks such as grasping and sorting in a logistics area. Its intelligence comes from large volumes of real-world scenario data.
After the Tianjin factory began production in June 2025, PaXini AI made data collection a key link between scenarios and R&D. Inside the data collection workshop, workers wearing self-developed five-finger tactile data gloves perform real-world tasks like grasping, assembly and sorting across 15 scenarios, including automotive manufacturing, healthcare and retail.
"Tianjin's diverse application scenarios across manufacturing, logistics and commercial services allow companies to continuously collect real-world data and validate their products," said Nie Xiangru, co-founder of PaXini AI. "Only when data is sufficiently rich and diverse can robots truly learn to perform tasks autonomously in complex environments."
At this year's fair, Tianjin released its first batch of 10 scenario innovation cases, covering fields including AI, robotics, brain-computer interfaces, life sciences, all-domain unmanned systems, smart factories, aviation equipment manufacturing, low-altitude economy and carbon reduction.
"We have built a scenario innovation service platform, which dynamically updates three lists, namely opportunities, capabilities and released projects, so private enterprises can match their technological strengths with available scenarios in a timely way," said an official with the Tianjin Development and Reform Commission. "We will also build a scenario validation center and a pilot-testing platform to provide testing grounds for private enterprises' new technologies and products."
Niu noted that China's continued efforts to open up scenarios, connect resources, and improve the business environment not only create application opportunities for private enterprises, but also offer them a broad stage for innovation-driven development, helping turn scenario-driven innovation opportunities into growth opportunities for the private economy. ■
