One EV sold every 100 seconds as Australia catches up to the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:02:40 UTC
13:02:40 KST

EV sales double in Australia as one in four new cars now electric
An electric car is being sold every 100 seconds in Australia, but there is still a long road ahead to decarbonise the country's transport sector, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.
The 10th anniversary edition of the annual State of Electric Vehicles Report shows how EVs have become mainstream within a decade, making up one in four new cars sold.
Sales have more than doubled within a year and last month, EVs outsold petrol and diesel cars for the first time.
"EVs are being taken up as a cost of living measure by households across Australia," Julie Delvecchio, CEO of the Electric Vehicle Council, said.
Owning an EV is no longer a luxury reserved for well-heeled inner-city dwellers as electric cars come close to price parity with petrol versions. Some are now selling for under $20,000.
This year's sales boom is being driven by suburban commuters, with the highest EV uptake in Tarneit, about 30 kilometres west of Melbourne.
"It's very much an average Australian suburb with people who have mortgages in the six to seven hundred thousands," Aman Gaur, the EVC's Head of Legal, Policy and Advocacy, said.
"They rely on their cars, they do not have access to three forms of public transport outside their front door, and for them, the sensible economic choice is to get into an EV."
Australians now have access to nearly 200 electric models, and incentives such as the fringe benefit tax exemption have helped to drive uptake.
The beginning of the conflict with Iran in February and the subsequent disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has seen fuel prices to surge this year, helping to further push the number of EVs currently on the road to more than 600,000.
"Australia is an island at the end of a long fuel supply chain, holding weeks' worth of reserves and importing almost all of its fuel," the Electric Vehicle Council (EVC) report said.
"Every car that plugs in instead of filling up is a permanent upgrade to our energy security."
Long road to meet climate goals
While 2026 may well become a turning point for passenger EVs, reaching Australia's climate targets will require a revolution in the national fleet.
There are about 21 million cars on Australian roads, and EVs make up just 3 per cent compared to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles.
"While the doubling of EV uptake over the last year is great news, Australia needs to maintain this momentum to be on track to reach its climate targets," Helen Rowe, the transport lead at the Monash University's Climateworks Centre, said.
The EVC report notes that Australia's EV uptake is not on track to meet the emission reduction targets of 43 per cent below 2005 levels by 2030, and 62 to 70 per cent by 2035.
"That 2035 target requires 5 million battery electric cars on the road by the middle of the next decade—a significant increase in pace from the current trajectory," the EVC's report said.
The other hurdle is charging infrastructure; it's increasing, but not quite keeping pace, according to the EVC's Aman Gaur.
"We do need to have a coordinated charging plan that will help Australians have confidence that they can get out onto the roads and charge either their car or their truck or their van," he said.
Addicted to diesel
Per capita, Australia uses more diesel than the US, China and Saudi Arabia.
And the biggest user of diesel is the transport and freight sector, which has barely started to electrify.
That's not because there are no electric trucks; while still more expensive, there are a growing number of options.
"China, the undisputed leader on truck electrification, saw monthly sales breach 50 per cent in December 2025 and already appears advanced in meeting its new 2030 target for 40 per cent heavy electric truck sales," The EVC report said.
Most freight operators in Australia are small businesses, running on very tight margins, and according to the EVC's Aman Gaur, the cost of switching to electric trucks was still prohibitive.
"There aren't enough financial incentives to get small mum and dad operators to make the switch to electric, which means that Australia is still importing diesel and our economy is still reliant on those imports," he said.
The EVC report called Australia a "global laggard" when it came to adopting electric trucks, with heavy vehicle rules such as road weight limits "complex and notoriously difficult to reform."
"With almost zero policy support and no dedicated charging infrastructure to speak of, electric trucks are yet to hit even 1 per cent of total truck sales.
"This contrasts with European markets and New Zealand, where strong freight electrification policies are moving heavy EVs beyond the 'early adopter' cohort to everyday trucking fleets.
"Electrifying Australia's heavy freight vehicles is the biggest unseized opportunity in Australia's energy transition."

Top AI and tech firms sign 'morally binding' accord to 'self-police' development after meeting at White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:01:15 UTC
13:01:15 KST

The accord comes amid massive global pressure from civilians and lawmakers alike to regulate the industry as reports of the technology breaking out of its confines continue to pile. Last week OpenAI revealed that its agent had hacked into an Australian government website during its testing phase.
US President Donald Trump said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies signed a voluntary accord on Tuesday that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology and its risks on humanity.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Trump and US House Speaker Mike Johnson met with leading executives from top tech and AI firms at the White House that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition.
The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, X and xAI – now part of SpaceX.
The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, late on Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.
It said the companies would implement “robust internal controls,” partner with an “independent external auditor” to assess whether the controls are working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.
“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said.
Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth."
Investment in data centres and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.
Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in AI development, said, “The technology has very real risks.”
“And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” he added.
Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding.” He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.
Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures these companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing.
The accord however does not introduce a set of legislation that introduces robust legal liability and regulation to guide the technology, which some in the industry have blown the whistle on, saying there is a chance it could outsmart humans and cause their extinction within a decade.
Trump, who has always vocally opposed instating such measures, said before the meeting that the US government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for “guardrails” or other restrictions.
“I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.”
Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centres cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
“You’re going to see, data centres are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, “they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”
Trump on Tuesday portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no “second place.”
The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington, but Trump underscored on Tuesday that he didn't want to cooperate too much with China.
"I didn’t want to do anything, because we’re leading. Why would I want to do anything?,” he said.

‘I do not know if the doctor survived’: young mothers recall ‘living hell’ of Nepal’s floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:11 UTC
13:00:11 KST

For three days, Pooja Pariyal waited on the roof of Trishuli hospital with her three-month-old daughter, Ridhika. On the ground below and around the building, most of her town had been destroyed and churned into a sea of mud in the catastrophic flash floods that surged through the Himayalan border region of Nepal and Tibet in August.
“Those three days were living hell for me, with no food, no working toilet and no one to help with the baby,” she says. “I had nothing to clean my baby’s soiled clothes. My milk supply had reduced because I was hungry and this poor little thing would cry her lungs out.
“I am so sorry you had to go through all of this,” she adds, breaking down in tears looking down at her baby.
Pariyal, 21, was one of about 50 patients – including five newborn babies – and medical staff stranded at the hospital. At night, the group went down into the hospital wards to rest – although Pariyal got little sleep – but come daylight they all climbed to the top of the building and spent the hours scanning the sky for helicopters.
On the fourth day, an army helicopter arrived to evacuate the stranded group. Now Pariyal and her baby, who was diagnosed with pneumonia shortly after their rescue, are living with about 125 other people, sharing 25 tents at Lamibagaichha holding centre, a temporary site in the town of Bidur, a couple of miles south of Trishuli.
In the weeks since a glacier high in the Himalayas collapsed on 26 August, plunging into the river below and triggering the floods that swept away dozens of villages, communities, roads and bridges, there have been landslips and further localised flooding adding to the misery of the people of the region.
More than 1,400 people have died, more than 5,700 are missing and more than 80,000 are still in need of humanitarian assistance, according to the latest Unicef assessment.
At 7.30am on the morning of the disaster, Pariyal left her house in Trishuli bazaar to get the bus to the hospital for a routine postnatal appointment. An hour and a half later a deluge of water, mud and debris tore along the Bhotekoshi River engulfing everything in its path, including a cluster of shops, hotels and houses where Pariyal lived. As she sat in the hospital waiting room, sirens and loudspeakers alerted people to the unfolding disaster.
“My baby’s third-month vaccination was due on 26 August, which is why I left for the hospital at 7.30 in the morning and was there when the chaos happened,” she says.
“It is only because of my baby that I am alive today.”
At the time, Pariyal had no idea of the scale of the flood. She worried that clothes she had left out to dry on the terrace at home might get washed away. It did not cross her mind that she would lose everything. Her now-destroyed house was rented, so she is not entitled to government compensation. “Maybe I will go back to my parents’ house when they get rehoused,” she says.
Aditi Aryal, a communications analyst at the UN Population Fund in Nepal, says 5,030 pregnant women are among those affected by the floods, with an estimated 750 of those having complications, and 550 due to to give birth next month in their nearest hospitals.
Kalpana Nepali, 23, from Rasuwa district, is living in another temporary shelter in Nuwakot, where men, women and children of all ages sleep together on the floor. There are mats and bedding for everyone. Nepali, who is seven months pregnant, was making soup in her kitchen when she had a phone call just after 8.30am from her husband who was on duty at the hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district. He told her to get away from the house and reach higher ground. “God knows how I managed to walk uphill in my nightdress. Maybe because I had a life to save before mine.”
She does not remember being rescued. “I had fainted and my first memory is feeling water on my face and realising I was in a helicopter with 10 other people. Later, I ate a whole packet of bread. I was stressed about the life inside me. My doctor had strictly advised me to eat every four hours. I do not know if the doctor survived the flood or not.”
Nepali’s husband was near the entrance of the tunnel so was able to escape. The pair are now living in a hall with about 80 other displaced people. “The toilet is not designated by sex, and there’s always a queue outside it,” she says.
Pregnant women staying in the shelters are being assigned to the nearest functioning health centre based on their estimated dates of delivery. Those with complicated or high-risk pregnancies will be airlifted to the maternity hospital in Kathmandu a week before they are due to give birth.
Nepali sits on a mat in the dormitory hall, a packet of biscuits in her hand. The disaster has taken away the luxury of eating to satisfy her pregnancy cravings, along with any sense of excitement about having her first baby. She is due in November and will give birth at Nuwakot health centre, before returning to the hall.
Lila Pieters Yahia, the United Nations resident coordinator in Nepal, warns: “Pregnant and lactating women might have a higher chance of experiencing trauma, shock and postpartum depression due to what they have experienced during pregnancy.”
Renuka Nepali is in the same shelter as Pariyal. The 27-year-old had just seconds to escape the flood with her two children, a 12-year-old son and an eight-month-old daughter in her arms. “I heard crying and shouting of ‘Daudanu-daudanu [run-run]!’ from my window while I was getting my son ready for school. When I opened the door, people were actually running. Without thinking, I held my daughter in my left arm, and grabbed my son with my right. I ran so fast my boy got a lot of bruises but these bruises are a sign of survival.”
Her relief at escaping is mixed with grief at the memory of her heavily pregnant friend and neighbour who could not outrun the flood. “She was trying to escape with me but she couldn’t keep up. She was swallowed by the flood while trying to grab a branch or something to hold on to.
“We have been through hell,” she says as she folds her clothes, which had been donated to the shelter. “This is what mother nature can do to you when you upset her. She doesn’t even spare the mothers.”

====================================================================================================

It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María Ramírez
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:11 UTC
13:00:11 KST

Maricarmen Abascal is a determined woman who uses a wheelchair to get around. She has needed her determination over the years she has spent fighting the real estate company that forced her out of her Madrid apartment last week. She had lived in the flat for more than 70 of her 87 years.
Police forced their way into her apartment after a judge approved Abascal’s eviction. By then, protesters had gathered around the building, including the actor Carlos Bardem, Javier’s brother. Teargas was used against them. Abascal was taken to a Madrid hospital, suffering from anxiety and extreme exhaustion, while her supporters chanted: “You are not alone.”
Demonstrations of solidarity with her and “all the other Maricarmens” have since erupted across Spain, with protest encampments springing up at Puerta del Sol square in Madrid as well as in Bilbao and Málaga.
Thousands of people are evicted from their homes in Spain every year. In the first quarter of 2026 alone there were, on average, 44 eviction orders a day, mostly for disputes about rent. Behind those figures, cases involving single mothers and elderly tenants often come to light. But no eviction has sparked such a public outcry, a national protest movement and a call for urgent political action like the tale of Abascal.
Evictions are actually in decline in Spain and are now about a third of what they were in the aftermath of the financial crisis. In 2014, there were more than 68,000 evictions compared with about 24,000 in 2025. Spain is one of the fastest-growing economies in the west. Employment and consumer data continue to defy the odds despite global economic uncertainty. But many young people and poorer older people surviving on pensions struggle to pay rent or buy a home, especially in the most prosperous cities.
In Abascal’s case, the real estate company Urbagestión bought her apartment in 2018, ending her rent-controlled arrangement. Her rent was initially increased from €500 a month to €2,650, way beyond what her pension could cover.
The Spanish supreme court upheld Urbagestión’s claim that the tenancy was invalid as it had been transferred twice, first to Maricarmen’s mother and later to her. But the original 1956 contract was signed by her father under Franco’s discriminatory laws against women.
As Abascal lay in hospital, the company and her representatives reached an agreement, mediated by Madrid city council, for her to return home. The monthly rent will be similar to the amount she has paid for years, about €500. This is a victory for the activism and solidarity of ordinary citizens who mobilised for a neighbour in need.
But her case reflects how property companies, banks and hedge funds profit from vulnerable tenants and their once-affordable homes. It is also a reminder of the failure of politicians to protect the right to “decent and adequate” housing that has been enshrined in the Spanish constitution since 1978.
The centre-left governing coalition has failed to change the law to protect the most vulnerable tenants from eviction, and to push through comprehensive housing reforms.
On Tuesday, Pedro Sánchez’s minority coalition finally introduced a new housing bill that would ban evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, limit rent hikes for two years and ban investment funds purchasing houses for two years. Now the bill needs to be approved by parliament within a month.
But Sánchez’s reliance on the support of a range of parties since 2023 has limited his room for manoeuvre.
The socialist PM’s leftwing coalition partner, Sumar, had pushed for reforms to prevent cases such as Abascal’s. But Sánchez had shelved the proposals until now, fearing rejection in parliament. The latest uproar is forcing his hand, even if it means including tax breaks sought by Junts, a rightwing nationalist Catalan party.
Madrid’s regional and municipal governments, in the hands of the conservatives, were slow to offer alternatives to Abascal until she was evicted, using the case instead to attack the national government. For the past three years, the Madrid regional government, led by the conservative Isabel Díaz Ayuso, has refused even to apply the existing national law to limit rent increases.
Spain’s highly decentralised system, with power divided at a local, regional and national level, is once again the perfect cover for politicians to do the minimum and blame each other while individuals suffer.
Spaniards repeatedly identify housing as the country’s biggest problem, but the issue has not earned the intense political attention it deserves.
A few days ago, Sánchez visited Zohran Mamdani, who is becoming a point of reference for the left in Spain and across Europe. Instead of trying to imitate the mayor of New York’s videos or his charm, fellow progressives could emulate his relentless focus on housing.
Mamdani supports solutions across the ideological spectrum, from pushing for the construction of new apartment buildings to taxing real estate investment funds. He is supporting public housing and protections for tenants in rent-controlled apartments, but also working with private developers, even exchanging pleasantries with Donald Trump to advance a proposal for a large urban development project over Sunnyside Yard in Queens, New York.
There are no magic bullets on housing. Fixing it will require hard work, smart planning, laser focus and an open mind. Winning progressive politicians have only now started treating this problem with the urgency it deserves.
Will Abascal’s eviction prompt a new era in housing policy in Spain? If it happens, change will have come at a high price. It should not take the forcible eviction of an 87-year-old woman who just wants to remain in her home for the corrosive effects of unaffordable housing to be taken seriously.
- 
  María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario.es, a news outlet in Spain

====================================================================================================

Economic growth and democratic decline: the ‘cotton king’ who reshaped Benin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:11 UTC
13:00:11 KST

In recent years, a building boom has reshaped Benin’s largest city, Cotonou, and a shiny new coastal road has reduced journey times to Ouidah, the west African country’s spiritual and cultural capital.
In the last decade, Benin’s annual GDP has grown from 3% to 6%, a regional high, and an industrial zone has been launched north-west of Cotonou to help industrialise the relatively small nation’s largely informal economy.
“Benin is now looking like a paradise,” said Savossou Stanislas, a 40-year-old tyre repairer in the official capital, Porto-Novo.
The rapid infrastructural development has been overseen by Patrice Talon, the president from 2016 till this May.
For years, Benin was so content being in the shadow of Nigeria, a neighbour about eight times its size and with about 16 times its population, that Talon’s predecessor, Thomas Boni Yayi, once quipped during a visit to Abuja that “Benin is the 37th state of Nigeria”.
Talon, who also enjoys good relations with Nigeria and called on it to help quell an attempted coup d’etat in December, chose a different path: to engineer enough growth for Benin to be recognised in its own right.
The Kagame model
Widely believed to be Benin’s richest person, Talon, known as “the cotton king”, made his name in agriculture but diversified into banking and hospitality. Before becoming president, he had financed the campaigns of Yayi and Yayi’s predecessor, Mathieu Kérékou.
Critics say his development agenda has come at a severe cost: once held up as a poster child for democratic transition in west Africa, Benin has also undergone democratic decline since Talon took power.
In many respects, Talon modelled his governance style on the leader of another relatively small African country: Paul Kagame. The archetypal “benevolent strongman”, Rwanda’s de facto leader since 1994 has also combined repression with policies aimed at economic and social transformation.
In time, the two men became allies and Talon even appointed two former Rwandan officials to head sensitive Beninese government agencies. Benin has also sought the east African nation’s help in countering a growing insurgency along the border with Nigeria.
By the end of Talon’s first term, strict new election laws and heavy registration fees had purged a lot of the opposition from parliament. In 2019, the government shut down the internet during a parliamentary election as people protested against the changes.
The judiciary was co-opted to muzzle dissent, resulting in the targeting of several dozen former allies and dissidents, including the opposition leader Reckya Madougou, who is in prison on charges of “undermining the state”, and the journalist Hugues Comlan Sossoukpé.
In April 2021, a month after Madougou’s arrest, Essowé Batamoussi, a judge at the court for the repression of economic offences and terrorism, resigned his post and fled to France to seek asylum. “There was no justice in her [Madougou’s] case,” Batamoussi said. “We received an empty file and a threat: if we did not put her in jail, we were in danger.”
Last November, it became apparent how deeply Talon had control of every major aspect of life in Benin. A controversial constitutional amendment, the second of his tenure, elongated the presidential term from five years to seven and introduced thresholds that kept opposition parties outside parliament. It also created a new senate, whose members are all appointed by government rather than elected.
Within a month of parliament approving the amendment, mutineers led by a former commander of the national guard attempted a coup, citing Talon’s authoritarianism and inability to tackle rising insecurity.
Only one opposition candidate was approved to stand in April’s presidential election, which was won by Talon’s hand-picked successor, Romuald Wadagni, with more than 94% of the vote. In August, Talon himself returned to centre stage as president of the senate.
Morgan Assogba, a Cotonou-based geopolitical analyst, described Talon as a “gigantic political actor with a good understanding of how politics works in Benin”, who had reshaped the political arena to suit his economic development drive.
For Guillaume Moumouni, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Abomey-Calavi, Talon’s dual policies of constitutional change and development constituted a “carrot and stick” approach to governing, aimed at ensuring the political environment did not jeopardise his economic objectives. In time, however, he added, there was “less carrot and more stick” as freedoms were increasingly suppressed.
What price progress?
During his campaign for the April election, Wadagni vowed to tackle extreme poverty, a tacit admission that economic growth had not been to the benefit of all Beninese.
The minimum monthly wage increased from 40,000 CFA francs to 52,000 CFA francs (£52-£68) in January 2023, but many still earn far less. In recent years, rent and electricity tariffs have also risen by at least 15%, while the price of fuel has almost doubled. “With the upcoming school term, we don’t know how we’ll manage,” said Stanislas, the tyre repairer, who has four children of school age.
Most of the development has been in Cotonou and Ouidah, Talon’s home town. Opposition figures have said there has been a lack of transparency in some of those projects, while civil society groups said some were awarded to entities linked to Talon’s political allies and business network. According to a 2023 report by Amnesty International, four development projects resulted in mass forced evictions that affected at least 6,000 people. The communication ministry was approached for comment.
Moumouni said economically Talon’s vision had brought net progress. “People are not gaining or enjoying much more in terms of cash, but they are enjoying [progress] in terms of social infrastructure,” he said. “There’s room for improvement for sure but compared to 10 or 15 years ago, there is quite a huge difference.”
Eugène Azatassou, the vice-president of the opposition Democrats party, feels differently.
“Development cannot be limited to roads and buildings,” he said. “It must also be measured by the quality of democracy, purchasing power, employment, security, improvement of living conditions … when a power continuously modifies political and electoral rules in order to conserve control of institutions, we have the right to ask ourselves if we are facing [only] a facade of development.”

Tern turnaround: colonies in England show signs of recovery after decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:10 UTC
13:00:10 KST

England’s most important tern colonies are showing signs of recovery after being hit by years of bird flu, flooding and increasingly unpredictable weather, new figures from the National Trust reveal.
The trust reported record numbers of little terns at Long Nanny in Northumberland, one of the UK’s most important breeding sites for what is the country’s second-rarest breeding seabird.
Numbers are also slightly up for arctic terns, the long distance superstars of the avian world that annually breed in places such as Northumberland before making the incredible journey south to Antarctica.
In Norfolk, more than 1,100 pairs of sandwich terns returned to breed at Blakeney Point after a two-year absence.
Ben McCarthy, the trust’s head of nature conservation, stressed there was no room for complacency.
But he said the figures showed “what can be achieved when internationally important breeding sites are carefully protected and managed.
“These results are particularly encouraging given the challenges seabirds have faced in recent years – from avian flu and extreme weather to wider pressures on the marine environment.”
The trust said there had been a “remarkable turnaround” for little terns at Long Nanny with at least 126 pairs nesting – doubling the previous site record.
At least 82 chicks are known to have fledged with the final total potentially exceeding 100 birds, rangers said.
Little terns are a particularly sensitive and vulnerable species that migrate from west Africa to breed, making nests, known as scrapes, on open sandy beaches.
The species had experienced “significant long-term declines nationally, making this year’s record breeding season especially significant”, the trust said.
The arctic tern colony at Long Nanny consisted of at least 730 breeding pairs this year with nests containing 1,346 eggs. That was slightly up and a sign of numbers “holding steady” after a torrid past few years for the species.
In 2023, Long Nanny’s arctic tern colony was devastated by avian flu, when rangers found more than 600 dead chicks. In recent seasons nests have been lost to high spring tides and extreme weather, the trust said.
James Porteus, the trust’s lead ranger for the Northumberland coast, said it was “incredibly encouraging” to see little terns doing so well, calling it an “exceptional season” after several years “dominated by bird flu outbreaks, flooded nests and concerns about declining numbers”.
He added: “To more than double the previous site record for breeding pairs is a remarkable achievement and a testament to the dedication of staff, volunteers and partner organisations who help protect the colony each year.
“It’s especially exciting to see so many chicks hatching and fledging. Little terns face huge challenges throughout their migration and breeding cycle, so every successful nesting attempt matters.”
Rangers in Northumberland also reported the return, for the seventh consecutive breeding season, of a black tern they have called Nigella. Black terns are not normally found breeding in the UK.
The trust stressed that the picture for breeding seabirds was “not universally positive”, pointing to a 27% fall in arctic tern numbers on the Farne Islands, Northumberland. Also there were no common terns there this year compared with five last year while sandwich tern numbers remained unchanged at two breeding pairs.

‘If people are in a bunker, business stops’: Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45m for every hour they halt businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:10 UTC
13:00:10 KST

Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, according to the country’s economy minister, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment.
Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to “destroy pretty much the entire economy”.
“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks.
Speaking from the heavily protected government building in Kyiv, Kravchenko, a former McKinsey executive who joined the government in the summer, said the attacks were forcing large parts of the economy into repeated standstills as workers were sent to shelters, with sirens lasting up to 10 hours a day.
“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” he said.
To ease the economic costs, the government recently introduced a new two-tier warning system designed to keep businesses operating during prolonged air raid alerts.
A “red” alert warns of a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning is used for drone threats, allowing many businesses to remain open.
More than half of businesses were continuing to operate during yellow alerts, Kravchenko said.
But a yellow alert is no guarantee of safety. That danger was made clear on Monday, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people while staff were still inside working.
It is one of the difficult trade-offs Ukraine faces as it tries to keep normal life moving while protecting people from an escalating campaign of Russian strikes.
Kravchenko said Russian attacks this year alone had caused an estimated $10bn in damage to fixed assets, with steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, most recently datacentres, among the targets. Russia has also effectively blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, which before the blockade carried the bulk of the country’s exports.
The minister believed the government was better prepared this year for what could be the “hardest, the harshest winter” of the war, with further pressure expected on energy supplies, infrastructure and businesses already weakened by months of strikes.
To protect against future strikes, the government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukraine’s air-defence system, the minister said, although he cautioned that businesses could never fully protect themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
The ongoing damage from strikes has added to an already severe strain on the state’s finances.
The president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged, despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027.
Kravchenko said the government had since narrowed the shortfall to $20bn through spending cuts and by identifying additional domestic reserves.
Kyiv was now seeking further support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potentially bringing forward loans that had been earmarked for next year, Kravchenko said.
“There is very active work with all our international partners to get additional sources of funding,” he said.
Kravchenko dismissed suggestions that the shortfall was the result of mismanagement or corruption. He also said it was not due to excessive spending under former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whose drive to overhaul military procurement and rapidly expand Ukraine’s drone programme had made him one of the government’s most prominent reformers before his dismissal in July, a move that triggered street protests.
Instead, he said the gap reflected both weaker-than-expected state revenues and the rising cost of waging the war.
“The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said, pointing to the need for more air-defence systems and for Ukraine to accelerate development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered weapons.
But high-profile corruption scandals have also reached Zelenskyy’s inner circle, straining trust in the government both at home and among western donors.
A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that corruption in government was the most cited concern among Ukrainians, named by 50% of respondents, ahead of mass missile and drone strikes at 40%. The same survey found that 72% believed Zelenskyy bore personal responsibility for corrupt actions by people around him.
Kravchenko said progress had been made to tackle the issue but admitted that Ukraine faced both corruption itself and a persistent perception problem both inside Ukraine and abroad.
“I very much appreciate the pressure of European partners on reforms,” he said, adding that Ukraine also needed to tackle perceptions of corruption at home and abroad.
Ukraine’s external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6bn, but only about $20bn has so far been secured, according to the minister, with further tax rises and spending cuts under discussion.
Asked whether the rise of parties sceptical of support for Ukraine in France and Germany could weaken western commitment to Kyiv, he said: “Am I worried? I think I should be, probably.”
“The overall fatigue is increasing in Europe,” he added.

‘I just saw this furry brown bottom disappear!’ In search of Samba – the fearless fugitive capybara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:09 UTC
13:00:09 KST

Samba the capybara is still at large. Along with her older sister, Tango, the intrepid rodent made her escape from Marwell zoo in Winchester in March. Tango all but gave herself up on day two; Samba broke for the marshy wetlands of the River Itchen. Word spread and within days the fugitive was an international social media star. But despite an intense search, the dense Hampshire countryside has afforded her a haven. Six months on, Samba remains elusive.
Marwell’s staff still aren’t sure how the capybaras escaped, although they have their suspicions. Tango and Samba were born on Jimmy’s Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk in the summer of 2025. They arrived at Marwell zoo on Monday 16 March, to great excitement. “They were a little bit shy when they got here, as you would expect,” says Laura Read, the chief executive of Marwell Wildlife. “But they were fine.” They were immediately placed in a quarantined habitat, as is standard procedure for new arrivals. The plan was to keep them there for 30 days.
The next day, the vet and zookeepers did their morning checks and everything was fine. But when they returned that afternoon, Samba and Tango had vanished. “There was no sign of them digging out – they don’t dig – and there was no sign of them chewing their way out,” says Darren Ives, a senior zookeeper who has been at Marwell for 15 years. He’s a member of the hoofstock team, who are responsible for “horses, equids, that kind of stuff … basically anything that’s big and shits a lot”. That includes capybaras – which are native to most of South America – although rather than hooves they have partly webbed toes.
“We think they really squeezed under a tiny gap in a gate,” says Read. “That’s the only explanation we have.” After 30 minutes of searching the enclosure, the alarm was raised. “In a situation like this, we are really well versed and have set drills that we practise regularly around animal escape.”
When an animal escapes at Marwell, a call identifying the species and type of emergency is sent out over the zoo’s radio network. Staff then send out searchers, contact the relevant authorities (Natural England, Winchester city council, the police) and mobilise drone support (provided by the University of Southampton, which Marwell already works with on population mapping conservation projects). Every species has its own emergency procedure, which includes determining whether a firearm response is required. Despite being the world’s largest rodents, capybaras do not demand a firearm response.
The search was initially confined to Marwell zoo’s 57 hectares (140 acres). By the evening, staff had located two warm bodies inside a dense section of tree and bush clippings used for composting. Neither was reachable. As dusk turned to night, staff did their best to secure the perimeter, laid out some food and left. The next morning, Tango left the compost pile and was captured with throwing nets (“without trying to stress her out too much,” says Read). Samba, however, had vanished.
Later that day, Marwell heard that Samba, who is about the size of a spaniel, had been spotted near the Ship Inn pub in Owslebury, nearly 2 miles away. A convoy of Land Rovers set off with transport crates and nets, while farmers were contacted to ask for permission to cross their land. Or, as Ives puts it: “In about five minutes, someone in Marwell uniform will be walking across – don’t shoot them.”
Read convened a crisis meeting, which looked at the threats to Samba’s wellbeing. “It was cars,” she says. “She’s got no natural predators here. She’s too big. We knew she’d probably seek out water as well, and they’re fantastic swimmers. Water would be her sanctuary.”
The decision was made to go public. Was there any hesitation? “That was the quickest way to find her and secure her welfare, so no. Our PR, you know, in terms of: ‘We’ve lost an animal,’ came second.”
Local people poured out to look for Samba, including a woman with a trained search dog. “But, in hindsight, did all that activity drive her further away from our direct locality?” Read wonders.
By Friday, the local press was taking an interest, then social media, with waves of AI capybara memes appearing. Soon, the story was being reported as far away as the US and Australia.
Glenn Moores also joined the search after seeing the hunt on social media. “I had a bunch of drones and a skill set that could help.” He runs Digital Fauna, a company that conducts wildlife surveys with drones, mostly counting deer (“there’s far more deer than anyone even estimated,” he says).
Moores’ involvement has been pivotal, says Ives. “It meant that he could search areas and go: ‘Don’t bother looking there.’” Staff would have to respond to every credible sighting, but “until we had him, we were literally just on foot … walking like a police search when they’re looking for a lost person.” Such was the quality of Moore’s thermal imaging that he was able to detect rats. “We were going out at six in the morning, we were going out at night, we were walking the fields around the river,” says Moores. “It’s amazing that nobody saw Samba in that time.”
Is he surprised how hard it has been to find her? “I’m used to counting deer at night, so we’re not strangers to finding animals about the size of a capybara with thermal imaging. That’s what we do. But finding one specific animal in an entire landscape is very different.” How long has he spent hunting for Samba? “My goodness. Days, days and days. Probably about three weeks’ worth of evenings.” His selflessness is not lost on the Marwell team. “All of his time has been given for free!” says Read, appreciatively. (Moores says he wants a free pass to the zoo.)
On Sunday morning, five days after Samba vanished from her enclosure, a member of the public was walking along the bank of the Itchen in Twyford when she spotted a capybara sunning herself. Then her dog, Growler, chased Samba into the river. The video she took of the incident found its way to Marwell and the focus of the search shifted: staff donned waders and mounted paddleboards. On land, they looked for tracks, droppings, a body. They flushed out barn owls, deer, a pheasant, but no capybara. Read is convinced she caught a flash of her. “I just saw this brown furry bottom disappear into the river.”
For the next week, the search was constant: at least six people a day, mornings and nights. “Everything went really quiet,” says Read. “We just couldn’t find any trace of her.”
Six months later, my own trip to Marwell begins with a capybara hunt. Peering into their enclosure – a mixed wetland habitat they share with two swamp-dwelling antelopes called sitatungas – I can’t spot Tango or her new companion, Ripple, a seven-year-old male. “They’re in there, definitely. Don’t worry,” says Read, who has just come from proofreading a press release about a monkey vasectomy performed at the zoo. It’s easy to see how Samba has evaded capture: “Try that in acres and acres and acres of an SSSI [site of special scientific interest] along the Itchen.”
Ten minutes later, Tango and Ripple waddle out to the grazing area. Ripple was brought in from a zoo in Blackpool a few months after the escape – partly to breed with Tango, but mostly to keep her company. Capybaras are sociable animals, Ives says, used to living in packs of between 10 and 20. Ripple is calmer and much bigger than Tango – the size of a small sheep, he weighs about 40kg. Capybaras can start breeding once they are about a year old and Tango has already started showing signs that she is in the mood to do so. “When you put the two of them together, they seem to complement each other,” says Ives.
So, how has Samba evaded capture for so long? For one, her biology. Capybaras are quick. “The things that would hunt these guys [in their native habitat] are jaguars. They need to be able to outrun them,” says Ives. Capybaras are quite angular, he says, making them streamlined when running – it’s an explosive speed, rather than one sustained over long distances. When chased, they head towards water and dive, barely breaking the water’s surface as they do so. Submerged, they can hold their breath for up to five minutes, or furtively breach the surface revealing just their eyes, ears and nose. “They’re designed to be quite stealthy. They’re very good at hiding in the undergrowth.”
Is Samba a danger to the public? “They’ve got a cracking set of teeth,” says Ives. “If she were to bite you, she’d probably take your finger off. But also if you get that close – I mean you’re doing better than us! – she would just run away. She would see you, smell you, hear you way before you see her.” As Read says, capybaras have “a reputation, shall we say, for being quite slippery customers in the zoo world”.
Also in Samba’s favour is her likeness to local wildlife, particularly muntjac deer. Marwell set up a hotline for sightings. “We had everything from: ‘We’ve seen her dead on the side of the M3,’ to: ‘She’s in my back garden,’” says Read. “We had one man who was absolutely adamant that she was in his back garden and was behaving weirdly. And we were like: ‘Right!’ We went down there … and it was a hedgehog.”
Some calls came from as far away as Stonehenge, about 40 miles away. More frustrating were the prank calls from drunk people in the middle of the night. “You very quickly got the gist of who was serious,” Read says. (If you think you have seen Samba, take a picture, record your exact location and send it to the zoo.)
In August, Marwell received an image of a rodent-like creature from a camera trap used to spot poachers. The zoo set up its own cameras and a week later received unmistakable proof of life. The first image: a hairy, rotund animal bottom. The second: Samba. “Without a doubt, that’s our girl looking fat and healthy,” says Read.
She was two to three miles away from the zoo, near where she had been chased by Growler. “It’s an ideal location for her to stay and disappear,” says Ives. The plan now is to make Samba feel comfortable in that area, allowing the keepers to narrow their search. They want to tempt her back to the same spot repeatedly with food (sweet potato and honeydew melons, apparently). They have laid more camera traps and put down bedding used by Tango and Ripple to see if she is enticed by their scent.
Read and her team insist they are doing everything they can, but interest in Samba has brought with it criticism of the zoo. “It’s been really upsetting for me and for the team, because we know how hard we’re working, still, on bringing Samba back,” says Read. “A lot of what we’re doing isn’t necessarily publicly visible, because it is things like drone flights at 6am, it’s camera traps, it’s someone sitting at a desk reviewing camera-trap footage hour after hour. It’s scientifically grid-mapping where we’re camera-trapping. We know that loads of boots on the ground will just drive her further away.”
She dismisses accusations of carelessness. “We’ve been here for 50 years. Our record speaks for itself. We’re award-winning for our animal welfare. No one did this because of carelessness. No one did this because they couldn’t be bothered or didn’t do their job properly. This happened because an animal did something that we could not have foreseen it doing.”
As for whether Marwell should have capybaras in the first place: “Just because the capybara itself is not an endangered species doesn’t mean that the ecosystems and the habitats that they occupy aren’t under threat,” says Read. The Amazon and Pantanal – the capybaras’ native habitats – are under threat and Read believes capybaras could be used to tell that story, not least because they are trendy and draw a crowd. “With the caveat that their welfare needs to be exceptionally well met,” says Read. “Yes, they’re here for conservation, for breeding programmes, for insurance and all the rest of it, but also they’re here to tell a story and to inspire people.”
Samba’s story will help with that, she hopes. “We are a conservation charity first and foremost,” says Read. “We are hands-on with our conservation work. We don’t just make donations to NGOs. We have teams in the field doing the work. We want to be really famous for the great work that we do and if Samba is one way of us doing that, then great. We’d like to shine a light on that as well as ‘we’ve lost a capybara’.” She pauses. “Although we did. We own that.”
Winter could prove crucial: with less vegetation, Samba may be easier to spot, but capybaras are not built for harsh weather. Is it a race against time? “If we got a really cold snap, we’d all be pretty worried,” says Read. If, on the other hand, it’s just “wet and windy, she’ll be fine with that. It’s more that we have no control over her welfare out in the world, whereas here we can give her everything she needs, including socialisation.”
Are they confident they’ll find her? “Well, technically, we’ve already found her!” says Ives. “We’ve seen her on the camera-trap footage. She’s very chunky. She’s very healthy.” If they do catch her, a reunion with her sister beckons. “But when – when, not if – we get her back, it’s going to be a very slow process to mix them, because she’s now a wild animal.”
How much longer she stays that way remains to be seen. For Samba, the net is closing in.

Can a mushroom make music? Devon exhibition explores ‘cultural world’ of fungi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:09 UTC
13:00:09 KST

For one of the installations, a musician spent hours in woodland “collaborating” with fungi to create a soundscape inspired by the electricity they emit.
Another is a kinetic sculpture of an extinct fungus that honours Beatrix Potter not for her tales of mischievous rabbits but for her lesser-known skills as a mycologist – a fungi expert.
These are just two of the exhibits playing starring roles in a rather extraordinary contemporary art show called Living Labyrinths, at the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery (RAMM) in Exeter, aiming to celebrate the “cultural world” of fungi.
Lara Goodband, the contemporary art curator at the RAMM, said it had been five years in the making. She suggested the south-west England was a good place to focus on fungi.
“We have great weather for it, warm and damp,” Goodband said. “But also, I think people here have a special affinity for fungi.”
She said a wide range of people in the south-west were fungi fans, from the ecologists who study the role they play in soil health to the ravers who enjoy the hallucinogenic properties of some mushrooms and the storytellers who work with the fairytale associations of toadstools.
RAMM is also an excellent place for this deep dive because of its Victorian collections of fungi. Specimens of stinkhorn and bird’s nest fungi appear alongside the modern pieces.
Goodband said interest in fungi had risen sharply over the past few years, partly after the success of Merlin Sheldrake’s book Entangled Life, which argued fungi provided a key understanding to the planet. “I think we’ve hit a moment,” said Goodband.
Among the highlights is a sound installation by the musician, composer and DJ Jason Singh, who spent hours hunkered down in two Devon woods, Fingle and Yarner, for his piece, The Intelligence Below.
He said he used biofeedback sensors to measure the electricity coming from mycelium – the rootlike networks of fungi – and translated these into sound.
Singh said: “So all the notes that you are hearing are translations of voltage being emitted from the living thing. This is music being generated by the living system of the mushroom.
“I’m interested in this idea that all living things generate and vibrate. This is a way for us to try to tune into and connect with other living things.”
Singh said he did get some odd looks from passersby when he was out in the woods collaborating with fungi. “But it’s magical being in a space recording mushrooms.”
Visitors to the exhibition will also be able to see watercolour studies by Beatrix Potter loaned by the Victoria and Albert Museum. Her work was overlooked in her lifetime but is recognised by modern mycologists.
Near them is a recent work called In Balance by the artist Jo Pearl based on a fungus called Potteromyces asteroxylicola, named after Potter in 2023 when it was identified in the collections of the Natural History Museum.
Another new piece is by Gemma Anderson-Tempini, who worked with scientists from the University of Exeter’s MRC Centre for Medical Mycology to create a map of her own mycobiome, the fungi dwelling within the human body.
Like Singh, Anderson-Tempini ventured out into the Devon landscape to gather material for her piece, Myco-Mother, 2026.
She collected pieces of red sandstone from Exmouth and chocolate-brown soil from Killerton, which she ground up to create the watercolours she used.
Anderson-Tempini believes her work is a first. “Every one of us is carrying a fungal ecology and until now nobody had drawn it,” she said. “Fungi is fashionable but Sheldrake and the rest stayed outside the body in forests and soil. This work turns it inward.”
- 
  Living Labyrinths opens on 3 October and runs until 21 February.

Living with disability in Denmark: “If we go anywhere, we have to plan everything,” says international mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Before Lyndsay takes her son Bjørn out, she has to find out where he can be changed. A bathroom marked accessible is no guarantee.
Bjørn is 22 and has cerebral palsy. He cannot move himself from his wheelchair onto a toilet or changing table. He also has scoliosis and osteoporosis, making an unsafe transfer especially risky. Lyndsay and her husband have changed him on public bathroom floors, in the back of a car and on a park bench, with her husband holding up a towel for privacy.
“When we take my son anywhere, we have to plan everything,” she said explaining:
“I have to pre-plan wherever we’re going: is there a toilet, or is there at least a toilet with a bench that we can change him on?”
For Lyndsay, who has lived in Denmark for 18 years, this is one measure of what it means to live here with a disability in the family.
Bjørn lives in a residence for people with disabilities, and Lyndsay said his care workers cannot take him out unless they have somewhere to move and change him safely.
When “accessible” is not enough
Denmark’s building regulations set out requirements for publicly accessible toilets, including level access, room for a wheelchair to manoeuvre and support rails. They do not require the ceiling lift and adult changing table Bjørn needs.
“You can’t call it an accessible bathroom because accessibility is for everybody,” Lyndsay said. She runs Changing Places Denmark, a nonprofit pressing for bathrooms with a ceiling lift, a height-adjustable adult changing table and enough space for a large wheelchair and a carer.
“They might have a changing table but they have no lift, and that does not work for somebody like my son,” she said.
“How does he get onto the table?”
Lyndsay first encountered a Changing Places bathroom while visiting a friend in the UK. When her friend said they needed to change her daughter during a supermarket trip, Lyndsay assumed they would use the floor.
Instead, they went into a room with the equipment they needed. “I was amazed by this bathroom,” she said.
“Everything was there that you would have at your home of somebody with a disability.”
She brought the idea back to Denmark. At the time of the interview, she said her organisation had certified six bathrooms and was checking others against its standards.
She hopes such facilities will eventually become “a norm rather than an exception”.
Lyndsay believes building rules are central to making that happen. She recalled contacting someone involved in a new restaurant building. He told her it would have an accessible bathroom, but it would not have the equipment she described. In her view, a builder can meet the rules while still leaving people like Bjørn without a usable facility.
The consequences can reach into working life, too. Lyndsay described another wheelchair user who, she said, had turned down a job opportunity because the workplace lacked suitable toilet facilities.
Finding help when you’re new to Denmark
For an international family, the first challenge may be knowing whom to ask. Denmark’s municipalities assess disability support case by case, including help with equipment and daily care. Lyndsay advises newcomers to tell the municipality about a disability when they register and speak with a sagsbehandler – a caseworker – about their needs.
“It’s been really challenging to sort of navigate the system here as an international,” she said.
Her husband is Danish, but he had never used disability services before their family needed them. “He was kind of going through the process with me for the first time too.”
Lyndsay recommends arriving at meetings with a clear account of what the person needs in daily life: what they can do independently, what equipment or assistance is missing, and what happens without it. When she sought a different residence for Bjørn, she sent his caseworker eight pages covering his medical needs and the experiences she wanted him to have, including outings.
She also encourages families to join parent groups, even if they need translation tools to follow discussions in Danish. Other parents helped her learn what questions to ask and which rules might apply.
“When I first came, I was like, what are these paragraph laws?” she said. Her advice is to check any suggested rule before relying on it in an application.
If a family disagrees with a decision, they can ask how to appeal and pay attention to the deadline stated in the decision. Denmark’s independent disability advice service, DUKH, offers free guidance on disability cases and can help people understand where to direct a complaint.
For Lyndsay, finding support has also meant finding community. Danish parents and disability organisations, she said, have welcomed her and switched to English when she could not find the right Danish words. “Whether you can speak English or Danish, you’re in the same boat because you have a child with a disability,” she said. “We’re just all trying to fight for the same thing.”
Is Denmark making progress?
There are signs of action, though Lyndsay thinks change is too slow. The UN disability rights committee welcomed a Danish parliamentary framework agreement on disability in 2024. In the same review, it raised concerns about uneven disability support across municipalities and barriers to accessibility in buildings, transport and services.
Lyndsay described how Antoniett, a wheelchair user who needs a lift to use a toilet, appeared before three politicians on the Danish television show “Signe Moldes Roadshow”.
According to Lyndsay, Antoniett explained that she had been unable to take a job because the workplace lacked suitable toilet facilities. The politicians expressed concern, but Lyndsay was struck by comments after Antoniett spoke publicly about the issue.
One person suggested she wear a nappy; another replied by asking how she would change it. Others suggested using a care home’s bathroom.
Lyndsay sees growing attention to disability and is working with groups in Norway and Sweden on bathroom standards. Her Danish organisation has three volunteers working alongside her but, she said, no funding yet. She believes people want conditions to improve, while questioning whether those with the power to change them understand what is missing.
That is why she asks people to look closely at the next accessible bathroom they see. A wheelchair may fit through the door. There may be rails beside the toilet. For Bjørn, the decisive question is still how he can get out of his chair.

Freedom and Architecture: Anneke Abhelakh on "The Albanian Files"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

For the past twenty years, Albania has been one of the most active construction territories in Europe. Dozens of international architects have been working there on projects that promise to alter the drawing, the structure, and the cities of a country still recovering from the regimes of the last century. To acknowledge that growth, and those changes in the landscape, is also to acknowledge that behind every form there is a story, and that there are files that tell us more than architecture itself.
Edited by Anneke Abhelakh and published by Lars Müller Publishers, with a foreword by Prime Minister Edi Rama, The Albanian Files has compiled two decades of work of sixty international architecture offices working in Albania into a dense publication whose format, color, and sheer presence amount to a statement in the reading of the country's recent history. The publication works as an extended document, a cartography of what these processes left behind. Much of what takes shape across its pages describes structures of power, patterns of commissioning, and positions whose consequences have proved controversial. Revealing is a sign of transparency, but it is also a sign that some things should never have been hidden in the first place. Albania, more than ever, with its aspirations to open a territory and its growing wish to engage with the world (through tourism and the prospect of EU membership), needs this clarity.

Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:58:33 UTC
12:58:33 KST

Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
- Date:
- September 29, 2026
- Source:
- Florida Atlantic University
- Summary:
- Wild blacktip sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from nearly 250 feet away, according to experiments conducted off the Florida coast. The sharks not only heard the sounds but sharply changed direction away from them, suggesting they could pinpoint where they were coming from.
- Share:
The ocean is filled with sound, and for sharks, those sounds can reveal what is happening well beyond their field of view. Noise produced by prey, predators, and other animals may provide important information about the surrounding environment. Yet scientists have had little direct evidence showing just how far a shark swimming freely in the ocean can hear, or whether it can tell where a distant sound originated.
A new study from Florida Atlantic University is beginning to answer those questions. Researchers studying blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) used an underwater speaker, a drone, and wild sharks swimming naturally in coastal waters. They found that the animals could detect sounds from substantial distances and abruptly turn away from the source, even when it was nearly 250 feet away.
The findings, published in Integrative Organismal Biology, provide the first quantified evidence that free swimming sharks can detect and orient away from sounds in the acoustic far field. The results offer a rare look at a basic shark sense that remains surprisingly poorly understood.
Testing Shark Hearing in the Wild
Blacktip sharks were especially well suited for the experiment because they gather predictably off Southeast Florida. Large numbers congregate along the Palm Beach County coast each winter, while smaller groups can be found there throughout the year. Clear, shallow water also allowed researchers to monitor individual sharks from above while minimizing interference with their natural behavior.
"Their abundance and accessibility made it possible for us to observe them from above without disturbing their natural behavior, while also presenting controlled underwater sounds," said Stephen Kajiura, Ph.D., senior author and a professor of biological sciences in FAU's Charles E. Schmidt College of Science.
Researchers carried out the tests in shallow coastal waters across Palm Beach County. After anchoring a boat, they placed an underwater speaker in the water and allowed it to drift with the current as far as 19 meters from the vessel. This setup helped reduce the possibility that the boat itself would influence the sharks.
The team played three groups of low-frequency sounds, covering 100 to 200 Hertz, 200 to 400 Hertz, and 400 to 800 Hertz. They also used a 10 kiloHertz control sound, which lies beyond the known hearing range of sharks. Rather than attempting to lure the animals toward the speaker, the researchers played the sounds loudly enough to provoke a startle response.
Sharks Responded From 243 Feet Away
Calibrated hydrophones allowed the researchers to measure sound levels at different locations, making it possible to determine what each shark was hearing at the moment it reacted. Meanwhile, a drone flying 40 to 50 meters above the water recorded the movements of free swimming sharks during both the experimental and control sounds.
The researchers then analyzed the footage frame by frame to determine how far each shark was from the speaker and how sharply its swimming direction changed.
The sharks reacted to all three low frequency sound ranges but showed no response to the 10 kiloHertz control. They detected low frequency sounds from distances of up to 74 meters (243 feet), substantially farther than had previously been demonstrated in freely swimming sharks.
Just as importantly, the animals often made rapid turns away from the speaker. That behavior indicates that they were not simply detecting the presence of a sound. They could also determine the direction from which it was coming.
More than 70% of the recorded responses occurred in the acoustic far field. The sharks were also most sensitive to lower frequency sounds, which they detected from greater distances and at lower sound levels.
"What makes this finding particularly interesting is that the sharks were responding to sounds beyond the acoustic near field, where the sound behaves differently than it does close to the source," Kajiura said. "This suggests that they are detecting the particle motion associated with sound even at considerable distances from the source -- something we have not previously been able to demonstrate in free-swimming sharks."
How Sharks Hear Without a Swim Bladder
The result is especially notable because sharks lack the gas filled swim bladder found in many bony fish. In those fish, the organ can contribute to the detection of sound pressure.
Sharks are instead believed to depend largely on their inner ears. These include a specialized sensory structure known as the macula neglecta, which may help them detect motion and vibrations generated as sound travels through water.
The research also demonstrates why studying shark hearing in the ocean can reveal information that is difficult to obtain in laboratory tanks. Inside a tank, sound can reflect repeatedly from the walls, producing complicated acoustic patterns that may make an animal's response harder to interpret.
"Trying to do hearing experiments in a tank results in the sound bouncing off the walls which causes complex and confusing signals -- it is like being in a house of mirrors. This is why it is so important to do these types of experiments in the ocean with wild sharks to get a natural response," said Caroline Sullivan, lead author who conducted this work as part of her master's degree in biological sciences.
Study co-author is Edmund Gerstein, Ph.D., a research director, Charles E. Schmidt College of Science.
A Hidden Sensory World in the Ocean
The findings suggest that sound may provide sharks with useful information about events occurring hundreds of feet away, long before those animals or objects enter view. Researchers now want to understand more precisely how the shark sensory system detects and processes these distant acoustic signals.
"The ocean is an acoustic environment, and sharks are clearly tuned into it in ways we are only beginning to understand," Kajiura said. "Being able to detect and respond to sounds from hundreds of feet away gives these predators an important source of information about their surroundings. The next question is how their sensory system allows them to pick up and interpret these distant sounds."
The work was supported by the Colgan Foundation, awarded to Kajiura, and the National Save the Sea Turtle Foundation, awarded to Sullivan.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Florida Atlantic University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- C L Sullivan, E R Gerstein, S M Kajiura. Orientation of Blacktip Sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) to Underwater Sound. Integrative Organismal Biology, 2026; 8 (1) DOI: 10.1093/iob/obag033

Spain’s rejection of Russian LNG to boost production costs in other industries — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:58:01 UTC
12:58:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Spain’s abandonment of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) could lead to higher fuel prices and increased production costs in a number of energy-intensive industries, like the chemical industry, metallurgy, and fertilizer production, political analyst Ilya Grashchenkov told TASS.
Earlier, Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said that Madrid intends to comply with the EU restrictions on the supply of Russian LNG despite the existing long-term contracts of Spanish companies. This January the EU Council approved a phased ban on imports of Russian gas. For LNG supplies under long-term contracts, the ban should come into effect from next year.
"The main risk is related precisely to the price. Higher gas prices will affect electricity and production costs. The most vulnerable sectors are the chemical industry, metallurgy, and the production of fertilizers, ceramics, glass, cement, and paper. The scale of costs will depend on the situation in the global LNG market," Grashchenkov said.
According to him, Spain will most likely be able to avoid a direct gas shortage. "Spain is technically ready to replace Russian LNG. It has a well-developed network of terminals, supplies from Algeria, and the ability to increase purchases from the United States, Nigeria, and other countries. This is why the risk of a shortage is low, but gas may become more expensive, especially during a cold winter," the expert noted.
Grashchenkov also drew attention to the possible legal consequences of the cessation of supplies.
"The EU ban gives Spanish companies grounds to claim force majeure, but it does not automatically cancel contracts. This is why the likelihood of compensation claims and lengthy arbitration disputes remains, especially regarding an agreement between Naturgy and Yamal LNG, he explained.
According to the political analyst, Spain’s well·developed LNG infrastructure will not allow it to fully take on the role of the main gas supply channel to other EU countries.
"Spain is capable of receiving large LNG volumes, but its capacity to transfer gas to France and further to Europe is limited. This is why it may become a regional hub, but not the EU’s main gas gateway. At the same time, Europe’s dependence on American LNG will indeed increase," Grashchenkov concluded.

Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violent
Unknown

Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violent
Tens of thousands of workers march nationwide, as police arrest 440 students in clashes at schools.
Tens of thousands of civil servants, including teachers, firefighters and healthcare workers, have marched in cities across France to demand higher pay, as students clashed with the police in separate protests over conditions at their schools.
Unions said some 300,000 people took part in the one-day strike action nationwide, while police on Tuesday estimated a turnout of 30,000 in the capital, Paris. The workers also demanded better working conditions and expressed anger at the government’s planned budget cuts.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Photos: Pope Leo draws hundreds of thousands for open-air Mass in Paris
- list 2 of 3France’s far-right National Rally gains ground in Senate vote
- list 3 of 3Photos: French students protest, public workers strike before budget cuts
Protests also took place at more than 400 schools, about 40 of which were blockaded and 44 of which faced attempted blockades.
Ten people, both students and staff members, were wounded, and at least 440 were detained, officials said.
The strikes and the student unrest came two days before the government is to unveil its draft budget and seven months before the presidential election. According to unions, the government proposes freezing base salaries for state employees in 2027 to save 2 billion euros ($2.3bn).
It would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze and the eighth during President Emmanuel Macron’s tenure. Unions say the freezes have cost workers a double-digit share of their purchasing power, and they are demanding a 6 percent raise.
‘Red alert’
Sophie Binet, general secretary of the General Confederation of Labor, called the protests “a red alert”.
“This anger is not going away. The government must look again at the budget,” she told Al Jazeera. She gave the government 48 hours to reverse the planned cuts before her union decides on further strike action.
The Education Ministry said just more than 11 percent of teachers and other school staff went on strike. French teachers are paid less on average than their counterparts in other European countries.
Fewer than 1 in 10 other civil servants took part, and fewer still in hospitals, with the loss of a day’s pay a likely factor in the turnout. France’s civil aviation regulator had warned of flight disruptions at some airports.
Professional firefighters, who say this summer’s huge wildfires exposed a lack of resources, were among those marching.
The government has already unveiled measures to help households cope with a spike in energy prices driven by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran, but it has failed to quell the discontent with Macron and his administration.
Student unrest
Students, meanwhile, have been protesting outside hundreds of schools over timetables, class sizes, teacher shortages and overheated classrooms during this year’s heatwaves. The demonstrations began in the Ile-de-France region around Paris and spread to other cities.
In addition to the 10 students and staff members who were hurt, 48 law enforcement officials were injured, authorities said, as students in some places set fire to rubbish bins and hurled projectiles, and officers responded with batons and tear gas.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told BFMTV that 440 people had been detained.
“We don’t have the final tally yet, but I’m told two thirds led to police custody,” he said. “Violence is never legitimate. There is nothing that justifies violence.”
Education Minister Edouard Geffray condemned the clashes on social media.
“This violence is unspeakable,” he wrote, adding that legal proceedings had begun. “To legitimize it or… call for an expansion of the blockades is to endanger both our students and public officials. It is irresponsible.”
‘Fewer cops, more money’
In Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income suburb of Paris, Bally Bagayoko, the district’s mayor and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed party, joined hundreds of students protesting at the Lycee Paul-Eluard.
He led them in singing the national anthem and called the protests “completely legitimate”, saying poorer areas received fewer resources than wealthier ones.
Outside the Arago school in Paris, students, some with their faces covered, sat on dumpsters to block the entrance beneath a placard reading “Macron explosion”. A banner at the Helene-Boucher school read “Fewer cops, more money”.
“We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally,” said Mael Breton, a final-year student there. “This is a real problem, especially when there is such a lack of funding… here at our school and in the national education system more broadly.”
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Monday condemned the high school protests as irresponsible but acknowledged that the “difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed”.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, a hard-left presidential contender, accused the government of steadily dismantling public services as he addressed protesters in Paris and urged his supporters to mobilise against the draft budget.
A Toluna Harris poll on Monday suggested that Melenchon and Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally, would advance to next year’s presidential run-off, with Le Pen best placed to win.

ChatGPT maker wants to be the App Store for AI as safety concerns grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:50:00 UTC
