What we know about the Cornell rape investigation
NEW YORK – Prosecutors have reopened an investigation into a 2024 report by a Cornell University student who said she was raped at a fraternity house, raising questions about how the case was initially handled by law enforcement officials and the school.
Her allegations surfaced again two weeks ago after the student, identified in a lawsuit as Jane Doe, sued seven men, the university, her sorority and the fraternity.
The case has led to fierce debate across the internet and drawn attention to the persistent problem of sexual assault on college campuses.
The district attorney for Tompkins County, home to Cornell in Ithaca, New York, said he would consider presenting the case to a grand jury. In 2024, immediately after her report, he declined to do so.
Here is what we know about the Cornell case.
What do we know about Jane Doe?
Because she is anonymous in the lawsuit, most of the details about her life are unknown.
Her lawyer has said she is from a small town about 1,610km away from Cornell.
She arrived at the university as an undergraduate in August 2022, then dropped out after she said she was raped in 2024.
She was 20 years old at the time and had been a member of the Tri-Delta sorority.
Her lawyer said she is struggling with the aftermath of the incident and is not in college.
What does the lawsuit say happened?
On Oct 19, 2024, according to the lawsuit, the woman was raped repeatedly over nearly seven hours at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca.
The lawsuit states that she started her night drinking vodka at the sorority house.
Around 8.30pm, she took an Uber to an event her sorority was hosting at a bar.
Although the bouncer correctly identified her as underage, she claims she was served at least one alcoholic beverage.
By about 11pm, she had decided to walk about a mile to Chi Phi’s fraternity house to see a man she considered a friend.
Once she arrived, according to the lawsuit, the man and his fraternity brothers gave her a beer, marijuana, rum and ketamine.
In the lawsuit, she claims she had not tried ketamine before and was pressured into snorting it.
The lawsuit then details a series of sexual assaults and continued drug use involving her friend and six other men.
At about 1.42am, one of the men sent a message to the Chi Phi Snapchat group inviting others to join in, using a crude term for female genitalia, according to a screenshot included in the lawsuit.
How did the police respond?
With the encouragement of friends, Jane Doe reported the incident to Cornell’s police department on Nov 8, 2024.
The Cornell police sent a crime alert to campus, stating that a victim had reported being “sexually assaulted by several males” and “coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs” at a fraternity house.
In a message to campus before that Thanksgiving, Cornell’s president said that the university police department was continuing its criminal investigation, and that a second, administrative investigation into the allegations was under way.
Some time that month, the Cornell police asked the Tompkins County district attorney’s office to review a statement from Jane Doe.
Criminal investigators advised the police that they did not think they could bring criminal charges under New York state law based on the statement.
Jane Doe’s lawyer said that after she gave her initial statement, no police or criminal investigators contacted her again.
It is unclear whether the police interviewed the men involved, or whether Jane Doe was told that her criminal case was not being pursued.
On Sept 28, the district attorney – who has released only excerpts from Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement – said that the statement did not make clear that she was forced into the sexual acts or that she was incapacitated, though she was under the influence of drugs and alcohol.
How did Cornell respond?
The university immediately placed the fraternity, and the seven men she named in the lawsuit, on interim suspensions, the suit said.
Meanwhile, Cornell’s administrative Title IX justice process swung into motion to determine any potential discipline for the accused men.
In May 2025, at least 12 hearings were held before a panel of faculty and staff, according to the woman’s lawsuit.
The accused men “were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”, according to the lawsuit.
Cornell does not deny that essays – which it calls reflection papers – were part of the punishment that the panel decided on for some of the men.
But it stated on Sept 28 that it was not the only consequence for any of them.
Cornell, citing student privacy rules, declined to give details about how the individual men were punished.
It said on Sept 28 that it gave the men “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions”.
Thomas Giuffra, the lawyer who represents Jane Doe, has said in interviews that only two of the men were expelled, and that his client did not feel justice had been done.
What has been the fallout from the lawsuit?
Millions of people have viewed the lawsuit or heard influencers and celebrities discuss the allegations online, bringing attention to the ongoing problem of sexual assault at Cornell and other college campuses.
The mayor of Ithaca said on Sept 28 that he is proposing a ban on permits for Cornell events until the university reforms its sexual assault policies.
The pressure and attention pushed the Tompkins County district attorney to reopen the criminal case.
A criminal investigator has reached out to Jane Doe’s lawyer, meaning that there could still be criminal charges in the case.
Governor Kathy Hochul has called for an independent investigation of Cornell’s handling of the case.
The names and photographs of the seven accused men are widely circulating online, as part of a mass movement that some see as a grassroots effort to bring accountability, and others view as a form of harassment of men not yet charged with any crime. NYTIMES

Heatwaves, wildfires expose a third of world to extreme ozone pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:31:15 UTC
11:31:15 KST

Heatwaves, wildfires expose a third of world to extreme ozone pollution
Heatwaves and wildfires helped expose 34 percent of the world’s population to “extremely poor” ozone air quality in the first eight months of 2026, according to a European Union report published Wednesday. Asia recorded the highest exposure, while ozone pollution remained difficult to curb despite decades of progress in reducing other harmful emissions.
Heatwaves and wildfires combined with human-caused emissions this year to expose one third of the world's population to extremely high levels of ozone pollution, a European Union report said on Wednesday.
In a new analysis covering the first eight months of 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) highlighted the close relationship between climate change and air pollution.
When heat and sunlight react with airborne emissions from wildfires, vehicles and industry, they create ground-level ozone pollution, which can damage lung tissue, cause breathing problems, trigger asthma attacks and lead to other health issues.
Despite progress in cutting the most harmful air pollutants in recent decades, ozone has proved more difficult to tackle as climate change fuels the conditions that favour its formation.
Read moreFrance puts out massive fire that torched 42,000 hectares and smouldered for 69 days
This year's ozone pollution was driven in part by record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires that seared Europe and North America and sent smoke well beyond their borders.
Indonesia has experienced major wildfires, while the warming El Nino weather pattern, which started in June and is due to peak later this year, could drive more fires in southeast Asia, according to the analysis.
"Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source," CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report.
'Extremely poor' air
CAMS uses satellite data and computer models to track air pollution and wildfires.
The report found that 34 percent of the global population was exposed to "extremely poor" air quality between January 1 and September 15, meaning concentrations of ozone were well above the World Health Organization's exposure guidance.
The WHO's guideline sets 100 micrograms of ozone per cubic metre as the maximum recommended level of exposure, averaged over eight hours.
Read moreWildfires, heatwaves threaten global air quality and health, UN warns
Another 17 percent of the world breathed "very poor" air, while five percent was exposed to "good" levels of ozone.
Asia has the highest rate of exposure to ozone pollution, with 53 percent of its population breathing "extremely poor" air. Another 22 percent was exposed to "very poor" ozone.
The continent's widespread emissions are driven by industrialisation, economic development and transport, as well as wildfires and the burning of agricultural residue.
New Delhi, Dhaka, Chinese megalopolis Chongqing and Pakistan's Lahore were among cities whose ozone levels were "extremely poor".
Two thirds of the population in North America and 45 percent in Europe were exposed to "poor" or "very poor" air quality.
EU regulation has been effective in reducing emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone, the report said.
Read moreFrance recorded 'hottest summer ever' in 2026, environment minister says
Ozone pollution is linked to 60,000 premature deaths per year in Europe, Ian Marnane, an official at the European Environment Agency, told a media briefing.
Ozone levels in North America also remained "relatively unchanged" despite ambitious emissions reduction policies, the report said.
Smoke from forest fires, crop burning and cooking are significant contributors to Africa's air pollution while Saharan dust travels as far as Europe.
Eight percent of Africa's population endured "extremely poor" air quality this year. It was "very poor" or "poor" for 19 percent of the continent.
Ozone levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro but the air quality was "good" or "fair" for 81 percent of South America's population.
One bright spot was Oceania, including Australia and New Zealand, where 66 percent of the population enjoyed "good" ozone levels and 34 percent lived under "fair" conditions.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Another 22% was exposed to “very poor” ozone.
The continent’s widespread emissions are driven by industrialisation, economic development and transport, as well as wildfires and the burning of agricultural residue.
New Delhi, Dhaka, Chinese megalopolis Chongqing and Pakistan’s Lahore were among cities whose ozone levels were “extremely poor”.
Two thirds of the population in North America and 45% in Europe were exposed to “poor” or “very poor” air quality.
EU regulation has been effective in reducing emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone, the report said.
Ozone pollution is linked to 60,000 premature deaths per year in Europe, Ian Marnane, an official at the European Environment Agency, told a media briefing.
Ozone levels in North America also remained “relatively unchanged” despite ambitious emissions reduction policies, the report said.
Smoke from forest fires, crop burning and cooking are significant contributors to Africa’s air pollution while Saharan dust travels as far as Europe.
In Africa, 8% of the population endured “extremely poor” air quality in 2026. It was “very poor” or “poor” for 19% of the continent.
Ozone levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro, but the air quality was “good” or “fair” for 81% of South America’s population.
One bright spot was Oceania, including Australia and New Zealand, where 66% of the population enjoyed “good” ozone levels and 34% lived under “fair” conditions. AFP

US imposes sanctions against Russian companies tied to Iran weapons procurement

The measures target 13 individuals and entities in Russia, Hong Kong, China, and Pakistan as the United States continues to exert economic pressure on Tehran under "Operation Economic Outcast" amid its months-long war with Iran.

Tehran and Moscow have increasingly strengthened relations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

US Senate blocks resolution seeking report on Americans killed in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:26:20 UTC

US Senate blocks resolution seeking report on Americans killed in West Bank
The resolution cites a ‘lack of accountability’ by Israel’s government and an ‘inability to secure justice’ by the US.
The United States Senate has blocked a resolution that would have required President Donald Trump’s administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.
The resolution failed 47-53 on Tuesday, with senators voting largely along party lines.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK pledges tougher stance on Israeli actions in Gaza, West Bank
- list 2 of 4Morocco’s pro-Palestine protests challenge Rabat’s deepening Israel ties
- list 3 of 4Palestine weekly: Israeli politicians vie to look toughest before election
- list 4 of 4Azeez Al-Shaair continues to honour slain Palestinians despite sanctions
It was brought to the floor by Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, and cited a “lack of accountability” from the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an “inability to secure justice” from the US government.
Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the only Democrat to vote against advancing the resolution, while Senator Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, joined Democrats in supporting it.
Van Hollen forced the vote under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, which allows individual members of Congress to demand a formal State Department report on the human rights practices of any country that receives US security assistance.
In a social media post after the vote, Van Hollen pledged to continue to press for justice.
“Tonight, 47 Senators supported my resolution to get accountability for the 9 Americans killed on the West Bank & for Palestinians who face injustices daily. That’s more support than we’ve ever had in this fight,” he wrote on X.
“Republicans blocked us, but we won’t stop until we get justice.”
Nine Americans killed
The resolution called for an unclassified report within 30 days of adoption. It would have detailed investigations into the deaths of the Americans, the treatment of US citizens held in Israeli prisons, and the conditions facing Palestinian children in Israeli military detention.
The measure cited the deaths of nine American citizens in the occupied West Bank since January 2022, including Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American journalist and Al Jazeera correspondent who was shot in the head and killed in May 2022 while reporting in the city of Jenin.
It also included Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, who was shot in the head and killed by an Israeli soldier in September 2024, and Sayfollah Kamel Musallet, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025.
The others were Amer Mohammad Saada Rabee, who was 14; Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohamed Ahmad Alkhdour, both 17; Omar Assad; Khamid Ayyad; Nasrallah Abu Siyam; and Khamis Rabee Jabara.
The resolution also noted the arrests of several Palestinian-American children by Israeli forces.
Among them was Mohammed Ibrahim, a 16-year-old from Florida, who was arrested in February 2025 and held in pretrial detention for nine months without contact with his family. It noted that US embassy officials and lawyers who met him told his family that he had lost nearly a quarter of his body weight, contracted scabies, and was beaten and tortured.
Other Palestinian Americans who remain in custody include Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah, 16, and Sama Safi, 20, a student detained in June in raids targeting students at Birzeit University.
The resolution cited rights groups that have documented the deaths of at least 44 Palestinians in Israeli military camps since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Those groups, it said, have documented widespread abuses, including beatings, sexual violence, harassment and threats, “pointing to systemic and deliberate mistreatment”.
It also went on to note a sharp escalation in Israeli settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, and stressed that there have been no convictions for the killings of Palestinian civilians by Israeli settlers since 2020.

Why Nirvana and Midnight Oil made the cut in Songs that Changed the World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:25:40 UTC
11:25:40 KST

Why Nirvana and Midnight Oil made the cut in Songs that Changed the World
In the new book Songs that Changed the World, author Andrew Clarke was aiming for a top 40, but couldn't do away with any two songs.
Here he tells the ABC's pop culture journalist why some songs made the list and others didn't.
You start the book with Strange Fruit. I want to talk about artists paying a personal price for their songs that change the world. You write in the book about Billie Holiday's final moments as well as some of what she went through in life. Tell me about that.
She did become public enemy number one. I mean, a Black woman singing about lynching in the United States was very confrontational, but she was a huge star and she had the power to do it. But the FBI and all the entities didn't really like that. So, she spent a lot of time being interviewed by police.
And you wrote that she didn't receive the medical treatment that she was due when dying in hospital.
Absolutely … the evidence is there to say that she could have got lots of things to help her, but no-one was willing to do that for her, and a lot of it was the pressure from the FBI.
It's pretty obvious why this particular song is on the list, but can you tell me what's going on in this song and why it's so powerful?
It is [written by] Abel Meeropol, who [was] a Jewish poet in New York City, and he saw a photograph of lynchings in Indiana, and he was so taken by that that he wrote this poem, which was later turned into the song Strange Fruit … the fruit is actually the Black people swinging in the trees as they're being lynched and the visual imagery of it is quite confronting.
When you go from that to something like Smells Like Teen Spirit, it seems like quite the jump. Why do both songs belong side by side in this book and tell me why the Nirvana classic made it in there?
I think the beauty of this is that the 42 songs tell different stories in most cases. Smells Like Teen Spirit is really about a disaffected youth finding a voice and finding some power, and maybe just understanding that they are a bit cranky at times … and that's the teen spirit because "you might think I'm just a stoner or lazy, but that's just the way we are and you guys need to understand it because we've got the power".
Would you describe this as a song that doesn't really have political messaging but still has an impact socially?
Oh, absolutely. And there's a couple of songs in this book like that that weren't designed to be political but the message in it was so strong and connected so strongly. Smells Like Teen Spirit [is a] song that connected to a generation in many ways. People I know who don't like that style of music still love that song. And … it gave people [the] feeling that it's OK to feel disaffected. But let's just get people to understand that we can still be productive, useful, and loved.
It appears in a lot of different places in pop culture. I hear the riff every day when I tune into The Breakfast Club — a radio show out of New York on a station that plays mostly hip hop and R&B — but I did go back and listen to the song after reading that part in your book because you mentioned that the lyrics, a lot of them don't even really make sense, and you're absolutely right.
It's pure genius when you think about it. It's just that great abstract way of thinking that older people didn't understand at the time.
Let's jump on to Beds are Burning. Tell me about this song and its impact, as well as the impact of Midnight Oil.
It's an interesting one because Midnight Oil had always been political to a degree, but this ramped it up. It's written specifically around the dispossession of the Pintupi people and it was the first time, I think, in Australia that anybody had really in a public way spoken about Aboriginal land rights, so something that we'd buried and hidden and didn't even want to talk about suddenly became something that we were singing along with … so it really brought that way of thinking into the mainstream.
There's something about having a catchy tune you're singing along to, but then it has this potent message.
It is good, isn't it? That's where some of these songs in the book, not just this one, hook you in without you knowing. You get entrapped by the music or entrapped by the melody, and then underneath it all are these great lyrics that are telling you a story and trying to ask you to think. And subconsciously, whether you like it or not, if you like the sound of that song, you are going to start to take in the lyrics in a way that you don't even understand.
It did make me wonder though why a song like Treaty by Yothu Yindi didn't make the list. Are there songs, Australian songs, that could have made the list but just missed out?
Oh, absolutely. Treaty is one of them, clearly. There's I was Only 19 by Redgum, Khe Sanh by Cold Chisel — they were all on the list that we considered. And hopefully we get to a point where we do a second book and they'll be in there.

The US Senate has rejected a discharge motion to bring forward a resolution introduced by Senator Chris Van Hollen concerning human rights practices in Israel and the occupied West Bank from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
The motion to discharge Senate Resolution 852 failed to attain the necessary majority, with 47 senators voting in favour and 51 opposing it.
Cross-party voting emerged during the ballot, with Democratic Senator John Fetterman voting against the motion, whilst Republican Senator Rand Paul voted in favour.
Republican Senators Bill Cassidy and Dan Sullivan did not cast votes.
The measure, titled the "Israel Human Rights Practices" resolution, directs the State Department to furnish Congress with detailed reporting on human rights conditions throughout the occupied West Bank, specifically regarding the circumstances surrounding the deaths and detention of American citizens.
Accountability demands for American deaths
Addressing the floor prior to the roll call, Van Hollen appealed directly to his colleagues to allow the resolution to advance to a full debate.
"I rise today to call up Resolution 852, a resolution to require the State Department to provide Congress with information on the growing violence and human rights abuses taking place in the West Bank, including against American citizens," he said.
Van Hollen pointed out that nine US citizens have been killed in the occupied West Bank over a four-year period by violent illegal Israeli settlers or members of the Israeli security forces.
"The United States government has repeatedly said that our number one priority overseas is to protect American citizens. And yet, as violent Israeli settlers continue to terrorise civilians in the West Bank, American citizens have been killed time and again, in many cases with the complicity of the government of Israel, the Netanyahu government," he said.
The senator challenged whether American authorities have demonstrated sufficient political will to pursue justice for citizens harmed in the occupied territory.
"How many more Americans must die in the West Bank before this administration takes serious, credible steps to secure accountability?" he asked.

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Atlanta has been confirmed as the first stop of the LA28 Olympic torch relay in the United States, with the flame set to travel across all 50 U.S. states before arriving in Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympic Games, organizers announced on Tuesday.
The relay will begin with the traditional lighting of the Olympic flame in Ancient Olympia, Greece, followed by a short relay across the country. The flame will then be handed over at the historic Panathenaic Stadium in Athens before beginning its journey across the United States.
Atlanta, host of the 1996 Olympic Games, was chosen as the first U.S. stop, linking the legacy of the last Summer Olympics held in the United States with LA28.
"Every Olympic Games begin with a single flame, and transporting that flame to Los Angeles is an honor and privilege that we'll share with every corner of the country, as Americans in all 50 states carry the flame on its path to our opening ceremony," said LA28 Chairperson and President Casey Wasserman.
After departing Atlanta, the flame will pass landmarks and visit major cultural and sporting events, with select cities set to host special celebrations along the way.
Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens welcomed the flame's return to the city.
"Thirty years ago, Atlanta welcomed the world. The 1996 Centennial Olympic Games changed this city," Dickens said. "When the flame returns to the U.S., Atlanta will be ready. Ready to welcome it from Greece. Ready to celebrate the spirit of the Games together as a community. And ready to send it forward toward Los Angeles and the next chapter of America's Olympic story."
Organizers said the complete route will be revealed in 2027, with the relay scheduled to begin in spring 2028 and conclude at the LA28 opening ceremony. ■

S. Korea's production, consumption, investment fall in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:21:29 CST
11:21:29 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's industrial production, private consumption and facility investment all fell last month, marking the first "triple decrease" in three months amid production disruptions in the automotive sector, statistical ministry data showed Wednesday.
The seasonally-adjusted index of all industry production, which excludes the agriculture, livestock and fishery sectors, dived 1.3 percent in August from a month earlier after sliding 0.1 percent in July, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
It recorded the steepest monthly contraction since October last year as summer vacations and partial labor strikes at some carmakers caused production disruptions in the automotive sector and subsequently dragged down related consumer spending.
Production among manufacturers tumbled 5.1 percent month-on-month in August due to a sharp fall in automotive production, which logged the fastest reduction since February 2020 with a 24.8 percent plunge.
The average capacity utilization rate in the manufacturing industry dipped 4.0 percentage points to 70.8 percent in the cited month.
Output in the construction industry rebounded 1.9 percent, but production in the public administration sector sank 2.9 percent.
Production in the services industry grew 0.5 percent in August from a month ago, turning around from a reduction of 1.4 percent in July.
The retail sales index, a key gauge of consumer spending, dwindled 1.8 percent in August, logging a second straight monthly fall after a 2.6 percent drop in July.
Sales of durable goods, such as passenger cars, retreated 4.5 percent, while non-durable goods, including food and beverages, decreased 1.6 percent in sales.
Facility investment turned negative, dropping 9.5 percent in August on a monthly basis after expanding 6.2 percent in June and 8.0 percent in July amid the semiconductor boom.
Investment in machinery, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment, swelled last month, but spending on transportation equipment plummeted 32.8 percent.
Construction completion, which measures the actual value of construction work performed, rose 1.9 percent month-on-month in August, rebounding from a slide of 1.0 percent in the previous month.
The cyclical variation factor for leading economic indicators, which gauges the outlook for future economic situations, slipped 0.1 point to 104.2 in August compared to the previous month.
The reading for coincident economic indicators, which measures the current economic condition, went up 0.5 points to 101.7 last month. ■

Nature-strip gardens boost urban biodiversity: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:21:11 CST
11:21:11 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Planting native gardens on suburban nature strips can boost urban biodiversity, with insect numbers increasing sevenfold and species numbers nearly doubling, an Australian study found.
Researchers studied the effects of planting habitat gardens on nature strips across the Merri-bek City Council in Melbourne's north in Australia to quantify the biodiversity benefits that these overlooked urban spaces can play in supporting native pollinators, according to a statement released Tuesday by the University of Melbourne.
After adding native gardens, insect abundance was seven times higher and species richness was about double that of conventional grass-covered nature strips, according to the study published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.
Insect pollinators such as bees, beetles and butterflies are vital to ecosystem functioning, yet many species are declining due to habitat loss and environmental change, said lead author Philippa Bell, a researcher at the university's School of Agriculture, Food and Ecosystem Sciences.
Bees showed the strongest response and were closely associated with the abundance and diversity of flowering plants, the researchers said, adding that butterflies and beetles also responded positively, although the effects were more variable.
Bell said nature strips, also known as road verges, were widespread across cities and offered an opportunity to create connected habitat for insect pollinators and other wildlife.
The researchers said the findings have important implications for local governments and policymakers seeking ways to improve biodiversity outcomes in urban environments. ■

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia's economy is expected to grow by 0.8 percent in 2026 and accelerate to 1.8 percent in 2027, according to the latest macroeconomic forecast released Tuesday by the Slovak Finance Ministry.
The ministry said the economy was poised to see a modest improvement despite continued external pressure, including trade tensions, the energy crisis, U.S. tariffs and declining competitiveness across the European Union.
A recovery in household consumption and exports is expected to support growth, with the gradual expansion of production at the Volvo car plant in Slovakia set to provide a significant boost.
Inflation is also projected to ease, with the annual rate dropping from 3.7 percent this year to 2.9 percent in 2027. The ministry said the continuation of an energy assistance scheme for households would also help curb price growth.
Real household incomes are expected to improve as well. Average nominal wages are forecast to rise by 4.5 percent this year, while real wages, adjusted for inflation, are expected to increase by 1.4 percent next year.
The ministry noted that the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development had lowered its forecast for eurozone growth in 2027 from 1.2 percent to 1 percent. Slovakia is therefore expected to outpace the eurozone average, with growth in France and Germany projected at 0.7 percent and 1.1 percent, respectively.
The Finance Ministry's Financial Policy Institute assessed risks to the forecast as broadly balanced. Persistently high energy prices could weigh on economic activity and strain public finances, while uncertainties related to military conflicts and trade barriers could delay the recovery in exports and weaken economic growth. ■

settle movable furniture installation forms temporary public interior in ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:10:39 UTC
11:10:39 KST

settle movable furniture installation forms temporary public interior in ireland
the installation draws on the adaptability of irish vernacular furniture.
Irish vernacular furniture informs settle public installation
settle, a temporary architectural installation designed and curated by TRESTLE, proposes a public interior for gathering and collective experience in the contemporary city. Drawing on the functionalism and adaptability of Irish vernacular furniture, the installation explores how an infrastructure of carefully considered objects can form a temporary public interior. Its components can be rearranged and reformatted for different events and gatherings, allowing the installation to adapt to different civic settings. Photographed by Willem Pab in St Luke’s crypt in Cork City, where it was presented in summer 2026, settle is set to be installed in a number of civic spaces over the coming months.
public interior by TRESTLE becomes framework for collective use
The project considers the public interior as a setting for collective experience within the modern city. Referencing Hannah Arendt’s writing on the importance of a shared ‘common world of things,’ Studio TRESTLE positions public interiors as part of this shared environment. The project responds to social structures that increasingly prioritize individual life, alongside the shift of everyday interaction toward digital spaces, by examining the role of tangible, situated rooms for public use.
settle explores a prototypical public interior through spatial order, thresholds, material character, repetition, and variation. These qualities are generated through a movable arrangement of objects and architectural gestures rather than a fixed interior. The installation can therefore be recast for different uses while maintaining a coherent spatial framework.
The project also considers reuse as a response to the climate emergency, focusing on how existing buildings can accommodate new forms of public life. Through a collection of functional, movable objects, settle creates a temporary civic interior that can be occupied, adapted, and reused across different locations.

name: settle
 designer: TRESTLE | @trestle___

award: 2026 Arts Council of Ireland Architecture Project Award

The Kaliningrad Non-Paper: Decoding Moscow’s Latest Warning to NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:10:07 UTC
11:10:07 KST

The unusually direct diplomatic clash between NATO and Moscow over the Kaliningrad exclave marks another escalation in Russia’s effort to use nuclear signaling and hybrid pressure against the Alliance.
By sending a formal “non-paper” to NATO headquarters in Brussels and warning that Russia was prepared to deploy its “entire arsenal” if Alliance members attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, Moscow appears to be drawing a deliberately threatening red line around one of its most strategically exposed territories.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska said in August that Russian nuclear rhetoric tends to intensify when Moscow faces setbacks on the battlefield or pressure on its critical infrastructure, arguing that such threats are aimed both at undermining Ukrainian resolve and weakening Western backing for Kyiv.
Nuclear saber-rattling to mask strategic vulnerability
Kaliningrad is one of Russia’s most strategically sensitive outposts.
Wedged between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea and geographically separated from mainland Russia, the exclave sits deep inside a region where NATO has substantially strengthened its military posture since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The accession of Finland and Sweden has further transformed the military geography of northern Europe, giving NATO members control of most of the Baltic coastline and increasing the strategic pressure surrounding Kaliningrad.
Latvia’s Russian Speakers Reject Putin’s ‘Russian World’ as Election Looms
For Moscow, that geography creates an obvious vulnerability. Russia has heavily militarized the exclave, but reinforcing and sustaining it in any serious confrontation with NATO would present major logistical and operational challenges.
The Kremlin’s answer is therefore increasingly asymmetric.
Its warning that Russia could deploy its “entire arsenal” appears designed to push the confrontation into the nuclear realm – raising the perceived costs of even conventional NATO activities around Kaliningrad and attempting to make routine deterrence measures politically harder for allied governments.
NATO has rejected that premise, stressing that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization remains a defensive alliance and that its exercises and deployments do not threaten Russian territory.
The Alliance has nevertheless dramatically reinforced its eastern flank since 2022, including through additional combat-ready forces, air and missile defense, surveillance and new regional defense plans. NATO says those measures are a response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and growing hostile activity against allied states.
The pivot to sub-threshold sabotage
The more important part of NATO’s response may be its linkage of Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric to Russia’s wider campaign of hybrid pressure.
As the conventional war in Ukraine continues, European governments and NATO officials say Russia has increasingly relied on sabotage, cyberattacks, electronic interference, drone incursions and other operations designed to remain below the threshold of open war with the Alliance.
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, has said Russia’s goal is to “break the will” of Ukraine’s allies, urging governments to expose and publicly attribute sabotage and destabilization operations when the evidence allows.
The Baltic region has become one of the most visible theaters for that pressure.
Commercial aviation is already contending with persistent GPS interference across the Baltic, severe enough that Finnair has modified pilot training and operational procedures to account for near-daily disruptions. The interference has intensified alongside Russia’s war against Ukraine and heightened electronic warfare activity in the region.
NATO has separately documented a broader Russian campaign involving sabotage, violence, cyber operations, electronic interference and disinformation across allied territory.
Against that backdrop, Moscow’s nuclear warning over Kaliningrad can be read as another layer of the same strategy: amplify fear at the strategic level while maintaining pressure below the threshold of conventional war.
NATO’s strategy of measured deterrence
NATO’s public acknowledgment of the Russian non-paper and its measured response suggest that the Alliance does not intend to accept Moscow’s framing.
By emphasizing that NATO is defensive and rejecting the threat of force, the Alliance is attempting to deny the Kremlin the argument that its own militarization and nuclear rhetoric are merely reactions to Western aggression.
At the same time, NATO leaders have made clear that Russian intimidation will not produce the outcome Moscow appears to want most: reduced Western support for Ukraine.
Secretary General Mark Rutte has repeatedly argued that Russian hybrid actions should trigger the opposite response, AFP reported.
“Our reaction will always be more support for Ukraine,” he said earlier this month, warning that Moscow’s attempts to create fear and division would not succeed.
Rutte returned to the same point last week, telling allies not to “fall into his trap” by allowing Russian hybrid attacks to distract attention from Ukraine. “Everything he does will lead to more support for Ukraine, not less support for Ukraine,” he said.
The danger, however, remains real.
The concentration of military forces around the Baltic, repeated airspace incidents, sabotage operations, electronic warfare and increasingly explicit nuclear rhetoric all increase the possibility of miscalculation.
Kaliningrad therefore remains one of the most dangerous pressure points in the NATO-Russia confrontation – not necessarily because either side is seeking a direct war, but because Moscow continues to use escalation itself as a political instrument.

New York governor urges review of Cornell response to assault case

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said on Sept 28 that his office reopened the case based on information in the civil suit and that he will present the matter to a criminal grand jury, which could vote to indict the individuals involved.
The plaintiff in the civil suit against Cornell, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, alleged she was “plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication”, resulting in “heinous criminal sexual acts”.

‘Hypocrisy’: US students are calling out college leaders for using AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:10:00 UTC
11:10:00 KST

‘Hypocrisy’: US students are calling out college leaders for using AI
Mark Arsenault and Alan Blinder
NEW YORK - College professors and administrators have been busting students for cheating with artificial intelligence for several years. Now, the professors and administrators are getting in trouble, too.
Dartmouth College in New Hampshire last week announced it was investigating its provost, Santiago Schnell, after the college’s student-run newspaper found that some of his published writing appeared written by AI.
Schnell, a mathematical biologist, is perhaps the most prominent in a growing cast of college professors and administrators who have been accused of using AI in a way that crosses ethical lines.
There have been instances of opinion articles, research papers and even campuswide messages to students showing traces of AI influence. He issued a statement apologising.
Administrators wring their hands, and sometime issue punishments, when students outsource writing assignments to a robot to save time or avoid the hard work of thinking.
Some students are calling out the examples of faculty doing the same thing as hypocritical.
“It just goes against all the values of our institution and the concept of academia,” Eli Moyse, a Dartmouth senior, said in an interview.
A working group at George Washington University said in a report in August that many students reported “doubts that faculty themselves are using AI ethically and transparently”.
And at Brown University in Rhode Island, a survey found that close to two-thirds of undergraduate students who responded had some worries about faculty members relying on AI to develop course lectures and other content.
At Dartmouth, Schnell’s AI use in public writing came up in an investigation in August by news site Semafor about AI-created writing appearing in the opinion pages of major publications.
That investigation said an Aug 9 commentary by Schnell in The Washington Post was written by AI. The opinion article was about AI cheating in school.
The Semafor investigation also found indications of AI writing in New York Times opinion articles.
The follow-up investigation in September by the student publication, The Dartmouth, found extensive AI use in Schnell’s published work in 2026.
Schnell told The Dartmouth in a statement that he used AI “for language refinement, copyediting, improving clarity and organisation and making writing processes more efficient”.
The newspaper then ran Schnell’s statement on his AI use through an AI detector, which flagged the statement itself as apparently written by AI.
Schnell did not respond to a request for comment.
In a note to her campus announcing the review of Schnell, Dartmouth’s president, Sian Beilock, said that being an early leader on AI was “messy”. Beilock recently called for more AI use at her university.
“There will be mis-steps,” she wrote, “and that’s part of how an institution learns”.
Dartmouth declined to comment beyond what Beilock had already written.
There should also be consequences, said Moyse, who called the AI scandal a “completely cartoonish” display of hypocrisy.
“He should resign immediately or get fired,” he said of Schnell. “Passing something off as your work when it isn’t your work is just plagiarism, even if it’s written by a robot.”
In a letter published on Sept 25 in The Dartmouth, the provost apologised for not always disclosing AI use in his public writing.
“Suffice it to say, I am more aware than ever of the need for robust intellectual discussions about the appropriate use of AI in the higher education landscape,” Schnell wrote.
The scope of AI use by university employees is not entirely clear, but one of the most comprehensive surveys, conducted in the autumn of 2025 by Elon University and the American Association of Colleges and Universities, found that about a quarter of the 1,057 faculty members from across the country who responded were not using generative AI tools.
Meanwhile, polling suggests US college students lean heavily on AI in their coursework. More than half say they use it at least weekly, and one in 5 say they use it every day.
Among faculty, nearly nine in 10 said they were not using AI for grading, according to the Elon survey.
And just 6% said they used AI “a lot” when preparing their own research papers.
Close to half, though, said they turned to AI at least somewhat as they created or changed “traditional assignments”.
At the University of California, Berkeley, the student-run paper, The Daily Californian, ran dozens of campus communications through AI detectors and found that some missives from top administrators were apparently written or altered by AI.
Dan Mogulof, a spokesperson for Berkeley, said in an e-mail that university leaders and communicators were using AI as a tool within certain guidelines and “so long as the final product accurately and authentically captures and expresses the author’s thoughts, perspectives, tone and objectives”.
He added: “We have found that not to be possible without extensive revision, editing and/or embellishment of whatever an AI agent might initially produce.”
Student journalists also tested a long essay published by Berkeley math professor Zvezdelina Stankova in The San Francisco Standard. AI detector Pangram flagged the essay as “33% AI-generated or AI-assisted writing”, the paper wrote.
Stankova, who declined to comment, told the student paper that she had used AI for editing, but the essay, about the shaky math skills of many new Berkeley students, was the result of “intensive human work and deliberation”.
Some schools have specific policies on AI use among employees.
At the University of Southern California, for instance, faculty and staff members cannot use AI to “independently make final decisions” about matters like admissions and discipline.
And USC says that artificial intelligence cannot be used in a way that defies any other university policy.
Still, a set of faculty guidelines for artificial intelligence at USC suggest the balancing act facing many professors: “There is a difference between what you can do with generative AI tools and what you should do.”
Whatever professors decide, the guidelines say, “faculty who require AI disclosure from students should generally hold themselves to the same standard”.
Even when institutions have AI policies in place, they – like most rules anywhere – are not always followed.
Stanford University has a detailed AI policy, for example.
But recently, the university used AI to remove a Hispanic man from a photograph, replacing him with a black woman, and to alter the appearances of two other students in the same image.
After the changes were discovered, the university acknowledged there had been a policy violation.
Experts say the controversies – and the uncertainty over how or whether to respond – can be traced to how quickly the technology is evolving on campuses.
Ethical standards have long governed matters like plagiarism and other forms of academic misconduct, but even written guidelines have not always explicitly kept pace with AI, leaving the normal boundaries murky.
“The big thing is there’s no social contract right now,” said Marc Watkins, who founded the Mississippi AI Institute for Teachers at the University of Mississippi. “We don’t have these sorts of priors to say what’s appropriate and what’s not.” NYTIMES

Diyar Güldoğan
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
A group of US House lawmakers is urging Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take immediate steps to curb settler violence in the occupied West Bank, protect Palestinian communities and investigate attacks involving American citizens.
In a Sept. 24 letter to Netanyahu, the lawmakers expressed “urgent concern” over escalating violence in the West Bank.
“We write with urgent concern regarding the growing outbreak of extremist settler violence in the West Bank, including violence that has killed and threatened American citizens,” they wrote.
They said continued settlement expansion and violence could affect Israel's long-term security and prospects for peace, prosperity and freedom for Israelis and Palestinians.
The lawmakers cited data they said showed a significant increase in settler violence in recent years. According to the letter, attacks by Israeli settlers, including incidents involving Palestinians and Israeli security forces, increased 27% in 2025, while serious incidents rose 63% during the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier.
They also cited UN figures indicating that 1,122 Palestinians, including civilians and combatants, were killed in the West Bank and East Jerusalem between Oct. 7, 2023 and July 24, 2026. They said 67 Israelis had been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank since the beginning of 2023.
The letter said settler violence had displaced residents from 107 communities since January 2023, affecting approximately 6,000 Palestinians. The lawmakers also cited more than 1,380 settler-related incidents documented by the UN across more than 250 Palestinian communities since the beginning of 2026.
"Israeli settler attacks have made daily life unsafe for Palestinians across large parts of the West Bank,” they said.
The lawmakers said attacks have affected Palestinian schools, farmers and families, with some residents reporting physical assaults, displacement from agricultural land and restrictions on movement.
“Nine American citizens have been killed in the West Bank since January 2022. To date, no one has been held accountable for any of these nine deaths. Many of us have heard directly from constituents, including American citizens who have themselves been threatened or harassed by settlers without cause,” they added.
The lawmakers asked Netanyahu's government to take three specific steps.
 
First, they called on the Israeli Police and Israel Defense Forces to defend Palestinian communities when they come under attack and to apply that standard regardless of who the attackers are.
Second, they called for a transparent and credible mechanism to investigate and prosecute violence against Palestinians, including Palestinian Americans. They also urged Israel to complete pending investigations into the deaths of the nine American citizens identified in the letter.
Third, the lawmakers called on Israel to halt additional settlement approvals and continue removing illegal outposts in the West Bank.
"Restoring the rule of law in the West Bank serves the security of Israelis and Palestinians alike. The safety of our constituents matters to us as the safety of your citizens matters to you.
"We ask that your government ensure that Americans living in or visiting the Israeli-controlled areas of the West Bank receive the security and the protection of property to which they are entitled," the lawmakers wrote.

In Brief
- New Greens leader David Shoebridge said his party would "fill the policy vacuum that's been left by the Labor Party".
- Shoebridge beat Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young in the vote, decided by the party's 10 senators and sole lower house MP.
New Greens leader David Shoebridge has vowed to "beat down One Nation" and expose Labor's "failures", signalling a greater focus on cost-of-living pressures after winning the first contested leadership ballot in the party's history.
Speaking in Sydney after becoming leader with six primary votes, ahead of senators Mehreen Faruqi on three and Sarah Hanson–Young with two, he said the party will fight the "1 per cent" and those "taking money out of the pockets of workers".
"As you travel around the country, the call I'm not hearing is: 'What do we want?' 'Gradual change'. 'When do we want it?' 'In due course'," he said.
"People are desperate for material change. They don't want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know isn't going to change their lives. They want to take on the vested interests."
Shoebridge replaces Larissa Waters, who stepped down as Greens leader on Tuesday due to ill health.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Shoebridge was elected as a senator in 2022 after almost 12 years in NSW state politics, and ran with the party's new deputy leader, Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May, who joined parliament two years ago after working for the United Nations and Greenpeace.
The party has struggled to increase its support base in recent polling, despite both major parties' decline and the rise of One Nation. At the 2025 election, the Greens lost three of their four seats and their leader, Adam Bandt. They later lost senator Dorinda Cox, who defected to Labor.
But the diminished party Waters took over has more leverage in parliament: it now holds the sole balance of power in the Senate on bills that are not supported by the Coalition.
Shoebridge's pitch on Instagram this morning said a party he led would stare "down the climate crisis, war, greed and an ever more unsure future".
Speaking after the ballot, he thanked Waters and former deputy leader Faruqi, before saying One Nation had run on a "short-term sugar hit, building on (and) feeding off people's quite legitimate anger".
"Their non-policies are being tested, and what we are going to do, collectively as the Greens, is fill the policy vacuum that's been left by the Labor Party," he said.
"We will point out the failure of the Labor Party, but we will point out what the solutions are," he said.
"We're not punching down on migrants. We're taking on the 1 per cent that have bought our parliament. They've bought the Labor Party. They've bought the Liberal Party. They've bought One Nation. Well, they bloody well haven't bought the Greens."
Treasurer Jim Chalmers responded to Shoebridge's comments by saying that despite never having met Shoebridge or Hodgins-May, he expected collaboration in the Senate.
"I think it's really important that we focus on the risks posed to workers and to our economy by One Nation, the Liberal Party, and the National Party," he said.
Faruqi voices disappointment over leadership process
Faruqi said she was "disappointed the party room chose another direction" and that "many others will feel the same way".
"I did not stand again for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team," she said in a post on social media.
She criticised the vote being decided among the party's 10 senators and one lower house MP, instead of party members being able to vote on the outcome.
"I've long advocated publicly that Greens leaders should be elected by members with enough time for thoughtful deliberation on who is best to grow our party. I share members' frustration that the opposite happened this week.
"Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party. I call on the new leadership team to set a timeline for one member, one vote."
Former MP Max Chandler-Mather, who now leads the Green Institute think tank, wrote to MPs on Tuesday saying grassroots members should help elect the next leader, the Sydney Morning Herald reported.
The Greens received almost two million votes last election, yet the direction of the party's leadership would be determined by just 11 representatives, he wrote.
Waters listed her achievements in the role as pushing the government to overhaul Australia's 25-year-old environment laws, new standards for native forest logging, strengthening controls on land clearing, and delaying coal and gas projects.
Under Waters, the Greens also helped Labor pass gun buyback legislation, and its budget tax package.
Waters will return as a "humble backbencher" after medical leave, saying she was "proud that our party is polling higher than ever before, amidst the surge to the right-wing forces of politics".

Germany has no plans to relaunch Nord Stream – Wadephul
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said this on Tuesday, September 29, in response to questions from members of the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly in Strasbourg, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“The federal government has no plans to restart Nord Stream. We became far too dependent on Russia, and it was a mistake. We cannot allow that to happen again,” Wadephul stressed.
He was responding to a question about the possible resumption of Russian gas supplies through the Nord Stream pipelines, an issue previously raised by representatives of the opposition right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
The German foreign minister also said that good relations with Russia could potentially be restored in the future, as Germany has nothing against the Russian people or the country as such. However, he said that Germany has nothing against the Russian people or Russia itself, but that the current Russian government is violating international law and waging a war of aggression against Ukraine.
“Therefore, for now, and probably for some time to come, we have to say that we will have security in Europe not together with Russia, but only against Russia,” Wadephul said.
To ensure security, European countries must strengthen their defense capabilities within NATO and the European Union, he stressed.
As reported, on September 26, 2022,explosions occurred on the Russian Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea, disabling three of the four pipeline strings. In February of the same year, shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the German government halted the certification process for Nord Stream 2, which was never put into operation.
Meanwhile, the opposition far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party supports resuming Russian gas supplies. In its 2025 election platform, the party called for the surviving Nord Stream 2 pipeline string to be put into operation as soon as possible and for the damaged sections of both pipelines to be repaired. The AfD argues that this is necessary to provide German industry with cheaper energy.

A little known greenhouse gas is quietly harming half of Europeans. This Italian city is hit hardest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:02:42 UTC
11:02:42 KST

People who suffer from asthma are the most at risk.
Half of Europeans were exposed to a little-known greenhouse gas during this summer’s record breaking heatwaves and wildfires.
Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that can “penetrate deep into the respiratory system and enter the bloodstream, allowing it to reach almost all organs within the body.” People who suffer from asthma are the most at risk.
Ozone forms from thousands of chemical reactions, triggered by sunlight and high temperatures. So the record-breaking heatwaves that gripped Europe from June to August this year led to ozone levels dangerous to human health. During this period, 50 per cent of Europe’s population was exposed to poor, very poor or extremely poor ozone levels, according to the European Commission’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS).
“Ozone pollution is a stark reminder of how interconnected our atmosphere, climate, health, and livelihoods really are, with pollution and our changing climate impacting the chemistry of the air we breathe, determining the health of our ecosystems, and even governing our ability to grow food,” says Laurence Rouil, Director of CAMS.
The good news is that EU efforts to combat other air pollutants are making a difference, so it is hoped that ozone levels can also be brought down with sustained effort.
Ozone illustrates the close relationship between air pollution and climate change
Air pollution, often called an invisible killer, causes more than four million premature deaths worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. In 2025, 56 deaths per 100,000 people in Europe and Central Asia were attributable to air pollution.
It is made up of many different gases. Ground-level ozone, not to be confused with upper atmospheric ozone which protects us from UV, is not as well known as others but it is especially concerning because of its close links with climate change.
“Ground-level ozone illustrates the close relationship between air pollution and climate change – a key societal challenge – due to its formation under high temperatures,” according to Atmosphere Watch, the first edition of a new report from CAMS on air quality.
Global temperatures are increasing and heatwaves are becoming more frequent and more extreme due to human-caused climate change. As ozone formation is triggered by high temperatures, the increase in heatwaves means more ozone.
Nitrogen oxides are part of the chemical reactions which lead to the formation of ozone and these, the report explains, are “mainly produced by the combustion of fossil fuels”. It names industry, solvents and road transport as sources of ozone, as well as biomass burning “further compounding the influence of climate change, with more extreme fires occurring under hotter and drier conditions”.
As a greenhouse gas, ozone is responsible for approximately 0.23°C of present-day warming, according to UK charity Clean Air Fund. It calls ground-level ozone a “super pollutant”.
How the EU has reduced levels of other air pollutants
Atmosphere Watch highlights that “air quality in Europe improved significantly regarding all pollutants regulated by the European Air Quality Directive.” Known as one of the most progressive air quality laws in the world, the 2024 directive requires EU countries to monitor pollutant limits and act when safe levels are exceeded.
A 2025 Copernicus report said: “Over the past decade, emissions of sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides have fallen by approximately three-to-five per cent per year across the European Union. The most significant reductions have been achieved in industry and road transport. Since 2015, industrial emissions of sulphur oxides have fallen by 59 per cent, while nitrogen oxide emissions from industry have declined by 39 per cent. Road transport emissions have also fallen substantially, with reductions of 40 per cent for nitrogen oxides and 34 per cent for fine particulate matter (PM2.5).”
Improving public transport, implementing low or zero emission zones for traffic, switching from fossil fuels to clean energy sources and consuming less meat are seen as some of the most successful ways to reduce air pollutants.
But, Atmosphere Watch says, “ozone shows no clear downward trend and remains an issue.”
Under the EU Ambient Air Quality Directive, the maximum eight-hour daily average ozone concentration should not exceed 120 μg/ m3 more than 18 days per year, with a long-term objective of 100 μg/m3 compliant with the WHO guidelines. The map above shows how much of Europe exceeded these levels during 2026 so far. It shows how levels get worse the further south you go on the continent – the areas where heatwaves were the hottest and most prolonged.
The extreme weather and unprecedented wildfires led to worse air pollution across the whole continent, not just in directly affected areas.
“Atmosphere Watch shows that air pollution knows no border. Wildfire smoke, ozone and dust can travel thousands of kilometres, affecting communities far from their source,” says Florian Pappenberger, Director-General of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
As an example, in August 2026 Belgium experienced its worst wildfire in 100 years. “The intense smoke columns travelled all the way through Germany, reaching Poland.”
Milan has some of the worst ozone levels in the world
While 50 per cent of Europeans were exposed to unsafe levels of ozone during the summer months, the exposure levels are even higher in other parts of the world.
So far in 2026, almost 40 per cent of the world’s total population has been exposed to extremely high levels of ozone, including 60 per cent of Asian citizens. Oceania was the least affected continent during the first eight months of the year – this is partly because the Northern Hemisphere is more sensitive to ground-level ozone pollution due to the higher landmass and population.
Roughly 50 per cent of the global population was exposed to very or extremely poor air quality due to ozone concentrations in 2026. Milan, Rio de Janeiro, Mexico City, Delhi and Cairo are the cities with some of the highest exposures. Only five per cent of the global population was exposed to ‘good’ long-term ozone levels and 15 per cent to ‘fair’ levels during 2026, according to the analysis.
“Ozone concentrations in all continents are likely to be affected by climate change: ground-level, and more generally, tropospheric ozone formation, is triggered by warm temperatures and sunlight. Therefore, in areas experiencing more heatwaves, local ozone concentrations will increase, partly offsetting the benefits of the mitigation strategies designed to reduce precursor pollutant emissions.”
How can ozone levels be reduced?
Ultimately responsibility for and power over ozone levels rests with governments. Experts recommend much better monitoring and reporting of ozone levels, as is done for other air pollutants. At the moment in the EU, only Croatia, France and Spain have developed or implemented air quality plans explicitly focused on ozone.
Countries and cities that are doing the best on limiting ozone are focused on improving forecasting for ozone concentration and understanding how ozone forms and its main sources, according to the European Environment Agency.
Making the public more aware of ozone and how it forms can also be helpful. On an individual level, we can all help to reduce ozone levels by walking or cycling rather than driving. If you must drive, adjust your habits so as to reduce emissions by lowering your speed and avoiding hard braking or rapid acceleration. Use environmentally safe paints and cleaning products whenever possible.

Taiwan plans US$850 million ammunition spend to prepare for potential PLA blockade
Taiwan should boost conventional ammunition stocks through local production while asking US to speed up weapons deliveries, analyst says
Taiwan’s military plans to spend more than NT$27 billion (US$850 million) to quadruple critical ammunition stocks to 120 days’ supply, strengthening its ability to sustain combat operations during a wartime blockade.
The proposed six-year “urgent ammunition replenishment” programme, running from this year until 2031, comes as Taipei seeks to strengthen its ability to keep fighting if a cross-strait conflict cuts external supply lines.
The spending proposal was revealed on September 26 and still requires legislative approval. The programme is expected to cost NT$27.59 billion, with NT$7.3 billion allocated this year through a supplementary budget. A further NT$7.3 billion is proposed for 2027 to accelerate procurement of various types of critical ammunition.
Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi, the strategic planning director of Taiwan’s defence ministry, said this month that the military aimed to gradually increase its combat-ready ammunition stocks from the current 30 days to 120 days.
He said more frequent combat-readiness drills and exercises in recent years had also increased ammunition consumption, requiring stocks to be replenished more quickly.

Family first: Le Pen clan tightens its grip as Bardella hits trouble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Marie-Caroline Le Pen, Marine Le Pen and Nolwenn Olivier arrive for Jean-Marie Le Pen's funeral in La Trinité-sur-Mer, France on Jan. 11, 2025. | Sebastien Salom-Gomis/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — In Marine Le Pen’s political world, family has a habit of finding its way back to the center of power.
That could now matter more than ever for Jordan Bardella.
The 31-year-old president of the far-right National Rally is battling allegations that he exchanged antisemitic messages as a young activist — accusations he has dismissed as “blatant falsehoods.” The controversy comes at an awkward moment for a party Le Pen has spent years trying to distance from the antisemitism associated with its past.
Advertisement
Le Pen has so far backed Bardella, offering her protégé an emphatic public defense. “The system will do anything — including the most disgusting things — to try to hinder this momentum,” she said, sitting next to him as they addressed reporters in the National Assembly Tuesday.
But Bardella’s difficulties inside the party predate the allegations — and the latest controversy now threatens to amplify them. His standing inside the National Rally had already grown precarious, with Le Pen drawing relatives and longtime loyalists closer as she prepares for next year’s presidential election.
Le Pen’s 27-year-old niece Nolwenn Olivier, Bardella’s former girlfriend, has been promoted to communications director. Another niece, Marion Maréchal, who broke with the party during the last presidential election, is back in favor and expected to play a frontline role. And Le Pen’s own brother-in-law, Philippe Olivier, an unofficial chief adviser, is taking part in many top campaign meetings.
At the same time, several figures associated with Bardella have been sidelined, passed over for promotion, or even ejected from the party. Once touted as a possible replacement for Le Pen, Bardella was not invited to speak at a recent National Rally parliamentary gathering, despite being party president and Le Pen’s presumptive choice for prime minister.
There is no indication Le Pen is preparing to cast Bardella aside. And yet, she has shown before that protecting the party can trump even the closest personal ties. In 2015, amid another controversy over antisemitic remarks, she backed the expulsion of the party’s founder — her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen.
That history leaves Bardella with little room for error as Marine Le Pen prepares for her fourth attempt at the presidency — and increasingly surrounds herself with people whose loyalty she has little reason to question.
Advertisement
Florian Philippot, once Le Pen’s right-hand man before abruptly leaving the party after the 2017 election, said some elements of Bardella’s treatment felt familiar.
“The little snubs, not being given a chance to speak,” Philippot said. “They are very telling.” Le Pen and her inner circle “would bring others back in and put them in the spotlight to show that you’re no longer the closest one,” he added.
Family affair
That Le Pen’s family would play a prominent role in her campaign was evident from the moment a court cleared the way for her on July 7 to run for office.
The next day she headed to La Flèche for her first campaign stop.
The town southwest of Paris is not just a National Rally stronghold. It is also a family one. Le Pen was welcomed by cheering crowds alongside her sister Marie-Caroline, who was running in the local senatorial race, and her brother-in-law Philippe Olivier.
They were accompanied, according to local press reports, by their daughter Nolwenn Olivier — Le Pen’s niece and future communications director for the campaign. Bardella, meanwhile, trailed Le Pen stony-faced as she worked the crowd and answered journalists’ questions.
Advertisement
Since then, Le Pen’s relatives and longtime loyalists have tightened their hold on her electoral operation.
Maréchal, who left the party but is now back in the fold, is expected to play a key role in the campaign, according to two National Rally officials. In an interview earlier this month, the 36-year-old said she could work on improving relations with the German and Italian governments if Le Pen were to win the presidency.
Beyond the family, longtime Le Pen loyalists have also been elevated. Her former chief of staff Renaud Labaye has been appointed deputy campaign director, while National Rally lawmaker Sébastien Chenu, another longstanding ally, is now in charge of local representatives.
Marine Le Pen and Marion Maréchal are pictured in Nice, France on Oct. 15, 2016. | Pool photo by Eric Gaillard via AFP/Getty Images
“For Marine Le Pen, it’s either a victory in 2027 or never,” said Jean-Yves Camus, a far-right specialist with the Jean-Jaurès Foundation. “And if it’s now or never, she needs to bolster her inner circle and have absolute trust in them.”
Those close to Le Pen described the tightening of the circle less as a liability than as a source of political strength.
“Some families just have politics in their blood,” said a person close to a member of the Le Pen family, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters. “Since when are members of the Le Pen family a handicap for the party?”
Advertisement
This summer, Philippe Olivier spent several weeks on holiday with Le Pen in the family bastion of La Trinité-sur-Mer in Brittany, giving him unusual access ahead of Le Pen’s campaign launch this autumn.
“He’s Marine Le Pen’s standard-bearer,” said a former National Rally adviser. “He spends his holidays with Le Pen, he has a degree of intimacy with her that is rare in politics. He’s loyal, writes her speeches.”
Olivier bristled at questions about the family’s role in the party, describing them as “insulting” in an interview with POLITICO.
“Reducing my presence in the party to my position as Marie-Caroline’s husband, when I’ve been a member of the political leadership for years — the reproaches are stupid,” he said.
Killer instinct
For veterans of the movement, it’s a familiar pattern.
The National Rally and its predecessor were run by the Le Pen family for nearly five decades before Marine Le Pen handed the reins to Bardella in 2021. Long before that, senior party figures had risen through the ranks only to find themselves eclipsed or shown the door when their ambitions collided with those of the family.
Advertisement
In the late 1990s, the party’s number two, Bruno Mégret, rebelled after being passed over as the lead candidate for the European Parliament election in favor of the wife of Jean-Marie Le Pen, Marine Le Pen’s father, who was then the party leader.
The feud split the movement — and the Le Pen family itself. As Marine’s sister, Marie-Caroline, sided with the rebels, Jean-Marie began pushing Marine to the forefront of the party.
“Marine is a killer, which is a strength in politics,” said Jean-Yves Le Gallou, a senior party figure at the time who joined the breakaway faction. She had “superior political skills that her father had likely detected.”
The two sisters later reconciled. Jean-Marie Le Pen would eventually discover firsthand how ruthless his daughter could be when asserting control. In 2015, after repeated clashes over his antisemitic remarks — including a description of Nazi gas chambers as a “detail” of history — the party she led expelled him.
The pattern resurfaced after the 2017 presidential election, when Philippot, then Marine Le Pen’s right-hand man and one of the architects of the party’s surge among working-class voters, abruptly left the party after losing an internal battle over its direction.
With Le Pen, said a former senior National Rally official, “you’re either in favor or out of favor. There’s no middle ground.”
Advertisement
Plan B
For Bardella, the problem is not simply that Le Pen’s family has moved closer. It is that his own role has narrowed sharply since July.
For months, he had been preparing for the possibility of having to replace Le Pen as the party’s presidential candidate. Once that prospect disappeared, Bardella was expected to fall back into line behind the woman whose political future he had been preparing to inherit.
According to a top National Rally official, Bardella himself acknowledged the difficulty of that position: He had to prepare seriously enough to become a credible “Plan B” candidate while showing enough deference to make clear that Le Pen remained the party’s undisputed standard-bearer.
Jordan Bardella arrives for an election night event in La Seyne-sur-Mer, France, on Sept. 27, 2026. | Thibaud Moritz/AFP via Getty Images
“His crime was that he really wanted to be [the presidential candidate] and he was disappointed,” said the former senior National Rally official. “He wasn’t able to hide it and morph overnight into the loyal foot soldier.”
Bardella’s reduced room for maneuver is also visible in the party’s policy direction.
His allies had pushed the National Rally toward greater fiscal caution, including a softer position on pensions. Le Pen has instead doubled down on promises to protect retirement benefits and cut taxes on fuel and electricity, while putting immigration and purchasing power back at the center of the campaign.
Advertisement
The focus now is to “mobilize our voters,” Philippe Olivier said. “They risk thinking that if we are not talking about immigration anymore, we’re dropping it.”
The latest controversy further complicates Bardella’s position.
In comments allegedly made when he was 17, shortly after he had joined the National Rally, Bardella said that “the Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them” and “all banks are held by the Jews,” according to the French investigative outlet Mediapart.
On Tuesday, the National Rally launched a counterattack, forcefully denying the allegations against Bardella. At a joint press conference with Le Pen, Bardella denounced “an attempt to destabilize their campaign.” Le Pen pledged her “absolute confidence” in the party president.
Bardella has also announced that he has filed a defamation lawsuit against Mediapart.
During the period when Bardella was expected to be his party’s presidential candidate, one of his main assets was his distance from the party’s toxic past. Le Pen’s political rivals have leaped to exploit the latest developments.
Advertisement
“The far right will remain the far right,” said Raphaël Glucksmann, a center-left presidential hopeful. “No communications agency, no window dressing will change that.” Marine Tondelier, leader of the Green party, called on Bardella to step down “from all his responsibilities.”
“I think this ruins [Le Pen’s] strategy to shed her controversial image,” said Gaspard Gantzer, a former adviser for ex-president François Hollande.
“It’s going to make people very uncomfortable,” he said.
