US forces exit Iraq, emboldening Iran’s proxies and Islamic State
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:02:50 UTC
09:02:50 KST

US forces exit Iraq, emboldening Iran’s proxies and Islamic State
- US forces withdrew from their remaining bases in Iraq on Sept 30, risking a security vacuum and allowing Iranian-backed militias and Islamic State to gain strength.
- Iran celebrated the US exit as a victory, with its proxies expected to expand influence and challenge Iraq's stability without Western military presence.
- Experts warn Iraq's security forces may be unprepared to handle threats, including a potential resurgence of Islamic State using advanced weapons like armed drones.
AI generated
BAGHDAD – US forces withdrew from their remaining bases in Iraq on Sept 30, raising fears of a security vacuum that would embolden Iranian-backed Shi’ite militias and allow ISIS to regroup.
The withdrawal of the final troops, mainly from an airbase in Erbil in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, was celebrated as a victory by Tehran and its allies, although many Iraqis were concerned that their own security forces were unprepared.
The pullout was agreed in 2024 under then US President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump’s administration even as it wages war against Iran next door.
It comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled dictator Saddam Hussein, triggering years of upheaval and chaos.
US troops initially left at the end of 2011 but returned less than three years later after ISIS fighters seized a third of Iraq.
More than 4,500 US troops died in America’s biggest war of this century, around twice as many as in the parallel war in Afghanistan.
The Iraq Body Count project says more than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed.
The Pentagon said the United States and its coalition partners had formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve, adding that the US would continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
The Iraqis are expected to lead the effort to secure the country, an ally of both Washington and Tehran, and keep the remnants of ISIS suppressed.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi said in a statement: “The end of the international coalition’s mission does not mean the end of our battle against terrorism, but rather Iraq’s transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability.”
Tehran has steadily entrenched itself through proxies in Iraq since the fall of Saddam.
While the departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, some worry that security forces trained and funded by the United States still cannot protect the country.
“The lesson from the past two decades is that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous,” said Jassim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi analyst who advises the security forces.
Adil Salman, 45, a high school English teacher, said Iraqis “should not rush to celebrate” the withdrawal. “Militias still operate outside the state’s control and (Islamic State) still has not disappeared,” he said. “I’m concerned that the US departure could lead to a new period of instability. In the end, people will judge this decision by one thing: whether security remains stable in the coming years.”
The presence of both US troops and armed groups allied to Iran in the region has pulled Iraq into the expanding Middle East conflict.
Of the 18 US service members listed as killed since Trump launched “Operation Epic Fury” alongside Israel against Iran in February, seven died in Iraq.
The last was an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Iran, allies are the winners
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a triumph for its “axis of resistance” of allied armed groups across the region.
The withdrawal raises “the possibility that Iran’s proxies will feel increasingly empowered in the absence of a Western military presence”, said Baghdad-based political analyst Ahmed Younis.
“These groups may attempt to expand their role in shaping state policies and consolidating their presence within key institutions.”
Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
The last time the US withdrew, the Iraqi army proved no match for ISIS. Soldiers took off their uniforms and fled when the group captured Mosul, Iraq’s second-largest city, in 2014.
Since ISIS’ self-proclaimed caliphate was defeated in 2017, US troops have been providing Iraqi security forces with critical intelligence on the group’s movements, aerial surveillance and reconnaissance.
Retired Iraqi Army General Mohammed al-Jubouri, who led a brigade in the war against ISIS, said: “The most important question now is whether Iraq’s security institutions have prepared a viable Plan B for the post-coalition phase.
“One of the worst-case scenarios would be Islamic State obtaining armed drones or improvised explosive drones at a time when Iraq still lacks sufficient air defence capabilities to counter such threats effectively.”

Finance presenter Alan Kohler retiring after three decades at ABC
After a brilliant 31-year career as the ABC's finance guru, Alan Kohler has decided to hang up his boots at the end of the year.
With a successful career in print before moving to television, Kohler has been one of the most influential journalists Australia has ever produced, as a former editor of The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and The Age and as an incisive columnist on all affairs financial.
"I love the ABC, always have, even more so after I joined it," he told ABC staff in a statement.
"I find it very hard to imagine this wonderful place not being part of my life, but I'm 74 and it's time to spend more time with my family, including the six grandchildren."
Kohler joined the public broadcaster in 1995 as business and economics correspondent for the 7.30 Report and went on to host Inside Business.
For the past 24 years, he has been the lead 7pm News finance presenter, unravelling the mysteries of financial markets for the audience with a format all his own that has often begun with: "Now, here's an interesting graph."
ABC managing director Hugh Marks said Kohler had made an extraordinary contribution to the organisation and the nation.
"For decades, he has helped Australians make sense of complex issues with insight, clarity and a uniquely engaging style, always delivered with warmth, humour and that trademark cheeky grin.
"I can't thank Alan enough for everything he has given to the ABC and our audiences. While this marks the end of an incredible chapter, it is certainly not the end of Alan's contribution, just the beginning of a new one."
Kohler hosted Inside Business for many years. He currently writes a weekly column and hosts a podcast, That's Business, every Friday.
While he is a distinguished editor, Kohler's biggest impact on the nation has been as a communicator.
After several stints as the chanticleer columnist for the AFR, he joined The Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) and The Age as senior business columnist, working with your correspondent during my time as SMH business editor.
A canny entrepreneur, he had by that stage already launched The Eureka Report and later left Fairfax Media when he added online news service Business Spectator to the mix.
Throughout his various incarnations, he has remained steadfastly loyal to the ABC and to his audience and is expected to continue his association with one-off specials.

Hong Kong’s executives are ‘ill prepared’ for AI era, report finds
The city’s firms have a severe lack of AI and cybersecurity expertise at the board level, leaving them ‘ill prepared’ for the coming era, report finds
Executives at Hong Kong’s largest listed companies have a severe lack of technological expertise, with fewer than 1 per cent of directors possessing dedicated artificial intelligence or cybersecurity skills, according to a new report by Grant Thornton Hong Kong.
The firm’s 15th annual Corporate Governance Review – which surveyed 100 major listed firms on Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Composite Index – found that 59 per cent of companies view cybersecurity or AI as principal business risks. Yet only 11 per cent had established specialised board committees to oversee digital threats and technology integration.
These gaps have persisted despite the introduction of updated Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) Corporate Governance Code standards last year, which introduced mandatory director training, board skills matrices and stricter overboarding limits.
“While overall disclosure quality on HKEX has improved, there remains a disconnect between acknowledged risks and technical expertise at the top,” said Barry Tong, head of advisory at Grant Thornton Hong Kong.

Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:58:52 UTC
08:58:52 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters living legend and grand final specialist
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who can call himself a grand final specialist.
Not that he ever would. The 35-year-old has for many years now been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.
A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.
He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.
Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.
Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.
"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.
"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."
That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.
But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.
His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.
In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.
In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.
Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.
It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.
"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.
"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.
"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."
It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.
Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.
But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.
None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.
"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.
"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

Hegseth to Slash 20 Percent of Generals and Flag Officers, Deepening Cuts to Top Ranks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:58:46 UTC
08:58:46 KST

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth plans to announce Sept. 30 a directive to slash the number of general and flag officers across the U.S. military by 20 percent, Pentagon officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Hegseth is doubling down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.
Hegseth’s announcement will come during a “State for the Force” address. The cuts will reduce the number of general and flag officer billets, meaning some moves may play out over time, rather than swiftly removing 20 percent of generals and admirals.
Fox News first reported the new cuts and details of the planned announcement. Pentagon officials later confirmed that account.
The “State of the Force” speech comes a year after Hegseth convened senior U.S. military leaders from commands around the globe to outline his philosophy for running the Pentagon—an extraordinarily rare gathering.
The services are expected to make the cuts by Jan. 1, 2027. How reductions will be apportioned among the services is, so far, unclear.
Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.
The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.
The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force about 30 generals, with plans to continue to grow that number.
In Hegseth’s Quantico address a year ago, he told the ranking military officers and senior enlisted advisers in the audience that “more leadership changes will be made” and asserted that “fat generals and admirals” were roaming the halls of the Pentagon.
A top Democratic lawmaker complained the cuts were arbitrary and Congress had not been consulted, and noted that Hegseth has removed senior officers from their roles with little explanation.
“Efficiency and streamlining in the military are worthy goals, but the size and structure of our military’s senior officer corps are matters in which Congress has a fundamental role,” said Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. “Article I of the Constitution assigns Congress the power to raise and support the armed forces and to make rules for their government. Reshaping the senior leadership of the world’s most powerful military is precisely the kind of decision that requires consultation with and justification to Congress.”
The new cuts are not the only step Hegseth is taking this week to reshape the military establishment. In a Sept. 29 memo released by the Pentagon, Hegseth directed military service academies to drop tenured positions for civilian professors. Hegseth said the move was needed because “civilian academic norms … dilute our focus on lethality.”
Critics have said the Pentagon’s efforts to reform the institutions could compromise the academic independence and the quality of education at the service academies, which include the U.S. Air Force Academy, the U.S. Naval Academy, and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.
USAFA only recently began offering tenure to civilian faculty.
Hegseth served on and off in the Army National Guard, reaching the rank of major. He has cast himself as a Pentagon chief who relates to rank-and-file troops.
His previous directive to reduce general officers mandated a 20 percent reduction in Active four-stars, a 20 percent cut in National Guard generals, and a 10 percent cut in overall general and flag officers. Hegseth has said that cuts were needed to reduce bureaucracy.

The signatories, in particular, reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, as well as for international law, including international humanitarian law.
We pledge to support efforts to identify and locate Ukrainian children who have been illegally deported or forcibly transferred, and to assist in verifying information related to each individual case
The signatories also pledged to "strengthen diplomatic engagement and practical mechanisms for the release and return of illegally detained civilians, as well as overcome the legal, administrative, and logistical obstacles hindering their return."
"We will continue to work together with Ukraine and international partners and engage all relevant parties in order to achieve these goals, uphold international law, support victims and their loved ones, and ensure that human dignity remains at the foundation of all peace-related initiatives," the document states.

helvetus uses FKM rubber to rethink integrated luxury watch strap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:55:34 UTC
08:55:34 KST

helvetus uses FKM rubber to rethink integrated luxury watch strap
helvetus develops reference-specific FKM rubber straps for rolex watches, combining precise case-fitting geometry with the material’s durability and resistance to everyday wear.
How Vulcanised Rubber Became a Luxury Material on the Wrist
Helvetus develops reference-specific FKM rubber straps for Rolex watches, combining precise case-fitting geometry with the material’s durability and resistance to everyday wear.
From industrial seals and aerospace applications to luxury timepieces, vulcanized FKM rubber has taken on a new role in contemporary watch design. Its chemical resistance, dimensional stability, and ability to hold a precise molded shape make it suited to straps that function as engineered components rather than simple accessories.
When the strap became part of the watch case
For much of the 20th century, a watch strap was essentially a strip of leather fitted between two lugs, with its design largely independent of the watch. Integrated cases changed that relationship. When Gérald Genta designed the Royal Oak in 1972 and the Nautilus in 1976, the bracelet became a continuation of the case, carrying its geometry from the bezel to the clasp.
Cartier had explored a similar approach much earlier with the Santos, designed in 1904 for pilot Alberto Santos-Dumont. Its exposed bezel screws and case geometry extended into the strap. The 2018 redesign made this connection more functional, introducing QuickSwitch for tool-free strap changes and SmartLink for bracelet adjustment.
The result is a category of straps designed around specific watch references. Once a strap must follow a particular case curve and interface, its geometry, thickness, and end pieces have to be developed for that model. Helvetus, for example, produces Cartier Santos straps for Medium and Large cases with curved ends that meet the lugs without a visible gap, while retaining the original buckle.
Why Helvetus chooses FKM instead of silicone
Silicone is common in watch straps, but it can attract dust and lint because of its electrostatic properties and may develop a tacky surface over time. FKM, a fluoroelastomer originally developed in the 1950s for seals and O-rings exposed to jet fuel, heat, and solvents, offers greater chemical resistance and dimensional stability across a wide temperature range.
FKM also retains its molded form instead of gradually relaxing into a curl. However, the material is more difficult to process. It must be vulcanized and is less receptive to color than silicone, contributing to the restrained palettes and higher prices of FKM straps.
Rolex’s own approach, the Oysterflex introduced in 2015, combines a titanium and nickel alloy blade with an elastomer overmold, functioning more like a bracelet with an elastomer exterior than a conventional rubber strap.
Aftermarket straps as a design discipline
Aftermarket components are often treated as secondary to the original, but their development involves a specific set of design constraints. The strap must fit a case it did not originally accompany, work with an existing buckle, and maintain the proportions and geometry of the watch.
Details such as end pieces machined to match a specific case curvature, flush-fitting keepers, and carefully controlled thicknesses help maintain the continuity of the original design. The FKM rubber range for Rolex follows this reference-specific approach, with straps organized around the Submariner, Daytona, GMT-Master II, Datejust, Day-Date, and Sky-Dweller rather than simply by lug width.
A replaceable layer of wear within the life of the watch
The use of a replaceable strap also changes how wear is distributed across the watch. A factory bracelet accumulates wear directly on the original component, while a replaceable strap concentrates everyday wear in a part that can be exchanged independently.
Keeping the original bracelet stored while using a replaceable strap therefore provides a way to reduce wear on the original components while preserving the watch’s factory configuration. In this sense, the strap becomes both a functional interface and a replaceable layer within the life of the watch.
project info:
name: The FKM Rubber Range For Rolex
 designer: Helvetus

Tarek Chouiref, Zein Khalil

Thousands of ultra-Orthodox Jews protested in West Jerusalem on Tuesday against compulsory military service, Israeli media reported.
Israel’s Channel 12 said the rally was held in honor of draft evaders recently released from military prison.
The march began in the Geula neighborhood, forcing the closure of several streets, the channel said.
It added that draft evaders were expected to receive hundreds of shekels each at the end of the rally.
Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth daily said the recently released men arrived by bus and were greeted enthusiastically by protesters.
Demonstrators carried signs saying “Release the hostages from Prison 10. They will never serve in the enemy army,” while others held placards saying “We will die rather than enlist.”
The dispute over military service has intensified since Israel’s Supreme Court ruled in June 2024 that ultra-Orthodox Jewish men are subject to compulsory military service and ordered the suspension of state funding for religious institutions whose students refuse to enlist.
Ultra-Orthodox Jews account for around 14% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million. Most oppose compulsory military service, arguing that full-time Torah study should take precedence and that military service threatens their religious way of life.

United States President Donald Trump has announced that he will spend 32 days travelling and campaigning for the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The upcoming race is widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term in office, and it could decide whether his political agenda faces legislative hurdles for the next two years.

“We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars,” Democratic Senator Patty Murray wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a letter on Tuesday.

RIO DE JANEIRO - Brazil’s patron saint has become a political flashpoint as the predominantly Catholic country’s leading presidential candidates make a last-ditch effort to court religious voters.
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has lashed out at President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva for apparently feeding rumours about his right-wing rival, with the saga exposing tensions between Brazil’s Catholic majority and its expanding evangelical population.
In recent days, the leftist incumbent has referred to claims that Bolsonaro plans to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of her patron saint status if elected.
Evangelicals, a booming denomination in Brazil with growing political power and an important right-wing voter base, do not recognise the saint as an object of worship.
“As long as I am president... no one is going to disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida,” Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term, said at a rally on Sept 28.
Bolsonaro, 45, has frequently invoked religion on the campaign trail, and denies the accusations.
“Everyone knows that I respect religions. All of them!” he said, accusing the government of spreading “fake news.”
‘Oxygen to rumours’
The quarrel erupted after media reports that figures in the Catholic Church were concerned about the future status of the beloved saint, who is depicted in Brazil as a black woman.
The unearthing of an abandoned 2007 Bill, initially proposed by a Bolsonaro-aligned lawmaker, to demote the patron saint subsequently unleashed rampant speculation online.
The president’s decision to “give oxygen to rumours” signals a sea change in how he engages with religious voters, said Victor Araujo, a comparative politics professor at the Britain’s University of Reading.
“By actively engaging with religious controversies and bringing them into the mainstream campaign, Lula is trying to neutralise Bolsonaro’s moral appeal and force his rival onto the defensive on religious grounds,” Araujo told AFP.
Lula currently has 48 per cent of Catholic voting intentions on Sept 27 compared with 29 per cent for Bolsonaro, according to a Quaest survey.
Evangelical voting intentions go in the opposite direction, with 46 per cent for Bolsonaro and 27 per cent for Lula.
Janaina, 51, a Catholic art teacher working in Rio de Janeiro, firmly believes that the right-wing camp has the saint in its sights.
“Religion has nothing to do with politics,” she said, voicing concern that Evangelicals “want this other religion to grow…and attack the Catholic Church.”
Andre Paschoal, a worshipper at the same church, is less convinced.
“Lula took advantage of this and he will certainly lose many votes because of it,” the civil servant, 58, told AFP.
“Instead of being sincere, he is making use of an artificial lie to sway Catholics or Evangelicals in his favour,” Paschoal believes.
‘Pure politics’
“It’s pure politics,” echoed Tereza Helael as she made her way to an evangelical service in the city centre.
“It’s meant to target a certain area, a certain group… just to get votes,” the 70-year-old artist said.
Brazil, known for its Christ the Redeemer statue looming over Rio de Janeiro, hosts the world’s second-largest Christian population after the United States, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Catholics have historically dominated that cohort, but rapid demographic changes in recent years have seen the country’s evangelical population shoot up.
Ultra-conservative actors from this community have provided crucial political backing to Flavio Bolsonaro’s father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup.
“This controversy is a reaction to these churches’ political activity becoming ever more aggressive in recent years,” said Rodrigo Nunes, a philosophy professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro.
However, he said, most Catholics are perturbed by the rumour “because it challenges their tacit, unspoken position as the dominant religion in Brazil.” AFP

Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani has condemned Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, saying whoever is responsible for the devastation in the besieged Palestinian territory is a “war criminal”.
Sheikh Mohammed, who is also Qatar’s foreign minister, made the remark on Tuesday on “Piers Morgan Uncensored” when asked about the nature of Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip.

He described the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as “a massacre” that “should be condemned”. He called for accountability for the perpetrators of that attack, but said the Israeli response was unjustified.
“Hospitals have been targeted, schools have been targeted. Whatever the justifications and the arguments, nothing is justifying this,” he added.
Sheikh Mohammed also criticised Israel’s near-daily violations of the “ceasefire” that took effect in October 2025, saying more than 1,400 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip had been killed since.
“There is more occupied territory – almost 70 percent of the Strip has been occupied and not allowed by the Israeli forces. They are not fulfilling their commitments of this agreement,” he said. “This is just showing that they have different intentions.”
He said Qatar’s efforts to broker a ceasefire had been repeatedly “undermined” by Israel “from day one of the war”.
He also condemned Israel’s strike on the Qatari capital, Doha, in 2025, which targeted senior Hamas officials who had gathered for negotiations. The attack, which caused a deadly explosion, was an unprecedented violation of Qatar’s sovereignty.
“We were attacked by Israel while we were mediating and trying to push for Trump’s proposal at that time in Doha,” he said, referring to United States President Donald Trump. “It was unacceptable and condemned. It’s setting a precedent of attacking the mediator that has never happened throughout the wars in history.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin “Netanyahu has crossed the line”, he added, “like he has crossed other lines before that”.
Sheikh Mohammed said that serving as a mediator had not been easy, but that he believed quiet diplomacy was the most effective way to make progress.
Qatar has also been playing a mediatory role, along with Pakistan, between Washington and Tehran following the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
“We are trying to do our best to give the best advice to the US government on how to reach a solution, as well as to the Iranians,” he said.
Sheikh Mohammed said that three matters needed to be resolved to end the war.
These are: an agreement on Tehran’s right to “peaceful nuclear power” and the removal of sanctions; agreement on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz according to international law; and reform of regional security arrangements, including the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Iran.
The last, he said, “wouldn’t happen without dialogue between Iran and GCC and setting the principles of what a good neighbourhood relationship should be”.
That should include, he said, “non-interference in each other’s affairs” and “non-aggression” against each other.
He added that if the region were to “build an area of common interest where we work together in areas of energy and economy, and trade and business”, it would “allow the chance for this region to unleash its potential”.

====================================================================================================

US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue deportation policy after judge labels it unlawful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:46:52 UTC
08:46:52 KST

The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let US President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.
The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on the policy to follow.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision to let the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of the litigation.
Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.
More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration - among his top priorities - since returning to office last year.
The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.
Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival welcomed the court's decision.
"A bad day for criminal illegals and open-borders activists alike," Percival wrote on social media.
Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the court has "allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture. That is a devastating result for people who may be put on a plane before they ever have notice or an opportunity to raise a fear claim."
Judge rules US immigration policy against immigration law, due process protections
In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.
The Supreme Court, which has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies, previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.
The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.
The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.
In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.
Deportees see sexual assault, unlawful transference, plaintiffs say
The policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries from which the US had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained, or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.
The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime US residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.
The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld most of the judge's ruling on September 18.
The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

European countries should have shown more solidarity and offered more support to Spain after the mass arrival in Ceuta of tens of thousands of migrants, Spanish King Felipe VI said on Tuesday during a gala dinner to mark a visit by French President Emmanuel Macron.
In an unusually outspoken address reflecting the depth of the crisis facing Spain following the Ceuta border rush that took place two months ago on Wednesday, the king said what happened in the enclave on the North African coast was "unacceptable" and generated an enormous security, public order and humanitarian challenge.
"It's a situation that ought to have as a consequence a reinforcement of collaboration between member states in resources and cooperation," he said. "The European countries that suffer the most pressure from being on the external borders of the European Union cannot alone bear a responsibility that also belongs to everyone."
The king spoke during a dinner at the Royal Palace in Madrid, also attended by Spain's Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, a rare European proponent of the benefits of migration who launched a mass regularisation of irregular migrants that concluded in the summer. Sanchez, however, has proposed possible changes to asylum rules to return arrivals more quickly, which NGOs and lawyers say would violate human rights conventions.
Asked in a news conference about the plans, territorial policy minister Angel Victor Torres said the government was "analysing the possibility" of a legislative amendment but that it was "not easy" due to questions of international law.
72,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta
Following the mass crossing of 72,000 migrants into Ceuta on July 30, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen commended Spain's swift action in returning most arrivals to Morocco. Other leaders were less understanding, however, with Italy suspending the European Union's border-free Schengen arrangements with Spain for one month.
European Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner unveiled a plan on Tuesday to strengthen EU border controls in the wake of Ceuta.
The plan, which requires the approval of member states, would strengthen the mandate of Frontex, the EU border protection agency, and give it a standing corps ready for immediate deployment.

The pro-Palestinian Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) filed a criminal complaint with Vietnamese authorities against an Israeli reservist who was vacationing in the country, accusing him of involvement in the destruction of civilian property during the war in Gaza, Walla learned on Monday.
The Belgium-based organization, which has pursued IDF soldiers traveling abroad after serving in Gaza and Lebanon, filed the complaint against H.G., a young Israeli, over what it described as his "involvement in the destruction of civilian targets during the genocide."
According to the foundation's statement, H.G., who was in Vietnam when the complaint was filed, is an Israeli reservist who served as a D9 bulldozer operator in the 605th Combat Engineering Battalion of the 188th Brigade during the IDF's ground operation in Gaza.
As in previous cases, the organization claimed that the reservist incriminated himself by documenting on social media the destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure in the Gaza Strip while operating a military bulldozer. According to the organization, he posted videos and photographs showing the destruction, demolition, and burning of buildings in Gaza City, Khan Yunis, and Rafah.
As of Monday, there was no indication that Vietnamese authorities had taken any action in response to the complaint.
IDF soldier said they 'flatten everything' if nothing suspicious found in Gaza sites
HRF pointed to a post it said was published on November 19, 2023, showing extensive destruction in Gaza. According to the organization's translation, the soldier described his unit's activities as follows: "We look for suspicious things, tunnels, military equipment, suitcases. When we find something, we call the senior commanders, and when there is nothing there, we complete the demolition and flatten everything."
The foundation claimed that H.G. was involved in two incidents. The first was the demolition of the Abbas police station in Gaza City's southern Rimal neighborhood between November 14 and 21, 2023. The second was the demolition of Palestine Square in Shejaia on December 18, 2023.
The organization alleged that the incidents involved the destruction of civilian property that was not justified by military necessity and attributed violations of international law to the reservist.
"This is another link in our systematic pursuit of accountability, wherever the perpetrators are," said the foundation's director-general, Lebanese-Belgian Dyab Abou Jahjah, who is identified with Hezbollah.
"We have already filed a complaint in Vietnam, and we continue to identify soldiers who regularly return there for vacation."
IDF order forbids photos taken from operation areas
A special IDF General Staff order titled "Soldiers' Use of the Online Space" is intended specifically to prevent complaints of this kind against soldiers.
The IDF emphasizes: "Do not photograph or publish pictures in uniform or from operational areas; avoid documentation that could be interpreted as harming the civilian population, and consider the international consequences of every post or photograph."
Despite the directives and what the article describes as a lack of significant enforcement within the IDF, HRF has used information uploaded online to file dozens of complaints in approximately 25 countries since the organization was founded roughly two years ago.
Those countries include Brazil, Argentina, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the UK, Cyprus, Greece, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, Canada, the US, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, India, and Vietnam.
A complaint was also filed in Slovenia against Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar. This represents the documented minimum, while the organization says it has also made approaches in additional countries.
Various proceedings were opened in Peru, Brazil, Romania, and Chile, but none resulted in punishment or sanctions.

Trump, tech executives release 'morally binding' accord amid rising fears over AI safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:46:31 UTC
08:46:31 KST

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said tech executives agreed to establish standards for AI and reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centers, as concerns mount over AI safety and the industry's growing footprint in communities.
Trump made the comments after a meeting with tech executives at the White House. The administration is facing increasing scrutiny over the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.
Data centers, which provide the computing power needed to train and run AI models, have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts. The backlash poses a political challenge for Republicans heading into the US midterm elections on November 3.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement between the companies. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president. And it really is a form of protection."
Trump released the one-page document on his Truth Social platform - which he had earlier described as "morally binding" - and that urged four layers of controls in companies.
First, the document asks companies to partner with an external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments of whether a company's AI control and monitoring systems were operating as intended.
Second, it urges companies to designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports from internal and external auditors and from teams operating AI controls.
Third, it asks for internal controls to monitor capabilities and alignment of AI models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats to ensure that models "do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
And fourth, it requests that companies have an internal team to ensure "all of the controls, monitoring and detection are operating as intended."
Luncheon spills into public view
What began as a closed-door lunch with technology executives spilled into public view when Trump joined House Speaker Mike Johnson and a lineup of CEOs on the White House driveway, an area rarely used by the president. He took questions for about 30 minutes on AI safety and other topics with the CEOs standing shoulder to shoulder behind him.
The unusual scene came as pressure has mounted on the administration to address the risks and rapid spread of AI, and underscored the alliance Trump has cultivated with leaders of the tech industry. Executives at the meeting included OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Google's Sundar Pichai and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Zuckerberg, pulled forward from the crowd of billionaire executives by Trump to speak, said that the companies agreed to develop "robust internal controls" for their AI systems, adding that auditors would check those procedures and report back to company boards. Trump said he is considering setting up a 10-person board to police the safety of AI tools, without specifying who would make up that group.
The document was signed by Trump and the bosses of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, social media platform X/Twitter, and NVIDIA.
'Makes sense' to transform steps into laws, White House says
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations. Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies is committed to doing this," the White House accord said.
"The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems," it added.
Trump doubles down on data centers
Trump separately told reporters at the White House that the tech companies would work to make communities "happy" about the construction of data centers.
Data centers are "going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial," he told reporters. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities."
Trump met with the executives the same day his aides announced a new AI tool that they said will make it easier for the public to use government services.
Silicon Valley executives attended the launch event on Tuesday morning, including Meta's Dina Powell McCormick and Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire. Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia led the design of the new tool. Silicon Valley companies Google, SpaceX, Meta and 8VC were listed in the launch event's program as sponsors.
Trump at the launch event said he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology, adding that doing so would make it harder for US companies to build better AI products than their Chinese counterparts.
Trump also said that he discussed AI with Xi when he visited the US last week, adding that the US already works with Xi's government "in so many ways."

‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:43:27 UTC
08:43:27 KST

He’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering the Los Angeles neighborhood again after he moved in and out of the crawlspace of another home.
“Yellow 2120”, as the black bear has been tagged, was spotted in the crawlspace of a home on Minoru Drive on Monday.
Steve Clark, whose in-laws live in the house, told NBC LA that they monitored their new neighbor through security cameras, and tried to scare him away by playing loud music and turning on a leaf blower.
“I didn’t even realize that the bear could get all the way back to that access point. He has to rip out ductwork and do a bunch of damage to get there,” Clark said.
Although those attempts to oust “Yellow 2120” from his adopted den failed, the bear later left on his own. While the homeowners have sealed up their crawlspace, their neighbors are on alert in case the bear decides to move in with them next.
“Yellow 2120” made headlines last year when he took up residence under another Altadena home for two months.
In November 2025, homeowner Ken Johnson noticed the bear leaving the crawlspace and later contacted California’s department of fish and wildlife for assistance removing it from under his home. Despite sweet-scented lures and ammonia-doused towels, “Yellow 2120” remained in place until January – when Johnson sought assistance from members of the Bear League, a volunteer organization that aims to help humans live in “harmony” with the animals, that was able to force the bear out with paintball guns.
“He’s a nuisance and he’s living under my house rent-free,” Johnson told the Orange County Register at the time. “We call him … unbearable, but he’s so cute. Once he gets out, we’ll call him bearable, but for now it’s unbearable.”
After the Eaton wildfire tore through the Angeles national forest and scorched parts of Altadena in January 2025, wildlife – including several bears – sought shelter in the community. In the weeks following the fire, at least two 500-plus-pound black bears sought refuge in homes evacuated during the wildfire. Although it’s unclear whether “Yellow 2120” was one of them, he had previously taken up residence under another Altadena home, said Cort Klopping, a fish and wildlife spokesperson.
As cities encroach closer on bear habitats, bear sightings are growing more common. In 2017, California registered 28 bear sightings in Los Angeles county. In 2023, that number rose to 455.
This month Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, told the Guardian that human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation feeding period. This year is on track to be record setting when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said.
Black bears – the only species of bear living in California – are largely non-confrontational, having killed only one person in the state in recorded history. The population is estimated to be between 49,000 and 71,000, with 50% living in the north coast and Cascade regions, and 40% in the Sierra Nevada.

The F/A-XX is designed as a carrier-based aircraft intended to extend the operational reach of the US Navy's aircraft carrier fleet.

Hurricane Polo sweeps over Mexico’s Pacific coast, heads inland
- Hurricane Polo hit Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm, causing roof damage, downed trees, and flooding but no serious injuries, with local authorities reporting little overall damage.
- The storm brought up to 20cm of rain to Sonora, raising concerns of life-threatening floods and mudslides amid a severe Pacific hurricane season driven by a Super El Nino.
- Emergency aid including food, water, and rescue equipment was deployed, while Tropical Storm Rachel threatens to intensify along the Pacific coast, adding to regional storm risks.
AI generated
PUERTO SAN CARLOS, Mexico - Hurricane Polo ripped roofs off houses, felled trees and flooded roads as it swept over Mexico’s Pacific coast but caused little serious damage and no reported injuries, according to initial assessments by authorities on Sept 29.
It made landfall late on Sept 28 in the south of Baja California peninsula as a Category 3 hurricane packing winds of up to 175kmh, according to the US National Hurricane Centre (NHC).
Polo raked across the peninsula and hopped the Gulf of California, then weakened to a tropical storm as it churned north-east into the Mexican mainland.
Up to 20cm of rainfall is expected in the state of Sonora, said the NHC, warning of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Winds have weakened considerably, to about 75kmh, according to the NHC.
It is the latest in a busy Pacific storm season turbo-charged by the El Nino weather phenomenon which has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.
The eye of the storm barrelled over the peninsular fishing village of Las Barrancas, which was largely unreachable after a swollen river caused a highway bridge to collapse.
Southward along the Baja California Sur coast, streets were flooded and the power was out in several towns including the small port of Adolfo Lopez Mateos and whale-watching town of Puerto San Carlos.
“The howling of the wind was terrifying; it sounded like the devil was on the loose,” Elvira Sanchez, who sat out the storm in a primary school acting as a shelter in Adolfo Lopez Mateos, told AFP.
Her home of salvaged wood was still standing after the storm but the tin roofs had been blown off the kitchen and bedroom.
“It barely brought any rain, it was mostly wind,” Victor Garcia, a resident of Puerto San Carlos, told AFP as he gathered branches that had fallen on his house.
The state power company was working to restore electricity and authorities promised to help with home repairs and to dredge flooded streets.
Baja California Sur’s governor Victor Castro, on a shelter visit, told AFP that local infrastructure has suffered “little damage.”
Nature, he said, had decided “to be kind this year.”
A military vessel docked in the area with 2,000 batches of food and basic supplies, drinking water, backhoes, heavy transport vehicles, inflatable boats, a demolition team, and a helicopter “to provide support to the population,” the Navy reported.
Baja California Sur is one of the Mexican states most exposed to major storms.
2026’s Pacific hurricane season is shaping up as more severe than usual, as a Super El Nino wreaks devastation across Central America, bringing historic droughts and flooding.
Meteorologists also issued Polo-related warnings of heavy rain and flooding in parts of 10 US states including Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, some of which are experiencing drought.
Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Rachel is paralleling Mexico’s Pacific coast and is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane by Oct 1. AFP

Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

08:33:34 KST

Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
- Published
Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city.
"Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.
Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September.
"All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.
Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded.
"We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.
At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.
Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.
This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia.
Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.
Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.
Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action.
"Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."
The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society.
Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014.
By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege.
Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih.
On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died.

- Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished? 
  - Published20 September
Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.
The situation, he admitted, was very difficult.
"It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."
Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center.
"In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC.
"This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average."
If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."
The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction.
Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.
Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware.
"We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.
There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.
Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon.
Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery.
"Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."
EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.
But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.
His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed.
"This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

Estonia says Russian intelligence ordered attack on defense firm supplying Ukraine
On Tuesday, Estonia said Russian security services ordered an August arson attack against Milrem Robotics, an Estonian defense company whose unmanned ground vehicles are used by Ukrainian forces.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said authorities had concluded “with certainty” that the Aug. 15 fire was a deliberate act of sabotage commissioned by Russian special services.
Russia Hits Kyiv With Ballistic Missiles, Killing 2 Women as Child Dies in Wider Region
Estonia’s Internal Security Service, KAPO, said the attack had been planned in advance and assessed that it was directly attributable to the Russian Federation. The agency said its methods were consistent with other suspected Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
Milrem Robotics produces THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles supplied to Ukraine. Fifteen were already operating in Ukraine by late 2025, according to company information cited by Breaking Defense, with more than 150 additional systems planned under a Dutch-funded program.
The fire broke out overnight on Aug. 15 at a building used by Milrem Robotics in Tallinn. Emergency crews contained the blaze, and nobody was injured.
Three suspects were subsequently detained in Latvia and transferred to Estonia, where they remain in custody as the criminal investigation continues.
Tsahkna said the operation formed part of a wider Russian campaign intended to intimidate European governments and weaken their backing for Ukraine.
Russia’s chargé d’affaires in Tallinn was summoned over the incident.
The Kremlin rejected Estonia’s findings. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the accusation unfounded and said Moscow would not take it seriously.
NATO: Russia failing to break support for Ukraine
The Estonian announcement triggered a wave of support from NATO and European leaders, who linked the sabotage to a broader campaign of Russian pressure against countries backing Kyiv.
“Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies,” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said.
“It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine,” he added, arguing that Moscow had failed both to achieve its objectives on the battlefield and to fracture allied unity behind Kyiv.
The EU also backed Estonia, describing the arson attack as reckless and saying Moscow would not succeed in forcing Europe to reduce its support for Ukraine.
European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand said Russia was attempting to frighten European countries into pulling back from Kyiv, but insisted that effort would fail.
French President Emmanuel Macron described the attack as a “dangerous escalation” and placed it within what he called a growing pattern of hostile Russian acts against European states.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys likewise said the incident demonstrated that Russian hostile activity did not stop at Ukraine’s borders, while Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics argued that the response should include further assistance for Kyiv.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called Estonia’s attribution “extremely serious,” while Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said such attacks would not weaken allied support for Ukraine.
The response reinforced a broader message from governments along NATO’s eastern flank: pressure attributed to Moscow has strengthened, rather than diminished, calls for stronger defenses and continued support for Kyiv.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have sharply increased defense spending since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and remain among Kyiv’s strongest supporters.

Jack Smith defends investigations into Trump during tense US Senate hearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:28:47 UTC
08:28:47 KST

Jack Smith defends investigations into Trump during tense US Senate hearing
Former US special counsel rejects claims that his probes improperly targeted Republicans and conservative groups.
Former Special Counsel Jack Smith has defended his investigations of President Donald Trump in a United States Senate hearing, though Republican lawmakers accused him of abusing his authority.
On Tuesday, Smith told the Senate Judiciary Committee that his investigations followed Justice Department policy and were based on evidence.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3FBI agents who investigated Trump file lawsuit alleging retaliatory firing
- list 2 of 3Key takeaways from Donald Trump’s controversial speech on election security
- list 3 of 3US intelligence director pick refuses to acknowledge Trump loss in 2020
He rejected accusations that political considerations influenced his decision to bring criminal charges against Trump, the first US president ever to be indicted.
“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation,” Smith said.
A former war crimes prosecutor at The Hague, Smith was appointed special counsel in 2022 to independently investigate allegations about Trump’s behaviour after the end of his first term as president.
In 2023, Smith ultimately brought two criminal indictments against Trump: one for his alleged attempts to subvert the 2020 presidential election and a second for his handling of classified documents while out of office.
Separately, two further criminal indictments were brought against Trump. One, in New York, accused Trump of falsifying business records to conceal unflattering information during his 2016 presidential campaign.
A second, in Georgia, also concerned allegations that Trump and his allies sought to overturn the 2020 election results.
Only one case – the New York indictment – was brought to trial, resulting in felony convictions. The rest were dropped after Trump was re-elected in 2024.
Smith himself resigned shortly before Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025. The Justice Department has a policy of not prosecuting sitting presidents.
Trump has denied all the charges against him and has accused Smith and former President Joe Biden of orchestrating a political “witch-hunt” against him.
Republicans focused much of Tuesday’s hearing on Smith’s investigative methods, including subpoenas that obtained phone records associated with members of Congress and financial information from Republican donors and organisations.
Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley accused Smith’s team of using its investigations to “map out and target the entire Republican Party”.
Smith, however, maintained that his office had a duty to pursue evidence relevant to the investigation.
He also defended obtaining phone records from lawmakers. He said the records helped corroborate evidence that Trump and his allies contacted members of Congress as they sought to delay certification of the 2020 election results.
Texas Senator Ted Cruz, whose records were among those sought, pressed Smith about why lawmakers were not notified of the subpoenas. Smith said prosecutors feared Trump and his associates could destroy evidence or interfere with the investigation if the subpoenas were disclosed.
“Is it a crime to be a Republican?” Cruz asked.
“Absolutely not,” Smith said.
Smith added that his office consulted the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section before obtaining the records.
The information Smith sought reveals the time and duration of the telephone calls but not their content. Critics have pointed out that there was no law against seeking such records during the course of Smith’s investigation.
During his testimony, Smith not only defended his investigative decisions but also accused the Trump administration of retaliating against the prosecutors and agents who worked on the two cases.
He argued that members of his former team had been fired for “doing their jobs”. Those firings have prompted legal challenges.
In March, three former agents with the FBI who investigated Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election filed a class-action lawsuit alleging they were illegally terminated as part of a “retribution campaign”. The lawsuit seeks their reinstatement.
Smith, who said Trump has threatened him with jail, framed the scrutiny of his work as part of a broader challenge to the independence of the Justice Department.
“As I appear before you today, it is my belief that the rule of law faces challenges unlike any we have experienced in our lifetime,” Smith said. “I will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution from the president or others.”

Norwegian Foreign Ministry State Secretary Eivind Vad Petersson noted that Russia's treatment of Ukrainians is a systemic issue that must receive a systemic response.

"I'm honored to be in this position, I'm honored to support Ukraine, and I'm honored to be able to call these people my friends," she added.

The accused were arrested for their alleged involvement in massive financial irregularities in the execution of ‘Jal Jeevan Mission’, an ambitious joint initiative of the central and state govts intended to provide functional household tap connections for safe and adequate drinking water supply.
NEW DELHI: Observing that the right to personal liberty of the accused becomes paramount if trial is unlikely to be completed in the near future, the Supreme Court has said bail must be granted in such cases.“It is a well-settled postulate of criminal jurisprudence that pre-trial incarceration cannot masquerade as punitive detention... This court must intervene to safeguard the right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution... when a trial cannot be reasonably concluded in the near future,” a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu said.The bench granted bail to ex-secretary of Rajasthan Water Supply and Sewerage Management Board Shubhanshu Dixit, who has been in custody since Feb 17, when he was arrested in a graft case.
Accused were held for ‘jal mission’ irregularities
The court also granted relief to a person who was allegedly operating as a broker on behalf of the then cabinet minister of the Public Health Engineering Department, Rajasthan, Mahesh Chandra Joshi.The accused were arrested for their alleged involvement in massive financial irregularities in the execution of ‘Jal Jeevan Mission’, an ambitious joint initiative of the central and state govts intended to provide functional household tap connections for safe and adequate drinking water supply.
Though the court accepted the plea of state govt that economic offences involving deep-rooted conspiracies must be viewed seriously, it granted relief to the accused.“Admittedly, the charges are yet to be framed and the trial is yet to commence for, inter alia, the following reasons: the investigation against some of the accused persons is still pending; two of the accused persons are absconding; and sanction under Section 19 of the PoC Act was granted on Sept 6 for the prosecution of six other co-accused persons who are public servants. Bearing in mind the sheer volume of evidence that must be led to prove the charges, the trial is bound to be a protracted exercise. In the conspectus of these aspects, we are of the view that it would serve no fruitful purpose to keep the appellants under further pre-trial custody. Resultantly, the present appeals succeed,” the court said.

Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:21:25 UTC
08:21:25 KST

Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives.
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection,” Trump said.
Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week.
“The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared.
The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests.
While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth.
The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment.
The document outlines four “layers of controls and audits” for AI companies. The first involves implementing internal safety monitoring during training – something that already exists at major labs and has failed to prevent testing failures thus far. The second calls for empowering an internal team to make sure the first layer of monitoring is operating correctly, while the third agrees to give an external auditor the ability to independently assess safety controls. Finally, the agreement calls for companies to designate an independent board to review reports about those safety controls.
None of the controls listed in the agreement involve government regulators or include a commitment to publicly detail the findings of independent evaluations. The agreement also appears to allow companies to pick their own evaluators, appoint their own oversight boards and decide whether to publish their results.
Trump made the remarks after holding a luncheon with tech leaders including Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO; Mark Zuckerberg, the Meta CEO; Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia; Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO; and other top industry executives. The tech industry, which has largely aligned itself with the Trump administration, has lobbied against strict regulatory oversight, arguing that it would stifle the economy.
Zuckerberg, flanked by Trump and other tech moguls, told a press conference after the lunch that he was proud of the agreement and said that it was created to assure the American public that their technology was trustworthy.
“This is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. “It was sort of a historic conversation.”
